title: How Routing Works in Next.js: Pages, Layouts and Links Explained
description:
Originally published on CodingCush.

In Next.js, routing is based on your folder structure instead of a configuration file: every folder inside the app directory becomes part of the URL, a file called page.tsx inside that folder becomes the page visitors see, and a file called layout.tsx wraps pages with shared parts such as a header and footer. You do not install a router or register routes — you simply create folders and files, and Next.js turns them into web addresses.

Routing Without a Router Library

If you have used plain React, this feels pleasantly strange. In a React single-page app you normally install something like React Router and then write route definitions by hand: this path shows this component, that path shows that one. Forget a route, and your page exists but nobody can reach it — a little like building a room and forgetting the door.

Next.js took the opposite approach, called file-system routing. The framework watches your app folder and builds the route table for you. A folder named about containing a page.tsx file automatically becomes the address /about. The official Next.js documentation on layouts and pages calls a page "UI that is rendered on a specific route", and that is the whole mental model: files are routes.

Your First Routes: page.tsx

Here is a tiny site with three pages. Read the folder tree as a map of the website:

app/
  page.tsx          ->  /
  about/
    page.tsx        ->  /about
  blog/
    page.tsx        ->  /blog

Each page.tsx simply exports a React component:

export default function AboutPage() {
  return (
    <main>
      <h1>About us</h1>
      <p>We build friendly websites.</p>
    </main>
  );
}

Notice what is missing: there is no route list anywhere. Add a folder, add a page file, and the URL exists. Delete the page file, and the URL politely becomes a 404. Beginners coming from other frameworks often waste an hour hunting for the routing file; in Next.js, the folder tree is the routing file. If the server/client split still feels fuzzy, our guide to Server Components vs Client Components in Next.js explains which of these files run where.

Layouts: The Frame Around Your Pages

Most pages on a site share furniture: a header, a navigation bar, a footer. Copying that furniture into every page works until the day you must change the menu in fourteen files. Next.js solves this with layout.tsx, a component that wraps the pages inside its folder:

export default function RootLayout({ children }) {
  return (
    <html lang="en">
      <body>
        <header>My Site</header>
        {children}
        <footer>(c) 2026 My Site</footer>
      </body>
    </html>
  );
}

The magic word is children: that is where the actual page appears, framed by your header and footer. Layouts can also nest. A layout inside app/blog/ wraps only the blog pages, inside the root layout — frames within frames. Better still, when a visitor moves between two pages that share a layout, Next.js keeps the layout on screen and swaps only the page content, so your header does not flicker or lose its state on every click.

The official Next.js Docs — the sidebar shows the routing topics this article covers: Layouts and Pages, and Linking and Navigating.

Dynamic Routes: One File, Many Pages

A blog has hundreds of posts but only one post design. Next.js handles this with dynamic segments: wrap a folder name in square brackets, and it becomes a placeholder that matches any value.

app/
  blog/
    [slug]/
      page.tsx      ->  /blog/my-first-post
                        /blog/hello-world
                        /blog/any-slug-at-all

export default async function BlogPost({ params }) {
  const { slug } = await params;
  return <h1>Post: {slug}</h1>;
}

Your component receives the matched value as params.slug and can load the right article from a database or files. One page file now powers every post on the blog — the same trick behind product pages on shops, profiles on social sites, and documentation pages like the ones you are reading about.

Linking Between Pages with next/link

To move between routes, use the Link component from next/link instead of a plain <a> tag:

import Link from "next/link";

export default function Nav() {
  return (
    <nav>
      <Link href="/">Home</Link>
      <Link href="/about">About</Link>
      <Link href="/blog">Blog</Link>
    </nav>
  );
}

It looks like ordinary HTML, but under the surface Next.js preloads the linked pages when they appear on screen, so clicks feel instant instead of triggering a full page reload. The React documentation's Learn React guide is a good companion here, because every page and layout is still just a React component with the same rules you already know. And if you are still deciding what to learn first, our comparison of React vs Next.js lays out the honest learning order.

Special Files: Loading, Error and Not Found

The App Router has a few more reserved filenames worth knowing, because they handle the moments beginners usually dread. Add a loading.tsx file to a folder and Next.js shows it automatically while that page's data is loading — no manual spinner logic — swapping in the real page the moment it is ready. Add an error.tsx file and it becomes a friendly safety net: if the page throws an error, visitors see your message and a retry option instead of a broken screen. And a not-found.tsx file lets you design your own 404 page in the same style as the rest of the site. Each of these is optional, each lives beside the page it serves, and each follows the same rule as everything else in this article: the filename is the feature.

Route Groups and Private Folders: Organising Without Changing URLs

As a site grows, the app folder can become crowded, and Next.js offers two naming tricks to tidy it. A folder wrapped in parentheses, such as (marketing), is a route group: it organises files and can even carry its own layout, but its name never appears in the URL — so app/(marketing)/about/page.tsx is still simply /about. A folder starting with an underscore, such as _components, is the opposite: it is private, completely opted out of routing, which makes it a safe home for shared components and helpers that should never become pages. Together, these two conventions let a large project stay organised without breaking a single address.

The App Router File Conventions in One Table

File or folder What it creates
page.tsx The visible page for that folder's URL
layout.tsx Shared wrapping UI for that folder and everything inside it
loading.tsx Loading UI shown while the page prepares
error.tsx Friendly error UI for that segment
not-found.tsx Your custom 404 page
[slug] folder A dynamic route matching any value in that segment
(group) folder Organisation only — invisible in the URL
_private folder Never routed — a safe place for shared code

Keep this table nearby for your first project. After a week of building, you will stop consulting it, because the conventions start to feel less like rules to memorise and more like common sense: of course the page file is the page.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I need React Router in Next.js?

No. Routing is built into Next.js through the file system. Installing React Router as well would duplicate the job and confuse both tools, so let the folders do the work.

What is the difference between page.tsx and layout.tsx?

A page is the unique content for one route. A layout is shared wrapping UI — headers, footers, sidebars — that surrounds pages and stays in place while you navigate between them.

What does [slug] mean in a folder name?

Square brackets mark a dynamic segment. The folder matches any value in that part of the URL, and your page receives the value as a parameter, so one file can serve many addresses.

Why is my new page showing a 404?

Almost always, the folder is in the wrong place or the file is not named exactly page.tsx (or page.jsx). Check that the folder sits inside app and that the file exports a default component.

Conclusion

Next.js routing rewards you for tidy folders: folders become URLs, page.tsx becomes the screen, layout.tsx becomes the frame, brackets become placeholders, and Link makes moving around feel instant. Learn those five ideas and you can build the skeleton of almost any website — no routing configuration required.

title: How v0 authenticates to Snowflake without exposing the user's OAuth token
description:
AI-generated applications often need to authenticate to external services on behalf of their users. That creates a problem: generated code shouldn't have access to the user's credentials.

We faced that decision when building the v0 Snowflake integration. It lets users connect Snowflake, inspect schemas, query data, and generate applications that run against their warehouses. That generated code has to authenticate to Snowflake, but it is written by a model and runs without human review, and prompt injection can steer it into exfiltrating whatever it can read, so the user's OAuth token should never enter the environment the code runs in.

We solved this with a Snowflake request proxy for v0 sandboxes, built on the Vercel Sandbox firewall. The sandbox can run normal Snowflake clients, but the real credential is resolved at request time in a server proxy outside the sandbox runtime. This lets existing Snowflake clients work inside the sandbox without exposing the user's credential to generated code.

The harder problem was deciding where the proxy could safely inject the credential. The obvious implementation, replacing a placeholder token wherever it appears, introduces another credential leak.

Isolation doesn't protect secrets

v0 runs generated applications in isolated sandboxes. Isolation protects the rest of the system from untrusted code, but it doesn't protect secrets inside the sandbox.

If a generated app can read a token from the filesystem, that token can be copied into logs, returned in an API response, embedded into generated client code, or sent to another host. Sandbox isolation limits what the application can access, but it does not help once the credential itself is available inside the sandbox.

For Snowflake, the credential represents the Snowflake role the user connected with. v0 should be able to help the user explore and build with data they are authorized to access, but generated code should not receive raw provider credentials just because it needs one.

Every Snowflake request goes through the proxy

The sandbox cannot talk to Snowflake directly. When code inside it sends a request to the user's Snowflake account host, the sandbox firewall forwards that request to the v0 Snowflake proxy:

The firewall terminates TLS with a certificate authority unique to each sandbox, which lets the proxy read and rewrite traffic that would otherwise be encrypted. The sandbox trusts that certificate authority automatically, so the Snowflake SDK and CLI run with their default certificate validation, OCSP included. The proxy then verifies the sandbox's OIDC token, looks up the v0 chat the sandbox belongs to, restores the user session bound to that chat, and retrieves a fresh Snowflake credential for that user.

The sandbox does not choose where a token-bearing request is sent. The proxy derives the Snowflake account host from the server-side credential and rejects invalid account URLs, keeping the credential scoped to the connected Snowflake account rather than trusting host information supplied by generated code.

Compatibility without credential exposure

As a stopgap, the first version of the integration wrote the user's real token into the sandbox's Snowflake token files. The proxy replaced that approach. Ideally, we would remove token files from the sandbox entirely, but Snowflake clients expect credentials in different locations depending on the authentication flow.

Some requests, such as Snowflake SQL API calls, authenticate with an Authorization: Bearer header. Other client flows read local token files and send the token as part of a login request. Once the client has authenticated, subsequent requests use Snowflake-issued session tokens, and the proxy passes those requests through untouched.

To preserve compatibility, v0 still writes a token-shaped placeholder into the sandbox. The placeholder is a fixed, public, 72-byte string that grants no access, and its only job is to let existing Snowflake SDK and CLI flows behave as if a token exists. The proxy never authorizes a request based on the placeholder itself. Instead, the proxy authorizes the request using the sandbox's server-side identity and its binding to the user's chat.

The real OAuth token, the reusable credential that represents the user, is never written into the sandbox. Snowflake does issue session tokens that live inside the sandbox after login, but each of those belongs to a single authenticated session.

Those sessions are short-lived in practice. The Snowflake helper in generated apps destroys its connection after each query, which ends the session right away. Closing the chat does not end a session on its own, but tearing down the sandbox takes the token with it, and Snowflake expires the session server-side after four hours of inactivity by default. When a request reaches the proxy, it decides whether and where to attach the credential.

Why blind replacement fails

The first version of the proxy searched each request for the placeholder and swapped in the real token wherever it appeared:

The problem is that generated code controls parts of the request, including where the placeholder can appear. A SQL statement, for example, is caller-controlled data. If a query contains the placeholder as a string literal, blind replacement turns that query into one containing the real OAuth token. If the database then returns that string, the real token comes back into the sandbox as query output, and the proxy would have leaked the token it was built to keep out.

Stricter matching does not close the hole. The proxy shouldn't inject a credential based on attacker-controlled text. Instead, it needs to know which field in each Snowflake request carries authentication.

Injecting credentials only into authentication fields

Snowflake requests reach the proxy in three shapes, and each shape puts authentication in a different place.

For Snowflake SQL API requests, the proxy sets the OAuth token on the Authorization: Bearer header. The body remains caller-controlled SQL and is not rewritten. If the placeholder appears in the SQL payload, the proxy rejects the request before it reaches Snowflake and logs it as placeholder misuse.

For Snowflake login requests, the proxy parses the JSON request body, sets the token structurally at the login token field, and serializes the body again. If the placeholder remains anywhere else in the request body, the proxy fails closed.

Post-login session requests authenticate with Snowflake-managed session tokens, so the proxy has nothing to inject.

Failing closed

The proxy rejects any request where:

  • The sandbox is not bound to a chat

  • No user-scoped credential can be obtained

  • The Snowflake account host cannot be derived

  • The placeholder appears outside an approved authentication field

  • A structured login body cannot be parsed safely

Requests are also bounded before inspection so that compressed or oversized bodies cannot turn the proxy into an unbounded parser. Every proxied request emits an observability event with the upstream outcome, status, duration, and injection location. This surfaces misuse and integration failures without exposing secrets.

Handling refresh and deploy

Token refresh cannot depend on an ambient browser cookie, because proxy requests originate from the sandbox, not from the user's browser session. v0 binds the user session to the sandbox instead, and the proxy mints and refreshes OAuth credentials from that binding.

The publish path uses Snowflake CLI flows with the same credential boundary. Deploy can write the placeholder into credential files, but never the real token.

After deployment, the application runs in Snowpark Container Services and authenticates as its own service user, with a token that Snowflake manages and rotates automatically, mounted at /snowflake/session/token. The user's OAuth token and the v0 proxy are no longer involved.

The resulting security boundary

For users, none of this is visible. Connect Snowflake, ask v0 to inspect schemas or build an app, preview the result, and deploy when it's ready.

The security model rests on five rules:

  • Credential injection happens only at each endpoint's authentication fields

  • Requests that use the placeholder outside an authentication field are rejected and logged

  • Token-bearing requests go only to the connected Snowflake account host

  • Credentials are minted and refreshed server-side

  • Generated code uses Snowflake without ever reading the user's OAuth token

In its first 15 days in production, the proxy attached credentials server-side for roughly 13,000 requests and recorded zero placeholder-misuse rejections.

Although we built this proxy for Snowflake, the same problem applies to other integrations: generated code often needs to authenticate without receiving the user's long-lived credential. The important part is to inject credentials only into protocol-defined authentication fields, rather than rewriting arbitrary request data.

The v0 Snowflake integration is now available in beta. Get started by reading the integration docs.

title: Calling an external service from Kafka Streams: size the threads, budget every call
description:
You have a Kafka Streams application, and one step needs an answer from somewhere else. It might be an AI model's decision, a fraud score, an address to geocode or a status from a provider's API. The most direct way to write it is a blocking call inside a mapValues:

stream.mapValues(value -> {
    HttpResponse<String> answer = http.send(requestFor(value), BodyHandlers.ofString());
    return withAnswer(value, answer.body());
});

This is where most applications start. It is kept bare on purpose: no timeout, no retries, no error handling.

What max.poll.interval.ms bounds in Kafka Streams showed what such a call can do to a thread's place in the group, run by run. This post is the other half: what to do about it. A blocking call caps a stream thread at one record per call, so we start by sizing the threads for it. Then we give every call an upper limit, and keep the slow step from holding up the rest of the stream.

Size the threads for the call

Kafka Streams gives each input partition a task and spreads the tasks over its threads, as the previous post opens with. A thread processes its tasks' records one at a time, so a blocking call blocks the thread it runs on.

Our runs called a stub, a small HTTP server of ours that stands in for the service. It waits a set time and answers. Everything else was real: a broker, a Kafka Streams application, HTTP calls over the network, and real vulnerability records, CVEs (how we measured). The first run had three partitions and one thread, so three tasks took turns on it. The arithmetic is short: at 300 ms a call, a thread does 3.3 records a second, however fast records arrive. With 600 records arriving at 20 a second, we measured 3.2 to 3.4 a second, and the stub never saw more than one call in flight.

More partitions alone do not help. A repartition to 32 before the call gives the calling step 32 tasks, and so does an input topic of 32 partitions, which is what we measured. With the same single thread, it still did 3.3 records a second, one call at a time.

It needs threads as well: 32 stream threads (num.stream.threads), one per task of the calling step, counted across all the application's instances. At 300 ms a call, we measured 3.3 records a second with one thread, 26 with eight and 106 with 32. With 32, the stub saw 32 calls in flight at once. Of a backlog of 3,393 records, 3,247 were done after 35 seconds. The rest took until 50 seconds. The records were spread unevenly over the 32 partitions, so as the emptier ones ran out, their threads went idle and the fullest finished alone.

How many threads a stream needs follows from Little's law: calls in flight equal the input rate times the call time. What a number of threads can do, and how fast they clear a backlog, is then one division and one subtraction. With the numbers of our runs:

calls in flight = input rate × call time
                    = 25 a second × 0.3 s = 7.5, so at least 8 threads

capacity = threads ÷ call time
  8 threads = 8 ÷ 0.3 s ≈ 27 a second (measured 26.4)
  32 threads = 32 ÷ 0.3 s ≈ 107 a second (measured 106)

backlog drains = capacity − input
  8 threads = 26.4 − 25 = 1.4 a second
  32 threads = 106 − 25 = 81 a second

service paused 45 s = 45 s × 25 a second ≈ 1,100 records
  8 threads = 1,100 ÷ 1.4 a second ≈ 13 minutes
  32 threads = 1,100 ÷ 81 a second ≈ 14 s (measured about 15)

The pause is from our last run. We paused the service for 45 seconds, and the backlog grew to about 1,100 records.

Eight threads only just keep up. The threads beyond that are headroom. Headroom is what clears a backlog, whatever builds it: a pause in the service, as in our run, a slow minute of it, a spike in the input or a restart. Headroom also covers a slower service. At 600 ms a call:

  8 threads = 8 ÷ 0.6 s ≈ 13 a second, below the input
  32 threads = 32 ÷ 0.6 s ≈ 53 a second, above it

With 8 threads, the lag would grow by about 12 records a second. With 32, it would still drain.

Is the stream keeping up?

Once a stream runs, the consumer group's lag tells you whether that sizing still holds. With Kafka Streams the lag needs reading with care.

Operators watch a consumer group's lag: the LAG column of kafka-consumer-groups --describe, or a lag exporter's line on a Grafana dashboard. That lag comes from the group's committed offsets, and Kafka Streams commits only every commit.interval.ms, 30 seconds by default. So a stream that keeps up does not show zero lag. Between commits the committed offset stays put while records keep arriving, so the lag climbs. At each commit it drops. A stream that kept up with 25 records a second showed a lag climbing to about 750, which is 25 a second times 30 seconds. It dropped to almost nothing at each commit, every 30 seconds.

A dashboard reads this curve at its own interval. Read every 20 seconds, the dashed line, the same healthy stream jumps between about 230 and 750. A reading just after a commit could show almost zero, but most readings show hundreds.

The next chart adds a slow stream. It had a 300 ms call and received the same 25 records a second as the healthy one. It got through only 3.3 of them a second, one thread's worth at 300 ms a call. Its committed lag climbed to about 3,000 in 135 seconds and never came back down.

Lowering commit.interval.ms makes the teeth smaller, but each commit is work. The thread flushes its producer and its store caches and writes its offsets to the broker, and it processes nothing meanwhile. Raising it to commit less often has a cost of its own for slow calls, which What max.poll.interval.ms bounds in Kafka Streams measures.

Give every call an upper limit

Sizing the threads used the typical call time. The rules in the next section start from a different number: the longest a call can take, every retry included. We call it the call’s budget. Without one, no setting keeps a thread in its group. A single call that never ends outlasts any poll interval.

The budget is the whole call, not one setting. It is the time to connect, the wait for the answer, the time to read the answer's body, every retry, and the backoff between retries. A client that tries four times with a 5-second timeout and a second of backoff between tries has a budget of about 23 seconds, not 5.

A timeout on the request is not always that budget. We checked the JDK's own HttpClient, on Java 25, against our stub, with a 5-second request timeout. When the service sent nothing for 10 seconds, the call ended at 5.01 seconds. When it sent its headers at once and its body over 20 seconds, the call did not end. It returned normally after 20.05 seconds, with the whole body. The Javadoc says only that the timeout fires "if the response is not received within the specified timeout".

What ended that call was a deadline around the whole of it:

HttpResponse<String> callWithin(HttpRequest request, Duration budget) throws Exception {
    CompletableFuture<HttpResponse<String>> call =
            http.sendAsync(request, BodyHandlers.ofString());
    try {
        return call.get(budget.toMillis(), TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
    } catch (TimeoutException e) {
        call.cancel(true);
        throw e;
    }
}

The caller was free at 5.02 seconds. The cancel also closed the connection: the stub's next write, a second later, failed.

Retries go inside the same deadline. Each try gets what is left of the budget, so the budget stays one number.

With another client. We ran one client, one call per case, and no retries. Check two things. Does its timeout end a call whose body arrives slowly? If not, put a deadline around the call. Does cancelling stop the call, or only free the caller?

The arithmetic on the budget

A stream thread has to call poll() at least every max.poll.interval.ms, 300 seconds by default, or the group takes its tasks away in a rebalance. So two limits apply between two polls, and each is a number of calls times the budget:

round = tasks per thread × budget
poll's worth = max.poll.records × budget

A round is a call for each of the thread's tasks. One poll returns up to max.poll.records records, a poll's worth. How many of them the thread works through before it polls again depends on its history: while the service is fast, Kafka Streams lets it take more. A cap on max.poll.records bounds that, whatever the history. The consumer's Javadoc gives the setting this job: to bound "the maximum that must be handled within each poll interval". Keep both under half of the poll interval, 150 seconds by default. The other half is margin: when an instance goes away, its tasks move to the others, and their rounds grow.

For the stream we measured, 25 CVEs a second at 300 ms a call on 8 threads, with a 2-second budget:

round
  8 partitions = 1 × 2 s = 2 s, under 150
  32 partitions = 4 × 2 s = 8 s, under 150

poll's worth
  1,000, the default = 1,000 × 2 s = 2,000 s, far over 300
  75 = 75 × 2 s = 150 s, just half

So max.poll.records can be at most 150 s ÷ 2 s, 75. Set it there, or lower.

The bound assumes every call takes its whole budget. That is not rare: when the service slows down, it slows down for every call at once. And even at the typical 300 ms, the default 1,000 records take 300 seconds, the whole poll interval.

Tasks per thread is the calling step's partitions over its threads, all instances counted. Leave commit.interval.ms at its default. If you raise it above a round, keep the round under a third of the poll interval instead.

The table adds two more services. Their numbers are calculated, not measured: we did not run them. Their threads come from the typical call, by Little's law. Their two limits come from the budget. In the CVE column the rate, the call time and the threads are our runs, and the budget is an example.

Fraud score CVE severity, our runs AI model decision
Records a second 200 25 5
Typical call 50 ms 300 ms 3 s
Calls in flight, rate × typical call 10 7.5 15
Threads, one task each 12 8 16
Budget, retries included 0.5 s 2 s 20 s
Round, with one task per thread 0.5 s 2 s 20 s
Poll's worth: max.poll.records, at most 150 s ÷ budget 300 75 7

Even the fast service needs max.poll.records cut, from 1,000 to 300. The AI model allows only 7 records a poll. That is the price of a 20-second budget, short of raising the poll interval.

Break either limit and the cost is not lag. The thread is evicted, its tasks start again from the last commit, and every call since then is made again. If the service charges per call, you pay each time. We ran three tasks on one thread with a 12-second call, against a poll interval scaled down to 30 seconds. The thread was evicted four times in 210 seconds and never committed, and the output held 17 records for 7 CVEs, where each CVE should give one. What max.poll.interval.ms bounds in Kafka Streams shows each bound run by run, and weighs the other levers, raising the poll interval among them.

Keep the slow step in its own stream

Threads are shared by all the steps of one application. So a fast step whose task lands on a thread with a slow one waits behind its calls. Two applications keep them apart. The first does the fast work and writes the records that need an answer to a topic. The second reads that topic, makes the call and routes the result. In our example, the first stream keeps the new CVEs that arrive without a severity score from their CNA, the organisation that assigned the CVE. The second asks the service for one.

The two-stream design.

The last run tested that, and the timeout, together. The first stream passed records on with no call. The second, with 32 threads, called the service. With records arriving at 25 a second, we paused the service for 45 seconds. With a 60-second timeout, the second stream simply waited out the pause, and its backlog grew to about 1,100. When the service came back, it caught up at about 100 a second in about 15 seconds. Nothing failed, and nothing rebalanced. With a 5-second timeout, 31 calls timed out together. The second stream went to ERROR, the client state that means it has stopped for good: Kafka Streams does not restart it, even after the service is back. In both runs the first stream never noticed.

The 5-second run stopped because of a default: a single call that throws sends the whole client to ERROR, with no retry, and a single connection error does the same. KIP-1033 added a handler in Kafka 3.9 that can change that policy. What to change it to, skipping the record, retrying it or sending it to a dead-letter topic, is a subject of its own. Until you have one, set the budget from what the service needs, not shorter.

Why not a separate worker

Another common way to handle a slow call is to take it out of Kafka Streams entirely. In our example, stream B would become a worker: a separate program of your own, built on a plain Kafka consumer rather than on Kafka Streams. It reads severity-requests, calls the service with many requests in flight at once, and writes the decided records to cve-decided.

Stream B needs a thread for every call in flight, because each call blocks its thread. A worker can use an asynchronous client instead: one thread sends many requests and handles each answer as it comes. For a very slow service that matters. At 25 records a second and 20 seconds a call, Little's law asks for 500 calls in flight: 500 threads and 500 partitions for stream B, a few threads for a worker.

In exchange, the worker has to do itself what Kafka Streams does for stream B, and all of it comes from the many calls it holds open. They finish in any order. So it commits an offset only when every earlier record of the partition is done, and keeps the order within a partition where that matters. And when it stops, or hands a partition to another instance, it has to finish or abandon the calls still open. Abandoned calls are made again by whoever reads the partition next.

It is also a second kind of application to watch. Its consumer group's lag shows like any other. But whatever shows you your streams, their state, threads and tasks, does not see the worker. Its health, its calls in flight and its failures need watching of their own.

Our call sits at the edge: stream B ends with it. A call in the middle of a stream, between a join and an aggregation, is harder to move out. The answers have to come back into the stream, joined to their records by key within a window. An answer later than the window needs a path of its own.

Two tools sit between stream B and a worker of your own: Confluent's Parallel Consumer and Responsive's async processor. We measured neither of them, nor a worker. The Parallel Consumer is the usual building block for a worker: more calls in flight than partitions, with order kept per key. The async processor keeps the call inside Kafka Streams and hands it to a thread pool, again with order kept per key.

The short version

  • A blocking call caps a stream thread at one record per call: throughput is threads over call time, up to the partitions.
  • Partitions alone do not help: a repartition without the threads to match only gives each thread more tasks.
  • Give every call a budget: the whole call, retries and backoff included. Without one, no setting is safe.
  • Keep a round, the tasks per thread times the budget, and a poll's worth, max.poll.records times the budget, under half of max.poll.interval.ms.
  • An eviction before a commit repeats the calls and writes duplicates.
  • With the defaults, one failed call stops the whole client.
  • Give the slow step its own stream, with the threads to match its partitions.

How we measured

We ran everything on one machine and one broker, against the stub, which waited a fixed time before it answered. A real service's time varies. Ours did not, so each run shows one latency at a time. The numbers describe the shape of the problem, not your cluster's. The records were real: newly published vulnerability entries, CVEs, from the National Vulnerability Database, replayed from one captured window. The runs used Kafka Streams 4.2.0 and the classic group protocol.

The stub, the replay script and the application that measured all of this are not published. If you want to run them against your own numbers, write to info@alginte.com and we will send them.

This post uses the NVD API but is not endorsed or certified by the NVD.

Related reading

  • Brice Leporini, Why you should not query a database in your stream processors (2022): the same problem from the database side, with a table join and a two-stage design as the ways out.
  • KIP-442: until Kafka 2.3, Kafka Streams set max.poll.interval.ms to effectively infinite, so older advice that a slow Streams application is never evicted predates it.
  • Sébastien Viale, Loïc Greffier and Valérie Servaire, Processing error handling in Kafka Streams (2025): the handler KIP-1033 added, written by two of its authors, with the built-in choices and the dead-letter queue support KIP-1034 added later.

In the next posts of this series, the service is an AI model that makes a decision on each event. To get them, follow the blog's RSS feed or @alginte_sw on X, where we post each one.

Handling 429 Email Rate Limit Errors in Logistics: Template Ownership
description:
Short answer: to handle 429 rate limit errors for an email API in Node.js, treat the response as a queue decision, not a send failure. Keep the verification event durable, honor the provider's Retry-After signal when present, retry with bounded jitter, and make template ownership explicit before the worker sends anything. For a logistics signup flow, I would keep the template in the application repository when its wording and variables are part of the product contract. A provider-managed template is the better runner-up when operations needs to change copy without a deploy and the application can validate the rendered result.

The important distinction is ownership. The retry loop controls when a message may leave. Template ownership controls what leaves after the delay. Mixing them creates a particularly nasty class of bugs: a verification token can be valid while the email body is stale, or a retry can send a different template than the first attempt.

The decision matrix

Template owner 429 behavior Change workflow Main risk
Application repository Queue the event and retry the same versioned render Code review and deploy Copy changes wait for release
Provider workspace Queue the event and resolve the template at send time Operations workflow A retry can observe a later template
Shared catalog service Queue the event with an immutable template version Catalog release process More coordination and another dependency

My default is application ownership for account verification. It gives the event a reproducible input: templateVersion, locale, recipient, and a token expiry. That matters more than shaving a step from the first call. A logistics signup link is a security boundary, not a newsletter.

What exactly should a 429 retry?

Retry the delivery attempt, never the HTTP request in isolation. The durable record needs an idempotency key, attempt count, next-attempt time, and the template version selected before enqueueing. A retry should not mint a second account, rotate a token by accident, or silently switch locales.

A 429 is also not permission to hammer the endpoint more politely. Respect Retry-After if the service supplies it. If it does not, use exponential backoff with random jitter and a cap. Stop after a defined deadline, then move the event to a reviewable state. The exact numbers belong in configuration for your traffic shape; the policy should be stable and observable.

This is where I usually reject clever client wrappers. A wrapper that retries every non-2xx response hides the difference between throttling, authentication failure, malformed input, and a provider outage. The caller needs a typed outcome.

Keep this boring.

The retry policy is a limitation, too: bounded backoff cannot make an expired verification token valid, and it cannot repair a bad sender configuration. Those cases need a terminal state and an operator signal, not more attempts.

How should Node.js handle 429 rate limit errors for email?

Suppose a driver signs up from a depot with a slow connection. The first request is accepted into your queue, but the downstream email API returns 429 twice. During those minutes, a copy editor changes “Verify your account” to “Confirm your dispatcher account.” With application ownership, the retry renders the recorded version. With provider ownership, it may resolve the new version unless the provider supports an immutable revision or the event stores enough information to pin one.

Neither choice is universally correct. Provider ownership is useful when a support or operations team must adjust wording quickly, especially for regional instructions. It needs a publish check, a preview test, and a rule that security-sensitive variables cannot be added by copy editors. Application ownership is easier to audit and test, but it makes copy a release artifact.

The decision criterion is not “which editor feels nicer?” It is replayability. Can an engineer reconstruct the exact body sent for a failed verification event six hours later? If the answer is no, the system has an audit gap.

A small Node.js worker with explicit outcomes

The worker below keeps transport policy separate from template rendering. It is intentionally boring. sendVerification is a generic adapter; the provider-specific SDK stays behind it.

type DeliveryResult =
  | { kind: 'sent'; providerId: string }
  | { kind: 'retry'; retryAt: number; reason: 'throttled' }
  | { kind: 'dead'; reason: 'invalid' | 'unauthorized' | 'expired' };

type SendError = {
  status?: number;
  retryAfterSeconds?: number;
  message: string;
};

function nextDelay(attempt: number, retryAfterSeconds?: number): number {
  if (retryAfterSeconds !== undefined) {
    return Math.max(1_000, retryAfterSeconds * 1_000);
  }

  const cap = 15 * 60 * 1_000;
  const base = Math.min(cap, 1_000 * 2 ** attempt);
  return Math.round(base * (0.75 + Math.random() * 0.5));
}

async function deliver(event: {
  id: string;
  attempt: number;
  templateVersion: string;
  expiresAt: number;
  recipient: string;
}): Promise<DeliveryResult> {
  if (Date.now() >= event.expiresAt) {
    return { kind: 'dead', reason: 'expired' };
  }

  try {
    const response = await sendVerification({
      idempotencyKey: event.id,
      recipient: event.recipient,
      templateVersion: event.templateVersion,
    });

    return { kind: 'sent', providerId: response.id };
  } catch (error) {
    const failure = error as SendError;

    if (failure.status === 429) {
      return {
        kind: 'retry',
        retryAt: Date.now() + nextDelay(event.attempt, failure.retryAfterSeconds),
        reason: 'throttled',
      };
    }

    if (failure.status && failure.status >= 400 && failure.status < 500) {
      return { kind: 'dead', reason: failure.status === 401 ? 'unauthorized' : 'invalid' };
    }

    throw error;
  }
}

The queue must make the state transition durable before acknowledging the job. On a retry, increment the attempt and preserve templateVersion. On a terminal result, record the provider response identifier when one exists. Metrics should separate 429, other 4xx, 5xx, queue age, and expired verification events. One counter called email_errors is not observability.

Do not use an unbounded in-process timer for this. A process restart should not erase delayed work. Use a durable queue, a database-backed schedule, or the equivalent mechanism already operated by your team. The implementation detail varies; the invariant does not.

How do provider limits affect a neutral policy?

The policy has to read the selected transport's contract instead of guessing from a status code. Amazon SES documents send rate and a rolling 24-hour sending quota as separate controls. SendGrid documents API rate limits and response headers for some endpoints. Mailgun documents API limits in its own API reference. These are different boundaries, even though all three can produce pressure that looks like “try again later.”

That difference changes what you measure. A send-rate ceiling calls for queue smoothing. A daily quota calls for admission control and an operator alert. An API-management limit may affect template lookup or status queries rather than message delivery. The adapter should translate those provider-specific signals into the small internal result type above, while retaining the raw status and headers for diagnosis.

I would test this at three levels: a pure backoff test with a fake clock, an adapter test that feeds a 429 with and without Retry-After, and a staging drill that confirms duplicate suppression after a worker restart. The last one catches the expensive bug. The code “works,” but the same verification email is sent twice when the acknowledgement is lost.

For the logistics case, choose provider-owned templates only when the team can pin revisions and review variable changes. Otherwise, keep the renderable contract beside the signup code, enqueue a versioned event, and let the worker retry delivery rather than recomputing business state. That is the runner-up's useful boundary: fast operational copy changes, at the cost of stricter release controls around template versions. Provider ownership is a poor fit when the team cannot audit revisions; application ownership is a poor fit when urgent copy changes cannot wait for deployment.

References

  • RFC 6585, Additional HTTP Status Codes, section 4 (429): https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6585#section-4
  • RFC 7231, HTTP Semantics, section 7.1.3 (Retry-After): https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7231#section-7.1.3
  • RFC 7208, Sender Policy Framework (SPF): https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7208
  • Amazon SES sending quotas: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ses/latest/dg/manage-sending-quotas.html
  • SendGrid API rate limits: https://docs.sendgrid.com/api-reference/how-to-use-the-sendgrid-v3-api/rate-limits
  • Mailgun API reference: https://documentation.mailgun.com/docs/mailgun/api-reference/send/mailgun-messages

title: A Privacy Budget for Email Test Data
description:
A Privacy Budget for Email Test Data

Email is often treated as harmless test plumbing. A CI job creates an inbox, a verification message arrives, a test reads the link, and the inbox is forgotten. In practice, those messages can contain names, account identifiers, reset tokens, invite URLs, and enough product detail to reconstruct a user journey.

The useful question is not “Which disposable inbox should we use?” It is “How much email data does this test actually need, for how long, and who can see it?” That is a privacy budget: a small, explicit limit on exposure that still lets engineers diagnose failures.

This framing is helpful for teams building web applications because it joins Privacy and Security with maintainability. The cheapest data to protect is the data we never retain.

Why email test data deserves a budget

Test email has a strange lifecycle. It starts as synthetic data, becomes a delivery artifact, then turns into a log attachment or a screenshot. Each copy has a different audience and retention period. A mailbox that is safe for a local smoke test may be a poor fit for a shared staging environment.

I use four questions to set the budget:

  1. Content: Does the test need the whole message, or only a token and delivery timestamp?
  2. Lifetime: Is the message needed for seconds, one CI run, or a week of investigation?
  3. Reach: Which people and systems can read the inbox, traces, logs, or artifacts?
  4. Reuse: Can one inbox accidentally reveal another test's message?

If the answer is vague, the data budget is already too large. The implementation get messy when a test stores a complete email simply because the assertion was easier to write that way.

Define the budget before choosing a tool

For a normal verification test, a reasonable default might be:

  • one generated address per test or isolated worker;
  • one expected message, with a bounded wait;
  • a retention period no longer than the CI run;
  • logs containing message ID, subject hash, and timing, but not the body;
  • a failure artifact containing a redacted excerpt only when the test fails.

This is not a universal policy. An OAuth flow may need a link target, while a rendering test needs HTML and CSS. The point is to name the minimum capability instead of granting an entire persistent mailbox.

Teams also need a vocabulary for search terms and operator mistakes. A developer may type tempail while looking for a temporary inbox, but that typo should never become a reason to broaden a production allowlist or retain more data. Small details like this prevent a test utility from quietly becoming an identity system.

A practical retention and access model

Separate the data plane from the evidence plane:

  • Data plane: the temporary inbox and message body, accessible only to the test worker.
  • Evidence plane: a small JSON receipt with correlation ID, delivery state, elapsed time, and a redacted failure reason.

The receipt should be enough to answer “Did delivery happen?” and “Where did it wait?” without answering “What did the user receive?” If debugging needs more, make the expansion deliberate, time-limited, and visible in the run record.

For flaky tests, Playwright traces for flaky email tests show why a timeline can be more useful than saving every message. The same principle applies to scheduled jobs: self-explaining cron runs make the outcome inspectable without preserving unrelated inputs.

Make failures useful without keeping everything

A test harness can emit a compact receipt like this:

{
  "correlation_id": "ci-1842-verify",
  "mailbox_scope": "worker-7",
  "message_seen": true,
  "delivery_ms": 842,
  "token_checked": true,
  "body_retained": false
}

The message_seen and delivery_ms fields help distinguish a provider delay from an application bug. token_checked confirms the assertion without printing the token. When the test fail, the harness can attach a redacted subject and the last polling event, then delete the inbox as part of cleanup.

Cleanup should be defensive, not aspirational. Put it in a finally block, make deletion idempotent, and record cleanup failure separately from the original assertion. A small ledger make retries understandable: created, message observed, assertion passed, deleted. It also makes a leak visible when deletion did not happen.

Checklist for the next review

Ask these questions in the next email-test review:

  • Does each parallel test have an isolated mailbox scope?
  • Are verification tokens absent from ordinary logs and traces?
  • Is the default retention shorter than the investigation window?
  • Can an engineer diagnose timing without opening the message body?
  • Does cleanup run after assertion failures and cancellations?
  • Are screenshots and CI artifacts covered by the same policy?

The goal is not to make testing slower or less observable. It is to make observability proportional. A privacy budget gives the team a shared tradeoff: retain the smallest evidence that explains the behavior, and require a reason before retaining anything more.

That small boundary usually improves reliability too. Fewer shared inboxes means fewer cross-test races, fewer misleading retries, and less uncertainty about which message belongs to which run. The test become easier to trust because its evidence has a clear owner and an intentional lifetime.

title: Make AI API Operations Idempotent
description:
Disclosure: I work on Modelflare, an OpenAI-compatible AI API gateway. The canonical version of this article lives on modelflare.dev.

Make AI API Operations Idempotent: a production guide with an explicit decision, reusable artifact, failure tests, operating signals, and source-qualified limits.

The operating rule

Make AI API Operations Idempotent should be implemented as a reliability control contract, not as a one-off configuration. Freeze the protocol, ownership, evidence, and rollback condition before traffic moves. The concrete control points in this guide are logical_request_id, idempotency_key, request_digest, durable_result.

Make side-effecting AI operations idempotent at the application boundary. Bind a caller-supplied idempotency key to one authenticated principal, operation, and canonical request digest; reserve the operation atomically; persist terminal success or failure; and return the same durable result on replay. Model call IDs are correlation data, not a substitute for this ledger.

Draw the failure boundary first

Separate the reader-facing task from the control-plane work behind it. Client setup owns the local file or environment variable; the gateway owns authentication, routing, limits, accounting, and attempt records; the provider owns its native protocol and volatile capability contract. A passing text prompt proves only that one path worked once.

Reliability controls must be defined on attempts and terminal states, not on a vague notion of a request “working.” Preserve the caller deadline, distinguish overload from permanent errors, and make rejection, cancellation, retry, fallback, and settlement observable as separate outcomes.

The owner record for this page is ai-api-idempotency; its frozen controls are logical_request_id, idempotency_key, request_digest, durable_result. Every value is reviewed at the wire or durable-state boundary and never inferred from a marketing label.

State and control contract: Make AI API Operations Idempotent

Use the following review record as the deployable artifact. Technical values are intentionally explicit so a reviewer can compare configuration, wire evidence, and durable state without relying on a screenshot or a successful-looking outer response.

Control point Fixed decision Evidence to retain
key_scope principal_plus_operation_plus_idempotency_key principal_id + operation + key
request_binding canonical_digest_must_match request_digest + schema_version
reservation atomic_pending_record_before_side_effect unique_constraint + created_at + owner
replay same_key_same_digest_returns_durable_result original_result_id + replay_count
conflict same_key_different_digest_rejected conflict_status + both_digests_without_payload
recovery stale_pending_requires_owned_reconciliation lease + side_effect_receipt + terminal_write

Exercise the critical transition

The example uses placeholders and deterministic inputs. Replace identifiers with reviewed values, never with credentials or customer content. Preserve the exact configuration snapshot alongside the probe result.

BEGIN;
INSERT INTO operation_ledger
  (principal_id, operation, idempotency_key, request_digest, status)
VALUES
  (:principal, :operation, :key, :digest, 'pending')
ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING;
-- only the transaction that owns the new row may perform the side effect
-- persist terminal result before returning it to the caller
COMMIT;

Verify behavior under failure

Run the ladder in order. A later check cannot compensate for a missing earlier boundary, and every attempt must remain attributable to one logical request.

  1. Freeze the current client, gateway policy, model alias, route set, and observable baseline. Evidence record for key_scope: enforce principal_plus_operation_plus_idempotency_key and retain principal_id + operation + key.
  2. Run one deterministic positive probe and capture the client-visible response, request ID, selected route, terminal state, and usage. Evidence record for request_binding: enforce canonical_digest_must_match and retain request_digest + schema_version.
  3. Run the paired negative, limit, or disconnect case and verify that it fails in the intended layer. Evidence record for reservation: enforce atomic_pending_record_before_side_effect and retain unique_constraint + created_at + owner.
  4. Repeat the probe through the actual protocol surface; do not infer native support from a neighboring compatibility endpoint. Evidence record for replay: enforce same_key_same_digest_returns_durable_result and retain original_result_id + replay_count.
  5. Roll out to a bounded cohort with an explicit owner, expiry time, stop threshold, and prepared rollback. Evidence record for conflict: enforce same_key_different_digest_rejected and retain conflict_status + both_digests_without_payload.
  6. Re-read durable configuration and accounting after the test, then remove temporary access or test data. Evidence record for recovery: enforce stale_pending_requires_owned_reconciliation and retain lease + side_effect_receipt + terminal_write.

Failure amplification to prevent

Treat each item below as a release blocker. A 200 response, attractive dashboard, or single successful demo does not override these failure conditions.

  • memory_only_deduplication — Process memory cannot protect retries after restart, failover, or concurrent execution on another node.
  • key_without_digest — Reusing a key for a different payload can return the wrong result or hide a caller bug.
  • check_then_act_race — Reading for an existing record and writing later allows two workers to perform the same side effect.
  • model_call_id_as_key — A model-generated call ID may change across retries and does not define the authenticated business operation.

Trip signals, denominators, and stop conditions

Monitor success and harm together. The threshold is a policy input, not a universal benchmark; choose it from the workload SLO and record the denominator before the observation window begins.

Signal Decision threshold Action
duplicate_side_effect_count 0 stop_operation_and_reconcile
idempotency_digest_conflicts review_each_event reject_and_alert_owner
stale_pending_age <_owned_recovery_deadline reconcile_with_external_receipt
replay_result_mismatch 0 disable_endpoint

Modelflare boundary and limitations

Modelflare can centralize OpenAI-compatible and native-protocol routing, scoped keys, groups, usage records, and failure handling. A configured channel is not proof that every optional field, model alias, retention promise, region, or fallback is supported. Verify the selected route with its native protocol, preserve explicit zero values, and use the final durable settlement as billing truth.

Idempotency does not mean every model generation becomes identical. It means the protected business operation has one durable outcome for the same authenticated request. Read-only generation may be retried under a budget, while payments, messages, database mutations, and tool actions need operation-specific keys and reconciliation.

Continue through the topic cluster

Use the linked parent for the broader decision, the sibling for the next implementation step, and the documentation route for current client configuration. These body links are deliberate because managed CMS articles do not currently carry a separate related-slug field.

  • Parent decision guide
  • Next implementation guide
  • Current setup documentation

Frequently asked questions

Is an HTTP POST automatically non-idempotent?

HTTP method semantics and application idempotency are related but different; the ledger defines replay behavior for the business operation.

Can the gateway invent the key?

The layer that understands the business operation should define it. A gateway request ID alone may not identify the user-visible side effect.

How are stale pending rows handled?

Use an owned recovery lease and external receipt lookup; never blindly repeat the side effect.

Sources and verification date

Sources were checked on 2026-08-07. They establish external contracts and engineering principles; they do not prove an untested route or future provider state.

  • RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics
  • OpenAI API reference: request IDs
  • OWASP: Transaction Authorization Cheat Sheet

title: Estimating Audio Transcription API Cost Per Minute in Go Before Production
description:
Short answer: estimate transcription spend from the audio duration before accepting the job, then turn that estimate into a quota and an alert threshold. Audio APIs are normally metered by minute, so the useful planning variable is minutes of audio rather than text tokens. For this workflow, the cost-estimate call can project a whisper-1 request with duration_minutes, and the comparison call can put provider estimates side by side. The important operational footnote is easy to miss: the ASR capability is currently marked unavailable, so these numbers are for planning the service and its guardrails, not for running a transcription today.

That distinction changes the first page an on-call engineer sees. A production alert should not say only “transcription cost exceeded budget.” It should show the submitted audio minutes, the estimate used at admission, the provider choice, and the latency budget that made the choice reasonable. Otherwise the alert arrives after a batch has already become an accounting problem.

What should the cost alert show first?

Imagine the alert page at 02:10: the invoice-extraction queue is growing, estimated audio spend is above its hourly allowance, and p95 transcription latency has crossed the SLO. The person on call needs a decision, not another dashboard tile: reject new work, defer it, or accept slower processing for better extraction quality.

Work backward from that page. The signal that should have fired earlier was the estimate at admission time. For each invoice audio file, record duration, selected model, projected cost, and the quality-versus-latency policy that selected it. Aggregate those records by tenant and time window. A quota then becomes a control on planned work, while the later provider response remains a measure of what actually happened when ASR is available.

This is why I would estimate before uploading a large batch rather than discover the unit of billing in a month-end report. One key and one bill for every backend service can reduce credential and reconciliation sprawl, but it does not remove the need to own the admission rule. Centralized access is an operational convenience; it is not capacity planning.

How can I estimate the cost of an audio transcription API per minute?

Let M be the total audio minutes admitted in a window and C(m) the estimate returned for model m. A simple guardrail is:

planned_spend = sum(C(model, duration_minutes))

Stop admitting work when planned spend reaches the tenant quota, or when the remaining latency budget cannot absorb the queue. The formula is intentionally boring. Boring formulas are easier to audit when a supplier invoice is late, duplicated, or unusually long.

Do not substitute token accounting for duration accounting. Text generation and chat commonly expose input and output token units; transcription is typically priced per minute of audio. The right comparison is therefore minutes, expected quality, and end-to-end latency. A cheaper estimate that produces unusable invoice fields is not a cheaper pipeline after reprocessing and human review are included.

The cost estimate is a planning input, not a quality score. Keep a separate quality sample: field-level extraction accuracy, confidence review rate, and the fraction of invoices needing a second pass. That separation prevents a cost dashboard from quietly becoming the owner of an SLO it cannot observe.

Which provider fits an invoice-extraction pipeline?

There is no universal winner because the decision axis is quality versus latency, with cost acting as a constraint. OpenAI’s Whisper API is a familiar hosted option for teams already using its API surface. Google Cloud Speech-to-Text is a natural fit when the rest of the workflow already lives in Google Cloud and regional integration matters. Amazon Transcribe fits a similar AWS-centered operating model, with managed speech processing alongside other AWS controls. Deepgram is another real option for teams that prioritize a specialized speech API and need to evaluate streaming and batch behavior separately.

Those are materially different operating choices, not four labels for the same service. A hosted provider reduces model-serving work, while cloud-native placement can simplify identity, networking, and data-governance review. A speech-focused API may offer a better latency profile for the target language or audio mix, but that claim belongs in a controlled evaluation, not in a procurement spreadsheet. Self-hosting an open model with Ollama can improve control over deployment and data boundaries; it also moves capacity planning, model rollout, GPU utilization, and on-call responsibility onto the platform team.

Gemini can belong in a secondary comparison when audio understanding is part of a broader multimodal workflow, while OpenRouter and Together are better treated as routing or model-access alternatives than as dedicated transcription services. Anthropic and Claude belong in the same adjacent-platform category. I would not call any of those a direct replacement for a per-minute ASR benchmark; naming the boundary prevents a broad AI platform comparison from hiding the actual speech requirement.

For an independent comparison, I would score the candidates against the invoice corpus rather than rank them by a single per-minute number:

Option Useful fit Cost and latency question Boundary
OpenAI Whisper API Existing OpenAI client and hosted transcription workflow Does its service latency meet the batch SLO at the target duration mix? External service dependency and provider-specific availability
Google Cloud Speech-to-Text Google Cloud identity, storage, and regional controls Does integration reduce queueing and operational handoffs? Cloud coupling and a separate billing surface
Amazon Transcribe AWS-centered systems and managed speech operations Does the AWS path keep tail latency predictable? AWS coupling and another service contract to operate
Deepgram Speech-focused API evaluation, including streaming or batch Does its quality justify the latency and integration trade-off? Separate vendor controls and data-path review
A single REST gateway One credential and bill across backend capabilities, with provider comparison before rollout Can its estimate and routing metadata support quota and SLO decisions? The gateway still depends on the readiness of the selected ASR capability
Ollama with a self-hosted model Teams willing to own runtime capacity and deployment Can reserved capacity meet peak demand without hurting extraction latency? Hardware, upgrades, and incident ownership stay in-house

The last row is not a free pass, and the gateway row is not a recommendation by itself. Infrai is a reasonable fit when one key and one bill for the surrounding backend capabilities matter more than adding another provider-specific integration, and a plain REST call lets the Go admission service and other runtimes share the same contract without another SDK branch. Its ASR readiness still has to be checked before rollout. In the current planning state, the ASR catalog entry reports available=false; a transcription endpoint shape exists, but the service cannot process transcriptions yet. That makes a pre-launch estimate useful for quotas and alert thresholds while making any claim about live transcription latency premature.

A small Go estimator with real failure handling

The implementation should make the planning boundary explicit. This example sends only the verified estimate inputs, reads the API key from the environment, checks every status, and backs off on rate limiting. It does not pretend that an estimate response means an audio job has been accepted.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "math"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func estimate(minutes float64) (map[string]any, error) {
    body, err := json.Marshal(map[string]any{
        "model":           "whisper-1",
        "duration_minutes": minutes,
    })
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }

    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }

    baseURL := os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL")
    if baseURL == "" {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_BASE_URL is required")
    }

    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPost, baseURL+"/ai/cost/estimate", bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        responseBody, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }

        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            delay := time.Duration(math.Pow(2, float64(attempt))) * time.Second
            if retryAfter := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"); retryAfter != "" {
                if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(retryAfter); parseErr == nil {
                    delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
                }
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }

        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("estimate failed with HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, string(responseBody))
        }

        var result map[string]any
        if err := json.Unmarshal(responseBody, &result); err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        return result, nil
    }

    return nil, fmt.Errorf("estimate failed after rate-limit retries")
}

func main() {
    result, err := estimate(12.5)
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    encoded, err := json.MarshalIndent(result, "", "  ")
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    fmt.Println(string(encoded))
}

There is no idempotency key in this sample because it estimates spend; it does not create, publish, or enqueue work. If the surrounding service later turns the decision into a write, give that write a client-supplied idempotency key and make the consumer idempotent as well. Retries are part of the design, not an afterthought added after the first duplicate invoice.

For provider selection, call the cost comparison operation during configuration or a controlled evaluation, then persist the chosen policy with the estimate record. Keep the comparison result out of the hot path unless provider readiness or latency changes require re-evaluation. A quota should be deterministic for the same input, or an operator will not be able to explain why an identical invoice was admitted yesterday and rejected today.

The threshold is a product decision with an SLO attached

Start with a conservative policy: estimate the whole audio duration, reserve headroom for the queue, and alert before the quota is exhausted. The exact headroom belongs to the workload. A ten-minute invoice batch and a call-center archive do not have the same burst shape, and neither should inherit a threshold because it looked tidy on a dashboard.

Measure two different failure costs. A low threshold creates false positives: useful jobs wait, on-call pages arrive during normal bursts, and users may retry into an even larger queue. A high threshold creates a budget surprise and can push latency beyond the extraction SLO. The right threshold is the point where the cost of a false alarm is visible and acceptable compared with the cost of admitting work the system cannot finish on time.

The present ASR limitation is therefore part of the rollout checklist. Build the estimate, quota, and alert path now; gate live transcription on the capability becoming available; then validate quality and latency with the same invoice corpus used to choose a provider. Planning data is valuable, but it is not production evidence.

  • Google Cloud Speech-to-Text documentation
  • Amazon Transcribe documentation
  • Deepgram documentation
  • Ollama

title: CodeBoo: Exorcising Your Codebase’s Hidden TODOs and Haunted Bugs
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

What I Built

We’ve all left a line like // TODO: fix memory leak before launch in a file, closed the editor, and promptly forgotten it ever existed. Over time, repos turn into digital haunted houses—populated by lingering code debt, unindexed security hazards, and ghost functions abandoned three years ago.

CodeBoo is a lightweight, local AI tool that brings those spectral bugs out of the shadows.

Point CodeBoo at any local directory or public GitHub repo link, and it scans the codebase to surface hidden TODOs, potential memory leaks, unhandled errors, and security issues.

Instead of dumping a terrifying, dry terminal log, CodeBoo ranks the issues by urgency and renders them as interactive, spooky-cute ghosts:

  • 👻 Harmless Spirits (Low Urgency): Cute, friendly little ghosts for routine TODO comments and cosmetic cleanups.
  • 🧟 Creepy Specters (Medium Urgency): Slightly unhinged ghosts for unhandled exceptions or inefficient loops.
  • 🎃 Nightmare Phantoms (High Urgency): Genuinely spooky, dark spirits for critical memory leaks, exposed keys, or potential null-pointer crashes. It turns technical debt triage into something clear, visual, and oddly charming.

Demo

Code

How I Built It

CodeBoo was built to run entirely on a mid-range developer machine (designed to consume under 5 GB of system memory, leaving plenty of room within an 8 GB free RAM budget).

  • The Model: Qwen2.5-Coder:7b (or gemma2:9b / gemma4:2b) running locally via Ollama. Code-focused open models are fantastic at reading multi-file context, understanding syntax semantics, and returning structured JSON without needing a cloud API key.
  • File Parser & Aggregator: A lightweight backend written in Python that walks through code files, strips non-essential whitespace to stay within model context limits, and flags candidate blocks.
  • Severity Ranking Engine: The LLM evaluates every discovered issue and assigns it an urgency rating (1 to 5), an issue category (Security, Leak, Refactor, TODO), a plain-English explanation (keeping jargon accessible), and a recommended fix.
  • Visual UI: A single-page web dashboard using CSS animations to display issue "cards" inside animated ghost sprites whose expressions and dark glow scale with the severity of the bug.

Limitations

  • Repository Size: Extremely large repos (thousands of files) must be scanned module-by-module to keep context window usage within RAM bounds.
  • Static Analysis Edge Cases: While local open-weight models excel at finding logic flaws and written TODOs, full runtime memory profiling still requires dedicated profilers.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

  • Codebase Confidentiality: Scanning code for security bugs or unhandled edge cases using a closed cloud API means sending your proprietary context to external servers. Local open-weight models guarantee your code never leaves your device.
  • Unrestricted Code Scans: You can run CodeBoo against massive personal repos or multiple commits without worrying about token limits, rate caps, or monthly bills.
  • Customizable Parsing: Because the inference runner and prompts are completely transparent, developers can swap out models or fine-tune prompt constraints for their specific language stack.

The Spirit of It

Prize Categories
