title: How I Measure a Server: The Knee, Percentiles That Lie, and Little's Law
description:
I did not trust latency numbers until I could make a server slow down on purpose. This post is what came out of three small experiments in my system-design-challenges repo. Each one changed how I read a metric I reach for every day. The code is real, and the numbers below are what the scripts actually measured on this machine, not what I hoped they would be.

Side note: this is the first challenge in a repo I keep for hands-on system design. It starts with the tools for measuring a service before it moves on to architecture, storage, and distributed systems. I work through it by running things, not just reading about them.

The setup: one worker, about 10 ms of work per request

The server is deliberately boring. Every request does roughly 10 ms of CPU-bound work in a spin loop that blocks the event loop, so the whole thing behaves like a single worker: a request that arrives while another is being served waits its turn.

// server.js: a tiny server with a simulated service time
const SERVICE_MS = Number(process.env.SERVICE_MS ?? 10);
const SLOW_CHANCE = Number(process.env.SLOW_CHANCE ?? 0);
const SLOW_MS = Number(process.env.SLOW_MS ?? 0);

function busyWork(ms) {
  const end = performance.now() + ms;
  while (performance.now() < end) { /* spin: this loop is the work */ }
}

const server = http.createServer(async (req, res) => {
  if (random() < SLOW_CHANCE) await sleep(SLOW_MS);
  busyWork(...);
  res.end("ok\n");
});

One worker doing 10 ms of work has a rough capacity of 1000 / 10 = 100 requests per second. Call that an estimate. Scheduling, random service times, and bursts change the measured result, and that uncertainty is the whole point of the first experiment.

Big word: utilisation. The fraction of a worker's capacity that is currently demanded, usually written as a percentage. At 70 requests per second, this server is about 70% busy.

Experiment 1: the knee, or where a queue stops being polite

The obvious way to load-test a server is to send more traffic and watch the average. The problem is that the average is the last number to admit something is wrong.

As incoming work approaches the server's maximum rate, a queue starts forming before every request becomes slow. The high percentiles move first, because the most recent arrivals wait the longest. The experiment ramps the request rate and looks for the point where tail latency bends sharply upward. The knee.

request/s p99
60 69.4 ms
70 157.6 ms

At 70 requests per second the server is about 70% busy. Not full. Yet the slowest 1% of requests have already more than doubled to 157.6 ms. The M/M/1 estimate W = 1 / (mu - lambda) gives 33.3 ms average at that rate, and the measured mean tracked it early on, then drifted as the run got noisier near the knee.

Where the easy answer is not the full truth: people say "a server is fine until it's 100% busy, then you scale it." Not really. A queue forms well before that, and the tail feels it first. The knee is usually a fair bit below full utilisation. Your headroom is yours to choose; the knee just tells you where the comfortable margin ends.

Experiment 2: percentiles that lie, or how fan-out magnifies a small problem

A mean is one number: add every latency, divide by the count. It is easy to compute and easy to quote. It is also very good at hiding the rare, slow call that decides what a real user experiences. Percentiles show the boundary the slower traffic actually crosses: p95 is the latency that 95% of requests meet or beat.

Fan-out makes the problem worse, because a page is only as fast as its slowest parallel dependency. Every extra call is another chance to pick up a slow one. This experiment gave each dependency a 2% chance of taking 200 ms, then drove pages at 40 requests per second with increasing fan-out.

calls per page mean p95 slow pages observed
1 4.0 ms 1.5 ms ~2%
20 63.1 ms 202.1 ms 31%

Read the mean column and the load test "sounds manageable": 4 ms to 63 ms. Read the p95 and the story inverts: 1.5 ms to 202.1 ms. And observe that about 31% of 20-call pages hit the 200 ms wall. The prediction 1 - (1 - 0.02)^20 ≈ 33% matches what the run observed. A 2% dependency, fanned out 20 ways, becomes a roughly one-in-three page failure.

Pros and cons of averaging. A mean gives you one stable number you can graph and compare. Its cost is that it averages away the rare slow calls that shape actual experience. Useful for spotting drift over time; dangerous as your only performance number.

Experiment 3: Little's law as a reality check on your own measurements

Little's law says the average number of requests in the system is L = lambda times W: the arrival rate multiplied by the average time each request spends in the system. The interesting bit is that it holds for almost any stable queue, so it works as a consistency check on your measurements.

rate/s L measured lambda x W M/M/1 L
50 0.95 0.95 0.89
70 2.06 2.06 2.00
80 3.50 3.50 3.41
90 9.11 9.11 6.94

Measured L matched lambda x W across all four rows. The M/M/1 prediction stayed close at low load and drifted farthest at 90 requests per second, which is exactly where you would expect the classroom model to wobble.

Big word: Little's law. The relationship L = lambda x W between requests in flight, arrival rate, and time in the system. Because it holds for almost any stable system, when your measured L and your lambda x W stop agreeing, something is off with your measurement or your model. Investigate.

What I take away

  1. Watch percentiles, not just the average. The mean hid the real damage in both the knee and the fan-out experiments.
  2. Account for fan-out in your tail budget. A 2% dependency turns into a 31% page failure when it is 20 calls wide.
  3. Queues grow before the server looks bad. Latency is the earliest signal of saturation; the knee marks the end of comfortable headroom.
  4. Use Little's law as a sanity check. When L and lambda x W stop agreeing, trust the mismatch and dig in.

Things that may matter, with no over-claiming on my part: these are finite runs on one machine. Event-loop scheduling, a seeded random source, and the load generator all add noise, and the M/M/1 formulas are a teaching model, not a promise. Treat the charts as tendencies and the relationships as intuition, not as a spec you can copy into a capacity plan.

Try it yourself

Clone system-design-challenges and run node challenges/challenge-1-measure-a-server/part-1-the-knee/knee.js, part-2-percentiles-lie/tail.js, and part-3-littles-law/little.js from the repo root. npm test from the root runs the checks. The repo grows module by module, and the numbers on your machine will be a little different, which is part of the lesson.

title: Making a WPF Expander Faster with UI Reuse and Virtualization
description:
Working with large collections in WPF can introduce performance issues that aren't always obvious at first.

Recently, I worked on optimizing an Expander in our application that contained around 1,000 sequences. Opening it was noticeably slow, so I started investigating what was happening behind the scenes.

The Problem

We had an Expander that displayed approximately 1,000 sequences.

Each sequence also had a three-dot (⋮) button that provided additional actions.

The problem was in how the UI was structured.

In the existing XAML implementation, a separate three-dot button was created for every sequence item.

This meant WPF had to create and manage a large number of additional UI elements when loading the collection.

With around 1,000 sequences, this introduced unnecessary UI creation overhead and affected the Expander's opening performance.

Finding the Bottleneck

I started examining the XAML structure and how the sequence items were being rendered.

I found that the three-dot button was being repeatedly created for individual items, even though its functionality and structure were reusable.

This was unnecessary work that could be optimized.

The Solution

I approached the problem in two ways:

  1. Reusing the Button

Instead of repeatedly creating the same button structure, I changed the implementation to reuse the button reference and avoid unnecessary repeated creation.

  1. Implementing UI Virtualization

I also implemented virtualization so that WPF would create UI elements only for the items needed for the visible portion of the collection rather than creating everything upfront.

This reduced the number of UI elements that needed to be generated and managed at once.

The Result

The Expander now opens significantly faster, even with approximately 1,000 sequences.

The improvement came from reducing unnecessary UI element creation and using virtualization to manage a large collection more efficiently.

What I Learned

This was another reminder that UI performance is not just about how much data an application handles.

It's also about how efficiently the UI framework creates, manages, and renders that data.

When working with large collections in WPF, consider:

  • Avoiding unnecessary UI element creation.
  • Reusing common UI definitions and resources.
  • Implementing UI virtualization.
  • Investigating DataTemplates and visual tree complexity.
  • Understanding when UI elements are actually created and rendered.

Sometimes, optimizing the UI structure can make a bigger difference than optimizing the underlying data operations.

title: Step-by-Step Email Event Notification APIs Explained — Auditable Compliance Records
description:
Short answer: a B2B SaaS compliance notice needs a small Node.js intake service that authenticates event notifications, writes an immutable evidence record, and keeps message content on a separate retention schedule. A delivery event is evidence of a downstream observation, not proof that a person read the notice.

The bill is usually shaped by retention, not by the outbound request. Duplicated raw payloads, rendered bodies, indexes, attachments, and logs outlive their purpose unless their life is designed. An example policy might retain normalized evidence for 30 days, raw event envelopes for 7 days, and no body after its hash and required metadata are recorded. Those are policy examples; legal requirements set the real window.

What is the bill actually storing?

Data Purpose Retention question
Notice metadata Links a notice to tenant and policy Is an ID enough?
Event envelope Preserves what the source reported When is the original shape no longer needed?
Normalized status Supports reports and reconciliation Can it outlive the raw payload?
Message content Supports review or discovery Is a hash sufficient?
Operational logs Explains retries and failures Can identifiers be logged without addresses?

Store the notice ID, tenant ID, recipient fingerprint, event type, source event ID, observed time, and content hash in durable evidence. Keep the raw payload in short-lived object storage only when investigation requires it. Keep message bodies in a separately governed store with a tested deletion job.

This is a trade-off. Expiring raw data can remove fields that were never promoted into the evidence schema. Expiring the body can leave an auditor able to prove what happened without reconstructing the prose. Define the evidence contract first. Retention is a data-model decision.

A delivered event can mean that a downstream system accepted a message; it does not establish that the recipient read it. A bounced event needs its reason and the time observed. Keep the system's notice ID beside the external event ID so a repeated notification does not become a second compliance notice.

Consider a 30-day audit window. On day one, the normalized record can answer which tenant issued the notice, which recipient fingerprint was targeted, which event source reported the outcome, and when the service observed it. On day eight, the raw envelope may be gone. That is acceptable only if the normalized schema already captured the event type, source identity, timestamps, content hash, and verification result. If the investigation needs a field that was left in the expired envelope, the retention policy has saved storage by spending auditability. This is the kind of failure that appears months after an apparently successful integration, when the team has forgotten which adapter supplied which field. Write the contract while the payload is still in view.

{
  "notice_id": "notice_01J9EXAMPLE",
  "tenant_id": "tenant_42",
  "recipient_fingerprint": "sha256:...",
  "event_type": "delivered",
  "provider_event_id": "evt_7f2",
  "observed_at": "2026-10-31T08:15:00Z",
  "content_sha256": "sha256:...",
  "raw_payload_expires_at": "2026-11-07T08:15:00Z"
}

Use a uniqueness rule on the source identity you trust. Record late events, but do not silently let them rewrite a newer terminal state. Do not put a full recipient address into ordinary logs. A fingerprint supports correlation, but it remains sensitive when the input and hashing process are available to an attacker.

How should the Node.js intake be wired?

This step-by-step integration has four boundaries: authenticate, parse and validate, normalize, and persist idempotently. Email APIs belong at the edge; the rest of the application should receive a narrow internal event shape.

import crypto from "node:crypto";

function fingerprintRecipient(address, secret) {
  return "sha256:" + crypto.createHmac("sha256", secret)
    .update(address.trim().toLowerCase()).digest("hex");
}

function normalizeEvent(payload, secret) {
  if (!payload.notice_id || !payload.type || !payload.event_id) {
    throw new Error("missing event identity");
  }
  return {
    notice_id: String(payload.notice_id),
    tenant_id: String(payload.tenant_id),
    recipient_fingerprint: fingerprintRecipient(String(payload.recipient), secret),
    event_type: String(payload.type),
    provider_event_id: String(payload.event_id),
    observed_at: new Date().toISOString(),
    content_sha256: payload.content_sha256 ?? null
  };
}

export async function acceptEvent(request, deps) {
  const payload = await request.json();
  await deps.auth.verify(request, payload);
  const event = normalizeEvent(payload, deps.secrets.recipientFingerprint);
  await deps.evidence.insertIfAbsent(event, { rawPayload: payload, expiresInDays: 7 });
  return { status: 202 };
}

202 means accepted for processing, not delivered. Parsing and signature checks need a bounded body size, replay protection where supported, and a defined malformed-event response. Write the original only after verification. If a write fails after success is returned, the service has lied; if an error follows a successful write, the sender may retry. Idempotency is correctness.

Which failure mode does each boundary contain?

Failure mode Containment Evidence
Duplicate delivery Unique source event ID and replay-safe insert First-seen time and duplicate count
Late event State ordering rule or event timeline Event time and observed time
Signature mismatch Reject before normalization Redacted request ID and reason
Database outage Bounded backoff or durable queue Attempts and final disposition
Unknown event type Quarantine for review Type and schema version
Accepted without delivery Separate accepted and delivered states Transition history

The subtle case is a retry storm. Separate permanent validation failures from transient infrastructure failures, cap attempts, and expose queue age. A dead-letter record should identify human work without becoming another uncontrolled payload copy.

SPF concerns a sending domain's authorization model. It does not define a webhook schema or prove that a recipient read a message. The intake still needs an authenticated event channel, replay protection, and a record of the verification decision.

Measure acceptance rate, verification failures, duplicate rate, time from receipt to durable evidence, queue age, and notices with no terminal observation after a chosen window. Measure by tenant too; a healthy aggregate can hide one tenant with a consistently wrong domain policy.

Test duplicate delivery, reordered events, unknown types, expired signatures, oversized bodies, and a database timeout after insert. Assert both the response and the evidence left behind. Add a schema version and preserve the old reader until the retention window closes. The cleanup job should count candidates, deletions, and failures.

How can I integrate email event notification APIs step-by-step?

Start with the evidence contract, then connect the email APIs, then exercise the failure paths. The order matters: integrating first and defining evidence later usually leaves a provider-shaped record that cannot answer a compliance question cleanly.

The first design often keeps every payload forever because storage feels cheap and evidence feels valuable. Access review later shows that the system retained more personal data than the audit question required. Promote the fields that answer that question, shorten the rest, and document what cannot be reconstructed after expiry.

One short rule is enough: preserve proof, expire copies.

The least complex implementation is a thin adapter, an idempotent evidence store, and an explicit retention policy. Add queues, reconciliation, or extra channels only when they remove a demonstrated operational burden, because each state transition must also be audited.

Further reading

  • RFC 7208, Sender Policy Framework (SPF): https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7208
  • RFC 5322, Internet Message Format: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5322
  • RFC 3339, Date and Time on the Internet: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3339

title: How to Learn CSS Flexbox and Grid (and Stop Guessing Which One to Use)
description:
For about two years my approach to CSS layout was trial and error. I'd type display: flex, add justify-content: center, watch nothing happen, swap it for align-items: center, and keep toggling properties in DevTools until the box landed roughly where I wanted. It worked, sort of. I just couldn't have told you why.

What fixed it wasn't another cheat sheet. It was learning a few ideas properly, in the right order, and then reviewing them until they stopped leaking out of my head. Here's the order I'd follow if I were starting again.

Learn the one idea that explains Flexbox

Flexbox has a main axis and a cross axis. That's most of it.

flex-direction sets the main axis. By default it's row, so the main axis runs left to right. justify-content moves items along the main axis. align-items moves them along the cross axis.

.toolbar {
  display: flex;
  justify-content: space-between; /* along the row */
  align-items: center;            /* up and down */
}

The reason I kept mixing up justify-content and align-items is that I'd memorized them as "horizontal" and "vertical". That's only true for rows. Switch to flex-direction: column and they swap. Once I stopped thinking in left/right and started thinking in main/cross, the guessing mostly stopped.

Then learn what flex: 1 actually means

The second thing that confused me was sizing. flex: 1 is shorthand for three properties:

.item {
  flex-grow: 1;
  flex-shrink: 1;
  flex-basis: 0%;
}

flex-basis is the starting size. flex-grow says how much of the leftover space an item takes. flex-shrink says how much it gives up when space runs out. If you've ever had an item refuse to shrink below its text, the fix is usually min-width: 0, because flex items default to min-width: auto. That one line has saved me more time than anything else in this post.

Grid is for two directions at once

Here's the rule I use now, and it's simple enough to remember. Flexbox is for laying things out in one direction, a row or a column. Grid is for rows and columns together.

A nav bar, a row of buttons, a card's header with a title on the left and an icon on the right: Flexbox. A page layout with a sidebar, header and main area, or a gallery where cards should line up in both directions: Grid.

.gallery {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(200px, 1fr));
  gap: 1rem;
}

That one declaration gives you a responsive gallery with no media queries. I'd suggest learning fr, repeat(), minmax() and gap before anything else in Grid. Named grid areas are nice too, and they read almost like a picture of the layout:

.page {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 220px 1fr;
  grid-template-areas:
    "header header"
    "sidebar main";
}

You can skip subgrid, grid-auto-flow: dense and explicit line numbering until a real layout asks for them.

Practice on things you'd actually build

Games help. Flexbox Froggy and Grid Garden are free and take an evening each. They're good for the first pass, but I forgot most of what I learned from them within a few weeks because I never used it on anything real.

What worked better was rebuilding layouts from sites I use. Pick a page, open it in DevTools with the layout overlays turned on (both Chrome and Firefox show Flexbox and Grid overlays), and try to recreate one section from scratch without looking at their CSS. Then compare. Doing this with five or six sections taught me more than the games did.

Josh Comeau's interactive guides on Flexbox and Grid are also worth reading once you've struggled a bit. They make far more sense after you've hit the problems they explain.

The part nobody talks about: forgetting it

My real problem wasn't understanding. I'd watch a good video on minmax(), get it completely, and three weeks later be back to guessing because I hadn't touched a grid since. CSS layout is a thing you use in bursts, so it fades between projects.

So I started reviewing. I keep a short list of the ideas that tripped me up (main vs cross axis, min-width: 0, auto-fill vs auto-fit, when to reach for Grid) and look at it again after a day, then a few days, then a couple of weeks. That's spaced repetition, and it's boring, and it works.

I ended up building Recl partly because of this. You share a video, article, reel or podcast to it, it writes a summary of the key points, files it under a topic like "CSS", and brings it back for review on a spaced repetition schedule. If you'd rather not use an app, a plain notes file you reread on a calendar reminder gets you most of the way there. What matters is seeing it again before it's gone.

A one-week plan

If you want something concrete:

  1. Day one: Flexbox Froggy, then rebuild a nav bar with Flexbox.
  2. Day two: build a card with a header, body and footer using flex-direction: column, and make the footer stick to the bottom.
  3. Day three: Grid Garden, then make a responsive gallery with repeat(auto-fill, minmax(...)).
  4. Day four: build a sidebar layout with grid-template-areas.
  5. Day five: rebuild one section of a real site you like, with DevTools overlays on.
  6. Weekend: write down the three things that confused you most, and review them next week.

You'll still open DevTools and fiddle. Everyone does. But you'll know which property you're fiddling with and why it moves things the way it does.

I build Recl, an AI learning app that saves your videos, reels, podcasts and articles, summarizes them, sorts them into topics, and uses spaced repetition so you remember what you learned.

title: GHOSTLIGHT: Stadium of Echoes Cover
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

Football Remembers the Scores. We Remember the People.

"Where memories never die."

A football match lasts 90 minutes.

Sometimes 120.

But a memory can last a lifetime.

For some people, it's the roar of thousands of supporters. For others, it's the smell of wet grass, the glow of floodlights through the rain, an old ticket kept in a drawer, or the feeling of holding someone's hand while watching a match for the very first time.

Years pass. Stadiums are renovated or torn down. Tickets fade. Results become statistics in databases.

But the memories remain.

Football remembers the scores. GHOSTLIGHT remembers the people.

That’s the idea behind GHOSTLIGHT: Stadium of Echoes — a cinematic, interactive digital sanctuary where forgotten football memories come back to life through locally running open-weight AI.


Hero: The Forgotten Stadium under midnight floodlights.

The Idea: A Stadium Full of Memories

The theme of the Hacktoberfest 2026 Ghost in the Machine challenge inspired me to explore a different kind of digital ghost.

Not a ghost that scares people.

A ghost that preserves something worth remembering.

I wanted to build an experience that connects football heritage, personal storytelling, open-weight artificial intelligence, and digital preservation.

The result is an interactive night stadium.

At first, it is almost completely dark. Its stands are silent. Only a few distant floodlights cut through the midnight mist.

Then someone leaves a memory.

An old matchday photograph. A ticket stub. A scarf. A few sentences about a football match experienced decades ago.

The AI helps transform that fragment into a living digital exhibit.

A section of the grandstand illuminates.

And the memory finds its eternal seat.

How It Works

GHOSTLIGHT is designed around a three-step emotional loop:

$$\text{Leave an Artifact} \longrightarrow \text{Awaken a Memory} \longrightarrow \text{Explore its Echoes}$$

1. The Forgotten Stadium

The experience begins in an atmospheric football cathedral at night. The interface uses a midnight palette of near-black, deep navy, and warm luminous gold.

Volumetric floodlights, animated fog, drifting particles, and editorial typography create the feeling of entering a place suspended between the past and present.

The main invitation is simple:

SOME MEMORIES NEVER LEAVE.

Users can awaken a new memory or explore the existing archive.

2. Leave an Artifact

Users can awaken a memory by entering:

  • A story or personal recollection: A heartfelt paragraph of what they experienced.
  • An approximate year: e.g., 1968, 1982, or 1998.
  • A football club or team: The colors they cheered for.
  • A stadium, if known: The cathedral where it occurred.
  • An optional photograph or visual artifact: Uploaded via drag-and-drop.

The uploaded artifact becomes the centerpiece of the exhibit.

The system does not require users to know every historical detail. An incomplete memory is still deeply worth preserving.

3. The Ghost Awakens — Gemma Meets Ollama

This is where open-weight AI becomes the heartbeat of the experience.

GHOSTLIGHT uses Google Gemma 3 4B, running 100% locally through Ollama.

Instead of sending personal family stories to a remote commercial cloud, the client communicates with a local Express backend, which prompts the local model with strict archival guardrails.

The model transforms the submitted recollection into structured exhibit data:

  • Title: An uppercase poetic exhibit name.
  • Approximate year: Historical era anchoring.
  • Theme and emotional character: e.g., "Ancestral Reverence", "First Floodlight Glow".
  • Narrative: An evocative, respectful story capturing the sensory atmosphere.
  • Closing inscription: A stone-carved epitaph for the grandstand plaque.
  • Tags: Connecting historical motifs.
  • Grounded recollections: Confirmed facts stated by the user.
  • Unknown or missing details: Respectfully cataloged as "Lost to the stadium winds".

The Ethical AI Principle: Enrich, Never Rewrite History

The system strictly distinguishes information explicitly provided by the user from details that remain unknown.

It never invents match results, fictional player lineups, attendance figures, or synthetic deceased voices simply to make a story sound complete.

A missing scoreline is not a bug to fix. It is part of what makes a human memory authentic.

4. The Memory Reveal

Once the memory has been processed during the floodlight power-up séance, the stadium begins to awaken:

  • A newly allocated seat in the grandstand lights up.
  • The exhibit title emerges in gold typography alongside the original uploaded artifact.
  • Two distinct columns tell the story:
    • Grounded Recollections: Details verified by the person who submitted the memory.
    • Lost to the Winds: Information that remains forgotten in time.

The closing inscription might read:

“Some matches never end.”

5. A Stadium That Speaks

I wanted the experience to engage the ears as deeply as the eyes.

GHOSTLIGHT includes two narration styles:

  • Tannoy: An authentic stadium announcer voice, preceded by a synthesized two-tone stadium bell chime (D5 587Hz -> A4 440Hz).
  • Whisper: A quieter, intimate museum-style narration.

The browser's native SpeechSynthesis API provides the voice. Meanwhile, a procedural Web Audio API soundscape adds a subtle stadium night hum, while the Rain Derby weather mode introduces synthesized rainfall and a stormy visual atmosphere.

Listening to a memory feels like attending a quiet private ceremony under the lights.

6. The Vintage Matchday Ticket


Vintage Matchday Ticket: A physical-digital keepsake generated dynamically on HTML5 Canvas.

One of the most distinctive details is the Vintage Matchday Ticket generator.

Every memory can become a high-resolution (1200x520px) digital keepsake:

  • Authentic perforated edges with cutout notches.
  • Archival exhibition title.
  • Stand, sector, and seat coordinates.
  • Period-inspired ink stamps (PRESS ARCHIVE • AUTHENTICATED or ALL HALLOWS' SPECIAL).
  • Procedural retro turnstile barcodes and serial numbers.

Users can toggle between the Museum Exhibit Plaque and the Vintage Matchday Ticket, exporting either as a print-ready PNG image. It turns fleeting digital text into a tangible souvenir worth keeping.

7. The Living Stadium and Echo Threads


Echo Threads: Luminous Bézier arcs connecting strangers through shared history.

The stadium is more than a backdrop — it is a living entity.

Every saved memory occupies an illuminated coordinate in the stands:

  • North Stand: Family devotions and childhood memories.
  • South Stand (Kop): Passionate chanting and terrace anthems.
  • West Grandstand: Press boxes and tactical heritage.
  • East Terrace: Historic standing terraces in the rain.

The Echo Threads feature takes this further: it automatically calculates and draws glowing Bézier curves between memories that share:

  • The same decade (e.g., the 1970s or 1990s).
  • The same football club.
  • A common emotional resonance.

Someone who remembers a rainy cup match in 1989 is visually connected to someone else who cheered for the same club in that era. The stadium becomes an illuminated web of collective human belonging.

8. A Museum That Belongs to Its Owner

Digital preservation should never mean handing ownership of personal memories over to an ad-driven cloud platform.

GHOSTLIGHT follows an uncompromising local-first approach:

  • All memories and high-res artifact images are stored directly in your browser's IndexedDB.
  • The archive provides full-text search, decade filters, card downloads, and JSON metadata exports.
  • The Time Capsule: Users can export their entire stadium collection into a self-contained .ghostlight.json file, and import it onto any other computer or browser.

The museum belongs entirely to the person who created it.

Technology Behind the Experience

Component Technology
Frontend React 19, TypeScript, Vite 8
Styling Tailwind CSS v4 (with zero-CLS theme variables)
Animation Framer Motion (spatial canvas transitions)
Backend Proxy Node.js, Express 5
AI Model Google Gemma 3 4B (Instruct)
Local Runtime Ollama
Persistence IndexedDB via idb
Narration Native Browser SpeechSynthesis
Acoustic Soundscape Web Audio API (realtime Tannoy chime + weather synthesis)
Graphics & Artifacts HTML5 Canvas 2D image renderer

Architectural Flow: 

  USER
    │
    ▼
  REACT 19 + VITE CLIENT
    │
    ├───► INDEXEDDB (Local Private Storage)
    │
    ▼
  EXPRESS 5 API (Port 3001)
    │
    ▼
  LOCAL OLLAMA ENGINE (Port 11434)
    │
    ▼
  GOOGLE GEMMA 3 4B (Strict JSON Mode)
    │
    ▼
  STRUCTURED MEMORY EXHIBIT
    │
    ▼
  MEMORY REVEAL (Seat Coordinates + Tannoy Audio + Vintage Ticket PNG)

The core AI workflow does not require a cloud LLM subscription or an API key. Everything runs on the hardware right in front of you.

Why Open Innovation Matters

Running an open-weight model locally is not merely an engineering preference for GHOSTLIGHT. It is a core product principle.

Personal photographs, deceased relatives' tickets, and intimate family memories are sacred. They deserve far better protection than being sent to third-party cloud servers for training or surveillance.

Using Gemma 3 through Ollama gives GHOSTLIGHT five vital guarantees:

  1. Privacy & Control: Memory text is processed on the user's machine without ever touching an external API.
  2. Independence: The application will work twenty years from now, even if commercial AI APIs vanish or change their pricing models.
  3. Accessibility: Anyone with consumer hardware can run the model locally.
  4. Ownership: The archive and its .ghostlight.json Time Capsule remain strictly under the user's control.
  5. Reproducibility: Any developer can clone the repository, pull gemma3:4b, and immediately experience the full installation.

What I Learned

One of the biggest lessons from this project is that AI applications do not always need to revolve around a conversational chatbot.

Sometimes the most profound interface for an AI system is a spatial experience.

Gemma does not need to act like a sports statistician or guess match scores. Its role is far more human: helping people structure raw emotions, giving them an archival form, and preserving the sensory essence of a moment.

The small details are what bring the soul to life:

  • The two-tone Tannoy chime before a story is spoken.
  • The perforated tear-off line on a vintage matchday ticket.
  • A single golden seat igniting in a darkened grandstand.
  • A glowing thread connecting two strangers across fifty years of football history.

These details transform GHOSTLIGHT from another AI demo into an authentic place of reverence.

What's Next?

GHOSTLIGHT began with football, but the underlying philosophy can expand into many cultural realms:

  • Supporter Club Heritage Archives: Preserving historic community memory before legendary stadiums are renovated.
  • Family Legacy Museums: Honoring passed generations and their shared passions.
  • Historical Places & Vanished Landmarks: Reviving theaters, concert halls, and community centers.

The long-term ambition is to give communities the tools to preserve the human stories that official archives overlook.

Try It Yourself

  • Project: GHOSTLIGHT: Stadium of Echoes
  • Source Code: []
  • Demo Video: []
  • Cover Image: Included in public/cover.png

Running Locally:

  1. Install Ollama and download the model: 
ollama serve
ollama pull gemma3:4b
  1. Clone and start the application: 
git clone https://github.com/budulay/ghostlight-stadium-of-echoes.git
cd ghostlight-stadium-of-echoes
npm install
npm run dev
  1. Open in your browser: 
http://localhost:5173

The sample memory can also be explored instantly without live AI inference. For real-time memory analysis, ensure Ollama is running with gemma3:4b.

The Final Whistle

I started with a simple question:

What if we could preserve the feeling of a football match, not just its score?

A stadium is far more than concrete, grass, and plastic seats.

It is a place where generations meet. Where friendships begin. Where families forge traditions. Where complete strangers hug in the pouring rain when a goal crosses the line in the 93rd minute.

And perhaps somewhere, in an old drawer, there is still a faded ticket from a match that nobody else remembers.

That ticket deserves a place.

That story deserves a light.

Football remembers the scores.

GHOSTLIGHT remembers the people.

The final whistle is not the end of a memory.

🏟️ GHOSTLIGHT: Stadium of Echoes — Where memories never die.

title: Chat SDK now supports XChat
description:
You can now build bots that hold end-to-end encrypted 1:1 and group conversations on XChat with the new XChat adapter for Chat SDK.

The adapter handles all encryption, key management, and signature verification automatically. Bots can also message users first, as long as the user has encrypted chat set up and follows the bot.

XChat has no markdown rendering, so the adapter falls back automatically: URLs and @mentions render as tappable links, tables as ASCII code blocks, and cards as text with a link preview. Streaming works through message edits.

Read the XChat adapter documentation to get started.

title: What if the history of a codebase could help explain the code nobody wants to touch?
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

NecroGit: A Little Séance for Legacy Code

Every codebase has a past.

Sometimes that past is a beautifully maintained changelog. Sometimes it is a function named do_not_delete_final2(), three deprecated imports, and a Git history that only the person who wrote it really understood.

Then that person leaves.

The code stays.

For Week 4's Ghost in the Machine challenge, I built NecroGit: a command-line tool that treats legacy-code maintenance like a bit of software archaeology. It looks for signs of bitrot, examines Git history for clues about how a project evolved, and uses an open-weight language model to help explain unfamiliar code and propose repairs.

The goal isn't to pretend a model can bring a developer back from the dead. It's to make the traces they left behind more useful to the next person who has to maintain the project.

What I Built

NecroGit is a Python CLI for developers inheriting repositories they didn't write.

It brings a few kinds of investigation into one workflow:

  • Inspect: scan Python files for known deprecated APIs and suspicious legacy patterns.
  • Summon: examine Git commits and author activity for historical context.
  • Explain: ask a language model to explain an unfamiliar function using the source and available repository context.
  • Patch: generate a proposed diff that a developer can review before applying.
  • Memory: keep a small repository dossier so useful context can carry between sessions.

The part I care about most is the connection between these steps. Finding a deprecated import is useful. Understanding why the surrounding code exists is better. Getting a proposed change that you can inspect, test, and reject if necessary is better still.

NecroGit is meant to assist the maintainer, not replace their judgment. Git history can offer clues about a previous developer's habits; it cannot tell us with certainty what that person intended. Likewise, an AI-generated patch is a proposal, not proof that the fix is correct.

Demo

Repository: github.com/avrojitduttaj/necrogit

The quickest way to see the workflow is to install the project in a Python environment, open a repository in your terminal, and try the inspection command:

necrogit inspect .

Then explore the other commands with:

necrogit --help
necrogit summon .
necrogit memory

The exact arguments for explain and patch depend on the installed CLI version; check each command's --help before running it.

Live demo / walkthrough: [Add a verified demo URL or video here]

I don't want to pass off a mockup as a working demo, so this post links to the source repository. If I add a hosted walkthrough, I'll put the verified URL here.

Code

The source is available here:

Explore NecroGit on GitHub

Live Deployment: NecroGit — The Repository Medium

A few of the implementation choices:

  • Python's ast module provides a structured way to inspect source code without executing it.
  • GitPython reads repository history and commit metadata.
  • Click provides the command-line interface, with Rich for readable terminal output.
  • HTTPX connects the engine to an OpenAI-compatible local model endpoint.
  • Repository dossiers can be stored locally, with optional Backboard integration in the project.

The intent is to keep the first step—static inspection—useful even when an AI model isn't available. The AI-assisted commands should fail clearly when inference isn't configured, rather than pretending they succeeded.

How I Built It

I built NecroGit around a simple question: what if Git history were more than a list of commits?

The scanner handles the deterministic part. It parses Python syntax and checks for patterns the tool knows about. The Git-history component gathers evidence such as authorship, commit dates, and commit messages. The AI engine can then use the available code and context to generate an explanation or a proposed diff.

For the open-model path, NecroGit is designed to work with Gemma 2 through Ollama, using a local OpenAI-compatible endpoint. That makes it possible to experiment with the model on your own machine rather than making a hosted, closed API the only way to run the project.

This separation matters:

  1. Rules find known patterns. They are predictable, testable, and don't need a model.
  2. Git history supplies evidence. It gives context, but it isn't a source of certainty about intent.
  3. The model helps interpret and draft. It can explain code and suggest changes, but its output still needs review and tests.

During development, I also added tests for deprecated-import detection, Git and non-Git directories, prompt construction, connection failures, local memory persistence, and CLI behavior. Those tests have been useful for catching mismatches between the intended user experience and what the command actually does.

One lesson from building a CLI is that a feature isn't finished just because the Python function works. Packaging, command registration, Windows paths, model endpoints, and readable error messages are all part of the product. I'm still tightening those edges, and I want to be honest about that rather than call the tool production-ready before it earns the label.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

For a tool that reads source code, where inference happens is part of the design.

A developer may be working with a private repository, a client's code, or an abandoned internal service. Sending that code to an external API should never be an invisible default. A local model gives the developer a path to keep inference on their own machine, subject to how they've configured the rest of their environment.

Open-weight models also make the system more replaceable. Developers can experiment with different models and local runtimes instead of tying the whole experience to one provider's API, pricing, or product decisions.

And the non-AI parts remain ordinary, inspectable software. The scanner's rules can be read and tested. The Git-history analysis can be audited. A proposed patch is visible as a diff.

That doesn't mean every setup is automatically offline or private: optional integrations and telemetry need to be configured and disclosed carefully. But open tooling gives developers more control over those trade-offs—and for a maintenance tool that may touch sensitive code, that control is important.

My Agent Session

[https://dev.to/agent_sessions/finding-the-necrogit-devrelay-session-link-xmpym5]

This section is optional. I will only link a real saved session; I won't invent an embed or session URL.

The Spirit of It

There's something eerie about opening a repository and finding a whole history of decisions with nobody left to explain them.

A commit message says “temporary workaround.” The workaround is still there six years later. A function has a strange name because it once fixed a production incident. A dependency is obsolete, but nobody remembers which behavior relied on it.

The ghost isn't really the old developer. It's the missing context.

NecroGit is my attempt to make that context a little easier to recover—from the code, from the commit history, and from the tools we can run ourselves. Not to resurrect the past exactly as it was, but to help the next maintainer move forward without blindly deleting it.

🏆 Prize Categories I'm Targeting

  • [ ] Overall Challenge Winner — $250

    NecroGit aims to make legacy-code maintenance easier by combining Git-history archaeology, AI-assisted code explanations, and safer patch proposals.

  • [ ] Best Use of Gemma — $200

    Gemma 2 powers NecroGit's local AI inference workflow, helping explain historical design decisions and draft modernization patches while keeping source code on the developer's machine.

  • [ ] Best Use of Backboard — $100

    NecroGit implements persistent repository dossiers, with local JSON storage and an optional Backboard synchronization path for retaining maintainer context across sessions.

  • [ ] Best Use of Sentry Agent Tracing — $100

    NecroGit includes instrumentation for tracing AI inference and memory operations, with breadcrumbs and structured context to help diagnose the resurrection workflow.

Deployment

NecroGit's web workbench is deployed on Render to make the project website accessible online. Render is used as a hosting and deployment platform, not as an AI integration.

The core NecroGit CLI remains a local developer tool, while the hosted website serves as the public-facing project experience.

Built by @avrojitduttaj.

If you've inherited a codebase that feels haunted, I'd love to know: what's the strangest piece of legacy code you've had to explain?

title: Would You Rather Have a Dumb Component or a Smart Component?
description:
A Component Doesn't Have to Be Dumb to Be Reusable

There's a long-running idea in frontend architecture:

Keep components dumb.

Let them receive data, render the UI, and leave everything else to something higher up the tree.

It sounds clean. And often, it is.

But there's a trade-off we don't always consider:

Making a component simpler can make the surrounding architecture more complicated.

Let's look at both approaches.

🔴 The Problem

Imagine a component that displays a list of users.

It needs to fetch the data, filter the results, and render them.

One approach is to put everything inside UserList.

function UserList() {
  const [users, setUsers] = useState<User[]>([]);
  const [query, setQuery] = useState("");

  useEffect(() => {
    getUsers().then(setUsers);
  }, []);

  const filteredUsers = useMemo(
    () => users.filter((user) => user.name.includes(query)),
    [users, query],
  );

  return (
    <section>
      <input value={query} onChange={(event) => setQuery(event.target.value)} />

      {filteredUsers.map((user) => (
        <div key={user.id}>{user.name}</div>
      ))}
    </section>
  );
}

This is a smart component.

It knows where its data comes from, manages its own state, handles filtering, and decides how everything is displayed.

Using it is simple:

<UserList />

But what happens when another part of the application already has the users?

Or when the same UI needs to display data from a different source?

Now the component's built-in behavior becomes a limitation.

🟢 The Other Extreme

We could separate those responsibilities.

The container handles the data. The presentational component handles the UI.

function UserListContainer() {
  const [users, setUsers] = useState<User[]>([]);

  useEffect(() => {
    getUsers().then(setUsers);
  }, []);

  return <UserList users={users} />;
}

function UserList({ users }: { users: User[] }) {
  return (
    <section>
      {users.map((user) => (
        <div key={user.id}>{user.name}</div>
      ))}
    </section>
  );
}

Now UserList doesn't care where the data comes from.

It can render users fetched by a parent, loaded from a cache, or passed in by a test.

That's a real benefit.

But splitting components isn't free.

The container needs to pass data down. Additional behavior may require additional props. And if the presentation component is only ever used in one place, the extra layer might not make the code any easier to understand.

We haven't necessarily removed complexity. We've moved it.

🔵 Reusability Has a Cost

A dumb component is often easier to reuse because it depends on fewer things.

It doesn't need to know about an API, a router, a global store, or a particular data-fetching library.

But reusability isn't the only thing that matters.

Sometimes, keeping behavior close to the UI makes a component easier to understand.

Consider a search box.

If its value, filtering logic, and displayed results always belong together, extracting every small piece into separate components and hooks can make a simple feature harder to follow.

On the other hand, if multiple screens need the same filtering behavior or visual list, separating those responsibilities may be worthwhile.

The useful boundary isn't necessarily between smart and dumb components.

It's between responsibilities that belong together and responsibilities that benefit from being independent.

🟣 So Where Should the Logic Live?

There isn't one rule that works for every component.

A few questions can help:

  • Does the component need to work with different data sources? Separating data access from presentation may help.
  • Does the behavior only make sense for this component? Keeping it local may make the code clearer.
  • Is the component coordinating several unrelated concerns? That may be a sign it has too many responsibilities.
  • Are you extracting something just to make a component smaller? Smaller doesn't automatically mean simpler.

You can also mix the approaches.

A component can own its local interaction state while receiving data from a parent. It can use a shared hook for behavior without becoming purely presentational.

These aren't mutually exclusive architectures.

🟠 What About Consistency Across a Codebase?

So far, we've looked at individual components.

But components don't always exist in isolation. They're part of a larger codebase, often maintained by multiple developers.

Imagine a team decides that components should follow a consistent architecture:

  • Components don't fetch data directly.
  • Shared state is accessed through established abstractions.
  • Business logic lives in hooks, services, or other dedicated modules.
  • Components receive the data they need through props.

There are good reasons to do this.

Developers know where to look for things. Responsibilities are predictable. Moving between different parts of the application feels familiar.

But there's a trade-off.

Some components might genuinely be simpler if they handled their own behavior.

Forcing them into the same structure could mean creating unnecessary hooks, adding extra layers, or splitting closely related logic across several files.

You gain consistency, but potentially lose simplicity.

And that's not necessarily a bad decision.

In a large team, predictable code can be more valuable than making every individual component follow its locally simplest implementation.

The important distinction is between consistent principles and identical implementations.

A codebase can have clear architectural rules without forcing every component to have exactly the same structure.

After all, you're maintaining a codebase, not just individual components.

⚡ The Takeaway

Smart and dumb components aren't competing goals.

A dumb component can be wonderfully reusable, but separating every bit of behavior can create unnecessary indirection.

A smart component can be convenient and cohesive, but accumulating unrelated responsibilities can make it difficult to change.

Neither approach is inherently better.

Don't optimize for dumb components. Don't optimize for smart components.

Optimize for clear responsibilities.

title: rustgrade: a Rust scanner for the habits coding agents leave behind
description:
For a few months I've been letting coding agents write a lot of my Rust. The code compiles, the tests pass, and then I read it and find the same things over and over: .unwrap() in library code, a std Mutex held across an .await, .clone() sprinkled around until the borrow checker stops complaining.

None of that is a compile error, so the agent has no reason to stop. I wanted something that would make it stop. That turned into rustgrade.

(Full disclosure: in this demo I told the agent to use unwrap so the hook would have something to catch. When I ran it without that instruction, it just wrote the Result itself.)

What it looks for

At its core it's a scanner built on syn. No LLM, no network calls, and it doesn't need to build your crate. Right now it has 8 rules: unwrap/expect outside tests, locks held across .await, unsafe without a // SAFETY: comment, unbounded channels, anyhow in public library APIs, clones and allocations inside loops, and &String / &Vec<T> style parameters.

Here are the three I see agents get wrong most.

Holding a lock across an await:

// Flagged
async fn bump(state: &std::sync::Mutex<Counter>, db: &Db) {
    let mut c = state.lock().unwrap();
    c.n += 1;
    db.save(c.n).await; // guard is still alive here
}

// Better
async fn bump(state: &std::sync::Mutex<Counter>, db: &Db) {
    let n = {
        let mut c = state.lock().unwrap();
        c.n += 1;
        c.n
    }; // guard dropped before the await
    db.save(n).await;
}

The first version makes the future !Send, and it can deadlock if another task on the same thread goes for the lock. It also compiles fine in a lot of setups, which is exactly why it slips through.

Unwrap in a library:

// Flagged
pub fn parse_port(s: &str) -> u16 {
    s.parse().unwrap()
}

// Better
pub fn parse_port(s: &str) -> Result<u16, std::num::ParseIntError> {
    s.parse()
}

Asking for &String when you mean &str:

// Flagged
pub fn greet(name: &String) -> String {
    format!("hello, {name}")
}

// Better
pub fn greet(name: &str) -> String {
    format!("hello, {name}")
}

If you want the reasoning behind any rule, rustgrade rules --explain <rule-id> prints a before/after and what the rule can't see.

The catch with reading only syntax

Skipping type information is what makes it fast, but it also means it guesses. clone-in-loop has no idea whether you're cloning an Arc (cheap) or a big Vec (not cheap), and it doesn't look inside macros. When it's wrong, you silence it inline, and you have to say why:

// rustgrade: allow(unbounded-channel) shutdown signal, at most one message per worker
let (stop_tx, stop_rx) = std::sync::mpsc::channel::<()>();

Those reasons stay in the JSON output, so they can be reviewed in CI instead of disappearing.

Yes, clippy already has lints for some of this (unwrap_used, await_holding_lock, undocumented_unsafe_blocks, ptr_arg, borrowed_box), and rustgrade audit runs clippy as well. The reason the scanner exists is timing. Clippy needs a build. The scanner took about 20 ms on a 445-line file on my machine, which is fast enough to run on every single edit an agent makes.

I also wanted to know how noisy it is on code written by people, so I ran it on 15 well-known crates (tokio, serde, regex, syn and others). They land between A and C, and every finding is in the repo if you want to argue with them.

Using it

You can use it on its own: rustgrade scan and rustgrade audit work in a terminal or in CI, with --fail-on thresholds and SARIF output for GitHub code scanning.

For agents, it installs as a skill plus a few commands in Claude Code, Cursor, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, Copilot and Windsurf. /audit gives a crate a grade from A to F using the scanner, clippy and your tests. /harden throws hostile input at your code and only fixes what a failing test proves is broken.

In Claude Code there's also a hook that scans every edit and hands the findings straight back to the agent.

Did it actually help?

I didn't want to just assume it did, so I measured it. 27 Claude Code runs with Sonnet, three tasks, 9 runs per setup. I counted unwrap/expect in library code with cargo clippy --lib, so test code doesn't count.

  • No rustgrade: 5 left over
  • A short rustgrade section in CLAUDE.md: 0
  • Just the hook, no section: 0

Cost per run barely moved: $0.23, $0.21 and $0.22.

To be honest about it, a plain instruction in CLAUDE.md did just as well as the hook here. The difference is that the instruction only works if the agent follows it, while the hook runs no matter what. In the hook runs the agent never loaded the skill or ran the scanner on its own, so those zeros came from the hook. Whether that matters more in long sessions, or for the other seven rules, is the next thing I want to measure.

It's a small sample, so I'm treating it as a first signal, not a conclusion. One thing that did surprise me: /harden found real bugs, including deadlocks, in thread pools the agent wrote during these evals. Those pools had passed their hidden tests. I reproduced the bugs separately to make sure they were real. Everything is in the repo, including the runs where it found nothing.

I built it with help from Claude Code.

Try it 

cargo binstall rustgrade
rustgrade scan

It's MIT-licensed and I'd love contributions: new rules, fixes for false positives, support for other agents. And since the rules are heuristics, the most useful thing you can send me is a false positive from a real crate, or a rule you think is just wrong.

Repo, numbers and demo: https://github.com/angeldevmobile/rustgrade

title: Shelf-Life Is Versioned Config, Expiry Is a Derived Field: Modelling Shelf-Life Studies, Lot Expiry and FEFO in a Food ERP
description:
By Isaac Muthui, CEO, Tamalaki Business Network Ltd. Originally published at factoraerp.com.

In most food ERPs, an expiry date is a column on a lot. Someone types it at packing, or the system adds a fixed number of days to the production date, and that's the end of it. But the number of days is not a constant. It is the output of a shelf-life study, it is only valid for a particular recipe, pack and storage condition, and it should change when any of those change. If the data model can't express that, the date printed on the pack quietly drifts away from the evidence behind it.

This post walks through how we think about modelling shelf-life and expiry in an ERP for food and agro manufacturers in East Africa. The operational checklist behind it is in the original article.

What the domain rules say

The requirements read like a spec:

  • Kenya's Food Hygiene Regulations (Cap. 254), regulation 14: each container marked "to identify the producing factory and the lot", and specified products carrying a date marking. Source
  • Codex CODEX STAN 1-1985, 4.7: day and month for products lasting up to three months, month and year beyond that, and storage conditions on the label "if the validity of the date depends thereon". Source
  • Codex CXC 1-1969, 13.4: records retained "for a period that exceeds the shelf-life of the product". Source
  • FSAI Guidance Note 18 (an Irish benchmark, not Kenyan law): set shelf-life before launch, redo it on "modification or reformulation", test at least three replicates from three batches per interval where no plan is specified, apply and document a margin of safety, and verify periodically. Source

Translated into engineering terms: shelf-life is versioned configuration with provenance, expiry is a derived field on a lot, and changes to recipe or packaging are invalidation events.

Shelf-life belongs to a product version, not a product 

ShelfLifeSpec (id, item_id, recipe_version_id, pack_spec_id, storage_condition,
               date_type, days, margin_days, study_id, approved_by, valid_from, valid_to)
               date_type IN ('use_by','best_before')
ShelfLifeStudy (id, item_id, recipe_version_id, design_json, lab_id, decision_note, closed_at)

The spec points at the recipe version and the pack specification it was proven for, and at the study that justifies it. days is what goes on the label; margin_days is how much was taken off the study result and why lives in decision_note. When either the recipe or the pack spec gets a new version, the old spec doesn't silently carry over. It needs a review.

Expiry is derived at the moment the lot is made 

expiry_date = production_date(lot, factory_timezone) + spec.days

Two details matter. First, compute it from the production date in the factory's time zone, not the server's, or a lot packed at 1 a.m. in Nairobi gets the wrong date. Second, store the derived date and the spec id on the lot, so that a later change to the spec doesn't rewrite history on lots already in the market.

In FactoraERP today, stock items have a trackExpiry flag and a shelfLifeDays value, and finished-goods lots get an expiry date calculated from their production date in the factory's time zone.

Invalidation: changes that should trigger a review

FSAI lists the triggers in plain language: no evidence for an existing date, and modification or reformulation of the food or its production. That's an event rule:

on RecipeVersionPublished(item_id)  -> flag ShelfLifeSpec(item_id) as 'review_required'
on PackSpecChanged(item_id)          -> flag ...
on SupplierApproved(key_ingredient)  -> flag ...
on ComplaintLogged(type='spoilage', lot.expiry_date > complaint_date) -> attach to ShelfLifeSpec as evidence

The last rule is the one most systems miss. A spoilage complaint before the printed date is shelf-life evidence, and it should land on the spec, not only in the complaint log.

FEFO is where the date earns its keep

An expiry date nobody uses for stock rotation is just ink. Dispatch should pick first-expired, first-out, and any exception should be a recorded decision:

-- lots skipped in a dispatch that expire earlier than the lot picked
SELECT l.lot_code, l.expiry_date
FROM lot l
WHERE l.item_id = :item_id
  AND l.status = 'sellable'
  AND l.qty_available > 0
  AND l.expiry_date < :picked_lot_expiry;

In FactoraERP, dispatching out of first-expiry order needs an operations manager or admin and a written reason, and the override is stored on the sale with who and when.

Study results are measurements, not a PDF

A durability study is a grid: batch × replicate × interval × test. FSAI recommends reading it at a high percentile (90th or 95th) rather than the mean, which needs at least three replicates per time point. That's a query, not an opinion:

SELECT interval_day, test,
       percentile_cont(0.95) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY value) AS p95,
       count(*) AS n
FROM shelf_life_result
WHERE study_id = :study_id
GROUP BY interval_day, test
HAVING count(*) >= 3
ORDER BY interval_day;

Takeaways

  • Version shelf-life by recipe, pack spec and storage condition, and link it to the study that proves it.
  • Derive expiry at lot creation in the factory's time zone, and store the spec id with it.
  • Treat recipe, packaging and supplier changes as invalidation events.
  • Route early spoilage complaints to the shelf-life spec as evidence.
  • Enforce FEFO and record every override with who, when and why.

The full 10-step operational checklist, with references to Kenya's food hygiene regulations, Codex CXS 1, CXC 1 and CXG 61 and FSAI Guidance Note 18, is on the FactoraERP blog.

title: Controlled input work depends on state placement: compare 10, 100, and 500 fields
description:
Field count alone does not determine whether a form should use controlled or uncontrolled inputs. Even with controlled inputs, placing state in each field meant editing one field invoked only one input component.

The experiment compared parent-owned values, field-local state, and DOM-owned values across forms with 10, 100, and 500 fields. Reducing repeated component work requires looking at state placement as well as whether inputs are controlled.

Count component calls for the same input operation

These are the three field components. trace is an experiment counter, not application state.

function ControlledField({ index, value, onChange }) {
  trace.fieldRenders++;
  return <input name={`field-${index}`} value={value} onChange={onChange} />;
}
function LocalField({ index }) {
  trace.fieldRenders++;
  const [value, setValue] = useState(initialValue(index));
  return <input name={`field-${index}`} value={value} onChange={event => {
    trace.fieldChanges++;
    setValue(event.target.value);
  }} />;
}
function UncontrolledField({ index }) {
  trace.fieldRenders++;
  return <input name={`field-${index}`} defaultValue={initialValue(index)} />;
}

The parent-owned version keeps a values array in state, replaces the changed position, and passes values to every input. The local version updates state inside LocalField. The uncontrolled version supplies an initial defaultValue and reads values through FormData on submission.

Field count and order stay fixed within each condition. The fixture uses position keys and does not delete, insert, or reorder fields.

Each input has a distinct name. A browser fill operation replaced the first field's field-0 value with edited. This was not a character-by-character typing test. Both controlled versions recorded one onChange call for that operation.

The measurement is the additional component-function calls caused by the edit, excluding initial rendering.

State placement Fields Additional parent-form calls Additional input-component calls
Parent-owned 10 1 10
Parent-owned 100 1 100
Parent-owned 500 1 500
Field-local state 10 0 1
Field-local state 100 0 1
Field-local state 500 0 1
DOM-owned 10 0 0
DOM-owned 100 0 0
DOM-owned 500 0 0

The production build used no React Compiler, memo, or Strict Mode. The table therefore compares the same unoptimized structure. Zero input-component calls does not mean the browser performs no input or painting work. Execution time, FPS, and memory use were not measured.

The React input reference describes updating a controlled value in onChange and moving state to the part of the tree that needs it. The observed results also show that controlled inputs do not inherently require the entire parent to rerun.

Verify collected values too

All 9 conditions produced as many FormData entries as there were fields, with edited as the first value after editing. This did not aggregate all field-local values into parent React state simultaneously. It collected values already reflected in the DOM using the submission method chosen for this experiment.

Immediate previews of all fields or validation across fields require an additional decision about where values are read. This fixture contains independent text inputs only. It excludes form libraries, IME composition, and asynchronous validation.

The same reset button produced different outcomes

After editing, pressing a type="reset" button left edited in both controlled versions. The uncontrolled version returned to field-0.

Approach After HTML reset Explicit reset method used in the experiment
Parent state edited Set state to an array of initial values
Field-local state edited Change the form key to remount it
Uncontrolled field-0 Call form.reset()

Changing the key in the field-local version tests whether remounting restores initial values. Remounting also recreates component state below that point. It should not be applied unchanged when a reset must preserve focus or other state.

After an explicit reset, all three approaches showed field-0 in the first field. Treat native reset and React state initialization as separate operations, then verify reset behavior for the chosen value ownership. The form reference also covers event-based submission and reading values with FormData.

The tests ran on September 11, 2026, with React and React DOM 19.3.0, Node.js 24.15.0, esbuild 0.28.2, macOS arm64, and Headless Chrome 152. The complete form fixture and results for the 9 conditions are available. These results do not establish that 500 fields always require uncontrolled inputs. Choose with both the values React needs during editing and the submission/reset behavior in view.

title: Introducing Vercel CI
description:
Coding agents are opening more pull requests than ever, and each one waits on CI before anyone can review or merge it. Most CI systems run the entire workflow on every push, even a one-line change. The more your agents push, the more time you spend waiting on CI.

Today, we're announcing Vercel CI in Beta. It runs only the tasks affected by your code change, and spins up only the compute those checks need, the same way Fluid compute scales with your traffic.

At Vercel, our CI now keeps up with our coding agents. Time from git push to "CI passed" is 2-6x faster than it was before.

How it works

Vercel CI uses Turborepo to understand your tasks and which ones depend on each other. It reads turbo.json, so if you're already using Turborepo, there's no separate CI config to write.

If you're not on Turborepo yet, add turbo.json and the turbo package. It works in single-package repos too.

Then tag the tasks you want Vercel CI to run.

"tags": ["ci"] is all you need to get started. No workflow YAML to maintain, no drift between your CI config and turbo.json, and Remote Cache is on by default.

When you or your agent push code, Vercel CI determines which tasks need to run based on the change. Tasks whose inputs haven't changed come from cache. The remaining tasks each run on their own machine, powered by Hive, Vercel's compute layer, and start as soon as their dependencies finish.

Vercel CI gives each task the compute it needs and nothing more.

Running your CI on Vercel

To get started, follow the documentation or prompt your agent from your repo:

Once set up, you or your agent can watch and inspect CI through the Vercel dashboard, Vercel CLI, or Vercel MCP. When something fails, go straight to the failing task, see what's blocked behind it, and open its logs, or search across recent runs to see whether a test has been flaky all week.

Vercel CI posts a check to your pull request on GitHub, so your existing branch protection rules can block merges on failure, the same way they do today.

Closing the loop

Vercel CI has already completed nearly 8 million tasks across our own repositories and the private beta, and we're just getting started. We're working to keep shrinking the time between writing code and running it in production.

As we work toward general availability, we plan to add:

  • Advanced observability

  • A vc ci CLI command for distributed execution before pushing code

  • More granular test selection

Vercel CI is available in Beta today on all plans. Read the docs and try it on your repository.

title: Looking for affordable image/video moderation API – pain points
description:
I've been evaluating content moderation APIs for a new project, and finding the right balance between cost, reliability, and data security is harder than expected.

Major cloud providers like AWS Rekognition and Google Cloud offer solid solutions, but their pricing can get steep fast, especially when processing video at scale. Smaller, specialized APIs like Sightengine and Clearview have more granular pricing, but I haven't used them extensively.

My priorities are straightforward: affordable per-image or per-video costs, reliable detection for adult content and violence, and clear data handling guarantees (no using my data for training). For indie projects, all three matter equally.

I'm leaning toward testing a couple niche providers that seem more indie-friendly, but I'd rather hear from anyone who's actually deployed these in production. What are you using, and have you run into hidden costs or reliability issues at higher volumes?

Happy to share findings once I've tested a few options.
