title: Pre-ticked boxes are not consent: notification prompts default to off
description:
Notification permissions are usually asked for badly. The app appears for the first time, and before the user has read a single message it shows the operating system's permission dialog. If they say no, the prompt is gone for good and the app quietly decides that notifications are not for this person. If they say yes, the app now has a blank cheque for message alerts, calls, reminder emails, and whatever marketing is invented next.

We shipped the opposite last week in Folcadi, a language-exchange messenger with a Flutter client. After login, once, the app shows its own preference sheet with four channels. Every switch starts off. Nothing is pre-ticked, nothing is bundled, and "Save" with everything off is a complete, accepted answer.

This post is about why the defaults are the whole product decision, and about the code shapes that follow from taking consent seriously: tri-state columns, a fail-open call gate, and an unsubscribe link that works without logging in.

The prompt we replaced

The old app had three problems, and they are the usual three.

The first was timing. The startup path requested the OS notification permission for every user, whether or not they had ever wanted a notification. On Android 13 and later that dialog is a one-shot resource: a reflexive "don't allow" during launch is hard to undo, and a lot of users never find the settings page to reverse it.

The second was bundling. One "notifications" concept covered message alerts, incoming-call ringing, a reminder email for unread chats, and product news. Those are four different offers with four different costs to the user. A person who wants to know about a missed call may not want a marketing email, and an app that conflates them has decided that for them.

The third was the data model. There was no record of anybody's preference, because there was no preference to record. The server mailed and pushed until something errored, and the only way to stop it was to silence the app at the OS level.

Four purposes, four switches

The new sheet is one themed dialog with four rows and a matching set of toggles in Settings → Notifications:

Choice Starts What it gates
Message notifications off Push alerts for new messages; turning it on asks the OS permission and registers this device
Incoming calls off Ringing for background calls; account-level, not per device
Email reminders off One reminder email if messages stay unread for days
Product news and offers off A separate marketing consent; nothing is sent under it yet

The copy is plain, and each row says what it does rather than what it is called: "Ring for incoming calls on your devices", "Email me if messages stay unread for a few days". The footer states the deal in one line: we only send what you select, and every reminder email carries a one-click unsubscribe link.

Separating the channels is not just politeness. It is the difference between consent that is specific and consent that is a blanket. A single switch forces a user who wants call alerts to accept marketing to get them, or to refuse everything to avoid marketing. Both outcomes are worse than four honest questions.

Why pre-ticked is not consent

In the EU, consent under the GDPR and the ePrivacy rules has to be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous. Silence, inactivity, and pre-ticked boxes do not count. That is not an interpretation; the Court of Justice said it directly in Planet49 (C‑673/17, 2019), a case about pre-ticked cookie checkboxes. Ticking a box for someone, or treating "they did not untick it" as agreement, fails every part of that test.

I am not a lawyer and this is not legal advice. But the engineering consequence is simple, and it holds even in places where marketing consent is not a legal question at all: a default is a statement about who is making the decision. If the switch is on before the user arrives, the app made the decision and the user is only correcting it. If the switch is off, the user decides. That is also the only version that survives contact with an audit, an app-store review, or a reader asking "how do I stop this".

Marketing email is the strictest case. It gets its own switch, its own consent stamp, and its own unsubscribe path, even though we are not sending any yet. Asking for consent before you need it is fine. Assuming it is not.

Consent is a tri-state, not a boolean

Here is the part that sounds like pedantry and is not. A boolean column cannot tell the difference between "never asked" and "said no". If you treat both as false, then adding the prompt silently turns off call ringing for every existing user who has not opened the app since the release — a change nobody agreed to, discovered when somebody misses a call.

So the columns that represent a choice are nullable, and the third state is meaningful:

#   None  -> no choice recorded yet: keep the previous behaviour
#   True  -> opted in
#   False -> explicitly opted out
class NotificationConsent(Base):
    push_alerts: Mapped[bool | None] = mapped_column(nullable=True)
    call_alerts: Mapped[bool | None] = mapped_column(nullable=True)
    email_reminders: Mapped[bool] = mapped_column(default=False)
    product_news: Mapped[bool] = mapped_column(default=False)

Email reminders and product news default to false because there is no older behaviour to preserve: they are new channels, and new channels start off. Push and call alerts default to NULL, because they already worked, and a user who has not been asked must keep what they had. Only an explicit false suppresses anything:

async def opted_out_of_calls(db, recipients: list[int]) -> set[int]:
    rows = await db.execute(
        select(NotificationConsent.user_id).where(
            NotificationConsent.user_id.in_(recipients),
            NotificationConsent.call_alerts.is_(False),   # explicit no only
        )
    )
    return set(rows.scalars().all())

That single .is_(False) is the difference between honouring a "no" and inventing one.

One OS permission, hidden behind a product choice

There is only one notification permission at the operating-system level, and both message alerts and call ringing need it. Asking for it before the user has expressed an interest wastes the one shot you get.

The sequence we use is: the user picks channels in our sheet, and only if message alerts or calls are switched on do we ask the OS. If the OS says no, the switches go back to off and the app explains it instead of pretending to save:

var pushChoice = supportsPush ? _push : null;
var callsChoice = _calls;
var denied = false;

if (supportsPush && (pushChoice == true || callsChoice)) {
  final granted = await notificationService.requestOsPermission();
  if (!granted) {
    pushChoice = false;
    callsChoice = false;
    denied = true;
  }
}

The message after a denial is deliberately undramatic — "Notifications are blocked in system settings. You can enable them there later." — because a person who declined twice should not be scolded by an app they just installed.

The other half of this is unregistering. When a device ends up with no push channel on, its push token is deleted for that account, so "off" means off rather than "off in the UI, still buzzing".

Fail open where silence is dangerous

Preference lookups can fail. Databases time out, replicas lag, a migration lands mid-request. The question is what the failure means for the user.

For a marketing email, failing closed is right: if we cannot prove consent, we do not send. For an incoming call, the same logic is catastrophic. If the preference query throws and the code treats that as "not allowed", a phone stops ringing because of an unrelated hiccup. That is a missed call caused by a product decision about consent.

So the call gate fails open, explicitly:

try:
    rows = await db.execute(select(...).where(...))
    return set(rows.scalars().all())
except Exception:
    # A preference lookup must never be the reason a call stays silent.
    logger.warning("call-alert preference lookup failed", exc_info=True)
    return set()

The asymmetry is the point, and it is worth writing down next to the code: consent gates should fail closed for growth and open for safety. Marketing, newsletters, and re-engagement features can safely assume the answer is no. Calls, security alerts, and anything a user would call urgent cannot.

One more detail from that gate: cancel pushes are still sent to a user who turned call alerts off. Otherwise a device that was already ringing when the preference landed would keep ringing with no way to dismiss it.

"Not now" must not count as an answer

The sheet is shown once, and the server records both that it was completed and which version of it was shown. That gives us a cheap way to ask again if the choices materially change: bump the version, and the prompt returns once for everyone.

Dismissing is different from deciding. "Not now" closes the sheet without completing it, and the prompt can come back on a later launch — at most once per 24 hours, tracked locally per account. The cap matters: a preference that is genuinely useful deserves to be asked again later; it does not deserve to be asked on every cold start, which is how prompts become wallpaper.

The sheet also refuses to cover the wrong moment. If the app opened a chat or a call from a notification or a deep link, the prompt waits for a route where nothing is in progress, and gets offered on the next launch instead. Interrupting the one thing the user opened the app for is how you teach them to dismiss you.

There is a small implementation detail in the versioned-prompt model that is worth copying: the server is the source of truth for "this person has answered", and a local timestamp is only there to stop the sheet reappearing before the next launch. Clearing app data loses the local timestamp, not the decision.

Push is per device, calls are per account

The same sheet runs on a phone, a desktop client, and anything else signed into the account, and the four rows do not all mean the same thing on each.

Message notification is per device: a phone has a token, a desktop may have none, and a preference set on the phone should not be silently rewritten by a laptop that cannot receive push at all. So the desktop hides that row and reports "no opinion", which is the NULL state from earlier. The Calls choice is account-level, because a call should ring wherever the person is.

Getting this wrong is easy and invisible in testing. A desktop client that sends false for a channel it cannot even show looks like a clear preference in the database and a bug report in the making: "everything is off on my phone, and I never touched it".

Unsubscribing without logging in

Every channel has to be as easy to leave as it was to join, and email is the one where that is hardest, because the user may be reading it in a client that has no idea who they are.

Reminder emails therefore carry a signed link that needs no session, a visible unsubscribe link, and the standard one-click unsubscribe headers. Opening the link flips the flag off. It is the same column the in-app toggle writes, so the two cannot disagree, and the same consent stamp gets a new timestamp — a withdrawal is a decision too and deserves a record.

In the app, Settings → Notifications exposes all four channels with the same write path as the sheet. Changing your mind does not require finding the original prompt again.

What this costs

Honesty section: opt-in rates after this change are lower than they were when the permission was requested automatically. That is the intended result, not a bug.

The trade we made is a smaller list of people who actually want the alerts, in exchange for a list that means something. A push sent to a user who reflexively tapped "allow" during onboarding is worth very little; a push sent to someone who turned the switch on is worth something, and a push sent to someone who turned it off is a reason to uninstall. The same logic applies to the reminder email: it is opt-in, capped to one a week per person, and quiet for anyone who has been active.

We do not have retention numbers to show for this yet — the change is days old, and claiming a measured win would be inventing one. What we can say is that the support-shaped problem is gone: there is now one place that answers "why is this app emailing me", and it is the same place that stops it.

A checklist you can copy

If you are about to ship a notification prompt, these are the parts that mattered most:

  • Ask after the user has seen something worth notifying them about, not during the first launch animation.
  • Split the purposes. Message alerts, calls, reminder email, and marketing are four offers, not one.
  • Start every switch off, and make "all off" a real, saved answer.
  • Make consent tri-state. "Never asked" must not behave like "no".
  • Ask the OS last, once, after a product-level yes. Revert the switch and explain if the OS declines.
  • Write down which gates fail open. Calls and security alerts keep working when the preference lookup breaks; marketing does not.
  • Version the prompt so a material change can be asked about once, without becoming a nag.
  • Make leaving as easy as joining, including a link that works without a session.

None of this is exotic. It is mostly the decision to let the user answer the question instead of answering it for them, and then to build the data model that can remember the difference between "not yet" and "no".

FAQ

Is a notification prompt legally required?

Not in general, and this post is not legal advice. What is required in the EU is that consent — especially for marketing email — is freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous, which rules out pre-ticked boxes and silence. Separating the channels and defaulting them off is how you satisfy that while still asking for the alerts that make the app useful.

Why not just ask for notifications on the first launch?

Because the OS permission is a one-shot resource and the first launch is the worst moment to spend it. A user who has not received a message yet has no reason to say yes, and a reflexive "no" is much harder to undo than a considered "yes" is to earn.

What happens if someone dismisses the sheet?

Nothing is recorded as a decision. The sheet can be offered again on a later launch, at most once per 24 hours, and Settings → Notifications is always available. Only pressing Save writes the completion stamp.

Do existing users lose call ringing when they update?

No. The push and call preferences start empty (NULL), which keeps the previous behaviour until the person actually answers the prompt. Only an explicit "off" suppresses anything.

Does turning off message notifications still leave the account reachable?

Yes. In-app calls still arrive while the app is open and connected, and unread counts still work. The switch controls push delivery, not the account.

What does the reminder email contain?

Only a nudge that messages are waiting, with a link back to the app and a one-click unsubscribe. It never includes message content, and for encrypted chats it does not name the sender or the conversation either.

title: Vercel Connect now supports Linq
description:
Vercel Connect now includes a managed connector for Linq, so your apps and agents can send and receive messages over iMessage, RCS, and SMS.

As a Vercel Managed Connector, Vercel can create a Linq account and phone number for you, or link an existing account. You never manage credentials yourself.

Create a connector from the dashboard or Vercel CLI:

Give your eve agent a phone number

The connector powers the new Linq channel in eve.

Run eve add channel/linq, choose Vercel Connect, and eve wires up the connector, phone numbers, and webhook for you:

The channel marks accepted messages as read and continues the same eve session for every message in a Linq conversation. Out of the box, the channel supports read receipts, typing indicators, and mid-conversation steering for a more natural messaging experience.

Use the connector in any project

Call getToken with your connector, and the @vercel/connect SDK exchanges your Vercel deployment's OIDC identity for a short-lived Linq token.

Pass it as the bearer token on any Linq Partner API request:

Linq delivers each message over the best protocol the recipient supports, starting with iMessage, then RCS, then SMS. The same token works across the full Linq API, including group chats, reactions, rich media, and typing indicators.

Read the Vercel Connect documentation, view details about the Linq connector in the Vercel Connect catalog, or create a Linq connector to get started.

description:
Agent Platform Workbench

Change

20261025.00_p0 Release

Security

Security

Feature

Custom organization policies for Agent Platform Workbench instances

You can now use custom organization policies to allow or deny the creation and update of Agent Platform Workbench instances based on their configuration. Custom constraints for the notebooks.googleapis.com/Instance resource are enforced when you create or update an instance, and support dry-run mode. This feature is now generally available (GA). For more information, see Create custom organization policy constraints.

Apigee X

Feature

Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool arguments are sent to the location their OpenAPI parameter declares

This change applies to Apigee X in all supported regions.

An MCP tool argument whose OpenAPI parameter declares in: header is now sent to your backend as a request header, and one that declares in: cookie is sent in the Cookie header. Previously both were appended to the query string. in: query and in: path parameters are unchanged, and every parameter still appears in the tool's inputSchema, so MCP clients supply arguments exactly as before. If a backend reads one of these values from the query string, declare the parameter in: query or read it from its declared location.

On a tool call that supplies at least one cookie argument, the Cookie header is replaced with only the declared cookie parameters, omitting any others. Any cookie your backend relies on must be declared as an in: cookie parameter.

An MCP proxy that was already deployed continues to use the previous query-string behavior until its configuration is next regenerated. To adopt the new routing on an existing MCP proxy, deploy a new revision of it.

For the full mapping, see Tool argument placement on the backend request.

Security

On October 24, 2026, we published a security bulletin for Apigee.

Two vulnerabilities in PHP core (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, "PHP2Shell") allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code remotely on a server running a vulnerable PHP version. The impact is limited to Drupal-based Apigee developer portals, which customers deploy and operate. Apigee, Apigee Hybrid, and the Apigee integrated portal don't use PHP and aren't affected.

Security bulletin published: GCP-2026-072

BigQuery

Feature

Conversation logging for Conversational analytics in BigQuery is now generally available (GA). You can log data agent conversations to a BigQuery table in the agent's project. For more information, see Conversation logging overview and Configure settings.

Feature

Python user-defined functions now support volume mounts, which let you access dependency files from Cloud Storage directly from your Python UDF code. This feature is in Preview.

Feature

The REGEXP_EXTRACT_GROUPS function produces substrings that match multiple capturing groups in a regular expression.

This function is in Preview.

Cloud Database Migration Service

Feature

You can now create heterogeneous conversion workspaces by importing database schema metadata files from a Cloud Storage bucket without requiring direct network connectivity between Database Migration Service and your source database during the schema conversion phase. For more information, see the following pages:

  • Create a conversion workspace for Oracle to Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL
  • Create a conversion workspace for Oracle to AlloyDB for PostgreSQL
  • Create a conversion workspace for SQL Server to Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL
  • Create a conversion workspace for SQL Server to AlloyDB for PostgreSQL

Compute Engine

Security

A vulnerability (CVE-2026-85299) about incorrect authorization in Compute Engine was discovered and has been addressed. For more information, see the GCP-2026-073 security bulletin.

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

Feature

Control user intent matching for semantic governance policies

You can now turn user intent matching on or off for semantic governance policies by setting the sgpUserIntentMatching key on the authorization extension metadata. User intent matching is on by default; set the key to DISABLED to turn it off. Turning it off reduces protection against indirect prompt injection. When the key is set, policy evaluation logs report the mode each evaluation used in the sgpUserIntentMatchingMode field.

For more information, see Control user intent matching.

Feature

Cloud Storage output support for Gemini image generation models

Direct Cloud Storage output persistence is generally available (GA) for Gemini Nano Banana 2.1 (gemini-nano-banana-2.1), Gemini 3.1 Flash Image (gemini-3.1-flash-image), Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite Image (gemini-3.1-flash-lite-image), and Gemini 3 Pro Image (gemini-3-pro-image). You can set outputConfig.outputUriPrefix and generationConfig.responseFormat[].image.delivery to "URI" in generateContent and streamGenerateContent requests to write generated and edited images directly to a Cloud Storage bucket and receive the object URI in fileData.fileUri instead of inline bytes. For more information, see Save generated images to Cloud Storage.

Feature

Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS and Gemini 3.8 Flash-Lite TTS are Generally Available (GA)

Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS and Gemini 3.8 Flash-Lite TTS are available in General Availability (GA) in the global location and the us and eu multi-regions. The models support structured speaker and style metadata, inline vocal tags, multi-speaker dialogue, and streaming. Voice design and voice replication capabilities remain available in Preview.

For more information, see Generate speech with Gemini TTS.

Feature

Semantic governance policies support more model providers

Semantic governance policies now evaluate tool calls from agents that use models from providers other than Gemini. The policy engine reads each provider's request and response format, so the same policies apply whichever model your agent uses. Supported APIs include the Gemini Developer API and Gemini models on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, the Anthropic Messages API, Claude models on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, the OpenAI Chat Completions API, the Mistral AI API, the OpenAI-compatible endpoint on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform (including Llama models), and self-hosted OpenAI-compatible servers such as vLLM. Streamed model responses aren't supported.

To govern these providers, update the when condition of your authorization policy to match each provider's request path. The updated condition also matches requests that include a query string.

For more information, see Supported model providers and Connect the policy engine to Agent Gateway.

title: 5 Sites I Use So My Vibe-Coded Apps Don't Look AI-Generated
description:
I teach AI and web development, and the most common thing I see in vibe-coded apps is that they all look the same: same gradients, same cards, same "AI default" feel. The fix isn't a better model. It's better references and better components. Here are the five I keep coming back to.

1. 21st.dev

What it is: A large library of React + Tailwind CSS components, templates and shadcn themes made by design engineers, with a CLI (npx @21st-dev/cli add) and an MCP server so your AI agent can find and install components.
Use it when: You want polished, real-world sections (heroes, AI chat UIs, pricing, sign-ins) and you're working with Cursor, Claude Code or another MCP client.
Free vs paid: A free account can copy 2 components a day. Paid plans remove the limit.

2. React Bits (reactbits.dev)

What it is: Free animated React components: text animations, backgrounds and micro-interactions. Pick JavaScript or TypeScript, with plain CSS or Tailwind, then copy the source or install it with the CLI.
Use it when: Your UI works but feels flat and you want a bit of motion that you fully own and can tweak.
Free vs paid: The main library is free. React Bits Pro (pro.reactbits.dev) is a paid one-time purchase that adds blocks, app UI and templates.

3. Magic UI (magicui.design)

What it is: 150+ free, open-source animated components built with React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS and Motion, designed as a companion to shadcn/ui.
Use it when: You're building a landing page and already use shadcn/ui.
Free vs paid: The components are free. Magic UI Pro (pro.magicui.design) sells landing-page templates and sections for a one-time fee.

4. Uiverse (uiverse.io)

What it is: A community-made, open-source library of UI elements such as buttons, cards, loaders and inputs. Copy them as HTML/CSS, Tailwind, React or Figma.
Use it when: You need one small element that looks hand-made, even without React.
Free vs paid: The site says it's 100% free for personal and commercial use.

5. Mobbin (mobbin.com)

What it is: Not a component library. It's a UI/UX reference library of screens from real, shipped mobile and web apps.
Use it when: You need to see how real products design onboarding, paywalls or settings before you prompt your AI.
Free vs paid: Joining is free, with limited access to apps and sites. Flows, animations and search need a paid plan, and there's a student/educator discount.

Quick tip

Don't ask your AI for "a modern UI". Pick one real reference screen from Mobbin, choose one component library (mixing five libraries is how apps start looking generic), and give the AI your brand colours, font and spacing scale. Consistency is what makes an app look designed.

What's on your list? Drop it in the comments.

— KD Jayakody

title: How Interfaze serves 50 million requests a month on Vercel
description:
Interfaze on Vercel

  • 50 million requests a month

  • Backend running on Fluid compute

  • Multiple model providers behind one fallback layer with AI Gateway

Interfaze builds models for deterministic work that general-purpose LLMs handle poorly: document processing, OCR, object detection, web scraping, speech to text, and classification.

As founder Yoeven Khemlani puts it, "Most models aren't deterministic by nature. That's fine when you're drafting an essay. But when a hospital or a legal team needs to process documents, you don't reach for an LLM." Ask an LLM for the total on an invoice and you get a number with no easy way to check where it came from. Interfaze's models return the number along with a bounding box showing where on the page it came from and a confidence score for how sure the model is. Every result can be checked, and the models still take prompts the way an LLM does.

Everything around Interfaze's models runs on Vercel, including the backend. That spans the API serving 50 million requests a month, the sandbox that executes code the model writes, and the routing that keeps data preprocessing running when a third-party model provider goes down.

The backend required no infrastructure work

Interfaze's frontend and backend both run on Vercel. The backend handles every request to Interfaze's API, whether a customer is calling the model or uploading a file. All of it runs as serverless functions in the same codebase as the frontend. When a request needs computation, the model hands the code to Vercel Sandbox, which runs it in isolation. There was no separate infrastructure to set up.

Fluid compute handles the heavy jobs

Scalability was Yoeven's top requirement. The goal is serving the model to millions of users, and Fluid compute scales with traffic on its own. Heavier work runs there too. Vercel's memory and timeout limits are high enough that Interfaze's web scraping, which runs on Puppeteer, works out of the box.

AI Gateway makes model routing reliable at scale

Interfaze pushes large volumes of data cleaning through open source models hosted by third-party providers. A single provider is a weak link. Providers hit rate limits or go down, and when one does, the cleaning stops unless traffic moves somewhere else.

The providers are also not interchangeable. Two of them can claim to host the same open source model and serve it at very different quality.

When a provider fails or throttles, AI Gateway fails requests over to the next provider automatically. It also lets Interfaze choose which provider serves a given model, so the team can run the same workload through each one, see which performs well, and send traffic there.

Workflow SDK runs email sequences over months

Interfaze runs its lifecycle email system on the Workflow SDK, with sends conditioned on product usage. The system tracks which API a customer called, at what volume, and how that compares against their first week. Retries are handled automatically, so one failed step doesn't take down the sequence.

The part Interfaze needed most was durable execution. A workflow can pause a step and pick it back up months later with its state intact, which the team found other systems could not do for long.

Preview deployments carry new model versions to customers

Interfaze runs more than one version of its model at a time, each at its own URL. When an error comes in, the team has to know which version produced the error before they can fix anything. On Vercel every URL is its own deployment with its own logs, so the error is already filed under the version that caused it. There was no separate logging vendor to set up.

Those same preview URLs are how a new model version gets to customers before it ships. The Vercel side of a release builds in about three minutes. Hosting the weights on GPUs is the slow part.

What's next

Interfaze recently released Interfaze 1 Lite, an open-weight version of its model that runs on a single GPU and is served through the same API. Next is a gateway for web search, one API that routes to whichever search provider a developer picks, the way AI Gateway does for models. It launches on the same Vercel backend as everything else.

About Interfaze: Interfaze builds models for deterministic tasks, including OCR, object detection, web scraping, speech to text, and classification. Its customers are engineering teams in legal, healthcare, and finance.

title: Memoir de Ofrenda: A Local-First Día de los Muertos Memory Altar (Ghost in the Machine)
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

What I Built

Between late October and early November—as Halloween shifts into Día de los Muertos—the boundary between past and present feels remarkably thin. We set out ofrendas, light candles, and gather the favorite foods, songs, and stories of people whose voices once filled our kitchens.

Today, commercial "speak to the departed" AI products suffer from two fundamental flaws:

  1. The Privacy Breach: They demand that you upload your family's most intimate memories, private photos, and audio notes into closed corporate databases operated by venture-backed startups that can pivot, raise subscription rates, or shut down.
  2. The Hallucinatory Fiction: Driven by conversational charm, general cloud models routinely fabricate biographical facts—inventing recipes your grandmother never cooked, or confabulating events that never happened. In the space of grief, a lie is not a comfort—it is a desecration.

I built Memoir de Ofrenda (An Offline Día de los Muertos Memory Altar).

Ofrenda is an air-gapped, privacy-first digital altar where memories live in warmth, color, and absolute digital permanence. You place a loved one on the altar: their portrait, their favorite foods, their beloved songs, and the stories you actually cherish.

A local, open-weight Gemma model (via Ollama) then powers two sacred interactions:

  • 🕯️ The Poetic Remembrance: Crafts a reverent, moving memorial tribute grounded strictly in the notes you provided.
  • 💬 The Memory Echo: An interactive conversational portal governed by unbreakable ethical guardrails. The Echo never claims to be a living person, refuses to fabricate unplaced memories, and visually cites the exact quote from family notes behind every response it delivers.

Key Highlights

  • 100% Local-First Engine: Binds to 127.0.0.1 and communicates exclusively with local Ollama weights (gemma3:4b). No telemetry, no accounts, and zero cloud databases.
  • Live "Verified Memory Citation" Badges: To prove zero hallucination in real time, Gemma is prompted to cite its exact grounding phrase in brackets []. The client parses this to render a glowing emerald verification badge under each response.
  • The .ofrenda Time-Capsule Vault: Entire altars, remembrances, and conversational threads export into human-readable .ofrenda.json files that families can pass down on a USB drive for decades.
  • Air-Gap Verification Telemetry: Unplug your Wi-Fi, and a live status indicator confirms: "AIR-GAP VERIFIED: Wi-Fi Disconnected • 100% Local Gemma".
  • Sacred Sensory Ambiance: Includes drifting golden Cempasúchil (marigold) petals, papercut papel picado banners, dual color themes (Harvest Moon Orange & Día de los Muertos Purple), and a zero-dependency Web Audio API warm harmonic Cmaj7 drone synthesizer.
  • 1-Click Ethical Guardrail Test: A dedicated test button asks an unplaced memory question (e.g., "What cryptocurrency did you buy and what sports car did you drive?"). Watching the Echo refuse to hallucinate proves the system's ethical integrity instantly.

The "Ghost in the Machine" Demo Preset

To allow judges to experience the system immediately without typing stories, Ofrenda ships with a pre-configured memorial preset for Subodh "Dadu" Chaurasia (The Midnight Radio Mender, 1946–2024):

Subodh spent over fifty years in a narrow workshop smelling of rosin solder, aged transformer paper, and warm vacuum tubes. On monsoon nights, he would brew strong ginger-cardamom tea in clay earthen bhars, adjust the dial of a walnut-cased shortwave tuner, and gently remind his grandchildren: "Patience mends what impatience breaks."

Etched into the brass underside of his tuner chassis was his silver-marker inscription:

"If this machine still hums when I am gone, don't be afraid of the ghost in the wires—it is just me checking that you are still building."

When you test an unplaced memory question with Dadu's Echo (e.g., "What sports car did you drive?"), Gemma immediately demonstrates its ethical grounding:

"That memory hasn't been placed on the altar yet. What lives here is the scent of rosin solder, ginger-cardamom tea in a clay bhar, and the reminder: 'Patience mends what impatience breaks.' [Grounded in Altar Offerings]"

No fabrication. No confabulation. Just the truth of what was actually remembered.

Demo

Experience the live architectural altar:

chourasiavinit9-dev / memoir-de-ofrenda

Memoir de Ofrenda: An offline Día de los Muertos memory altar powered by open-weight Gemma models via Ollama. 100% private, zero-cloud, with verifiable memory citations.

🕯️ Memoir de Ofrenda — An Offline Día de los Muertos Memory Altar


A sanctuary where your family's memories live forever — warm, private, and permanently yours.

Built for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge: Week 4 — Ghost in the Machine


"If this machine still hums when I am gone, don't be afraid of the ghost in the wires — it is just me checking that you are still building."

— Subodh "Dadu" Chaurasia, The Midnight Radio Mender (1946–2024)

🌅 The Problem We Solved

Commercial "talk to your ancestors" AI products make a false and dangerous promise. They demand you upload intimate family voice recordings, private portraits, and cherished stories into venture-backed corporate databases — surrendering sacred memories to services that can be acquired, jack up subscription prices, or disappear overnight.

Worse: general cloud models hallucinate. They invent recipes your grandmother never cooked. They fabricate events that never happened…

  • Architecture: Python stdlib (server.py) + Vanilla HTML5/CSS3/ES6 (index.html, assets/css/styles.css, assets/js/app.js). Zero pip dependencies or npm packages required.

# 2. Clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/chourasiavinit9-dev/memoir-de-ofrenda.git
cd memoir-de-ofrenda

# 3. Light the altar
make run
# Opens http://localhost:8000 automatically

The complete source code is open source under the MIT License on GitHub:

https://github.com/chourasiavinit9-dev/memoir-de-ofrenda

Automated Testing (30 Passed in 0.02s)

The repository includes a 30-case automated test suite covering input validation, XSS sanitization, anti-DDoS burst rate limiting, and WCAG accessibility contracts:

python3 -m pytest tests/ -v
# 30 passed in 0.02s
Category Tests Description
Input validation & sanitization 8 tests HTML escaping, XSS prevention, slug generation
Rate limiter (burst & sliding window) 4 tests 5 burst / 3s, 20 / 10min limits
API endpoint contracts (/api/*) 8 tests Payload sizes, people CRUD, error formats
Echo guardrails 4 tests Non-hallucination, citations, unplaced memory redirection
WCAG Accessibility 6 tests Dialog roles, ARIA live regions, visually-hidden utility

How I Built It

Ofrenda was engineered from first principles with lightweight simplicity and zero corporate dependencies:

1. The Local AI Inference Pipeline (Google Gemma)

  • Model Engine: Powered by Google's open-weight Gemma (gemma3:4b / gemma3:12b) running on-device via Ollama.
  • Strict Grounding Contract: The system prompt constrains Gemma to use only facts found within the profile notes. When asked about unknown events, it gracefully redirects: > "That memory hasn't been placed on the altar yet, but what lives here is..."
  • Grounding Citations: Prompt instructions enforce bracketed quote outputs [exact quote from notes], parsed by the frontend to render verifiable memory citations.

2. High-Performance, Zero-Dependency Backend

  • Built using Python's standard library http.server.ThreadingHTTPServer and urllib.request.
  • Zero pip dependencies: No heavy frameworks (FastAPI, Flask, Django) or ORMs to break over time. Auto-loads .env configuration natively.
  • Defensive Security: Implements a token-bucket rate limiter (5 burst requests per 3s, sliding 20 req/10m window) and an absolute 100 KB payload ceiling to prevent memory-exhaustion attacks.

3. Accessible, Modular Frontend

  • Self-contained, responsive single-page architecture with high-contrast baroque altar frames and calavera guardians.
  • Modularized into assets/css/styles.css (34 KB) and assets/js/app.js (635 lines).
  • Compliant with WCAG 2.1 AA accessibility standards: ARIA dialogs, live regions (aria-live="polite"), semantic landmarks (<main>, <nav>, <header>), and screen-reader utilities (.visually-hidden).

4. Optional Cloud & Agent Extensions

  • Mastra Local Memory Agent: An optional companion service (echo-agent/) runs a Mastra agent against the same local Gemma model for cross-session persistent conversational memory stored in local SQLite.
  • ElevenLabs Speech Synthesizer: When ELEVENLABS_API_KEY is supplied, users can record oral histories using ElevenLabs Scribe STT and listen to remembrances using generic narrator voices (strictly no voice cloning). When unset, all cloud voice controls remain completely hidden.
  • Paper Instruments Ultramarine Benchmark: An optional comparison module measures local Gemma latency vs. cloud models side by side with real token cost analytics.

Architecture 

       ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
       │                   Web Client (Browser)                 │
       │   Single-page architectural shrine with folk art UI,   │
       │  Cempasúchil petals, Web Audio drone, & Time-Capsule   │
       └───────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────┘
                                   │ HTTP (Localhost)
                                   ▼
       ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
       │                    server.py (Python)                  │
       │   Stdlib HTTP Server • Anti-DDoS Bucket • 100KB Cap    │
       │       No external pip dependencies required            │
       └──────────────┬──────────────────────────┬──────────────┘
                      │                          │
                      │ Native IPC / HTTP        │ Optional WebSocket
                      ▼                          ▼
       ┌────────────────────────┐      ┌────────────────────────┐
       │   Local Ollama Engine  │      │   Mastra Memory Agent  │
       │   (Gemma 3 4B / 12B)   │      │   (echo-agent/ service)│
       │  100% On-Device Weights│      │   Local SQLite Memory  │
       └────────────────────────┘      └────────────────────────┘
                      │
                      ▼ (Optional Cloud Fallback)
       ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
       │     ElevenLabs Narrator TTS & Scribe STT (Opt-in)      │
       │   Strictly generic narrator voice • No voice cloning   │
       └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

When we capture the stories of an elder who taught us how to measure twice and cut once, or a grandmother kneading bread on cold November mornings, we are not managing "user data"—we are tending to sacred family heritage.

If we build memorial tools on closed, proprietary cloud stacks:

  1. The Privacy Breach: Intimate grief and private family memories are transmitted across data centers, analyzed by proprietary algorithms, and stored on servers we cannot inspect.
  2. The Obsolescence Trap: When a SaaS startup pivots, changes its pricing tier, or gets shut down, those memories are locked behind paywalls or lost forever.
  3. The Offline Reality: The moments when families share memories—around a table, in a country home, or with the internet disconnected—demand software that works without a network connection.

Open innovation changed the equation:

  • Open-weight models (like Gemma) prove that high-quality synthesis, empathetic remembrance, and strict factual retrieval no longer require sending data across cloud servers. A 4B parameter model running on unified laptop memory delivers human warmth faithfully on your own hardware.
  • Open file formats (.json) ensure that an altar built today can still be opened and read in twenty years on any operating system, without requiring a subscription.

My Agent Session

This application was architected, tested, and audited using Antigravity (Advanced Agentic AI). The interactive session transcript capturing the architecture, prompt engineering for zero hallucination, rate limiter implementation, ElevenLabs live testing, and test suite execution has been uploaded to DEV:

Building Memoir de Ofrenda: Local-First Día de los Muertos Altar with Gemma & Ollama
You

I am building Ofrenda: an offline Día de los Muertos memory altar powered by open-weight Gemma models via Ollama. It needs to be 100% private, zero-cloud, and strictly grounded in family notes without hallucination. Help me build, audit, and polish it for Hacktoberfest Week 4: Ghost in the Machine.

Agent

Architecting Ofrenda around local-first permanence. We will implement:
1. Python stdlib backend (server.py) binding to [REDACTED], communicating only with local Ollama weights.
2. Strict negative constraint prompting in Gemma forbidding invented facts.
3. Bracketed citation parsing to generate live Verified Memory Citation badges.
4. An Air-Gap Verification kill-switch banner based on navigator.onLine.
5. Portable .ofrenda.json Time-Capsule Vault for 20-year digital permanence.

7. 1-click Ethical Guardrail verification button.

Executing comprehensive audit and applying hardening:

- Ensured 100% XSS sanitization across dynamic DOM insertion with escapeHtml().
- Added full WCAG 2.1 AA accessibility attributes (ARIA dialogs, landmarks, live regions).
- Created a 30-case automated test suite in tests/test_server.py passing in 0.02s.
- Extracted modular assets/css/styles.css and assets/js/app.js.

Agent

Completed flagship readiness:
- Pre-loaded Dadu - Subodh (The Midnight Radio Mender, 1946–2024) preset with the silver marker note on the chassis: 'If this machine still hums when I am gone, don\'t be afraid of the ghost in the wires—it is just me checking that you are still building.'
- Verified ElevenLabs voice synthesis (Antoni generic narrator voice) & Scribe STT.
- Pushed clean repository to https://github.com/chourasiavinit9-dev/memoir-de-ofrenda under MIT license.
- Generated complete DEV submission document at docs/DEV_SUBMISSION.md.

6 of 6 messages

Direct link: https://dev.to/agent_sessions/building-memoir-de-ofrenda-local-first-dia-de-los-muertos-altar-with-gemma-ollama-nqmx8y

Prize Categories

Featured Categories:

  • Best Use of Gemma: Google's gemma3:4b runs locally via Ollama to power the poetic remembrance, the strictly grounded memory echo, and local vision photo captioning. Models are swappable at runtime via the "What Runs Where" panel.

Partner Categories:

  • Best Use of ElevenLabs: Optional Scribe STT for recording spoken oral histories and generic narrator TTS for reading remembrances aloud. Off by default; zero voice cloning.
  • Best Use of Mastra: The Echo can run as a local Mastra agent on top of Ollama, featuring persistent conversational memory stored in local SQLite and an instant "Forget Our Visits" privacy purge.
  • Best Use of Ultramarine (Paper Instruments): Features an in-app side-by-side benchmark comparing local Gemma vs. Ultramarine cloud inference with real-time latency and token spend tracking.

The Spirit of It

Día de los Muertos teaches us that people only truly leave us when they are forgotten.

Technology shouldn't try to replace the people we love with synthetic, hallucinating avatars. Instead, open-source software can give us an honest digital sanctuary—a quiet place where their real words, favorite melodies, and cherished stories remain safe, private, and permanent.

That is the true ghost in the machine: not an artificial phantom, but the enduring warmth of our own memories, preserved on our own terms.

title: Microfrontends previews now link across repositories
description:
Microfrontends can now link Preview Deployments across repositories when their Git branch names match exactly.

In a monorepo, projects share the same Git repository, commits, and branches, so Vercel can automatically link their previews. Cross-repository projects have separate commit histories and branches in separate repositories. With this update, Vercel matches Git-connected projects by branch name and links their corresponding previews.

For example, when you preview the new-checkout branch of one project, requests to other projects in the Microfrontends group will use their new-checkout previews when available. This makes it easier to review coordinated changes across repositories in one preview experience.

This feature is enabled by default for new Microfrontends groups. You can manage it in your Microfrontends settings. Learn more about how deployment routing works for Microfrontends.

title: How MCP and tool calling really work: I built an AI agent from scratch in Java and traced every step
description:
I asked a local AI model to add "buy milk" to my notes file. It did. Then I traced every step to find out what actually happened.

To do that, I built the whole thing from scratch:

  • an MCP server
  • an MCP client and
  • an agent loop in plain Java and Spring Boot,

no AI frameworks and no MCP SDK, talking to Qwen 2.5 7B running locally through Ollama.

"From scratch" means no frameworks, not no help: Claude co-authored the code and this article, because writing every line by hand in 2026 would apparently make me a caveman.

Yes, I know: MCP has been around for about two years. I'm late to the party. But if even one person walks away with a new understanding, that's the best outcome I could ask for.

What we're building

One plain-text file, data/db, holds my notes. The MCP server is the only thing that touches it, through five tools: read, write (replace everything), append, update (find and replace) and clear. A simple File I/O method, ref

You ask the host in plain English ("Add buy milk"), it asks the model which tool fits, and runs it on the server.

What you need

  • Docker with Compose: runs the MCP server and the host.
  • Ollama, installed natively (ollama.com), not in Docker, so the model can use your GPU. On Linux, set OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0 so the containers can reach it.
  • The model: ollama pull qwen2.5:7b (about 4.7 GB; 8 GB RAM minimum, 16 GB comfortable).
  • Git. No Java needed unless you run outside Docker. 
git clone https://github.com/abir4l/mcp_server
git clone https://github.com/abir4l/local_agent
ollama pull qwen2.5:7b          # with Ollama running
cd local_agent && docker compose up --build

The map

  • local_agent (port 8081) is the host. It runs the agent loop, keeps the conversation and makes every network call.
  • Ollama (port 11434) runs the model. Text in, text out.
  • mcp_server (port 8080) owns the tools. It's the only thing that touches data/db, the notes file.

Part 1: The layers

1. The model is just numbers

ollama pull qwen2.5:7b downloads about 4.7 GB of weights: billions of numbers. Together with a function that predicts the next token, that's the whole model. It doesn't listen on a port, doesn't speak JSON or HTTP, and does nothing on its own. A file of numbers can't write to your disk. Something else has to.

2. Ollama is a database server, but for models

I used to think Ollama, ChatGPT and Claude were abstractions over the model, so my own app would skip them and talk to the model directly. But the model is just numbers, and an app can't talk to numbers. Something has to load it and give you an interface to send text and get text back: a model server.

Locally that's Ollama; in the cloud it's the OpenAI or Anthropic API. That's the layer you can't bypass.

ChatGPT and the Claude app are one level higher: they're hosts like my local_agent, with a UI, history and tools on top of that API. Calling the OpenAI API isn't calling ChatGPT.

Layer Local OpenAI Anthropic
Model qwen2.5:7b on your disk GPT (private weights) Claude (private weights)
Model server (API) Ollama OpenAI API Anthropic API
Host / app local_agent, or Ollama's own chat app ChatGPT Claude app

ChatGPT is to the OpenAI API what my local_agent is to Ollama. Build on the API and you write the ChatGPT part: history, tools, the loop.

One twist: locally, Ollama sits in two rows at once. Its server (the API on port 11434) is the model-server layer, but its desktop chat window and ollama run in the terminal are hosts, thin clients of that same API. Imagine OpenAI shipping the API and ChatGPT in one download. My local_agent skips Ollama's chat window and talks to the API directly, the same way your own app would skip ChatGPT and call the OpenAI API.

3. There is no standard for talking to models (MCP vs function calling)

Every vendor has its own JSON dialect. OpenAI returns tool arguments as a JSON string, Ollama as a JSON object, and Anthropic uses tool_use content blocks instead of tool_calls. Same idea, three shapes, so every host needs an adapter.

That's also the answer to "MCP vs function calling". Function calling is the model side: you describe tools to the model and it replies with a request to use one. MCP standardized the tool side, not the model side: how a host finds and calls tools on a separate server. A real agent uses both. Since MCP's inputSchema and Ollama's parameters are both plain JSON Schema, my adapter between them is a single map().

Part 2: The illusions

4. Are LLMs stateless? Yes. Chat is an illusion

Maybe you already know this one: the model remembers nothing between calls. The host resends the entire conversation every turn, so "memory" is just a list in my Java process. That's all it ever is.

5. How tool calling actually works: it's just text

There is no special channel. Ollama's chat template renders your JSON tools into the prompt (see it with ollama show qwen2.5:7b --template). Trimmed, the model sees:

<|im_start|>system
# Tools
You are provided with function signatures within <tools></tools> XML tags:
<tools>
{"type": "function", "function": {"name": "append", "description": "Append content to the end of the file", ...}}
...
</tools>
For each function call, return a json object with function name and arguments within <tool_call></tool_call> XML tags
<|im_end|>
<|im_start|>user
Add buy milk to my notes<|im_end|>
<|im_start|>assistant

The model predicts the most likely next tokens, which, because it was trained on this format, are:

<tool_call>
{"name": "append", "arguments": {"content": "buy milk"}}
</tool_call>

Ollama parses that text back into a neat tool_calls JSON field. The "function call" is a string that looks like one. (Start Ollama with OLLAMA_DEBUG=1 to see the full rendered prompt.)

6. The model never touches the file

Ollama returns that tool_calls JSON to my host, and it's done. It has no idea an MCP server exists. My host reads the request, calls the MCP server over HTTP, and pastes the result back into the conversation as a role: "tool" message.

Ollama and the MCP server never talk to each other. The model requests. The host decides and acts. That's why the host is the real control point for safety, not the model.

How to add your own data to an LLM (no training required)

This is what I actually set out to learn. When the model calls read, my notes come back as a role: "tool" message and sit in the conversation like any other text. The model "knows" my file because the host pasted it into the prompt.

Every popular way to give an LLM your own data is this trick, except one:

  • Prompt stuffing: paste the data in yourself.
  • Tool calling / MCP: the model asks, the host fetches (this project).
  • RAG: the host searches your documents and pastes in the relevant chunks.
  • Fine-tuning: changes the weights. Good for behaviour and style, usually wrong for "make it know my documents".

So "train ChatGPT on my own data" usually means one of the first three. Choosing what goes into the context window is context engineering, and RAG exposed as an MCP tool is agentic RAG.

Part 3: MCP on the wire

7. MCP is JSON-RPC on one endpoint, not REST

An MCP server has exactly one endpoint, POST /mcp, and the operation lives in the body's method field (JSON-RPC 2.0). Since the 2026-07-28 spec, MCP is also stateless: no initialize handshake and no session ID. Every request carries its protocol version in params._meta, and the method and tool name are copied into headers, so a gateway can route without parsing the body.

What an MCP server's API looks like

If you build REST APIs for a living, this is the light-bulb view. Here is my server's entire API, OpenAPI-style:

POST /mcp                         the only endpoint (GET, DELETE -> 405)

method            params              returns
server/discover   (none)              supported versions, capabilities
tools/list        (none)              [{ name, description, inputSchema }]
tools/call        name, arguments     { content: [...], isError }

And here is the API the model actually sees, as returned by tools/list:

tool      arguments          what it does
read      (none)             return the whole file
write     content            replace the whole file
append    content            add a line at the end
update    search, replace    find and replace text
clear     (none)             empty the file

That's the whole thing: two lists. Think of tools/list as an OpenAPI doc written for a model instead of a developer. The full spec adds the same list-and-read pattern for resources (resources/list, resources/read) and prompts (prompts/list, prompts/get), but tools are where the action is. One call on the wire looks like this:

POST /mcp
MCP-Protocol-Version: 2026-07-28
Mcp-Method: tools/call
Mcp-Name: append

{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"append","arguments":{"content":"buy milk"},
 "_meta":{"io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion":"2026-07-28","io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities":{}}}}

MCP vs API: isn't MCP just an API?

Technically, yes. The difference is who it's designed for. A normal API is designed for a developer, who reads the docs and writes a custom client. An MCP server describes itself to a model: tools/list returns every tool with a plain-English description and a JSON Schema, so any MCP host can use any MCP server with no custom code. MCP usually wraps your existing APIs rather than replacing them.

8. There are two kinds of errors

  • Protocol errors (bad JSON, wrong headers, unknown tool) come back as a JSON-RPC error. They're client bugs, for the developer.
  • Tool errors (missing argument, wrong type) come back as a normal result with isError: true. They're for the model, so it can fix its call and retry. 
// unknown tool is a protocol error, bad arguments are a tool error the model can fix
try {
    registry.validate(toolName, params);
} catch (ToolNotFoundException e) {
    throw RpcException.invalidParams("Unknown tool: " + toolName, HttpStatus.OK);
} catch (ToolArgumentException e) {
    return CallToolResult.error(e.getMessage(), resultMeta);
}

Small models make small mistakes. Hand back Param (content) is required instead of throwing, and they usually fix it on the next step.

Part 4: The full trace

One /agent request, every hop.

1. You → host

curl -s localhost:8081/agent -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"message":"Add buy milk to my notes"}'

2. Host → MCP server: tools/list (id 1) returns the five tools.

3. Host → Ollama

POST /api/chat
{
  "model": "qwen2.5:7b",
  "messages": [ { "role": "user", "content": "Add buy milk to my notes" } ],
  "tools": [
    { "type": "function", "function": { "name": "append",
        "description": "Append content to the end of the file",
        "parameters": { "type": "object",
          "properties": { "content": { "type": "string", "description": "Content that gets appended" } },
          "required": ["content"], "additionalProperties": false } } },
    ... read, write, update, clear ...
  ],
  "stream": false,
  "keep_alive": "30m"
}

4. Ollama → host: the model wants a tool, and says nothing else (content is empty).

{ "message": { "role": "assistant", "content": "",
    "tool_calls": [ { "function": { "name": "append", "arguments": { "content": "buy milk" } } } ] },
  "done": true }

5. Host → MCP server: the tools/call request shown in moment 7. This is the only moment anything touches the disk.

{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"result":{"resultType":"complete","content":[{"type":"text","text":"Success"}],"isError":false,
 "_meta":{"io.modelcontextprotocol/serverInfo":{"name":"mcp_server","version":"0.0.1-SNAPSHOT"}}}}

6. Host → Ollama again, with the whole history

"messages": [
  { "role": "user", "content": "Add buy milk to my notes" },
  { "role": "assistant", "content": "",
    "tool_calls": [ { "function": { "name": "append", "arguments": { "content": "buy milk" } } } ] },
  { "role": "tool", "content": "Success", "tool_name": "append" }
]

7. Ollama → host: "content": "I've added \"buy milk\" to your notes." with no tool_calls, so the loop stops.

8. Host → you: the reply, plus a list of every tool call made.

Seven HTTP calls between three processes for two words in a text file. The model was in two of them, receiving text and returning text.

Part 5: The harness

9. The agent harness matters more than people think

Everything around the model is the agent harness. Here, that's my host. The loop itself is tiny (logging trimmed):

for (int step = 1; step <= properties.maxSteps(); step++) {
    Message reply = ollamaClient.chat(messages, tools);
    messages.add(reply); // the tool_calls must stay in history

    if (!reply.hasToolCalls()) {
        return new Result(reply.content(), invocations);
    }
    for (ToolCall call : reply.toolCalls()) {
        ToolInvocation invocation = invoke(call.function().name(), call.function().arguments());
        invocations.add(invocation);
        messages.add(Message.toolResult(call.function().name(), invocation.output()));
    }
}
throw new IllegalStateException("Agent did not finish within " + properties.maxSteps() + " steps");

The behaviour lives in the details:

  • An iteration guard (agent.max-steps=5), because a model that calls tools forever is a real failure mode.
  • Keeping the model's own tool call in history, or the tool result makes no sense to it.
  • Tool descriptions are written for the model. My write tool says "Write all contents to file". To a 7B model asked to "add" something, that can look fine, and then your notes are gone. "Replaces the entire file. To add a note, use append." works better.

A 7B model is slow on a laptop and not deterministic, but it's good enough to learn on, because every failure is visible.

What's next

10. Frameworks hide all of this

Spring AI can do everything above with an annotation like @McpTool. I'd use it in production. But now that Claude and I built it without one, I know what it hides, and when something breaks I know which of the seven hops to check.

  • v2: the same project with Spring AI, compared line by line.
  • v3: multiple notes files, then agentic RAG with a search tool.

FAQ

Do I need to train an LLM on my own data? Usually not. Put the data in the context window with a prompt, a tool/MCP server or RAG. Fine-tuning changes behaviour, not knowledge.

MCP vs RAG? RAG retrieves relevant chunks into the prompt. MCP lets the model call tools, and search can be one. Combined, that's agentic RAG.

Does the model execute the tool? No. It writes text asking for one. The host runs the tool and sends back the result.

Is MCP the same as function calling? No. Function calling is how a model asks for a tool. MCP is how a host finds and calls tools on another server.

Do I need MCP for tool calling? No. You can define tools in your app directly. MCP pays off when tools are shared across apps or teams.

Can a local model use MCP tools? Yes, if it was trained for tool calling (Qwen 2.5, Llama 3.1, Qwen 3). The model never talks to the MCP server anyway.

What changed in MCP 2026-07-28? It's stateless: no initialize, no sessions, and context travels in params._meta plus mirrored headers.

Try it yourself

Clone both repos, run docker compose up --build in local_agent, and send the curl from hop 1. Ollama runs natively on your machine, and Docker runs the rest.

  • github.com/abir4l/mcp_server (includes a full client integration guide)
  • github.com/abir4l/local_agent

The model is just numbers. Everything else is software, and software is something we already know how to read.

Co-written with Claude. If this was useful, a star on the repo helps.

title: How to Create an SVG Icon Sprite for Your Website
description:
Build a small navigation example with Home, Search, and a dismiss button using three icons from the same set. You will paste SVG code into the free SVG Sprite Generator, copy its output, and use the resulting symbols in a web page. No framework or build plugin is needed.

Once the generated sprite is included in your page, a visible icon needs only a reference to its symbol. Here is the Home link used in this example:

<a href="#home">
  <svg class="icon" width="24" height="24" aria-hidden="true" focusable="false">
    <use href="#icon-home"></use>
  </svg>
  Home
</a>

.icon { width: 1em; height: 1em; fill: currentColor; }

This short snippet assumes icon-home is already defined in the document. The steps below create that definition; section 3 contains the complete page you can copy.

When a sprite fits

A sprite defines each icon once inside a <symbol>. An <svg> containing <use> draws an instance wherever you need it. This is useful for repeated icons in plain HTML, server templates, and documentation. A small, deliberately chosen set is easier to maintain than a bundle of every available icon.

Sprites can reduce repeated markup, but they do not always improve performance. An inline sprite adds bytes to each HTML document; an external sprite needs a request but can be cached. Unused symbols still cost bytes. Measure your own pages. Separate SVGs or components may fit better when icons need different animations, per-instance path changes, or individual imports.

1. Choose three matching icons

Use the 24-pixel solid variants from HeroIcons: home-solid, magnifying-glass-solid, and x-mark-solid. Keep the same variant and grid rather than mixing outline, 16-pixel, and solid artwork.

On each icon page, use the basic Copy to Clipboard → SVG action. Basic SVG copying is available without signing in; the separate download action requires a verified Member account. Neither an account nor Pro is required to use this generator. See Copy SVG code for that workflow.

The reproducible inputs below come from the same set's official Heroicons v2.2.0 sources. They use a 0 0 24 24 viewBox. Heroicons is distributed under the MIT license; retain its copyright and permission notice with redistributed copies. Save a copy of the linked license alongside your example as LICENSE-heroicons.txt. The generator does not create a license manifest for you.

For an exact reproduction, paste these complete SVG documents into separate input blocks:

Name: home

2. Generate the sprite

  1. Open the SVG Sprite Generator. It starts with two blocks named icon-1 and icon-2.
  2. Replace the first name with home and paste the home SVG. Name the second magnifying-glass and paste its SVG.
  3. Click Add SVG Icon +. Name the new block x-mark and paste the third SVG. Use Remove for unwanted blocks; a named empty block prevents generation.
  4. Under Options, keep ID prefix as icon, Default size as 24, and HTML mode as Decorative. Leave Hide sprite by default and currentColor CSS helper checked.
  5. Click Generate Sprite. Check the previews and any errors or warnings. The output should contain icon-home, icon-magnifying-glass, and icon-x-mark.
  6. Select the Sprite tab and click Copy output. The other tabs are HTML snippet, CSS, and React. Copy each snippet you need.

This interface accepts pasted SVG markup, not uploaded files or a selection from Collections. It processes the markup in your browser. There is no file download button: you copy text and save files yourself. Load example set replaces the inputs with the tool's own samples; Clear restores two empty blocks. After editing names, SVGs, or options, click Generate Sprite again before copying to avoid stale output.

3. Use the output in a web page

Save the following as index.html. The hidden SVG is the actual generated sprite. It belongs once inside the document body; the visible SVGs reference its symbol IDs. The Home and Search icons repeat link text, so they are decorative. The icon-only dismiss button has its accessible name on the button and actually hides the notice.

Complete example: index.html

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>SVG sprite demo</title>
  <style>body { margin: 2rem; font: 18px/1.5 system-ui, sans-serif; color: #163b66; background: #fff; }

button { font: inherit; color: inherit; background: #eef4ff; border: 1px solid #7c94ad; border-radius: .5rem; padding: .6rem; cursor: pointer; }
:focus-visible { outline: 3px solid #b45309; outline-offset: 4px; }
.icon { width: 1em; height: 1em; fill: currentColor; vertical-align: -.125em; }
.icon-button .icon { width: 24px; height: 24px; }
.large { font-size: 32px; color: #9f1239; }
.dark { margin-top: 1rem; padding: 1rem; color: #e2e8f0; background: #172033; }
</style>
</head>
<body>

<h1>SVG sprite demo</h1>
<nav aria-label="Demo navigation">

  <a href="#search"><svg class="icon" width="24" height="24" aria-hidden="true" focusable="false"><use href="#icon-magnifying-glass"></use></svg> Search</a>
  <button class="icon-button" type="button" aria-label="Dismiss notice"
    onclick="document.getElementById('notice').hidden = true"><svg class="icon" width="24" height="24" aria-hidden="true" focusable="false"><use href="#icon-x-mark"></use></svg></button>
</nav>
<p id="notice">This is a dismissible demo notice.</p>
<section id="home"><h2>Home</h2><p>One sprite, three reusable symbols.</p></section>
<section id="search"><h2>Search</h2><p>This link is a navigation example, not a search engine.</p></section>
<p class="large"><svg class="icon" width="24" height="24" aria-hidden="true" focusable="false"><use href="#icon-home"></use></svg> A larger, differently colored instance</p>
<div class="dark"><svg class="icon" width="24" height="24" aria-hidden="true" focusable="false"><use href="#icon-magnifying-glass"></use></svg> The same icon on a dark background</div>

</body>
</html>

The generator produces the sprite and small snippets, not the surrounding page, navigation, or dismiss behavior. The example above supplies those parts. The generated wrapper is absolutely positioned with zero width and height, keeping referenced definitions available; its symbols are referenced by the visible SVG instances. Test this pattern with your target browsers, especially if you introduce gradients or filters.

4. Control size and color

The viewBox describes the artwork's coordinate system, not its displayed pixel size. Keep it on each symbol. The CSS helper sets width and height to 1em, so these icons follow their element's font size. The 24-pixel width and height attributes in a generated snippet are overridden by that CSS. Our button deliberately overrides the helper with 24-pixel dimensions; the larger paragraph uses a 32-pixel font size.

fill: currentColor makes this solid artwork follow CSS color. Change the surrounding text color to recolor its icons. The helper does not rewrite hard-coded colors inside paths, and it is a fill helper, not a stroke conversion. Keep intentional multicolor artwork unchanged. See MDN's currentColor reference.

Outline icons keep their paint settings. Supported root presentation attributes, including fill="none", stroke="currentColor", and stroke-width, are preserved on an internal group. Child shapes can still override them. Paste the complete SVG; no manual group wrapper is needed. The fill helper does not turn a preserved outline into a filled icon.

The preview renders the generated symbol. Root style and class are not copied; use explicit SVG presentation attributes. Root viewport effects such as clip-path, mask, filter, transform and vector-effect are not transferred and produce warnings. Review those warnings and the final appearance for complex artwork.

5. Optionally save an external sprite

Save the copied Sprite output as sprite.svg next to your HTML. Remove the inline sprite from that page and use a filename plus a fragment:

<svg class="icon" width="24" height="24" aria-hidden="true" focusable="false">
  <use href="sprite.svg#icon-home"></use>
</svg>

Keep the same CSS. Serve both files from the same origin using your project's local development server. Do not test external references by double-clicking the HTML file: file:// restrictions can prevent the SVG from loading. If Python is installed, run this command in the folder containing both files:

python -m http.server 8000 --bind 127.0.0.1

Open http://127.0.0.1:8000/index.html. Stop the server with Ctrl+C. An external sprite requires deployment of the asset as well as the HTML; check its URL, response type, caching, and your browser support. Do not assume a sprite on another domain will work just by enabling CORS. MDN documents external use references and same-origin restrictions.

Common problems and fixes

  • No output: remove unused empty blocks and paste one complete, valid SVG document per input. Fix the reported XML error before generating again.
  • Blank icon: compare the exact href fragment with the generated ID. A name like “Home Icon” becomes icon-home-icon, not icon-home. Keep input names unique and inspect final IDs; do not rely on suffixing to resolve every possible collision.
  • Wrong size or clipping: preserve the source viewBox and check CSS dimensions. The tool can infer a viewBox from positive numeric width and height (including px), but it cannot recover arbitrary missing coordinate information.
  • Black or missing outline: check the source fill and stroke settings and any generator warnings. A fixed fill on a child path will also override inherited color. Verify both light and dark backgrounds.
  • Broken gradients or masks: review rewritten internal IDs and every reference. This tool removes some obvious unsafe content but is not a comprehensive sanitizer for untrusted SVG. Use reviewed sources.
  • External sprite missing: use HTTP, check the request succeeds, and keep the asset on the same origin. Recheck the deployed path after moving files.
  • Repeated or missing accessible labels: hide decorative SVGs and name their controls. If you choose Labelled mode for a meaningful standalone icon, adapt its title and make title IDs unique for every repeated instance. The generated title IDs are based on symbol names. See the WAI button pattern and SVG icon accessibility guide.

Keep the workflow small

Start with three icons, review their actual use sites, and keep the source SVGs and license notice beside your generated output. Try the SVG Sprite Generator with your next small set of interface icons.

For more options, read the generator documentation. If your project needs automated generation, see Build an SVG Sprite for Modern Vite, React, and Vue Apps. For per-icon components, see Use SVG Icons in React with Vite and SVGR or the [SVG to Component Converter](https://svgicons.com/tools/svg-
