title: I don't have a single photo of my great-grandparents. So I built an altar for the people nobody remembers.
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

There is an idea from Día de los Muertos that I keep coming back to.

A person dies three times. Once when their body stops. Once when they are buried. And a final time, when the last person who remembers them is gone.

I went looking for a photograph of my great-grandparents to put on an ofrenda. There isn't one. Nobody in my family has a single picture of them. I don't know their faces at all.

So I went to the public archives instead, and found page after page of people in the same situation as my great-grandparents. Portraits from India, a hundred years old and more, labelled with a single line:

Unidentified woman.

Milk-woman, studio photograph.

Indian Christian, India, ca. 1910.

Someone loved each of these people. Someone paid for that photograph, dressed them in their best clothes, told them to hold still. And now nobody knows their names.

So I built them an altar.

A woman photographed for a lantern slide around 1910. Her name was not recorded. Above, the photo as it survives. Below, the same photo after Living Portraits.

What I Built

Living Portraits is a digital ofrenda for old photographs. You place a photo on the altar, and it comes back to you in one short sequence I call the Return:

  1. The photo appears as it is today: faded, creased, black and white.
  2. A thin line of candlelight passes down the photo and mends it.
  3. Colour spreads outward from the person's face, the way a memory comes back.
  4. The portrait settles into depth. Move your cursor, or tilt your phone, and it shifts gently, as if you were standing in front of a real print, while candlelight flickers brighter on whatever is nearest to you.

Under every portrait is everything we know about them, which is often almost nothing. A name if there is one. Her name was not recorded if there isn't. A link to the archive the photo came from and its licence, so you can check it is real. And a number showing how closely the restored face still matches the original.

Light a candle

If the final death comes when no one remembers you, the smallest thing we can do is remember.

Under each portrait there is one button: Light a candle. A fourth candle catches on the altar's shelf, and the server keeps count, one candle per visitor. It isn't much. But a woman whose name nobody wrote down, a hundred years ago, now has a number next to her that only goes up.

You can also place your own family's photos on the altar, and save their Return as a short video to send to the family group.

The Version I Threw Away

My first version animated the faces. One open-source model, a few lines of code, and Srinivasa Ramanujan's portrait from 1913 turned its head and broke into a wide, toothy grin.

It looked impressive for about two seconds. Then it felt scary and awkward. A man who never smiled like that for any camera was smiling at me because a model decided he should. These are real people. They can't agree to be made to smile for us, and they can't be asked.

So I deleted it. In Living Portraits the face is never moved, never re-posed and never given words. The photo comes back to life through light, colour and depth, the way a real photograph does when you carry it to a window. Every download is labelled AI-restored.

That decision changed the whole project, and I think it made it better.

Demo

Try it live: http://139.59.7.49 (light a candle for someone while you're there)

Watch the 68-second demo: demo video. A photo is placed on the altar, processed live on DigitalOcean, returns, and gets its first candle. The narration was generated with ElevenLabs.

Here is a photo being placed on the altar and processed live on the DigitalOcean server:

How It Works

Four open-source models run one after another on a single small server. The browser does the rest.

Mend. GFPGAN v1.4 repairs blur, scratches and damage on the face. I blend its output with the original at 60% instead of 100%, so the person keeps their own face rather than a polished stranger's.

Colour. DDColor predicts colour for black-and-white and sepia prints. It only predicts the colour; every bit of light and detail comes from the original photograph.

Depth. Depth Anything V2 estimates how near or far each part of the photo is. That depth map is what lets the portrait shift when you move, and what makes the candlelight fall on the face before the wall behind it.

Check. A face-recognition model (ArcFace, through facexlib) compares the face before and after restoration, and that score is printed under every portrait.

The server, a small FastAPI app, sends back three images: the photo as it was, the photo restored, and the depth map. The Return itself is a short WebGL shader running in your browser. The candlelight sweep, the colour spreading out from the face (located by the face detector), the depth and the flicker are all drawn live, so the original photo is never baked into a video.

Three Problems I Didn't Expect

1. Restoration makes everyone look like a stranger

Face-restoration models are trained to make faces look good, and "good" drifts toward young, smooth and symmetrical. For a stranger's photo, that's fine. For someone who can't tell you what they really looked like, it's a quiet kind of erasure.

So I measure it. The ArcFace check compares the face before and after for every photo. Across the eleven archive portraits I tested, ten scored 0.88 or higher, and the median was 0.94. On this scale, around 0.5 already means "probably the same person". The one low score, 0.74, was a side profile, which face models struggle with in general.

2. Sepia is not colour

Most 19th-century portraits are albumen prints: brown ink on cream paper, not black on white. My first black-and-white detector looked at saturation, decided these prints were already in colour, and skipped them. Half of my archive photos came back untouched.

The fix was to stop asking "is there colour?" and ask "does the colour depend on anything except brightness?" In a toned print, dark means brown and light means cream, and that's all. So I fit colour as a function of brightness and look at what's left over:

def is_black_and_white(img_bgr):
    small = cv2.resize(img_bgr, (256, 256))
    lab = cv2.cvtColor(small, cv2.COLOR_BGR2LAB).reshape(-1, 3).astype(np.float32)
    L, a, b = lab[:, 0] / 255, lab[:, 1], lab[:, 2]
    X = np.stack([np.ones_like(L), L, L * L, L ** 3], 1)   # colour as a curve of brightness
    leftover = sum(np.std(c - X @ np.linalg.lstsq(X, c, rcond=None)[0]) for c in (a, b))
    return leftover < 4.0   # sepia and grey prints leave almost nothing behind

Real colour photos leave a lot behind. Sepia and grey prints leave almost nothing. It now sorts every archive photo I have correctly.

3. The colours were too loud

DDColor's first results were vivid in a way old photographs never are: magenta suits, orange hands. I scale the predicted colour back by a quarter. The portraits look less like an advert and more like a hand-tinted print, which is closer to the truth of the era.

Built on DigitalOcean

The whole altar lives on one DigitalOcean CPU-Optimized Droplet, and DigitalOcean is a big part of why one person could build and ship this in a weekend.

It sits close to the people it's for. The portraits are from India, and so are many of the families I hope will use it, so the Droplet runs in DigitalOcean's Bangalore region.

Dedicated cores, steady timing. Restoring a photo is heavy, continuous number-crunching. On a CPU-Optimized Droplet with 4 dedicated vCPUs, a photo takes about 12 seconds, every time, with no noisy neighbours slowing it down.

One machine runs everything. The four models, the FastAPI server, the candle counts and the web page itself all live on the same Droplet as a single systemd service. There is no separate GPU service, no third-party AI API, and nothing else to keep in sync.

From a blank Droplet to live with one script. setup.sh in the repo installs the models on a fresh Ubuntu Droplet, and the service file keeps the app running across restarts. Every update during the build was a copy and a service restart.

It doesn't need a GPU. I planned to rent a GPU Droplet. Then I removed the face animation, the heaviest model, and found everything else fits comfortably on CPU: about 12 seconds per photo on the Droplet, against about 5 seconds on my laptop's 4 GB RTX 3050.

The cost is small and predictable. The Droplet costs $0.125 an hour, which works out to roughly $0.0004 of compute per photo, and the whole build ran on DigitalOcean's Hacktoberfest credit.

That matters for who can use this. A family, a small local archive or a school history project can run their own altar for a few dollars a day, or switch it off when no one is visiting.

Where It Falls Short

  • Colour is a guess. DDColor doesn't know what colour her sari really was. The page says so under every portrait.
  • Side profiles are harder. Face models are trained mostly on faces looking at the camera.
  • Faded sepia prints get only a hint of colour, because the paper tone dominates.
  • Hand-tinted prints are left alone. One 1860s portrait was read as already coloured. It may well be hand-tinted, so leaving it untouched is the honest result.

Why Open Source Matters Here

Commercial apps already "bring old photos to life". To use them, you upload your family's photographs to a company's servers, usually on a subscription, and accept whatever the model decides to do to the faces of people who can't object.

Every decision that shaped this project was only possible because the models were open:

  • When face animation felt wrong, I could remove it.
  • When restoration drifted away from the real face, I could measure it and turn it down.
  • When the colours were too loud, I could change them.
  • When sepia prints were skipped, I could fix the detector that a closed API would have hidden from me.

And the photographs never leave a server the family controls. Nothing is sent to an AI company, and nothing can be taken away by a subscription ending or an app shutting down. A memory deserves at least that.

The Moment It Landed

Her first candle was lit while I was recording the demo.

The script uploaded a portrait from the 1880s, a young woman in her best sari with every ornament she owned, captioned Her name was not recorded. The Return played, the colour came back into her face, and then the button was pressed and the count changed from nothing to 1 candle lit.

It's a small number. But it's one more than she had yesterday. Her portrait is in the gallery on the live site. If you visit, light one for her.

Prize Categories

Best Use of DigitalOcean. The entire app, from the four models to the API, the candle counts and the page, runs on one DigitalOcean CPU-Optimized Droplet, deployed with the setup script and systemd service in the repo. It shows that open-source image models don't need a GPU to be useful to a family.

Best Use of ElevenLabs. The demo's narration was generated with ElevenLabs, and the repo includes the script and the tools that cut the screen recording to each narrated paragraph.

Code

Tanhaker / living-portraits

Restore, colour and give depth to old family photos for the ofrenda. Open-source AI, the face is never changed.

Living Portraits

Bring an old family photo to the ofrenda. Living Portraits mends its creases, returns its colour and gives it depth, using only open-source models on a server you control.

The face is never moved, re-posed or given words. The photo comes back to life through light, colour and depth instead.

Built for the DEV Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 4: Ghost in the Machine.

The Return

When a photo is placed on the altar, the page plays one short sequence on a WebGL canvas:

  1. The photo appears as it is today: faded, creased, black and white.
  2. A line of candlelight sweeps down and mends it.
  3. Colour blooms outward from the person's face.
  4. The portrait settles into depth. It shifts gently with your cursor or as you tilt your phone and candlelight flickers brighter on what is nearer.

The page can record the Return as a video to…

View on GitHub

Built with help from an AI coding assistant. Every portrait shown is public domain or CC0, from Wikimedia Commons, with sources listed in the repository README.

title: Mistral Large 4 updated weights and lower pricing on AI Gateway

Then select mistral/mistral-large-4 in the agent. See the coding agents guide for details.

AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries, failover, and performance optimizations for higher-than-provider uptime. It includes built-in custom reporting, Zero Data Retention support, budgets for API keys, routing rules, and more.

AI Gateway reflects provider pricing with no markup and does not charge a platform fee on inference, including on Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) requests.

You can view all language models available on AI Gateway.

title: Designing Photo Slots for Multi-Person AI Video Templates
description:
A photo-to-video interface becomes more complicated as soon as a template supports two people or a group. A generic upload box does not tell users which photo belongs to which performer.

Dame Hombro AI is the product example here: fourteen dance and freestyle templates cover solo adults, duos, groups of three, cats and dogs. Outputs are 15-second, 720p MP4 clips with generated audio. The following is a practical interface design checklist for this kind of workflow, rather than a claim about any particular model architecture.

Treat each upload as a role assignment

A template should define its required cast before the user chooses files. Label the slots with the same role names used in the preview. For a duo, two distinct slots are easier to inspect than a single gallery of attachments. For a pet preset, make the expected animal type explicit.

Keep the selected template and its photo assignments together. If a user switches from a solo scene to a group scene, show the newly required roles before allowing generation. Do not silently treat a missing performer as an optional input.

Separate preparation from generation

Choosing a file, preparing an upload and starting a paid generation are different actions. The interface should make those boundaries visible. A useful review screen answers four questions: which template is selected, which photo fills each role, which aspect ratio will be generated, and what the request costs.

Dame Hombro AI offers 9:16 and 16:9 output and charges one credit per video. Its credit packs are one-time purchases; unused credits do not expire, and failed generations restore the credit. These are product rules worth showing before a request starts.

Validate the brief, then review the result

Input validation can confirm required slots and file constraints. It cannot guarantee that a generated face, hand or dance movement will look right. Completion therefore needs a second review step: watch the whole clip, including its audio, before downloading or sharing it.

For this product, photos must be authorized. Human subjects must be adults, and minors, celebrities and public figures are excluded. The result is a new AI interpretation, so the UI should not promise exact identity preservation or frame-by-frame replacement.

Describe audio independently

A dance template can evoke a movement style without including a commercial recording. This service creates new audio; it does not promise the original song, lyrics or an artist's voice. Dame Hombro AI is independent of Bulin 47 and Kevin Wai.

For builders, the useful design boundary is between the reference, the request and the generated result. Make each one inspectable, and users have a clearer basis for deciding what to create and what to share.

title: Shift‑Left Testing: Bringing Quality Forward in the Development Pipeline
description:
In modern software delivery, waiting until the end of a sprint—or worse, production—to discover defects is both expensive and demoralizing. Shift‑left testing flips that model by embedding quality activities early, where they can be acted upon quickly and cheaply. Below is a practical guide to adopting the mindset and habits that make early testing effective without discarding the valuable role of dedicated QA.

The Core Idea

  • Test earlier, not just more – Quality isn’t a phase; it’s a continuous activity. Involving QA during requirements gathering and design catches misunderstandings before any code is written.
  • Cost curve argument – The classic defect cost curve shows that fixing a bug in design can be 10‑100× cheaper than fixing the same bug after release. Early detection reduces rework, shortens feedback loops, and protects the budget.

Where It Starts

  • QA in requirement reviews – Bring a QA representative into backlog refinement and requirement workshops. Their perspective highlights ambiguous language, missing edge cases, and non‑functional expectations that developers might overlook.
  • Unit tests written with the code – Encourage developers to write unit tests alongside implementation, not as an afterthought. When the same person who writes the logic also defines its verification, the test suite stays tightly coupled to the intended behavior.

Practical Habits

  • Three Amigos sessions – Regularly schedule short meetings where the developer, QA, and product owner align on acceptance criteria. Translating user stories into concrete, testable statements ensures everyone shares the same definition of “done.”
  • CI runs tests on every commit – Configure the CI pipeline to execute unit, integration, and contract tests on each push. Immediate feedback (often within minutes) lets the team correct regressions before they accumulate, keeping the codebase healthy throughout the sprint.

What It Is Not

  • Not eliminating QA – Shift‑left does not replace dedicated testing roles. QA expertise is still essential for exploratory testing, usability assessments, and complex scenario coverage that automation cannot fully emulate.
  • Not skipping later‑stage testing – Early testing complements, not substitutes, regression, performance, and security testing performed closer to release. The goal is a layered safety net, not a single checkpoint.

Do / Avoid

Do

  • Involve QA at requirements/design stage, not just before release.
  • Write acceptance criteria as testable statements up front.
  • Run automated checks on every commit, not just nightly.

Avoid

  • Treating shift‑left as “developers test, so QA isn’t needed.”
  • Skipping late‑stage regression just because you shifted left.
  • Bolting “shift‑left” onto a process where nothing else changed; the whole workflow must adapt to early feedback.

Shift‑left testing isn’t a shortcut—it’s a disciplined expansion of quality practices that saves time, money, and frustration by catching problems where they’re cheapest to fix.

title: Introducing Virtual Models on AI Gateway
description:
Today, we are introducing Virtual Models on AI Gateway.

Virtual Models are an abstraction of the model string and configurations your apps and developers use. With a single virtual model ID, you can change and update models, configure fallbacks and priority, and enforce Zero Data Retention centrally. The virtual model configuration applies wherever the ID is used.

Assign a virtual model ID to an agent task, and pass it as the model string wherever that task is called. You can then change the model and settings behind the virtual model ID in AI Gateway, and your apps and agents will pick up the new configuration automatically, without code changes or redeploys.

New models use the same virtual model ID

In the last 90 days, 125 new models from more than 10 labs became available on AI Gateway. That adds up to about 10 a week. AI Gateway already makes switching a one-line change. You call any of those models by ID, and AI Gateway routes each request to a healthy provider and can fall back to others when one fails.

That one line still lives in your code, so switching usually means a redeploy.

Virtual Models move model selection and configuration to AI Gateway. You create an ID for a task, like vmc/coding-agent, and then configure the model and the settings it should use:

You can then use that virtual model ID as the model string wherever the task runs:

For coding agents like Claude Code, Codex, and others, connect them with vercel ai-gateway setup, then select your virtual model in each harness's model picker or configuration.

When a different model is available, including one from another provider, edit the virtual model. Every app and agent that calls vmc/coding-agent picks it up within a few minutes, with no code change or deployment needed:

Give each task its own model

An agent task like support ticket triage can run hundreds of times an hour and needs to be cheap. Other tasks, like legal contract review, may only run a few times a day, but require a high level of reasoning.

You can now give each task a purpose-built virtual model and easily evolve that model and configuration over time:

Settings such as fallbacks, Zero Data Retention, and tags stay with the virtual model when you switch models. Provider options apply per provider, so an Anthropic-specific setting stops applying when you point the virtual model at an OpenAI model. Review your provider options whenever you switch providers.

Before you switch a virtual model that serves production traffic, point a second one, like vmc/coding-agent-candidate, at the new model and run your evals against it. If quality drops after the switch, point the original back at the previous model.

Govern which models your team uses and how

Anyone on your team can call a virtual model, and team roles control who can make changes to it. Platform and security teams can centrally govern and test models and settings, while still easily giving teams access to new models as they are released.

Settings on a virtual model win over the same settings in a request, so callers can't override the provider order, fallbacks, or service tier you chose. For example, you can configure the fallback models for vmc/storefront-assistant centrally, and every app using that virtual model ID will use the same failover configuration, even if a request specifies different fallbacks.

If a virtual model requires Zero Data Retention or providers that don't train on request data, those configurations are enforced even if a request explicitly sets zeroDataRetention or disallowPromptTraining to false.

Tags on a virtual model replace any tags sent with the request, so spend lands on the task no matter how each app tags its calls. The Virtual Models page shows requests, spend, and success rate for each task.

Get started

Create a virtual model from your team dashboard or with the Vercel CLI.

About AI Gateway

AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries, failover, and performance optimizations for higher-than-provider uptime. It includes built-in custom reporting, Zero Data Retention support, budgets for API keys, routing rules, and more.

AI Gateway reflects provider pricing with no markup and doesn't charge a platform fee on inference, including on Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) requests.

Virtual Models work with every model type on AI Gateway, including image, video, speech, embedding, and realtime models, and with the AI SDK and the OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible APIs. See the Virtual Models documentation for every setting.

title: Node.js Code for Verifying Property-Management Phone Numbers with SMS (Audit Evidence)
description:
Short answer: for a property-management portal, use a managed OTP boundary when the requirement is proving control of a resident's phone, but keep the decision, expiration, attempt count, recipient, and provider response in your own audit record. Send through /v1/sms/otp, validate the submitted code in your application, and treat resend as a new rate-limited action through /v1/sms/resend/{id}. That gives the platform a reviewable record without making the SMS vendor the system of record.

Infrai fits this boundary when one REST API and one key can cover the communications call alongside other backend capabilities, while the property application keeps its own evidence policy. Its public discovery surface is self-describing and does not require a key, so the request schema can be reviewed before implementation rather than inferred from an SDK.

The important distinction is between delivery and evidence. An SMS provider can create and deliver a challenge; it cannot, by itself, explain why your leasing workflow accepted a phone number, which policy version applied, or why a number was suppressed after repeated failures. Those are application decisions.

What should the property portal actually prove?

The login flow has two separate questions: did the service send a challenge to the claimed number, and did the person presenting the code satisfy the verification policy? A successful provider response answers only the first question. Your database must bind the challenge to the account, record an expiration policy, count failed attempts, and retain enough provider metadata for an auditor to reconstruct the decision.

This is also where bounces and invalid recipients matter. A failed delivery is not proof that the person lacks access to the phone, but it is a useful signal for pausing future sends. Keep a suppression decision separate from the OTP decision: a number may be temporarily blocked for abuse, permanently invalid, or merely awaiting a delivery-status check. Do not turn a transient delivery failure into an irreversible identity judgment.

For a platform team, the invariant is simple: no accepted login without a valid, unexpired challenge tied to the intended account; no retry that can create an accidental second accepted state; and no resend path that bypasses the same abuse controls as the first send. The audit trail is part of the feature, not logging polish added after launch.

Which architecture fits the evidence requirement?

There are two viable shapes.

The first is a specialist verification service. Twilio Verify, Vonage Verify, and Amazon Cognito's MFA features each represent a different version of this approach: the provider owns more of the challenge lifecycle, while your application integrates at a narrower boundary. Twilio Verify is a focused verification product with a mature channel and country footprint; Vonage Verify is another managed verification option with its own regional and policy constraints; Cognito fits best when the identity system already lives in AWS and the application is willing to adopt its user-pool model. The trade-off is control. A specialist can reduce the amount of OTP machinery you operate, but it may leave your property-specific evidence model, suppression policy, and cross-channel records split across systems.

The second is an application-owned policy layer over a communications API. Your service owns challenge state, account binding, expiry, attempt limits, suppression decisions, and audit exports. The API owns SMS submission and the provider-facing delivery surface. Infrai is a deliberate option in this shape: its communications capabilities sit behind one REST contract, so adding adjacent backend capabilities does not require another SDK, key, and integration boundary. Its public discovery surface also exposes request and response schemas and runnable examples, which makes an API review easier to repeat during a control assessment.

I would choose the second architecture for a property-management platform when compliance evidence must connect the phone challenge to the resident, lease context, suppression decision, and policy version in one record. I would choose Twilio Verify, Vonage Verify, or Cognito when the team explicitly values a more managed identity workflow and can accept the provider's lifecycle and evidence boundaries. There is no honest universal winner here; the right answer follows the ownership boundary.

Decision Application-owned policy over a communications API Specialist verification service
Evidence One property-specific audit record can contain the decision inputs Provider records are more central, application context may be separate
Operating load You own expiry, attempts, suppression, and reconciliation More challenge lifecycle is managed for you
Lock-in Communications contract is narrower, policy remains yours Identity and verification workflow can be more provider-shaped
Best fit Compliance review needs account and property context together The team wants a pre-shaped verification product

How should Node.js code verify a phone number with SMS?

The send operation should create a pending challenge before calling the provider, then mark it sent only after a successful response. The provider's identifier belongs in that record. Store a hash or otherwise protected representation of the one-time code, never the usable code in plaintext, and expire the challenge according to the policy your security review approved.

The sample below keeps the provider payload outside the example because the verified contract is discoverable and the exact request schema should be copied from that live capability definition, not guessed from a blog post. It still shows the important operational properties: explicit POST, bearer authentication from an environment variable, status checking, Retry-After handling, and a bounded exponential retry for 429 responses. The application should supply a request body generated from the discovered schema through OTP_REQUEST_JSON. It uses only the Go 1.22 standard library.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func sendOTP() ([]byte, error) {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    payload := os.Getenv("OTP_REQUEST_JSON")
    if key == "" || payload == "" {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY and OTP_REQUEST_JSON are required")
    }

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPost, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/sms/otp", bytes.NewBufferString(payload))
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")

        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            wait := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); parseErr == nil && seconds > 0 {
                wait = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(wait)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("otp request failed with HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("otp request exhausted retries")
}

func main() {
    body, err := sendOTP()
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Println(string(body))
}

For a real create operation, add an idempotency key derived from the pending challenge before retries, using the provider's documented convention. The same key must not be reused for a separate resend. A resend is an explicit state transition, and the application should retain its own attempt and cooldown record before invoking /v1/sms/resend/{id}.

Keep it boring.

What does verification and rollback look like?

Your application endpoint should load the pending challenge, reject an expired or already-consumed record, compare the submitted code against the protected value, and atomically mark success. Rate-limit by account and phone number as well as by source address; otherwise an attacker can rotate one of those dimensions while brute-forcing the same challenge. Keep the failure response deliberately unhelpful so it does not reveal whether a phone is registered.

The rollback story deserves equal attention. If the SMS call fails, leave the challenge in a failed-send state and make the next attempt create a fresh pending record. If delivery later proves invalid, add the recipient to the appropriate suppression workflow and stop automatic sends until a reviewed action clears it. Since the relevant event surface is pull-based rather than webhook-driven, reconciliation needs a scheduled poll and a visible freshness timestamp. A dashboard that says “verified” without showing when its delivery evidence was last refreshed is not a compliance control.

Before production, test these cases explicitly: a successful first send, an expired code, a reused code, four consecutive rate-limit responses, a resend after cooldown, an invalid recipient, and a provider error with a non-2xx body. Rollback should disable new sends behind a feature flag while preserving already-created audit records. Do not delete evidence to make a failed migration look clean.

The conditional recommendation is therefore narrow: try Infrai for the communications boundary when one consistent REST surface and a discoverable, broad backend capability set reduce integration ownership, while your service remains responsible for property-specific OTP evidence and suppression policy. Choose a specialist verification product when managed identity lifecycle is more valuable than keeping that policy layer in your application. For the Infrai boundary, start with the SMS OTP guide and verify the current request schema before shipping.

References

  • RFC 4226: HOTP: An HMAC-Based One-Time Password Algorithm
  • RFC 6238: TOTP: Time-Based One-Time Password Algorithm
  • Twilio Verify documentation
  • Vonage Verify API documentation
  • Amazon Cognito MFA documentation
  • Infrai SMS OTP guide

title: phantom-cli: A Haunted Terminal That Possesses Your Shell with Open-Source AI
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

What I Built

Meet phantom-cli, a lightweight, cross-platform terminal pranking utility that turns your ordinary shell into a haunted environment.

When you or an unsuspecting friend type routine commands like ls, dir, or cd, the terminal executes its normal tasks without breaking your workflow. Simultaneously, however, it quietly fires an asynchronous request to a cloud-hosted open-weight AI model in the background. Within seconds, an ancient, glitchy "phantom" trapped inside the operating system outputs eerie, personalized commentary reacting directly to the command you ran and the folder you are currently viewing.

Demo

Code

GitHub Repository: phantom-cli

How I Built It

To make phantom-cli accessible to any developer regardless of hardware limitations (since I couldn't run a large model locally on my machine), I designed a zero-dependency, thin-client architecture:

  • Shell Hook Overrides: The project provides dedicated setup scripts (install.ps1 for Windows PowerShell and install.sh for Unix/Linux/macOS Bash/Zsh) that safely remove conflicting command aliases and append intelligent wrapper functions into your $PROFILE or ~/.bashrc/~/.zshrc.
  • Native OS Tooling: No Python, Node.js, or heavy runtimes are required on the host machine. It uses native shell features like PowerShell's Invoke-RestMethod and Unix curl.
  • Open-Weight AI Integration: It hooks directly into lightning-fast open-weight models (such as llama-3.3-70b-versatile hosted on Groq) via API, injecting dynamic path and command context into the prompt on the fly.
  • Pre-Flight Safety Checks: Both installers prompt securely for your API key and verify connection stability before making any modifications to your terminal configuration.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Open innovation was absolute core to making this project work:

  1. Escaping Corporate Guardrails: Closed commercial AI models come wrapped in heavy enterprise safety filters that immediately panic or refuse to participate if you prompt them to act like a spooky, glitchy machine ghost. Open-weight models gave me total creative freedom over the system prompt to build atmospheric horror and creative developer tools.
  2. Democratizing AI on Standard Hardware: Because I couldn't run heavy models locally, pairing lightweight client-side shell hooks with cloud-hosted open weights proved that developers on standard, resource-constrained laptops can still build rich, interactive experiences without expensive hardware.
  3. Transparent Extensibility: Having full control over the open architecture allowed me to structure prompt payloads and background threads cleanly without being locked into a proprietary vendor ecosystem.

The Spirit of It

Nothing beats testing this on a colleague or friend's machine, watching them type a routine ls or cd to look for a file, and suddenly seeing the terminal talk back to them with cryptic warnings about the directory they are in! It brings a playful, haunted pulse to everyday developer workflows.

title: Integrate Node.js Library for Error Tracking: Auditable 2026 Support Pricing Practices
description:
Short answer: keep the pricing decision and its audit record in the customer-support application, then put the error-tracking library behind a narrow capture boundary that carries a request ID, operation ID, rule variant, and redacted user context. Evaluate Sentry, Rollbar, Datadog Error Tracking, OpenTelemetry, and Infrai with the same failure fixtures. Choose the capture service that preserves that evidence without becoming the authority for the pricing result.

This is a governance problem disguised as a Node.js integration task. A support ticket that fails during a new pricing-rule rollout can tell the team which path failed and which cost bucket received the operation. It cannot, by itself, prove what the customer was charged. That proof belongs in the application audit trail.

What must an error record prove before it can attribute cost?

The useful event is deliberately narrow. It contains a request_id, an operation_id, the flag key, the selected variant, a pseudonymous user identifier, and the exception context needed to reproduce the failure. The support ticket body, payment credentials, and authentication material stay out of the event even if the selected library accepts arbitrary metadata.

The operation ID is the join key between two records with different responsibilities. The pricing service owns the durable decision and its idempotency key. The error service owns a report about what happened while that decision was being attempted. A repeated error report must not apply the pricing rule twice, and a failed report must not roll back or alter a successful pricing operation.

I initially treated the flag value as sufficient context for this kind of investigation. It is not. A value such as new_rule says nothing about which support action produced it, while an email address is both a weak correlation key and an avoidable privacy liability. A stable operation identifier plus a pseudonymous user key gives the investigation a join without copying the customer record into an observability system.

That distinction also sets the retention boundary. A compliance review can ask for the authoritative pricing decision, the reason for the decision, and the related error evidence, but an error tracker should not become a second ledger. Document that boundary before installing an npm library; otherwise, convenient context fields tend to become an accidental data export.

How should Node.js integrate an error-tracking library in practice?

Install the selected Node.js error-tracking library during process setup, initialize it with project-specific settings, and register its middleware for uncaught exceptions and HTTP errors. Add custom logging only around critical sections that need business context. A wrapper around every function creates a noisy record rather than an auditable one.

The integration test should use a fixed, redacted fixture instead of a production traffic dump. Give it one ordinary HTTP error, one uncaught-exception path, one duplicate report attempt, and one simulated 429 response. Assign the fixture deterministically to an old or new pricing variant, then send the identical event envelope through every candidate adapter.

The pass criteria are concrete:

  1. The receiving system contains the operation ID and variant.
  2. The business result is unchanged when error delivery is retried or fails.
  3. Sensitive support and payment fields are absent from the serialized event.
  4. A 429 response causes bounded backoff and honors Retry-After when present.
  5. A deliberately triggered sample error can be found using the operation ID.

Reject the candidate if the adapter hides a non-success response, duplicates the business operation, or requires an incident feature that it does not provide. Do not report benchmark numbers from this test. It is an acceptance test for evidence and ownership, not a performance study.

Keep the fixture boring.

The following wire-level probe uses the only verified capture route in this comparison. The 2026-11-01 discovery snapshot is the reference point for the route and capability claims here. INFRAI_ERROR_PAYLOAD must contain the redacted JSON envelope produced by the application; keeping that envelope in an environment variable makes the route test independent of any unverified request-field names. The explicit method, bearer token, and idempotency key are visible so the request can be inspected before it is placed behind a library adapter.

set -eu

: "${INFRAI_API_KEY:?INFRAI_API_KEY is required}"
: "${INFRAI_ERROR_PAYLOAD:?INFRAI_ERROR_PAYLOAD is required}"
: "${ERROR_OPERATION_ID:?ERROR_OPERATION_ID is required}"

response_file="$(mktemp)"
trap 'rm -f "$response_file"' EXIT

for attempt in 0 1 2; do
  status="$(curl --silent --show-error --output "$response_file" --write-out '%{http_code}' \
    --request POST 'https://api.infrai.cc/v1/errors/capture' \
    --header "Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY" \
    --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    --header "Idempotency-Key: $ERROR_OPERATION_ID" \
    --data-binary "$INFRAI_ERROR_PAYLOAD")"

  case "$status" in
    2*) cat "$response_file"; exit 0 ;;
    429)
      [ "$attempt" -lt 2 ] || { cat "$response_file" >&2; exit 1; }
      sleep_seconds="$((2 ** attempt))"
      sleep "$sleep_seconds"
      ;;
    *) cat "$response_file" >&2; exit 1 ;;
  esac
done

The probe is intentionally not the pricing transaction. The application writes its own decision record with its own idempotency key, and the capture adapter reports the resulting error with the same operation identifier. That separation makes a retry safe even when the observation service is unavailable.

Which service preserves the evidence without owning the decision?

Sentry and Rollbar are reasonable choices when the dominant requirement is a focused application-error workflow with a Node.js SDK. Datadog Error Tracking is a reasonable candidate when error investigation needs to live alongside an existing Datadog operations environment. OpenTelemetry has a different role: its Logs signal defines portable telemetry concepts and correlation fields, but it is an instrumentation and collection approach rather than a complete incident-triage product.

Those distinctions matter more than a feature checklist. A specialist can be the right answer when alert routing, source-map processing, session replay, or a mature incident workspace is a release requirement. A portable signal can be the right answer when the team wants to operate the collector and choose downstream storage. The correct comparison unit is the capture boundary, not the vendor logo.

Infrai is a measured candidate for that boundary. Its public discovery surface is self-describing and available without a key; the capability description includes request and response schemas, billing information, and runnable examples. The live discovery snapshot describes 295 routes across 20 modules, and documented capabilities have runnable examples in 10 languages. Those facts make it possible to inspect a contract before the Node.js adapter is deployed.

There is a second, different advantage for this support workflow: Infrai offers one key and one bill across the broader backend surface, rather than forcing the API process, queue worker, and reconciliation job to coordinate separate provider credentials and invoices. The breadth is real, while the interface remains a plain REST contract. In practical terms, a team can keep one application-owned capture method while changing the service behind it; the callers continue to depend on the boundary, not on a provider-specific SDK.

I recommend trying Infrai for the capture leg of a small, vendor-neutral error pipeline when the team values a self-describing REST contract and a replaceable backend across Node.js and worker processes. I would choose Sentry or Datadog when built-in incident workflows are mandatory, OpenTelemetry when portability and operated collection are the main requirement, and Rollbar when a focused error-monitoring product is the better organizational fit. The recommendation is conditional because the evidence boundary must remain useful even when the capture provider changes.

The limitations belong in the decision record. Threshold alert or notification routes, distributed-trace span-tree queries, source-map or crash-symbolication processing, Session Replay, and heartbeat monitoring for a job that never ran are outside Infrai's supported capability. Its flags lack change audit logs, evaluation statistics, parent-child dependencies, and a recycle bin; clients poll. Logs lack a user-deletion endpoint for a GDPR erasure workflow, or bulk export and subscription endpoints. A support platform with those obligations needs complementary systems and should not describe trace_id or span_id fields as a span-tree query system.

Option Boundary style Strong fit Boundary to verify
Sentry Node.js error-tracking SDK Context-rich application error investigation Alerting, retention, and privacy configuration still need ownership
Rollbar Node.js error-monitoring SDK A focused error workflow Confirm framework coverage and duplicate-report behavior
Datadog Error Tracking Error tracking within an operations platform Teams already using Datadog for operational analysis The wider platform becomes part of the investigation workflow
OpenTelemetry Instrumentation and collector Portable logs and correlation fields Downstream analysis and incident handling remain yours
Infrai Plain REST capture request A replaceable capture leg across runtimes Alerting, span-tree investigation, and erasure workflows need other systems

The table is a boundary map, not a ranking. The same fixture, the same redaction rules, and the same operation identifier should be used for every row.

How should rollout evidence survive a pricing-rule change?

Record the flag key, variant, operation ID, and pricing decision in the system that owns the support transaction before the rollout percentage changes. Send only the redacted diagnostic context to the error adapter. When a capture attempt is retried, reuse the operation-linked idempotency key for the report and keep the business idempotency key unchanged.

During the first rollout, inspect a deliberately triggered error from each variant and verify the join in both directions: from the support operation to its error evidence, and from the error evidence back to the authoritative operation record. A successful search is useful; it is not proof that the pricing result was correct. Reconciliation remains the authority.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai error-capture discovery reference, then run the same redacted fixture against the other candidates before selecting a production adapter.

Sources

  • OpenTelemetry Logs signal concepts
  • Sentry Node.js error monitoring

title: Here Lies My Toaster
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

What I Built

Every house has a drawer of dead things: the earbuds that play on one side, the charger with the split cable, the phone with the spiderweb screen. Nobody mourns them. Halloween ends tonight and Día de los Muertos begins tomorrow, two days for remembering the departed, so I gave the drawer an obituary page.

Here Lies is a small web app that runs on your own laptop. You take a photo of something that died, and Gemma 4, running through Ollama on the same machine, writes it a straight-faced newspaper obituary: a name, a cause of death, a life of service, who it leaves behind, a request in lieu of flowers, an epitaph. You can download the card as a PNG.

The rule: the model may invent a name. It may not invent a scratch. Every physical detail on the card has to point at something the model listed when it looked at the photo, and plain Go code checks that before you see it.

Living things get a notice instead.

In my tests the cat, the dog, the monstera and the person were turned away every time.

Demo

More cards on the landing page: https://nazboyko.github.io/here-lies/


The toaster survived. Mr. Chester Golden-Crust did not: "In lieu of flowers, please wipe the crumbs from beneath the toaster tray."


Agnes Petalbrook: "Survived by a terracotta shard and the faint smell of potting mix."


Mr. Arthur Glowwick: "It shone when asked, and dimmed when done."


The app, on another run of the same toast. On the right: what the model saw, and which sentence used each detail.

Run it yourself. You need Ollama, Go 1.26 and Node 20 or newer.

ollama pull gemma4:e4b
git clone https://github.com/nazboyko/here-lies && cd here-lies
make run
open http://localhost:8787

Code

nazboyko / here-lies

Obituaries for the things that died in your house, written by a local open-weight model.

Here Lies

Obituaries for the things that died in your house, written by a model on your own laptop.

Take a photo of something that died: a cracked phone, burnt toast, shoes with holes, last week's pumpkin. Gemma 4 runs on your computer through Ollama, looks at the photo and writes the thing a straight-faced newspaper obituary. The model may invent a name. It may not invent a scratch: every physical detail on the card has to point at something the model listed when it looked at the photo, and plain Go code checks that before you see it.

Point it at a cat, a person or a healthy plant and it refuses: "Still alive. Give it a treat instead."

Landing page: https://nazboyko.github.io/here-lies/

Run it

You need Ollama, Go 1.26 and Node 20 or newer.

ollama pull gemma4:e4b
git clone https://github.com/nazboyko/here-lies && cd here-lies
make run

Then open http://localhost:8787…

View on GitHub

How I Built It

  • Look. Gemma 4 gets the photo and returns JSON: thing, person, animal, living plant or unclear; what the object is; and what it sees, in three lists: damage, wear, features. Code numbers the details d1, d2, d3.
  • Gate. Plain code. People, animals and healthy plants get the still-alive notice.
  • Write. A second Gemma call, text only. It turns the numbered list into an obituary in JSON, and every sentence about the body carries the ids it uses.
  • Check. Plain Go, no model. The cause of death must cite a real damage or wear id, every life sentence must cite a real id, and everything must fit the column. A failing draft goes back once with the problems listed. If the rewrite fails too, code keeps what passes, rebuilds the rest from the detail texts, and the page says what it repaired.

Why two calls? The writer never sees the photo. It can only describe what the looking step wrote down, and because each reference is an id, my code can verify it. One call doing both would hand me prose I could either trust or not.

To measure it, I ran 17 photos from Wikimedia Commons through the real pipeline: 11 dead things, a cat, a dog, a healthy monstera, one person, an intact mug and a blurry shot. Then I opened every photo next to its details and marked each one true, false or unsure.

Measure Result
Photos 17
Gate decision correct 16 of 17
Obituaries printed 13
Passed the check on the first draft 12 of 13
Rewritten once after the check 1
Repaired by code after the rewrite 0
Details on printed cards 65
Really in the photo, checked by eye 53 true, 4 false, 8 unsure
Causes of death resting on a false detail 2
Median seconds 0.8 to look, 2.4 to write and check

Machine: Apple M5 Max, 64 GB, gemma4:e4b through Ollama 0.35.1. A card takes about 3 seconds. The one rejected draft was the charger's: its third life sentence cited no detail, and the rewrite fixed it.

The honest failure. My first look prompt asked for one list of details, each tagged damage, wear or feature. Gemma tagged almost everything as a feature. Burnt toast came back as "dark brown toasted surfaces", so the check found no injury and printed "Natural causes. It was simply no longer needed." Only 6 of 11 dead things had any damage or wear listed, and a split laptop charger became "white wired earbuds".

So I split the schema into three lists and asked for damage first. On the next run all 11 dead things had an injury. That run had its own bug: the model wrote "no visible damage" as an entry in the damage list, the check accepted it as an injury, and a blurred green glow was buried as Miss Petunia Bloomsworth, who "passed away due to no visible damage." Code now drops entries like that.

The table shows the check's limit. It proves that each sentence points at a listed detail, not that the detail is real. Two causes of death rested on details I could not find in the photo: a cassette adapter "suffered a missing screw hole" while its real injury, heat warping, went unmentioned, and a folded umbrella died of "torn fabric". That is why the card footer prints the model's list: you can hold the obituary up against the photo.

How it was tested:

  • 48 Go unit test cases: the check, the gate, the repair step, the HTTP routes, and the Ollama client against a fake server (bad JSON, missing model, Ollama down, timeout).
  • The live run above, plus two extra passes on three photos. The details barely moved, since the look step runs at temperature 0.2. The names changed each time, except the pumpkins, who were Mr. Josiah Gourdington twice.
  • 10 Playwright tests against the real server and model: upload, card, sentence-to-detail mapping, PNG download, still-alive notices, phone width, keyboard, missing model, Ollama down, the LAN address, and a full run that fails if any request leaves the machine.

Stack: Go 1.26 with net/http serving a React, Vite and TypeScript page; Gemma 4 E4B through Ollama; html-to-image for the PNG; Old Standard TT and UnifrakturMaguntia fonts bundled from Fontsource. The Ollama request pattern (structured JSON output, timeouts, plain-language errors) comes from my earlier project Backpack. The code here is new.

Photo credits, all from Wikimedia Commons: jack-o'-lanterns by Giulia Forsythe (CC BY 2.0), burnt toast by Sheep purple (CC BY 2.0), succulent by stephen boisvert (CC BY 2.0), light bulb by Shixart1985 (CC BY 2.0), and the shoes on the cover by Wolfmann (CC BY 4.0).

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

These photos show the inside of your home: the kitchen counter, the bathroom shelf, whatever is headed for the trash. With an open-weight model on the laptop they never leave it. No upload, no account, no retention policy. The server holds the photo in memory for one request and never writes it to disk.

It works with Wi-Fi off. The browser test records every request during a full run, and the count going to any host outside the machine is zero. Each obituary costs nothing.

Because the model runs on my machine, I could cut its job into two strict steps and check the output in my own code. The schemas, the temperatures and the check live in my repository, not behind an endpoint that can change or disappear, and HERELIES_MODEL swaps in any other Ollama model.

The limit is the eyesight of a small model. Gemma called the broken mug a "creamer jug" with a spout it does not have, and 4 of 65 details were wrong. I can see those mistakes because the pipeline shows them to me, and I prefer that to a better answer I cannot inspect.

The Spirit of It

The most surprising result was a refusal. In the first run Gemma looked at a rotting succulent, translucent and black at the edges, and decided it was alive: "This plant is still with us. Water it." Once the prompt said that brown, mushy or translucent leaves mean dead, Agnes Petalbrook got her obituary.

Día de los Muertos is about remembering through stories. A dead charger is not a grandmother, but it deserves a better send-off than the trash can: a name, a cause of death, and someone to survive it. In its case, "a set of mismatched plugs and a seldom-used surge protector."

Prize Categories

Best Use of Gemma: Gemma 4 runs locally through Ollama, does both the looking and the writing, and code checks its output against what it saw.

title: RunPod em reais: o que custa a hora, a sessão de 4 horas e o pod que ninguém desligou
description:
R$ 134, R$ 239, R$ 480. São três contas de GPU alugada na RunPod que ninguém quer receber: o que se paga ao deixar um pod ligado por 48 horas numa RTX 3090, numa 4090 e numa A100.

Os preços saíram da tabela de preços da RunPod (marcada como atualizada em 28/10/2026, consultada em 31/10/2026). Converti com US$ 1 = R$ 5,397 e 3,5% de IOF, ou R$ 5,59 por dólar; o spread do seu banco não está incluído. Não rodei teste na plataforma, é conta sobre a tabela.

A hora, em reais

A 3090 de 24 GB custa US$ 0,50 por hora, R$ 2,79. A 4090 (24 GB), US$ 0,89, R$ 4,97. A L40S de 48 GB, US$ 1,09, R$ 6,09. A A100 de 80 GB, US$ 1,79, R$ 10,00. A H100 PCIe, US$ 2,89, R$ 16,14. Uma sessão de 4 horas fica entre R$ 11 (3090) e R$ 65 (H100).

Memória é o que você está comprando

Entre a 4090 e a A100 há R$ 5 de diferença por hora e 56 GB de memória. Se o seu modelo cabe nos 24 GB, esses 56 GB ficam parados. Começaria numa 3090 ou 4090 e só subiria para a L40S (48 GB) quando o erro de memória aparecesse.

Se for criar a conta, este é o meu link de afiliado da RunPod. Eu rodaria primeiro um script pequeno para ter certeza de que ele funciona antes de alugar hora cara.

O disco, que o pod parado não desliga

A tabela de armazenamento mostra o Volume Disk a US$ 0,10 por GB por mês com o pod rodando e US$ 0,20 com ele parado. Para 100 GB de modelos, são R$ 112 por mês parado. O Network Storage padrão, a US$ 0,07 por GB abaixo de 1 TB, daria R$ 39 pelos mesmos 100 GB; leia na documentação o que diferencia os dois antes de decidir.

Quando nem vale alugar GPU

Se o seu código só chama API de terceiros, o que você precisa é de um servidor pequeno, como a VPS da Hostinger (comparei promoção e renovação aqui). GPU só quando o modelo roda na máquina alugada.

Links de afiliado: se você assinar por eles, o Sinal Aberto pode receber uma comissão, sem custo extra. Texto produzido com assistência de IA.

title: React's XSS protection didn't save this app — a ref callback killed it
description:
Exploiting stored cross-site scripting in OopsSec Store's product review functionality to execute JavaScript in every visitor's browser.

The product reviews feature in OopsSec Store doesn't sanitize input. At all. You can drop a <script> tag into a review, it gets saved to the database, and it runs in every visitor's browser. Here's how to go from a comment box to stealing a flag.

Lab setup

From an empty directory:

npx create-oss-store oss-store
cd oss-store
npm start

Or with Docker (no Node.js required):

docker run -p 127.0.0.1:3000:3000 leogra/oss-oopssec-store

The app runs at http://localhost:3000.

Vulnerability overview

Users can submit reviews on product pages. Those reviews get stored in the database and displayed back when someone loads the page. The problem: the server saves whatever you type without sanitization, and the frontend renders it as raw HTML. If your "review" happens to be a script tag, the browser will execute it.

Here's what happens:

  1. Submit a review containing JavaScript
  2. The backend stores it as-is
  3. Any user who visits the product page gets the review injected into their DOM
  4. The browser executes the script in that user's session

Locating the attack surface

Go to any product page and scroll down to the reviews section. There's a list of existing reviews and a form to add your own.

Submitting a review sends a POST to /api/products/[id]/reviews. The backend stores the content directly, the frontend renders it without escaping.

Exploitation

Discovering the target

Looking through existing reviews, there's a comment from "Mr. Robot":

"Heard the devs left some old flags lying around at the root... files that say exactly what they are. Classic mistake!"

A flag file at the application root. Given the naming convention, /xss-flag.txt is the obvious guess.

Crafting the payload

First, confirm the XSS works:

<script>
  alert("XSS");
</script>

If that pops an alert, input is being executed as code.

Now the real payload -- fetch the flag and display it:

<script>
  fetch("/xss-flag.txt")
    .then(r => r.text())
    .then(flag => alert("Flag: " + flag));
</script>

Executing the attack

  1. Open any product page in OopsSec Store
  2. Scroll to the reviews section
  3. Paste the payload into the review textarea
  4. Click Submit

The API saves it as a regular review. No validation, no filtering.

Triggering the vulnerability

Refresh the page. The malicious review loads from the database, gets injected into the DOM, and the browser sees the <script> tag and runs it.

The script fetches /xss-flag.txt (same-origin, no CORS issues) and pops the flag:

OSS{cr0ss_s1t3_scr1pt1ng_xss}

Anyone who visits this product page from now on triggers the same script.

Vulnerable code analysis

Server-side: no input sanitization

The API endpoint stores whatever the user sends:

const review = await prisma.review.create({
  data: {
    productId: id,
    content: content.trim(), // No sanitization performed
    author,
  },
});

trim() strips whitespace. HTML and JavaScript pass through untouched.

Client-side: raw HTML injection

The frontend injects review content into the DOM through a ref:

<div
  ref={el => {
    reviewRefs.current[review.id] = el; // Raw HTML injection
  }}
  className="text-slate-700 dark:text-slate-300"
/>

This sidesteps React's built-in XSS protection. Normally React escapes anything passed as a JSX expression, but setting HTML through a ref bypasses that.

Remediation

Server-side sanitization

Strip dangerous HTML before it hits the database. DOMPurify handles this:

import DOMPurify from "isomorphic-dompurify";

const review = await prisma.review.create({
  data: {
    productId: id,
    content: DOMPurify.sanitize(content.trim()),
    author,
  },
});

Script tags and event handlers get removed before anything is saved.

Client-side safe rendering

Let React do what it's designed to do -- escape HTML:

<div className="text-slate-700 dark:text-slate-300">{review.content}</div>

Passing content as a JSX expression means React escapes HTML entities automatically.

Apply both fixes. Server-side sanitization stops malicious content from entering the database. Client-side escaping stops it from executing even if something slips through. Either one blocks this attack on its own, but XSS is one of those things where you really want both layers.

title: Building an In-Browser 478-Point Facial Landmark & Symmetry Analyzer (Zero Cloud Uploads)
description:
Most facial measurement and "rating" applications on the market today share two huge flaws:

  1. They charge aggressive subscription fees.
  2. They upload users' personal biometric selfie photos to centralized cloud servers.

I built FaceIQ as an open web application that executes 100% client-side in the browser.

How It Works Under the Hood

Using Google's MediaPipe 478-point landmark topology and WebAssembly/WebGL, the application computes:

  • Bilateral Cranial Symmetry: Evaluates lateral deviation across 32 anatomical mirror pairs.
  • Palpebral Canthal Tilt: Accurately measures inner-to-outer canthus inclination in degrees.
  • Facial Thirds & FWHR: Bizygomatic cheekbone width to midface height proportions.
  • Golden Ratio (Phi 1.618): Mathematical alignment against classical neoclassical cannons.
  • PSL Scale Rating Calculator: Quantitative facial harmony scoring.

Because the entire inference model runs in local browser memory via WebAssembly, zero bytes of photographic data ever touch a remote server.

Check out the live web app: Link

Would love to hear technical feedback and suggestions for additional craniofacial ratios to implement!

title: Virtual models now available on AI Gateway
description:
Virtual models are now available on AI Gateway.

A virtual model is a saved configuration that tells AI Gateway which model and settings to use. Your apps and agents call it with a custom model ID, such as vmc/coding-agent. You can change the model or settings centrally in AI Gateway without redeploying your apps or reconfiguring your agents.

Use virtual models to:

  • Configure coding agents: Set reasoning effort, fast mode, prompt caching, and other options even when your agent doesn’t expose them.

  • Control routing and compliance: Choose providers, configure fallback models, and enforce requirements such as Zero Data Retention.

  • Attribute spend: Attach custom reporting tags to every request that uses the virtual model.

To create a virtual model, open the Virtual Models page and click Create Virtual Model. Enter a slug, choose the underlying model, configure the settings you want requests to use, and save.

Or create one with the Vercel CLI:

To use a virtual model, replace the provider model ID in your AI SDK or compatible API requests with vmc/<slug>, such as vmc/coding-agent.

For coding agents, connect to AI Gateway with vercel ai-gateway setup if needed, then select your virtual model in the agent’s model picker or configuration.

Virtual models work with every model type on AI Gateway. Read the launch post for examples or learn more in the virtual models documentation.
