title: 👻 RepoGhost: Bringing Forgotten Codebases Back to Life with Local AI
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine.

What I Built

I built RepoGhost, a local AI-powered repository analyzer designed to bring forgotten and abandoned codebases back to life.

Every repository has a story, but understanding an unfamiliar project can sometimes feel like exploring a haunted house. There may be unfinished tasks, confusing file structures, undocumented functions, and code that nobody remembers writing.

That's where RepoGhost comes in! 👻

Users can upload a repository as a ZIP file, and RepoGhost scans it to discover:

  • Repository Overview: Detects source files, programming languages, and project structure.
  • Forgotten Tasks: Finds TODO, FIXME, and HACK comments that may have been left behind.
  • Python Syntax Findings: Identifies basic Python syntax issues.
  • Chat with the Ghost: Ask questions about the repository and get AI-powered explanations.
  • Haunted Project Report: Generates an AI-assisted report to help developers understand their codebase.

I interpreted the theme Ghost in the Machine as giving a voice to forgotten codebases. RepoGhost acts like a friendly ghost that helps developers understand what is happening inside a project, even when its original developers are no longer around.

Demo

🎥 Video Demo:

Note: RepoGhost is designed primarily for local execution, so the demo can showcase the application running on your machine.

Code

💻 GitHub Repository: https://github.com/Sourodip1804/RepoGhost

Contributions, feedback, and suggestions are welcome!

How I Built It

I built RepoGhost using a combination of open-source technologies and local AI inference.

AI Model:

  • Qwen2.5:3B – An open-weight language model used to understand repository context, answer questions, explain code, and generate reports.
  • Ollama – Runs the model locally, allowing RepoGhost to communicate with the AI without depending on a hosted AI API.

Backend:

  • Python
  • FastAPI
  • Repository scanning and file analysis
  • ZIP extraction and processing
  • REST API endpoints for uploading repositories, chatting, and generating reports

Frontend:

  • React.js
  • Vite
  • CSS
  • Lucide React icons

How it works:

  1. The developer uploads a repository ZIP file.
  2. The FastAPI backend safely extracts and scans the repository.
  3. RepoGhost identifies programming languages, source files, and unfinished task markers.
  4. Relevant repository context is prepared for the AI model.
  5. Qwen2.5:3B processes the context through Ollama and generates explanations or answers.
  6. The frontend displays scan results, AI conversations, and the generated project report.

One of my main goals was to keep the AI workflow local. The project does not need a paid cloud AI API to perform its core AI tasks.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Open innovation made this project possible in a way that would have been difficult to achieve with a closed AI API alone.

Using an open-weight model like Qwen2.5:3B with Ollama gave me the opportunity to experiment with local AI inference, understand how models interact with application backends, and build an AI-powered tool without depending on paid API access.

It also offers some important advantages:

  • Privacy: Repository source code can remain on the developer's machine when using the local setup.
  • Accessibility: Developers can experiment without needing a paid AI API subscription.
  • Customization: The model and AI workflow can be modified according to project requirements.
  • Transparency: Developers have more control over the tools and infrastructure powering their AI applications.
  • Community: Open-source models and frameworks make it easier for developers to learn, contribute, and build on existing work.

For me, open innovation is not just about using free tools. It is about having the freedom to understand, experiment, modify, and build something useful.

The Spirit of It

The most interesting part of building RepoGhost was thinking about how much knowledge gets trapped inside old repositories.

A developer might leave a project unfinished, forget how a particular function works, or return to an old codebase after months or years.

Instead of manually exploring every file, imagine asking:

"Hey Ghost, what is this project actually doing?"

And getting an explanation from the code itself.

That is the idea behind RepoGhost: every codebase deserves a second life.

Prize Categories

  • Open-Source AI Challenge – Ghost in the Machine (Week 4)

Building RepoGhost has been a great learning experience. I explored local LLM integration, Ollama, FastAPI, React, repository analysis, and the practical challenges of connecting an AI model with a real application.

There is still plenty of room to improve, and I would love to hear your feedback and suggestions!

Let's bring forgotten codebases back to life. 👻

Hacktoberfest #OpenSourceAI #Ollama #Qwen #React #Python #FastAPI #OpenSource #AI

title: I made my tmux sessions reachable from a 2002 Nokia
description:
I run my work in tmux: builds, logs, servers, and lately a lot of AI coding agents. The thing about an agent in a pane is that it stops and waits for me. "May I run this?" "Which of these three?" "Done." And I am never at that keyboard when it asks. I am in the kitchen, on the train, on a walk.

So I built muxway: a small Go agent next to tmux on each machine, a hub, and clients. The clients got out of hand. There is a browser one, an Android one with a Wear OS watch face, one for Even Realities G2 glasses, and a Java ME MIDlet that runs on a Nokia 6310i from 2002.

That phone has a 96 by 65 pixel screen, GPRS, and cannot do modern TLS. It reads Claude Code and answers it. This post is about why the Nokia was the useful one to build, not the silly one.

The agent calls you

The part I use most is the notification. Claude Code, Codex and Antigravity tell muxway, through their hooks, when they ask a question, want a permission, go idle, or finish. The pane lights up in every client, the phone and the watch buzz, the glasses show a banner at the foot of whatever I am reading. Then I answer from wherever I am: a tap, Enter, y, a number, a few words, or I hold the microphone and say it. The hub transcribes, the words land on the input line, and nothing is sent until I confirm.

In the browser I get up to four tiles from any mix of machines, all live and typable. Drag a header to swap, drag a divider to resize, and tiles that are one tmux window's panes move that window on the host as I rearrange them.

A lens for tiny screens

A terminal does not fit on a watch or a pair of glasses, and certainly not on 96 by 65 pixels. What does fit is the conversation. A lens knows what an agent's screen looks like and reshapes it: the box drawing, the status line and the spinner go, the question and the prompt stay. On the glasses that is eight short lines. On the Nokia it is whatever the screen holds, and you scroll with a key. Whatever the agent suggests in its input box is offered as the first answer, so most of the time the reply is one key.

The lens is also why the Nokia was worth doing. If the API is small enough that a MIDP 1.0 phone can be a client, in under 30 KiB of JAR, then anything can. The protocol has a plain text mode: one authenticated GET returns a pane wrapped to the width you ask for. A phone of that age cannot speak current HTTPS, so it goes through a small relay that terminates TLS for it. The MIDP 2.0 build, on a Nokia 7310 from a few years later, adds colour, Unicode and the camera: take a photo of a whiteboard, it lands in an inbox on the host, and the path is typed into the reply for the agent to read.

It is a remote shell, so build it like one

Whoever can type into a tmux pane owns that machine. I did not want a "trusted network" bypass or a convenience mode that becomes the default.

  • Panes are opt-in. Nothing is reachable until its owner marks it with muxway expose.
  • A token names which hosts and panes it may read, and separately which it may type into. Read and write are different grants.
  • Input is text and a fixed grammar of named keys. Clients never send raw escape sequences.
  • Every authentication step is rate limited and locked out. Secrets are hashed, compared in constant time, never logged.
  • Every write to a pane is audit logged on the host: who, when, which pane, how many bytes.
  • The agent dials out to the hub over a signed, encrypted WebSocket. Nothing listens on your machines, and clients never reach them directly.
  • One static Go binary per role, one third party dependency, no cgo.

The hub signs people in with OpenID Connect if you have an identity provider, or with tokens if you do not. It serves the web client from files embedded in the binary, so there is nothing else to deploy.

Getting it running 

go install github.com/notmarkopadjen/muxway/cmd/muxway@latest

# on the hub
muxway hub serve --listen 127.0.0.1:7600 --public-url https://hub.example.com --trust-proxy &
muxway hub pair-code --host alice-laptop

# on the machine with tmux
muxway agent pair <code>
muxway agent run &
muxway expose -t work:1.0 --write --name build
muxway hooks claude-code

# back on the hub: a token for a client
muxway hub token create --name phone --read 'alice-laptop/*' --write 'alice-laptop/@build'

Open the hub in a browser and paste the token. For a script or your own client, a pane is one request away:

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Accept: text/plain" \
  "https://hub.example.com/v1/panes/alice-laptop/@build?width=40&lines=20"

Build your own client

That last request is the whole point. The protocol is documented with examples and a diagram for every flow: bearer tokens, JSON and text mode, long polled events, the key grammar, rate limits, error codes. The four clients I wrote are proof that it holds up from a React app down to a feature phone. If you have a device I do not, a Kindle, an e-ink badge, a Game Boy with a link cable, the API will not be what stops you.

Where it is

It is young and I use it every day. Everything is Apache 2.0:

  • muxway: hub, agent, web client and the protocol. First tagged release v0.1.0, static binaries for Linux and macOS.
  • muxway-android: phone and Wear OS, APKs on the releases page.
  • muxway-glasses-even: the Even Realities G2 app.
  • muxway-midp: the Nokia, MIDP 1.0 and 2.0 JARs on the releases page.

Claude Code, Codex and Antigravity are the agents I have tested the hooks and the lens with. Another CLI needs its hooks to call muxway notify on the host and a lens for its screen, and that is a pull request I would be glad to see. If you try it, the thing I most want to hear is where the security model gets in your way, because that is where I would rather hear it from you than find out later.

title: How to Learn React Hooks (and Stop Fighting useEffect)
description:
The first React app I wrote with hooks had a useEffect that fetched a user profile. It worked on the first load. Then I added the user ID to the dependency array because the linter told me to, and the network tab filled up with the same request, over and over, until the tab froze.

I fixed it by deleting the dependency array. That was the wrong fix, and it took me an embarrassingly long time to understand why.

Most people learn hooks the way I did: copy a pattern, hit a bug, paste a Stack Overflow answer. You end up knowing a dozen workarounds and none of the ideas underneath. Here's the order I'd learn them in now.

Start with what a render actually is

Before any hook makes sense, you need one mental model. Every time state changes, React calls your component function again, top to bottom. Every variable inside it is created fresh. Every function you define inside it is a new function.

That's why this logs a stale value:

function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

  function handleClick() {
    setCount(count + 1);
    console.log(count); // still the old number
  }

  return <button onClick={handleClick}>{count}</button>;
}

count belongs to the render that created handleClick. It isn't a live variable that updates in place. The new value only exists in the next render. Once that clicked for me, half my "hooks are weird" complaints went away. They weren't weird. I just thought my component was an object that stuck around, and it's really a function that runs again.

useState: learn the updater form early

You'll use useState constantly, so learn the one detail that bites people. If the new state depends on the old state, pass a function:

setCount(c => c + 1);

Call setCount(count + 1) three times in one handler and you get +1, because all three read the same count. Call setCount(c => c + 1) three times and you get +3. I'd also learn that objects in state get replaced, not merged, so setUser({ ...user, name }) is the habit to build.

useEffect is for syncing with things outside React

This is where most of the pain is, and the React docs rewrite at react.dev is the best thing I've read on it. The short version: an effect is for keeping your component in sync with something React doesn't control. A network request, a subscription, a timer, a DOM API, a third-party widget.

The dependency array isn't a list of "when to run". It's a list of every value from the render that the effect reads. If you lie to it, you get stale data. If you include an object or function that's recreated every render, you get my infinite loop.

The fixes I reach for, in order:

  1. Move the function inside the effect, so it isn't a dependency at all.
  2. Depend on primitive values (user.id) instead of whole objects (user).
  3. Ask whether this needs to be an effect in the first place.

That third one matters most. The docs page You Might Not Need an Effect is worth reading twice. Filtering a list, computing a total, resetting a form when a prop changes: none of these need useEffect. You can calculate them during render. A lot of my old bugs came from effects that set state that could have just been a variable.

And write the cleanup. If an effect subscribes, starts a timer or opens a socket, return a function that undoes it. In development, Strict Mode runs your effects twice on mount to flush out missing cleanups, which is why your fetch shows up twice in the console. That's on purpose.

useRef, useMemo and useCallback can wait

useRef is simple once you see it as a box that survives renders without causing one. Use it for DOM nodes and for values you need to remember but never display, like an interval ID.

useMemo and useCallback are performance tools. I'd skip them until you have a real reason, like a slow calculation or a memoized child component that keeps re-rendering. Wrapping everything in them makes code harder to read and usually doesn't make it faster.

Custom hooks come last, and they're just functions that start with use and call other hooks. The first time you pull a useDebounce or useLocalStorage out of two components that both had the same effect, you'll get why they exist.

Build small things that break

Reading about hooks only gets you so far. These four tiny projects cover almost every common mistake:

  1. A counter with a "+3" button, to learn the updater form.
  2. A search box that fetches results as you type, to learn dependencies, cleanup and race conditions.
  3. A stopwatch with start and stop, to learn useRef for the interval ID.
  4. A dark mode toggle saved to localStorage, pulled into a custom hook.

Do them without a tutorial open. When something loops or shows stale data, that's the lesson.

Then make it stick

My actual problem with hooks wasn't understanding them once. I'd read the effects docs, get it, and a month later on a different project write the same broken fetch again. The rules of the dependency array are the kind of thing you know in theory and forget in practice.

What helped was reviewing the handful of ideas that kept tripping me up: renders are snapshots, the updater form, dependencies are what the effect reads, maybe you don't need an effect. I'd look at those notes after a day, then a few days, then a couple of weeks. That's spaced repetition, and it works better for this than rereading a tutorial when you're already stuck.

I built Recl for exactly this kind of learning. You share a video, article, reel or podcast to it, say a conference talk on effects or the react.dev page itself, and it writes a summary of the key points, files it under a topic like "React", and brings it back for review on a spaced repetition schedule. A plain notes file with calendar reminders does the same job if you'd rather not use an app. What matters is seeing it again before the next bug does the reminding for you.

I build Recl, an AI learning app that saves your videos, reels, podcasts and articles, summarizes them, sorts them into topics, and uses spaced repetition so you remember what you learned.

title: Secure Amazon S3 Buckets Using IAM Policies and Bucket Policies
description:
Introduction

Amazon S3 is one of the most widely used AWS services, and also one of the most common sources of data leaks. Almost every S3 breach in the news comes down to one thing: a misconfigured access policy.

In this article, I'll explain the two main ways of controlling access to S3, IAM policies and bucket policies, show when to use each, and walk through a hands-on example you can try in your own account.

How S3 Access Is Evaluated

Before writing any policy, it helps to know how AWS decides whether a request is allowed:

Everything is denied by default.
An explicit Allow in a relevant policy grants access.
An explicit Deny always wins, no matter what else says Allow.
For requests within the same account, access is granted if either the IAM policy or the bucket policy allows it (and nothing denies it).

Remember this rule: Explicit Deny > Allow > Default Deny.

IAM Policies vs Bucket Policies
Feature IAM Policy Bucket Policy
Attached to IAM user, group, or role The S3 bucket
Answers the question "What can this identity do?" "Who can access this bucket?"
Has a Principal element No Yes
Cross-account access Needs help from the other side Supported directly
Best for Managing permissions for your users and roles Bucket-wide rules, cross-account access, enforcing conditions
Size limit 2 KB (users), 6 KB (groups), 10 KB (roles) 20 KB

Simple way to remember it:

IAM policy = identity-based ("what can I do?")
Bucket policy = resource-based ("who can touch this bucket?")
Hands-On: Secure a Bucket Step by Step
Step 1: Create a Private Bucket
Open the S3 console and choose Create bucket.
Give it a unique name, for example vishal-secure-demo-bucket.
Keep Block all public access turned ON.
Enable Bucket Versioning.
Enable Default encryption (SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS).
Choose Create bucket.

Tip: Block Public Access is your first line of defense. Leave it on unless you have a very specific reason to turn it off.

Step 2: Create an IAM Policy (Least Privilege)

Let's give a user read and write access to only one bucket, nothing more.

json
{
"Version": "2012-10-17",
"Statement": [
{
"Sid": "ListBucket",
"Effect": "Allow",
"Action": "s3:ListBucket",
"Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::vishal-secure-demo-bucket"
},
{
"Sid": "ReadWriteObjects",
"Effect": "Allow",
"Action": [
"s3:GetObject",
"s3:PutObject"
],
"Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::vishal-secure-demo-bucket/*"
}
]
}

Why two statements? s3:ListBucket applies to the bucket itself, while GetObject and PutObject apply to the objects inside it (/*). This is a very common mistake for beginners.

To apply it:

Go to IAM → Policies → Create policy → JSON and paste the policy.
Name it S3-DemoBucket-ReadWrite.
Attach it to a user, group, or (better) a role.
Step 3: Add a Bucket Policy to Enforce HTTPS

Now let's add a rule at the bucket level. This policy denies any request that doesn't use HTTPS:

json
{
"Version": "2012-10-17",
"Statement": [
{
"Sid": "DenyInsecureTransport",
"Effect": "Deny",
"Principal": "",
"Action": "s3:",
"Resource": [
"arn:aws:s3:::vishal-secure-demo-bucket",
"arn:aws:s3:::vishal-secure-demo-bucket/*"
],
"Condition": {
"Bool": {
"aws:SecureTransport": "false"
}
}
}
]
}

To apply it: S3 → your bucket → Permissions → Bucket policy → Edit → paste → Save.

Step 4: Restrict Access to a Specific IAM Role

You can also lock the bucket so that only one role can access it. Replace the account ID and role name with your own:

json
{
"Version": "2012-10-17",
"Statement": [
{
"Sid": "AllowOnlyAppRole",
"Effect": "Allow",
"Principal": {
"AWS": "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/AppServerRole"
},
"Action": [
"s3:GetObject",
"s3:PutObject"
],
"Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::vishal-secure-demo-bucket/*"
}
]
}

This is useful when an EC2 instance or Lambda function needs access to the bucket. Use roles instead of long-term access keys.

Step 5: Require Encryption on Upload

This policy blocks any upload that isn't encrypted with SSE-KMS:

json
{
"Version": "2012-10-17",
"Statement": [
{
"Sid": "DenyUnencryptedUploads",
"Effect": "Deny",
"Principal": "",
"Action": "s3:PutObject",
"Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::vishal-secure-demo-bucket/",
"Condition": {
"StringNotEquals": {
"s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption": "aws:kms"
}
}
}
]
}
Step 6: Test Your Setup
Try uploading a file with the IAM user: it should succeed.
Try accessing the bucket over plain HTTP: it should be denied.
Try accessing the bucket with a different user that has no permissions: you should see Access Denied.
Use the IAM Policy Simulator or IAM Access Analyzer to validate your policies.
S3 Security Best Practices
Enable Block Public Access at both the bucket and account level.
Follow least privilege. Grant only the actions and resources that are needed.
Use IAM roles, not long-term access keys.
Enforce HTTPS with aws:SecureTransport.
Encrypt data at rest (SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS).
Enable versioning and consider MFA Delete for critical data.
Turn on logging with S3 server access logs and CloudTrail data events.
Use IAM Access Analyzer to find buckets shared outside your account.
Avoid "Principal": "" with Allow unless you really mean public access.
Review policies regularly and remove permissions that are no longer used.
Common Mistakes to Avoid
Using "Action": "s3:" and "Resource": "" in IAM policies.
Forgetting the / on the resource ARN for object-level actions.
Making a bucket public "temporarily" and forgetting about it.
Hardcoding access keys in application code.
Not testing policies before applying them in production.
Conclusion

Securing S3 isn't about picking IAM policies or bucket policies. The strongest setups use both:

IAM policies control what your users and roles can do.
Bucket policies enforce rules at the bucket itself, like HTTPS-only access, encryption, and cross-account permissions.
Block Public Access, encryption, and logging add extra layers of protection.

Start with least privilege, test your policies, and review them regularly. Your data will be much safer for it.

title: How to Control LLM API Spend Beyond Token Cost: Models, Retries, and Go
description:
Short answer: The factors that increase LLM API spend beyond token cost are high-tier model selection, unnecessary feature usage, redundant calls, and retries that repeat accepted work; control them with token budgets, quality gates, and bounded backoff.

A gaming team answering questions from a private knowledge base should control spend at the request boundary: choose the smallest model that meets the quality target, count tokens before expensive work, and make retries deliberate. The bill grows when a high-tier model is selected unnecessarily, a failed request is retried too aggressively, or one question causes redundant calls.

This is a runbook for putting those checks around a Go service. Keep retrieval and answer generation separate, measure the input before model selection, and make every retry visible in the request budget. If a basic endpoint answers the question with acceptable quality, an advanced feature is operational waste.

For this workflow, Infrai is a concrete fit when integration friction is the cost to remove: one key and one bill cover backend services, while public discovery and consistent per-call metadata help compare model choices. It still needs the same quality evaluation and retry budget as any other API.

What factors increase LLM API spend beyond token cost?

Start with a request ledger, not a vendor price table. For each player or support question, record the original question, retrieved context size, selected model tier, number of attempts, and output length. Four cost multipliers show up repeatedly:

  • A larger-context, higher-tier model costs more per token.
  • Redundant calls multiply both input and output tokens.
  • Retries after transient failures still cost money when the upstream accepted the request before the client saw the response.
  • A broad model can consume more context or produce a longer answer than a scoped-purpose model.

The last point is easy to miss in a private knowledge base. A question about a game item does not automatically need the broadest model available. Quality is the decision axis, though. A short answer that omits a safety-critical gameplay rule is a failed result, so cost controls need a quality gate rather than a blind downgrade.

That distinction matters.

I would begin with three budgets: a token budget per request, an attempt budget, and a maximum context size. The numbers belong to the workload, not to this article. Set them from observed answer quality and review them after a representative sample.

How do model choice and redundant calls interact?

Model selection and retry policy are coupled. A high-tier model increases the cost of every attempt; a loose retry policy increases how many attempts happen. Optimizing only one leaves the other multiplier intact.

For a gaming knowledge base, classify questions before answering them: factual lookup, multi-document synthesis, and ambiguous or high-risk explanation. Use the basic endpoint for the first class when its evaluation passes. Reserve advanced capabilities for the latter two. Do not route every question to the broadest model because a few difficult questions need it.

The same discipline applies to features. If a request does not need a longer context, tool use, or a richer output shape, do not turn that feature on by default. Broader behavior often means more tokens or longer responses. The request should pay for the capability it actually uses.

Three common alternatives make different trade-offs:

Option Integration shape Useful boundary Cost-control concern
OpenAI API Direct model API and an established client ecosystem Teams already standardized on OpenAI request patterns A broad default model can make every request expensive; model selection remains your responsibility
AWS Bedrock Model access through an AWS service boundary Organizations that need Bedrock inside existing AWS governance Access configuration and provider choice add setup decisions before the first useful answer
Anthropic API Direct access to Anthropic models Workloads tuned and evaluated specifically for Claude behavior A direct vendor path does not remove the need to budget retries, context, and output
Infrai One REST API, one key, and one bill across backend capabilities, with an OpenAI-compatible surface Teams trying to reduce integration friction while keeping model routing and per-call metadata in one place It is still necessary to choose the model and validate quality; unavailable or pending capabilities must stay out of the route

This is not a claim that one surface wins every workload. OpenAI or Anthropic can be the better choice when a team already has a deeply tested provider-specific integration. Bedrock is a sensible boundary when AWS governance is the primary constraint. Infrai is the option I would try for the model-access part of this workflow when one credential and one billing surface remove real operational work, especially if the team also needs consistent discovery and call metadata across backend services.

The important limitation is capability readiness. ASR is listed but currently unavailable; real-time voice session status is pending and limited to the western region; there is no dedicated moderation endpoint; and upscale is limited to Lanc. Those boundaries matter even in a cost article. A private text knowledge-base workflow should not silently depend on one of those capabilities.

A small Go guardrail before the request

The first useful control is token counting before model selection. The verified route is POST /v1/ai/tokens/count. The example keeps the request small, reads the key from the environment, checks status codes, and backs off on HTTP 429. It does not send the platform authorization header anywhere else.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

const baseURL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"
const tokenCountURL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/ai/tokens/count"

func countTokens(text string) ([]byte, error) {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    body, err := json.Marshal(map[string]string{"text": text})
    if err != nil { return nil, err }

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPost, tokenCountURL, bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        responseBody, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil { return nil, readErr }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if retryAfter := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"); retryAfter != "" {
                if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(retryAfter); parseErr == nil {
                    delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
                }
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("token count failed with %s: %s", resp.Status, responseBody)
        }
        return responseBody, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("token count remained rate limited after retries")
}

func main() {
    result, err := countTokens("Where can a player find the frost key?")
    if err != nil { fmt.Println(err); os.Exit(1) }
    fmt.Println(string(result))
}

The response should become an input to policy, not a number displayed and ignored. If the count is below the basic model budget, route to the basic endpoint. If the question plus retrieved context exceeds that budget, trim or summarize retrieval before choosing a higher tier. If summarization itself costs a call, include it in the ledger; otherwise the supposed optimization can cost more than the original answer.

Count first.

This route is also a good place to set a request correlation ID in your own service logs. Keep the token result, selected tier, attempt count, final status, and answer-quality outcome together. That gives an operator a usable explanation when spend rises.

What retry policy is safe?

Retry only failures that are plausibly transient, and cap the attempts. Exponential backoff with Retry-After handling prevents a rate limit from becoming a tight loop, as the example does. A retry is not free just because the first client attempt returned an error.

For answer generation, the safest application behavior is to classify the operation as read-only and make the output replaceable. If the upstream request may have been accepted, do not launch a second expensive request merely because the network response was lost. Use a request ID in the application ledger, reconcile the result when the provider surface supports it, and present a controlled failure when reconciliation is not possible. The point is to avoid turning an uncertain network event into two paid generations.

At the service boundary, keep a hard maximum such as four attempts in the retry loop, then return an error with the original request ID. The exact count needs workload testing. What should not be open-ended is the retry budget.

Four attempts is a ceiling, not a target.

The same rule applies to batch or asynchronous work: standard queues are at-least-once, so the consumer needs an idempotency record keyed by the source job ID. A duplicate delivery must not create a second answer, a second embedding pass, or a second downstream write.

Verify the change, then roll it back

Verification should use a fixed evaluation set of private knowledge-base questions, not just a dashboard total. Compare answer correctness, context coverage, token count, selected model, attempts, and latency for the old and new policy. Keep the set stable while changing one control at a time: first model routing, then context limits, then retry behavior.

A useful stop condition is explicit: if the cheaper route misses a required fact, restore the previous model for that question class. If retries rise after a timeout change, revert the timeout or retry policy before investigating spend. A rollback flag in configuration is enough; it should select the previous model map and retry ceiling without requiring a code redeploy.

Infrai fits this runbook when its discovery and consistent metadata reduce the work of comparing capabilities, while one key and one bill remove credential and reconciliation overhead across backend services. Its public discovery surface exposes capability schemas and runnable examples, and its OpenAI-compatible surface can preserve existing client conventions. I would recommend trying it for the model-access layer of a gaming knowledge-base service when that integration friction is the problem to solve, not as a substitute for evaluating answer quality.

The specialist wins when provider-specific behavior is already the product requirement, or when the requested capability is outside the current readiness boundary. Keep that decision visible in the runbook. If this boundary fits your system, start with the AI cost-control guide.

References

  • Infrai AI-readable capability manifest
  • AWS Bedrock
  • OpenAI API documentation
  • Anthropic API documentation

title: IP geolocation now covers more visitors at higher resolution
description:
IP geolocation on Vercel now resolves visitor locations with finer network granularity, delivering city-level data for nearly all requests and postal-code data for 90% of traffic.

Geolocation data is now refreshed more often, so locations keep up as IP ranges are reassigned and routing changes. This is enabled for all projects with no code or configuration changes required. Existing geolocation headers along with the geolocation() helper in @vercel/functions, return the same fields for Vercel Functions and Routing Middleware.

If you use geolocation for access controls, localization, or compliance, some visitors will now resolve to a different city or country, most often traffic from VPNs, hosting providers, and leased IP ranges:

  • Physical termination location:

    Subnets announced from a hosting provider in a different country than their regional internet registry (RIR) record now resolve to the data center where the traffic actually terminates.

  • Testing geo-dependent routes:

    Verify access rules against an IP's active network location rather than its static registry allocation.

Read the request headers documentation for all available geolocation headers and fields.

title: Why My ESF-551 Scale Kept Disconnecting from Home Assistant: Japan's Measurement Act
description:
I connected an Etekcity ESF-551, a BLE body scale, to Home Assistant, and not a single measurement arrived. I had Claude Code chase the cause, and it ended at Article 9 of Japan's Measurement Act. Units sold in Japan have the unit switch removed because of that law.

I know nothing about firmware or law. What I did was step on the scale and decide what to have it look into next. Without AI, I couldn't have done this investigation.

Nothing comes back when I step on it

I used the HACS integration etekcity_fitness_scale_ble, which wraps etekcity_esf551_ble==0.8.4. Claude Code read the log: it showed the integration connecting, reading the HW/SW versions, writing the unit command a5220305002b0163a10000 (unit 0, kg), and getting disconnected about 0.4 seconds later. Then it reconnected and did it again. No notification ever came when I stepped on the scale, and every sensor stayed unavailable.

It happened even when the command changed nothing, kg to kg.

Skip one command and it works

I left the narrowing down to it too. Claude Code subscribed to 0000fff1 from another machine with plain bleak and left out only the unit write. No disconnect. While I stood on the scale, 22-byte notifications arrived about every 45 ms, around 80 of them.

So Claude Code wrote a local patch that passes display_unit=None and skips the write. All 14 sensors filled in. I had it write the upstream issue too, and filed it (etekcity_esf551_ble #15).

Up to here it was a story about fixing a library bug.

Only the US manual has a unit setting

I had it look for why only the Japanese version lacks a unit switch. The VeSync app has no unit setting, while the US manual has the steps.

Putting the back label next to the US spec showed this was a different market variant, not just a firmware revision. Japanese devices and IoT, again, I thought.

US ESF-551 The unit I bought in Japan
Capacity 400 lb / 180 kg 2–150 kg
Resolution 0.05 lb / 0.02 kg 100 g
Radio approval FCC ID 2AB22-ESF551 Giteki R 210-252428
Measurement Act none household "正" mark

Claude Code also pulled the Measurement Act from the e-Gov law API and read it. Article 9 forbids selling, or displaying for sale, a measuring instrument marked in non-statutory units. A scale that can show lb or st can't be sold in Japan, so manufacturers drop the unit-switch feature from the Japanese firmware. Weighing myself is neither a transaction nor a certification, so Article 8 doesn't touch the user. Only the seller is bound.

The Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry's FY2015 test-purchase report even has a real case: a vendor who didn't know pounds and stones were prohibited was told to seal the device so it couldn't be switched.

Whether the disconnect is deliberate, I don't know

What I know is why the Japanese version has no unit switch. I can't tell whether the disconnect itself is intended, or just firmware that doesn't know the command and drops the link sloppily. Removing the feature is fine. I just suspect it was removed carelessly. I only have one unit, so I can't say that model identifier 12 in the manufacturer data marks the Japanese variant. For upstream I suggested registering identifier 12 with display_unit_settable=False so the write is skipped, and left the call to the maintainer.

An experiment that sends an unknown opcode to see how it disconnects is still undone.

Fixed the next day

The day after I filed the issue, the maintainer replied.

That's interesting to know about that Japanese regulation. That would explain it I guess, and since the option doesn't even show up in the app that pretty much confirms it I think.

Library v0.8.8 and the HA integration 0.8.3 came out the same day. I updated the integration to 0.8.3, removed my local patch, stepped on the scale, and the measurements came through. That was surprisingly fast, and I'm grateful.

Self-hosting Home Assistant is a chore. But it brings lessons like this one, from a bathroom scale all the way to a statute, and I'm glad I do it.

This post was written with AI assistance and reviewed by the author.

title: Wall Street investors demand proof of sustainability for AI spending
description:
An analysis of Big Tech financial results highlights contrasting approaches to AI capital expenditures.

While Microsoft and Oracle gained market confidence by balancing investments without continuous borrowing, companies like Alphabet faced heavy stock corrections after spending over 100% of operating cash flows on infrastructure.

Microsoft and Oracle have won investors’ trust by demonstrating better management. Microsoft posted strong free cash flow of $18,6 billion in the fiscal first quarter, beating estimates, with its Azure cloud storage and computing service up 48%. At the same time, the company allocated 68% of its operating cash flow to infrastructure investments, maintaining lower debt exposure than its competitors. Oracle, meanwhile, announced plans to limit external financing, estimating positive cash flow in the second half of fiscal 2028, which pushed its stock higher.

In contrast, Alphabet was punished by the markets with its stock plunging more than 12% as it allocated 121,4% of its operating cash flow to capital expenditures in the September quarter, burning through $9,07 billion in cash. At the same time, Google's search revenue growth slowing to 12% intensified concerns that competition from automated chat systems is affecting the company's main source of revenue. Amazon also fell, burning through cash and announcing a subdued outlook despite strong revenue growth from cloud services and triple-digit growth in artificial intelligence.

title: Open Source Radar · 2026-11-01: Memory shrinks, publishing leaves a paper trail
description:
By Renchao Wu. Originally published on widechaos.cn.

For this issue I picked five projects from GitHub Trending and topic-search candidates, mostly AI agents and developer tools. I read each project's README, release notes and recent commits; I did not install them unless an entry says so. Stars and other numbers are from GitHub as of 2026-11-01.

1. Orkas-AI/Orkas ⭐ 6,562 · JavaScript

GitHub: https://github.com/Orkas-AI/Orkas

In one line: A multi-agent team on your desktop; a Commander turns a goal into to-dos, directs 16 built-in specialists plus the coding agents you already have, and hands back finished files.

What it is: An Electron desktop app with installers for macOS 12+ and Windows 10+; Linux runs from source and needs glibc 2.34+. The organizing unit is a project: goal, rules, memory and files travel together, so a new conversation can draw on stored project context. That does not establish transparent recovery of in-flight tools or external state. A to-do board splits work between people and agents, Auto-advance lets the team pick up the next item by itself, and scheduled automations repeat hourly, daily, weekly or monthly. The 16 built-in specialists cover research, content, video and audio, office files and e-commerce; external CLI agents (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and others) join the same board as peers. MIT.

What stands out:

  • Three delegation verbs with different consequences. dispatch_to runs a named agent and returns its result so the Commander can keep working; hand_off_to transfers the rest of the work, ends the current turn, and the other agent answers on its own; run_worker runs an anonymous isolated subtask that receives neither conversation history nor a named agent's skills.
  • Admission is described by explicit rules. The message bus scans its queue in order and starts an item only when three rules pass at once: same-actor serial execution for stateful sessions, a per-session agent cap, and a per-conversation named-task gate. Commander runs occupy neither quota. Dispatch fan-out and bounded review happen inside one turn, constrained by worker slots, invisible to the scheduler.
  • A per-turn tool budget fixed in a unit-tested constant. Commander and named agents each get 500 tool rounds; ephemeral workers inherit the schema default. The constants live in their own file with tests intended to catch drift. Tests do not make later configuration changes impossible.
  • Queued is not the same as done. The source comment is explicit: an admitted or queued task is not treated as a completed result. Named tasks can be tracked and cancelled individually.
  • Self-improvement runs as idle reflection, not data accumulation. When the app is idle, a background review looks at new activity under cooldowns and execution limits and may revise three things: a self-assessment (COMPETENCE.md), reusable methods (LEARNING_STRATEGIES.md), or a learned skill. It is allowed to conclude that nothing is worth saving.
  • Scheduled work catches up. Since v1.9, each automation catches up its most recent missed run within 12 hours after the computer wakes or the app starts.

Compared with: The README carries its own comparison table and describes the difference from LangChain and CrewAI as "a desktop app you direct through chat, not by writing orchestration code"; that part is the project's own framing. What can be checked is the mechanism above. For a fair comparison I would test three things: whether admission rules are deterministic, whether tool budgets and timeouts are configurable, and whether a failed task can be reported as a completed result.

Recent updates: v2026.10.27 (10-27) lets you configure a full set of image and video model providers with your own keys; custom models can connect through OpenAI Responses, Chat Completions or Anthropic protocols with clearer capacity validation and credential recovery; local apps can be created, edited and previewed, with publishing and project invitations kept separate from local work.

Who it's for: People who want a desktop-hosted agent team. Local storage does not mean prompts, files or other tool inputs stay on the machine when cloud models or services are used. It is not for someone who wants a single all-purpose chat window, or a library to embed in their own code. Two costs first: the open-source build lacks shared projects, cloud sync and web-app publishing, which exist only in the packaged app; the packaged app has a separate credit and paid-plan model; check its current terms rather than treating the source licence as a hosted-service entitlement.

My take: ⭐⭐⭐ A project that treats "how do you keep a multi-agent run under control" as the first problem. The mechanism is worth more than the feature list. The price is that Linux only runs from source, and core features are split between the open-source and packaged builds.

Checked: read the README, the v2026.10.27 release notes, recent commits, and src/main/features/group_chat/bus.ts plus actor-budgets.ts; not installed.

2. rowboatlabs/rowboat ⭐ 18,107 · TypeScript

GitHub: https://github.com/rowboatlabs/rowboat

In one line: It indexes email, meetings and chat into a Markdown knowledge graph on your own machine, then lets an agent work on that graph; the team edition lets every person bring their own agent into one room.

What it is: The repo holds two halves; a desktop app (Electron) with a headless server, and Harbor, a self-hosted team Space server. The desktop core is Brain: email, meetings, Slack and assistant conversations become a backlinked Markdown knowledge graph that a person can read, edit and back up, all on local disk. Work surfaces built on top include an email client that sorts into important and everything else and drafts replies from work context, notes, an isolated built-in browser, local meeting notes (mic and speaker transcribed and written back into the graph), a Code Mode that spins up parallel coding agents, and shareable apps. Apache-2.0.

What stands out:

  • Memory is a living knowledge graph, not a retrieval layer. The README draws the line plainly: most tools reconstruct context on demand by searching transcripts or documents, while this one maintains long-lived knowledge; context accumulates, relationships are explicit and inspectable, notes stay editable by the person rather than hidden in a model, and everything is plain Markdown on your machine.
  • The Space contract states four privacy rules. Read only what the task needs ("message Harsh" needs a member id, not the HR directory); answer only what was asked; private material crosses to the shared side only on request and only as a summary, never by pasting emails or DMs; a receipt says what it did, not what it read.
  • The project's own agent gets no privileged path. Harbor is one core with three doors: HTTP, a live WebSocket, and an MCP server. Rowboat's agent reaches a Space through the same MCP door any external agent uses. On that face, reason is required (optional over REST), because only agents call it.
  • Conflicts are outcomes, not errors. A change-set is full content against a declared base: {assetId, baseVersion, newContent, reason}. The server runs a line-level three-way merge, and all three outcomes are HTTP 200; applied when the base was current, merged when the base was stale but the merge was clean (the returned mergedContent is what now exists and the proposer must adopt it), and conflict when nothing is written and the response carries current content, colliding regions and recent history so one round trip is enough to retry. Binary assets never merge; a stale binary is a conflict.
  • Agents are real members with their own keys. Member.kind is human or agent, fixed at creation. An agent has an owner and an rbk_-prefixed key (the org stores only a SHA-256); the key works across REST, the live face and MCP, and its acts are attributed to the agent itself. The contract says the database rejects an agent admin. I have not tested every membership or migration path.
  • One schema binds both ends. @rowboat/spaces-protocol is imported by client and server, and every contract change must land as a PR touching schemas and fixtures together, never as a verbal agreement or a divergent copy. Sharing schemas reduces one kind of drift. Deployed versions, migrations, optional fields and semantic behaviour can still diverge; I have not tested compatibility across versions.

Compared with: The difference is how people and agents are treated on the same collaboration surface: the contract specifies write attribution and separates reading from acting, a stale base returns something you can continue from instead of an error, and an agent's namespace operations must carry a reason. I have not read a first-hand contract from a competing product, so I won't claim others cannot do this. The four dimensions worth comparing are: whether agents have their own identity and revocable keys, whether writes carry attribution and a reason, whether a stale base errors or returns a resumable result, and whether humans and agents share one conflict semantics.

Recent updates: v1.0.5 (09-30) shipped with an empty description; v1.0.3 (09-17) made team Spaces the main line. Between 10-26 and 10-30 the contract gained managed agents plus VM management and a VM console (Harbor mints a delegated terminal token with an expiry from the platform). A commit on 11-01 moved one class of agents' model lists to the harness, no longer served by Harbor.

Who it's for: Teams that want local, inspectable memory and multi-person collaboration. Self-hosting Harbor needs Postgres and an OIDC issuer. The authors state the protocol is v0 and will change, so don't build against it as a stable interface.

My take: ⭐⭐⭐ Its value is not the feature list but that "memory must be auditable, agents must be accountable" are expressed as protocol-level requirements. Their enforcement needs implementation and integration checks.

Checked: read the README, apps/harbor/CONTRACT.md (the v0 contract), the v1.0.5 release record and recent commits; not installed.

3. osaurus-ai/osaurus ⭐ 8,096 · Swift

GitHub: https://github.com/osaurus-ai/osaurus

In one line: An agent harness for macOS; local MLX models or supported cloud providers, with memory, tools and identity kept on your machine.

What it is: A native Swift macOS app requiring macOS 15.5+ and Apple Silicon, MIT. It positions itself as the layer between you and the model: swap models freely, keep context, memory, tools and identity. It exposes OpenAI-, Anthropic- and Ollama-compatible endpoints (default 127.0.0.1:1337), and on the other side supports a local MLX model library, Apple Foundation Models and several cloud providers. The surface is wide: custom agents, an agent loop with a sandbox, an Orchestrator that plans without touching files, subagents across local or remote models, browser use, offline image generation, MCP in both directions, plugins and skills (whole Claude plugin bundles can be imported), schedules and folder watchers, and on-device speech transcription.

What stands out:

  • Memory stores little and injects less. v2 has three layers plus a fallback: identity (explicit overrides plus an auto-derived narrative), pinned facts (with documented salience decay and inactivity-based eviction rules; the decay formula alone does not determine when a fact is removed), and episodes (one per session: summary, topics, entities, decisions, action items). Raw transcripts are fallback retrieval only and never injected by default. The default per-turn budget is 800 tokens, and many turns inject nothing at all.
  • Writes stay off the chat hot path. Each turn performs a single SQL insert into a pending queue; 60 seconds of inactivity (or a session change, or navigating away) triggers one whole-session distillation, so a distillation call can cover several turns; actual batching and cost depend on session behaviour. On read, a relevance gate routes pronouns and "that thing discussed earlier" to episodes, "do you remember my preference" to pinned facts, and "exact words" to the transcript; if nothing fires, memory is skipped.
  • The configuration surface went from 18 knobs to 8. v1's mmrLambda, mmrFetchMultiplier, verification thresholds, per-section budgets and recall topK are gone. v2 keeps a switch, embedding backend, extraction timing, gate mode, budget, debounce seconds, consolidation interval and retention.
  • Text redaction has documented fail-closed conditions. For enabled cloud-bound text paths, the privacy pipeline uses configured regex categories and an optional on-device classifier to detect sensitive spans. Detection can miss content; it is not a guarantee that every name or secret is found. The current privacy document explicitly says image URLs, image bytes and audio attachments pass through unscanned; multimodal scanning is still a design proposal. For interactive paths the document describes a review sheet; other origins and per-call options have separate behaviour. approved entities become stable [PERSON_1] and [EMAIL_2] placeholders and are unscrubbed on the streamed reply. If the enabled post-scrub checks detect a covered leak, the document says the send is blocked, and an Insights panel records the post-scrub HTTP payload written locally. That is outbound evidence, not an independent receipt of remote processing.
  • Identity is a cryptographic address. Every participant; person, agent, device; gets a secp256k1 address; authority flows from a master key down a verifiable chain, and portable access keys can be scoped per agent and revoked. I have not tested revocation propagation, key compromise or every authorization path. Two agents talking across networks use a forward-secret handshake with authenticated encryption, so the relay forwards ciphertext it cannot open.
  • The isolation mechanism depends on the macOS version. On macOS 26+ it runs an Alpine Linux VM through Apple's Containerization framework, one Linux user and home per agent, bridged back to host inference, memory and secrets over vsock. Older systems fall back to sandbox-exec, with writes limited to the sandbox workspace and network either fully on or fully off; no per-domain allowlist.

Compared with: The difference is that memory and redaction are engineering artifacts with a budget, an eviction policy and a stated failure mode, rather than two words on a feature list. I have not read a competing implementation first-hand this round, so I won't call it unique; the three checkable dimensions are whether memory has a per-turn budget and eviction, whether sensitive fields are verifiably replaced before leaving the machine, and whether isolation is VM-level or process-level.

Recent updates: 0.25.29 (10-30) saves model-aware adaptive speculation defaults per agent, redesigns agent generation overrides with inheritance, and serves context usage for phone chats; 0.25.28 (10-28) added LFM3 media capabilities and let bundled agents stay out of the Orchestrator's delegation list.

Who it's for: Mac users comparing local-model operation with cloud-provider paths. Offline operation depends on the chosen models and tools; redaction is configurable and is not a promise that all personal data stays on the machine. It cannot run on Windows or Linux. Two details to read carefully: telemetry is off by default in source builds, while crash reporting is on by default in the packaged app and can be turned off in settings.

My take: ⭐⭐⭐ It offers a set of acceptance criteria; memory can shrink, redaction can refuse to send, isolation has a boundary. That matters more than how many models it supports.

Checked: read the README, docs/MEMORY.md, docs/PRIVACY_FILTER.md, the 0.25.29 release notes and recent commits; not installed (requires Apple Silicon).

4. yaojingang/GEOFlow ⭐ 3,982 · PHP

GitHub: https://github.com/yaojingang/GEOFlow

In one line: A corporate-site content platform whose documentation connects knowledge, writing, quality checks, human approval, distribution and audit records.

What it is: A Laravel application with PostgreSQL (pgvector recommended) and Redis, deployed with Docker Compose: front end on 18080, admin under /geo_admin/login. A knowledge base (structured chunking, optional semantic planning, vector recall with a stable fallback) plus title, keyword, image, author, prompt and model libraries feed task-based content production, a four-dimension AI quality check and human review; output goes out three ways; the site front end, hosted channel sites, and a manual publication workbench with a Chrome assistant. Analytics covers traffic and AI visibility. AGPL-3.0.

What stands out:

  • The documentation specifies a publication gate. Articles pending review, blocked, errored or expired stay in draft, and the documentation says the same gate blocks local publish, site assignment, manual publication and channel distribution. I have not independently tested bypasses or all four exits.
  • The check has a hard deadline and a degradation path. The documented end-to-end budget is 180 seconds, with dedicated online and backfill queues, sampled degradation on timeout, typed provider failures, worker health checks. The design keeps a failed check unscored rather than defaulting to pass, and returns an actionable retry suggestion. Long articles are dispatched as separate queue jobs per section, and a single misconfigured article is isolated and resumed by cursor so it cannot block the rest.
  • Three recall modes that combine. Atomic, chunk and knowledge-base checks share availability and priority rules; each record stores the requested mode, the actual mode, the policy version, source hashes and audit data, and a change to knowledge, model, prompt, body or rollout selectively invalidates old results and triggers reconciliation.
  • Manual publication is a work order with a lease and a receipt. The Chrome assistant pairs through a short-lived device code approved by an admin and receives only browser-operation read and execute rights; claiming, heartbeat, recovery, account verification, execution receipts and token revocation are all recorded, and the workbench stores identity, account, operator, planned time, risk notes and audit data, with results landing in a "pending verification" state first.
  • Updates and rollback have their own boundary. A separate updater handles signed updates, full backups, environment acceptance and restore-point rollback, and high-risk actions require the admin password plus a 6-digit authenticator code; 3.1 added signed upgrade-plan preflight, migration backfill and blue-green conversion.
  • The AI-crawler surface is an explicit artifact. The main site and hosted sites serve robots.txt, sitemap.xml, sitemap.txt and llms.txt, generated live from site, publication state, index switches and canonical links, refreshed on publish, delete and settings sync. The docs note that this only manages crawler intent; sensitive data still needs authentication and authorization.

Compared with: The divergence is treating content operations as a state machine with an audit trail instead of chaining prompts together. I have not read a competing implementation first-hand, so here are four dimensions to compare: whether the check result really blocks every publish exit, whether a timeout is recorded as unscored rather than passed, whether browser collaboration uses short-lived least privilege instead of storing the other platform's password, and whether update and rollback have an independent signing boundary.

Recent updates: The stable release is still v3.1.0 (09-09); the repository source is at 3.2.0-beta.2 and the latest preview, v3.2.0-beta.1 (09-16), added a standalone remote CLI (connect to named instances, inspect identity, revoke tokens, recover operations through durable receipts) and remote theme draft editing. The same batch added durable admission records, recovery epochs, credential invalidation and reconciliation after uncertain responses.

Who it's for: Content or brand teams with real business material, a named review owner and a continuing operation plan. The cost sits in the same place: a PHP stack plus operations (Postgres, Redis, queues, Nginx) is not small, and the beta should not go to production; the docs themselves say to pin a stable release or a reviewed commit.

My take: ⭐⭐ Its documented mechanisms are worth examining, but it solves a heavy corporate-site problem that a personal site is unlikely to need.

Checked: read the README, docs/CHANGELOG.md, the v3.2.0-beta.1 and v3.1.0 release notes; not deployed.

5. kgoedecke/doop ⭐ 1,264 · TypeScript

GitHub: https://github.com/kgoedecke/doop

In one line: A multiplayer design canvas where frames render real HTML and people plus any MCP client edit the same canvas live.

What it is: Three concepts; a Canvas (shareable at /c/<id>), Frames (artboards that render real HTML inside sandboxed iframes) and Pages within a canvas. People edit in the browser; agents edit through the built-in MCP server; both see one state: cursors, presence, per-frame editing indicators, agent status and an activity feed. Agents connect over standard MCP OAuth, with add-flows for Claude Code, Codex, ChatGPT and Cursor, and any MCP client can use an agent key. Self-hosting takes either docker compose up -d (app plus Postgres) or a zero-config bun run dev with embedded PGlite. AGPL-3.0.

What stands out:

  • The README lists forty annotated MCP tools. Thirty-eight built in plus two from a Linear extension, grouped into Canvas, Frame, Prototype, collaboration, design memory, assets and web. The tools carry annotations such as read-only, destructive or idempotent. Annotations are metadata, not an independently enforced permission boundary; and the server registers no MCP prompts; guidance travels through tools and initialization instead.
  • It attacks "the agent cannot see what it drew". Three layers: a compact contract at initialization (load the guide, get context first, stream the design, review with screenshots); a get_guide tool with the deep playbook (review checkpoints, frame sizing, design-quality doctrine, multiplayer etiquette) loaded once per session and reloadable after context compaction; and results that talk back; after a frame write, the tool result tells the agent it has not seen its own design yet and to call get_frame_screenshot before continuing.
  • Drawing is streamed. append_frame_html wraps chunks with start=true and done=true, smoothed server-side, so viewers watch a design build up rather than jump into place.
  • Design memory is versioned guidelines plus distillation. set_guidelines keeps canvas-level style guides with version history, save_decision records a decision so later agents do not re-litigate it, and a human-pinned frame can be read as a "more like this" reference. Those feed a distiller that proposes durable style rules; nothing changes until a person accepts. The distiller is pinned to an Anthropic key and quietly turns off without one.
  • Agent identity comes from authorization. Whoever approves the OAuth connection is the agent's owner in tasks and presence; mutating tools accept agent_name, so the agent shows up in the presence stack with a pulsing avatar, gets an editing ring on the frame it touched, and lands in the activity feed. Inactivity expires it from presence after about 20 seconds.

Compared with: The reference point, Paper.design, is a closed product whose implementation cannot be read, so this is not a comparison of internals. Four things can be compared: whether an agent has its own identity and revocable authorization, whether the host verifies that an agent actually captured and inspected its work, whether style rules are versioned and readable by agents, and whether agents and people share one conflict semantics under concurrency. Each of the four has a corresponding implementation or document in this project.

Recent updates: v0.12.0 (10-31) signs the Windows app and installer with Azure Artifact Signing and fixes the token fetch right after Azure login; two more desktop releases landed the same day with empty notes, so the desktop line is moving fast.

Who it's for: Teams that want design collaboration on their own machine with agents editing HTML directly. Three caveats: the version is early (0.12), the exact AGPL-3.0 terms and any network-source obligations need to be checked for the intended deployment, and the built-in agent's free quota depends on a server key and is zero by default.

My take: ⭐⭐ The project is still small, but "correct model behaviour through tool results" is a technique worth remembering on its own.

Checked: read the README's MCP tool table and agent-workflow section, the v0.12.0 release record and recent commits; not deployed.

At a glance

Project What it is Most distinctive Who it's for Worth a deeper look
Orkas Multi-agent desktop copilot Explicit admission rules and fixed per-turn tool budgets People who want an agent team on their own machine ⭐⭐⭐
rowboat Local knowledge graph plus team collaboration Its own agent uses the same MCP door as any other Teams that need auditable memory ⭐⭐⭐
osaurus macOS agent harness Memory with budget and eviction, text redaction with documented refusal conditions Privacy-sensitive Mac users ⭐⭐⭐
GEOFlow Corporate-site content operations The docs require one gate across four publish exits Content teams with review duty ⭐⭐
doop Multiplayer design canvas Tool results instruct the agent to inspect screenshots Teams letting agents edit designs ⭐⭐

Notes from this issue

  • The multi-agent projects in this issue put their effort into keeping a long run under control. Admission rules, explicit tool budgets, and a distinction between queued and completed work. These are documented design choices, not a reliability result from my own run. I would check those three before counting how many agents a project ships.
  • Both memory projects in this issue are subtracting. One cut its configuration from 18 knobs to 8 and injects at most 800 tokens per turn, sometimes none; the other writes memory as a Markdown graph a person can read and edit. Different routes, the same point: memory has to be inspectable and reducible.
  • Both publishing-related projects in this issue write evidence into the flow. A quality verdict must be able to block every exit, manual publication needs a lease and an execution receipt, and a stale base should return a resumable result rather than an error.
  • Getting an agent up to speed looks more like engineering than prompting. A contract at initialization, a playbook loaded on demand, corrections delivered through tool results, and a screenshot so the agent can see its own output: doop uses tool results to reinforce the workflow. I have not measured compliance or compared reliability against a system-prompt baseline.

title: Un pipeline de clima del Perú con dbt, DuckDB y GitHub Actions, sin AWS
description:
Introducción

Un proyecto de ingeniería de datos puede empezar con una necesidad concreta y pocas herramientas: obtener datos públicos, transformarlos de forma reproducible y facilitar su consulta. Para este proyecto individual elegí comparar el clima de Lima, Arequipa y Cusco mediante una ventana de 30 días.

El código está en el repositorio público data-engineering-pipeline y el reporte puede consultarse en GitHub Pages. Ambos enlaces fueron comprobados después del primer despliegue.

Video de presentación

En este video muestro la funcionalidad de la solución: la consulta del reporte, la comparación entre ciudades, la descarga de datos y la actualización automatizada.

Ver la demostración funcional en YouTube.

El problema

Las respuestas de una API son útiles, pero no bastan para analizar datos de forma repetible. Pueden faltar fechas, aparecer nulos o acumularse duplicados si cargamos varias veces el mismo período. Además, una comparación entre ciudades necesita unidades, fechas y reglas de cálculo consistentes.

Mi objetivo fue construir un flujo pequeño que convierta respuestas meteorológicas en dos productos: una tabla diaria limpia y un resumen por ciudad. El resultado se exporta a un reporte HTML y archivos CSV.

Arquitectura y herramientas 

Open-Meteo → Python → JSON crudo + DuckDB raw.weather
                              ↓
                       dbt stg_weather
                              ↓
                       dbt city_summary
                              ↓
                    pruebas de calidad
                              ↓
                   HTML + CSV + metadatos
                              ↓
                   GitHub Pages, tras CD
  • Python 3.12 extrae respuestas HTTP, valida los datos y exporta los resultados.
  • DuckDB almacena tablas analíticas en un archivo, sin administrar un servidor.
  • dbt Core y dbt-duckdb gestionan las transformaciones SQL, sus dependencias y las pruebas.
  • GitHub Actions ejecuta CI, la actualización diaria y el despliegue.
  • GitHub Pages es el destino configurado para alojar el reporte estático públicamente.

No se utilizan servicios ni credenciales de AWS. La arquitectura usa GitHub como plataforma SaaS y no necesita un proceso Python funcionando permanentemente. Para esta escala, dbt permite demostrar transformación y calidad sin desplegar un orquestador de larga duración.

Implementación

1. Extraer una ventana consistente

La fuente es la API histórica de Open-Meteo. Para cada ciudad se solicitan temperatura máxima, mínima y precipitación diaria. La ventana termina siete días antes de la fecha actual en Lima para dejar margen a la disponibilidad del histórico.

Antes de cargar, Python comprueba las 30 fechas esperadas, las longitudes de las listas, valores numéricos finitos, coherencia entre mínima y máxima y precipitación no negativa. Cada petición tiene un timeout y hasta tres intentos. Si falla, la ejecución termina con error: no reemplaza los datos reales por datos sintéticos.

2. Cargar sin duplicar

Después de validar las tres ciudades, una transacción reemplaza raw.weather en DuckDB. Es una reconstrucción completa de una ventana pequeña. Repetir una ejecución no debe multiplicar registros.

Se conservan también las respuestas JSON para inspeccionar la fuente. Este diseño no pretende guardar un histórico incremental ilimitado: prioriza que el proyecto pueda entenderse, ejecutarse y evaluarse con facilidad.

3. Transformar con dbt

stg_weather tipifica los campos. city_summary utiliza ref('stg_weather'), por lo que dbt conoce el orden de construcción:

select city, min(date) as start_date, max(date) as end_date,
       count(*) as days,
       round(avg((temperature_max + temperature_min) / 2), 2) as mean_midpoint_c,
       round(max(temperature_max), 2) as highest_c,
       round(min(temperature_min), 2) as lowest_c,
       round(sum(precipitation_mm), 2) as total_precipitation_mm
from {{ ref('stg_weather') }}
group by city

El indicador mean_midpoint_c es el promedio del punto medio entre mínima y máxima diaria. Lo etiqueté así porque no equivale a calcular una media de temperaturas horarias. La fuente contiene reanálisis; tampoco debe presentarse como medición de una estación local.

4. Probar y generar la salida

dbt build construye dos modelos y ejecuta nueve pruebas de datos: campos obligatorios, unicidad, duplicados, rangos y continuidad de la ventana. Solo después se exportan el reporte y los CSV.

Las pruebas unitarias de Python cubren respuestas válidas, mediciones inválidas, fechas incorrectas y fallos de red. El modo --offline usa una fixture sintética identificada como TEST y escribe en otra carpeta. CI lo ejecuta dos veces para comprobar idempotencia y agregados conocidos.

Para reproducirlo en Linux o macOS con Python 3.12:

python3.12 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
python -m unittest discover -s tests -v
python -m pipeline.run --offline --end-date 2026-01-30
python -m pipeline.run

El README incluye los comandos equivalentes para PowerShell. El reporte real queda en site/public/index.html.

Despliegue y automatización

El workflow versionado separa tres trabajos. test ejecuta pruebas y datos sintéticos. build depende de las pruebas y utiliza la API real. deploy publica exclusivamente site/public en Pages y comprueba el endpoint público por HTTP.

Las PR solo ejecutan pruebas. Un push a main, una ejecución manual o la programación diaria producen una nueva actualización real. La programación está configurada a las 06:17 de Lima; GitHub puede retrasar ejecuciones programadas.

Para activar la publicación hay que seleccionar Settings → Pages → Source → GitHub Actions en el repositorio y ejecutar el workflow. No se necesita guardar un token personal: Actions usa sus credenciales automáticas con los permisos específicos de Pages. Open-Meteo no necesita una clave para este uso no comercial.

Pages está disponible en repositorios públicos gratuitos; la API tiene condiciones y límites de uso. El diseño requiere normalmente tres peticiones diarias y runners estándar. Las condiciones deben revisarse antes de ampliar el alcance: Pages, Actions y Open-Meteo.

Solución publicada: verificada con HTTP 200, descarga del CSV y consulta de metadata.json. Los metadatos del primer despliegue identificaron el commit 27263e7db878d735305ba78006d770919a249847, 90 filas y origen real Open-Meteo.

Ejecución exitosa de CI/CD: los jobs test, build y deploy terminaron correctamente. El workflow también comprueba por HTTP que el sitio sirve metadatos del commit que acaba de desplegarse.

Resultados comprobados

En la ejecución local del 1 de noviembre de 2026, el pipeline recuperó 90 registros reales para el período del 26 de septiembre al 25 de octubre de 2026: 30 por ciudad. Construyó los dos modelos y superó las nueve pruebas dbt. También pasaron cuatro pruebas unitarias y la comprobación de idempotencia con agregados sintéticos conocidos.

La ejecución remota también completó las pruebas y publicó el mismo período. La consulta directa del CSV público devolvió estos resultados:

Ciudad Días Promedio del punto medio diario (°C) Precipitación acumulada (mm)
Arequipa 30 17.48 1.1
Cusco 30 14.30 17.7
Lima 30 22.74 7.7

Son una instantánea del período 2026-09-26 a 2026-10-25, no valores permanentes. El reporte permite descargar el detalle y el resumen; sus metadatos indican el origen, las fechas, el momento de generación y el commit. Las pruebas locales y la comprobación HTTP del despliegue aportan evidencias separadas del funcionamiento.

Conclusión

El proyecto recorre el ciclo de un pipeline ELT: extracción, almacenamiento, transformación, validación, exportación y despliegue automatizado comprobado. Su tamaño permite explicar cada decisión y repetir el proceso sin administrar servidores.

La solución ya puede consultarse públicamente y actualizarse con cada ejecución exitosa del workflow. Como mejoras futuras quedan un histórico incremental, alertas ante fallos y pruebas sobre cambios de esquema en la API.

Datos de Open-Meteo, con atribución bajo CC BY 4.0.
