title: My fix checker found two missing tests. Then it wrote them.
description:
In my last post, Bite checked some well-known projects and found a few small gaps: changes that no test would notice if they broke. Two of them:

  • In Rich, Markdown <kbd>Ctrl</kbd> is drawn in bold yellow, and no test checks it.
  • In chi, a Go web router, a change made XML responses get compressed by default. The commit did add a test, but that test counts the list against itself, so it still passes with the change taken out.

Finding a gap is the easy half. Someone still has to write the test. So this week Bite got a new option, --write-tests, that tries to write it.

How it works

For each change no test noticed, a fresh AI worker writes one small test on a copy of the project. Then Bite doesn't take its word for it. It runs the test itself:

  1. With the change in, the test must pass, twice.
  2. With the change taken out, the test must fail, and fail for a real reason (not just a crash on loading).

If either part goes wrong, Bite throws the test away and says so. It uses your own Anthropic API key, and --budget caps what a run spends.

What happened

Gap Bite's test With the change Without it Cost
Rich <kbd> prints <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>, checks Ctrl is bold yellow passes, twice fails: Ctrl not bold yellow $0.14
chi XML sends XML through chi's compressor, checks it comes back gzipped passes, twice fails: XML not gzipped $0.10

Total: $0.34. That's more than the two rows add up to, because of the next part.

The first chi try got thrown away, and that was Bite's fault. Go runs tests by folder, not by file, and Bite asked Go to run one file alongside the whole project. Go refused before running anything. Bite's rule caught it: a test that fails before it even runs doesn't count. So it threw the test out instead of showing a fake result. The fix is in PR #67, and the second try worked.

Did it write the right test?

Before Bite could do this, Claude had already written a test for each gap the slow way, to confirm the gaps were real. So there was an answer key.

  • Rich: Bite's test checks the same thing as the answer key: Ctrl comes out bold bright yellow.
  • chi: the answer key (chi #1246, still open) adds XML to chi's existing list test. Bite's test goes further: it sends a real XML response through the compressor and checks it gets zipped. Different route, same claim.

Here's the Rich one, exactly as Bite wrote it:

# Guards that <kbd>…</kbd> in Markdown renders its text in the markdown.kbd style.
from rich.console import Console
from rich.markdown import Markdown


def test_kbd_inline_html_is_styled():
    console = Console(
        file=__import__("io").StringIO(),
        force_terminal=True,
        color_system="truecolor",
        width=40,
    )
    console.print(Markdown("Press <kbd>Ctrl</kbd> now"))
    output = console.file.getvalue()
    assert "\x1b[1;93mCtrl\x1b[0m" in output

Then we tried the whole loop

On my own copy of Rich, Bite ran as a GitHub Action on a pull request. It found the <kbd> gap, wrote the test, and opened a small pull request with the test in it. I merged that pull request, and Bite's check on the original pull request turned green. Gap found, test written, test merged, without anyone typing a test.

What I took from it

  • Don't trust a test you didn't watch fail. The pass-and-fail check is the whole point. An AI can write a test that looks right and checks nothing, just like the chi commit's own test did.
  • Throwing things away is a feature. The chi test that never ran would have looked like a catch. Bite saying "no" there is what makes its "yes" worth something.
  • Two gaps is a small trial. It worked twice, on two languages. That's a start, not proof it always works.

It's in v0.7.0 (pipx upgrade bite-check). On your own computer: bite --write-tests. In GitHub Actions, the setup is in Bite's README. Since this trial, Bite also asks a second fresh check whether each test is fair before showing it.

Disclosure: I'm not a coder. Claude ran these trials, wrote Bite's code and helped me draft this post. The numbers come from the run logs.

title: Introducing Vedha: New Testing framework for Agentic World. Test your web app with an AI agent in 5 minutes (and catch the bugs it would miss)
description:
AI agents are good at clicking through a web app. They're bad at knowing whether it actually worked. An agent sees "Order placed" on the screen and reports success, even when the API behind it returned 500 and saved nothing.

This tutorial sets up an AI agent that tests your app in a real browser and checks what the server did. You'll go from zero to a test you can keep in CI in about five minutes.

We'll use Vedha, an open-source MCP server built on Playwright. It works with Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code and any other MCP client.

Step 1: Add Vedha to your agent (1 minute)

In Claude Code:

claude mcp add vedha -- npx -y @vedhajs/mcp --allow-domain localhost --out ./vedha-out

For Cursor, VS Code or Claude Desktop, add this to your MCP config:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "vedha": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@vedhajs/mcp", "--allow-domain", "localhost", "--out", "./vedha-out"]
    }
  }
}

Two things to note:

  • --allow-domain localhost is required: the agent can only browse the domains you list. Point it at your dev server, not the open web.
  • If you've never used Playwright on this machine, run npx playwright install chromium once.

Optional: install the agent skill, which teaches the agent how to test with Vedha (declare checks, mark writes, never retry an unknown outcome):

npx skills add HMAKT99/VEDHA

Step 2: Ask the agent to test something (1 minute)

Start your app, then ask:

Test the checkout on localhost:3000: place an order for Ada and confirm it worked.

The agent opens the page and works through the flow with vedha_act. Each call is one browser action, and it can say what success looks like. Here is the call an agent sends to fill the form and submit it:

{
  "op": "fill", "intent": "enter name", "target": { "label": "Name" }, "value": "Ada",
  "then": [{
    "op": "click", "intent": "place the order",
    "target": { "role": "button", "name": "Place order" },
    "mutating": true,
    "expect": { "text_contains": "Order placed" }
  }]
}

mutating: true tells Vedha the click changes data, so it should check what the server did, not just the page.

On a healthy app, this is what the agent gets back (real output, trimmed):

step 1 (step-2): verified
result: verified
effect: server confirmed (POST /api/orders 201; read-back /api/orders confirms POST /api/orders)
changed on the page (3 added, 3 removed):
  + status: Order placed

Vedha saw the 201, then read the order list back to confirm the order is really there.

Step 3: Watch it catch a bug the page hides (1 minute)

Now the same test against a broken backend: the API returns 500, but the frontend still shows "Order placed". This is what the agent gets back (real output, trimmed):

step 1 (step-2): verified
result: failed (health_check_failed): declared checks passed, but the page reported: POST /api/orders returned 500
hint: treat this action as failed: the server or page reported an error even if the page looks fine
requests: POST /api/orders 500
  + status: Order placed
open failure: "place the order" - declared checks passed, but the page reported:
POST /api/orders returned 500. Do not report success unless a later step fixed it.

"Order placed" is on the page, and the agent's own check passed. Vedha still reports the step as failed, says why, and reminds the agent not to claim success. A browser tool that only checks the screen would have reported a pass.

Two more things Vedha does here without being asked:

  • If a submit times out and Vedha can't tell whether the order went through, it reports outcome_unknown and refuses to click "Place order" again until a read-only check settles it. No duplicate orders from a retrying agent.
  • The agent can check server state without leaving the page with vedha_probe (for example GET /api/orders).

Step 4: Turn the run into a Playwright test (1 minute)

Once a flow is verified, ask the agent:

Save that as a Playwright test.

It calls vedha_promote, which writes a plain @playwright/test spec from the verified steps. This is the real output for the order flow above:

// Generated by Vedha from an explored session. Review before committing.
import { test, expect } from "@playwright/test";

test("places an order", async ({ page }) => {
  await test.step("open the shop", async () => {
    await page.goto("/");
  });
  await test.step("enter name", async () => {
    await page.getByLabel("Name", { exact: true }).fill("Ada");
  });
  await test.step("place the order", async () => {
    await page.getByRole("button", { name: "Place order", exact: true }).click();
    await expect(page.locator("body")).toContainText("Order placed");
    await expect.poll(async () => {
      const res = await page.request.get("/api/orders");
      const body = await res.json();
      const items = Array.isArray(body) ? body : [body];
      return items.some((it) =>
        Object.entries({ name: "Ada", qty: 1, product: "Widget" }).every(([k, val]) => it[k] === val),
      );
    }).toBe(true);
  });
});

Notice the last assertion: because Vedha confirmed the order on the server during the run, the generated test checks the server too, not just the text. It also lists its assumptions at the top, so review it before committing.

Step 5: Keep it honest in CI (1 minute)

Commit the spec and run it with your normal Playwright setup. One more line makes the rest of your suite safer too:

npm install -D @vedhajs/playwright-test

import { test, expect } from "@vedhajs/playwright-test"; // instead of "@playwright/test"

With that import, any test whose own checks pass while the app answers with a 5xx, or a write request fails, fails instead of going green. That covers tests written by your agent and by people. (More on guard mode here.)

What you get

  • An agent that tests in a real browser and reports verified, failed or unknown, never "looked fine".
  • Bugs caught that the screen hides: 5xx behind a success message, rejected writes, writes that weren't stored (where the API allows a read-back).
  • Plain Playwright tests to keep, with server checks included.

How much difference does it make? In a small pilot (one model, held-out tasks, 3 trials each), the agent missed 9 seeded bugs with Vedha against 26 with Playwright MCP, using about 30% fewer tokens. Details and limits here.

Try the demo without your own app 

git clone https://github.com/HMAKT99/VEDHA && cd VEDHA
pnpm install && pnpm build
npx tsx examples/demo/run.ts

Repo, docs and benchmark data: https://github.com/HMAKT99/VEDHA (Apache-2.0)

If you try it on your app, I'd like to hear what it caught, and anything it got wrong.

title: Session Timeout UX: Show What Survives Sign-In in Your Public Demo
description:
A useful session timeout UX demo shows the work before expiry, the sign-in transition, and the exact state afterward. Make it clear which values were saved and which were still drafts. Returning to the same screen does not prove that unsaved work survived, and seeing text in a field does not prove it was stored successfully.

For a developer building a SaaS in public, that sequence gives peers a concrete continuity problem to review. It is more informative than a screenshot of a “Session expired” message or an unqualified claim that the app keeps everything safe.

The project-note editor below is fictional. All example values and states are prepared for explanation. This is a review workflow, not a report of testing a real app, and it does not recommend changing a production authentication policy for the sake of a recording.

Define the activity that should continue

Imagine a planning app with a project title and a longer meeting note. The user has saved the project title, then started editing the note without submitting the latest changes. Their authenticated session expires while that note is open.

There are several different things to inspect: the saved title, the unsaved note, the user's location in the task, and their permission to continue. Give each one an explicit expected state in your own review notes.

Do not use “restore the session” as a catch-all phrase. A new authenticated session, a restored page, and recovered draft data are separate results. A product can achieve one and fail another.

Keep the public demonstration scoped to the activity. You do not need to expose authentication tokens, internal account information, or a customer's workspace to show whether a prepared note remains available after sign-in.

Prepare a before-expiry record

Use distinctive, harmless sample values that a viewer can recognise later. The note might contain a short prepared agenda with an unfinished final line. A generic paragraph of filler makes an accidental reset harder to spot.

State whether the displayed note is already saved. If the interface has a save indicator, include it in the recording and check what that indicator actually means in the implementation. Do not call a value server-saved merely because a spinner stopped.

Record the expected outcome before triggering expiry. That prevents a successful-looking return from becoming the standard after the fact. The demonstration should answer a question you deliberately chose to inspect.

Keep a copy of the prepared values in your private review record. After sign-in, compare against that record rather than relying on memory or assuming that similar-looking text is identical.

Trigger expiry under known test conditions

Use a suitable test environment and a supported way to exercise the expired-session path. Describe the relevant conditions without publishing credentials or turning a temporary test configuration into advice for production.

Distinguish a real expiry from a mockup that displays the message. A simulated screen can help review wording, but it cannot establish that the application handles an expired credential, redirects correctly, or preserves a draft.

If you shorten a test session for the demonstration, say that the timing is a test condition. A recording with an edited pause should also say that the waiting period was compressed.

Do not claim that every expiry path behaves identically. Inactivity, an explicitly ended session, and an account change may have different consequences. Choose the path you intend to show and keep other cases in a separate check list.

Show what the person can do at the interruption

When the app asks the person to sign in again, record the available action and the explanation beside it. A viewer should be able to understand whether their work is still present, temporarily unavailable, or known to be lost.

Do not promise draft preservation in the message before the behavior supports it. If the system cannot recover a draft, the explanation needs to reflect that limit while the product team investigates the design.

Avoid replacing the whole flow with a still image of a warning. The transition matters: does the interruption cover the editor, replace it, or take the person to another page? Those choices affect what someone thinks has happened to the note.

Ask a peer to describe their next action from the visible state. Their answer can reveal unclear wording. It cannot verify the authentication or storage behavior behind the interface.

Compare the state after sign-in

Complete sign-in using a prepared test account through the normal supported flow. Return to the project and compare the saved title, unsaved note, and task location with the before-expiry record.

Show the full relevant note, including its unfinished final line. A restored first paragraph can hide lost edits farther down. Check whether the interface distinguishes a recovered draft from the last stored version.

If the note reappears, establish what that result means. It might still be an unsaved draft awaiting submission. The demo should not imply that recovery automatically completed the user's original action.

Then perform the intended save under the current authenticated state and check the supported confirmation. Treat that as a further step. Recovery, permission to save, and successful persistence each deserve their own observation.

Use accessibility guidance with its actual scope

The W3C explanation of re-authentication describes a Level AAA criterion: after an authenticated session expires, the person can continue their activity without losing data when they authenticate again. It explains why losing work can especially affect people who need more time.

That gives the review a useful goal. It does not mean a short clip proves that the whole application conforms to WCAG, or that one particular storage design is required in every system.

Review the interaction with the input methods and assistive technology relevant to your actual implementation. A pointer recording does not establish focus behavior, an accessible explanation, or a usable route back for a keyboard user.

State the checks performed and their limits. A public demo can show a specific continuity path while a separate implementation review addresses the rest of the criterion and the broader product requirements.

Keep recovered data tied to the right person

Preserving a note is not the only requirement. The application must also handle the identity and access under which that note can be viewed or submitted. Do not treat any successful sign-in as permission to attach previous work to the new account.

For the fictional editor, record an unresolved account-change case separately from the same-account demonstration. It may need a design decision about how to explain available drafts without exposing another person's content.

Do not improvise a storage workaround merely to make the public sequence look smooth. Local retention, shared devices, server storage and deletion have different implications that belong in the actual product's design and security review.

The public artifact should report what was observed under the stated conditions. A preserved sample note is useful evidence for one path, not a certificate that draft recovery is safe across every device, identity and failure condition.

Ask founder peers one continuity question

Buildside is the founder-community context for this review. Uriel Bitton builds and runs Buildside, which is this article's publisher relationship. A prepared demo gives peers a specific interaction to assess without asking them to inspect private customer work.

Choose one question: can they tell what survived, can they identify what still needs saving, or does the return location match their understanding of the task? Keep implementation findings separate from opinions about the message.

If you make a revision, repeat the relevant before-and-after sequence. A clearer sentence is a useful improvement, but it does not repair lost state by itself. Show the state comparison again when behavior changes.

Keep the version, conditions, prepared values and unresolved cases in your development notes. Your next build-in-public update can report one checked improvement and the boundary around it. That gives readers useful progress while preserving an honest account of the work still left to verify.

Hey I'm Uriel Bitton. I write about building in public strategies and growing startups.

Subscribe for more stories on growing your audience by building in public.

title: Bring your agent to Notion with Chat SDK
description:
Your team already works in Notion. Now your agent can too.

With the new Notion adapter for Chat SDK, the same agent you run on Slack, Discord, GitHub, Teams, or WhatsApp can join comment discussions on your Notion pages, no separate codebase required.

Each Notion page maps to a channel and each comment thread to a thread, so replies stay threaded automatically.

The adapter supports mentions, message editing, conversation history, and up to three file attachments. By default, your bot replies when @-mentioned and where mentions aren't available in a workspace, it can trigger on a keyword or on all comments instead.

Notion doesn't support buttons, modals, or reactions, and cards render as markdown. Discussions can start at the page or block level, but not on inline text ranges. History fetches return only open comments.

Read the documentation to get started, browse the directory, or build your own.

Read more

title: Control AI crawlers and assistants separately in Vercel Firewall
description:
You can now log or block requests from AI crawlers and AI assistants separately with the AI Bots managed ruleset in Vercel Firewall.

  • AI crawlers: bots that collect content for indexing and model training

  • AI assistants: bots that fetch pages in response to user actions or search queries

For example, you can block AI crawlers while allowing AI assistants to retrieve your content to answer users’ questions. Vercel updates the rules as new bots are added.

To configure these controls, open your project’s Security > Firewall > Rules. Under Bot Management, enable AI Bots and select the gear icon beside it. Set an action for AI crawlers and AI assistants, then review and publish your changes.

You can also modify these rule settings using the Vercel CLI:

Review the changes with vercel firewall diff, then apply them with vercel firewall publish.

title: How Vercel Agent accesses production safely
description:
An agent working on production systems needs permission to act. A request like “fix this deployment” doesn’t tell you upfront which actions it will take or what access it will need. Grant agents broad access and a mistake can affect unrelated resources. Ask for approval at every step and the user has to approve individual actions before they know how the agent intends to solve the problem. Repeated prompts can turn that review into a habit of clicking approve.

Vercel Agent starts by investigating the problem, then proposes a plan showing what it would do and what access it would need. Approving that plan grants the additional permissions to carry it out, so the user can review the proposed fix before authorizing any changes.

The plan determines the permissions

For a broken production deployment, Vercel Agent might inspect recent deployments and build logs, then compare the failed deployment with the last known-good one. Read-only access lets that investigation run automatically. If it leads to a proposed redeploy, Vercel Agent requests the additional access in a plan the user can review and approve in one decision.

Access is defined by scopes, the named capabilities recognized by the Vercel authorization system. Any plan requesting access beyond the read-only baseline waits for approval as a whole, including any read-only tasks it contains. In this example, the investigation runs under a separate read-only plan before Vercel Agent proposes the redeploy:

Plan

Work

Requested scope

Investigate the failure

Inspect recent deployments and build logs, then compare the failed deployment with the last successful one

read:deployment

Redeploy the last known-good build

Create a deployment

read-write:deployment

A short read-only lookup can run without a plan. For longer investigations, Vercel Agent creates a read-only plan so the user can follow its tasks and progress while it runs automatically.

The plan connects what the user wants done to what Vercel Agent is allowed to do:

  • Intent: The outcome the user asks for.

  • Work: The tasks Vercel Agent proposes to achieve it.

  • Access: The scopes those tasks require.

  • Enforcement: The credentials and API checks that enforce access limits.

Each stored plan records its tasks and progress, with requested scopes attached to each task. The task descriptions explain why access is needed, and the scopes are combined across the plan.

The read-only baseline currently includes every registered scope beginning with read:. Plans need approval when they request access beyond that baseline or include supported external actions, such as opening a GitHub pull request. Read-only operations can still expose sensitive information, so automatic approval does not mean the work is harmless.

Vercel Agent can only use permissions the user already has

Vercel Agent runs as a Vercel App, which the user authorizes to act on their behalf within a team. That authorization is limited by the user’s existing permissions, so approving a plan cannot grant access the user does not have.

The Vercel OAuth service exchanges that authorization for shorter-lived tokens with specific scopes. These scopes define which capabilities the token permits, such as reading deployments or changing project settings. Vercel APIs check the token on each request to enforce those limits.

A user may authorize Vercel Agent for a team with dozens of projects. A redeploy plan requests deployment write access. Editing environment variables, changing domains, and managing team membership each require their own permissions.

Deployment write access is broader than a single redeploy. Naming deployment X in a plan does not, by itself, restrict the token to that deployment. The runtime, the software that coordinates Vercel Agent’s execution, checks that the plan is active before selecting its approved credential. Vercel APIs check each request against that credential’s permissions.

Approval determines which permissions Vercel Agent can use

When a user approves a plan that needs additional Vercel access, its requested scopes are checked again and a token is prepared containing the read-only baseline plus the approved permissions. The runtime, the software that coordinates Vercel Agent’s execution, checks that the plan is active before selecting its approved credential. That credential remains subject to its scopes, team, the user’s permissions, and expiry.

The credential used depends on the work:

Work

Credential

Read-only investigation

A baseline token with read-only scopes

Approved Vercel changes

A token with baseline scopes plus the approved additional scopes

External actions

Credentials and permissions specific to that provider

The model’s instructions tell it when to propose a plan and request approval. If it attempts an operation outside the token’s permissions, Vercel APIs reject the request, even if the model considers the action necessary to complete the task.

A single plan can include Vercel changes and a GitHub pull request. The user reviews both in one plan, while each provider uses separate permissions and credentials. GitHub pull-request access is tied to an owner and repository, so approval to open a pull request in acme/storefront applies to that repository even if the user also has access to acme/payments. Opening a pull request there requires its own approval.

Plans and tokens use the same permission definitions

A proposed plan can request a permission that has been renamed or removed. We initially maintained a separate permission list for Vercel Agent, which could fall out of sync with the OAuth service that issues its tokens. We moved to the same scope definitions so those mismatches could be caught during planning.

At session setup, Vercel Agent loads those definitions from the Vercel scope registry into an in-memory catalog. Fetching the registry requires authorization for the team, while the scope definitions themselves are shared across teams. The catalog supplies the definitions used at three stages:

  • Plan validation: Requested scopes are normalized, and unknown or malformed names are rejected before the plan is stored or presented for approval.

  • Approval: The requested scopes determine whether the plan fits within the read-only baseline or needs additional access.

  • Token preparation: Valid scopes define the credentials for approved work.

For example, a task to update firewall rules might request an outdated scope. The system rejects the proposed plan and returns valid scopes so Vercel Agent can correct it before requesting approval. This catches the mismatch during planning and requires an explicit correction instead of a fallback to broader access.

Fetching the registry adds latency and a service dependency, so Vercel Agent caches the catalog and uses that copy to check stored plans when they are loaded. Those checks reflect the cached definitions until the catalog is refreshed with changes from the registry.

Resuming work requires an active, approved plan

Vercel Agent may receive approval after the original chat request has ended, or lose its connection before carrying out an approved redeploy. The stored plan includes its state, who approved it, and when, alongside its tasks and requested permissions. That record connects the proposed work to the access the user authorized and allows the approval to be checked when work resumes.

Before resuming, the runtime reloads the plan and checks that it is active before selecting a credential with its approved permissions. A stopped plan fails that check, even if its token has time remaining before expiry.

If approval and a request to stop arrive together, the plan can move from waiting for approval to active only if the stop has not already changed its status. The runtime then checks again that the plan is active before using the approved credential.

If the investigation reveals that the current plan needs replacing, Vercel Agent can propose another. A replacement requesting elevated access needs its own approval, giving the user a chance to review the revised work and permissions together.

Where permissions need more precision

As Vercel Agent reached more of the platform, we had to correct access rules for actions that involve multiple resources or have different consequences. Attaching a domain can require both domain and project permissions, while staging a firewall rule and publishing it need different levels of access. Scopes need to capture these distinctions while keeping each plan’s access request manageable.

Matching those scopes to a proposed fix requires care throughout planning:

  • Choosing scopes: Vercel Agent chooses scopes with incomplete information, so it can request too little access and leave a task blocked, or too much and grant more authority than the work needs. Task-level guidance helps it choose, while validation catches invalid scope names. Even a valid scope can grant broader access than necessary.

  • Describing the work: “Redeploy the last successful build” gives the user a concrete action to assess, while scope names alone leave them to work out the consequences. The plan needs to explain the intended change and make clear which limits the token actually enforces.

  • Understanding denials: A denied operation could indicate a missing scope, an incorrect resource, or an operation that should remain blocked. Vercel Agent needs to distinguish those cases before requesting additional permissions.

Even with the right permissions, a redeploy requires judgment about whether the selected commit is safe to ship. That depends on the application, the failure, and the proposed fix. The user needs enough information to assess the choice, and Vercel Agent still has to execute it correctly.

Read-only investigation also needs controls for the information it retrieves, including sensitive project configuration and operational details. We chose a read-only baseline so Vercel Agent can investigate before asking for approval, and that choice needs continued review as scopes and the information they expose change. Other systems may need a narrower baseline. Separate controls must govern how retrieved information is handled and where it can go.

Vercel Agent can make a wrong decision or encounter malicious instructions in content it reads, such as build logs. Scoped credentials limit which operations it can perform in either case, but permitted operations can still cause harm. Plans therefore work alongside sandbox isolation, network policy, secret handling, rate limits, audit logs, and service authorization. Our work on security boundaries in agentic architectures explains the separation between an agent, its credentials, and the code it executes.

From investigation to approved action

Authority stays attached to the work that required it. The runtime selects the approved credential for an active plan, and its scopes define the operations Vercel Agent can perform. With the investigation already done, the user can assess a proposed fix and its requested access together.

Try Vercel Agent to investigate an issue in your project. Review what it finds and, if it proposes a change, assess the plan and requested access before approving it.

title: How to Reconcile Logistics Platform Usage and Internal Counters for Billing in Go — 2026
description:
Bill from the platform's usage record; use your own counter to explain the bill. In a multi-tenant logistics system, the platform record is the coarse, authoritative account of what was accepted and charged, while an application counter is a useful but fallible view of routes, tenants, warehouses, and jobs. Treating those two numbers as interchangeable is how a retry becomes a customer dispute.

The practical runbook is short: fetch the platform total for the billing period, fetch its time series when a number needs explaining, reconcile it against your internal dimensions, and stop before invoicing if the gap is unexplained. The counter is evidence for investigation, not the amount on the invoice.

Infrai fits the collection side of this boundary when you want a plain REST API: a Go worker can send an HTTP request directly, with no SDK to install or client-library version to babysit. That is useful operationally because the same access pattern works across languages, while the platform record remains the thing you audit.

It also keeps the backend boundary to one key and one account bill. That does not replace reconciliation, but it removes a class of month-end work in which an operator has to map several service credentials and invoices back to the same logistics tenant before investigating a gap.

The operational advantage is one key, one bill for the platform boundary, not a claim that local counters become trustworthy.

The public discovery surface is another useful detail: an operator can inspect the documented capability surface without a key before wiring the reconciliation worker, which makes endpoint and schema review part of the change rather than an outage-time guess.

Use the first record.

Should platform usage records or internal counters drive the invoice?

Invoice from the platform record. Your own counter can drift when a worker crashes after accepting an event but before incrementing its metric, or when a retry increments a metric twice while the platform deduplicates the request. Those are normal failure modes in an event pipeline, not proof that the platform is wrong.

The distinction matters during an outage. A dashboard can show that a tenant produced 9,998 shipment-label events while the platform reports 10,000 billable events. The two missing events might be sitting in a queue, or they might have completed just before a process died. At 3am, the useful question is not “which graph looks cleaner?” It is “what page fired, and which record can the customer independently verify?”

Keep the internal dimensions anyway. The platform cannot see a warehouse ID, carrier, route, or your retry class unless you put that information into your own system. Those dimensions make a bill explainable and help locate the broken part of the pipeline. They do not turn an application counter into an authoritative ledger.

The distinction is the boundary.

Keep that boundary visible.

A small reconciliation worker in Go

The worker below retrieves the account usage total and its time series, retries a rate-limited request with exponential backoff, honors Retry-After when it is present, and fails loudly on other non-success responses. It deliberately treats the response as JSON data rather than inventing field names that the endpoint may change; the reconciliation service can persist the raw responses alongside its period, tenant mapping, and decision.

Set INFRAI_API_KEY, USAGE_START, and USAGE_END before running it. The dates are sent as query parameters because the account usage API is the boundary for the platform record; validate the period against the billing calendar in the calling system.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func getUsage(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, path, start, end string) ([]byte, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        u, err := url.Parse(path)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        q := u.Query()
        q.Set("start", start)
        q.Set("end", end)
        u.RawQuery = q.Encode()

        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, u.String(), nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
        req.Header.Set("Accept", "application/json")

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }

        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if retryAfter := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"); retryAfter != "" {
                if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(strings.TrimSpace(retryAfter)); parseErr == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                    delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
                }
            }
            if attempt == 4 {
                return nil, fmt.Errorf("rate limited after retries: %s", strings.TrimSpace(string(body)))
            }
            timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done():
                timer.Stop()
                return nil, ctx.Err()
            case <-timer.C:
            }
            continue
        }

        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("GET %s returned %s: %s", path, resp.Status, strings.TrimSpace(string(body)))
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("unreachable retry state")
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    start := os.Getenv("USAGE_START")
    end := os.Getenv("USAGE_END")
    if key == "" || start == "" || end == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY, USAGE_START, and USAGE_END are required")
    }

    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 30*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}

    usage, err := getUsage(ctx, client, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/account/usage", start, end)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    timeseries, err := getUsage(ctx, client, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/account/usage/timeseries", start, end)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Printf("usage=%s\ntimeseries=%s\n", usage, timeseries)
}

The decision after collection is intentionally boring. Store the platform payload as the invoice input. Store the internal aggregate and the gap as reconciliation data. If the gap is non-zero, open an investigation and hold the invoice until an operator can account for it; do not “correct” the platform total with a local guess.

There is a security detail worth keeping in the runbook: the API key comes from the environment in this example, not source control or a log line. Secrets handling is an operational dependency, and OWASP's guidance on secret storage and rotation is a better reference than a team convention written from memory.

How do retries and outages change the evidence?

An event should have a stable identity before it enters the worker. Keep that ID through queue redelivery, HTTP retry, and persistence. Your own meter should record whether it saw the event, whether processing completed, and which tenant dimensions applied. A crash can leave those states split across systems, so the reconciliation job must compare states rather than incrementing a number in the error path.

For reads, retrying a 429 with backoff is appropriate. For writes elsewhere in the pipeline, use a client-supplied idempotency key and persist the result before acknowledging the queue message. A retry without identity is not resilience; it is an invitation to double count. The sample only reads the platform endpoints, so it has no write-side idempotency header to demonstrate.

Run reconciliation monthly at minimum, before the invoice is generated. The monthly job should compare the platform total and time series with internal totals per tenant and operational dimension, retain the raw responses, classify each gap, and record who approved the final decision. If a gap first appears on an invoice, the process has already failed its auditability test.

Which metering system fits the boundary?

There is no universal winner here. The right choice depends on which system owns the evidence and which dimensions the billing team must defend.

Option Useful boundary Limitation to accept
Platform usage records Authoritative account-level consumption and charged totals Coarse: internal warehouse, route, and retry dimensions are outside the platform view
Internal counters Tenant-level operational detail, anomaly detection, and customer explanations Drift under crashes, redelivery, and counter placement; unsafe as the sole invoice source
Stripe Billing Invoice and subscription workflows after you have a trusted usage quantity It does not remove the need to establish which event quantity is authoritative in your application
Lago Open-source metering and billing workflows when you want to operate the metering boundary yourself You own the durability, reconciliation, and operational correctness of that boundary
OpenMeter Event-based usage metering when real-time windows and product dimensions are central It adds another usage system to reconcile with the platform that actually charged the underlying account

Infrai is a reasonable fit for the platform-record side of this workflow when the account usage endpoints are the source you need to audit. Its plain REST API means a Go worker can call it directly with an HTTP request, without installing an SDK or tracking a client-library version; the consistent response metadata also gives an operator useful request context while investigating a gap. That reduces integration glue, but it does not make internal dimensions appear in the platform record.

My explicit recommendation is to try Infrai for collecting the authoritative platform usage record in a multi-tenant logistics backend when auditability of that account-level access matters and a language-neutral REST boundary is useful. Keep an internal meter beside it. Choose Stripe Billing when invoice lifecycle and payment collection are the primary boundary, Lago when operating an open-source billing stack is deliberate, and OpenMeter when event-level product metering is the central capability rather than a supporting audit trail.

Verify, then roll back the decision

Verification is a query, not a dashboard glance. Re-run the same closed billing period, compare the total and time series, and inspect the stored request IDs and raw payloads. Check the internal event ledger for duplicate IDs, missing acknowledgements, worker restarts, and tenant reassignments. A clean-looking graph is not evidence that those transitions did not happen.

If the gap is unexplained, pause invoice publication for the affected period, preserve both records, and route the case to the owner of the ingestion boundary. Do not rewrite the platform record, and do not silently overwrite your local aggregate. Once the cause is known, correct the internal explanation or issue the appropriate billing adjustment through the normal review process, while retaining the original reconciliation decision.

The customer-facing answer should include the platform quantity used for billing and a readable breakdown from your own dimensions. Never present only your own number to a customer who can compare it with the amount they were charged. That is an avoidable credibility failure.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and verify the account usage response for the period you actually invoice.

The practical second advantage is Infrai's single key and single bill account boundary: one credential covers the backend capabilities used by the workflow, so the reconciliation job does not need a new key and invoice relationship for every service it touches. Its public discovery surface also exposes capability schemas without a key, which makes the contract easier to inspect during a review. That reduces integration friction; it does not make the platform a replacement for a dimension-rich metering store.

req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/account/usage", nil)
if err != nil {
    panic(err)
}
req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))

References

  • Infrai official documentation
  • Stripe Billing usage-based billing
  • Lago documentation
  • OpenMeter documentation
  • OWASP Secrets Management Cheat Sheet

title: I Built DTDb — An IMDb for Developer Tools
description:
We developers have strong opinions about the tools we use every day.

Vim vs. VS Code. PostgreSQL vs. MySQL. Ubuntu vs. Arch. Python vs. Go. And now, with AI coding agents becoming part of everyday development, there are even more tools to compare.

But where can you actually see what developers think about these tools?

There are plenty of comparison articles, sponsored rankings, benchmarks, and opinionated blog posts. But I wanted something a little different.

So I built DTDb — Developer Tools Database.

👉 https://dtdb.dev

What's the idea?

Think of IMDb, but instead of movies, we're ranking developer tools.

The concept is simple:

  • Developers rate the tools they actually use.
  • Tools are organized into categories.
  • Each month, ratings are frozen into a ranking.
  • You can follow how rankings change over time and see which tools are gaining or losing popularity.

The goal is to create a community-driven picture of the developer tools ecosystem.

What can you find there?

I've started with several categories:

  • Database engines — PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle Database, and others.
  • Linux distributions — Ubuntu, Debian, Arch Linux, etc.
  • Programming languages — Python, JavaScript, Java, and more.
  • AI coding agents — Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, OpenAI Codex, etc.
  • IDEs and code editors — VS Code, Visual Studio, Notepad++, and others.

This is just the beginning. There are plenty of categories and tools I'd like to add.

Why monthly rankings?

I didn't want DTDb to become just another leaderboard where positions constantly fluctuate.

Freezing ratings into monthly snapshots makes it possible to look back and understand how developer preferences evolve.

For example, it'll be interesting to see how AI coding agents compete over the coming months, or whether developers' preferences for programming languages and databases actually change.

What's next?

There are plenty of things I'd like to improve:

  • More categories and developer tools.
  • Better ways to explore historical rankings.
  • More community participation.
  • Improvements based on actual user feedback.

But before going too far, I'd love to hear what other developers think.

I'd love your feedback!

A few questions I'm particularly interested in:

  1. Does the IMDb analogy make sense for developer tools?
  2. What categories would you like to see?
  3. Which tools do you think are missing?
  4. Would you actually use something like this to discover or compare developer tools?

This is an independent project, and I'm still figuring out the best direction for it.

Check it out: https://dtdb.dev

Any feedback, criticism, or suggestions are very welcome!

title: AI Agent Cancellation: Stop Work That Continues After the User Clicks Stop
description:
A Stop button can be honest in the browser and still be a lie in production. The chat stream disappears, but a model request may be generating, a browser tool may be clicking, and a background worker may be one step away from sending an email.

That is not a cosmetic bug. It is a broken contract. Users interpret “Stop” as “do not do more work for me.” Your system needs to translate that request across every layer, record what actually stopped, and make the remaining uncertainty visible. This guide gives you that contract.

The key idea is simple: cancellation is a state transition, not a boolean and not a client disconnect.

The five meanings hidden behind “Stop”

Teams often store one cancelled flag and call it a day. That collapses several different facts:

Event What it proves What it does not prove
Browser aborts a stream The browser stopped listening The server or model stopped working
API accepts a cancel request The request was recorded Every child task observed it
Worker sees the request New work should not begin An in-flight tool did not finish
Provider accepts cancellation The cancellation reached that provider No already-buffered output or usage exists
Run becomes terminal Your ledger has a final outcome An external write was reversed

Keep those facts separate. A robust lifecycle might be:

running → cancel_requested → cancelling → cancelled

with other terminal paths such as completed, failed, and needs_reconciliation. The last state is important. If a payment, ticket, or record write was in flight when cancellation arrived, pretending it is cancelled can make a later retry unsafe.

Define the cancellation contract before wiring a button

Write down the semantics your product promises. A useful default is:

  1. A user can request cancellation for a run they are authorized to control.
  2. No new model turn, tool call, or queued step starts after the durable request is observed.
  3. In-flight work gets a best-effort cancel signal and has a deadline for acknowledging it.
  4. The API never reports cancelled until the orchestrator records a terminal decision.
  5. Side effects already dispatched are reconciled, not guessed away.
  6. A cancelled run does not silently resume; resumption creates a new attempt or requires an explicit resume action.

This contract gives product, API, and operations teams the same vocabulary. It also prevents a dangerous UX pattern: changing the button label to “Stopped” the moment the browser disconnects.

Use one durable run record

Put the authoritative state in a database or workflow engine, not in a process-local abort controller. A minimal record can look like this:

type RunStatus =
  | "queued" | "running" | "cancel_requested" | "cancelling"
  | "cancelled" | "completed" | "failed" | "needs_reconciliation";

type AgentRun = {
  id: string;
  tenantId: string;
  status: RunStatus;
  cancelRequestedAt?: string;
  cancelReason?: "user" | "deadline" | "policy" | "operator";
  activeStepId?: string;
  version: number;
  terminalAt?: string;
};

The version field enables compare-and-set updates. It stops a late worker from replacing cancel_requested with running after another worker has already processed the stop request.

Your POST /runs/:id/cancel endpoint should be idempotent. It records the request once, returns the current state, and publishes a cancellation event. Repeated taps, reconnects, and retries should all produce the same outcome.

async function requestCancel(runId: string, actorId: string) {
  return db.transaction(async (tx) => {
    const run = await tx.runs.lockForUpdate(runId);
    assertCanCancel(actorId, run);

    if (["completed", "failed", "cancelled"].includes(run.status)) return run;

    const next = await tx.runs.update(runId, {
      status: "cancel_requested",
      cancelRequestedAt: new Date().toISOString(),
      cancelReason: "user",
      version: run.version + 1,
    });
    await tx.outbox.insert({ type: "run.cancel_requested", runId });
    return next;
  });
}

The transactional outbox is not required by every stack, but the principle is: persist the decision before notifying workers. A process crash between an in-memory publish and a database write should not make a stop request disappear.

Propagate cancellation across every boundary

An agent run usually crosses more boundaries than a normal web request. Treat cancellation as a signal that travels with the run.

Browser and streaming edge

AbortController can stop fetch and response-body consumption in the browser, as MDN documents. Use it to stop rendering and then call your durable cancellation endpoint. Do not rely on disconnect detection alone: mobile networks reconnect, tabs sleep, and a user may close a page without meaning “cancel.”

const controller = new AbortController();

stopButton.onclick = async () => {
  controller.abort("user_pressed_stop"); // end local streaming now
  await fetch(`/api/runs/${runId}/cancel`, { method: "POST" });
  showStatus("Stopping…");
};

The status is “Stopping,” not “Stopped,” until the run event feed reports a terminal state. If an SSE connection reconnects, replay events from a monotonic sequence number rather than starting another run.

Orchestrator and model calls

At step boundaries, read the durable record. In long model streams, also pass a cancellation primitive that can close the network request or invoke a provider-specific cancellation API where available. A close tells your HTTP client to stop waiting; it does not automatically prove upstream inference stopped or that no tokens were billed.

Use an absolute run deadline as well. Pass the remaining time, not a fresh full timeout, to each downstream call. A run that spends 50 seconds retrieving should not receive another 60 seconds of model time merely because each layer starts its own clock.

Parallel tools

Parallelism makes cancellation interesting. If a run launches a search, an internal lookup, and a write tool together, cancellation must reach each child. But not all children have the same policy:

  • Read-only tools can normally be abandoned or cancelled.
  • A write before its commit point can be cancelled.
  • A write after dispatch needs a receipt or authoritative read-back.
  • Cleanup work may need a short shielded window so it can record the correct final state.

In Python, cancellation is cooperative: asyncio injects CancelledError at an await point, and the official guidance is to use try/finally for cleanup and generally propagate the exception afterward. Do not catch it broadly and continue doing more agent work.

async def execute_step(run_id: str):
    try:
        await assert_not_cancelled(run_id)
        result = await call_tool_with_deadline(run_id)
        await persist_result(run_id, result)
    except asyncio.CancelledError:
        await record_step_interrupted(run_id)
        raise

Queued and durable work

A cancellation request must invalidate queued messages too. Workers should acquire a lease, re-check the run state immediately before each externally visible action, and release the lease on exit. A message already in a queue is not permission to execute it.

For longer-running orchestration, model cancellation and external-step cancellation as explicit workflow commands. Systems such as Temporal distinguish cancellation commands from ordinary completion; the general lesson applies even if you use Postgres and workers instead of a workflow engine.

If you need the underlying persistence pattern, see AI Agent Durable Queue: Stop Long-Running Work From Dying Mid-Task.

Never confuse cancellation with rollback

Cancellation prevents future work. Rollback tries to compensate for past work. They are related but not interchangeable.

Imagine an agent creates an invoice and then receives a stop request before it records the tool response. The correct terminal state is often needs_reconciliation, not cancelled. Query the payment system by a stable operation key. If the invoice exists, show it as created and offer a distinct authorized reversal. If it does not, mark the step cancelled.

This is why every write tool needs an idempotency key and an operation ledger. The full pattern is covered in AI Agent Idempotency: Prevent Duplicate Charges, Emails, and Records. Cancellation reduces how often you enter an unknown state; it never removes the need to resolve one.

Design an honest user experience

The UI should expose progress without flooding people with internals:

State User-facing message Allowed action
running Working Stop
cancel_requested Stopping work Hide or wait
cancelling Finishing safe shutdown View details
needs_reconciliation Checking an action before closing Retry check or contact support
cancelled Stopped; no new work will run Start a new run

Do not show partial generated text as a completed answer. Mark it as interrupted, keep it separate from the final result, and never automatically feed it into the next agent turn. It may have been cut off mid-instruction or before a tool result arrived.

Structured errors help clients make this distinction. An error envelope should include a stable code, whether a retry is safe, the run state, and a correlation ID. Agent Tool Error Envelopes shows a compatible pattern.

Test the race conditions, not just the button

The happy path is easy: click Stop and see the stream close. Production correctness lives in the races. Add deterministic test hooks before model calls, before a tool dispatch, after dispatch but before receipt storage, and while a worker holds a lease.

Your cancellation test matrix should cover at least:

  1. Cancel while queued: no worker starts the first step.
  2. Cancel during token streaming: client stops, provider result is recorded as interrupted or reconciled.
  3. Cancel between model output and tool dispatch: no tool begins.
  4. Cancel during two parallel tools: every child reaches a known terminal state.
  5. Cancel after a write dispatch: reconciliation runs; the write is never blindly retried.
  6. Cancel during a process crash: a replacement worker respects the durable request.
  7. Duplicate cancel calls: one lifecycle transition and no duplicate cleanup.
  8. Resume attempt after cancellation: it creates a new attempt with explicit provenance.

Capture traces for each test and replay them when the runtime changes. AI Agent Trace Replay is useful for turning an escaped cancellation race into a permanent regression test.

A practical implementation checklist

  • Store run lifecycle state durably, including cancellation reason and timestamps.
  • Make cancellation requests authorized and idempotent.
  • Send a durable signal to workers; do not trust page disconnects as intent.
  • Check for cancellation before every new turn and side effect.
  • Propagate an abort signal and remaining deadline to streams and tools.
  • Record a confirmed terminal state only after worker cleanup finishes.
  • Reconcile writes that crossed a commit boundary.
  • Preserve interrupted output as partial, never as final.
  • Emit lifecycle events that reconnecting clients can replay.
  • Test cancellation at every boundary and after simulated crashes.

A Stop button is a promise about control. Keep that promise by treating cancellation as a first-class workflow outcome, not a disappearing HTTP connection.

FAQ

Does aborting an LLM stream stop the model?

Not necessarily. It reliably stops your client from consuming the response, but the provider may stop asynchronously, may have already buffered output, and may still report usage. Record provider request IDs and reconcile their final status when the distinction matters.

Should a cancelled AI agent run be retried automatically?

Usually no. Cancellation expresses changed user intent. Create an explicit new attempt instead. Only retry internal cleanup or a clearly idempotent read when that work is necessary to reach a known terminal state.

What is the difference between a timeout and cancellation?

A timeout is a system deadline; cancellation can come from a user, policy, operator, or parent workflow. Both can use the same propagation mechanism, but record the cause separately because the correct product response differs.

How do I cancel an agent tool that has already started a write?

Request cancellation, then query the target using the operation key or receipt. If the write committed, treat it as completed and use a separate compensating action if appropriate. Never assume a network timeout means the write failed.

Can I resume a cancelled agent run?

You can, but make it explicit. Persist a checkpoint with its inputs, completed steps, and evidence. Start a new attempt that references the old one, re-checks policy, and never repeats uncertain writes without reconciliation.

What metrics show whether cancellation works?

Track time from request to terminal state, cancelled runs with work still starting afterward, orphaned tool calls, reconciliation rate after cancellation, duplicate cancellation requests, and the fraction of partial outputs mistakenly shown as final.

title: Character limits have two numbers: building an ad preview around warnings and blocks
description:
Disclosure up front: I run Maestro, a B2B paid media company, and this post is about a free tool we built, the Maestro LinkedIn ad mockup. Nothing here needs you to use it. The problems are the same for anyone building a form, an editor or a preview against a platform's published limits.

The tool does one narrow job. You enter a LinkedIn single-image ad (company name, intro text, image, headline, optional description, CTA and destination URL), compare desktop and mobile views, and export a mockup plus a production brief for whoever approves the ad. It runs in the browser, needs no sign-in, and doesn't upload your creative.

Most of the interesting engineering wasn't in drawing the card. It was in deciding what the tool is allowed to say. This post walks through those decisions: how to model a limit, how to count characters when the platform doesn't tell you how it counts, how to show truncation you can't reproduce exactly, and how to test all of it.

A field has two limits, not one

LinkedIn's single image ad specifications publish two numbers for most text fields: a shorter length to avoid truncation and a hard maximum.

Field Avoid truncation Hard maximum
Introductory text 150 characters 3,000 characters (up to 10 emojis)
Headline 70 characters 200 characters
Description 100 characters 300 characters
Destination URL n/a must start with http:// or https://; up to 2,000 characters
Ad name (optional) n/a 255 characters

A single maxLength can't represent that. Set it to 3,000 and people ship intro text that gets cut off after the first line. Set it to 150 and you block copy LinkedIn would accept, which is worse, because the writer now has a tool telling them something false.

So the tool treats the two numbers as different kinds of rule:

  • Past the recommendation: show a warning. The copy may be fine. A longer intro can be a deliberate choice, and the writer decides.
  • Past the published maximum: block the review export until the field is fixed. This copy can't work.

That split, "you should look at this" versus "this can't ship", is the single most useful idea in the tool. It applies to any field with a soft and a hard limit: meta descriptions, SMS segments, push notification titles, app store subtitles.

Model the limit as data, with its source

Constants scattered through components break the first time the platform changes a number. Limits are facts with a source and a date, so they belong in one table that the UI, the validator and the export all read. Here's a simplified sketch of that shape:

type Severity = "warning" | "error";

type Rule = {
  field: "introText" | "headline" | "description" | "destinationUrl" | "adName";
  kind: "recommendation" | "maximum";
  limit: number;
  unit: "characters" | "emoji";
  source: string;      // URL of the published spec
  checkedAt: string;   // ISO date the spec was last read
};

type Finding = {
  field: Rule["field"];
  severity: Severity;
  count: number;
  limit: number;
  method: CountMethod;  // see the Unicode section
  message: string;
};

const severityFor = (rule: Rule): Severity =>
  rule.kind === "maximum" ? "error" : "warning";

Two details matter more than they look.

First, kind drives severity, not the number. Nobody has to remember that 150 is a warning and 3,000 is an error. A recommendation can never block, by construction.

Second, every rule carries checkedAt. Our page states that the limits were checked against LinkedIn's specs on September 27, 2026, and the exported brief carries the same date. If a refresh of the source fails, the honest state is "Unknown currency", not a silent pass on old numbers.

One green check is a lie: keep the states separate

The most common failure in review tools is a single status that quietly means several things. "Ready" might mean the preview renders, or the copy is within limits, or someone approved it, or the platform accepted it. Those are four different questions with four different owners.

The tool keeps them apart:

  • Preview: can the draft be pictured, with any missing fields labeled?
  • Technical check: do the supplied copy, URL and image pass the supported rules?
  • Production handoff: is the record complete enough for a named reviewer to check?
  • LinkedIn: has the intended Campaign Manager account supplied dated approval and native-rendering evidence?

Sketched as types:

type PreviewState = "Preview available" | "Preview incomplete";
type TechnicalState = "Pass" | "Needs changes" | "Unknown" | "Unsupported";
type HandoffState = "Ready for review" | "Hold";
type PlatformState = "Not checked" | "Externally verified";

type ReviewStates = {
  preview: PreviewState;
  technical: TechnicalState;
  handoff: HandoffState;
  platform: PlatformState;
};

Nothing inside the tool can set platform to "Externally verified". That value only arrives with dated, account-scoped evidence from someone who looked in Campaign Manager. A mockup can be ready for production review while LinkedIn is still Not checked, and the UI says exactly that instead of collapsing it into a checkmark.

If you build anything that previews a third-party platform, I'd start here. Write down which states your tool can know and which it can only record from someone else, and make the second group impossible to set from local code.

What counts as a character?

This is where most counters quietly go wrong. In JavaScript, "ðŸ‘ðŸ½".length is 4. A user sees one thing.

I ran a handful of strings through Node 20 to show how far the common methods drift apart:

Input .length (UTF-16 units) Code points Grapheme clusters
Hello 5 5 5
ðŸ‘ 2 1 1
ðŸ‘ðŸ½ (thumbs up + skin tone) 4 2 1
ðŸ‘©â€ðŸ’» (ZWJ sequence) 5 3 1
ðŸ‡ºðŸ‡¸ (regional indicator pair) 4 2 1
Ã© (precomposed) 1 1 1
Ã© (e + combining accent) 2 2 1
1ï¸âƒ£ (keycap) 3 3 1

The two Ã© rows look identical on screen and count differently under two of the three methods. Normalizing to NFC first collapses the second one to length 1, which is worth doing before you count anything.

Grapheme clusters are the closest match to what a person thinks of as a character. Browsers expose them through Intl.Segmenter, which MDN lists as available across browsers since April 2024:

const segmenter = typeof Intl !== "undefined" && "Segmenter" in Intl
  ? new Intl.Segmenter(undefined, { granularity: "grapheme" })
  : null;

export function countCharacters(text) {
  const s = text.normalize("NFC");
  if (segmenter) {
    let n = 0;
    for (const _ of segmenter.segment(s)) n++;
    return { count: n, method: "grapheme (Intl.Segmenter)" };
  }
  return { count: [...s].length, method: "code point fallback" };
}

Note the return shape. The count travels with the method that produced it. If an older runtime falls back to code points, the export says so.

The part you can't know

Here's the honest problem: LinkedIn doesn't publish every detail of its Unicode counting logic. It says 150 characters "including spaces, emojis, and punctuation" and a limit of 10 emojis, but not whether a skin-toned thumbs up is one character or two.

So our count is a local review count, and the tool labels it that way. Copy that lands near a boundary gets a note to test it in Campaign Manager before launch. I'd rather show an honest "approximately 150, check natively" than a confident number that turns out to be wrong at exactly the point where it matters.

Counting emoji is its own trap

The 10-emoji limit needs an emoji detector, and the obvious regex doesn't agree with itself. Testing the same strings against two Unicode properties in Node 20:

  • /\p{Extended_Pictographic}/u matched ðŸ‘ and ðŸ‘©â€ðŸ’», missed ðŸ‡ºðŸ‡¸ and 1ï¸âƒ£, and matched a plain Â© with no emoji presentation selector.
  • /^\p{RGI_Emoji}$/v (the newer v flag) matched ðŸ‘, ðŸ‘ðŸ½, ðŸ‘©â€ðŸ’», ðŸ‡ºðŸ‡¸ and 1ï¸âƒ£, did not match a bare Â©, and did match Â©ï¸ with the variation selector.

The v-flag version is closer to what a person would call an emoji, but neither is guaranteed to match LinkedIn's rule. The approach I'd use: segment into graphemes first, test each grapheme, record the counting and emoji-sequence method in the export, and treat an emoji count near 10 as a boundary to check natively.

Truncation you can't reproduce exactly

The point of the 150 and 70 recommendations is truncation, so people want the preview to show where the "â€¦see more" lands. You can't get that exactly right from outside the platform. Truncation depends on fonts, viewport width, line height and rules the platform doesn't publish.

What we did instead:

  1. Pick fixed, documented card widths. The preview uses a 552 CSS-pixel desktop card and a 358 CSS-pixel phone card inside a 390px model, and stays responsive down to 320px. Those are product decisions, written down, not claims about LinkedIn's layout.
  2. Clamp by lines in CSS, not by slicing characters. Cutting the string at character 150 is wrong for two reasons: you might split a grapheme cluster, and the platform truncates visually, by lines. A line-clamp with a More/Less toggle is closer to the real behaviour and never corrupts text.
  3. Keep the text selectable and complete. The collapsed state is presentation. The exported brief always contains the full copy, even when the preview is collapsed.
  4. Label every export. Mockup images carry the caption "Approximate feed preview â€” check the final ad in Campaign Manager", plus the mode and variant. Production artwork is exported separately, with no card chrome or crop guides on it.

If a stakeholder screenshots the mockup and forwards it, the caption goes with it. That's cheaper and more honest than chasing pixel-perfect truncation.

Don't fake unsupported states

LinkedIn's spec says paid vertical (4:5) images serve on mobile devices only. A desktop/mobile switch could squeeze a portrait image into the desktop frame anyway, and it would look plausible. It would also show a placement that doesn't exist.

So the desktop view renders an explicit unsupported state for portrait creative. The same thinking applies to the description field. LinkedIn says the description shows on LinkedIn mobile and desktop when the image is less than 200 pixels wide, or when the ad runs beyond the feed through the LinkedIn Audience Network. For a normal large feed image, the tool doesn't promise the description will be visible.

A rule of thumb I took from this: if the honest answer is "this doesn't render here", render that answer. An empty state that explains itself is better than a convincing picture of something that won't happen.

Validate images against published ranges, and stop there

The image rules come from the same LinkedIn page:

Ratio Recommended Minimum Maximum
Landscape 1.91:1 1200 Ã— 628 640 Ã— 360 7680 Ã— 4320
Square 1:1 1200 Ã— 1200 360 Ã— 360 4320 Ã— 4320
Vertical 4:5 720 Ã— 900 360 Ã— 640 2430 Ã— 4320

LinkedIn accepts JPG, PNG or GIF up to 5 MB. Our first version takes JPG and PNG only. Animated GIFs are rejected with a clear message rather than silently frozen on their first frame, because a frozen frame would misrepresent the ad.

Two things we deliberately did not do:

  • Infer a ratio tolerance. LinkedIn publishes rows, not a tolerance. Is 1200 Ã— 630 "close enough" to 1.91:1? The spec doesn't say, so the tool doesn't guess. It offers the recommended presets and Fit/Crop controls, and records the crop rectangle and focal point in the export.
  • Pretend our caps are LinkedIn's. The tool has its own limits, 5,000,000 bytes in and out and 24,000,000 decoded pixels, to keep the browser responsive. The UI calls them tool limits, not platform rules.

URLs: validate syntax, keep everything

Destination checks are simple on paper: an http:// or https:// prefix and up to 2,000 characters. LinkedIn also warns that some special characters in the query string, such as < > # % { } [ ], can cause errors.

export function checkDestination(raw) {
  const findings = [];
  let url;
  try { url = new URL(raw); } catch {
    return [{ severity: "error", message: "Not a valid URL." }];
  }
  if (!/^https?:$/.test(url.protocol))
    findings.push({ severity: "error", message: "Must start with http:// or https://." });
  if (raw.length > 2000)
    findings.push({ severity: "error", message: `Over 2,000 characters (${raw.length}).` });
  const query = raw.includes("?") ? raw.slice(raw.indexOf("?")) : "";
  if (/[<>{}\[\]]/.test(query))
    findings.push({ severity: "warning", message: "Query string contains characters LinkedIn says can cause errors." });
  return findings;
}

Note that the query check reads the raw string. new URL("https://x.com/?a=<b>").search comes back as ?a=%3Cb%3E in Node 20, so testing url.search would miss the characters the user actually typed.

Two cautions. Store the raw string exactly as entered, including every tracking parameter. Normalizing it through URL and writing back url.href can re-encode characters and change what gets launched. And syntax validity proves nothing about the page. The brief records the destination headline and next action separately, so a reviewer can judge whether the ad's promise matches the page.

Edits invalidate checks, presentation doesn't

Once there are reviews in the record, every edit raises a question: which checks does this edit invalidate?

We split inputs into two groups:

  • Content: image, crop, copy, CTA, destination and evidence. Changing any of these invalidates the checks and exports that depend on it, while unrelated evidence survives.
  • Presentation: desktop/mobile mode, collapsed/expanded copy, theme, crop overlay. Changing these changes what you see and nothing else.

One simple way to implement it: store, with each review, a hash of the content fields it covered. On edit, recompute the hashes and drop any review whose hash no longer matches. That's easier to reason about than event-driven invalidation, and it makes "why did my approval disappear?" answerable: the field it covered changed.

Import is all or nothing

Users can export a structured JSON record and import it later. The record embeds the original, delivered and logo image bytes with hashes, so a file that only contains a path isn't treated as lossless.

Import validates the whole record first: schema, embedded assets, hashes and size caps. Only then does it replace the current work, in one step. If anything fails, the current work stays as it was. A half-imported record is worse than a failed import, because it looks fine.

How to test it

These are the tests I'd write for any tool like this. Each one maps to a behaviour our tool's page commits to:

  • Boundary triplets for every rule. 149, 150 and 151 characters of intro text should give no finding, no finding and a warning. 2,999, 3,000 and 3,001 should give a warning, a warning and an error. Same pattern for 70/200 and 100/300. A 151-character intro must never produce an error.
  • A Unicode fixture file. The strings in the table above, plus the two forms of Ã©, run through countCharacters, with expected counts per method. When a runtime changes its segmentation data, this file is where you'll find out.
  • State-separation tests. Load the worked example, and no real approvals come with it. The sample ships with clearly labeled simulated review records, and loading it into the editor clears them, so it opens on Production handoff: Hold. Assert that no code path sets the platform state to verified.
  • Invalidation tests. Approve, change the headline, assert the copy review is gone and the asset review survives. Toggle desktop/mobile, assert nothing is gone.
  • Import round-trips. Export, import, and compare byte-for-byte. Then corrupt one embedded image hash and assert the import fails with the current work intact.

What I'd tell someone building one of these

  • Put limits in data, with the source and the date they were checked.
  • Give recommendations and maximums different kinds, so severity follows from type.
  • Count graphemes, say which method you used, and label the number as local.
  • Clamp visually, never slice strings, and caption every exported image as approximate.
  • Render unsupported states instead of plausible fakes.
  • Keep "we checked it" and "the platform accepted it" in separate fields that local code can't merge.

The tool isn't an official LinkedIn preview and can't predict approval, delivery or performance. It's a review step before Campaign Manager, and the final check still happens there. If you want to poke at the decisions above, the Maestro LinkedIn ad mockup is free and runs entirely in your browser.

Disclosure: I'm Tim Keen and I run Maestro, the B2B paid media company that makes the tool. LinkedIn limits in this post were taken from LinkedIn's single image ad specifications page; the tool's page records them as checked on September 27, 2026. Unicode results come from Node 20.
