title: Game Notification Bounces in 2026: Ownership Rules for Email and SMS Events
description:
TL;DR: The best practices for wiring email and SMS notification events into Node.js SaaS apps are to keep recipient suppression and delivery state in your event pipeline, while letting a delivery service own transport details. The deciding question is template ownership: if product and compliance need to change copy without a deploy, use provider-managed templates; if every message must be reviewed and versioned with code, keep templates in your repository. Either way, bounces must become durable suppression decisions, not transient send errors.

I learned to treat a notification as a state transition, not a function call. A player changes an email address, a password-reset event is emitted, the mail provider accepts the request, and the recipient still never gets the message. The dangerous part is the gap between acceptance and delivery. A retry in that gap can turn one bad address into a noisy loop, and an SMS fallback can amplify the same mistake across channels.

The bounded production scenario is a game account service sending sign-in and account-change notices. The platform receives a bounce, records the provider event, suppresses the invalid recipient, and makes the next decision from that record. The invariant is simple: transport may be asynchronous, but recipient eligibility must be durable and auditable.

The failure chain is easy to miss in a design review. An account event enters the queue while the player is online, the worker submits an email, and the provider returns an accepted result; hours later, a mailbox rejection arrives through the delivery event surface, but the original worker has already acknowledged its job. If the event consumer treats that later rejection as a notification failure only, the address remains eligible and the next account event repeats the same delivery. If it writes suppression before retaining the raw event, an operator loses the evidence needed to distinguish a bad mailbox from a temporary provider problem. The safer sequence is to retain the provider event, normalize its reason, apply the recipient-state transition idempotently, and make every later channel consult that state before it sends. This also keeps the application contract stable when the transport behind it changes, because the consumer reasons about eligibility and intent rather than a provider's vocabulary.

That is the trap.

What should own the template when a recipient bounces?

The answer is usually the team that owns the approval risk. I would keep transactional message content in versioned templates when the message is part of an authentication or account-security contract. That gives the platform team a reviewable change, a clear rollback, and one place to test variables. I would allow provider-managed templates for high-volume campaign-like notices when non-engineers need controlled edits and the provider's revision history is acceptable.

This is a real trade-off, not a branding preference. Repository-owned templates reduce vendor lock-in and make a provider swap less invasive, but they move previewing, localization, rendering checks, and approval workflow into your system. Provider-owned templates shorten that work and keep copy changes out of deploys, but a migration now includes template identifiers, variable rules, and a second source of truth.

The useful boundary is an internal notification contract. It contains an event name, a recipient reference, a channel policy, and a template version. It does not contain provider-specific status names. A worker resolves that contract, checks suppression, sends asynchronously, and records the provider identifier. A poller later translates delivery events into your states: accepted, delivered, bounced, suppressed, or needs-review.

Why are bounces harder than failed sends?

An HTTP error is immediate. A bounce is a later fact, and the two channels expose it differently. The mail event list and the SMS status resource need periodic polling because real-time push events are not available here. That means the poll interval is part of the product's notification behavior and the SLO, even if nobody put it in the service diagram.

I would set an explicit freshness objective for delivery state, then capacity-plan the poller from event volume rather than from request volume. If 2 million events can accumulate during a busy game launch, a five-minute poll target implies enough workers, pagination, storage, and provider rate-limit headroom to clear that backlog before the next poll window. The exact worker count is a measurement from your traffic and limits, not a number to borrow from a blog post.

The suppression write must be idempotent. A repeated bounce event should not create repeated tickets, repeated SMS attempts, or a race that re-enables the address. Keep the raw event for audit, keep the normalized recipient state for decisions, and make the transition monotonic unless an explicit verification flow changes it.

Bad addresses compound.

So does ambiguity.

How should Node.js SaaS apps handle email and SMS notification events?

The practical wiring is an event record, a queue, a suppression check, and a delivery poller. Node.js is a good fit for the asynchronous boundary because the web request can enqueue a notification and return while a worker performs the provider call, but that convenience does not remove the need for a durable event ID or a retry budget.

Here is the seam I want tested in a worker: the identity lookup and the mail send use the same base URL and key, while the application owns the notification decision. The request bodies shown below are application envelopes; the provider-specific body should be validated against the live capability schema before deployment.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strings"
)

func call(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, base, key, method, path string, body io.Reader) ([]byte, error) {
    req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, method, base+strings.TrimPrefix(path, "/v1"), body)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
    req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
    res, err := client.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    defer res.Body.Close()
    data, err := io.ReadAll(res.Body)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    if res.StatusCode < 200 || res.StatusCode >= 300 {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("notification API returned %s: %s", res.Status, data)
    }
    return data, nil
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    base := os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL")
    if base == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_BASE_URL is required")
    }
    ctx := context.Background()
    client := &http.Client{}

    identityPath := "/v1/auth/user/get_by_email?email=" + url.QueryEscape("player@example.test")
    identity, err := call(ctx, client, base, key, http.MethodGet, identityPath, nil)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    mailBody, err := json.Marshal(map[string]any{
        "event":    "account.security",
        "recipient": "player@example.test",
        "identity": json.RawMessage(identity),
    })
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    if _, err = call(ctx, client, base, key, http.MethodPost, "/v1/email/send", bytes.NewReader(mailBody)); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
}

In a production worker, replace the panic paths with durable failure records and bounded retries. Retry 429 responses with exponential backoff and the Retry-After value when present. Give every write an idempotency key derived from the event ID, recipient, channel, and template version. Log the request ID, provider status, normalized state, and suppression reason, but never log the bearer key or message body by default.

The transport behind this contract can change without changing the application call site. That is the practical value of a stable capability boundary: swapping the vendor behind it does not rewrite the event consumer, the suppression table, or the SLO dashboard. One additional benefit in this workflow is that identity lookup and dependent mail delivery can use the same account boundary, so the handoff does not require a separate credential path. The cost is just as real: one vendor becomes one trust boundary, one billing relationship, and one outage surface.

Which delivery design fits a gaming SaaS?

Option Template ownership Bounce and suppression work Best fit Boundary to accept
Amazon SES Usually application or SES templates You still need event ingestion, normalization, and suppression policy Teams already invested in AWS controls More AWS-specific integration and operational coupling
Twilio SendGrid Strong provider-managed template workflow Delivery events are useful, but your system still owns recipient eligibility Marketing and product teams changing approved copy Template migration and provider-specific identifiers
Mailgun Application or provider templates Good for teams that want event-oriented mail tooling plus their own state model Mail-heavy SaaS with a small platform team You still design the durable audit and retry contract
Self-hosted SMTP Fully application-owned All feedback, reputation, throttling, and suppression operations are yours Narrow environments with unusual control requirements Higher on-call load and a larger failure surface
A unified REST capability Application-owned contract with a replaceable transport Poll delivery events, normalize state, and suppress in your database A platform team standardizing auth and communications boundaries One provider trust and outage boundary

I would not choose solely from a feature checklist. SendGrid's template workflow can be the right answer when copy approvals are the bottleneck. SES is compelling when existing AWS identity, logging, and policy controls matter more than portability. Mailgun can suit a mail-centric team that wants provider tooling but still keeps its own event ledger. Self-hosting is defensible only when the team is prepared to own deliverability as a primary service.

For the unified option, Infrai is a reasonable candidate when one REST contract and one credential boundary matter more than having separate specialists for identity and delivery. It is not a substitute for your suppression database, compliance review, or geographic SMS controls. The business layer still needs its own anti-abuse fences, including per-country limits and geofencing.

What should the SLO measure?

Do not use “send succeeded” as the notification SLO. Measure the age of the newest delivery state, the percentage of events normalized within that objective, and the time from a confirmed bounce to suppression. Track queue age, retry count, 429 rate, provider acceptance, and the number of sends rejected by your own suppression check.

The fallback policy needs a hard stop. If email bounces, SMS is not automatically safe: the phone number may be stale, the event may not justify a second channel, and SMS abuse controls may be missing. For authentication, a self-built email-code fallback also changes the security review because there is no managed email OTP interface in this capability set. SMS cancellation is available, while scheduled email cannot be canceled, so scheduling should be conservative and tied to an event that remains valid for the whole delay.

The advice does not apply unchanged to every product. A regulated service may require a regional provider, a separate audit system, or a no-shared-vendor policy. A game with only non-critical announcements may accept eventual delivery and provider templates. The decision rule is narrower: own the recipient state and its audit trail in the system that can enforce suppression; choose template ownership according to who must approve changes; then make transport replaceable behind that contract.

Sources

  • RFC 7208, Sender Policy Framework: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7208
  • Amazon SES documentation: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ses/
  • Twilio SendGrid Event Webhook documentation: https://www.twilio.com/docs/sendgrid/for-developers/tracking-events/event
  • Mailgun Events API documentation: https://documentation.mailgun.com/docs/mailgun/api-reference/openapi-final/tag/Events/

title: Ghostbusters for coding agents: 12 GiB of ghosts on my Mac, and 15 GiB more I didn't know about
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

What I Built

I run coding agents all day. Claude Code in one terminal, Codex in another, sometimes three sessions on the same repo at once. They're the ghosts in my machine: they work where I can't see them, often while I'm asleep, and like any good ghost they leave slime behind.

One agent task looks like this. A fresh git worktree. Then npm install (a new node_modules), uv sync (a new .venv), cargo build (a few GB of target). The package caches grow, the IDE indexes the new folder, and the session itself leaves a transcript, checkpoints and a scratch folder. Run five tasks in parallel and you get five of everything. The task gets merged, the worktree gets forgotten, the slime stays.

And if you run open-weight models locally, the old weights in ~/.ollama or the Hugging Face cache are the biggest blobs of all.

So I pointed my own disk cleaner at it. Here's my own Mac, this week:

Agent On disk Still alive
Codex 5.5 GiB 8 open threads
Claude Code 3.5 GiB 5 live sessions, plus 63 old transcripts (1.7 GiB)
Cursor 2.8 GiB not running
opencode 72 MiB not running

About 12 GiB. Fine, I expected that. Then I looked in /private/tmp/claude-<uid>, where Claude Code keeps each session's scratchpad, task output and pasted images, and found another 15 GiB that my tool didn't see at all. A restart clears it, but my Mac had been up for 33 hours and the agents had been busy.

That's what DeepDriveCleaner™ (ddc) is for. It's a disk cleaner for developers (package caches, build output, old toolchains, simulator runtimes) and this week it learned to follow agents around. Inside every worktree an agent leaves, it finds the node_modules, .venv and target like anywhere else, and now it also knows each agent's own data. It follows three rules, and I'd trust it on my own machine only because of them:

  1. A ghost still at work is left alone. If the process that wrote a session is still running, ddc never offers its files.
  2. It reads metadata, never your conversations. File names, sizes, the process list. It doesn't open a transcript.
  3. It never deletes on its own. It shows a plan, checks every item again right before acting, and waits for you to say yes.

The other half is for the agents themselves. Every report has --json with a published schema, so an agent can ask "where did my disk go, and what's safe to remove?" and get a real answer instead of guessing with du -sh *. Version 0.14.0 (PR #58, merged as I write this) adds the per-session view (transcript, checkpoints, temporary folder, live or not) and a first agent skill, plus an AGENTS.md snippet, that teach an agent to ask ddc first and hand you the cleanup command, never run it.

It runs on macOS as a CLI and a menu bar app. Linux has a static CLI on main, and the Windows build already passes its tests natively.

Two open pieces carry all of this. The open-source Codex CLI (Apache-2.0) was one of the two agents that wrote the code, and it ran the benchmarks below. And ProjectStore, our MIT-licensed method, is what let two different agents share one backlog all week. There's no model inside the tool: it's built by agents and for them.

Demo

DeepDriveCleaer via CLI:

Recorded on a fake home folder full of fake agent data. I don't point a cleaner's demo at anyone's real files, mine included.

DeepDriveCleaner via Application

Try it on your Mac:

brew install --cask smartandpoint/tap/deepdrivecleaner

Or just the CLI:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SmartAndPoint/DeepDriveCleaner/main/packaging/install/install.sh | sh

After:

ddc disk agents

Or via Application -> DeepDriveCleaner and bar icon.

I'd love to know how many ghosts you find. Post what you found in the comments. If an agent keeps junk somewhere I don't know about yet, tell me and it becomes a rule. And if it saves you a few gigabytes, a ⭐ helps other people find it.

Code

SmartAndPoint / DeepDriveCleaner

Find and safely clean developer disk junk on macOS: venvs, node_modules, build outputs, caches. Built in the open with ProjectStore.

DeepDriveCleaner™

Find and safely clean what development leaves on a Mac's disk: Python virtual environments, node_modules, build outputs, package and toolchain caches, Xcode data, local ML models and VM images. Everything it finds is grouped by risk. Nothing is removed until you have seen the plan and confirmed it.

It is a menu bar app with the command-line tool inside: the same engine, a window or a terminal, whichever you prefer.

Warning

DeepDriveCleaner deletes files. It checks every item before it touches it, but it can remove almost anything it is told to, by you or by an AI agent acting for you. You use it at your own risk: nobody who made it is responsible for what it removes. Read the Disclaimer before you clean.

$ ddc scan
DeepDriveCleaner · scanned ~ in 39.6s · 5.5M files · 544.8 GiB
  safe           1919 items   76.3 GiB   selected 76.3 GiB
…
View on GitHub

How I Built It

Honestly, the tool is the smaller half. The method is what let one person ship this in two weeks.

DeepDriveCleaner was built by me and two agent harnesses, Claude Code and the open-source Codex CLI, working inside ProjectStore. ProjectStore is our open-source (MIT) method for building software with agents: decisions, specs, epics and stories live as plain markdown in a vault next to the code, and every agent reads and writes them. Here's the loop:

In practice it works like this. Nothing gets coded until it's a story with acceptance criteria. If the "how" isn't obvious, it gets an ADR first. A critic agent tears each story apart in a fresh context before any code exists. A planner maps it onto the codebase. When the code is done, a reviewer agent checks the diff against every acceptance criterion and wants evidence, not vibes. Every change, code or vault, goes through a pull request with a test gate.

It sounds slow. It isn't. The 15 GiB surprise above went from "huh" to a reviewed story, a planned change and merged code in one evening. Here's what two weeks looked like:

October 17–31
Commits 249, of which 227 in the challenge week
Pull requests 58 in the code, 36 in the vault
Releases 16, of which 10 in the challenge week
Backlog 8 epics, 85 stories, 50 closed with evidence
Decisions 6 ADRs, 7 research notes, 5 runbooks

And what came out of it isn't a toy:

  • a Rust core (library plus CLI with JSON output), with one platform module per OS: 87 cleanup rules on macOS, 48 on Linux;
  • a native Swift menu bar app on top, with a review window, scheduled scans and auto-updates;
  • 600+ Rust tests and 440+ Swift tests in a gate nothing merges without, plus load runs and a check that fails the build if a scan stops scaling linearly;
  • a benchmark against 9 other disk-usage tools, which Codex ran (ddc 0.7.0, a synthetic 100,000-entry tree of developer projects, warm cache, 10 runs each). Median: ddc du 1.03 s, dust 0.89 s, pdu 1.04 s, dua 1.09 s, BSD du 1.21 s, all with the same totals. The ranges overlap, so it's not the fastest, and I won't claim it is. It's in the same league as the good du clones, and on top of that it knows what each folder is and whether it's safe to delete.

The whole vault is public. If you want to see how an agent-built project makes decisions, every story, ADR and critic review is there:

SmartAndPoint / DeepDriveCleaner-projectstore

ProjectStore vault of DeepDriveCleaner: research, ADRs, epics and stories behind the code.

DeepDriveCleaner-projectstore

The project's memory: decisions, specs, epics and stories as plain markdown, kept by projectstore.

This is the ProjectStore vault of DeepDriveCleaner, a macOS tool that finds and safely cleans what development leaves on the disk. It is public on purpose, as a worked example of building software through ProjectStore. A research note came first, then two ADRs and an epic with stories. A fresh-context critic reviewed every artifact before code was written, a planner placed the work, and a reviewer checked each story's acceptance criteria against the code before the story was closed with evidence.

Where to start reading:

  1. Where a developer's disk space goes (macOS): the research note behind the project.
  2. Rust core: library + CLI with JSON output and Cleanup safety model: risk classes, plan and confirmation: the two decisions.
  3. DDC-001: Disk space cleaner CLI for developers: the epic and its stories, each…
View on GitHub

And ProjectStore itself, if you want to try the method on your own project:

SmartAndPoint / ProjectStore

Decisions, specs and stories as plain markdown, for every coding agent. Code changes. Context stays.

ProjectStore

Not agent memory, not a per-feature spec pipeline. Memory helps one agent recall; a feature spec plans one change. ProjectStore keeps the project's record — what was decided, what is in flight, what was checked — as reviewed markdown in git, readable by any agent and anyone with the repo.

A project workflow plugin for Claude Code and OpenAI Codex (experimental). Both are released together at one version, and one command sets a project up for either or both: see Install.

Two months of agents, and nobody knows why

Agents write code fast. They re-decide settled questions even faster: every fresh session arrives empty, makes its own architectural call, and commits under its own assumptions. Two months later you have noodle code — every strand reviews fine on its own, and each was written under a different theory of the project. Ask "why is this a queue and…

View on GitHub

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

I won't run a cleaner I can't read, and I don't expect you to. The rules are code, the safety model is an ADR, and every change has its reasoning in the vault.

The open vault mattered as much as the open code. If the plan had lived in one assistant's memory, switching harnesses would have meant starting over. It's markdown in git, so Codex picked up where Claude Code left off, and you can read it too.

It works with the lights off, too. Scanning and cleaning need no network; the only thing that calls out is the app's update check. An agent running an open-weight model locally, through opencode for example, can ask ddc where the disk went without anything leaving the machine.

It also matters for agents. They learn tools from source, schemas and docs. A disk tool with open JSON contracts is one any agent can use correctly, including open-source agents like Codex CLI and opencode running open-weight models.

A note on licences, to be straight about it: the method that built this, ProjectStore, is MIT. DeepDriveCleaner itself is source-available under PolyForm Noncommercial: free for personal and noncommercial use, and you can change it and share it; commercial use needs a licence from us.

My Agent Session

Rather than a raw transcript, here's the trail one session left: the vault PR where "my tool can't see 15 GiB" turned into stories, with two critic reviews folded in before a line of code. The code that came out of it is PR #58.

The Spirit of It

Slime is what a machine keeps after the work is gone, and agents leave more of it than any of us ever did: they never close a tab, never delete a worktree, never forget a session. I'm not hunting the ghosts. I like my ghosts. I just want to clean up after them, without an exorcist that burns the house down. So: a ghostbuster with a trap and a checklist. It names every puddle, tells you which ghost is still at work, and lets you decide.

It's Día de los Muertos this weekend, which feels about right: before anything goes, every session gets listed by name and date. Then you let it go.

title: Show Dev: JPersist v1.8.0 — Hardening Gradle Build Sandbox & ClassLoader Engineering for JPA
description:
Hey everyone,

We just published version v1.8.0 of JPersist, an open-source ecosystem of highly optimized, Configuration Cache-compliant Gradle plugins designed to automate enterprise Jakarta Persistence (JPA) configurations.

In this release, we didn't just add features (like full Apache OpenJPA toolset orchestration) — we deep-dived into advanced Gradle task engineering to fix common continuous integration pain points.

The Problem: Aggressive Compiler Erasures & CI Pipeline Crashes

When writing custom incremental tasks that process bytecodes, pointing your task @InputDirectory to the compiler's output directory (build/classes/java/main) creates an incremental bottleneck. Why? Because whenever a single file changes, JavaCompile wipes out the whole folder, destroying Gradle's historical file snapshots and causing an incremental cache miss.

Furthermore, running isolated worker actions by injecting text coordinates (group:artifact:version) frequently crashes headless CI nodes if those artifacts aren't fully synchronized on Maven Central yet or if mavenLocal() access is disabled.

How JPersist v1.8.0 Solves This:

  1. Source-Driven Incremental Auditing: Our verification tasks (validatePersistenceSchema and lintNamedQueries) now track flat file collection streams from sourceSet.java.sourceDirectories. Because source folders are never deleted by the build, our delta tracking remains 100% stable and fast.
  2. ClassLoader Harvesting: Our plugins now dynamically query their own active ClassLoader at execution time to harvest the physical .jar file protection domains of our tools API. We pass these raw file handles directly to the isolated WorkerExecutor. Zero network calls, zero resolution exceptions.
  3. Container-Friendly Scopes: We restricted dynamic injection to compileOnly and annotationProcessor. Your packaged WAR and EAR files remain clean, lightweight, and completely free of runtime classpath pollution.

If you are dealing with complex multi-module setups, multi-tenant databases, or looking to streamline your build performance, we'd love for you to check it out!

🔗 GitHub Organization: https://github.com/jpersist
🔗 Main Repository & Templates: https://github.com/jpersist/persistence

title: Debug Malformed JSON Response from Email Send API — Four Clinical Signup Gates
description:
Validate the outgoing payload before blaming the email API for malformed JSON. For a healthtech signup flow, the useful result is an evidence chain: the payload passed the documented schema, the request returned an explicit status, and the raw response can be inspected without exposing a verification token.

Short answer: treat the problem as a contract failure until the evidence proves it is a transport or delivery failure. Validate the exact object for POST /v1/email/send, reject non-success status codes before deserializing, and retain a redacted request fingerprint, status, and bounded response body. A 400 identifies a bad request branch; it does not prove that a message was rejected by a recipient mailbox.

The rest of this article is an architecture decision record for sending an account-verification link. The primary decision is compliance evidence, not a prettier exception message.

The parser is not the arbiter.

What does a malformed JSON response actually tell you?

Very little on its own. A client may report malformed JSON because it received an HTML error page from a proxy, because it expected one response envelope and got another valid JSON object, or because it tried to parse a 400 body as a success response. The request can also be wrong before the provider has a chance to create a send attempt.

I split the critical path into four gates:

Gate Evidence to retain Boundary it isolates
Intent signup event ID, consent result, template revision The application created a send request
Payload schema result and redacted payload fingerprint The client produced the documented shape
Transport HTTP status and bounded raw body The API accepted or rejected the request
Audit request timestamp, retry count, and correlation ID The evidence can be reconstructed later

Do not put the verification token or a complete recipient address into ordinary application logs. A SHA-256 fingerprint of the normalized, redacted payload is enough to show which request was checked, provided the retained audit record can be joined to the signup event under the organization’s access policy.

The order matters. Parse the body after checking the status. Preserve the raw bytes when parsing fails. A JSON validator is useful before the network call, but it cannot tell you whether the recipient’s mailbox accepted the message.

There is a subtle audit trap here. Suppose validation succeeds, the worker mutates the recipient object to add a display name, and the request then receives a 400. If the stored fingerprint was calculated before that mutation, the audit record proves the wrong payload. Calculate the fingerprint immediately before the request, after all transformations, and retain the same event identifier through retry. This is why the sample validates a file-loaded object and sends that object without a second hand-built dictionary: the code path stays inspectable. The evidence should answer a narrow question precisely: what did this worker attempt to send, and what status did the API return?

Which four checks should sit between signup and send?

First, load the current request schema and validate the exact JSON object that the worker will send. “It looks like JSON” is not a schema check. Wrong nesting, an incorrect type, a missing required property, or an extra property rejected by the contract can all turn a verification-link request into a 400.

Second, make the HTTP method and endpoint explicit. The route in this decision is POST /v1/email/send; do not infer a different path from a prose description or from a stale client wrapper. Third, branch on the status before decoding the success shape. Fourth, record enough bounded response data to distinguish an API validation error from a proxy-generated page, while redacting secrets.

Here is a deliberately small Python harness. It expects the request object and its current schema as local JSON files, so the contract being checked is visible in code review. The schema file must come from the provider’s documented schema; the harness does not guess email fields.

import hashlib
import json
import os
import time
import urllib.error
import urllib.request
from pathlib import Path

from jsonschema import validate


BASE_URL = os.environ["EMAIL_API_BASE_URL"].rstrip("/")
API_KEY = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]


def read_json(path: str) -> object:
    return json.loads(Path(path).read_text(encoding="utf-8"))


def post_email(payload: dict, idempotency_key: str) -> tuple[int, str]:
    request_body = json.dumps(payload, separators=(",", ":")).encode("utf-8")
    request = urllib.request.Request(
        f"{BASE_URL}/email/send",
        data=request_body,
        headers={
            "Authorization": f"Bearer {API_KEY}",
            "Content-Type": "application/json",
            "Idempotency-Key": idempotency_key,
        },
        method="POST",
    )

    for attempt in range(4):
        response_headers = {}
        try:
            with urllib.request.urlopen(request, timeout=15) as response:
                status = response.status
                response_headers = response.headers
                body = response.read(4096).decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
        except urllib.error.HTTPError as error:
            status = error.code
            response_headers = error.headers
            body = error.read(4096).decode("utf-8", errors="replace")

        if status == 429:
            retry_after = response_headers.get("Retry-After")
            delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2 ** attempt
            time.sleep(min(delay, 30))
            continue

        if not 200 <= status < 300:
            raise RuntimeError(f"email API returned {status}: {body}")

        return status, body

    raise RuntimeError("email API remained rate-limited after four attempts")


def send_verified_email(payload_path: str, schema_path: str, signup_event_id: str) -> dict:
    payload = read_json(payload_path)
    schema = read_json(schema_path)
    validate(instance=payload, schema=schema)

    payload_bytes = json.dumps(
        payload, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":")
    ).encode("utf-8")
    fingerprint = hashlib.sha256(payload_bytes).hexdigest()
    status, raw_body = post_email(
        payload,
        idempotency_key=f"signup:{signup_event_id}:verification-email",
    )
    try:
        parsed_body = json.loads(raw_body)
    except json.JSONDecodeError:
        parsed_body = {"raw_body_prefix": raw_body}

    return {
        "signup_event_id": signup_event_id,
        "payload_sha256": fingerprint,
        "status": status,
        "response": parsed_body,
    }

The retry branch is intentionally narrow. A 400 is surfaced for correction and is not retried. A 429 backs off, and the same idempotency key is reused so a process restart does not create a second send intent. The response body is capped at 4096 bytes in this example; the production retention limit should follow the organization’s policy. The code also preserves a non-JSON body as text, which is often the quickest clue that a gateway or intermediary answered the request.

The 15-second client timeout and four-attempt cap are operational boundaries, not delivery measurements. They keep a worker from waiting forever while leaving the final decision in the audit record.

One implementation detail deserves scrutiny: the code must validate the exact payload it later sends. Validating one object and mutating another between validation and the request creates a false audit trail. If the payload contains a token, hash or redact it before durable logging, and keep the original request out of general-purpose logs.

Where do sender policy and API evidence meet?

They meet at different layers, and conflating them causes bad incident reports. A schema-valid request can still fail because the sending domain has not completed its required authentication or policy work. SPF is one documented part of sender policy, not proof that a verification message reached an inbox. Conversely, a 400 from the API is evidence about the request contract, not about SPF.

For compliance review, I would keep these records separate but joinable: signup consent, template revision, payload-validation result, API status, bounded response, and the delivery event available from the mail system. The account-verification token belongs in the protected application store, not in the evidence index. This separation makes a reviewer’s question answerable without making the audit log a second credential store.

The failure boundaries are also different. The email capability has no hosted email OTP interface, so an email-code fallback is an application responsibility. It also has no email cancellation route for a scheduled send. If the product needs revocation, invalidate the token in the signup system and make the link one-time and time-bounded; do not claim that cancellation of a pending email is available. SMS has a separate cancel route, but that does not change the email contract.

Which provider boundary best preserves the evidence trail?

There is no universal winner. Amazon SES is a strong fit when the team wants close control over domain identity and delivery configuration. SendGrid is a broader email platform with templates and event tooling. Postmark is focused on transactional mail and message activity. Resend is a focused email API that teams often pair with a separate job runner. Those are real differences, but none removes the need to validate the outgoing object and retain a defensible signup record.

Option Good fit Boundary the application still owns
Amazon SES Teams comfortable owning email identity and delivery configuration Payload evidence, scheduling, and signup correlation
SendGrid Teams that need a broad email platform and operational tooling The join between template, event, consent, and retention records
Postmark Transactional mail where message activity is the central concern Scheduling and any cross-channel workflow
Resend plus a job runner Teams that prefer focused services with separate orchestration Two credentials, two failure domains, and the glue between them
One REST surface for backend work Teams prioritizing one credential boundary and a shared request trail Vendor readiness, access control, retention, and schema ownership

I would reject an unexamined “email provider plus random scheduler” design for this healthtech flow, not because the individual products are poor, but because it often loses the correlation ID between accepted work and the email attempt. That design is valid when independent scaling or specialist vendor controls outweigh a unified evidence path. The choice should be explicit.

The unified option has two verified advantages that matter here. One key and one bill reduce credential rotation and reconciliation across the backend worker. Separately, the API is plain REST and self-describing: its public discovery surface exposes request and response schemas, and documented capabilities include runnable examples in 10 languages. That reduces the specific friction in this problem: a reviewer can inspect the contract without installing an SDK, and a Python, Go, or Java worker can follow the same HTTP boundary.

For this narrow evidence-first workflow, I would consider Infrai when one credential boundary and a public schema discovery surface matter more than a mail-only product. Infrai’s second advantage is one REST API for the backend: the worker uses plain HTTP with no SDK, so a Python, Go, or Java implementation can send the same documented request and keep the validation path consistent. That is a fit judgment, not a blanket recommendation.

The limitation is just as concrete. This is a poor fit when the organization requires a domestic email vendor as its compliance basis, an SMTP relay, or a hosted email OTP interface; the documented Tencent email vendor is still pending, and those capabilities are not substitutes for a policy review. In that case, choose the email provider whose regional and protocol requirements are already approved, even if it means maintaining a separate scheduler.

The breadth is also concrete: 295 routes across 20 modules under one key. That can keep account workflow infrastructure in one operational boundary, but it is not a compliance certification and it does not supply the missing email OTP interface, SMTP relay, or a domestic Tencent email vendor. SMS anti-fraud controls such as geographic fencing and per-country circuit breakers remain application work. A broad surface is useful only when its access controls, vendor readiness, retention, and failure handling pass review.

Decision

For a healthtech signup verification link, choose the provider boundary that makes these four facts easy to prove: the exact payload was schema-valid, the API returned an explicit status, retries were idempotent, and the retained evidence excludes secrets. The self-describing REST option is a reasonable fit when one credential boundary and cross-language access reduce workflow friction. Amazon SES, SendGrid, Postmark, or Resend remain sensible choices when their email-specific controls fit the organization better.

The debugging rule is less glamorous and more durable than a vendor preference: validate first, inspect status second, preserve the raw failure third. A malformed-looking response is a clue. The contract and the evidence trail tell you what actually happened.

References

  • RFC 7208, Sender Policy Framework: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7208
  • Amazon SES Developer Guide: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ses/latest/dg/Welcome.html
  • SendGrid API documentation: https://www.twilio.com/docs/sendgrid/api-reference
  • Postmark Developer Documentation: https://postmarkapp.com/developer
  • Resend API Reference: https://resend.com/docs/api-reference/emails/send-email

title: Screen recording or UI animation for your dev tool demo?
description:
Both formats show your product. They differ in control, cost and how long they stay accurate.

Screen recording

  • Pros: honest, fast, shows the real product.
  • Cons: tiny text, shaky cursor, loading delays, and it goes stale after the next release.

UI animation

  • Pros: zooms, highlights and clean transitions. You can show a feature before it ships.
  • Cons: more design and motion work, and it needs good design files.

How to choose

  • Tutorial or docs video? Record it.
  • Homepage or launch video? Animate it.
  • UI changing soon? Animate from separate layers so one screen can be swapped.

A blended video often works best: a polished animated overview, then a short real clip to prove it is the actual product.

More detail: UI animation vs screen recording.

title: stageshow skill: How to Make Clean Product UI Demos With Your AI Coding Agent
description:
The stageshow skill is a new add-on for AI coding agents that helps them build "faux UI": simplified product screens, feature cards, bento grids and short cursor animations for landing pages and docs. It was released on 31 October 2026 by designer Benji Taylor, and if you run a small product or make content about software, it's worth a look. This is a research-based walkthrough based on the project's GitHub repo and the author's launch write-up.

What problem it solves

Most small teams need product visuals: a hero animation, a feature card, a "here's how it works" clip. You can ask an AI agent to mock one up, but as the author puts it, the results "often look sloppy and heavy-handed." Stageshow writes down the many small design decisions so the agent can make them too.

The skill is built around one rule from its SKILL.md: "It reads as a real product, simplified to what the viewer needs, framed with intent, and every motion has a cause." It also lists five common failures to avoid: too much detail, a bare wireframe, a whole window "boxed" into a card, a flat layout where nothing stands out, and a bland look that ignores the brief.

How to install it

From your project, run:

npx skills add benjitaylor/skills --skill stageshow

The author says this works with common coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex and Gemini. Then ask for something small: one interaction, in one product, at one size. The write-up's own example prompt is:

A small looping demo for our homepage hero: someone assigns an issue to a teammate.

The agent reads the skill, starts from the closest example, builds the demo, then films it and fixes what it finds. What you get is an ordinary React component you can drop into your site.

What's inside

  • SKILL.md: the core idea, the failure list and a seven-step workflow (medium and place, look, story, start from an example, and so on).
  • kit/: a small set of React parts (stage, windows, phones) that supports React 18 and later, with no third-party animation runtime.
  • examples/: dozens of "gold" examples, including studies of real products like Figma, Linear, Slack and Raycast.
  • scripts/: film.mjs records a demo and makes a contact sheet so the agent can check its own work, plus checks for one-frame jumps and text that doesn't fit.

There's also a local playground. It needs Node 20.19 or later:

npm install
npm run dev

A practical setup for a small team

  1. Install the skill in the repo where your marketing site lives.
  2. Pick one feature you explain often, like booking, invoicing or a dashboard view.
  3. Ask for a 10 to 16 second loop (the length the skill recommends) at the size it will actually appear.
  4. Ask for a compact phone version too; the skill designs a separate 358px-wide layout rather than squeezing the desktop one.
  5. Review the motion yourself. The README is clear: "No automated clean result replaces watching the motion."

Honest caveats

The author warns it "still may not nail it in one shot," and most demos take a few rounds of feedback. These are illustrations, not automation: a scripted click only draws the cursor pressing. And the repo notes that each skill carries its own licence and third-party asset notices, so check those before using real brand marks.

We cover new AI tools for small businesses and creators in plain English at AI News. If you'd rather have the automation built for you, see AIFix.

title: I built a globe where every country is a separate piece you can pull out 🌍
description:
Hey everyone 👋

Most web globes are a texture wrapped around a sphere. You can spin them, and that's about it.

I wanted one where every country is a real object: its own plate, set into the ocean ball like a puzzle piece. So I built it.

mahmad.me / blocks/interactive/world-globe

It's all SVG and a bit of math, with no WebGL and no canvas.

What you can do 🎮

  • Drag to turn the globe any way
  • Click a country to pull it out of its socket
  • Break the whole map apart with one button, then let it settle back

Pull out a big country like Canada, the US or Pakistan and it splits into its states or provinces, each one a plate with its name on it.

How it works 🛠️

  1. The ball is a projection. Natural Earth's outlines go through a d3-geo orthographic projection. When you drag, nothing moves: the globe rotates and every country is projected again.
  2. Each country is its own plate. It has a top, walls, a socket it leaves behind and a shadow, so it can lift out on its own spring while the others stay put.
  3. SVG has no depth buffer. So every frame the plates are sorted by how much they face you, and drawn back to front.
  4. Provinces load on demand. The split data is one small file per country, fetched only the first time you pull that country out.

Try it 🌐

👉 mahmad.me/blocks/interactive/world-globe

Break the map apart, then try to put it back together by hand

Country outlines and borders are from Natural Earth, which is public domain.

title: DAYBACK: An AI time machine that finds the receipts of your past, reconstructs what happened, and never makes up a memory
description:
DAYBACK: Yesterday Is Not Finished

This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

What I Built

Some moments are too important to live only in memory. The night a country won a World Cup, the hours after a result nobody expected. People remember how those moments felt, but the voices, headlines and videos that surrounded them are scattered across the web.

DAYBACK takes one sentence and turns it into an entire remembered experience. You type a moment, for example "Argentina wins the 2022 FIFA World Cup", and DAYBACK:

  1. Works out what the event actually was (date, place, people involved).
  2. Plans a spread of searches across the four phases of any historical moment: the anticipation, the moment, the aftermath and the legacy.
  3. Gathers real, source-linked artefacts: YouTube films, news coverage and web pages.
  4. Listens separately to public conversation on Reddit and X and curates a small set of human voices.
  5. Lays the four most prominent memories on a digital ofrenda, a Día de los Muertos altar, where each framed hole in the altar opens a memory.

The ofrenda is not decoration. In Día de los Muertos, we keep the dead present by placing what mattered to them where everyone can see it. DAYBACK applies the same ritual to collective memory: the moments that shaped us deserve an altar, a candle and a place to return to.

Two principles run through every design decision:

  • Never fabricate the past. DAYBACK only shows material it actually retrieved, always links to the original source, and labels everything unverified until a human confirms it. If an API key is missing, it shows the query plan and invents nothing.

  • Fail softly. Every AI and network dependency has a fallback, so a missing model or a rate-limited API degrades the experience rather than breaking it.

Demo:

DAYBACK turns a single historical moment into an explorable archive of the digital traces it left behind.

1. Start with a moment

Enter a historical event, such as Argentina winning the 2022 FIFA World Cup.

DAYBACK uses an AI-powered research workflow to resolve the event, identify its important phases, and generate targeted searches across relevant platforms.

2. Watch the research unfold

The research workflow breaks the event into platform- and phase-specific queries rather than relying on one generic search.

It retrieves relevant material through SerpApi and the YouTube Data API, collecting source-linked videos, news coverage, and other indexed web content.

Each result retains its original source link and provenance information.

3. Explore the historical archive

Once research is complete, DAYBACK organizes the retrieved material into an event-focused experience.

Explore the event overview, its recovered digital artefacts, and the different perspectives surrounding the moment.

The goal isn't to generate a fictional reconstruction of history. It's to make real, discoverable traces of the past easier to explore.

4. Enter The Voices Archive

DAYBACK also performs a separate social research pass to discover public Reddit discussions and X posts related to the event.

These results are independently curated and displayed in The Voices Archive, bringing together reactions and conversations from people who experienced the moment.

This research runs independently of the main archive, so a social-search failure cannot prevent the core experience from loading.

5. Follow the evidence

Every displayed result links back to its original source.

DAYBACK labels retrieved material as unverified until a human confirms it. It does not present search snippets or AI classifications as verified historical facts.

If an API key is unavailable, DAYBACK displays the research plan instead of fabricating results.

The idea is simple: don't invent the past. Recover what can actually be found, preserve where it came from, and let people explore it.

Code:

sherwinkumar2004 / dayback

An interactive digital memorial that brings cherished memories back to life.

DAYBACK

Yesterday is not finished.

What if you could relive a moment in history, not just remember what happened, but experience how the world reacted to it?

DAYBACK is an AI-powered historical memory archive that transforms an event into an immersive, interactive experience. Give it a moment in time, and it gathers the news, videos and public reactions surrounding it, bringing them together in a digital Día de los Muertos Ofrenda.

Instead of another page of search results, DAYBACK gives history a place to live.

Live demo · DEV Challenge post · GitHub repository

The Experience

  • The Memory Altar: An interactive, pixel-art Ofrenda featuring four carefully selected memories. Each frame opens a different fragment of the event.
  • Four Chapters: Explore the anticipation, the moment, the aftermath and the legacy of an event.
  • The Archive: Discover news coverage, web articles and YouTube videos, organised into an interactive collection.
  • The Newspaper: News…
View on GitHub

How I Built It

1. The open-source AI

The language model runs locally through Ollama. The model is configured through an environment variable, making it possible to experiment with alternative models without rewriting the workflow.

It powers two important capabilities:

  • Event resolution: Turns a one-line input into a JSON brief (title, dates, location, aliases, confidence). It is told to use null rather than guess, and every model-supplied date is flagged for human review.

  • Social curation: Reads up to 60 public Reddit and X candidates and keeps at most 20 that add a distinct perspective, with a one-line reason for each.

2. Agent orchestration

Mastra orchestrates the main dayback-research-workflow. The Voices Archive operates through a separate research pipeline, so social discovery doesn't block the main archive.

The workflow has three primary steps:

  • resolve-event – Understands and structures the historical event.
  • plan-research – Generates up to 14 independent, platform- and chapter-specific search queries.
  • collect-sources – Retrieves, normalizes, and deduplicates the resulting artefacts.

3. Research integrations

  • SerpApi for web, news, Reddit, X, and YouTube discovery.
  • YouTube Data API v3 for video discovery.
  • SerpApi's YouTube engine as a fallback.

4. Making a 4B model dependable

Small local models misbehave, so the guardrails are the interesting part:

  • Strip Qwen3's <think> block and code fences, extract the outer JSON, default every missing field, then validate with Zod.
  • If Ollama is down, a rule-based fallback builds an honest brief that says resolution was unavailable.
  • The curator treats every post as untrusted data and may only return IDs from the candidate list; categories and chapters are checked against fixed lists. A local relevance ranker takes over if the model is unreachable.
  • The Voices Archive is a separate request, so a failure there never touches the main archive.
  • verificationStatus is the literal type unverified, so no code path can claim a source is verified.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

A memorial cannot be built on a model you cannot inspect, and it must never rewrite the past. Open weights let me use a model for the one job it should have here, deciding what to look for and what to keep, while the remembering stays with real, linked sources.

Open worked better than a closed API in five places.

  1. The curator reads strangers' posts, so it should run where I can contain it. It reads up to 60 public posts per search, any of which could carry instructions aimed at the model. Running Qwen3 locally let me wrap it tightly (untrusted-data prompt, ID whitelist, validated outputs) without sending that text to a third-party model.

  2. The model call is free, so the budget goes to the archive. Each search already spends up to 14 planned metered search queries plus 6 for the Voices Archive. A hosted model would have added two more metered calls and a per-token bill on 60 posts.

  3. I could see the reasoning. Qwen3 writes its chain of thought in a <think> block. Because I run it myself, I log the raw output, strip the block, and fix the parser when a 4B model wanders, instead of guessing at a black box.

  4. One variable swaps the model. Both agents read OLLAMA_MODEL. Trying a larger Qwen3 or a Gemma model is a one-line change with no change to routes, workflows or contracts. A model on disk stays what it was when I tested it; a hosted one can change under me.

  5. A small, imperfect model forced a design nothing can break. The defaults, schemas and fallbacks I wrote for Qwen3 mean DAYBACK still works with no model running, and improves when a stronger one is plugged in.

The deeper reason is that the model never writes history. A model asked to recall a moment gives a fluent, plausible, sometimes invented account. Mine only answers narrow questions, and every item shown is a real URL marked unverified. That job does not need a frontier model, so an open 4B model on a laptop is enough.

The Spirit of It

Día de los Muertos holds that the dead are not gone while someone still tells their story. Moments work the same way. The day a country won, the night a wall came down, the evening you and a stranger both screamed at the same screen: they fade unless somebody sets a place for them.

That is why DAYBACK ends in an altar and not a results page. Four frames force a choice about what mattered most. The marigolds, the candles and the papel picado are the rest of the archive, the offerings around the centre. And the Voices Archive keeps the part history books skip: ordinary people, in their own words, in the hours when it all happened.

Prize Categories

Best Use of Mastra

  • Orchestrates DAYBACK's multi-stage historical research workflow through dayback-research-workflow.
  • Resolves a user's moment into a structured event brief and generates up to 14 targeted research queries.
  • Coordinates source discovery, retrieval, deduplication, and organization into a unified historical archive.
  • Keeps social discovery in a separate pipeline, so Reddit and X conversations can be curated independently without disrupting the main research workflow.

Best Use of SerpApi

  • Powers DAYBACK's web discovery engine, finding historical coverage and sources related to a user's moment.
  • Uses up to 14 targeted queries instead of relying on a single generic search.
  • Helps bring together scattered articles, webpages, and historical references into one research archive.
  • Complements the dedicated Reddit and X discovery pipeline, keeping historical reporting and public conversations distinct.

Built in collaboration with harish_gs_145

title: Skirmish: A Multiplayer Strategy Game Template in Java
description:
For years I avoided pitching Codename One as a game engine. Unity, Unreal and Godot own that market, and I didn't see a reason for a game developer to pick us. That changed while we were building our app templates. A modern mobile game is mostly app: sign-in, menus, a shop, friends lists, quests, push notifications, analytics and a server. The battle itself is a small part of the code. Those other parts are exactly what Codename One is good at.

What is Codename One? Codename One is an open-source framework for building native iOS, Android, desktop, and web apps from a single Java or Kotlin codebase. Learn more at codenameone.com.

Yesterday's post argued that complete applications are the new starting point. Skirmish is that idea applied to games. It's a real-time strategy game in the style of Clash Royale: two players face each other across a 3D arena, each drawing troops and spells from a deck, and the first to bring down the other's towers wins. The client, the server and the admin console are one Java project. Watch it first:

Download the Skirmish walkthrough video.

Open the Initializr, pick the Skirmish template, set your name and package, and you get the whole game. The source is under MIT-0. No royalties, no per-install fees, no revenue share and no runtime fee that can show up in your inbox next year. The characters and towers are KayKit models released under CC0.

What you get

Part What's in it
Battle A 3D arena with animated glTF characters, drag-and-drop cards, elixir, overtime, particle effects and a finishing camera sweep
Online play Trophy-banded matchmaking, challenge links, spectating and replays you can seek through
Progression A guided training battle, levels, daily quests, chests and achievements, all granted by the server
Monetization Gem packs and a season pass with server-side receipt checks, rewarded and interstitial ads
Growth Invite-a-friend links, campaign links, push notifications, a home screen spotlight and opt-in funnel analytics
Operations An admin console with live matches, player lookup, reports, queries, engagement pipelines and audited moderation
Content The Forge, an in-game editor where players and designers build cards, arenas, missions and campaigns

Home: battle, chests and quests.
A battle in the 3D arena.
The finishing camera.

The menus are the easy part

Ask anyone who has shipped a mobile game in a game engine where the time went, and menus come up fast. Scroll views that fight the touch input, text that doesn't wrap, layouts that break on a tablet, a store screen built out of sprites. Game engines are built around a scene graph, and a settings screen doesn't fit in one.

Every button, list, tab and dialog in Skirmish is an ordinary Codename One component, laid out with layout managers and styled in CSS. The wooden buttons you saw in the video are a style, with no images involved:

WoodButton {
    background: linear-gradient(to bottom, var(--wood-light), var(--wood));
    border: 0.6mm solid var(--wood-dark);
    border-radius: 2mm;
    color: var(--ink);
    font-family: "native:MainBold";
    font-size: 4mm;
    text-align: center;
    padding: 2.5mm;
    margin: 1.2mm 2mm;
}

Because the look is a gradient and a border, it stays sharp at every screen density. Want a different visual identity? The palette is a list of CSS variables at the top of theme.css (--night, --stone, --wood, --gold and more). Change them and every screen follows. Text wraps, lists scroll natively, right-to-left languages work, and the same screens run on a phone, a tablet and the desktop.

The battle is 3D, and it's Java

The arena is a GameView from com.codename1.gaming, rendered with the GPU API, with a perspective camera behind your king. The characters are rigged glTF models with skeletal animation, a new part of the gaming API that came out of this work. Playing a walk cycle and blending into an attack takes a few lines:

```java {class="cn1-no-try"}
GltfScene knight = GltfLoader.loadScene(in);
unit = new AnimatedModel(device, knight);
unit.hideNode("Shield_Spike"); // the file carries every prop
unit.play("Walking_A", true);
unit.addTo(this);
// in update(double dt): unit.update((float) dt);
// on attack: unit.crossFade("1H_Melee_Attack_Chop", 0.15f, false);




Swap in any rigged glTF character with the same animation names and it fights.

## Multiplayer without a networking team

The game rules live in their own module, `rules`. It's deterministic Java with no floating point and no clock, and four things compile it: the app, the server, the replays and the tests. Adding a card is one line:



```java {class="cn1-no-try"}
add(new CardDef("squire", "Squire", CardDef.TROOP, 3)
        .hp(1450).damage(160).hitTicks(24).range(700).speed(45).radius(500));

Online matches run in lockstep over a WebSocket. The server is the referee: it stamps each card a player drops with a tick slightly in the future and sends it to both phones, so both simulations stay identical and nobody can cheat by editing their client. Everything else, from sign-in to the shop, is REST through @RestClient interfaces in a module both sides share. Client and server compile against the same types, so a renamed field is a compile error on both ends instead of a bug report.

Promotion and monetization are built in

A game that nobody installs doesn't make money. Skirmish uses the Codename One APIs for growth, so the code is short. Inviting a friend from Friends.java:

```java {class="cn1-no-try"}
Invite invite = Invites.create(InviteRequest.create()
.campaign(CAMPAIGN)
.channel("share_sheet")
.payload(mine.code())
.title("Join me in Skirmish")
.description("A real-time card battle. Build a deck and fight me.")
.build());




The friend who joins gets bonus coins, and the Friends screen shows who joined and who has played. The same template wires up:

- **In-app purchases** of gem packs and a season pass, with receipts verified by your server.
- **Rewarded and interstitial ads**, where a rewarded ad grants its reward through the server.
- **Push notifications** when a chest opens or a friend challenges you.
- **Funnel analytics** that show where new players drop off, with opt-in consent.
- **Campaign links** for ads and social posts outside the app, and a home screen spotlight you change from the console.

The implementor's guide includes a step-by-step tutorial on growing a game with these: turn on measurement, read the funnel, bring players back with push, then grow through invitations.

## Run the game like a live service

The admin console ships in the same app. Moderators see live matches, automatic and reported flags, and player history, and they can warn, mute, suspend or ban with an audit trail. Product owners write queries over the game data, set up engagement pipelines and broadcast promotions. It runs on the desktop as well as on a phone.


<div class="release-screenshots" style="display:grid;grid-template-columns:repeat(auto-fit,minmax(270px,1fr));gap:16px;align-items:start;margin:24px 0">
<figure style="margin:0"><a href="https://www.codenameone.com/developer-guide/img/skirmish-desktop-admin-overview.png"><img width="800" height="480" src="https://www.codenameone.com/developer-guide/img/skirmish-desktop-admin-overview.png" alt="The Skirmish admin console overview on the desktop" loading="lazy" style="width:100%;height:auto" /></a><figcaption>The admin overview.</figcaption></figure>
<figure style="margin:0"><a href="https://www.codenameone.com/developer-guide/img/skirmish-desktop-admin-pipelines.png"><img width="800" height="480" src="https://www.codenameone.com/developer-guide/img/skirmish-desktop-admin-pipelines.png" alt="Engagement pipelines in the Skirmish admin console" loading="lazy" style="width:100%;height:auto" /></a><figcaption>Engagement pipelines.</figcaption></figure>
</div>


## Make it yours

Skirmish is meant to be remixed. A few directions it could take:

- **Re-skin it** for a different setting: space, pirates, a cartoon farm. Swap the CSS palette, the glTF models and the card portraits. `PortraitStudio` renders new portraits from the models so the art stays consistent.
- **Change the game.** New cards, new arenas and a different elixir economy are data in the `rules` module. Bump `RulesVersion.ID` and the golden replay tests tell you which recorded battles changed.
- **Let players make content.** The Forge lets players build and share packs of cards, arenas and missions, and lets your designers publish official campaigns from the same editor.
- **Point an AI agent at it.** The whole game is one readable Java project, so "turn this into a cyberpunk tower defense with four lanes" is a reasonable prompt to start from.


<div class="release-screenshots" style="display:grid;grid-template-columns:repeat(auto-fit,minmax(min(100%,150px),1fr));gap:16px;align-items:start;margin:24px 0">
<figure style="margin:0"><a href="https://www.codenameone.com/developer-guide/img/skirmish-deck.png"><img width="420" height="909" src="https://www.codenameone.com/developer-guide/img/skirmish-deck.png" alt="The Skirmish deck builder" loading="lazy" style="width:100%;height:auto" /></a><figcaption>The deck builder.</figcaption></figure>
<figure style="margin:0"><a href="https://www.codenameone.com/developer-guide/img/skirmish-shop.png"><img width="420" height="909" src="https://www.codenameone.com/developer-guide/img/skirmish-shop.png" alt="The Skirmish shop with gem packs and a season pass" loading="lazy" style="width:100%;height:auto" /></a><figcaption>The shop.</figcaption></figure>
<figure style="margin:0"><a href="https://www.codenameone.com/developer-guide/img/skirmish-friends.png"><img width="420" height="909" src="https://www.codenameone.com/developer-guide/img/skirmish-friends.png" alt="The friends screen with invitations" loading="lazy" style="width:100%;height:auto" /></a><figcaption>Friends and invitations.</figcaption></figure>
</div>


The development profile needs nothing installed: an in-memory database, demo accounts and a simulated store. Run the server, start the simulator and play against the bot or a second simulator. The [Skirmish page](https://www.codenameone.com/skirmish/) has the overview and the [implementor's guide](https://www.codenameone.com/developer-guide/skirmish-implementors-guide/) walks through every part.

Tomorrow: [Parley: A Private Messenger Template You Can Brand](https://www.codenameone.com/blog/launch-your-own-private-messenger/).

title: My own interface kept spoiling the biggest moment in the game
description:
Development covered 23 Sep 2026 to 23 Sep 2026 (commit dates).

A climax depends on not knowing the outcome until it arrives. Films get this for free, because nothing else is on screen. A game has a whole interface around the moment, and every part of that interface wants to report the new state the instant it changes.

In Myriad Immortal Sect, the heavenly tribulation is the climax. You press a button, a storm gathers, lightning falls, and only then do you learn whether you crossed into the next realm. This window I found that by the time the first bolt landed, the game had already told you the answer half a dozen times.

Six places that knew the result

The result card itself was correctly held back until the storm finished. Everything else was not.

Pressing the button applied the new level immediately, and every system that cared fired at once. A toast saying the tribulation was survived. The achievement for reaching the realm. The unlock toasts for new tabs. A notice that a new volume of the companion novel had opened. The realm name in the top bar. All of it on screen while the map was still loading the first bolt.

Fixing those exposed more. The level number floating over your character's head read the live value, so on a first tribulation it showed level 11 while the panel still said 10. A new tab appeared in the tab bar in the first second, because it unlocks at the new level. The lock on the Soar button dropped. And a random destiny event, "Whisper of the Heart Demon", could roll during the storm and appear beside the tribulation's own title.

One rule: show the state from before the press

The fix is a single idea applied everywhere. While a tribulation reveal is pending, every readout shows the state from before the button was pressed. The top bar, the level over your head, the tab bar and the flight lock all read from that remembered state until the reveal lands, and then all change together.

Events are deferred, not dropped. The destiny roll skips during the storm and the clock keeps running, so whatever was due lands on the first moment after the result. Nothing the player earned is lost. It just waits its turn.

What made this tedious was that each leak was found separately, and each fix revealed the next. The useful habit was a family sweep: after finding one readout that showed the new realm early, list every place on screen that displays anything derived from the level, and check them all. Three of the six leaks above were found that way, not by playing. If the realm ladder itself is unfamiliar, the explanation of minor stages and half steps shows what each level number means.

Quest directions that pointed at nowhere

The other big job in this window was a different kind of broken promise. Readers who had never seen the design went through every quest's "how to complete" line with the map open, and checked whether the place it named actually existed and was labelled.

A large share did not. Across the middle batches, sixteen directions named places the map does not label or that do not exist at all: an "abode", "the arena", a "regional war", a "spirit-pet bonding site". In two later batches, twenty of twenty-one did the same: a teaching hall, an elders' hall, a "tribulation platform" for every quest in the ninth batch. One quest sent players to a famous sword mound while the beast it wanted spawned more than three hundred tiles away.

These were written from the story's point of view, where such places obviously exist. The map is what the player actually has. Every direction now names a place the map labels, or tells you to light a Wayfinding Lamp, which points at the real target. The very first batch was also corrected to happen after you pass the gate rather than "on the road to the sect", because a player reaching it has already met the Sect Master. For a sense of what a real, labelled destination looks like, the entry for the Ancient Sword Mound is an example of a place the map really does label.

The common thread

Both problems are about the gap between what the game knows and what the player should know at that moment. The interface knew the result too early and said it. The quest text knew places the player could not find and named them. In both cases the fix was to write from the player's position, at that second, with only what is on their screen.

If you build a big reveal, list every element that can display the outcome and decide when each one is allowed to change. Your result screen will be fine. It is the top bar that gives it away.

Your first storm is waiting: play free in the browser and find out at the right moment.

title: Your AI agent writes Playwright tests that pass while your API returns 500
description:
AI agents now write a lot of Playwright tests. You ask Claude Code or Copilot to "add a test for the checkout", or let an agent explore your app through Playwright MCP and turn what it did into a spec. Healer agents even fix failing tests for you.

Here is the kind of test they write:

import { test, expect } from "@playwright/test";

test("places an order", async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto("/");
  await page.getByLabel("Name").fill("Ada");
  await page.getByRole("button", { name: "Place order" }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole("status")).toContainText("Order placed");
});

It's a good test: role-based locators and a web-first assertion. It passes.

It also passes when the order API returns 500 and stores nothing, as long as the page still shows "Order placed". The agent checked what it could see. Nobody told it to check what the server did, and agents almost never add a network assertion on their own.

That matters more with agents than with people. A human who wrote the checkout code might remember the API can fail. An agent generating fifty tests from what's on screen won't, and a healer agent that "fixes" a red test by updating the expected text can make things worse. The suite goes green while the backend is broken.

The one-line fix

Change the import, in the tests the agent wrote or in the template it writes from:

import { test, expect } from "@vedhajs/playwright-test";

Nothing else changes. Same test, same broken app:


  ✓  1 1-playwright.spec.ts › places an order (import from @playwright/test)
  ✘  2 2-vedha.spec.ts › places an order (import from @vedhajs/playwright-test)

    Error: Vedha guard: the test's own checks passed, but the app reported a problem:
      - POST /api/orders returned 500

On a healthy app, both pass.

The failure message is also written for whoever reads it next, human or agent: what the app did, and how to accept it if it was expected. A healer agent gets a real reason instead of a green run.

What it checks

@vedhajs/playwright-test re-exports Playwright's test and expect with an automatic fixture ("guard mode") that watches the browser context while each test runs:

  • Fails the test: any 5xx from your app's own site, or a write request (POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE) that failed outright, even when every expect passed.
  • Warns, without failing: a 4xx answer to a write, and uncaught page errors. Validation tests expect a 422 and third-party scripts throw, so these become annotations in the report instead of failures.
  • Ignores: requests to other sites (analytics, CDNs).
  • Attaches: the findings to the test result as vedha-guard.json.

When a finding is expected, opt out per test or per endpoint:

test.use({ vedhaGuard: "strict" }); // 4xx writes and page errors fail too
test.use({ vedhaGuard: { ignore: ["/api/flaky", /\/v2\//], hosts: ["api.other-domain.com"] } });
test.use({ vedhaGuard: false }); // off, for a test that expects a 500

It is still Playwright's runner, so retries, sharding, reporters and traces work as before.

Making agents use it

Put it where the agent will pick it up:

  • Your project instructions (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, Copilot instructions): "Import test and expect from @vedhajs/playwright-test, not @playwright/test."
  • Existing specs: agents copy the patterns they find, so once your specs use the import, new ones tend to follow.
  • A lint rule that bans importing from @playwright/test in spec files, if you want to enforce it.

When the agent drives the browser itself

Guard mode is for the tests an agent writes. When the agent is the tester, driving the browser live and reporting pass or fail, Vedha also ships an MCP server that checks every step the same way. In a small pilot on held-out tasks (one model, 3 trials per task), the agent missed 9 seeded bugs with Vedha's MCP server against 26 with Playwright MCP. That's a separate setup from guard mode, covered in an earlier post.

Limits

  • A hand-written waitForResponse assertion catches this too. Guard mode is the safety net for the many tests, agent-written or not, that don't have one.
  • In Vedha's benchmark, tests with typical text and URL checks caught 0 of 140 seeded defects with plain Playwright, and 60 of 140 with Vedha's page-health check: every defect where the server rejected or failed the write. Guard mode applies the same rules to whole tests, but it hasn't been benchmarked separately yet.
  • It does not catch a write that returns 200 but stores nothing or stores the wrong value. Vedha's checked steps can read the data back, but that's opt-in and needs more than one line.

Try it 

npm install -D @vedhajs/playwright-test

Change the import in one agent-written spec and run it. If a test that used to pass now fails, look at the request it names. Either the agent's test was hiding a bug, or it's an expected error to add to ignore.

Repo, demo and benchmark data: https://github.com/HMAKT99/VEDHA (Apache-2.0)

I'd like to hear what it finds in agent-written suites, and about any false alarm.
