The result is 1,522,476 rows from 3000 configurations with 1024 distinct paths. The reconciliation adds up: 1,516,476 leaves and 6000 XML attributes in the source give the same number. The assignment of value to path was checked separately for this article, against a single pass that computes the position for each of the 1.5 million leaves. A comparison with EXCEPT over configuration, path and value yields zero differences in both directions. The ordinals of the parts turn three paths into twelve, those of the wheels four paths into eight, the rest are the 1004 paths of the catalog including the XML attributes /Drivetrain/@kind and /Brakes/@type. For the configuration from the excerpt, the table delivers under /Drivetrain exactly the six rows one would expect: the XML attribute and the five hub attributes.

In total, the XML route in SQL Server looks like this. The runtime per script was measured in a Docker container under Docker Desktop on a current desktop machine: Intel Core i7-14700KF with 28 logical cores, 62 GB RAM and an NVMe SSD under Ubuntu, of which 28 cores and 8 GB go to the Docker VM, the SQL Server container limited to 4 GB of memory, SQL Server 2022 build 16.0.4265.3 without further tuning, in the second run in the same container. The numbers are orders of magnitude on this one system, not benchmarks. For perspective: a three-year-old laptop with an Intel Core i7-1165G7 needed, in an earlier measurement with a smaller version of the catalog, around three times as long for the whole route and around ten times as long for the XQuery steps pass 1 and pass 2.

Step Time
Load as SINGLE_BLOB and split into 3000 configurations 8 s
Pass 1: all leaves with ancestor names 1.8 s
XML attributes 0.5 s
Detection of repeated parent elements 0.7 s
Pass 2: ordinals for the repetitions 0.9 s
Merge, index and reconciliation 2.4 s
total around 15 s

The same with JSON and OPENJSON

If the catalog arrives as JSON, there is no detour through pass 1 and pass 2, because an array brings its ordinals with it. The file is loaded as SINGLE_CLOB and split with STRING_SPLIT at the line breaks into one row per configuration. That STRING_SPLIT guarantees no order does not matter here, because every line is a self-contained configuration. After that, a recursive CTE opens every node with OPENJSON: the anchor is the document, the recursive part opens everything that is an object or an array and appends the key or the index to the path. Whatever is neither object nor array is a leaf.

  1: -- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  2: -- 147007: The same catalog as JSON Lines - recursively with OPENJSON (SQL Server)
  3: -- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  4: -- One row per configuration; attributes follow the xmltodict convention (@kind),
  5: -- repeated elements are arrays. Array indexes are counted from 1, as with XML.
  6: DROP TABLE IF EXISTS [stage].[raw_json];
  7: SELECT
  8:    CAST(T02.value AS nvarchar(max)) AS doc
  9: INTO [stage].[raw_json]
 10: FROM
 11:    OPENROWSET(BULK '/tmp/configs.jsonl', SINGLE_CLOB) AS T01
 12:    CROSS APPLY STRING_SPLIT(CAST(T01.BulkColumn AS nvarchar(max)), CHAR(10)) AS T02
 13: WHERE
 14:    LEN(T02.value) > 2;
 15: 
 16: -- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 17: -- Open recursively: objects (type 5) and arrays (type 4) are shredded further,
 18: -- everything else is a leaf. OPENJSON returns key/value in Latin1_General_BIN2,
 19: -- hence COLLATE DATABASE_DEFAULT on both sides of the recursion.
 20: -- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 21: DROP TABLE IF EXISTS [stage].[leaf_json];
 22: WITH
 23: CTE_node AS
 24: (
 25:    SELECT
 26:        CAST(JSON_VALUE(doc, '$."@id"')  AS nvarchar(20))  COLLATE DATABASE_DEFAULT AS config_id
 27:       ,CAST(JSON_VALUE(doc, '$."@type"') AS nvarchar(20))  COLLATE DATABASE_DEFAULT AS config_type
 28:       ,CAST(doc AS nvarchar(max))                         COLLATE DATABASE_DEFAULT AS node
 29:       ,CAST(N'' AS nvarchar(400))                         COLLATE DATABASE_DEFAULT AS path
 30:       ,CAST(5 AS int)                                                              AS json_type
 31:    FROM
 32:       [stage].[raw_json]
 33:    UNION ALL
 34:    SELECT
 35:        CAST(T01.config_id   AS nvarchar(20))  COLLATE DATABASE_DEFAULT
 36:       ,CAST(T01.config_type AS nvarchar(20))  COLLATE DATABASE_DEFAULT
 37:       ,CAST(T02.value       AS nvarchar(max)) COLLATE DATABASE_DEFAULT
 38:       ,CAST(T01.path
 39:             + CASE WHEN T01.json_type = 4
 40:                    THEN N'[' + CAST(CAST(T02.[key] AS int) + 1 AS nvarchar(10)) + N']'
 41:                    ELSE N'/' + T02.[key] END
 42:             AS nvarchar(400)) COLLATE DATABASE_DEFAULT
 43:       ,CAST(T02.type AS int)
 44:    FROM
 45:       CTE_node T01
 46:       CROSS APPLY OPENJSON(CASE WHEN T01.json_type IN (4, 5) THEN T01.node ELSE N'[]' END) AS T02
 47:    WHERE
 48:       T01.json_type IN (4, 5)
 49: )
 50: SELECT
 51:     config_id
 52:    ,config_type
 53:    ,CAST(path AS varchar(400)) AS path
 54:    ,CAST(node AS varchar(200)) AS value
 55: INTO [stage].[leaf_json]
 56: FROM
 57:    CTE_node
 58: WHERE
 59:    json_type NOT IN (4, 5);
 60: 
 61: SELECT
 62:     COUNT(*)             AS leaves
 63:    ,COUNT(DISTINCT path) AS paths
 64: FROM
 65:    [stage].[leaf_json];
 66: -- 1528476   1026

Two details make the difference between a query that runs and one that does not even compile. First, OPENJSON returns the columns key and value in the collation Latin1_General_BIN2, while the columns of the anchor carry the collation of the database. In a recursive CTE, anchor and recursive part must have identical types, collation included, otherwise SQL Server reports "Types don't match between the anchor and the recursive part". The COLLATE DATABASE_DEFAULT on both sides is therefore mandatory. Second, OPENJSON counts array indexes from zero, XML ordinals count from one. The + 1 in the path aligns the two, so that both routes deliver the same paths.

The JSON route needs around 25 seconds for loading and recursion together. It delivers 1,528,476 rows with 1026 paths, that is, 6000 rows and two paths more than the XML route. The difference are @id and @type, which JSON carries as paths of their own, while they are columns on the XML route. All 1,522,476 rows of the XML route reappear with configuration, path and value in the JSON result, the ordinals of the lists included. The code, a single script, is much shorter than the five scripts of the XML route from pass 1 to the merge, but at around 25 seconds the runtime is above the around 15 seconds of the XML route. Whoever has the choice, because the catalog is converted anyway, can skip the XML shredding. What the conversion looks like in Python is shown by the twin of this article, which follows shortly.

Inventory: reading the schema off the data

With the path/value table, the actual question of the project becomes a grouping: which type carries which paths, and how often? Per type and path, the values are counted, as are the configurations in which the path occurs. The share of all configurations of the type then says what one is dealing with.

  1: -- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  2: -- 147009: Inventory - which type carries which paths, and how often (SQL Server)
  3: -- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  4: DROP TABLE IF EXISTS [stage].[inventory];
  5: WITH
  6: CTE_configs AS
  7: (
  8:    SELECT
  9:        config_type
 10:       ,COUNT(DISTINCT config_id) AS configs
 11:    FROM
 12:       [stage].[leaf]
 13:    GROUP BY
 14:       config_type
 15: )
 16: SELECT
 17:     T01.config_type
 18:    ,T01.path
 19:    ,COUNT(*)                                                                         AS n_values
 20:    ,COUNT(DISTINCT T01.config_id)                                                    AS n_configs
 21:    ,CAST(100.0 * COUNT(DISTINCT T01.config_id) / MAX(T02.configs) AS decimal(5, 1)) AS share_pct
 22: INTO [stage].[inventory]
 23: FROM
 24:    [stage].[leaf] T01
 25:    INNER JOIN CTE_configs T02
 26:    ON
 27:      T02.config_type = T01.config_type
 28: GROUP BY
 29:     T01.config_type
 30:    ,T01.path;
 31: 
 32: -- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 33: -- Required or optional: from a share of 99 percent a path counts as required for
 34: -- the type, everything below is optional or belongs to a variant.
 35: -- The threshold is deliberately not 100 percent. In real data a required value is
 36: -- missing in a few configurations, and the path should stay required so that
 37: -- exactly these gaps show up. For strict counting use 100.0.
 38: -- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 39: SELECT
 40:     config_type
 41:    ,COUNT(*)                                           AS paths
 42:    ,SUM(CASE WHEN share_pct >= 99.0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS required_paths
 43:    ,SUM(CASE WHEN share_pct <  99.0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS optional_paths
 44: FROM
 45:    [stage].[inventory]
 46: GROUP BY
 47:    config_type
 48: ORDER BY
 49:    config_type;
 50: -- cargo_bike      640   34   606
 51: -- road_bike       634   29   605
 52: -- trekking_bike   640   29   611
 53: 
 54: SELECT
 55:     path
 56:    ,n_configs
 57:    ,share_pct
 58: FROM
 59:    [stage].[inventory]
 60: WHERE
 61:        config_type = 'trekking_bike'
 62:    AND path LIKE '/Drivetrain/%'
 63: ORDER BY
 64:    path;
 65: -- /Drivetrain/@kind             980   100.0
 66: -- /Drivetrain/Belt              367    37.4
 67: -- /Drivetrain/Chainline         613    62.6
 68: -- /Drivetrain/Chainrings        613    62.6
 69: -- /Drivetrain/CoasterBrake      367    37.4
 70: -- /Drivetrain/FrontDerailleur   613    62.6
 71: -- /Drivetrain/GearRange         367    37.4
 72: -- /Drivetrain/GearRatio_max     613    62.6
 73: -- /Drivetrain/GearRatio_min     613    62.6
 74: -- /Drivetrain/Gears             367    37.4
 75: -- /Drivetrain/HubType           367    37.4
 76: -- /Drivetrain/RearDerailleur    613    62.6
 77: -- /Drivetrain/Sprockets         613    62.6

A path with a share close to one hundred percent is a required attribute of the type. The query draws the line at 99 percent and not at 100, so that a required attribute missing in a few configurations stays required and exactly these gaps show up. The classification is a finding from the data and not a schema statement. Whether an attribute is required in the business sense is decided by the business side, and an element that is present but empty counts as present here. A path with a small share is optional. And a path that occurs in a fixed fraction of the configurations belongs to a variant. The drivetrain of the trekking bike shows this without any prior knowledge: /Drivetrain/@kind appears in all 980 configurations, the chain attributes appear in 62.6 percent of them, the hub attributes in the remaining 37.4 percent. The two variants of the drivetrain can be read off the count, and so can the fact that they exclude each other. The inventory takes under half a second.

The same count is, as a side effect, a data quality tool. A path that occurs in only three out of a thousand configurations is either a rare extra or a typo in the element name. A required attribute at 99.8 percent has two configurations in which it is missing. And a path that counts more values than configurations is either a repetition that pass 2 did not resolve, or a pair of element names in the same configuration that differ only in upper and lower case and collapse under the database's default collation. This metric, n_values greater than n_configs, is a plausibility check for paths that are assigned more than once within a configuration. In the catalog it applies to no path. Whether the shredding was complete, it does not answer. That is what the reconciliation of the row counts at the end of the merge is for. Whoever wants to derive check rules from such metadata finds the idea continued in Deriving data quality rules from the schema, there for relational schemas.

Generate views instead of writing them

Nobody writes a view with six hundred columns by hand, and nobody should have to. The inventory knows every path per type, and every path becomes a column: MAX(CASE WHEN path = '…' THEN value END) grouped by configuration. STRING_AGG assembles the column list, QUOTENAME turns the path into a valid column name and the type into a valid view name, and sp_executesql runs the DDL. Because paths and type come from the data, they pass through QUOTENAME as identifiers and through a REPLACE that doubles single quotes as literals. With XML names that is mere caution, because they cannot contain single quotes. With keys from JSON it is necessary. List paths with an ordinal stay out. They get views of their own with one row per list element, otherwise columns like accessories_part_3_name would arise that stay empty for anything but four parts.

  1: -- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  2: -- 147010: Generate the views from the inventory instead of writing them (SQL Server)
  3: -- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  4: -- One view per object type with one column per path. List paths (with [n]) stay
  5: -- out; they get views of their own with one row per list element.
  6: -- Run the script once per object type: first as it stands with 'trekking_bike',
  7: -- then with 'road_bike' and with 'cargo_bike' in @config_type. Every run creates
  8: -- the view of its type (vw_trekking_bike, vw_road_bike, vw_cargo_bike).
  9: -- CREATE VIEW must be alone in its batch, hence the DDL runs through
 10: -- sp_executesql. The typed view and the sample query at the end belong to the
 11: -- trekking bike and assume that its run was the first.
 12: -- Identifiers pass through QUOTENAME, literals through REPLACE('''') - paths from
 13: -- JSON, unlike XML names, may contain single quotes.
 14: DECLARE @config_type varchar(20) = 'trekking_bike';   -- then 'road_bike', then 'cargo_bike'
 15: DECLARE @sql         nvarchar(max);
 16: 
 17: SELECT
 18:    @sql = N'CREATE OR ALTER VIEW [dbo].' + QUOTENAME(N'vw_' + @config_type) + N' AS'
 19:         + N' SELECT config_id'
 20:         + STRING_AGG(
 21:              CAST(N', MAX(CASE WHEN path = ''' + REPLACE(path, '''', '''''') + N''' THEN value END) AS '
 22:                   + QUOTENAME(LOWER(REPLACE(REPLACE(SUBSTRING(path, 2, 400), '/', '_'), '@', 'attr_')))
 23:                   AS nvarchar(max))
 24:             ,N'') WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY path)
 25:         + N' FROM [stage].[leaf] WHERE config_type = ''' + REPLACE(@config_type, '''', '''''') + N''' GROUP BY config_id;'
 26: FROM
 27:    [stage].[inventory]
 28: WHERE
 29:        config_type = @config_type
 30:    AND path NOT LIKE '%[[]%';
 31: 
 32: EXEC sp_executesql @sql;
 33: 
 34: SELECT
 35:    COUNT(*) AS columns_generated
 36: FROM
 37:    INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COLUMNS
 38: WHERE
 39:    TABLE_NAME = 'vw_' + @config_type;
 40: -- XML route:  trekking_bike 621, road_bike 615, cargo_bike 621
 41: -- JSON route: trekking_bike 623, road_bike 617, cargo_bike 623
 42: GO
 43: -- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 44: -- Second layer: typing where it is needed. All values of the generated view are
 45: -- text; only here do price, weight and lumen get their types.
 46: -- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 47: CREATE OR ALTER VIEW [dbo].[vw_trekking_bike_typed]
 48: AS
 49: SELECT
 50:     config_id
 51:    ,general_model                                        AS model
 52:    ,TRY_CONVERT(smallint,       general_modelyear)       AS model_year
 53:    ,TRY_CONVERT(decimal(10, 2), general_price)            AS price
 54:    ,TRY_CONVERT(decimal(6, 2),  general_weight)          AS weight_kg
 55:    ,frame_material                                          AS frame_material
 56:    ,drivetrain_attr_kind                                         AS drivetrain_kind
 57:    ,TRY_CONVERT(tinyint,        drivetrain_gears)              AS gears
 58:    ,TRY_CONVERT(smallint,       lighting_front_lumen)            AS lighting_front_lumen
 59: FROM
 60:    [dbo].[vw_trekking_bike];
 61: GO
 62: SELECT
 63:     frame_material
 64:    ,COUNT(*)                        AS n
 65:    ,CAST(AVG(price) AS decimal(10, 0)) AS price_avg
 66: FROM
 67:    [dbo].[vw_trekking_bike_typed]
 68: GROUP BY
 69:    frame_material
 70: ORDER BY
 71:    frame_material;
 72: -- Aluminum   246   3178
 73: -- Carbon     246   3443
 74: -- Steel      248   3426
 75: -- Titanium   240   3116

The view for the trekking bike has 621 columns and comes into being in under half a second. The script creates the view of one type per run. For the road bike and the cargo bike it runs once more with the respective type in @config_type and delivers views with 615 and 621 columns. A query over it, say the average price per frame material over 980 configurations, runs in around 40 milliseconds. This is the moment the approach pays off: a new attribute in the catalog requires no change to shredding, inventory and view generator. It is a new row in the inventory and, on the next run, a new column in the view. Manual work remains only for the typed view, if the attribute is to get a type there.

All values of the generated view are text, just as they stood in the XML. They get types in a second layer, and only the columns that someone needs typed. TRY_CONVERT is the right tool for that, because a single faulty value must not bring the whole view down. What to watch out for per data type is covered in Safe type conversion with T-SQL.

Three limits belong to this. A column name is an identifier of at most 128 characters. For longer input QUOTENAME returns NULL, and because STRING_AGG skips NULL values, the column silently disappears from the view. The column count at the end of the script is therefore more than a control output: 620 paths without ordinal plus config_id must give 621 columns. Furthermore, the mapping of path to column name is not unique. /A/B and /A_B both become a_b, and the view fails with the message that column names must be unique. The same happens with /A/@b and /A/attr_b, which both become a_attr_b, and with Gears and gears as soon as the path column carries a binary collation and the two spellings sit in the inventory as separate paths. Whoever has such names appends a running number from the inventory. SQL Server allows 1024 columns per view, Postgres 1600, where in Postgres a materialized table additionally requires the row to fit into an 8-KB block. With a thousand attributes and one view per type that still works out, with two thousand it no longer does. Then views are generated per assembly instead of per type, that is, one view for the frame, one for the drivetrain, and the consumers join through the configuration ID. And the path/value table itself is an intermediate format, not a target model. It has no types, no constraints, and every query has to pivot first. Whoever uses it as the data model for applications builds the entity-attribute-value pattern with all its well-known drawbacks. As a landing zone for a document with an unknown schema it is exactly right, and the generated views are the layer the consumers see. If a view is queried often, it can be materialized as a table.

Postgres bridge

The same route leads through JSONB in Postgres, and there it is even the fastest. COPY loads the JSON Lines file as one row per configuration, where CSV mode with impossible delimiter and quote characters makes sure that backslashes in the text are not read as escapes. The recursive CTE opens objects with jsonb_each and arrays with jsonb_array_elements including the ordinality, and both happen in one lateral join, so that one recursion serves both cases.

  1: -- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  2: -- Load JSON Lines: one row per configuration. CSV mode with impossible quote and
  3: -- delimiter characters keeps backslashes in the text from being read as escapes.
  4: -- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  5: DROP TABLE IF EXISTS stage.raw_json;
  6: CREATE TABLE stage.raw_json
  7: (
  8:     doc   jsonb NOT NULL
  9: );
 10: COPY stage.raw_json FROM '/tmp/configs.jsonl' WITH (FORMAT csv, QUOTE E'\x01', DELIMITER E'\x02');
 11: 
 12: -- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 13: -- Flatten recursively: objects via jsonb_each, arrays via jsonb_array_elements
 14: -- with ordinality; anything that is neither object nor array is a leaf.
 15: -- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16: DROP TABLE IF EXISTS stage.leaf_json CASCADE;   -- CASCADE: the views of an earlier run depend on it
 17: CREATE TABLE stage.leaf_json AS
 18: WITH RECURSIVE
 19: CTE_node AS
 20: (
 21:    SELECT
 22:        doc ->> '@id'  AS config_id
 23:       ,doc ->> '@type' AS config_type
 24:       ,doc            AS node
 25:       ,''::text       AS path
 26:    FROM
 27:       stage.raw_json
 28:    UNION ALL
 29:    SELECT
 30:        T01.config_id
 31:       ,T01.config_type
 32:       ,T02.node
 33:       ,T01.path || T02.step
 34:    FROM
 35:       CTE_node T01
 36:       CROSS JOIN LATERAL
 37:       (
 38:          SELECT
 39:              '/' || key AS step
 40:             ,value      AS node
 41:          FROM
 42:             jsonb_each(CASE WHEN jsonb_typeof(T01.node) = 'object' THEN T01.node ELSE '{}'::jsonb END)
 43:          UNION ALL
 44:          SELECT
 45:              '[' || ordinality || ']'
 46:             ,value
 47:          FROM
 48:             jsonb_array_elements(CASE WHEN jsonb_typeof(T01.node) = 'array' THEN T01.node ELSE '[]'::jsonb END) WITH ORDINALITY
 49:       ) T02
 50: )
 51: SELECT
 52:     config_id
 53:    ,config_type
 54:    ,path
 55:    ,node #>> '{}' AS value
 56: FROM
 57:    CTE_node
 58: WHERE
 59:    jsonb_typeof(node) NOT IN ('object', 'array');

Loading takes under half a second, the recursion just under four, and the result is row-identical to the OPENJSON route: 1,528,476 rows, 1026 paths. More on COPY and its variants is in Transferring data.

XML directly works in Postgres as well, with xmltable instead of nodes(), and with a trap that is bigger than anything in SQL Server. The function xmltable over the whole 27-MB document with the row path /Catalog/Configuration//*[not(*)] was still running after 36 minutes in the measurement with Postgres 18.6. It reacted neither to pg_cancel_backend nor to pg_terminate_backend and only ended with the container. That was no outlier, as a follow-up measurement with partial catalogs shows: for 50, 100 and 200 configurations the same query takes 4, 17 and 99 seconds, that is, a good five times as long per doubling, and for 3000 configurations that would be hours. The obvious explanation is a call into the XML library libxml2 that does not check for interrupts. What the measurement proves is only the behaviour, not the cause. After the split into one row per configuration, the same xmltable runs as a lateral join over the fragments in around four seconds, and it does so even when it computes the positions right away, because count(preceding-sibling::*) is cheap on a 9-KB fragment. The ordinals only for repeated siblings then come set-based with dense_rank() over configuration, parent path and name. The script for it is in the XML download for Postgres. Postgres generates the views from the paths with format() and runs the DDL with \gexec, three views with around 620 columns each, each in around ten milliseconds.

  1: -- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  2: -- Generate the views from the paths: format() builds the DDL, \gexec runs it.
  3: -- List paths (with [n]) and the two attributes of the configuration stay out.
  4: -- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  5: SELECT format(
  6:           'CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW stage.vw_%s AS SELECT config_id%s FROM stage.leaf_json WHERE config_type = %L GROUP BY config_id;'
  7:          ,config_type
  8:          ,string_agg(
  9:              format(E'\n   ,max(value) FILTER (WHERE path = %L) AS %I'
 10:                    ,path
 11:                    ,regexp_replace(lower(trim(both '/' from path)), '[^a-z0-9]+', '_', 'g'))
 12:             ,'' ORDER BY path)
 13:          ,config_type)
 14: FROM
 15:    (SELECT DISTINCT config_type, path FROM stage.leaf_json WHERE path NOT LIKE '/@%' AND path NOT LIKE '%[%') T01
 16: GROUP BY
 17:    config_type \gexec
 18: 
 19: SELECT
 20:     table_name
 21:    ,count(*) AS columns_generated
 22: FROM
 23:    information_schema.columns
 24: WHERE
 25:    table_name LIKE 'vw\_%'
 26: GROUP BY
 27:    table_name
 28: ORDER BY
 29:    table_name;
 30: -- vw_cargo_bike      621
 31: -- vw_road_bike       615
 32: -- vw_trekking_bike   621

Limits and decisions

The method has a fixed frame, and that frame should be known before using it.

  • Depth: The ancestor names are columns, and their number is fixed. Four levels cover the catalog, a document with ten levels needs ten columns or a different way of building the path, and the check from pass 1 shows whether the reserve is enough. The recursive CTE of the JSON route does not know this limit, but in SQL Server it knows another one: after 100 recursion levels it stops with an error, until OPTION (MAXRECURSION 0) lifts the limit. Postgres recurses without a limit.
  • Namespaces: local-name() ignores namespaces, which is intended here. Two elements with the same local name from different namespaces thus fall onto one path. Whoever has to tell them apart adds namespace-uri() as a further column. A name() with prefix does not exist in SQL Server's XQuery, and the prefix would only be a spelling of the URI anyway. To address a namespace in the path on purpose, there is WITH XMLNAMESPACES.
  • Spelling and collation: XML names are case-sensitive, the text columns of the database with the default collation SQL_Latin1_General_CP1_CI_AS are not. Two elements Gears and gears thus collapse onto one path in the inventory, and the detection of repetitions wrongly reports their parent element as repeated. Whoever has such names creates the name and path columns with a binary collation such as Latin1_General_100_BIN2. If both spellings sit in the same configuration, the inventory shows the case through the same metric as a missing ordinal: more values than configurations. If they are spread over different configurations, the metric stays silent, and the case only shows up once the paths are counted under a binary collation.
  • Column widths and character set: Names with varchar(100), values with varchar(200) and paths with varchar(400) are tailored to the catalog, whose longest path has 32 and whose longest value has 19 characters. Longer strings are silently truncated by value() to the target width, without error and without warning. Just as silently, characters that the code page of varchar does not know are lost: Łódź becomes Lódz. Whoever expects such values takes nvarchar. For foreign documents the widths are adjusted to the data. A first pass with wide columns and MAX(LEN(…)) shows what is needed. A blanket varchar(max) is no option for the path: it is the key of the index on the path/value table, and a max type cannot be an index key.
  • Mixed content: Text alongside child elements falls through [not(*)]. Such documents need an additional pass over text() nodes.
  • Elements with XML attributes only: An element like <Warranty years="2"/> has neither text nor children. Pass 1 matches it nonetheless and delivers a row with an empty value, because [not(*)] only asks about child elements. The XML attribute is collected correctly by its own pass as /General/Warranty/@years. The empty row disappears if the predicate is extended by [not(@*) or text()]: leaves without XML attributes are kept even when empty, leaves with XML attributes only if they have text. A plain [text()], by contrast, would also discard deliberately empty elements such as <Belt/>. Whoever reaches for normalize-space() for this gets an error, because the function is missing in SQL Server's XQuery.
  • Types and localization: All values are text. Decimal point or comma, date formats and yes/no spellings are decided only in the typed view, and there with TRY_CONVERT, not with CONVERT.
  • File size: An xml value holds up to 2 GB, and SINGLE_BLOB reads the whole file at once. With documents in the gigabyte range the split is the bottleneck, and from a certain size a streaming parser outside the database is the better choice. That is the topic of the twin article on Python.
  • Known, small schema: Whoever has twenty attributes and knows them needs none of this. A nodes() with twenty value() columns is then shorter and faster. The generic route pays off when the schema is large, variable or unknown.

As a decision aid:

Starting point Recommended route
XML, schema large or unknown, file fits into memory Split, pass 1, detection, pass 2, inventory, generated views
JSON, schema large or unknown One row per document, recursive CTE with OPENJSON or JSONB, inventory, generated views
XML, but conversion to JSON planned anyway Convert, then the JSON route
Schema small and known nodes() with fixed value() columns, no path/value table
File in the gigabyte range Streaming parser outside the database, load as JSON Lines, rest in SQL

Summary

  • The hours in that project did not come from the programming language but from the design: code per type, access per attribute, schema in your head.
  • The database route does not know the attributes in advance. It loads raw, shreds generically into path and value, and afterwards counts what exists. What it requires are the element of the sub-documents, an upper bound for the depth, and lists in which an element name repeats in at least one configuration.
  • In SQL Server, the split into one row per configuration is the decisive step. After that, one pass over nodes() with the parent axis delivers all leaves in around two seconds.
  • Computing positions for all 1.5 million leaves raises the runtime from around two to around 40 seconds. They are therefore computed only for the elements that repeat according to pass 1.
  • The inventory makes required, optional and variant attributes per type visible, and from it the database generates the views with hundreds of columns itself.
  • JSON does without the second pass, in Postgres JSONB is the fastest route, and xmltable over a whole large document is a trap there.
  • The path/value table is a landing zone, not a data model. The generated and typed views are the layer for the consumers.

FAQ

How do I read XML with an unknown structure in SQL Server?

Load the document as an xml value, split it with nodes() into one row per sub-document, and then fetch every leaf element with nodes('//*[not(*)]'). The parent axis local-name(..) delivers the names of the ancestors, from which the path is built, and value('.') delivers the value. The result is a path/value table from which a grouping makes the schema readable. Required are the element of the sub-documents and an upper bound for the depth of the tree. The method recognises lists only when an element name repeats within them in at least one configuration.

How do repeated elements get their position in SQL Server?

The XQuery expression let $p := . return count(../*[local-name() = "Part"][. << $p]) + 1 counts the same-named siblings that precede the current element in the document, and thus delivers its position. For all 1.5 million leaves this expression is too expensive. It raises the runtime from around two to around 40 seconds. So pass 1 fetches all leaves without position, a grouping reads off at which positions elements repeat at all, and pass 2 computes the position only there. A ROW_NUMBER() over the output of nodes() looks simpler, but does not guarantee the document order.

Isn't the path/value table exactly the EAV model everyone warns about?

Yes, in form. No, in role. The entity-attribute-value pattern is a problem when it is the permanent data model of an application, because types, constraints and simple queries are missing. Here the table is an intermediate stage between the raw document and the generated views. It is filled once per load run, counted once, and the consumers see views with real columns. Whoever queries the views often materializes them and is back at an ordinary table model.

XML or JSON: what should I load if I have the choice?

JSON, if the ordinals of lists matter and the conversion happens anyway. An array brings its order with it, and the recursive CTE needs no second pass. XML directly, if the file arrives that way and should not be touched again. In SQL Server the XML route took around 15 and the JSON route around 25 seconds for 1.5 million values. In Postgres, JSONB was clearly ahead at around four seconds.

Why not OPENXML?

OPENXML with sp_xml_preparedocument delivers an edge table of the whole document in which every node is a row with an ID and a parent ID, in document order. That sounds like exactly the generic access this article is looking for. In the measurement, the edge table alone for 3 million nodes took around 55 seconds, the text column arrives as ntext and cannot be indexed, and the prepared document occupies memory until it is explicitly released. The route through nodes() was around thirty times faster in this measurement and needs no handles.

Why not just nodes() with fixed paths per attribute?

Because that is exactly the loop in the code, only in SQL: one value() call per attribute, a thousand calls per type, and a change for every new attribute. For a known schema with twenty attributes that is the right way. For a thousand attributes that nobody knows completely, the generic shredding with a subsequent inventory in SQL is the version that does not have to change with every catalog change.

Related articles

Upstream:

  • Set-Based vs. Row by Row: PostgreSQL Refresh from 114 to 12 Seconds (the general argument against the loop per element)
  • ETL vs. ELT — How to Tell Which Pattern You Actually Built (load raw, then transform in SQL)
  • Design Pattern // The Architecture of an ETL Process (the layers into which the path/value table fits)

Downstream:

  • Deriving Data Quality Rules from the Schema (the inventory as a data quality tool)
  • Design Pattern // Safe Type Conversion with T-SQL (the typed second view layer)
  • Transferring Data: bcp, COPY, pgloader, ETL (loading on the Postgres side)

  • XML route for Postgres: catalog as XML, generator and script (ZIP)

title: Terraform: un plan de cambio que se pueda explicar
description:
Cuando un cambio de infraestructura falla, el problema no siempre es que Terraform haya calculado mal. Muchas veces el plan era correcto, pero nadie pudo explicar a tiempo qué iba a cambiar, qué evidencia faltaba o cómo volver atrás. Para una guardia SRE, un plan útil es también un contrato de comunicación.

El síntoma: un plan correcto que nadie entiende

El incidente suele empezar con una frase pequeña: “solo son unos recursos”. Después aparecen decenas de líneas, un -/+ inesperado y una aprobación que se hace con prisa. El plan pasa, pero la confianza no.

He visto que el riesgo sube cuando el equipo revisa el número de recursos en vez de revisar las consecuencias. Crear dos recursos no es automáticamente seguro; reemplazar uno puede romper una dependencia que no aparece en el título del pull request. Un plan sin contexto se vuelve una lista, no una decisión.

La primera señal de alerta es que la persona que aprueba no puede contestar tres preguntas:

  1. ¿Qué comportamiento cambia para el usuario?
  2. ¿Qué dependencia puede quedar inestable?
  3. ¿Cuál es el paso concreto para recuperar el servicio?

Si la respuesta es “lo vemos después del apply”, ya hay deuda de operación.

Qué debe responder un buen plan

Un plan de Terraform debería ser legible para alguien que no escribió el módulo. Antes de mirar los detalles, dejo un resumen corto en el pull request:

  • Intención: qué capacidad se añade o qué problema se corrige.
  • Alcance: cuentas, regiones, clusters y entornos afectados.
  • Cambio sensible: reemplazos, permisos, reglas de red o datos que se destruyen.
  • Dependencias: qué servicio debe estar sano antes de aplicar.
  • Recuperación: qué se revierte y qué no puede revertirse automáticamente.

Luego comparo ese resumen con el plan real. Si el texto dice “actualizar una regla” pero Terraform muestra un reemplazo, el cambio se detiene. Esa pausa es barata; una sorpresa en producción no lo es.

También conviene guardar el hash del commit, la versión del proveedor y el workspace usado. Parece detalle menor, pero evita discutir sobre un plan que ya no corresponde al código actual. En la practica, muchos minutos se pierden por esa confusión.

Un flujo de revisión que funciona en guardia

Uso cuatro pasos, incluso para cambios que parecen rutinarios.

1. Generar el plan en un entorno reproducible

El job debe registrar el commit, la versión de Terraform, los proveedores y el estado remoto. Si el estado cambia durante la revisión, se genera un plan nuevo. No se aplica un archivo viejo solo porque ya tiene una aprobación.

2. Separar cambios esperados y cambios laterales

Marco los recursos que forman parte de la intención y dejo aparte todo lo demás. Un cambio lateral puede ser drift, una variable compartida o una lectura distinta del proveedor. No lo escondo para que el diff se vea bonito: lo investigo.

3. Probar la explicación, no solo la sintaxis

Otra persona lee el resumen y responde qué pasará si el proveedor devuelve un error a mitad del apply. Si no entiende el flujo, falta documentación. Esta revisión funciona como una pequeña prueba de contrato entre Terraform y la operación.

En cambios que disparan notificaciones o validaciones por correo, dejo una evidencia verificable y con tiempo de expiración. Para depurar señales de correo tras un drenado, puede servir señales de correo en un drenado de nodo; la idea es la misma: cada señal debe llevar contexto suficiente para no depender de memoria humana. A veces el test aparece escrito como “tamp mail com” o “temp org mail” en una nota antigua; lo trato como texto de prueba, no como una identidad real.

4. Acordar una ventana de observación

El apply no termina cuando el comando devuelve código cero. Defino qué métricas mirar, durante cuánto tiempo y qué umbral detiene el cambio. En flujos con email también conviene validar la evidencia de un email, porque un mensaje enviado no significa que el usuario haya completado el paso siguiente.

Cómo dejar preparado el rollback

Un rollback confiable empieza antes del apply. Primero clasifico el cambio:

  • Reversible: se puede volver al commit y aplicar sin migración adicional.
  • Reversible con cuidado: necesita restaurar una variable, una regla o un secreto.
  • No reversible: modifica datos, consume una migración o cambia una dependencia externa.

Para los dos últimos casos, el runbook incluye una copia o exportación comprobada, el propietario de la decisión y una condición clara de parada. “Ejecutar el commit anterior” no es suficiente si el recurso ya fue reemplazado o si el proveedor conserva un efecto fuera del estado.

Un patrón práctico es usar dos artefactos: el plan que se va a aplicar y un documento breve de recuperación. El segundo contiene comandos, señales esperadas y el último punto seguro. No incluyo secretos en ninguno de los dos. Si el rollback requiere improvisar, todavía no está listo.

Checklist antes de aplicar

  • [ ] El plan fue generado desde el commit que se revisó.
  • [ ] La cuenta, región y workspace están confirmados.
  • [ ] Los reemplazos y permisos tienen una explicación explícita.
  • [ ] El drift fue investigado o aceptado con un dueño.
  • [ ] Existe un último punto seguro y un procedimiento de recuperación.
  • [ ] Las métricas y logs de observación están abiertos.
  • [ ] La ventana permite esperar el resultado, no solo lanzar el comando.
  • [ ] El equipo sabe quién puede detener el cambio.

Si una casilla queda vacía, el cambio puede esperar. La presión de “aplicar antes del stand-up” rara vez compensa una dependencia que nadie ha mirado.

Conclusión

Terraform produce un plan técnico, pero la guardia necesita una decisión operable. Un buen flujo conecta intención, diff, dependencias, observación y recuperación. Cuando cualquiera del equipo puede explicar qué cambia y cómo parar, el plan deja de ser una salida de consola y se convierte en una herramienta SRE.

No hace falta añadir más automatización a cada incidente. A veces basta con un resumen honesto, un artefacto reproducible y un rollback que otra persona pueda ejecutar sin adivinar. Esa claridad es pequeña, pero aguanta mejor cuando la noche se complica.

title: 5 Things Every Small Business Homepage Needs Above the Fold
description:
"Above the fold" is the part of your homepage people see before they scroll. On a phone that's a tiny space, and it's where most small business sites lose people. Here are the five things I check first on every small business homepage.

1. A headline that says what you do and where. "Welcome to our website" tells nobody anything. "Family dentist in Austin, TX" or "Same-day plumbing repairs in Tampa" tells visitors (and Google) they're in the right place.

2. One obvious call-to-action. Pick the one action that matters most — Book now, Get a quote, Call us — and make it a big, high-contrast button. Three competing buttons usually means none get clicked.

3. A tap-to-call phone number. Many local customers are on mobile and just want to call. Use a tel: link so it's one tap, and keep it visible in the header.

4. Proof. A star rating, a review count, or one short testimonial near the top builds trust instantly. Real reviews beat stock badges.

5. A real photo. Your actual team, shop, or finished work beats generic stock photos. It makes the business feel real and local. Compress it so it doesn't slow the page down.

Quick test: open your homepage on your phone and ask a friend what you do, where, and how to contact you — in five seconds. If they can't answer, the top of the page needs work.

I'm with ENZORA. We build websites for US small businesses and offer a free website and SEO audit: https://enzora.vercel.app

title: Why your design looks fine on screen and broken on a shoe: three constraints, three consequences
description:
I build a browser-side customizer for printed sneakers. You upload artwork, it gets sliced across the shoe panels, and you preview it on the actual shoe before ordering: bukefootwear.com. The slicing geometry is in the first post, the magnification math in the second, the render pipeline in the third, the deploy budget in the fourth, and the routerless storefront in the fifth.

This one is different. It is not about a bug I fixed. It is about three physical properties of a shoe that decide what the software can and cannot promise, and the three places where ignoring them produced a page that looked correct and was not.

The failure mode is not ugly, it is plausible

Every bad custom-print result I have seen looked acceptable on a laptop. That is the problem. When a canvas render is wrong in an obvious way — black output, a stretched image, a 404 texture — you fix it in a minute. When it is wrong in a plausible way, it ships.

A design that loses four millimetres of its border at the seam still looks like a design. A motif that breaks across the toe cap still reads as a motif. A palette that shifts half a shade on a fabric substrate still reads as the same palette. You only find out after the pair is made.

So the useful framing is not "how do I rasterise artwork onto a shoe". It is "which constraints can the browser check, and which ones can only the person looking at it check". Three constraints turned out to matter more than everything else I did.

Constraint one: the surface is not developable

A t-shirt is a flat rectangle. You can print it in one pass and the artwork behaves like a poster glued to cardboard. A shoe upper is a curved shell. There is no isometric mapping from a plane onto a doubly-curved surface that preserves both distances and angles — this is Gauss's theorema egregium, and it is the reason a basketball cannot be wrapped in gift paper without creases.

The engineering consequence is that you do not flatten the shoe. You decompose it. A pair of low-tops in our pipeline resolves into dozens of separate cut pieces, each with its own outline, its own safe area and its own transform back into shoe space. The user's single upload becomes dozens of independent renders.

The consequence inside the code is that there is no single "the design" object after slicing. There is an array. Anything that assumed one image, one bounding box, one transform is now wrong, and it fails quietly: each panel renders fine in isolation, and the composition is broken.

If you are building anything similar, the data model has to be decided before the renderer. Ours looks roughly like this:

{ code: 'toe-cap', path: Path2D, safeArea: Path2D, warp: Float32Array }

The warp is the part people skip. A panel outline tells you where a piece is on the shoe. It does not tell you how the artwork bends to sit on it. Those are two different pieces of data and conflating them is the single most expensive mistake in this class of project.

Constraint two: the seam eats the edge

Panels are joined by stitching, and stitching needs material to hold. Every panel therefore carries a seam allowance — a strip along its outline that will be folded under or consumed by the join. Artwork placed there is not printed, or is printed and then hidden.

This converts a design problem into a clipping problem, and the clipping is where the silent failure lives: an out-of-bounds design gets cropped, and cropping is not an error. A drawImage call whose destination rectangle extends past the canvas does not throw, does not warn, and does not return a status. It draws what fits.

I have written about the mask layer specifically elsewhere, but the general lesson is worth stating plainly: in a canvas pipeline, geometry violations are not exceptions. The only way to catch them is to compare the intended area against the safe area yourself, before drawing, and to surface the result to the user as a number or a highlighted region — not as a console message nobody reads.

The practical rule I ended up with: never let the renderer be the first thing that discovers a bounds problem. Validate the placement against the safe area on input, and treat the renderer as an optimiser for a decision already made. This is the same reasoning as validating a form on submit rather than trusting a database constraint to reject it later.

Constraint three: the substrate is not paper

Paper holds ink on the surface. A shoe upper is a textile or a synthetic leather: it absorbs, it stretches over a last, and it moves with the foot. Three things follow, and none of them are visible in a canvas preview:

Colour shifts. Ink on a woven or microfibre surface sits differently than ink on a coated paper. A mid-tone that reads neutral in sRGB can go warm or muddy on a warm-grey substrate. There is no browser API for "how will this CMYK-adjacent stack land on this material" — the material sample is the oracle.

Edges soften. Small type and one-pixel hairlines do not survive the transfer intact. This is not a resolution problem in the usual sense; it is a material problem. Our answer was to stop specifying DPI and start specifying pixels against a measured magnification factor, which is what the second post covers.

The preview can only be honest about the first two constraints. A canvas render can show you cropping and composition truthfully. It cannot show you colour on material or edge softening. Any claim otherwise is a lie dressed up as a feature, so the preview needs to say what it does not model — and that statement belongs on the page, not in a FAQ.

What the constraints cost in pixels

Once the surface is non-developable and the pieces are small, magnification does the budgeting for you. Measured across panels, a single uploaded image is stretched by a factor between roughly 2.9× and 4.8× depending on where the panel sits. Working backwards from a target print resolution gives a hard floor on upload size rather than a preference: around 2,000 px lands near 78% of target, 2,400 px near 98%, and about 2,916 px clears it.

That number is not interesting on its own. It is interesting because it is derivable, and because it can be shown to a user before they upload anything. "Minimum 2,900 pixels on the long edge" is a rule a person can act on. "High resolution required" is not.

The acceptance problem

Put the three constraints together and you get a class of defect that no unit test catches: each panel is individually correct, the composition is wrong. The only reliable check is a human looking at the assembled result.

So the thing I actually shipped for this is not a spec sheet, it is an acceptance surface. There is a page that renders one artwork across the panel set at real proportions, side by side with an assembled preview, so a person can see whether the pattern breaks at a seam or loses its border: panel-preview. It is the same data the customizer uses, presented so that the failure is visible instead of plausible.

The written version of the same reasoning — why an eighteen-panel curved shell is a genuinely different problem from a printed t-shirt, and what that means for what you can promise a customer — is at why shoes are harder than shirts.

What this changes about the build

None of this is exotic graphics programming. It is constraint accounting. The three things I would tell anyone starting a project that maps flat artwork onto a curved, seamed, non-paper object:

  1. Decide the panel data model before the renderer. Outline, safe area and warp are three separate facts. Conflating them produces a renderer that cannot be fixed, only rewritten.
  2. Treat geometry violations as validation, not exceptions. Canvas will happily crop your design out of existence and return success.
  3. Be explicit about what the preview does not model. Colour on substrate and edge softening are outside the browser's knowledge. Say so.

The results, if you want to see whether the constraints are actually being respected rather than just described, are four prints on four different base shoes — a woven geometric, a botanical, a chain motif and a tonal Art Deco fan — each with the full seven-view set on its own page. They are collected at the featured designs gallery; Onyx Deco is the clearest test of the third constraint, because a tonal print with almost no contrast is exactly the case where a colour shift stops being subtle.

And if you want to test the whole pipeline against your own artwork, the customizer is the same one I have been describing: design your own.

The numbers in this post come from measurements on our own panel set, not from a general model. If your panel count, seam allowance or substrate differ, the constants move — the constraints do not.

title: Bridging Python and Rust: Building Type-Safe Data Quality Pipelines with PyO3 and JSON Schema 2020-12 #rust #python #pyo3 #jsonschema
description:
Introduction

What happens when Python's flexibility meets Rust's performance in a data engineering pipeline?

Imagine processing millions of rows of data, only to discover that a critical column contains unexpected null values, duplicate records, or an incompatible data type.

You could catch these problems after processing. But what if you could define quality rules before the data reaches your warehouse—and enforce those rules through a high-performance Rust engine?

That's the engineering challenge behind combining Python, PyO3, Rust, and JSON Schema Draft 2020-12.

In this article, we'll explore the architecture, schema design, native Rust integration, and testing strategy behind a declarative data quality gate.

The goal: Make configuration validation predictable, keep the Python–Rust boundary clean, and separate structural validation from runtime data checks.

Executive Summary

When building data profiling and data quality pipelines, engineers face a classic dilemma: Rust delivers zero-cost abstractions, fearless concurrency, and high-performance data processing, while Python provides data teams with expressiveness, rich ecosystem tooling, and declarative configuration.

In dataprof, the core profiling engine is written in Rust and exposed to Python via PyO3 native bindings. However, enterprise pipelines require declarative Quality Gate Policies to verify null thresholds, uniqueness constraints, distinct value bounds, and column data types before committing data to downstream warehouses.

This case study explores the architecture described in PR #1061 (schema architecture and test suite) and PR #863 (production error subsystem), focusing on the relationship between JSON Schema Draft 2020-12 and native Rust profiling kernels.

The central engineering principle is straightforward: validate configuration early, keep the interoperability contract explicit, and evaluate data-dependent invariants where the actual data is available.

1. The Architectural Challenge

Data profiling engines may need to inspect datasets containing millions of rows. Meanwhile, quality policies are authored by data engineers or orchestration systems in YAML or JSON.

The challenge is to translate human-readable configuration into reliable rules that a native Rust engine can evaluate.

Architecture Overview 

          DATA ENGINEER
            YAML / JSON
                 |
                 v
      +----------------------+
      | JSON Schema 2020-12  |
      | Policy Validation    |
      +----------------------+
                 |
                 v
      +----------------------+
      | Python Validation    |
      | Clear Error Messages |
      +----------------------+
                 |
                 v
      +----------------------+
      | PyO3 Boundary        |
      | Python <-> Rust      |
      +----------------------+
                 |
                 v
      +----------------------+
      | Native Rust Engine   |
      | Quality Evaluation   |
      +----------------------+
                 |
                 v
        QUALITY GATE RESULT

The Pitfalls of Naive Implementations

1. Schema Draft Incompatibilities

Older JSON Schema drafts, such as Draft 4 and Draft 7, differ from Draft 2020-12 in their supported keywords and semantics.

Modern keywords such as $defs and prefixItems require a compatible validator. Using an older validator without checking its behavior can result in unsupported keywords not being enforced as expected.

2. Wildcard Resolution

Policies often apply default rules across multiple columns while allowing column-specific overrides.

For example, a global rule might require columns to contain no null values, while a particular column may explicitly disable that restriction.

{
  "*": {
    "null_count": {
      "max": 0
    }
  },
  "user_notes": {
    "null_count": null
  }
}

The intended behavior is that the global rule applies by default, while the specific column overrides it.

Implementing this behavior requires a clear rule-resolution strategy. JSON Schema can validate the configuration's structure, but the application's policy evaluator must implement the actual wildcard matching and precedence semantics.

3. Runtime-Only Semantic Boundaries

Not every invariant belongs in JSON Schema.

For example, a schema can validate that a column name is a string. It cannot independently establish that the column actually exists in a particular Parquet or CSV dataset.

That check belongs in the runtime evaluation layer, where the dataset's metadata and profiling results are available.

Separating structural validation from runtime semantics makes the system easier to reason about and maintain.

2. Designing the JSON Schema Draft 2020-12 Policy Specification

A maintainable policy format should be explicit, modular, and strict enough to catch configuration mistakes.

JSON Schema Draft 2020-12 provides useful features for this purpose:

  • $defs allows reusable schema definitions.
  • $ref allows one schema component to reference another.
  • patternProperties applies schemas to object properties whose names match regular expressions.
  • additionalProperties: false rejects properties that are not otherwise permitted.

Example JSON Schema

The following illustrates the intended schema architecture. The referenced TableRules definition must be supplied in a complete implementation.

{
  "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
  "$id": "https://github.com/AndreaBozzo/dataprof/schemas/quality_policy.json",
  "title": "DataProfQualityPolicy",
  "type": "object",
  "additionalProperties": false,
  "properties": {
    "version": {
      "type": "string",
      "enum": ["1.0"]
    },
    "global_rules": {
      "$ref": "#/$defs/TableRules"
    },
    "columns": {
      "type": "object",
      "patternProperties": {
        "^[a-zA-Z0-9_*.-]+$": {
          "$ref": "#/$defs/ColumnRuleSet"
        }
      },
      "additionalProperties": false
    }
  },
  "$defs": {
    "MetricBound": {
      "type": "object",
      "additionalProperties": false,
      "properties": {
        "min": {
          "type": ["number", "null"]
        },
        "max": {
          "type": ["number", "null"]
        }
      }
    },
    "ColumnRuleSet": {
      "type": "object",
      "additionalProperties": false,
      "properties": {
        "null_count": {
          "$ref": "#/$defs/MetricBound"
        },
        "distinct_ratio": {
          "$ref": "#/$defs/MetricBound"
        },
        "expected_type": {
          "type": ["string", "null"]
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

Key Architecture Highlights

Pattern-Based Column Matching

The patternProperties keyword allows property names matching a regular expression to be validated against a specified schema.

This can support naming conventions and wildcard-like policy keys. However, actual wildcard matching—such as interpreting prefix_* as a prefix matcher—must be implemented by the policy evaluator. A JSON Schema regular expression does not automatically provide glob-matching semantics.

Explicit Null Handling

Allowing null in a schema makes it possible to represent explicit null values in the configuration.

However, the meaning of null must be defined by the application. If null disables an inherited rule, the policy evaluator must implement that behavior explicitly.

Strict Property Validation

Using additionalProperties: false helps reject unexpected properties and catches configuration typos instead of silently accepting unknown keys.

Reusable Definitions

Using $defs and $ref avoids repeating the same rule definitions throughout the schema. This makes future changes easier to manage.

3. Bridging with PyO3 Native Rust Extensions

The next challenge is translating validated configuration into structures that Rust can process.

Serde provides serialization and deserialization support, while PyO3 allows Rust functions to interact with Python.

A practical architecture separates responsibilities:

  1. Python receives the configuration.
  2. A Draft 2020-12-compatible validator checks its structure.
  3. The validated configuration is serialized or passed across the Python–Rust boundary.
  4. Rust deserializes the configuration into typed structures.
  5. The native evaluator applies the rules to the dataset profile.
  6. The result is returned to Python.

Rust Data Structures

The following example illustrates how policy components can be represented using Serde.

use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
use std::collections::HashMap;

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct MetricBound {
    pub min: Option<f64>,
    pub max: Option<f64>,
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct ColumnRuleSet {
    pub null_count: Option<MetricBound>,
    pub distinct_ratio: Option<MetricBound>,
    pub expected_type: Option<String>,
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct QualityPolicy {
    pub version: String,
    pub columns: HashMap<String, ColumnRuleSet>,
}

These structures provide a typed representation of the policy.

The Option<T> type represents an optional Rust value. However, when configuration semantics distinguish between a missing property and an explicitly supplied null, additional deserialization logic may be required to preserve that distinction.

PyO3 Integration

A simplified PyO3 function can accept a JSON string, deserialize it, and invoke a native evaluator.

use pyo3::exceptions::PyValueError;
use pyo3::prelude::*;

#[pyfunction]
fn evaluate_quality_gate(
    policy_json_str: &str,
) -> PyResult<bool> {
    let policy: QualityPolicy =
        serde_json::from_str(policy_json_str)
            .map_err(|e| {
                PyValueError::new_err(e.to_string())
            })?;

    // Invoke the native policy evaluator here.
    // The evaluator must be implemented separately.
    let is_valid = run_policy_evaluation(&policy)
        .map_err(PyValueError::new_err)?;

    Ok(is_valid)
}

Here, run_policy_evaluation is a placeholder for the native evaluation implementation and must be defined before the example can compile.

Why This Separation Matters

Python handles configuration validation.

Python provides access to JSON Schema validators and can generate detailed validation errors for configuration authors.

Rust handles typed evaluation.

Rust can evaluate rules against native profiling structures without requiring every operation to pass through Python.

PyO3 provides interoperability.

PyO3 exposes native functionality to Python while keeping the interface explicit.

Serde provides structured deserialization.

Serde maps JSON values into Rust data structures. Ordinary JSON deserialization should not automatically be described as zero-copy; that depends on the implementation and the data being processed.

The key design objective is to keep the boundary simple and ensure that both sides agree on the policy's semantics.

4. Practical Example: Defining a Quality Gate

Consider a dataset containing customer records.

Before loading the dataset into a warehouse, a team may want to verify that customer IDs do not contain null values and that email addresses have the expected type.

A policy could look like this:

{
  "version": "1.0",
  "columns": {
    "customer_id": {
      "null_count": {
        "max": 0
      }
    },
    "email": {
      "expected_type": "string"
    }
  }
}

The schema validates the configuration's structure. The runtime evaluator then interprets the rules against the actual dataset profile.

For example, if the profile reports that customer_id contains three null values, a rule requiring a maximum null count of zero should fail.

The evaluator should return a meaningful result that identifies the violated rule rather than merely reporting that the overall policy failed.

A production implementation should also define:

  • How missing columns are handled.
  • How global rules interact with column-specific rules.
  • Whether explicit null disables a rule.
  • How conflicting rules are resolved.
  • How invalid configuration differs from failed data quality.
  • How errors are reported to Python callers.

These details are essential for predictable behavior in real data pipelines.

5. Exhaustive Parity Verification: 30 Test Cases

Schema validation and native evaluation must remain consistent as the policy format evolves.

A useful test suite should cover ordinary configurations, edge cases, invalid inputs, and serialization behavior.

The original case study reports 30 test cases distributed across four categories.

Test Suite Category Verification Invariants Reported Result
Baseline Policy Conformance Minimal versioned schema, table-level bounds, column metric boundaries 10 / 10 PASSED
Wildcard & Column Mapping Universal wildcard *, prefix patterns, column-specific rule overrides 8 / 8 PASSED
Strict Rejection & Negative Tests Unknown keys, additionalProperties: false, negative bounds, invalid types 7 / 7 PASSED
Encoding & Serialization Parity UTF-8 BOM handling, null-pointer safety, Serde deserialization parity 5 / 5 PASSED
Total 30 reported test cases 30 / 30 PASSED

Running the Tests

The case study identifies the following test command:

pytest tests/test_quality_policy_schema.py -v

Reported output:

========================= 30 passed in 0.18s =========================

These results are reproduced from the case study and have not been independently verified here.

Additional Tests Worth Considering

Beyond baseline validation, a robust implementation should consider the following cases.

1. Missing Versus Explicit Null

Verify whether an omitted rule and an explicitly supplied null have different meanings.

2. Wildcard Precedence

Verify that a specific column rule overrides a global rule according to the documented precedence rules.

3. Unknown Column References

Verify how the evaluator responds when a policy references a column that does not exist in the dataset.

4. Invalid Numeric Bounds

Test reversed minimum and maximum values, negative values where prohibited, and non-finite numeric values where relevant.

5. Schema-to-Rust Compatibility

Verify that configurations accepted by JSON Schema can be deserialized into the Rust policy structures, and that unsupported configurations are rejected with useful errors.

6. Error Reporting

Ensure configuration errors can be distinguished from runtime evaluation failures.

7. Large Policies

Measure performance and memory consumption for configurations containing many column rules.

These tests help protect the contract between configuration authors, the Python validation layer, and the native Rust evaluator.

6. Key Engineering Lessons

1. Shift Schema Validation to the Language of the Caller

Validate human-authored configuration in Python using a Draft 2020-12-compatible JSON Schema validator before passing it across the PyO3 boundary.

This makes it possible to report actionable validation errors close to where the configuration originates.

2. Keep the FFI Contract Lean

Pass JSON-serialized configurations or structured Python objects that map clearly onto Rust data structures.

The best approach depends on the size of the policy, interoperability requirements, and performance measurements.

The interface should remain explicit, predictable, and easy to test.

3. Decouple Syntax Validation from Runtime Semantics

JSON Schema validates structure and types.

The native Rust evaluator validates domain-specific conditions against the actual dataset profile.

Keeping these responsibilities separate avoids trying to solve data-dependent problems during static configuration validation.

4. Define Null and Override Semantics Explicitly

A configuration format is only reliable when its behavior is unambiguous.

If explicit null disables an inherited rule, document that behavior and implement it consistently in both validation and evaluation.

5. Test the Contract, Not Just Individual Components

Unit tests for Python validation and Rust evaluation are useful, but integration tests are equally important.

They establish whether the complete pipeline behaves consistently from configuration input to final quality-gate result.

7. Final Thoughts

Bridging Python and Rust is not just about making code faster. It is about assigning the right responsibilities to each layer.

In this architecture:

  • JSON Schema defines the structure of a quality policy.
  • Python validates human-authored configuration and produces actionable errors.
  • PyO3 provides the boundary between Python and native Rust code.
  • Serde maps JSON data into typed Rust structures.
  • Rust evaluates policy rules against dataset profiles.

The key lesson is simple: validate configuration early, keep the interoperability contract explicit, and evaluate data-dependent invariants where the actual data is available.

A well-designed Python–Rust boundary can make data quality systems easier to maintain, test, and extend.

Let's Discuss

If you were designing a production-grade Python–Rust data quality engine, how would you handle schema evolution, wildcard precedence, and error reporting across the FFI boundary?

Would you prefer JSON serialization for a simple contract, or structured Python objects for tighter integration?

I'd love to hear how other engineers approach this problem.

title: The golden set: 100 labelled examples as the acceptance test for an AI feature
description:
If you ask three people whether an AI feature "works", you will get three answers, each based on the last few examples they happened to see. A golden set replaces opinions with a number: a fixed collection of real inputs with agreed correct answers, run every time something changes. About a hundred items is enough to start.

Why a hundred

With 100 items, one mistake moves the score by one point, and you can still read every failure by hand. That is the point of the first set: not statistical perfection, but a measurement the whole team can inspect. As the feature matures you grow it; you do not start with thousands.

A caution on precision: with 100 items the uncertainty is wide. A 95% score can plausibly hide a true rate anywhere from roughly 89% to 98%. Treat it as a tripwire, not a guarantee, and say so in the acceptance document.

What goes into it

Sample from real data from the process, not from examples someone invented. Then deliberately cover:

  • The typical case, in proportion to how common it is (most of the set).
  • The boring variations: different phrasings, formats, languages, typos.
  • Known hard cases: the pairs people confuse, the odd layouts.
  • Things that must be refused or escalated: out-of-scope questions, missing fields, items the system should hand to a human.
  • A few adversarial ones: instructions hidden in the input, empty input, absurdly long input.

Tag each item with its category so you can report per-category results, not just one average that hides a weak spot.

Who labels it

The process owner, or someone they trust, decides the correct answer. Two people labelling independently, then discussing disagreements, finds the ambiguous items early. Ambiguity found at this stage is a requirements problem, and it is cheaper to fix now than after launch.

How to use it

  1. Freeze it. The set is not training data. Never tune on it after you start reporting from it, or the score only reflects what you memorised.
  2. Run it on every change: a new prompt, a new model version, a new threshold.
  3. Write the pass bar before the first run, as a number per category. Example: "at least 95% correct on automated items, and every must-refuse item refused".
  4. Read the failures, all of them. Each one is either a bug, a labelling error, or a missing rule.
  5. Keep a changelog of scores per version so regressions are visible.

A minimal runner is a few lines:

def evaluate(system, items):
    results = [(it, system(it["input"])) for it in items]
    ok = [r for it, r in results if r["answer"] == it["expected"]]
    return len(ok) / len(items), [it for it, r in results if r["answer"] != it["expected"]]

Refresh it slowly

Every month or so, add 10 to 20 fresh real items, especially ones that came out of the review queue as corrections. Retire items that no longer reflect the process. Keep a separate untouched holdout if you tune a lot.

Takeaways

  1. Start with about 100 real, labelled items.
  2. Cover typical, hard, and must-refuse cases and tag them.
  3. Freeze it, write the pass bar first, run it on every change.
  4. Be honest about the uncertainty that comes with a small set.

title: Build a Self-Supervised Pretext Task in 25 Lines of Python (No Labels Required)
description:
Most teams don't have a data problem. They have a label problem: millions of raw documents or images and only a few thousand annotated ones. Self-supervised learning (SSL) gets around this by making the data label itself.

The easiest way to understand that is to build the label generator yourself. Here's a minimal masked-token pretext task, the same idea BERT is pretrained with, in plain Python.

Step 1: Start with raw, unlabeled text 

corpus = [
    "the engineer deployed the model to production",
    "the server returned an unexpected error",
    "the model detected a damaged component",
]

No sentiment tags, no categories, no annotators.

Step 2: Turn every sentence into (input, target) pairs automatically 

import random

MASK = "[MASK]"

def make_pretext_examples(sentence, mask_prob=0.15, seed=None):
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    tokens = sentence.split()
    inputs, targets = [], []
    for tok in tokens:
        if rng.random() < mask_prob:
            inputs.append(MASK)
            targets.append(tok)      # the hidden word is the label
        else:
            inputs.append(tok)
            targets.append(None)     # no loss on visible tokens
    return inputs, targets

for i, s in enumerate(corpus):
    print(make_pretext_examples(s, mask_prob=0.3, seed=i))

Output (Python 3, exactly as printed):

(['the', 'engineer', 'deployed', '[MASK]', 'model', 'to', 'production'], [None, None, None, 'the', None, None, None])
(['[MASK]', 'server', 'returned', '[MASK]', 'unexpected', 'error'], ['the', None, None, 'an', None, None])
(['the', 'model', '[MASK]', '[MASK]', 'damaged', 'component'], [None, None, 'detected', 'a', None, None])

Notice the first two sentences mostly hid easy words like "the" and "an". That's exactly the shortcut problem covered below; real pipelines mask subword tokens and use smarter masking strategies.

That's the whole trick. The target came from the original sentence. Nobody wrote it by hand.

Step 3: What a real model does with these pairs

In a real pipeline you would:

  1. Tokenize with a subword tokenizer instead of split()
  2. Feed inputs to a Transformer encoder
  3. Compute cross-entropy only on the masked positions (the Nones are ignored)
  4. Repeat over millions of sentences

The encoder can't predict "detected" in the third example without understanding that models detect damaged components, so it ends up learning syntax and meaning as a side effect. That side effect, a reusable representation, is what you actually want.

Step 4: Throw away the head, keep the encoder

After pretraining, you discard the token-prediction head and fine-tune the encoder on your small labeled dataset (say, 2,000 support tickets tagged by intent). This is where SSL pays off: far fewer labels for the same accuracy.

Three gotchas we learned the hard way

  • Too-easy masks teach shortcuts. Masking only stop-words ("the", "a") gives the model nothing to learn.
  • Masking is a design decision. In images, a random crop can cut out the exact defect or tumour you care about. Choose transformations that keep the meaning you need downstream.
  • Low pretraining loss ≠ a useful model. Evaluate with a linear probe and with fine-tuning on the real task.

Beyond masking

Masked modeling is one of four big SSL objective families. The others are contrastive learning (SimCLR), teacher-student methods without negatives (BYOL), and redundancy reduction (Barlow Twins, VICReg). We cover all four, plus a decision framework and how to evaluate SSL models properly, in our complete guide: Self-Supervised Learning Explained: How AI Learns Without Labeled Data.

What would you mask in your own dataset? Tell us in the comments.

— The AheadMint Team
