title: My demo refused 96% of off-topic questions but only 39% of tricky ones. I know because of a test set
description:
Here are two numbers from my document Q&A demo. Ask it about something that is not in the knowledge base at all, and it refuses correctly 96.1% of the time. Ask it a question that sits close to a document but is not answered by it, and it refuses only 39% of the time.

If I had tried the demo by hand, I would have asked a few questions, seen it say "not in the docs" a couple of times, and called it good. The 39% only showed up because there was a labelled test set. That set is the subject of this post: a golden set, the cheapest acceptance test an AI feature can have.

What it is

A golden set is a list of real inputs with the answer a human accepts for each one. Nothing more. It is not training data and it is not a benchmark you publish. It is the thing you run after every change to ask one question: did it get better or worse?

Without it, every change is judged by whichever three examples someone happens to try. With it, "works pretty well" becomes a number you can argue about.

How I would build one in an afternoon

  1. Take real inputs. 100 is enough to start. Pull them from the actual process: tickets, invoices, questions people really ask. Not examples you invented to look nice.
  2. Cover the ugly cases on purpose. Roughly: most of it typical, a quarter hard or ambiguous, and a handful that must be refused or sent to a human. The ugly part is where the demo above found its 39%.
  3. Label it with the person who owns the process. The owner says what "correct" means. If two people disagree on a label, that disagreement is a finding, write it down.
  4. Freeze it. Do not tune the system on these examples. Tune on a separate split and touch the golden set only to report. In my ticket-triage demo the threshold is chosen on a validation split and the test set is used once.
  5. Write the acceptance rule before you run it. For example: "at least 97% correct on what is handled automatically, everything else goes to a person." Then the run is a pass or a fail, not an opinion.

What it showed me in my own demos

These are public demos on public datasets (test data, not client results):

  • Ticket triage. If everything were automated, accuracy would be 90.2%. Handle only the confident 75.9% and accuracy on those is 97.7%. The golden set is what made the trade-off visible.
  • Document Q&A. Out-of-base questions are refused 96.1% of the time, but near-miss questions only 39.4%. The cited answers hit 93% precision against a 95% target. I reported the gap instead of hiding it, and it points to the next fix: a reranker or an LLM for exactly those near-miss cases.

In both cases the number told me where to work next. A hand-tried demo would have told me nothing.

Pitfalls

  • Leakage. If the system has seen the golden examples while being tuned, the score is fiction.
  • Too clean. A set made only of easy cases gives 99% and a false sense of safety.
  • Never refreshed. Real inputs drift. Add new failures to the set whenever production surfaces one.
  • One number for everything. Report per category. A fine average can hide a category that fails every time.

Takeaways

  1. A golden set is real inputs plus answers a human accepts.
  2. Build it before the pilot, with the process owner.
  3. Include the ugly cases deliberately.
  4. Freeze it, and write the pass rule first.
  5. Report per category, and add every new production failure to it.

If you can only do one thing before your next AI pilot, label 100 examples. It is the cheapest hour of the project.

  • pg_qualstats is upgraded from 2.1.2 to 2.1.4.

  • pglogical is upgraded from 2.4.5 (for PostgreSQL 17 and earlier) and 2.4.6 (for PostgreSQL 18) to 2.4.8.

  • pgTAP is upgraded from 1.3.0 to 1.3.4.

  • pgtt is upgraded from 4.0 to 4.6.0 for PostgreSQL 12 and later.

  • PL/Proxy is upgraded from 2.11.0 to 2.12.0.

  • PostGIS is upgraded from 3.5.2 (for PostgreSQL 13 through 17) and 3.6.0 (for PostgreSQL 18) to 3.6.4 for PostgreSQL 13 and later.

  • roaringbitmap (pg_roaringbitmap) is upgraded from 0.5 to 1.2 for PostgreSQL 12 and later.

The new maintenance version is [PostgreSQL version].R20261013.02_04. If you use a maintenance window, then the updates to the minor and extension versions happen according to the timeframe that you set in the window. Otherwise, the updates occur within the next few weeks.

For more information about checking your maintenance version, see Perform self-service maintenance. To find your maintenance window or to manage maintenance updates, see Find and set maintenance windows. For more information about supported extensions, see Configure PostgreSQL extensions.

Change

Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL now supports enabling Managed Connection Pooling on existing Private Service Connect instances. Previously, Cloud SQL supported enabling Managed Connection Pooling only on new instances using Private Service Connect.

For more information, see Managed Connection Pooling overview and Configure Managed Connection Pooling.

Dialogflow

Feature

gemini-3.5-flash-lite has become generally available (GA). See Generative quotas for how to request quota for Gemini 3 and later models.

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Configure citations for custom MCP data stores

You can configure the citation_mappings parameter for custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) data stores using the REST API to display source citation chips when Gemini Enterprise answers questions using tools on your custom MCP server. This feature is generally available (GA).

For more information, see Configure citations for custom MCP data stores.

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Connect workflows in Workflow Builder to Confluence Data Center and Jira Data Center

You can connect workflows in Workflow Builder to Confluence Data Center and Jira Data Center to search data and automate actions across these third-party apps.

For more information, see Workflows overview.

Google Cloud Contact Center as a Service

Announcement

Advanced reporting dashboards prerelease notes 6.16

Here are the pre-release notes for updates to the advanced reporting dashboards and other reporting in CCAI Platform. When we release these updates, we expect the new capabilities to be as shown here.

Important: The next version of the advanced reporting dashboards could be greater than 6.16.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where the Agent Performance tile on the Real-time Agent Monitoring dashboard executed redundant database queries during auto-refreshes.

  • Updated advanced reporting filter prompts so they behave consistently across all dashboards and display the complete list of configured values:

    • List-backed filters now open directly into a searchable list on the first click.

    • Dropdowns that previously returned empty or partial lists now display the full configured list, including Agent Name, Agent Email, Agent Custom ID, Agent Teams, Location, Language, Answered By, and Projection Result.

    • Disposition Codes and Disposition List filters now display the codes configured for your instance.

    • Agent Teams and Team Name filters now match agents in any of their assigned teams.

    • Configuration renames (Queue Group, Queue, Agent Team, Disposition Code, Location, Role, and Skill) now appear in filter dropdowns within 30 minutes instead of up to six hours.

    • The Projecting filter on the live Queued dashboards is now clearable, so you can reset it to show all queued interactions, and offers only Yes.

    • Fields without a predefined list of values (such as consumer phone numbers and ID fields) now display a plain text box with an operator so you can type a value directly.

    • Call Status and Deflection Type filters now display values that existed in the data but were previously missing from the list.

    • Channel now reports a value on the live Voice and Chat dashboards, and on historical Chat dashboards, for interaction types that previously appeared blank (including internal, API-initiated, campaign, UCaaS, callback, and extension calls).

    • On the Agent Audit dashboard, the Change Details table now displays its timestamp column and sorts it correctly.

    • Consumer phone number filters now accept a single value instead of multiple values. Saved filters or links that pass multiple numbers apply only one.

    • On the Missed Interactions dashboards, the Activity Status column and filter are renamed to Projection Result.

    • Actor values describing who answered, ended, or disconnected an interaction are now standardized as Human Agent, Virtual Agent, End User, and System. Saved filters, Looks, and schedules that used the previous wording must be reselected.

Google Kubernetes Engine

Change

For GKE Standard CPU node pools, GKE can now upgrade nodes by updating the existing Compute Engine VM in place, instead of deleting the VM and creating a new one. Because the node keeps its underlying VM, it also keeps its compute capacity during the upgrade. This lowers the risk that a node upgrade fails or stalls because resources aren't available.

To enable this type of upgrade, use surge upgrades with the maxUnavailable field set to a value greater than 0. For more details about when GKE reuses the same Compute Engine instance, including exceptions, see maxUnavailable: GKE makes an existing node unavailable to recreate it.

This change applies to all GKE versions. To opt out, contact Cloud Customer Care.

Vertex AI Search

Change

Agent Search: Update to the stable model

The stable model for answer generation is updated to gemini-3.5-flash/answer_gen/v1 from gemini-2.5-flash/answer_gen/v1.

For more information, see Answer generation model versions and lifecycle.

title: Gravespeaker: Giving the Person Behind the Headstone a Voice
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

TL;DR: Gravespeaker turns a headstone photo into a researched ghost story, spoken aloud by ElevenLabs. Gemma reads the inscription and writes the monologue; Mastra orchestrates the research and storytelling, with SerpApi supplying the search results. The hard part was keeping the theater without inventing the person. Try it here.

What I Built

I used to make up their stories 🪦

Growing up, I was always intrigued by the paranormal and graveyards especially. I would go hang out in the cemetery just for the fun of it, coming up with wild stories about each person buried there: who they were, where they lived, and how they died. I wanted to know everything and what I didn't know, I made up.

That idea is where this app comes from: go to a graveyard, snap a picture of a tombstone (or upload a test copy), and the app will give you facts transformed into story mode by Gemma 4. ElevenLabs is responsible for the voice, which can be either male or female.

When you put it all together, it's just like the stories I used to imagine walking through the cemetery, except this time I have actual records to work from. Apparently, making up the entire biography was the easy version.

Why it needs the theater 🎭

My primary objective was to turn this into a theatrical story without diluting the person who lived behind the gravestone. That's why the search engine and fact engine were so important to this build: without raw facts, the theatrics have nothing to play with, and without theatrics the whole app turns into another obituary in the daily paper (for those of you old enough to remember those).

It's for the person who stops to read a name and wonders what happened between those two dates. That was me long before I had an app for it.

AKA Cool Things to Watch For

There's a lot going on behind the scenes in this application that you'd never notice unless you know to look for them. Here's a short list:

  1. Gemma reads the inscription, but ordinary code decides whether the search results match that person.
  2. Proposed facts have to carry quotes that can be checked against their sources.
  3. A narrator is selected from cues in the records, with a voice selector if you'd rather hear the other one.
  4. When the research can't support a biography, the story stays with the stone.

Demo

One stone, one life, one story 🪦

Try Gravespeaker

Turn on your sound for this one. The tunnel effect is intended to make the voice sound like it's coming from below the stone, which is a perfectly reasonable thing to want your phone to do in a cemetery.

  1. Take or upload a photo and let Gemma read the inscription. If the stone names more than one person, choose whose story to tell.
  2. Read the generated story, then press play beside Hear their story.
  3. For a researched story, open Facts for the inscription and Sources for its records.

The app selects its research candidate automatically and labels generated stories as AI reconstructions. A story drawn only from the inscription says so, without research tabs pretending there's more to see.

You can try a photo from the reviewed fixture collection. The manifest records the original photographers, source links, and licenses.

Code

anchildress1 / gravespeaker

Photograph a headstone. Discover a life. Hear the story the records left behind.

🪦 Gravespeaker

Photograph a headstone. Discover a life. Hear the story the records left behind.

  • About
  • Features
  • Tech Stack
  • Architecture
  • Project Structure
  • Getting Started
  • Configuration
  • Deploying
  • Benchmarks
  • Security
  • License
  • Author

About

Gravespeaker is a mobile-friendly web app. Upload or snap a photo of a gravestone, check what the AI read from the stone, and hear a short theatrical story built only from facts checked against public records you can click through.

The story is openly fiction, labelled "Story generated with AI", but it states only facts that appear in a cited source. If the records can't establish who the person was, the app says so instead of making something up.

Built for Hacktoberfest 2026, Week 4: Ghost in the Machine. The PRD has the full scope, schedule and definition of done.

Features














Step What you get
Read Name and life dates from a photo, shown read-only. Maiden names are split
…



View on GitHub


⚖️ The project uses Polyform Shield 1.0.0 with supplemental terms. The application is source-available; Gemma is open-weight and Mastra is the open-source framework at its core.

The app is built with SvelteKit and TypeScript, deployed on Cloud Run, with Gemma 4 26B hosted through the Gemini API. The source and saved experiments include the inscription benchmarks, recorded search results, and story evaluation harness.

The local unit suite passes 379 tests, covering namesakes, conflicting dates, failed searches, and unsupported story claims. The generated stories have their own evaluation harness, because a mocked model is remarkably cooperative about saying exactly what the test expects.

How I Built It

Reading the stone is more than reading the words 🪨

First, the image is captured (or uploaded) and sent to Gemma 4 26B for analysis to read the gravestone. I thought about doing this deterministically instead, but there are so many variants to account for plus wear and tear on the gravestone itself.

Plus I didn't just want to read the results, I needed to know which part was the name, whether it's a maiden or married name, whether it's a dual burial plot and if so are there two people or just one, when did they die, is the full date present or just a year, does the gravestone define a birthday. Technically speaking, this is the sort of problem AI handles exceptionally well.

The saved reading run scored 57/58 fields across 20 photos, with no extra people or request/JSON errors. That's a small smoke test with one call per image, including the app's normalization, and the remaining mistake matters: a worn 1818 still came back as 1848.

An earlier run also produced a person literally named "[]". I can reject a name with no letters in ordinary code. A plausible but wrong year is harder, and it can send the search after the wrong person. The benchmark notes keep the prompts, failures, and scoring details available for inspection.

Challenge one: finding the right person 🧭

As it turns out, searching for people isn't as easy as it sounds. I guess that's why there's specialized sites for this kind of thing, but I didn't have that. So I made my own instead.

There were two primary challenges I faced in this build and one of those was getting the search criteria just right. I didn't want AI in charge of a search when it makes more sense to call SerpAPI with deterministic data points. When I first read the specs, I thought that I'd have everything I possibly needed to make this whole idea come to life.

I was wrong...

SerpApi: five search engines and a disappearing credit balance 🪙

I tried a variety of different search combinations, including the person's name, date of birth, date of death, and burial location.

One Google search did not return enough reliable data about a person given their name, date of birth, or death date. So I attempted to correct that by adding in other search providers with the same search lookup — which worked right up until Claude helpfully pointed out that I'd run out of credits before I finished testing the app at the rate I was using them.

So one search provider went to five and back down to two. Finding more results helped, but I still needed to know whether they belonged to the person on the stone.

Saving the results so I could afford to test 🗂️

I used Mastra to orchestrate the search pipeline and spent my free credits running tests to figure out which sources actually belonged to the person on the stone. This required up to 100 credits per test run until I started saving SerpAPI results for reuse. Yes, there's a cache, but that doesn't give me a fixed set of results to test against. Storing results was my solution.

Google added another complication: some result links went through redirects that didn't reliably return a destination while recording. The replay harness preserves those resolved links and rejects incomplete recordings. I wanted to change the matching logic and see what changed, not wonder whether Google had handed me a different experiment. Replaying the saved responses runs the research workflow without spending more search credits.

Mastra: which search to try next—and when to stop 🧭

Mastra runs this as a workflow with explicit inputs and outputs: plan the searches, run the next one, resolve the candidates. There is no model deciding which query to try or whether a birth year matches. That's ordinary code, and I can replay it against the same responses without asking an LLM to reconsider arithmetic.

The app starts with the name and fully readable birth and death years, trying plain queries and then obituary, grave, or cemetery terms. Yandex goes first, then Google if it doesn't find a dated match. Later queries can add a town from browser location, photo GPS, or the inscription. I'm working from the assumption that most people are buried close to where they lived.

Mastra handles retries, and the workflow stops when it finds a medium- or high-confidence candidate, runs out of queries, or encounters repeated provider failures.

The stopping rule made a measurable difference on the same nine-person replay set:

Search strategy Search attempts, including retries Cases with a dated match
Wait for three sources 136 5/9
Try each query plain, then with keywords; stop at the first dated match 72 5/9

Requiring more sources sounded reassuring until it cost almost twice as many attempts without finding another dated match. In replay 25, only two cases stop after the first search. A dated match is the engine's assessment, not independent proof that the entire biography is correct.

For example, Ethan John Chartre takes four attempts in the saved replay: the plain name-and-dates query on both engines, then the version with obituary terms. The fourth returns a funeral-home result that the matcher grades high. Same person, same dates, different search wording—and finally something useful to work with.

What makes a match convincing enough? 🪪

High confidence means the name and every available birth or death year match, with at least one year present. Medium means the name and one year match while another year remains unconfirmed. A name alone is useful as a lead and pretty terrible as permission to start narrating somebody's life, so it needs date evidence from the page or fallback snippet before it can support a researched story.

The identity tests cover middle initials, generational suffixes, and pages that mention the right person inside somebody else's obituary. Jr. and Sr. are doing quite a lot of work when the alternative is giving a son his father's life story.

The gravestone didn't come with a Facebook username 🪧

I also wanted to be able to search social media for people who passed away since 2010 — a completely arbitrary date meant to tune appropriately in the future after proper benchmarks and data integrity checks are complete. However, SerpAPI's Facebook profile endpoint required a profile identifier—a username or numeric ID—and I was unable to find a way to link a gravestone with a profile identifier by the challenge deadline. General web searches can still turn up social links; the dedicated profile lookup didn't make it into this build.

Challenge two: keeping the theater without inventing a life 🎭

Finding a plausible search result is only the beginning. The app fetches the source pages, checks their date evidence, and drops pages that contradict the inscription. Gemma extracts proposed facts with supporting quotes, and code checks those quotes against the source text before they reach the storyteller. If a page can't be fetched, the available search snippet is the fallback evidence.

Gemma turns those supported facts into a first-person monologue. If the research doesn't supply enough evidence, it works from the stone; if no generated sentence survives the checks, the UI shows a plain epitaph. Running out of records doesn't mean the app gets to invent some.

The evaluator was taking the theater out 🧪

The evaluator needed to understand the difference too. If someone died at 96, calling it a long life is reasonable. If they died at 45, the same line needs another look. A ghost talking about the wind around the grave is atmosphere. A ghost watching their children grow has just acquired children, and I need a source for that.

The evaluator originally pushed too far in the other direction and started taking the theater out with the unsupported facts. I pushed back. I wasn't building all of this just to have a second model reduce the story to a list of dates with dramatic punctuation.

The story evaluation harness now has two kinds of input: recorded research cases and deliberately constructed cases that tempt specific mistakes. The written cases include good and bad reference stories, so the evaluator has to demonstrate that it can tell the difference before its scores mean much.

Mastra's createScorer runs a Gemini Flash judge that separates life claims from atmosphere and identifies supporting evidence. Code then checks that the quoted evidence actually appears in the supplied records. An unsure verdict counts as a failure, and a separate check catches years outside the person's lifespan. Each generated case gets three attempts, because one lucky paragraph is a very convenient way to fool myself.

The production checks catch new names, numbers, and certain contradictions; the evaluator tackles what the sentences actually mean. That evaluation work is still in progress, and I'm not claiming a complete passing score for generated stories. Getting the judge to recognize the problem is part of solving it.

ElevenLabs: a voice from below the stone 🎙️

ElevenLabs reads the finished paragraph using Callum or Matilda. Callum is slowed to 0.85 speed; Matilda stays at 1.0. Both use a tunnel effect with distance added, because the intention is for the voice to come from somewhere below the stone instead of sounding like a cheerful assistant reading an obituary.

The narration endpoint streams MP3 audio using Flash v2.5 when the visitor presses play. The starting voice comes from pronouns and relationship cues in verified quotes, then a name-based guess. It's a narrator, not verified gender or a recreation of the person's actual voice, and the visitor can switch it.

I also wanted narration to change based on when the person died, but that hasn't made it into the build. The speed and effects are fixed. Getting the facts right took priority over giving every century its own dramatic entrance.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

What choosing Gemma let me change 🪛

I didn't start by assuming the open model would win. I tested hosted Gemma against Gemini Flash, and smaller Gemma variants locally through Ollama and LiteRT-LM. The local models struggled with worn inscriptions, including inventing surnames, so I kept the larger hosted model for this build.

That ability to try local inference matters for this project. A cemetery is a fairly inconvenient place to discover that the app needs a better signal, and open weights give me a route toward running the model myself instead of making the hosted endpoint a permanent requirement. This version uses hosted services; the local experiments show both the possibility and how much work remains.

Mastra gives me the same room to work on the orchestration. Its open-source workflows and scorer let me put ordinary code around the model, replay the research, and define what a good story means for this particular app. Someone else can inspect those choices, reproduce the experiments, or decide my ghost needs a different set of rules. They don't have to start by rebuilding the framework.

My Agent Session

Entire: keeping the reasoning with the code 🧵

Entire records the agent sessions and ties checkpoints to commits. That matters when the finished code tells me what a rule does but doesn't tell me which argument, failed experiment, or particularly convincing wrong answer put it there.

The recorded session preserves the disagreement over atmosphere in the story evals, including the decision to undo a prompt change that was stripping out valid language. Without that context, tightening the prompt again would look like progress. It would also put me right back in the argument I'd already had.

There's a concrete example in the confidence-label fix. Codex caught a case where a source page was rejected for contradicting the stone, but its search confidence could still help label the final story as matching every date. Claude added a regression test and changed the grade to use the remaining evidence when a page gets dropped.

That commit carries Entire checkpoint 01M68EC8YQA3S5V7J8WWQ9ARF3, including the tradeoff behind the more conservative grade. It's useful context to keep beside the code, especially when another helpful AI decides the stricter rule looks unnecessary.

With the repository and checkpoint data available locally, the session can be inspected with:

entire checkpoint explain e003abf

The Spirit of It

Why I wanted the stone to answer 🕯️

I wanted the experience to feel a little unsettling, like you've stopped to read a gravestone and someone on the other side has decided to answer. That's where the first-person story and the voice come together. Reading a name and hearing a story addressed to you are two very different ways to spend a few minutes in a cemetery.

That's my interpretation of Ghost in the Machine: give someone a reason to stop at a stone they might otherwise walk past, let the theater pull them into the story, and leave them with something about the person who actually lived.

Prize Categories

Category Its role in Gravespeaker
Best Use of Gemma Reads the inscription, extracts proposed facts, and writes the theatrical monologue; the reading comparisons and story eval harness are linked above.
Best Use of Mastra Runs the research and story workflows, owns search-step retries and stopping, and supplies the custom story scorer.
Best Use of Entire Preserves the agent sessions and checkpoints behind the implementation, including the evaluation decisions and confidence-label fix.
Best Use of SerpApi Supplies Google and Yandex results for identity matching and research; saved responses make the workflow experiments repeatable.
Best Use of ElevenLabs Streams the selected narrator with the pacing and tunnel effect described above.

Still curious about the person behind the stone 🪦

Growing up, I wanted to know everything, and what I didn't know, I made up. That was half the fun. Building this means figuring out how to keep that curiosity and theater without making up somebody else's life.

🛡️ The Ghostwriter Has Been Identified

Codex helped draft this post from the project files and composed this footer, apparently unwilling to remain an anonymous apparition.

The saved benchmark results are available for inspection; the ghosts have declined peer review.

title: Before You Ship a Task App, Test Its Data Export
description:
A task app can look great during a demo. You create a task, assign it to someone, add a deadline, and move it across a board.

Then you click Export.

The download contains task titles and dates. The comments are missing. Attachments are only links. Completed work has disappeared because a filter was active.

The file opens, but it does not contain everything the team expected.

For developers, this is a useful reminder: an export button is a feature with its own requirements. Downloading a file is only the first step.

I run WhatsOnTech, where we publish guides about software and everyday business technology. This article looks at a question that matters to both software buyers and developers: can people take their work with them in a form they can actually use?

The example below uses a fictional task app. It is a suggested testing approach, not a claim that I tested every product mentioned.

Disclosure: I run the website linked in this article. This article was prepared with AI assistance.

Decide What the Export Is Supposed to Do

Before choosing a file format, decide why someone needs the export.

A manager preparing a weekly report may only need task names, owners, deadlines, and status.

A team moving to another app may need much more: descriptions, comments, checklists, attachments, and the relationships between records.

Someone recovering from data loss needs a tested restoration process.

These are different jobs.

An export designed for reporting can be useful without recreating an entire workspace. The problem starts when the interface calls that file a complete backup.

Write a clear description of the feature before building it:

Export the selected tasks and their main fields for spreadsheet reporting. Comments and attachment files are not included.

That explanation may sound less impressive than “Export everything,” but it sets an expectation the product can meet.

Understand the Work Before Choosing the Fields

A personal reminder and a shared project do not carry the same amount of information.

“Send the invoice” might need a title, deadline, and completion status.

“Prepare the new website homepage” could involve several people, review comments, image files, subtasks, and approval history.

This difference also matters when choosing software. Our Microsoft To Do vs Trello comparison explores the distinction between simple lists and work organised into stages.

For developers, the lesson is to export the information that gives a task its meaning.

A card titled “Update the page” is not very useful after migration if the page address, feedback, and assigned person have been lost.

Start by listing the fields people rely on during normal work. Then decide which export includes each field.

Use a Small Dataset With Deliberate Edge Cases

Testing with three tasks called “Task 1,” “Task 2,” and “Task 3” will miss many problems.

Instead, create a small test workspace with records that challenge the export.

Include:

  • Two tasks with the same title but different IDs.
  • One completed task and one archived task.
  • A task without a deadline.
  • A description containing commas, quotation marks, and line breaks.
  • Text in more than one language.
  • A task with several checklist items.
  • Two attachments that share the same filename.
  • A task with more than one comment.
  • A deadline with a specific time.
  • A date-only deadline with no time attached.

Record what you expect before downloading anything.

For example, your fictional workspace might contain 12 tasks, 7 comments, 4 checklist items, and 3 attachments.

Those counts give you something concrete to compare against. They are not proof of completeness by themselves, but they make missing data easier to notice.

Use invented information for this test. Real customer records are unnecessary.

Make Export Scope Visible

A common source of confusion is the difference between “what I can see” and “everything in the workspace.”

If a user filters the screen to show open tasks, should Export include only those tasks?

Either behaviour can be reasonable. It needs to be explicit.

The export screen could offer:

  • Current filtered view.
  • All tasks I am allowed to access.
  • Include completed tasks.
  • Include archived tasks.

Show a summary before the download:

This export includes 12 tasks, including completed tasks. Archived tasks are excluded.

For larger systems, the export should also explain its timing. If a team changes records while a long export is running, the resulting file may contain information collected at different moments.

Use a consistent snapshot where practical, or document how the export handles changes during generation.

The user should not have to guess what “all” means.

Choose CSV or JSON for a Clear Reason

CSV is useful for rows and columns. People can open it in a spreadsheet, sort tasks, and create simple reports.

JSON can represent nested information such as a task with several comments and checklist items.

Neither format guarantees completeness.

Format Useful for What needs attention
CSV Spreadsheet reports and simple transfers Nested records, text formatting, dates, and spreadsheet interpretation
JSON Structured records and custom migration tools Schema documentation, relationships, and importer compatibility
ZIP package Records plus attachment files File organisation, missing files, and a contents summary
PDF A readable snapshot Limited usefulness for importing structured data

A well-documented CSV may be more useful than an unexplained JSON file.

For a structured export, include a format version, export time, field descriptions, and a clear explanation of how records connect.

Keep stable identifiers. Two tasks with identical titles should remain distinguishable after export.

Learn From a Real Export Limitation

Trello provides a practical example of why these details matter.

According to Atlassian’s export documentation, board members can export raw JSON, while boards in Premium Workspaces can also be exported as CSV. Comments are not included in the CSV export.

For Workspace exports, including raw attachments is a separate option. Without it, the export links to attachments hosted on Trello.

Atlassian also states that importing the exported JSON or CSV to recreate a Trello board is not currently supported.

That does not make the exports useless. It means exporting, reporting, migration, and restoration are separate capabilities.

When evaluating any app, check the documentation for the exact export option you plan to use. Different formats and export levels can include different information.

Check Attachment Files, Not Just Their Names

An attachment entry may contain a filename and a web address without containing the file itself.

That can work while the original account remains available. It may fail later if permissions change, the file is removed, or the link expires.

If an export promises attachment files, check that they are actually present.

Download a sample package, disconnect from the original service, and try opening the included documents and images.

Also test duplicate filenames. Two different files named “brief.pdf” should not overwrite each other.

A package can keep files in separate folders based on task or attachment IDs. A contents list can connect each file to its original record.

If a file could not be included, report it clearly. A successful download message should not hide skipped attachments.

Keep Dates and Text Meaningful

Dates deserve more attention than they usually receive.

“05/06/2026” can mean different dates depending on the reader’s locale.

A date-only deadline should remain a date. Converting it unnecessarily into a timestamp can make it appear on a different day in another time zone.

For timed events, use a documented representation with a time-zone offset or UTC convention. Where local scheduling matters, preserve the relevant time-zone information too.

Text needs similar care.

Check that:

  • Commas stay inside the correct field.
  • Quotation marks survive the export.
  • Multiline notes remain attached to one record.
  • Urdu and other non-English text remains readable.
  • Identifiers with leading zeros stay intact.

A file that opens without an error can still contain changed values.

Compare actual field values, not just the appearance of the first few rows.

Separate Export, Sync, and Backup

These three features are related, but they serve different purposes.

An export provides a copy of selected information.

Sync carries changes between connected locations.

Backup is intended to support recovery under defined conditions.

A team may use all three.

For example, syncing a folder can make an exported file available on another computer. It does not automatically protect that file from a deletion that also syncs.

Our guide to cloud backup versus sync explains this distinction from the user’s perspective.

For your own app, describe recovery in practical terms:

  • Which records can be recovered?
  • How old can the recovery point be?
  • How long are copies retained?
  • Are attachment files included?
  • What access is required to restore them?
  • Has the recovery process been tested?

An occasional manual export can contribute to a backup plan. Its value depends on its coverage, storage, age, and whether someone can use it to recover the information they need.

Test the Return Journey

If your app promises restoration, test the complete journey.

Create a test workspace, export it, and restore it into a separate empty test environment.

Then compare the result with the original.

Check record counts, field values, attachment contents, and relationships. Make sure comments belong to the correct tasks and checklist items retain their completion status.

If the destination creates new IDs, verify that the relationships are mapped correctly rather than expecting every ID to remain unchanged.

Repeat the import.

Does it create duplicates? Update existing records? Refuse to continue? The behaviour should be deliberate and documented.

If your app supports export but not import, say so. Do not describe a readable archive as a tested restore package.

Never delete the original workspace just to find out whether restoration works.

Treat Spreadsheet Export as a Security Feature

User-entered text may behave differently after it leaves your application.

Some spreadsheet programs interpret values beginning with certain characters as formulas. This creates a risk known as CSV or formula injection.

Correctly escaping commas and quotation marks does not, by itself, solve that problem.

OWASP notes that protections depend on the spreadsheet application and how the file is opened, saved, and reopened.

For a related DEV discussion, see spreadsheet exports and formula-injection controls.

Keep the original data unchanged in your application. Apply suitable handling when creating a spreadsheet-facing export, and test it with the applications you support.

A separate machine-readable export may be appropriate when users need exact original values.

Export permissions also matter. The download must not reveal private fields or other users’ records simply because the export query has fewer restrictions than the normal screen.

Make Large Exports Honest About Failure

A small workspace may export quickly. A large one may require background processing.

Give the job clear states such as preparing, ready, failed, or completed with omissions.

If only part of the data was exported, say so. Provide a useful summary of what was included and what failed.

Avoid giving every download the same filename. A descriptive name with an export date makes older copies easier to distinguish.

Protect the generated file appropriately. A private workspace should not become a publicly accessible download.

If download links expire, tell users when they need to create another export.

Use a Release Checklist

Before releasing an export feature, check more than the download button.

Check What a useful result looks like
Export scope Included and excluded records are clear
Record counts Counts match the selected scope
Text Quotes, line breaks, and different languages survive
Dates Date-only values and timed events retain their meaning
Attachments Promised files are present and open correctly
Relationships Comments and subtasks remain linked correctly
Permissions Restricted records and fields stay restricted
Spreadsheet behaviour Untrusted text is handled for supported applications
Repeated import Duplicate handling follows the documented rule
Partial failure Missing items are reported
Restoration Tested if recovery is promised

Keep the test dataset so you can run these checks again when the data model changes.

A newly added field is easy to display in the app and easy to forget in an export.

Build the Exit Alongside the Entrance

Onboarding helps people bring their work into an app. Export helps them keep control of that work later.

Both deserve careful design.

Start with a clear purpose, test with realistic sample records, and explain the limits of each format. If you promise recovery, test recovery.

The goal is not to produce the largest possible download. It is to give people a copy they can understand and use for the purpose you promised.

Before shipping another task feature, try taking the existing work out of your app. What survives that journey tells you a great deal about the quality of the export.

title: Honest-ofrenda: an AI remembrance writer that has to show what it made up
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

What I Built

I gave an AI eight facts about a grandmother and asked for a short remembrance. It gave her a smile that wasn't in the facts.

That is why I built honest-ofrenda. You type 6 to 8 facts about someone you remember for your ofrenda: their name, a year, a favourite food, a story. An open-weight model (Qwen3-8B) turns them into a few warm sentences. Then plain Python code checks what the model wrote against your facts and shows you everything it added.

For the theme, the ghost in this machine is what a language model does without being asked: it adds details. A smile. A candle. A prayer. In a remembrance for someone who has died, those invented details are the haunting. So I didn't try to hide the ghost. I built a tool that makes it show itself.

I took the Día de los Muertos side of the theme: honoring the past, not the spooky side. It is for anyone who wants help with the words but doesn't want an AI inventing memories. Both people in this post, Sunanda Kulkarni and Ramesh Joshi, are made up. I have not run it on a real family's facts.

Demo

There is no live demo. It runs on my own laptop, and any public version would send visitors' text to a hosted API. Here is a real run on the made-up grandfather:

I remember Ajoba teaching me how to whistle while fixing bikes.
He kept a blue notebook with train times for 120 routes.
He loved shrikhand and would eat it every Sunday.
...

Checker: FLAGGED
- name: Sunday
Review by hand (soft claims not in your facts): every

His facts say he whistled while repairing bicycles, kept a notebook with 120 train times, and that shrikhand was his favourite food. The model turned that into teaching me to whistle, 120 routes, and a Sunday ritual nobody mentioned.

Runs took between 38 and 46 seconds each. They were single runs, and the first included a cold start, so please don't read them as benchmarks.

Code

DkHrR / honest-ofrenda

honest-ofrenda

What it is

honest-ofrenda is a tool that turns biographical facts about a remembered person into a short remembrance for an ofrenda. The open-weight language model writes the wording, while deterministic code checks that the draft introduces no names or numbers absent from the provided facts.

Run it

Install dependencies:

pip install -r requirements.txt

Set your Tinker key in .env:

API_KEY=your_api_key_here
MODEL=Qwen/Qwen3-8B

Run the tool:

python -m ofrenda.cli samples/sunanda.txt --save out/sunanda.md

Use it for someone you remember

Copy samples/template.txt into a folder named my_facts/ (which is git-ignored), and fill in 6 to 8 facts about the person. Run the tool:

python -m ofrenda.cli my_facts/yourfile.txt --save out/yourfile.md

Read every sentence yourself, and compare it with your facts because the checks catch only some changes. Note that your facts are sent to the Tinker hosted API. The tool has been run only on the two made-up samples, not on a…

View on GitHub

MIT licence. 42 tests pass, and none of them call the model.

pip install -r requirements.txt
# put your Tinker key in a .env file (API_KEY=...)
python -m ofrenda.cli samples/sunanda.txt --save out/sunanda.md

There is also a blank samples/template.txt for using it on someone you remember, and a README section on how.

How I Built It

My rule was: the model proposes, plain code checks.

  1. The model (Qwen3-8B on Tinker, thinking turned off) writes 4 to 6 sentences from your facts only. The prompt tells it not to add names, numbers, places, foods or songs, and not to describe feelings or looks unless a fact says so.
  2. A checker compares every number and every capitalised word with your facts. A made-up year, price or name gets flagged.
  3. A soft-word list flags words like always, every, smile and warmth when they aren't in your facts.
  4. An evidence view shows, for each sentence, the closest fact and the words that appear in no fact. It has false alarms ("selling" vs "sold"), so it's a review aid, not proof.
  5. A local web page. python serve.py opens a small page on your own computer, with no live demo. It asks for at least 4 facts besides the Name line and shows the same checks.

What went wrong

  • A leaked token. The first output ended with <|im_end|>, the model's own end marker. I added a cleaner.
  • A smile the checker couldn't see. The first run ended with "the way she smiled and the warmth she brought". The checker said nothing unsupported, because that line has no name or number. That is why the soft-word list and the evidence view exist.
  • 7 of 12 sentences drifted. I read the two saved pages against the facts by hand. "Teaching me how to whistle", "120 routes", "every Sunday", "for the first time", "with care and pride", "loved making puran poli" and "a quiet presence, steady and strong" are all additions or changes. The checker and soft-word list flagged 2 of those 7 sentences. The evidence view listed unmatched words in all 7. This is my own hand count of 12 sentences, not a benchmark.
  • One fact is a trap. In the browser I once gave it a single fact. The model wrote six sentences of invented ritual: candle, marigolds, photo, water bowl, altar, prayer. The checker said nothing unsupported. The evidence view marked 5 of the 6 sentences as matching no fact. That is why the page now requires at least 4 facts.
  • The smile came back. Running the made-up grandmother again in the browser, the model wrote "She always had a smile on her face". This time the soft-word list caught always and smile, but it still missed "She loved making puran poli" (her favourite food, not her hobby).

What I did not do

  • No real person's facts, and no first user yet.
  • No fine-tuning, no local model and no comparison with a closed model.
  • No test with facts that contain instructions.
  • No live demo. The web page runs only on my laptop.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

I'll be careful here. This does not run offline, and your facts are not kept on your machine. Qwen3-8B runs on Tinker's hosted API, because my 4 GB laptop can't run an 8B model. Your facts are sent to that service, and the README says not to use it for anything you wouldn't send to a hosted service.

What the open pieces gave me:

  • A model I can name and swap. Which model writes the text is one line in a settings file. I did not test another model, so that is a design point, not a result.
  • A checker that doesn't depend on the model. It is plain Python, so it behaves the same whichever model writes the text. That matters most here, because the model is the part I can't trust.
  • Weights anyone can download. Someone with a bigger machine could run the same model at home. I haven't tried that.
  • Code you can read and fork. MIT licence, and the whole pipeline fits in a few small files. The model call still depends on Tinker, so if that host went away you'd need to point it at another one.

I didn't compare this with a closed model, so I can't say the open one did better. I can only say what it did: it made up details, and the code around it caught some of them.

My Agent Session

I wrote the code with Google's Antigravity (Gemini) and planned each step with Claude. I checked every report against the raw output, because the agent overstated things. Twice it also broke my rules. It opened its own log files outside the project folder. And when my safety scan flagged a harmless pattern in the error-cleaning code, it split the string in two so the scanner would stop seeing it. That is a funny thing to catch in a project about not letting a machine quietly change the facts. I left it in and I don't call it a security feature. No saved session link.

The Spirit of It

The moment it landed was small. Across my runs on the made-up grandmother, the model kept reaching for the same kind of ending: a smile, warmth, "a quiet presence, steady and strong". Nice words, generic, and nobody gave them to it.

A real remembrance is made of specific things: 5 marigold plants on a balcony, 6 kilometres walked to see a first film, a favourite food. Those came from the facts. The additions were the vague ones. I'd rather have the five plants.

I haven't shown it to anyone yet, and this post won't pretend I have. The tool's job is to help a person write what they remember, and then to point at everything that wasn't theirs.

Prize Categories

Entered in the overall Week 4 challenge, on the Día de los Muertos side of the theme. No partner category. Tinker's category needs a fine-tune with a measured improvement over a baseline, and I only used inference, so I didn't enter it.

title: Cloudflare’s Post-Quantum GeoKey Manager Enters Closed Beta Without Attribute-Based Encryption
description:
Cloudflare has moved a post-quantum rebuild of GeoKey Manager into closed beta, guarding geo-fenced keys with hybrid ML-KEM-768 and X25519 instead of the attribute-based encryption used since 2022. Keys live only in kernel memory on verified regional servers, and any failed check rejects the request, a fail-closed choice practitioners ask could cause a regional outage. GA is planned for Q1 2027.

By Steef-Jan Wiggers

title: # My Python Learning Journey – Understanding Python Fundamentals 🐍
description:
Introduction

Today, I continued my Python learning journey and explored some important Python fundamentals.

As a beginner, I learned how objects, functions, methods, variables, and attributes work. I also explored function overloading, naming conventions, and PEP 8.

Let's look at what I learned today with simple examples.

1. What is an Object?

An object is an instance of a class.

In Python, almost everything is an object, including integers, strings, lists, and functions.

Example:

name = "Python"
age = 25

print(type(name))
print(type(age))

Here, "Python" is a string object and 25 is an integer object.

2. What is a Function?

A function is a reusable block of code that performs a particular task.

We use the def keyword to define a function.

Example:

def greet():
    print("Hello, Welcome to Python!")

greet()

Output:

Hello, Welcome to Python!

Here:

  • def is the keyword used to define a function.
  • greet is the function name.
  • greet() calls the function.

3. What is a Method?

A method is a function associated with an object or class.

Example:

name = "python"

print(name.upper())

Output:

PYTHON

Here, upper() is a string method that converts lowercase letters into uppercase letters.

4. What is a Variable?

A variable is a name that refers to an object.

Example:

name = "Sam"
age = 25

print(name)
print(age)

Here:

  • name refers to a string object.
  • age refers to an integer object.
  • = is the assignment operator.

5. What is an Attribute?

An attribute is a name associated with an object or class.

Attributes can store data or represent behavior.

Example:

class Student:

    def __init__(self, name, age):
        self.name = name
        self.age = age

s1 = Student("Sam", 25)

print(s1.name)
print(s1.age)

Here:

  • Student is a class.
  • s1 is an object (instance).
  • self refers to the current instance.
  • self.name and self.age are instance attributes.
  • __init__() is an initializer method.

6. What is an Instance?

An instance is an individual object created from a class.

Example:

class Student:
    pass

s1 = Student()
s2 = Student()

Here, s1 and s2 are two separate instances of the Student class.

A simple way to remember:

  • Class = Blueprint
  • Instance = Individual object created from that blueprint.

7. Class Attributes vs. Instance Attributes

Class Attribute

A class attribute is defined inside a class but outside its methods. It is shared by instances by default.

Instance Attribute

An instance attribute belongs to an individual object.

Example:

class Student:

    school = "ABC School"

    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

s1 = Student("Sam")
s2 = Student("David")

print(s1.school)
print(s2.school)

Output:

ABC School
ABC School

Both objects access the same class attribute.

Changing a class attribute through an object 

s1.school = "XYZ School"

print(s1.school)
print(s2.school)

Output:

XYZ School
ABC School

Here, Python creates an instance attribute named school for s1. It does not change the original class attribute.

Changing the class attribute 

Student.school = "DEF School"

print(s1.school)
print(s2.school)

Output:

XYZ School
DEF School

The s1 object continues using its own instance attribute, while s2 accesses the updated class attribute.

8. What is Function Overloading in Python?

Function overloading means using the same function name with different parameters.

Python does not support traditional function overloading directly. If we define multiple functions with the same name, the latest definition replaces the previous one.

We can achieve similar behavior using default arguments and *args.

Using default arguments 

def add(a, b, c=0):
    print(a + b + c)

add(10, 20)
add(10, 20, 30)

Output:

30
60

Using *args 

def add(*args):
    print(sum(args))

add(10, 20)
add(10, 20, 30)

Output:

30
60

*args allows a function to accept multiple positional arguments.

9. Naming Conventions in Python

Naming conventions are guidelines used to name variables, functions, classes, and constants.

Snake Case

Words are separated by underscores.

student_name = "Sam"

def calculate_total():
    pass

Commonly used for variables and functions.

Pascal Case

Each word starts with a capital letter.

class StudentDetails:
    pass

Commonly used for class names.

Camel Case

The first word starts with a lowercase letter, and subsequent words start with uppercase letters.

studentName = "Sam"

It is valid Python, but snake_case is preferred for variables and functions.

Upper Snake Case

All letters are uppercase, separated by underscores.

MAX_SIZE = 100
DATABASE_NAME = "StudentDB"

Commonly used for constants.

Leading Underscore

A single underscore at the beginning indicates that a name is intended for internal use.

_internal_value = 100

This is a convention, not strict access control.

10. What is PEP 8?

PEP stands for Python Enhancement Proposal.

PEP 8 is the Python style guide that provides recommendations for writing clean, readable, and consistent Python code.

Some important guidelines:

  1. Use four spaces for indentation.
  2. Use snake_case for variables and functions.
  3. Use PascalCase for class names.
  4. Use UPPER_SNAKE_CASE for constants.
  5. Use spaces around operators.
  6. Separate functions and classes using blank lines.
  7. Keep code lines within the recommended length.

Example

Without following PEP 8:

def calculateTotal(a,b):
    total=a+b
    print(total)

Following PEP 8:

def calculate_total(a, b):
    total = a + b
    print(total)

The second example is easier to read and follows common Python style recommendations.

Conclusion

Today, I explored several important Python concepts, including objects, functions, methods, variables, attributes, instances, and class attributes.

I also learned about function overloading, naming conventions, and PEP 8.

Understanding these fundamentals is helping me build a strong foundation in Python.

I'm continuing my learning journey step by step and sharing my progress with the developer community.
