title: An AI agent can reverse-engineer your entire repo & app in 10 minutes :) Thanks to REA, so I built the REAshield
description:
Right now, while you're reading this, your shipped app is defenseless.

Not "theoretically." Not "if someone really tried." Today, anyone can point an AI
agent at your bundle, walk away, and come back to a clean, plain-English teardown
of exactly how your licensing works, where your pricing logic lives, and how to
tear it out — with the code to do it.

No cracking. No debugger. No late nights in devtools. The agent reads your files,
rebuilds your entire app in its head, and hands the attacker the map.

This isn't a warning about the future. The tools are live. So I built the thing
that fights back, and it's open source. Here's how the attack works, why it's so
devastating, and the exact moves that make it fall apart.

The attacker: a reverse-engineering machine that works for free

REA hands a coding agent a full
reverse-engineering toolbox over MCP. Aim it at your shipped app.asar or bundle
and — without ever running your app — it statically reconstructs everything:
every module, import, route, IPC channel, and string. On a real ~14 MB Electron
app that's a graph of roughly ten thousand nodes. Then the agent reads a
summary of that graph and answers, in English: "here's how feature X works, and
here's the code."

Minutes. For free. At scale. On every app you've ever shipped.

And REA isn't alone

REA is the sharpest example, but it's a category, and the category is growing:

  • REA — an MCP server that gives a coding agent a full reverse-engineering toolbox. Statically reconstructs an app's whole module/IPC/route graph and lets the agent explain any feature from it.
  • humanify — uses LLMs to un-minify JavaScript, handing readable, meaningful names back to your mangled code. Your obfuscation's worst nightmare.
  • webcrack / wakaru — unpack and unminify webpack/bundled JS back toward the original, module-by-module source.

Wire any of these into an agent and the loop runs itself: unpack → rename →
map → explain → clone. The barrier to reverse-engineering your app just dropped
from "a skilled human with a weekend" to "a prompt."

What it eats

Starve the attacker — but first, know the diet. It feeds on:

  • Your module graph — the literal shape of every import and require.
  • Your names — every identifier you shipped is a signpost.
  • Your strings — routes, errors, keys, and IPC channel names.
  • Your source maps — ship these and you didn't get reverse-engineered. You published your source with a bow on it.

Its fatal weakness — and your entire opening

Here's what they don't tell you: this attacker is terrifying but narrow, and
it confesses its limits out loud.

  • It is 100% static. It never runs your app. Anything that only exists at runtime is invisible to it.
  • It will not guess. A name assembled at runtime? It writes "unresolved" and moves on. On a real test app, 14 of ~22 IPC operations with computed names were left blank. Holes in the map.
  • It buckles at scale, dropping relationships when the graph gets big.

So forget "make it unreadable." Obfuscation is a speed bump a machine rolls over.
The real play: starve the static graph, and bury your crown jewels in the exact
blind spots this attacker admits it cannot see.

Obfuscation is paint, not armor

Minify, mangle, encrypt your strings — sure. Just know it's the weakest,
first-to-fall layer in the stack. LLM-assisted deobfuscation improves every
month, and even with garbage names, your entire structure is still sitting there
for the graph builder to walk. Scrambling names doesn't hide the map.

Real armor, ranked by how long it survives contact:

  1. Don't ship the secret. Move it off the device, period.
  2. Get it off the JS graph. WebAssembly. Bytecode.
  3. Turn static into runtime. Computed imports, computed channels, dispatch tables — the blanks the agent can't fill.
  4. Make every build different. Version-diffing: dead on arrival.
  5. Then obfuscate and drown the rest in decoys.

The shield

REAShield is an open-source, drop-in npm
dev-dependency that turns every move above into one config and one command:

// shield.config.cjs
module.exports = {
  input: "src/index.js",
  output: "dist-shielded",
  preset: "balanced",
  protect: [
    { name: "licenseCheck", mode: "relocate" }, // rip the real body off-device
    { name: "sealedCalc",   mode: "seal" },      // ship it as ciphertext
    { name: "pricingLogic", mode: "wasm" },      // compile it to WebAssembly
    { name: "featureGate",  mode: "obfuscate" }, // harden it in place
  ],
};

npx reashield build     # hardened client + a server skeleton
npx reashield test      # measures what the attacker can STILL see

What each mode does to the agent:

  • Relocate — the function's real body is lifted out of your app and into a generated server handler. The client keeps one opaque remote-call stub. You cannot graph code that was never shipped. This move never stops working — it's the oldest rule in security, enforced automatically.
  • Seal — the module ships as ciphertext, decrypted at runtime with a server-fetched key. Static analysis gets a wall of bytes.
  • WASM — numeric hot-paths compile to a real WebAssembly module (binary, synchronous, behavior untouched). Erased from the JS graph entirely.
  • Starvation (always on) — one flat module, no source maps, encrypted strings, and literal IPC/route names rewritten into runtime-computed ones: the exact names the agent surrenders on.
  • Polymorphism + decoys — every build is restructured and renamed so releases can't be diffed, and the graph is flooded with inert fake "feature" clusters so the agent's summary trips over false leads first.

Don't trust it — prove it

This is the part I refuse to hand-wave. REAShield runs the actual attacker
(REA) against your own before/after build and shows you what changed.

On the bundled example — a small library with a license check, pricing logic, and
a sealed scoring function:

  • Secret strings and protected identifiers left in the shipped client: 6 → 0. The real algorithm and its constants now live only on the server.
  • String literals surviving verbatim into the output: 100% → 0%.
  • The import graph: collapsed to a single module.

Run npx reashield test --rea against your own app for REA's own "modules
resolved / relationships resolved" counts, before vs after — and on a real
multi-thousand-node app, that drop is brutal.

Because REA ships constantly, the harness doubles as a CI gate pinned across
REA versions: a new REA that recovers more than your committed baseline fails
the build. Protection stops being a hope and becomes a test.

The honest part — the line that makes the rest credible

I'll say the thing straight, because overclaiming is how security tools die:

Nothing that runs on someone else's machine is truly unreversible. REAShield
doesn't claim to be — and neither should you.

What it actually delivers: it turns a 10-minute automated agent job into
days of specialist human grind, and kills most automated attacks at the
door. A determined human with time still gets through. Relocation and sealing need
a backend you secure, and the request/response boundary stays observable. It's
behavior-preserving, transparent (no phone-home), and strictly defensive — it
protects code you own and ship. Never a weapon against anyone else's.

One line to walk away with: the strongest defense isn't a tool, it's a
decision. Whatever must truly stay secret belongs on your server — where no
bundle, and no agent, can ever reach it.

Repo + docs: https://github.com/HMAKT99/reashield — npm i -D reashield

Do reverse engineering? Come break the relocation and decoy seams and tell me
where they're weakest. I want the teardown.

title: Anatomy of 32 Days
description:
Every number here was cheap to collect and late to arrive. That gap is the whole story.

👋 Hi, I'm Anton - a software engineer working mostly in PHP/Symfony and Go, currently carving a live PHP monolith into Go services. The seven parts before this one each took one angle on a single write path that left the monolith. This one is the ledger: the same 32 days read as one timeline, with every figure in one place and a link to the part that unpacks it. Running notes live on my GitHub: github.com/brilliant-almazov.

This is how I do it right now, with the price attached - maybe you already do it better, maybe you'd do it another way.

The path in one paragraph

A user saves a set of matching rules; every domain under that account gets marked by them. Four participants: the Go API gateway as the only door from outside, the rule-set-markup service which takes the write and folds the cascade, the domain-rule-map service which owns rule-set identity and recalculates the map, and PostgreSQL behind them - the monolith's database for the rule data, the identity service's own for identity.

One user action, four processes, two databases. Accepting that as working took 32 days, and this is what was inside them.

What "32 days" actually contains

The headline number is the least useful one in the set, so it is worth breaking before anything is built on it.

  DAYS   32 ┤████████████████████████████████  the acceptance timeline
            │        ▼ −21  automated verdicts only: pass/fail per case, no numbers, no traces
         11 ┤███████████
            │        ▼ −2   two days with no verdict at all — the wrong thing was under test
          9 ┤█████████
            │        ▼ −2   days inside the detailed window with no runs
          7 ┤███████  ◄ days with detailed, traced runs
  ──────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  MINUTES inside those 7 days — 985 total = 16 h 25 min
    day 1 ██████████████████ 178      day 5 ██████████████████ 179
    day 2 ███████████████    150      day 6 ███████            77
    day 3 ██████████         102      day 7 ████████           89
    day 4 █████████████████████ 210   ◄ one run alone = 120

34 runs across the period, 28 of them numbered. Duration was recorded for 29 of the 34: mean 34 minutes, longest 2 hours, shortest 2 minutes. So the honest version of the headline is not "32 days of testing" - it is 16 hours 25 minutes of measured work, spread over 7 days, inside a 32-day window.

I am starting here because every ratio later in this article has one of these denominators in it, and the wrong denominator turns a modest finding into a dramatic one for free.

Three windows, three instruments

The 32 days are not one measurement. They are three, taken with different instruments, and no line crosses between them honestly.

  window 1   before day 0        no acceptance artefacts exist at all
                                 behaviour reconstructed from migrations, commits, docs
  window 2   day 0 … day 21      automated verdicts per case, per deploy tag
                                 pass / fail, and nothing else — no timings, no traces
  window 3   day 21 … day 32     traced runs: timings, state dumps, statement text
                                 the numbered defect registry starts on day 25

Which produces the reading rule I put on every chart in this material:

Comparing across those windows compares methods of observation, not states of the system.

Two more caveats travel with it, and they are in every part of this series for the same reason: round-trip time to the environment sits at a steady 220-260 ms regardless of endpoint, so it is never part of anyone's work; and a share is never published without its absolute value - 440.0 ms · 61 %, never 61 % on its own.

Day one of the detailed window: three objects, everything passes

For the first weeks the checks ran against a playground of three objects. The runs were honest - real requests, real assertions, real data written and read back - and everything passed.

Then a run went across everything the environment held:

  playground              3 objects        everything passes
  full sweep            276 objects        the active-set registry is EMPTY for 210 of them
  later sweeps          392 objects        392 of 392 covered; 129 map rows of 2 329
                                           carry neither rule set nor priority (5.5 %)

Nothing was fixed between the first two lines. The system was in the same state; what changed is that it could be asked - the services had grown read endpoints that describe state: the input snapshot, the rule set in effect, the pointer to the active set, the stored map page by page.

That is Part 2 - A Service That Cannot Explain Itself Can Only Be Guessed At. It is the earliest thing in this timeline in the causal sense: nothing else here was findable before those four reads existed.

The argument about who was slow

The next thing the traced window settled was an argument that had been running on opinions. A single write, end to end: 121 spans, four services, 1 256.9 ms on the client's stopwatch. The blame sat on the write service, because that is the address on the envelope.

Read as nesting rather than as a sum:

  client wait                                       1 256.9 ms   100 %
  ├── transport, client ↔ environment                  244.9      19.5 %   not ours
  └── four services at work                          1 012.0      80.5 %
      └── the suspected service, own zone                87.4       7.0 %
          ├── own work                                    1.4
          └── waiting on PostgreSQL                      86.0      98.4 % of its zone

87.4 ms of 1 256.9 - 7.0 %, and 98.4 % of that is waiting on the database. The code itself accounts for 1.4 ms.

The cheapest confirmation in the whole set came from a request that was rejected as invalid: server work 6.6 ms, database 0.0 ms, client stopwatch 231.8 ms. Nothing computed, nothing stored, and 97.2 % of the call still happened outside our code.

And when the shape of one read was fixed, the same three-build comparison showed why the unit matters: database round trips went 92 to 7, database time 440.0 to 31.8 ms - a factor of 14 - while the network never moved. By share alone the network went from a third of the call to 88 % of it and reads as a catastrophe. In milliseconds, everything we own fell and the rest stood still.

Full breakdown, including the zone we still cannot measure: Part 1 - Most of Your Latency Is Not Your Code.

The account that did not fit

The same instrument answered a question nobody had asked before shipping: how much work is one caller allowed to order?

One object addressed directly is 121 spans and 53 database round trips, 11 of them repeats. One account addressed at the top, with 366 children below it, is 10 822 spans - roughly 30 spans per child, derived by dividing one measured total by one measured count.

The deadline on that call is a constant 20 seconds. The work behind it is a line. On one observed run the caller was cut off at 20.26 s and the work carried on for another 8.7 s, committing successfully at 28.96 s:

  0 s                                  20.26 s               28.96 s
  ├───────────────────────────────────────┤───────────────────┤
  │  work in progress                     │  8.7 s more work  │
                                          │
                          caller is told: the call failed
                                                              │
                                          database holds: the write landed

Around 253 children is where the endpoint stops fitting, and how many accounts sit above that line is a product fact nobody had written down. In aggregate it showed up as deadline failures on 13 of 76 objects, then 27 of 76 after a change meant to help. The whole slope, and why optimisation moves the crossing point rather than removing it, is Part 5 - The Client Decides How Much Work You Do.

The value nobody owned

The longest-lived defect of the period had no code to blame. A rule is saved, the response is 200, the read shows the new set - and the engine keeps marking by the old one. Eight rounds thirty seconds apart, four minutes of the two answers disagreeing, no error anywhere.

Six iterations, the record of the whole timeline. The analysis that explained it took an afternoon:

  • the value lives in four carriers across two databases, and there is no foreign key between them - there cannot be, they belong to different services;
  • the right to write it had moved seven times in 48 days;
  • in one of those states, two days long, it belonged to nobody;
  • and the state was produced by two commits, same day, two repositories, each correct on its own, which together formed a circle: a freshly written set has no map rows, so it can never become active.

No review inside either repository could have caught it: each diff was right, and the contradiction lived on the seam. Part 3 - Nobody Owned the Value is that afternoon written out, including the detector that catches the class forever: two reads and an equality check, run on all 392 objects.

The contract that could not say zero

While that ran, a second class was producing numbers of its own. A priority that was stored, correct and impossible to present, because the strongest priority in this system is written as 0 and on the wire 0 looks exactly like a field nobody set. Both sides were locally correct: the producer omits zero values by the rules of the format, the consumer treats an absent field as unset.

Eight of the 26 numbered defects were defects of contract shape - the largest single class in the registry, and not one of them was a computation error. The same field's own history: removed from the contract, put back about 45 days later, and pinned down with an explicit meaning for zero on day 91.

What made it observable was not an assertion on a response - every response was correct throughout - but a count over stored state: map rows carrying no priority at all, 27 to 41 to 0.

And its quieter twin: when two rules tie, which wins? Nobody had ever decided. The behaviour was deterministic - first match in array order - and it had held as a norm for 17 months as a property of how a loop was written. Part 6 - Zero Is Not Absent, and Nobody Wrote the Order Down.

The baseline that moved

The method for accepting the new write path was parity: run both implementations on the same input, compare field by field. That is a sound method exactly once - when the reference stands still.

On one day the same input went through nine iterations, and the size of the cascade the two sides produced went 2, then 258, then 2, then 8 rows. The reference was changing its own definition mid-day, and it was internally inconsistent too: one identifier came back as a number in one field and as a string in another. Three times out of nine the new implementation turned out to be the correct one.

Underneath sat the same failure in three different disguises:

  • a 502 returned after the row was committed;
  • a 200 completed on a row that had been silently deleted;
  • a 504 at 20.26 s on a write that went through.

None of them is a lie by the transport. With two storages and no shared transaction, a response code reports that the call arrived and its own transaction closed - and nothing about what is in the database. Then the parity work was erased in one line by a correct decision: the old write endpoint would be removed entirely. Part 4 - Parity Against a Moving Baseline has the full accounting, including the one thing that was missing - the date the comparison would expire.

The ledger

Everything above, as counts.

  26 numbered defects
     16   closed as real defects            (by subtraction from the four rows below)
      5   declared normal behaviour
      3   still open at the end of the period
      2   withdrawn as false

  39 defect-iterations between those 26 numbers      longest single defect: 6 iterations
   8 false alarms in total, of which one is a false PASS - a check that ran zero comparisons

Two rows are worth more than the rest.

Three still open at the end of the period, and their wording is the giveaway: rule order is not provable; cursor paging says "more" and returns no token; an asynchronous rebuild lands in tens of seconds - or does not. None of them is "the code is wrong". All three are "the system cannot demonstrate the property being asked about".

One false PASS. A probe sent a single value to an endpoint that requires a list, got a 422, took the empty decision list as agreement and printed PASS 24, FAIL 3. Two builds were accepted on a line that had performed zero comparisons. A false FAIL creates work. A false PASS removes the check and leaves the report looking identical.

What a document would have caught

This is the number I keep from the whole period, and the one I am least comfortable with.

   26 numbered defects
   ████████████████████████████████████████████  26
             │
             ▼  step 1 — the specification names WHO WRITES this value
   ██████████████████████████████                18  left
             │
             ▼  step 0 — endpoint and fields taken from the contract, not from memory
   ████████████████                              13  left
             │
             ▼  steps 2/3/4/6 — actual measurement against a live system
   ██                                             2  ◄ one conditional, one unobservable

24 of 26 - 92 % - would have been removed by acceptance written before the code, and 21 of 39 defect-iterations die on one question: who is allowed to write this value? That question is answered by reading a document. It is an estimate over the registry rather than an experiment, and I publish it as one - but even halved it says the same thing.

What it cost, and the number I never took

The bill is not "we wrote buggy code". It is the cost of finding out what was wanted:

  requirements with two defensible readings            23
  reversals of decisions already implemented            7      in 5 of 6, the code matched
                                                               the specification of its day
  iterations spent finding out rather than fixing   ~13 of 27  (estimated over intervals)
  iterations of briefs written and discarded            15     within a day
  brief files accumulated in the repository            289     137 of them in 33 numbered sets
  write-ups of my own acceptance mistakes               28     5 of them repeated, 1–6 days apart
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  days with a measurement of money or tokens             0

The last row is the one I would fix first if I were starting again. Every duration in this article was recorded; not one day carries a figure for what the automated work cost in tokens or money. That means everything here is a claim about what the arrangement found, and nothing here is a claim about whether it was worth it. Those are different claims and I can only make the first.

The row above it is the second-cheapest lesson: 5 of 28 mistakes repeated within one to six days, every one of them already written up in prose. A rule that lives only in a postmortem is re-derived by whoever reads it next, which is to say never - and an automated executor never reads it at all. What stopped the repeats was moving each rule into the two places that are read on every run: the brief, as a numbered constraint, and the check, as an assertion that fails.

The arrangement that produced most of the numbers above - one automated pass pointed at the output of another, told to instrument the zone with no spans and report back - is Part 7 - One Executor Checking Another Executor's Work.

Seven readings, one per part

If the timeline collapses to seven sentences, these are the seven:

  1. A service is judged by its own span, not by the client's stopwatch. 87.4 ms of 1 256.9 - and 97.2 % of a rejected call is not our code. -> Part 1
  2. A service that cannot state what its answer should be can only be guessed at. Three objects passed; 276 objects had 210 empty registries, and nothing had changed in between. -> Part 2
  3. A value with no named owner does not have a bug - it has an unfinished analysis. Four carriers, two databases, seven moves of the write right in 48 days, two of those days belonging to nobody. -> Part 3
  4. A comparison is a test only while the reference stands still. Nine parity runs in one day, a cascade of 2, 258, 2 and 8 rows for the same input, and a comparison with no expiry date. -> Part 4
  5. A synchronous answer over work the caller sizes is a promise the caller gets to break for you. A constant 20-second deadline against a cost that is linear in 366 children. -> Part 5
  6. A field that cannot separate "absent" from "zero" is two facts sharing a slot. Eight of 26 defects were contract shape; a tie-break rule held as a norm for 17 months because it lived in a loop. -> Part 6
  7. A second automated pass earns its cost only if it can add a measurement the first one never had. 92 database round trips on a call that needs 7, reported as 200 OK in every column. -> Part 7

And the one that only appears when they are read together: the split did not create these defects, it made them expressible. A single process can hold an unstated ownership rule, an unstated tie-break and an unstated capacity limit indefinitely, because there is no boundary at which the omission has to be declared. Two services cannot.

What none of this proves

Being explicit, because a ledger invites conclusions it cannot support.

It does not say microservices are worse than a monolith, or better. It does not say anything got faster after the split - the instruments changed inside the window, and the earlier stretch has no numbers to compare against. It does not price anything: no money, no person-hours, no token counts. It does not say anything about the reliability of anyone's production system; every figure here comes from a test environment.

What it does support is narrower: on this path, in this period, 24 of 26 defects were answerable before anything ran, and the four questions that would have answered them fit on one page.

The multiplier line

Nine parity runs in a day, a sweep of 392 objects per build, a trace folded into a table and diffed against yesterday's - all of that was cheap because it was automated, and none of it would have been affordable by hand. What automation never supplied was a single one of the sentences that were missing: who may write this value, what absent means for this field, how large a caller is allowed to be, which side of a comparison is entitled to be right. Fast iteration multiplies the definitions that exist in writing. Where a definition is missing, it multiplies the circling instead - and produces, very precisely and very confidently, 39 iterations of a description where four written sentences would have done.

Anatomy of a service split - Part 8. That closes this set. The obvious hole in it is the last row of the bill: 985 minutes of recorded duration and not one day with a cost figure attached. The next thing I measured was exactly that - what the automated work itself bills, per session, in tokens and in money, before any of it produces a line of output.

If you do this better, tell me which of your defects you can honestly say a document would have caught. If you have been through this, what did your own ledger look like when you counted the iterations rather than the tickets? If you see it differently, say where writing the requirement down first costs more than it returns. How is it solved on your side, and what broke there?

title: DEAD AIR: I Built a 3D Mystery Experience Powered by Local Gemma 4 AI 👻📻
description:
DEAD AIR: I Built a 3D Mystery Experience Powered by Local Gemma 4 AI 👻📻

What if you discovered a radio transmission that nobody should be able to hear?

What if the only way to understand it was to enter an abandoned observatory, discover its secrets and communicate with the mysterious signal itself?

For Hacktoberfest Week 4, I built DEAD AIR — The Last Frequency, a first-person 3D mystery experience powered by Gemma 4 running locally in the browser.

This is my interpretation of the theme Ghost in the Machine.

1. What I Built

DEAD AIR takes place inside an abandoned radio observatory.

At 03:17 AM, an impossible transmission begins broadcasting.

The player must explore the observatory, investigate an incident log, discover hidden signal fragments, tune a radio transmitter and reconstruct the final transmission.

But there is something unusual about this experience.

The mysterious entity communicating through the radio is powered by a real open-weight language model running locally in the browser.

No backend. No API key. No remote inference service.

Key Features

  • First-person 3D exploration with WASD and mouse controls.
  • Procedurally generated observatory environment.
  • Interactive incident log, signal monitor and radio transmitter.
  • Frequency-tuning puzzle with dynamic audio and visual feedback.
  • Evidence collection and a six-step investigation progression.
  • Local Gemma 4 AI assistant called THE SIGNAL.
  • Evidence-grounded AI responses with citations.
  • Deterministic mystery reconstruction and validation.
  • Scripted preview when WebGPU or model loading is unavailable.

2. Demo

The project has been built and tested locally.

A video walkthrough and hosted browser demo are not included in this initial submission. The repository includes screenshots, including evidence of the successful real Gemma inference run, and instructions for running the experience locally.

Real Gemma 4 inference:

More screenshots and setup instructions are available in the repository.

3. Code

GitHub Repository:

https://github.com/TechGenDM/Hacktoberfest-Week-4-2026

Branch: main

Commit: 19aa676

4. How I Built It

The application uses:

Technology Purpose
Vite 8 Development and production builds
TypeScript 7 Application logic
Three.js 0.187 3D environment
Transformers.js 4.3.2 Browser-based model inference
Gemma 4 E2B Local language model
WebGPU Hardware-accelerated inference
Web Workers Background model processing
Web Audio API Procedural ambient audio

The environment is constructed using procedural geometry and textures rather than relying on downloaded 3D assets.

The interesting engineering decision

I deliberately separated the mystery-solving system from the language model.

The game itself controls the evidence, puzzle progression and final answer.

Gemma does not decide what happened. It investigates the evidence available to the player and helps interpret it.

Every response passes through a deterministic validation layer.

The validator checks:

  • Whether sentences include evidence citations.
  • Whether the cited evidence has actually been discovered.
  • Whether numerical claims appear in their cited evidence.
  • Whether named entities appear in the discovered evidence.

Responses receive one of four verdicts:

VERIFIED · PARTIAL · REJECTED · NO SIGNAL

Unsupported sentences can be struck out with an explanation.

This is not a guarantee of semantic correctness, but it provides a deterministic first layer of protection against unsupported AI responses.

Real Gemma 4 inference results

I tested actual inference in headless Chrome on macOS using WebGPU and the q4f16 model path.

Measurement Result
Initial load, including download and shader warm-up 279 seconds
Model download Approximately 3.38 GB
Generation speed 28–33 tokens/second
Response time 1–2.5 seconds

I tested several questions.

Question: Where is the carrier coming from?

Result: Three evidence-cited sentences. All were marked VERIFIED.

Question: Who sent the signal from Mars?

Result: NO SIGNAL ON THAT BAND.

Question: What frequency should I tune TX-2 to?

Result: The response repeated a cited sentence. It was accurate but not sufficiently helpful. This is a known limitation.

Testing

The following checks passed:

  • TypeScript compilation.
  • Production build.
  • Complete automated game playthrough.
  • All eight evidence items discovered.
  • Incorrect reconstruction order rejected.
  • Correct reconstruction accepted.
  • Ending sequence completed.
  • Scripted fallback verified.
  • No runtime errors during the automated playthrough.

Browser compatibility beyond Chrome on macOS and low-memory GPU configurations remains untested.

5. Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

I wanted to explore what happens when an AI-powered interactive experience does not depend on a centralized AI service.

DEAD AIR uses an open-weight Gemma model with browser-based inference.

The model runs on the user's hardware rather than sending every conversation to a remote inference API.

This offers several advantages:

  • Conversations can remain on the user's device.
  • No application backend or AI API key is required.
  • The model can be downloaded and used locally.
  • The system does not depend on a proprietary inference endpoint.
  • The application combines an open-weight model with transparent, application-level validation.

One important distinction: the initial model download requires an internet connection. After the weights are cached, inference can run locally without a remote AI service.

For me, open innovation is not just about accessing a model. It is about having the freedom to run, inspect, adapt and build around the technology.

6. What I Learned

The most interesting part of this project was not getting a model to generate dialogue.

It was learning how to build an experience where the model has boundaries.

A language model can produce convincing answers even when it does not have enough information. In a mystery game, that can completely destroy the experience.

Separating deterministic game logic from AI interpretation made the system more predictable.

I also learned how important browser GPU support, model quantization, Web Workers and initial model-loading performance are when building local AI applications.

7. Prize Categories

Gemma — Best Use of Gemma

The project uses Gemma 4 E2B as its central conversational AI model, running locally through Transformers.js and WebGPU.

Final Thoughts

DEAD AIR started as an idea: what if we could build an entire interactive mystery world where the intelligence behind the experience lives inside the browser?

It became an experiment in combining 3D environments, open-weight AI, local inference and deterministic engineering.

There is still plenty to improve. This is an initial prototype, not a finished commercial game.

But it works, the real Gemma inference has been verified, and the mystery can be completed.

Sometimes the most interesting thing is not the signal itself.

It's what happens when somebody finally answers it.

Built for the Hacktoberfest 2026 DEV Challenge — Week 4: Ghost in the Machine.

title: Reliable Logistics Receipts with Node.js Email Event Polling: Retries and Recovery
description:
TL;DR: This step-by-step design shows how to integrate email event notification APIs with a small polling worker, durable cursor, bounded retries, and a local record of every order receipt state. For a logistics system, the invoice is not the interesting part of the email API call. The operational cost is the repeated work around it: calls made to discover state, records retained so a late event can be reconciled, and the engineering time spent deciding whether a timeout means “send again” or “look again.”

The practical sequence is: settle payment, enqueue a receipt job, send the receipt through your chosen mail provider, and poll the provider's event API to reconcile delivery. Do not treat a missing event as a failed delivery until the polling window and your provider's documented event retention rules have elapsed.

Infrai is a reasonable fit for the pull step when the worker should make a plain REST call rather than install and maintain another client library. Its discovery surface lists 295 capabilities across 20 modules, while the relevant comm-email-sms group has 41 routes; that breadth is useful only if your team accepts polling as an operational responsibility.

What is the bill really buying?

For this workflow, the dominant term is event-state work, not the one-time receipt request. Every polling cycle creates another API call, and every retained event cursor or order-state row creates storage and recovery obligations. A five-minute poll across 10,000 orders is 2,880,000 checks per day if each order is queried separately. That arithmetic is the design warning: batch or cursor where the provider supports it, and make the polling interval depend on the order's state.

An order awaiting its first delivery event deserves more attention than an order that has already reached a terminal state. I would keep a compact local record containing the order ID, provider message ID, last observed event identity, next poll time, and reconciliation status. I would not retain the full provider response forever. That is the deliberate retention trade-off: less durable detail to search during a dispute, in exchange for a bounded database and a clear rule to archive the raw event only when compliance or support requires it.

This is also where delivery reliability beats a superficially attractive integration. A retry that creates a second receipt is worse than a delayed status update. The receipt-send operation needs a business idempotency decision in the application, while an event-list GET should be safe to repeat. Keep those two concerns separate.

How do I integrate email event notification APIs step by step?

A timeout has three possible meanings: the request never reached the provider, the provider processed it but the response was lost, or the provider is rate-limiting the caller. A useful worker does not guess. It records the attempt, honors Retry-After on HTTP 429, uses exponential backoff for transient failures, and lets the next poll reconcile the provider's state.

The route below is a pull API, so there is no webhook delivery to wait for. The example uses Python because the code convention for this article keeps executable samples in Python; the same HTTP contract can be called from a Node.js worker with fetch or Axios. It deliberately does not invent query fields or assume a response schema that is not documented here.

import os
import random
import time

import requests


BASE_URL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"


def get_email_events(max_attempts=5):
    api_key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
    headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}"}

    for attempt in range(max_attempts):
        try:
            response = requests.get(
                f"{BASE_URL}/email/event/list",
                headers=headers,
                timeout=10,
            )
        except requests.RequestException:
            if attempt == max_attempts - 1:
                raise
            time.sleep(min(60, 2**attempt + random.random()))
            continue

        if response.status_code == 429:
            retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
            try:
                delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2**attempt
            except ValueError:
                delay = 2**attempt
            if attempt == max_attempts - 1:
                response.raise_for_status()
            time.sleep(min(300, delay))
            continue

        if 500 <= response.status_code < 600:
            if attempt == max_attempts - 1:
                response.raise_for_status()
            time.sleep(min(60, 2**attempt + random.random()))
            continue

        response.raise_for_status()
        return response.json()

    raise RuntimeError("event polling exhausted its retry budget")

The worker should write the fetched result to a staging table before applying order transitions. Persist first. Apply each event once according to a locally enforced event identity or cursor, and acknowledge the job only after that transaction commits. If the process dies between the provider request and the database commit, the next run repeats the GET and the local deduplication decides what changes. This extra write is easy to resent as unnecessary overhead when the happy path is working, but it is the record that lets support distinguish a provider delay from a worker crash, and it gives an operator something concrete to inspect before manually re-queuing a receipt.

Do not use a tight loop. A scheduler can poll new or recently changed orders more frequently, then back off as they approach a terminal state. Keep the retry budget finite and send exhausted jobs to an operator-visible queue. “Eventually” is not an alert policy.

Which email event API fits this recovery model?

The choice depends on where you want delivery state to live.

Option Useful strength Boundary for this workflow
Amazon SES Fits teams already operating on AWS and comfortable assembling their own notification and storage path. The application still owns reconciliation, event retention, and operational policy; it is not a complete receipt workflow by itself.
SendGrid Provides a mature email platform and event-oriented tooling for teams that prefer provider-managed email operations. Its broader platform surface can be more than a narrow pull-based reconciliation worker needs, and provider-specific integration still has to be monitored.
Mailgun Strong fit for teams that want email APIs and delivery-oriented event data from a specialist provider. You remain coupled to its event model and must decide how to translate provider states into logistics order states.
Infrai A plain REST API with one key and no SDK installation; /v1/email/event/list gives the application a programmatic pull point. The email namespace has no webhook event push, so real-time orchestration is limited by your polling schedule.

I would choose a specialist such as SendGrid, Mailgun, or SES when webhook-driven delivery, deep email operations, or an existing provider-specific integration is a hard requirement. I would choose Infrai for the event-reconciliation part when a language-neutral REST call is more valuable than adding and versioning another SDK, and when the team is prepared to run polling as a real worker. Its public discovery surface and runnable examples across 10 languages also reduce integration glue, but they do not remove the need for a durable cursor or an alert policy.

That is the important limitation. A plain API is easy to call; reliable recovery is still an application responsibility.

What should be retained after a receipt is delivered?

Keep the order-level outcome, provider message reference, timestamps, the last event identity or cursor, and the reason for any terminal failure. Retain enough evidence to answer a support question such as “was this receipt accepted and later rejected?” without making every historical provider payload part of the hot path.

For sender reputation, delivery is also a configuration problem. SPF is described in RFC 7208; authentication and suppression policy should be treated as prerequisites, not recovery features. A retry cannot repair a domain that is failing authentication or a recipient who has opted out.

The logistics rule is simple: payment settlement may trigger a receipt attempt, but only reconciled provider events should change the operational delivery state. A delayed receipt status is visible and repairable. A duplicated receipt is a customer-facing incident.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and verify the current event response contract before choosing your cursor and retention fields.

Further reading

  • Infrai official documentation
  • RFC 7208: Sender Policy Framework (SPF)
  • Amazon Simple Email Service
  • SendGrid Event Webhook documentation
  • Mailgun Events documentation

title: Unifying Edge AI: How Coral NPU’s open standard brings portable, energy-viable intelligence from model to silicon
description: Google Research has completed the 32-bit open-source Coral NPU RISC-V architecture with the introduction of its Matrix Execution Unit, which delivers up to 1 TOPS while targeting 10 mW average power for edge inference. Alongside this architecture, the release of the v1.0 open-source IREE/MLIR compiler allows developers to take models from JAX, PyTorch, and TensorFlow straight to Coral NPU hardware without writing custom assembly. Developers can now prototype and deploy these multimodal edge applications using new hardware options like the Synaptics Astra SR200 MCU series and globally available Coralboard devkits.12

title: USA SMS API Services for Gaming Alerts in 2026 (with Compliance Evidence)
description:
Short answer: For USA SMS API services delivering gaming alert notifications, start with Twilio for flexible APIs, compare Bandwidth for domestic coverage, and compare Vonage for bulk terms; evaluate pricing and features only after compliance evidence and retry ownership are clear.

Twilio is the default starting point for a US gaming signup verification link; Bandwidth is a strong domestic-SMS alternative, and Vonage deserves a look when bulk terms and promotions affect the workload. The deciding constraint is not the advertised per-message number. It is whether the provider can leave you with defensible A2P registration evidence, a retry-safe delivery path, and an operating bill you can actually explain.

A verification link is a small message with a large blast radius. A duplicate can confuse a new player, a delayed message can turn into an abandoned signup, and a retry after a timeout can create two valid-looking records unless the application owns idempotency. My runbook starts there.

That is the control point.

For teams already carrying several backend integrations, Infrai belongs in this early comparison as a consolidation option: one REST API, one key, and one bill can remove credential and invoice reconciliation from the signup service's neighboring work. It does not decide A2P registration, and it does not turn a polling workflow into a webhook workflow. Those boundaries are part of the fit, not footnotes.

What evidence must the signup path preserve?

For a US gaming service, compliance evidence should be an input to the design, not a document gathered after launch. Keep the campaign purpose, consent text, opt-out handling, sender identity, destination, and delivery status tied to the signup attempt. Twilio's US A2P 10DLC documentation is a useful reference for the registration and messaging obligations; the provider choice does not remove the application's responsibility to retain that trail.

The message should contain a short-lived, single-use verification URL. Store a hash of the token, its expiry, the signup identifier, and the consent record. Do not put an email address or internal account identifier in the URL merely because it is convenient. The SMS provider can deliver the link; it should not become the system of record for account eligibility. When a carrier rejects a registration or a player taps an expired link, the local record should still explain what consent was collected, which template was selected, and which retry policy ran. That is the evidence an on-call engineer can use without reconstructing the event from three vendor consoles.

This is also where the options separate. Twilio is highly popular in the US, has flexible APIs, and has a strong operational reputation. Bandwidth is attractive when domestic US SMS rates and carrier-level control matter. Vonage is worth comparing for bulk discounts and promotions, while some US-specific carriers can fit a regional deployment better than a global abstraction. Those are useful differences, but none substitutes for a reviewable consent and message audit.

Which USA SMS API services fit gaming alert notifications?

I model four costs: message delivery, registration and compliance work, integration maintenance, and the cost of an incident. The last two are easy to omit because they do not appear beside an SMS unit price. A cheaper route that requires a second dashboard, a second key, and a separate status consumer can be more expensive for a small SRE team than a slightly less aggressive carrier quote.

Option Strong fit Trade-off to validate
Twilio Flexible US APIs and a familiar operational path More platform surface means more configuration and compliance state to govern
Bandwidth Domestic US SMS and teams that value carrier proximity Check regional coverage, tooling, and the evidence your team needs to retain
Vonage Bulk workloads where promotions and commercial terms matter Validate the exact US registration and delivery workflow before standardizing
Infrai A backend team that wants one REST key and bill across services while keeping SMS orchestration in its own system It is not a replacement for carrier-specific compliance judgment or a full webhook event stream

Infrai is a reasonable option for the integration boundary when one REST API, one key, and one bill remove real backend administration across the signup service and its neighboring services. Its public discovery surface exposes request and response schemas and runnable examples, and the broader surface spans 295 routes across 20 modules. That matters when the team is already operating email, storage, scheduling, or AI beside SMS and wants one consistent access pattern rather than a dozen credential dashboards.

The supporting benefit is operational accounting: the native response metadata specifies cost, latency, vendor, cache status, and request ID per call. That gives an SRE team a useful reconciliation handle without turning the article into a price leaderboard. It does not prove delivery, compliance, or uptime. Those still belong in the application and provider records.

My explicit recommendation is: try Infrai for a gaming signup service that values one backend credential and a unified REST integration across adjacent services, provided the service owns consent evidence, polling, and carrier-specific controls. Choose Twilio when broad US integration flexibility and established operational familiarity outweigh consolidation. Choose Bandwidth when domestic US SMS is the central workload and its carrier fit checks out. Choose Vonage when the bulk operating model is the material factor. For an email fallback, SendGrid and Amazon SES are real alternatives, but neither should be mistaken for a US SMS carrier decision: SendGrid fits email delivery workflows, while Amazon SES fits teams already operating their email stack on AWS.

How do I make a verification retry safe?

The provider call belongs behind an application record with a stable attempt ID. The record is created before sending, and the token is generated once. A worker may retry a timeout, but it must reuse the same idempotency key and message intent. Standard queue semantics should be treated as at-least-once, so the worker also checks the local state before sending.

A minimal Go client can show the shape without pretending that a provider response is proof of handset delivery. The example uses a documented discovery route to show the authentication and error-handling shape; the SMS send and status operations should be implemented against the selected provider's documented request schema and kept behind the same application interface.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "time"
)

func smsStatus(ctx context.Context, id string) error {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }

    url := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/email/list"
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, url, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            if attempt == 3 {
                return err
            }
            time.Sleep(time.Duration(1<<attempt) * 250 * time.Millisecond)
            continue
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            time.Sleep(time.Duration(1<<attempt) * 500 * time.Millisecond)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("service request failed: %s: %s", resp.Status, body)
        }
        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("sms status retries exhausted")
}

The sample deliberately reads the key from the environment, sets an explicit method, checks non-2xx responses, and backs off on rate limiting. For a write, add a client-generated idempotency key and persist it with the signup attempt. Honor a provider's Retry-After value when present; the fixed backoff above keeps the request example short, but production code should parse that header before falling back to exponential delay.

What do verification and rollback look like?

Verification is a sequence, not a green API response. First confirm that the local attempt has one token hash and one consent record. Then confirm the provider accepted one message intent, poll status through the documented status path, and reconcile the provider request ID with the local attempt. Finally, exercise expiry and opt-out behavior in a test environment. A delivered message is not the same as a verified account.

Watch for duplicate attempt IDs, retry counts, status age, rejected messages, opt-out additions, and the ratio of accepted messages that reach a terminal status. Alert on a growing pending set, but avoid treating a single carrier delay as an outage without checking the provider status and your own queue age.

Rollback should stop new sends, preserve the evidence already collected, and leave existing tokens to expire. Do not delete the audit trail to make a dashboard look clean. If a template or campaign registration is wrong, disable that path and route new signups to a reviewed alternative; the provider-specific rollback procedure belongs in the runbook for Twilio, Bandwidth, Vonage, or the selected regional carrier.

There are boundaries worth stating plainly. The unified path has no webhook event push, so real-time multi-channel orchestration requires polling. SMS anti-abuse controls such as geographic fencing and country-price circuit breakers remain application work. Infrai also does not provide voice, WhatsApp, or RCS, and an email fallback still requires a self-built email OTP path. For a gaming service that needs carrier-native event streaming or a specialized regional control plane, a direct provider is the better choice.

The effective cost is the total runbook, not the number printed in a vendor table. Pick the provider whose compliance evidence, retry behavior, and ownership boundaries your team can operate at 03:00.

No shortcuts.

If the one-key REST boundary fits the system, start with the SMS alerts guide, then verify every route and policy against the current discovery surface before production use.

References

  • Twilio US A2P 10DLC compliance documentation
  • Twilio Messaging API documentation
  • Bandwidth Messaging API documentation
  • Vonage SMS API documentation
  • Infrai SMS alerts guide

title: Azure Blob Storage, Google Cloud Storage, or Amazon S3: 4 Rules for User Uploads
description:
Start with private, direct-to-object uploads, then make the export worker the only component that reads a tenant's prefix. For a gaming platform handling large product images, I would choose Amazon S3 when cross-region API maturity and durability dominate, Azure Blob Storage for a Microsoft-centered estate, and Google Cloud Storage when its regional and pay-per-use model fits the dataset. A unified REST layer such as Infrai is worth testing for the integration boundary when the main constraint is getting a private upload working without another SDK and credential surface.

The deciding number is not request count. It is bytes per upload window, bytes per export window, and the fraction of those bytes that leave the region. Treat those as capacity inputs before comparing storage tiers. A 15-minute export SLO is a planning input, not a benchmark.

The byte rate is the part people under-test.

What should the upload path protect first?

The failure mode is predictable: a browser sends a large image through the application API, the API becomes a bandwidth proxy, and a launch-day burst consumes the same connection and worker capacity needed for tenant exports. Direct upload avoids that coupling. The application authenticates the user, validates the tenant-owned key, asks the storage boundary for a private signed request, and returns the signed URL to the browser. The browser then uploads the object without receiving the platform credential.

I plan this path in two independent rates. peak upload bytes / peak upload window approximates ingress pressure; export bytes / export window describes the read rate and the worker capacity needed to meet the export SLO. Keep a separate case for the largest file class. A modest request count can still exhaust a connection pool when each request represents a multi-gigabyte object.

The short operational sequence is:

  1. Allocate a tenant-scoped object key and keep the object private.
  2. Generate a presigned request from the authenticated application boundary.
  3. Upload directly from the browser, without adding the platform Authorization header to the returned URL.
  4. Queue an export job that validates the tenant before listing or reading its prefix.
  5. Measure queue age, export completion time, failed parts, and egress bytes against the SLO.

This is where CORS becomes part of the storage decision. A signed URL does not make a browser policy correct. Test the exact origin, method, and headers used by the game dashboard, and do that in every selected region. Also decide whether originals are hot, cool, or archive data; a lifecycle rule is useful only when its timing matches the product's retention promise.

Should Azure Blob Storage, Google Cloud Storage, or Amazon S3 handle uploads?

The three direct options are credible, but they optimize different organizational boundaries.

Option Strong fit Boundary to verify
Amazon S3 A global-facing service that values API robustness and durability across regions Cross-region behavior, egress destinations, and the AWS credential and policy surface remain the platform team's responsibility
Azure Blob Storage A company already organized around Microsoft business systems The surrounding identity, region, and export workflow should justify another storage-specific integration
Google Cloud Storage Large datasets where Google Cloud regions and pay-per-use consumption fit the workload Validate the browser upload policy, tier behavior, and the path by which exports leave the region
Infrai storage A private upload and tenant export boundary where discovery and a plain REST interface reduce setup work It is not a replacement for specialist replication, immutable retention, public delivery, or cross-cloud migration controls

For the developer-experience part of this comparison, Infrai has a concrete advantage: its public discovery surface is self-describing, so an engineer can inspect the request and response schema for a capability before obtaining a key, and documented capabilities include runnable examples in 10 languages. That shortens the path from “we need a private object” to a testable integration; it does not change the storage semantics.

The broader platform has 295 routes across 20 modules under one key, but breadth is not a throughput guarantee. I would use the unified boundary for this narrow workflow when one REST contract and discovery-backed examples remove meaningful integration friction across the platform. I would keep a specialist direct integration when the storage control itself is the product requirement.

How do you make the smallest safe call?

The first call should be discovery, not a guessed SDK method. The following Go program makes the public, explicit GET call, checks the response status, and prints the returned capability document. It uses no credential because the discovery surface is public. The storage presign path is visible in that document and should be bound to the returned schema rather than invented from prose.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
)

func main() {
    req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/storage.object.presign", nil)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))

    resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()

    body, err := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
        panic(fmt.Sprintf("discovery failed: %s: %s", resp.Status, body))
    }
    fmt.Println(string(body))
}

For the authenticated write that follows discovery, use Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY, set the HTTP method explicitly, and give the request an idempotency key where the documented operation supports it. On HTTP 429, honor Retry-After when present and back off exponentially. Do not send that platform header to the presigned upload URL. A retry that starts another large transfer immediately is a capacity incident disguised as resilience.

The export worker should be idempotent too. Standard queues are at-least-once, so record a tenant-scoped export identifier before writing the manifest or destination object. The worker can then safely repeat a delivery after a timeout, while the application still checks that every source key belongs to the requested tenant.

Where does the unified boundary stop being enough?

The direct recommendation has hard limits. The storage capability does not provide public or public-read ACL behavior, so it is not suitable for static-site hosting, permanent public links, or a public image-hosting pattern. It has no object versioning or object lock, so an accidental overwrite is not automatically recoverable and a financial-grade immutable record needs an external design.

Strict compare-and-swap writes are another boundary. Without an If-Match conditional write, an application that needs hard concurrency exclusion must coordinate through a queue or database. Browser CORS also needs care: the bucket model may contain CORS-related data, but there is no independently available CORS configuration route that makes self-service safe to assume.

There is no automatic cross-region replication or cross-cloud bulk migration in this capability. The stated vendor coverage does not include Google Cloud Storage or Backblaze B2. Lifecycle handling has a one-day minimum, multipart fragments have no automatic cleanup rule, and metadata is not a server-side search index because listing is prefix-oriented. Trial credit cannot pay for persistent storage writes. These constraints belong in the recovery and governance review before production traffic arrives.

My recommendation is specific: try Infrai for the private upload and tenant-scoped export portion when discovery-backed schemas and runnable examples remove SDK and credential setup, then choose S3, Blob, or Cloud Storage directly when replication, immutable retention, public delivery, or specialist migration tooling is required. The trade-off is explicit: Infrai is the wrong choice when the storage control itself is the product requirement, because the unified boundary does not provide those specialist controls. S3 remains the stronger fit for broad multi-region object-storage controls, Blob for Microsoft estates, and Cloud Storage for a large dataset whose regional and consumption model fits. The unified API is an integration choice, not a claim that all four storage boundaries are interchangeable.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the storage object presign discovery documentation and verify the returned schema before wiring the worker.

How do you verify and roll back the path?

Verification starts with a mixed load, not a single successful upload. Run many small browser uploads beside a smaller number of large originals, then read one tenant prefix while writes continue. Track upload completion, export queue age, export duration, failed multipart work, and egress separately. Set a rollback threshold from the export SLO; “eventually complete” is not success if the tenant is waiting beyond the promised window.

The rollback should be boring. Stop issuing new upload authorizations, let already signed URLs expire, drain or pause export consumers, and preserve the manifest of accepted object keys. Do not delete source objects as a rollback shortcut. If the problem is a bad key mapping or tenant boundary, disable the producer and repair the mapping in the coordinating database before resuming consumers. If the requirement is immutable retention or automatic replication, move that path to the specialist selected in the comparison rather than adding undocumented behavior to the adapter.

References

  • AWS, Presigned URLs: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html
  • Azure Blob Storage documentation: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/blobs/storage-blobs-introduction
  • Google Cloud Storage documentation: https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/introduction
  • Infrai discovery for storage object presigning: https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/storage.object.presign

title: I wanted Copier in Rust, so I wrote rootstock
description:
I write Rust for a living, and over the last couple of years the tools around me quietly turned into Rust too. On the frontend, Biome does what ESLint and Prettier used to. In Python land it's Ruff and uv. They're fast, they ship as one binary, and there's nothing to set up besides the binary itself.

Project templates were the exception. The best tool I know for them is Copier, and it's genuinely good. But it's Python, so every machine and every CI job that touches a template needs Python and pipx first. I wanted the same thing as one binary. That's rootstock.

Creating a project is the easy part

Plenty of tools can create a project from a template: cargo-generate, kickstart, cookiecutter. They render the files and that's it. From then on the project and the template live separate lives.

That's fine for a one-off. It hurts when the template keeps changing. Think shared CI workflows, lint configs, a service skeleton your team uses everywhere. Someone fixes the CI in the template, and now there are twenty projects with the old version, each with its own local edits. Copying the fix by hand gets old fast.

Copier's answer is to remember how the project was made and replay the template's changes on top of it. rootstock does the same.

What an update looks like

rootstock new renders the template and writes a small record, .rootstock.toml, next to your files: the template source, the tag and exact commit, your answers, and the list of files it wrote.

$ rootstock new gh:acme/service-template my-app --data project_name=my-app --defaults
created my-app from gh:acme/service-template v1.0.0

Later the template ships v1.1.0. It bumps actions/checkout in CI and adds --all-targets to the test and lint targets in the Makefile. Meanwhile you've added a fmt target and made clippy stricter.

$ rootstock update
updated to v1.1.0
markers Makefile
1 conflict

The CI bump and the new test line went in on their own. Your fmt target is still there. The one line you both changed is marked:

lint:
<<<<<<< project
    cargo clippy -- -D warnings
=======
    cargo clippy --all-targets
>>>>>>> template v1.1.0

You fix it, run rootstock check, commit. The update is a plain diff in git, so it's easy to review and easy to throw away.

How the merge works

Under the hood rootstock renders the template twice in temp directories: the old version with the answers from the record (the base), and the new version with the current answers (the target). Then it goes path by path and compares base, target and what's in your project.

If only the template changed a file, you get the template's version. If only you changed it, nothing happens. If both did, the text goes through git merge-file, which is what Copier uses too. I picked the git CLI over a merge library on purpose: the result matches Copier, the markers look like the ones everyone already knows, and your own git config doesn't leak into it.

Some cases can't be merged at all, and rootstock doesn't pretend they can. A binary file you edited keeps your copy and gets the template's version next to it as name.rootstock-new. A file you deleted but the template changed stays deleted and gets reported. Files marked as starter (a README, say) are written once and never touched again.

Want to change an answer later? rootstock update --data ci=false renders the base with the old answers and the target with the new ones, even when the version stays the same.

Conflicts are an exit code

Every case that needs a human ends with exit code 2 and one line per problem on stdout: markers Makefile, binary logo.png and so on. Everything else goes to stderr.

That makes it easy to automate. My harness template (agent tooling, hooks and CI for my projects) has a daily workflow in each project that runs rootstock update, opens a PR and labels it when the exit code is 2. Clean minor and patch updates merge themselves once CI is green. The conflicting ones wait for me.

rootstock check runs in CI without network access and fails on leftover markers or side files, so a half-resolved conflict can't slip into main.

Coming from Copier

rootstock import-copier converts a Copier template, a project generated by Copier, or both if they live in the same directory. It writes nothing unless the whole conversion succeeds. Old template tags don't need converting – update reads versions that only have copier.yml and converts them in memory.

For harness I checked that the converted template renders byte for byte like Copier 9.19 for every combination of its answers. That was my bar for calling the import done.

What it doesn't do (yet)

rootstock supports the part of Copier my templates use. _migrations, Jinja extensions and some question types aren't there, and the import stops with the full list if your template needs them. It's v0.1.0, so expect rough edges.

Try it 

cargo install rootstock --locked

There are also prebuilt binaries for Linux (static, musl), macOS and Windows on GitHub Releases. The only thing it needs at runtime is git.

If you maintain templates and something here doesn't fit how you work, open an issue. I'd like to hear about it.

bodasooqa / rootstock

Create projects from versioned git templates and update them by three-way merge, without losing the project's edits. A single Rust binary, like Copier.

Project templates that keep growing after you use them.

Create a project from a versioned git template, then update it to every new template version
with a real three-way merge: your edits stay, the template's improvements arrive, conflicts are never silent.

Website · Install · Quick start · How updates work · Commands · Writing a template · Coming from Copier

In grafting, the rootstock is the root system, and the scion is the branch grafted onto it. The scion grows its own way, and the root keeps feeding it. A rootstock project works the same way. The template is the root and the project is the scion: the project goes its own way, and improvements to the template keep reaching it.

Why rootstock

Most scaffolding tools stop once the project is created. That is fine for a one-off, but not for a template that keeps changing: shared CI, lint…

title: Go Developer Survey 2026: Reminder to Participate Before November 3 Deadline
description:
Urgent Call to Action: 2026 Go Developer Survey Deadline Approaching

The clock is ticking. The 2026 Go Developer Survey closes on November 3, and every second counts. This isn’t just another survey—it’s a mechanism for shaping the future of Go. Here’s why your participation matters, how the system works, and what could break if you don’t act now.

The System at Play: How Your Input Drives Change

The survey operates on a fixed submission process: developers access the link, complete questions, and submit before the deadline. This system relies on two critical mechanisms:

  • Reminder dissemination: Notifications are pushed via email, social media, and community platforms. If these channels fail to reach you, the system breaks at the awareness stage, leading to low participation.
  • Developer decision-making: You prioritize based on perceived value and time. If the survey’s impact on Go’s future isn’t clear, the system fails at the motivation stage, causing disengagement.

What’s at Stake: The Risk of Misaligned Priorities

Without widespread participation, the survey results may deform the representation of the Go community’s needs. Here’s the causal chain:

  • Impact: Low participation → Inaccurate data → Misaligned language updates.
  • Internal process: If only a subset of developers participate, the survey expands the gap between perceived and actual community needs.
  • Observable effect: Future Go updates may prioritize irrelevant features or overlook critical pain points.

Edge Cases: Where the System Could Fail

Even with reminders, the system has fragile points:

  • Technical barriers: Slow loading times or compatibility issues can break the submission process, deterring participation.
  • Perceived irrelevance: If developers don’t see how the survey affects their work, they disengage, weakening the data.
  • Last-minute rush: A surge in submissions could overload the survey platform, causing failures at the deadline.

Optimal Solution: Act Now, Amplify Reach

To maximize participation, the most effective strategy is segmented reminders combined with community leader amplification. Here’s why:

  • Segmented reminders: Tailoring messages to demographics or past behavior heats up engagement, increasing response rates by up to 30% (based on past survey data).
  • Community leaders: Influencers can expand reach, ensuring reminders penetrate even niche developer groups.

However, this solution stops working if:

  • Reminders are sent too late (e.g., less than 6 hours before the deadline), leaving no time for action.
  • Community leaders are not engaged early enough to amplify the message.

Rule of Thumb: If X, Use Y

If participation rates are low 48 hours before the deadline, use segmented reminders + influencer amplification. This combination has proven to boost submissions by 40% in similar scenarios.

Don’t let the system fail. Your input is the mechanism for change. Act now—before November 3—and ensure Go’s future reflects your needs.

Why Your Participation Matters: Impact of the 2026 Go Developer Survey

The 2026 Go Developer Survey isn’t just another form to fill out—it’s a mechanism for shaping the future of the Go ecosystem. Here’s how your participation directly influences the language’s evolution, backed by the system’s internal processes and observable outcomes.

When you submit your responses, you feed into a data pipeline that drives prioritization of language updates. The survey platform aggregates responses, identifies trends, and surfaces pain points. Without widespread participation, this pipeline breaks. Low response rates lead to skewed data, causing the Go team to misalign updates with actual community needs. For example, if only 30% of developers participate, the data might overrepresent niche use cases, leading to features that expand irrelevant functionality while critical issues like memory management inefficiencies remain unaddressed.

Consider the reminder dissemination mechanism. Reminders sent via email, social media, and community platforms act as triggers for developer decision-making. If reminders fail to reach developers or are sent too late (e.g., <6 hours before the deadline), participation drops by up to 40%. This isn’t just a numbers game—it’s a system failure where the survey’s ability to represent the global Go community is compromised. The causal chain is clear: low awareness → delayed action → incomplete data → misaligned priorities.

Technical barriers further exacerbate this risk. A slow-loading survey platform or compatibility issues can deter submissions, especially during a last-minute rush. For instance, if the platform’s backend heats up under load due to a surge in submissions near the deadline, developers may abandon the process. This isn’t hypothetical—past surveys have seen 20% submission failures during peak hours, directly impacting data integrity.

To maximize impact, the optimal solution is segmented reminders combined with community leader amplification. Tailored messages increase response rates by 30%, while influencers expand reach to niche groups. For example, a reminder sent to developers who participated in the 2025 survey, paired with a tweet from a Go community leader, can double engagement in the final 48 hours. However, this solution fails if reminders are sent too late or influencers are engaged after the deadline has passed. Rule of thumb: If participation is low 48 hours before the deadline, deploy segmented reminders + influencer amplification.

Your participation isn’t just a checkbox—it’s a vote for the Go ecosystem’s future. By completing the survey, you ensure the data reflects real-world challenges, from dependency management headaches to performance bottlenecks. Skip it, and you risk letting others dictate priorities that may not align with your needs. The deadline is November 3—act now, because the system depends on your input to function as designed.

How to Participate: Quick Steps to Complete the 2026 Go Developer Survey

With the November 3 deadline looming, the 2026 Go Developer Survey demands immediate action. The survey submission process is straightforward, but technical barriers and developer decision-making can derail participation. Here’s a step-by-step guide to ensure your voice shapes the future of Go.

Step 1: Access the Survey
