title: I Gave Two GitHub Repositories a Terrible Idea. Then I Gave It Life.
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine.

The monster had a complaint:

Stop trying to feed me those foreign files, I can't steer my legs properly while chewing!

One parent was a tool that digests repositories. The other was a simulated fly. Gemma had given their imaginary child a problem neither parent could have alone: eating code made it difficult to walk.

That was the moment FrankenRepo started to feel alive.

What I Built

FrankenRepo is a gothic laboratory where two public GitHub repositories become one very questionable monster.

Choose a brain. Choose a body. Inspect their observable DNA. Select Useful, Cursed, or Chaotic, then pull the lever. Gemma invents a name, personality, inherited traits, a curse, first words, and a speculative useful mutation. The lab turns them into a downloadable Monster Birth Certificate.

I wanted repository discovery to feel like opening a cabinet of strange specimens. A web framework and a JSON processor become a specter suffering through nested brackets. A repository-eating crab meets a fly with simulated motor behavior. Familiar tools suddenly have a family resemblance.

The monster is fictional. The parents and their source links are real.

The standby creature above is original interface artwork. Model-generated certificates appear after an actual successful ritual.

Demo

The demo follows Flask + jq in Cursed mode through the local browser application: inspect the donors, invoke Gemma, reveal the creature, inspect its DNA, and export a PNG. It uses the actual provider and application, with no fixture responses or replayed model result.

52-second continuous local recording, captured on 1 November before the deadline. There is no public hosted application yet.

The new creature is The Scribe of Bracketed Sighs. Its proposed mutation gives Flask the web server and jq the JSON-log filtering: two recognizable roles, with feasibility still left to a human.

A second real specimen, The Scavenging Glider, supplied the chewing complaint in the opening:

HungryCrab supplied repository digestion; desktop-fly supplied simulated motor behavior. Gemma supplied the chewing problem. The suggested digest-to-movement integration is still speculative: a funny character can arrive before a workable adapter.

Code

Source and published v0.1 preview on GitHub · Saved real-run evidence · Asset credits

The source is MIT licensed. Use Node 24 and npm 11:

git clone https://github.com/drevendev/FrankenRepo.git
cd FrankenRepo
npm ci
npm run dev

Open http://127.0.0.1:5173. The interface opens without model credentials; generation requires an explicitly configured provider. The README explains setup. The newer persistence and orchestration work described below is a local update beyond the published v0.1 preview.

How I Built It

The stack is TypeScript workspaces, React/Vite, Hono, and Zod. The verified model is Gemma 4 26B A4B IT, served through Cloudflare Workers AI as @cf/google/gemma-4-26b-a4b-it. Gemma writes the creature; an original deterministic SVG kit draws it. This keeps the visual style consistent and makes PNG, SVG, and alt-text exports practical.

The important design decision was giving the laboratory three distinct kinds of truth:

Layer What belongs there
Observed DNA Public GitHub metadata and bounded README excerpts, with source links and observed commits
AI interpretation The model's explanation of how a trait relates to those observations
Imaginary offspring The creature's personality, curse, and proposed mutation

That separation runs through the UI and the data contract. The model can invent an anxious archivist; it cannot invent a source that proves the archivist exists.

Inspection uses fixed GitHub API endpoints, with request and response limits. FrankenRepo never clones or executes donor code. Missing observations stay unknown. README content is untrusted input, so it has no authority to change the application's tools or rules.

Gemma returns structured JSON. Zod checks its shape, and evidence validation checks that cited source IDs exist. A ritual gets at most two model calls: an initial attempt and one bounded repair, or an eligible deliberate revision. It eventually returns a result or a visible failure.

Keeping the experiment under control

The local update adds a private MongoDB Atlas archive and durable reservations. A restart preserves consumed allowances; an unknown provider outcome keeps its reservation. Saving a card is separate from consent to publish it. Private recovery keys never belong in public URLs.

Mastra runs the donor, context, model/validation, and reveal steps. Sentry records linked agent, tool, and inference spans with model IDs, timing, and token metadata, without sending raw prompts or card text. A Browserbase research session retrieved a pinned donor paragraph that entered a real model input. These integrations have local evidence; the category entries below describe their completed scope. Public hosting remains pending.

The update passed 78 unit/contract/policy tests and 18 desktop/mobile browser tests. Browser success fixtures test application behavior; the real Gemma receipts and recording establish provider use. They answer different questions.

The failure that changed the project

A structurally valid creature can still make an unsupported technical claim.

One early result turned the crab-and-fly pairing into an automated bug-finding insect. The name worked. The sources supplied no mechanism for finding bugs. Source IDs existed, but the proposed connection did not follow from them.

Later, an optional Ultramarine second opinion led to a real Gemma revision using the same frozen donor snapshots. The original survived unchanged. The revised text still promised a "verified lineage report" that the evidence could not support. The plumbing worked; the idea still failed review.

That changed my acceptance criteria. I added targeted checks for the failure classes I had observed. A subsequent Useful run was rejected after its bounded repair instead of showing a substitute creature. Those checks cover specific mistakes; semantic review is still necessary.

Three Paper Instruments requests changed the observed credit balance by $0.00108065. Cloudflare's billed cost and Neuron consumption were not captured, so I leave them unknown. A model's opinion and a dashboard estimate both need that same discipline: say exactly what was observed.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

The open-weight model provides the central creative behavior, and the application exposes how that behavior is constrained. The prompt, schemas, provider adapters, source observations, and original artwork are inspectable. Someone can change the experiment instead of accepting an opaque personality generator.

The verified path uses hosted Gemma. An Ollama adapter also exists as a local inference option; I have not qualified it as equivalent to the hosted model. Moving inference locally would still leave live GitHub inspection dependent on the network.

Open innovation also shaped the game itself. A public project can become inspiration for something unexpected while keeping its author, purpose, and evidence visible. The imaginary child does not inherit a license grant or become a real merger of its parents' code.

The Spirit of It

For Ghost in the Machine, I wanted the haunting to come from software's recognizable habits: a parser that cannot stop sorting, a fly that cannot stop twitching, an archivist demanding paperwork from a metaphor.

The best creature was the one whose complaint made sense once you met its parents.

So there is a large lever, a quiet music box, and a birth certificate stamped CERTIFIED IMAGINARY. Sound starts off; keyboard controls and reduced motion are supported.

The machine should enjoy its theatrical entrance. The evidence should survive the lights coming back on.

Prize Categories

The following entries use completed local scenarios. Public application hosting is still pending.

Category What actually ran
Best Use of Gemma Source-linked creature generation and real browser exports, including the continuous demo above.
Best Use of Mastra The actual donor → context → Gemma/contract → reveal workflow; real run IDs, step timings, and a failed run are retained.
Best Use of MongoDB Atlas Private save → API restart → read, wrong-key denial, consented public read → unpublish/delete, and competing durable budget reservations.
Best Use of Browserbase A real cloud browser retrieved a pinned donor README paragraph that entered a real Gemma input. This is research-context use, without a public-site E2E claim.
Best Use of Ultramarine Two real second opinions through the official OpenAI SDK, with recorded token usage and the credit cost reported above.

The Browserbase context came from HungryCrab's README at the observed commit, and was supplied as a separately identified browser excerpt. Ultramarine identified the missing code-to-stimulus interface in the crab/fly proposal; its own proposed fix remained an opinion. Atlas denied reads after revocation and deletion, including an attempted recreation of a deleted operation.

Public hosting, a gallery, the proposed memory corpus, and the apprentice-training experiment remain unfinished. Render, Backboard, and Tinker are not entered. No deployed service or trained checkpoint is claimed.

Built with AI-assisted coding and drafting. Real model outputs are preserved as evidence; test fixtures and illustrated interface specimens are labelled separately.

title: .NET 10 + Pinecone: como integrar com um banco de dados vetorial
description:
🧭 1. Introdução

A integração entre .NET 10 e Pinecone permite desenvolver aplicações capazes de armazenar, pesquisar e recuperar informações por similaridade semântica.

Essa abordagem é especialmente útil em projetos de:

  • Inteligência Artificial (IA).
  • RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation).
  • Assistentes virtuais e chatbots.
  • Busca semântica de documentos.
  • Sistemas de recomendação.
  • Recuperação inteligente de conhecimento.
  • Aplicações baseadas em LLMs (Large Language Models).

Diferentemente dos bancos relacionais tradicionais, que normalmente consultam dados por condições e valores exatos, o Pinecone foi projetado para trabalhar com vetores (embeddings).

Esses vetores representam o significado de textos, documentos e outros conteúdos em um espaço matemático. Dessa forma, conseguimos encontrar informações relacionadas pelo contexto, mesmo quando as palavras utilizadas são diferentes.

Neste artigo, vamos implementar uma integração utilizando:

  • .NET 10 e C#.
  • Pinecone Vector Database.
  • API REST do Pinecone.
  • HttpClient e IHttpClientFactory.
  • Injeção de dependência.
  • Arquitetura organizada em camadas.
  • Operações de inserção e pesquisa vetorial.

🧠 2. O que é Pinecone?

O Pinecone é um banco de dados vetorial gerenciado, desenvolvido para armazenar e consultar embeddings em larga escala.

Seu principal objetivo é permitir pesquisas por similaridade entre vetores, oferecendo uma infraestrutura especializada para aplicações de IA.

Como funciona?

Imagine uma aplicação que armazena documentos sobre desenvolvimento de software.

Podemos cadastrar os seguintes conteúdos:

  • Documento 1: Como implementar autenticação JWT com .NET.
  • Documento 2: Como proteger endpoints de uma API.
  • Documento 3: Como configurar um banco de dados SQL Server.
  • Documento 4: Como implementar autorização baseada em políticas.

Quando um usuário pesquisa:

"Como proteger uma API desenvolvida em C#?"

Uma busca tradicional pode depender da correspondência exata das palavras.

Já uma busca vetorial pode encontrar documentos semanticamente relacionados, como o documento sobre autenticação JWT ou autorização baseada em políticas.

Principais conceitos

Conceito Descrição
Vector Representação numérica de um conteúdo
Embedding Processo de transformar conteúdo em vetor
Index Estrutura onde os vetores são armazenados
Namespace Divisão lógica dos registros
Metadata Informações adicionais associadas ao vetor
Similarity Search Pesquisa por proximidade entre vetores
Upsert Inserção ou atualização de vetores
Query Consulta por similaridade

🔄 3. Arquitetura de funcionamento

Uma integração com Pinecone normalmente envolve três etapas principais:

  1. Transformar o conteúdo em embeddings.
  2. Armazenar os embeddings no Pinecone.
  3. Gerar um embedding para a pesquisa e consultar os vetores mais próximos.

É importante entender que Pinecone e o modelo de embeddings possuem responsabilidades diferentes.

O Pinecone armazena e pesquisa vetores. O modelo de embeddings transforma textos em representações numéricas.

Fluxo de inserção 

flowchart TD
    A["Aplicação .NET 10"] --> B["Documento / Texto"]
    B --> C["Modelo de Embeddings"]
    C --> D["Vetor Numérico"]
    D --> E["Pinecone API"]
    E --> F["Vector Index"]
    F --> G["Armazenamento"]

Fluxo de pesquisa 

flowchart TD
    A["Usuário realiza uma pesquisa"] --> B["API .NET 10"]
    B --> C["Modelo de Embeddings"]
    C --> D["Vetor da consulta"]
    D --> E["Pinecone Query"]
    E --> F["Pesquisa por similaridade"]
    F --> G["Documentos relacionados"]
    G --> H["Resposta para a aplicação"]

Em aplicações RAG, os documentos recuperados podem ser enviados posteriormente para um LLM, que utiliza esse contexto para construir uma resposta.

🏗️ 4. Criando o projeto .NET 10

Vamos começar criando uma Web API.

dotnet new webapi -n PineconeIntegration
cd PineconeIntegration

Para este exemplo, utilizaremos a API REST diretamente por meio do HttpClient.

Essa escolha evita acoplar a aplicação a uma biblioteca específica. O repositório do SDK oficial C# foi arquivado em julho de 2026, portanto vale avaliar cuidadosamente seu estado de manutenção antes de adotá-lo em novos projetos.

Estrutura sugerida 

PineconeIntegration/
│
├── Controllers/
│   └── DocumentsController.cs
│
├── Application/
│   ├── DTOs/
│   │   ├── DocumentRequest.cs
│   │   └── SearchRequest.cs
│   │
│   └── Interfaces/
│       ├── IEmbeddingService.cs
│       └── IPineconeService.cs
│
├── Domain/
│   └── Entities/
│       └── Document.cs
│
├── Infrastructure/
│   ├── Embeddings/
│   │   └── EmbeddingService.cs
│   │
│   └── Pinecone/
│       ├── PineconeOptions.cs
│       └── PineconeService.cs
│
├── appsettings.json
└── Program.cs

A separação permite manter as responsabilidades organizadas:

  • Api: exposição dos endpoints HTTP.
  • Application: contratos, DTOs e regras de aplicação.
  • Domain: entidades e conceitos do negócio.
  • Infrastructure: integração com serviços externos, embeddings e Pinecone.

🔑 5. Criando uma conta e configurando o Pinecone

Para utilizar o serviço, acesse:

https://www.pinecone.io/

Após criar sua conta:

  1. Acesse o painel de controle.
  2. Crie um projeto.
  3. Gere uma API Key.
  4. Crie um Index.
  5. Configure a dimensão dos vetores.
  6. Selecione a métrica de similaridade.
  7. Aguarde o índice ficar disponível.

Configuração do Index

Para nosso exemplo, considere:

Configuração Valor
Nome dotnet-documents
Tipo Dense Vector
Dimension 384
Metric Cosine
Deployment Serverless

Atenção: a dimensão 384 é apenas ilustrativa. Ela precisa corresponder exatamente à dimensão produzida pelo modelo de embeddings escolhido.

A métrica Cosine é uma opção comum para pesquisas semânticas, mas a escolha deve considerar as características do modelo e da aplicação.

Obtendo o Index Host

Depois de criar o índice, obtenha seu endereço de acesso (host).

O formato é semelhante a:

https://dotnet-documents-xxxxx.svc.region.pinecone.io

O endereço real será fornecido pelo Pinecone. Não utilize um endereço fictício na aplicação.

Em produção, prefira utilizar o host específico do índice nas operações de dados.

⚙️ 6. Configurando as variáveis da aplicação

Vamos utilizar o padrão Options do .NET para centralizar as configurações.

PineconeOptions.cs 

namespace PineconeIntegration.Infrastructure.Pinecone;

public sealed class PineconeOptions
{
    public const string SectionName = "Pinecone";

    public string ApiKey { get; set; } = string.Empty;

    public string IndexHost { get; set; } = string.Empty;

    public string Namespace { get; set; } = "documents";

    public int Dimension { get; set; } = 384;
}

appsettings.json 

{
  "Pinecone": {
    "IndexHost": "",
    "Namespace": "documents",
    "Dimension": 384
  }
}

A API Key não deve ser armazenada no arquivo de configuração versionado.

Configure-a por variável de ambiente:

Pinecone__ApiKey="SUA_API_KEY"
Pinecone__IndexHost="https://SEU_INDEX_HOST"

Durante o desenvolvimento, também é possível utilizar o Secret Manager:

dotnet user-secrets init

dotnet user-secrets set "Pinecone:ApiKey" "SUA_API_KEY"

dotnet user-secrets set "Pinecone:IndexHost" "https://SEU_INDEX_HOST"

🔌 7. Criando o contrato de integração

Vamos definir uma interface para abstrair as operações do Pinecone.

IPineconeService.cs 

namespace PineconeIntegration.Application.Interfaces;

public interface IPineconeService
{
    Task UpsertAsync(
        string id,
        float[] embedding,
        string content,
        CancellationToken cancellationToken);

    Task<string> SearchAsync(
        float[] embedding,
        int topK,
        CancellationToken cancellationToken);
}

Essa abstração permite trocar a implementação futuramente sem alterar os controllers ou as regras principais da aplicação.

🧮 8. Implementando o serviço de embeddings

Antes de enviar informações para o Pinecone, precisamos transformar o texto em um vetor.

Para isso, utilizamos um modelo de embeddings.

Podemos utilizar modelos de provedores externos ou executar um modelo localmente.

Neste exemplo, vamos definir um contrato independente do fornecedor.

IEmbeddingService.cs 

namespace PineconeIntegration.Application.Interfaces;

public interface IEmbeddingService
{
    Task<float[]> GenerateAsync(
        string text,
        CancellationToken cancellationToken);
}

EmbeddingService.cs 

using PineconeIntegration.Application.Interfaces;

namespace PineconeIntegration.Infrastructure.Embeddings;

public sealed class EmbeddingService : IEmbeddingService
{
    public Task<float[]> GenerateAsync(
        string text,
        CancellationToken cancellationToken)
    {
        // Exemplo didático.
        // Substitua pela chamada real ao modelo de embeddings.

        throw new NotImplementedException(
            "Configure um provedor real de embeddings.");
    }
}

Não devemos utilizar vetores aleatórios ou gerados artificialmente em uma aplicação real.

O modelo precisa produzir embeddings semanticamente consistentes tanto para os documentos armazenados quanto para as consultas.

Regra fundamental: utilize o mesmo modelo e a mesma configuração de dimensão nas duas operações.

📦 9. Criando o serviço Pinecone com HttpClient

Agora vamos implementar a comunicação com a API REST.

O Pinecone oferece operações de Data Plane para armazenar e pesquisar vetores.

Utilizaremos:

  • POST /vectors/upsert
  • POST /query

As chamadas serão direcionadas ao host específico do índice.

PineconeService.cs 

using System.Net.Http.Json;
using System.Text.Json;
using PineconeIntegration.Application.Interfaces;
using PineconeIntegration.Infrastructure.Pinecone;

namespace PineconeIntegration.Infrastructure.Pinecone;

public sealed class PineconeService : IPineconeService
{
    private readonly HttpClient _httpClient;
    private readonly PineconeOptions _options;

    private static readonly JsonSerializerOptions JsonOptions =
        new(JsonSerializerDefaults.Web);

    public PineconeService(
        HttpClient httpClient,
        Microsoft.Extensions.Options.IOptions<PineconeOptions> options)
    {
        _httpClient = httpClient;
        _options = options.Value;
    }

    public async Task UpsertAsync(
        string id,
        float[] embedding,
        string content,
        CancellationToken cancellationToken)
    {
        ValidateEmbedding(embedding);

        var request = new
        {
            vectors = new[]
            {
                new
                {
                    id,
                    values = embedding,
                    metadata = new
                    {
                        content
                    }
                }
            },
            @namespace = _options.Namespace
        };

        using var response = await _httpClient.PostAsJsonAsync(
            "/vectors/upsert",
            request,
            JsonOptions,
            cancellationToken);

        response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode();
    }

    public async Task<string> SearchAsync(
        float[] embedding,
        int topK,
        CancellationToken cancellationToken)
    {
        ValidateEmbedding(embedding);

        if (topK is < 1 or > 1000)
        {
            throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(topK));
        }

        var request = new
        {
            vector = embedding,
            topK,
            includeMetadata = true,
            includeValues = false,
            @namespace = _options.Namespace
        };

        using var response = await _httpClient.PostAsJsonAsync(
            "/query",
            request,
            JsonOptions,
            cancellationToken);

        response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode();

        return await response.Content.ReadAsStringAsync(
            cancellationToken);
    }

    private void ValidateEmbedding(float[] embedding)
    {
        ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(embedding);

        if (embedding.Length != _options.Dimension)
        {
            throw new ArgumentException(
                $"Expected {_options.Dimension} dimensions, " +
                $"but received {embedding.Length}.");
        }

        if (embedding.Any(value => !float.IsFinite(value)))
        {
            throw new ArgumentException(
                "Embedding contains invalid numeric values.");
        }
    }
}

Entendendo a implementação

UpsertAsync

Envia um vetor para o Pinecone com:

  • ID único.
  • Valores numéricos do embedding.
  • Metadata com o conteúdo original.
  • Namespace de armazenamento.

Se o ID já existir, a operação atualiza o registro.

SearchAsync

Recebe o vetor de pesquisa e solicita os registros mais próximos.

O parâmetro topK determina a quantidade máxima de resultados solicitados.

A propriedade includeMetadata permite recuperar os dados associados aos vetores.

🔐 10. Configurando autenticação e injeção de dependência

Vamos registrar o HttpClient e os serviços no container de dependências do .NET.

Program.cs 

using PineconeIntegration.Application.Interfaces;
using PineconeIntegration.Infrastructure.Embeddings;
using PineconeIntegration.Infrastructure.Pinecone;

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

builder.Services.AddControllers();

builder.Services
    .AddOptions<PineconeOptions>()
    .Bind(builder.Configuration.GetSection(
        PineconeOptions.SectionName))
    .Validate(
        options => !string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(options.ApiKey),
        "Pinecone API Key is required.")
    .Validate(
        options =>
            Uri.TryCreate(
                options.IndexHost,
                UriKind.Absolute,
                out var uri) &&
            uri.Scheme == Uri.UriSchemeHttps,
        "A valid HTTPS Index Host is required.")
    .Validate(
        options => options.Dimension > 0,
        "Dimension must be greater than zero.")
    .ValidateOnStart();

builder.Services.AddHttpClient<IPineconeService, PineconeService>(
    (serviceProvider, client) =>
    {
        var options = serviceProvider
            .GetRequiredService<
                Microsoft.Extensions.Options.IOptions<PineconeOptions>>()
            .Value;

        client.BaseAddress = new Uri(
            options.IndexHost.TrimEnd('/') + "/");

        client.Timeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30);

        client.DefaultRequestHeaders.Add(
            "Api-Key",
            options.ApiKey);

        client.DefaultRequestHeaders.Add(
            "X-Pinecone-Api-Version",
            "2025-10");
    });

builder.Services.AddScoped<IEmbeddingService, EmbeddingService>();

var app = builder.Build();

app.UseHttpsRedirection();

app.MapControllers();

app.Run();

A versão da API utilizada no exemplo é 2025-10, conforme a documentação de referência consultada. Antes de publicar em produção, verifique a versão estável mais recente e a compatibilidade dos endpoints utilizados.

📥 11. Criando o endpoint para cadastrar documentos

Vamos disponibilizar um endpoint para receber textos e armazenar seus respectivos embeddings.

DocumentRequest.cs 

using System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations;

namespace PineconeIntegration.Application.DTOs;

public sealed record DocumentRequest(
    [Required]
    [StringLength(10000, MinimumLength = 3)]
    string Content);

DocumentsController.cs 

using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc;
using PineconeIntegration.Application.DTOs;
using PineconeIntegration.Application.Interfaces;

namespace PineconeIntegration.Controllers;

[ApiController]
[Route("api/documents")]
public sealed class DocumentsController : ControllerBase
{
    private readonly IPineconeService _pineconeService;
    private readonly IEmbeddingService _embeddingService;

    public DocumentsController(
        IPineconeService pineconeService,
        IEmbeddingService embeddingService)
    {
        _pineconeService = pineconeService;
        _embeddingService = embeddingService;
    }

    [HttpPost]
    public async Task<IActionResult> Create(
        [FromBody] DocumentRequest request,
        CancellationToken cancellationToken)
    {
        var embedding = await _embeddingService.GenerateAsync(
            request.Content,
            cancellationToken);

        var id = Guid.NewGuid().ToString();

        await _pineconeService.UpsertAsync(
            id,
            embedding,
            request.Content,
            cancellationToken);

        return Created(
            $"/api/documents/{id}",
            new
            {
                Id = id,
                Message = "Document successfully indexed."
            });
    }
}

Exemplo de requisição 

POST /api/documents
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "content": "O .NET 10 permite desenvolver APIs modernas utilizando C#."
}

O processo será:

  1. Receber o documento.
  2. Gerar seu embedding.
  3. Criar um identificador.
  4. Enviar o vetor para o Pinecone.
  5. Retornar o resultado da operação.

🔎 12. Criando o endpoint de pesquisa semântica

Agora vamos implementar a pesquisa.

SearchRequest.cs 

using System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations;

namespace PineconeIntegration.Application.DTOs;

public sealed record SearchRequest(
    [Required]
    [StringLength(2000, MinimumLength = 2)]
    string Query,

    [Range(1, 20)]
    int TopK = 5);

Adicione o endpoint ao DocumentsController:

[HttpPost("search")]
public async Task<IActionResult> Search(
    [FromBody] SearchRequest request,
    CancellationToken cancellationToken)
{
    var embedding = await _embeddingService.GenerateAsync(
        request.Query,
        cancellationToken);

    var results = await _pineconeService.SearchAsync(
        embedding,
        request.TopK,
        cancellationToken);

    return Ok(new
    {
        Query = request.Query,
        Results = results
    });
}

Exemplo de requisição 

POST /api/documents/search
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "query": "Como desenvolver uma API moderna com C#?",
  "topK": 5
}

O Pinecone retornará os registros mais próximos do vetor da consulta.

Cada resultado pode conter:

  • ID do vetor.
  • Score de similaridade.
  • Metadata.
  • Conteúdo original, quando armazenado na metadata.

O score representa uma medida de similaridade conforme a métrica configurada no índice. Não deve ser interpretado automaticamente como uma porcentagem de confiança.

🤖 13. Integrando Pinecone com RAG

Uma das aplicações mais interessantes do Pinecone é a construção de soluções RAG.

RAG significa Retrieval-Augmented Generation e combina recuperação de informações com geração de respostas por modelos de linguagem.

Como funciona?

Imagine um chatbot corporativo que responde perguntas sobre documentos internos.

O fluxo pode ser:

  1. O usuário envia uma pergunta.
  2. A aplicação gera o embedding da pergunta.
  3. O Pinecone pesquisa os documentos mais relevantes.
  4. A aplicação recupera os conteúdos encontrados.
  5. Os conteúdos são adicionados ao contexto do LLM.
  6. O modelo gera uma resposta fundamentada nas informações recuperadas.

Arquitetura RAG 

flowchart TD
    A["Usuário"] --> B["API .NET 10"]
    B --> C["Embedding da pergunta"]
    C --> D["Pinecone Vector Search"]
    D --> E["Documentos relevantes"]
    E --> F["Construção do contexto"]
    F --> G["LLM"]
    G --> H["Resposta contextualizada"]
    H --> A

Essa arquitetura pode ser aplicada em:

  • Chatbots de atendimento.
  • Assistentes de documentação técnica.
  • Sistemas de suporte interno.
  • Pesquisa de contratos.
  • Consulta de manuais.
  • Bases de conhecimento corporativas.

Importante: a recuperação de documentos não garante, por si só, que o LLM responderá corretamente. É necessário controlar o contexto, as permissões, as fontes e a qualidade das respostas.

🧱 14. Boas práticas de arquitetura e desenvolvimento

Para utilizar Pinecone em aplicações corporativas, recomendo observar alguns pontos.

🔐 Segurança

  • Nunca exponha a API Key no frontend.
  • Utilize variáveis de ambiente ou um cofre de segredos.
  • Restrinja as permissões das credenciais.
  • Utilize HTTPS.
  • Implemente autenticação e autorização na API .NET.
  • Separe os namespaces conforme as necessidades de isolamento.
  • Não permita que o usuário escolha livremente namespaces sem validação.

⚡ Performance

  • Utilize IHttpClientFactory.
  • Configure timeout adequado.
  • Avalie operações em lote para grandes volumes.
  • Evite gerar embeddings repetidos para conteúdos que não mudaram.
  • Utilize IDs estáveis quando precisar atualizar documentos.
  • Recupere apenas os metadados necessários.
  • Avalie o custo e a latência das consultas.

📊 Observabilidade

Monitore:

  • Tempo de geração dos embeddings.
  • Tempo de resposta do Pinecone.
  • Quantidade de vetores cadastrados.
  • Quantidade de resultados recuperados.
  • Erros de autenticação e comunicação.
  • Consumo e custos associados às operações.

Evite registrar API Keys, documentos confidenciais ou informações pessoais nos logs.

🧩 Consistência dos embeddings

O modelo de embeddings utilizado na indexação deve ser compatível com o modelo utilizado na consulta.

Se trocar o modelo, a dimensão ou a estratégia de geração, considere criar um novo índice e reprocessar os documentos.

🧪 15. Estratégia de testes

Uma integração bem estruturada também precisa de testes.

Sugestões:

Cenário Resultado esperado
Inserção de documento Vetor armazenado
Atualização de documento Registro atualizado
Consulta válida Resultados encontrados
Vetor com dimensão incorreta Validação rejeitada
API Key inválida Erro de autenticação
Index Host incorreto Falha de comunicação
Pinecone indisponível Tratamento de falha
Consulta sem resultados Lista vazia
Namespace incorreto Isolamento respeitado

Uma boa estratégia é utilizar mocks para testar os serviços de aplicação e testes de integração controlados para validar a comunicação real com o Pinecone.

🏛️ 16. Evoluindo a solução

Depois de implementar as operações básicas, podemos evoluir a arquitetura para suportar cenários mais complexos.

Funcionalidades futuras

  • Upload e processamento de PDF.
  • Divisão de documentos em chunks.
  • Pipeline assíncrono com RabbitMQ.
  • Processamento em lote.
  • Integração com Azure OpenAI ou outros provedores de LLM.
  • Busca híbrida: semântica e textual.
  • Filtros por metadata.
  • Controle de acesso por usuário e organização.
  • Versionamento de documentos.
  • Estratégias de reindexação.
  • Monitoramento com OpenTelemetry.

⚠️ 17. Pontos importantes antes de utilizar em produção

O exemplo apresentado demonstra o fluxo essencial, mas uma aplicação real precisa de algumas evoluções:

  1. Implementar um provedor real de embeddings.
  2. Criar uma estratégia de chunking para documentos extensos.
  3. Implementar políticas de retry e tratamento de erros transitórios, respeitando os limites do serviço.
  4. Definir limites de tamanho e quantidade de registros por requisição.
  5. Criar uma estratégia de atualização e exclusão de documentos.
  6. Garantir isolamento entre clientes e organizações.
  7. Validar a compatibilidade entre dimensão e modelo de embeddings.
  8. Implementar monitoramento de custos e latência.
  9. Tratar indisponibilidade do serviço externo.
  10. Avaliar a retenção e proteção dos dados armazenados.

Outro detalhe importante: Pinecone não substitui necessariamente um banco relacional. Uma arquitetura pode utilizar SQL Server ou PostgreSQL para os dados transacionais e Pinecone para a recuperação semântica.

🎯 18. Conclusão

A integração entre .NET 10 e Pinecone abre possibilidades interessantes para aplicações que precisam trabalhar com Inteligência Artificial, recuperação de conhecimento e pesquisas semânticas.

Com uma arquitetura organizada, utilizando interfaces, injeção de dependência e HttpClient, conseguimos manter a integração desacoplada e preparada para evoluções futuras.

O Pinecone pode atuar como uma camada especializada de recuperação vetorial, enquanto o .NET 10 permanece responsável pelas regras de negócio, exposição das APIs, segurança e orquestração dos serviços.

Mais do que integrar um banco de dados, estamos construindo uma base para aplicações inteligentes, capazes de recuperar informações pelo significado e não apenas pela correspondência exata de palavras.

O futuro das aplicações modernas não está somente em armazenar dados, mas também em conseguir interpretar, relacionar e recuperar conhecimento.

  • Pinecone — GitHub C# Client
  • Microsoft — IHttpClientFactory
  • Microsoft — .NET 10

title: CI Can Be Green While the macOS Installer Fails: Stage-by-Stage Acceptance from a Real Controller Migration
description:
This is the English edition of an article first published in Japanese on Zenn: https://zenn.dev/asagiman/articles/macos-installer-actual-acceptance

Even after CI turns green, the macOS Installer can stop. This happens at the final real-machine acceptance step even when development relies on AI agents. The tests have passed and no problem has been found in the built package. Yet a product cannot ship until the user's Mac accepts the installation and the authorized work actually runs.

During the migration of the Controller that Netsujo is developing, the internal records show that, within the two days of October 16 and 17, 2026 alone, we ran the real macOS Installer eleven times. Four runs succeeded (three generation-update stages and one limited diagnostic without authentication) and seven failed (three generation-update stages and four stages involving the administrator's own authentication). All seven failures passed preinstall and then stopped in postinstall, and the operating system recorded a failed installation. In one of the authentication runs, part of the changes had already been applied to the machine when the run failed. There were also real-machine failures and successes before and after these two days. On October 30, 2026, another installation stage succeeded on the real machine and passed readback, but a normal authenticated AI job had not yet been accepted.

Below is a way to record evidence so that the next decision can be made without losing the proof of stages that did succeed, separated into five boundaries: source (including CI), package, OS installation, authorization, and a real AI job. It ends with a check you can run quickly with a disposable test package.

The two-day real-machine results are based on internal records from October 16–17, 2026. The October 30 result and the current status were confirmed by checking the same internal records on November 1, 2026. As of November 1, 2026, the overall Controller migration and acceptance of a normal authenticated job are still in progress. Credentials, internal recovery procedures, secrets, and confidential configuration values are excluded.

What happened: a built package stopped in postinstall

CI runs tests against a specified source, environment, and input. It can find many problems that are reproducible on the development side in advance: types, unit tests, static checks, and package generation.

When the macOS Installer is involved, the existing OS state, pre- and post-install scripts, the actual user and permissions, the administrator's own authentication, and migration state from earlier generations all affect the result. Some of these conditions cannot be fully reproduced in a CI environment.

In the Controller recovery work, we used the real installation logs to separate the progress of preinstall from the later postinstall failure. In the failed runs, postinstall returned an error, and the OS recorded the installation failure together with a PackageKit error (PKInstallErrorDomain Code=112). A separate diagnostic that succeeded is valid only for the diagnostic's own scope; the failed package stays on hold and needs its own acceptance.

The first thing a developer needs to establish is which candidate, which stage, and which recorded outcome were involved. Fixing on a single cause too early risks treating failures from different generations as the same phenomenon.

Sorted by type, the records showed that different candidates succeeded at different stages

The table below organizes the observations by type, within what can be published. The rows are not in chronological order. "Observed evidence" shows what an actual record exists for; "Supported conclusion" shows what that record supports.

Stage (by type) Observed evidence Supported conclusion
Source and CI checks Test and CI success records for the target candidates Source accepted within the specified check scope
Limited unauthenticated diagnostic Record of Installer success on the real machine, with its output read back Processing on macOS confirmed under the diagnostic conditions
Generation-update stage Records of both success (3 runs) and postinstall failure (3 runs), depending on the candidate Only the candidates that succeeded met OS acceptance for that stage
Authentication-related stage Records in which the authentication child process did not finish normally and the Installer also failed (4 runs) The authentication-dependent sequence remained unaccepted
State inspection after failure In one failed run, part of the changes had already been applied to the machine Partially applied changes exist
Real AI job No complete authorized launch, delivery, durable record, and independent acceptance Final acceptance of the Controller migration remains open

The real logs tell us the terminal state of each stage. Even when an authentication-related process fails, an OS denial or nearby warning that appears in the log at the same time cannot simply be taken as the root cause. Establishing causality requires a safe reproduction that isolates the failure conditions.

We therefore adopted a rule: a stage that succeeded for one candidate is never reused as a success for another candidate. The evidence of the successful diagnostic is preserved, and a new package requires new acceptance evidence.

First, identify "the same subject"

In long-running development, conversations, PRs, CI, release files, and host logs are each updated at different times. Even after a commit moves on following review, a package built from an older revision can remain on disk. When this happens during incident response, it becomes easy to attach past check results to the current candidate by mistake.

So we pin the identity of the subject being accepted.

Subject Main information to retain Question answered
Source Repository, commit SHA, reviewed changes Which code was evaluated?
CI Target SHA, job, result, timestamp Which checks passed against which code?
Package Hash, size, build origin, signature and composition checks Do the delivered file and the checked file match?
OS execution Scope of execution authority, real-machine result, log, partial state Was the package actually applied?
Authorization and use Valid authority, real job result, saved output, independent acceptance Can the intended work be completed through the legitimate path?

For example, a package's SHA-256 can confirm file identity: it checks that the file a reviewer approved matches the file a user is about to install. Even when the hash matches, the postinstall terminal status and authentication success must be confirmed separately.

When reporting a single failure, save at least "the candidate identifier, the stage executed, the observed terminal status, and the remaining unknowns" in the same record.

Why a simple retry is dangerous

An installer may update some files or state before it fails. In our records, too, there was a run that failed after part of its changes had been applied. A rerun then starts from a different initial state. Even if only the second attempt succeeds, the cause of the first failure can be lost.

Privileged operations and authentication add a question of authorized scope. If an operation run under a one-time approval fails, treat that approval as used and stop. If a developer removes a protection through an environment variable or a different execution path, the result may look like a technical success, but the legitimate permission model breaks.

After a failure, our practice is to review the preserved logs and remaining state, organize the source, and re-confirm the target file and authorization before rerunning the same operation. The eleven runs above are records of different packages; none of them is a rerun of the same package.

What to check after a failed stage

  • Which terminal state the OS recorded: success, failure, or interruption.
  • Whether any changes were applied before the failure, and how far to preserve the parts that cannot be confirmed.
  • Whether the next run would make additional changes to existing data or managed state.
  • Whether the existing approval was consumed by the run, and who decides the next authorization.
  • Whether a local reproduction environment exists where the same input can be tested safely.

Checking these five points lets you explain why the next operation is needed, even during an urgent recovery. Retrying without checking adds one more partial state of unknown cause.

Put a safe preflight first to make failure cheap

Some operations change the environment's state the moment they succeed. Separating the conditions that can be inspected read-only before execution reduces failures that happen after irreversible changes.

As a general design, consider the following order.

  1. Fix the input and the subject: identify the acceptance candidate, the package to run, and the authorized scope.
  2. Static checks: inspect composition, dependencies, format, and hash.
  3. Non-destructive environment checks: confirm the required OS conditions and readable state within the authorized scope.
  4. Recovery assessment: evaluate in advance what state remains after an interrupted run and how to reconcile it.
  5. Authorized change: execute according to an approval that matches the subject and the operation.
  6. Real-machine readback: compare the OS terminal record with the durable result.
  7. Normal job acceptance: confirm authentication and roles, shutdown, output persistence, and independent review.

This order is a design proposal. We do not claim that the current Controller implementation follows it. Acceptance of a normal job remained incomplete as of November 1, 2026.

What RED→GREEN should confirm

What follows is a generalized approach, not a result carried out on the Controller. Once you find a failure condition, first pin a local counterexample. For example, remove an environmental condition that the package-building logic assumes, using a safe fixture, and confirm that the preflight stops correctly. That is the RED state.

Next, add the minimum condition check or recovery and confirm that the same fixture turns GREEN. Loosening a protection mechanism for testing at this point can weaken the production permission guarantee. Keep the operations that must be refused refused, and give a reason only to the operations that are needed. Testing only the happy path is not enough; include the conditions that must fall explicitly into a hold.

Abnormal case Expected behavior
Package hash mismatch Do not proceed to the real-machine operation; hold
Execution authority expired or mismatched with the subject Stop and await a new, correctly scoped approval
Inconsistent existing-generation information Preserve history and investigate the cause
Preflight finds a missing condition Report the failure before any state change
postinstall exits nonzero Save the OS result as a failure and inspect partial state
Child-process termination unconfirmed Stop promotion to SUCCESS
Real job output cannot be saved Hold job acceptance and inspect the durable record

This table generalizes the refusal and stop conditions to aim for. When applying it to a real product, build tests that fit the assets being protected and the OS specification.

Keep acceptance as a record per stage

Bringing AI into the development process increases the number of times an agent reports "implementation complete" or "tests passed". If the granularity of those reports is vague, a source fix gets taken as a successful start of operations.

We treat each stage as an independent unit of acceptance. The following is a generalized design example. It was constructed to explain the stages and is separate from the actual state names of any product. There are six state names, and they map to the five boundaries from the introduction as follows: SOURCE_REVIEWED and CI_ACCEPTED are "source", PACKAGE_VERIFIED is "package", OS_INSTALL_ACCEPTED is "OS installation", and AUTHORIZED_REAL_JOB_ACCEPTED covers "authorization" and "a real AI job". The final INDEPENDENT_OPERATIONAL_REVIEW is not a boundary but an independent check of the whole.

SOURCE_REVIEWED
      |
      v
CI_ACCEPTED
      |
      v
PACKAGE_VERIFIED
      |
      v
OS_INSTALL_ACCEPTED
      |
      v
AUTHORIZED_REAL_JOB_ACCEPTED
      |
      v
INDEPENDENT_OPERATIONAL_REVIEW

For each stage, record the subject identifier, the observed result, who authorized it, and when it ran. If a stage fails, mark it HOLD and keep the evidence of the earlier stages that succeeded. When the candidate changes, re-examine the stages affected by the change. Keep unknowns visible as unknowns until an authorized observation resolves them.

Example acceptance record 

{
  "candidate": "example-source-revision",
  "packageDigest": "example-package-digest",
  "check": "os_install",
  "observed": "failed",
  "partialState": "requires_reconciliation",
  "authorization": "consumed",
  "realJobAccepted": false,
  "nextGate": "independent_review_before_new_approval"
}

This is fictional data for explanation. It contains no real identifiers or credentials. The record keeps failure and uncertainty as values and does not promote them to success. Any mechanical judgment also needs a design that never promotes an ambiguous value to success.

What to ask an independent review for

An independent review confirms what each piece of evidence actually proves. A review of source changes and tests looks at reproduction of the problem, the changed code and its impact, and boundary conditions including abnormal cases. A review of the package and the real machine looks at the identity of the target bytes, the actual macOS Installer result, and whether anything was partially applied. A review of security and operations looks at the permission boundary and validity of approval, and at output persistence, shutdown, and independent acceptance of the formal job.

The role of an independent review is less about running more tests and more about verifying assumptions the implementer may have missed. For operations that change permissions and OS state in particular, confirm that the reviewed source matches the actual subject of the operation that is later approved.

A minimal check you can run yourself

You can observe what does not become "success" when postinstall fails, using a test package that contains nothing confidential. The steps below were run and confirmed on macOS 26.6.2 on November 1, 2026. They use no administrator privileges and target the user's home directory. The package is empty, and no files are installed.

  1. Create and enter a temporary directory, then create scripts/postinstall and make it fail on purpose. 
work=$(mktemp -d) && cd "$work" && mkdir -p scripts
printf '#!/bin/sh\necho "demo postinstall: failing on purpose" >&2\nexit 1\n' > scripts/postinstall
chmod +x scripts/postinstall
  1. Build the package and record its hash. 
pkgbuild --nopayload --scripts ./scripts --identifier com.example.demo --version 1.0 ./demo.pkg
shasum -a 256 demo.pkg
  1. Install into the user domain and record the exit status and the log. 
installer -pkg demo.pkg -target CurrentUserHomeDirectory; echo "exit=$?"
grep 'com.example.demo\|demo.pkg' /var/log/install.log | tail -5

In our run, installer printed "The install failed" and ended with exit=1, and /var/log/install.log recorded PKInstallErrorDomain Code=112 (the explanatory text in parentheses depends on the display language; if you cannot find the log line, search for Code=112). If you cannot read the log, the exit status alone is enough to identify the failure. For comparison, rebuilding with exit 0 instead of exit 1 gave exit=0 and "The install was successful". An empty package does not appear in the list of installed packages (pkgutil --pkgs) even when it succeeds, so its absence from that list cannot be used as evidence of failure.

  1. In the same shell as step 1, delete the temporary directory. /var/log/install.log keeps a record of the run, which is an ordinary system log entry. 
[ -f "$work/demo.pkg" ] && cd / && rm -rf "$work"

What this confirms is the gap that a package whose identity is confirmed by its hash can still fail OS installation. One observation is complete when you write "observed": "failed" in the acceptance record above and inspect the remaining state before any rerun.

Where to start when applying this to another product

First, write down the scope your usual CI protects. Then list the execution environments outside CI. For the macOS Installer, that is the OS installation result; for a web service, the deployment target and the anonymous production page; for an AI agent, legitimate authentication and the completion of a real task.

You do not need to build a large management platform from the start. Linking the source SHA, check results, release file, and real-environment acceptance result for a single change into one record is enough to make it easier to see where the work stopped. Next, add the person responsible for each stage and its stop conditions.

When a check fails, look at that record before starting any additional run. Reuse valid results for subjects that have not changed, and safely isolate only the parts whose cause remains.

Summary: the last thing to confirm is whether the work actually ran

The Controller migration confirmed that failures can remain in the OS installation and authentication stages even after CI succeeds. The fact that the unauthenticated diagnostic succeeded is kept as valid evidence, while the authenticated stages and the real job need additional acceptance. Work that is still in progress as of November 1, 2026 is not treated as a completed result.

Completing real operations requires evidence that the machine accepted the specified package, started the work with legitimate authority, and finished output persistence, shutdown, and review. Even when AI raises development speed, responsibility for this final confirmation stays with the development team.

Go one step beyond source and CI acceptance: include real-environment and real-use confirmation in the plan, with separate evidence for each stage.
That is the lesson that generalizes from these failures and the recovery process.
