title: 50% of CPU time was memory stalls, so I re-ran the test
description:
50% of CPU time was memory stalls, so I re-ran the test

Pivot's October 28 post makes a claim that sounds like an excuse until you read the perf counters: on a naive hash GROUP BY over 99 million ClickBench rows, the CPU reported 100% busy while spending 50.1% of its slots stalled on memory and only 16.1% actually retiring instructions. Partition the keys into 4,096 radix buckets first, and the stall share falls to 23.5%, retiring rises to 32.2%, DRAM traffic drops from 4.5 GB to 1.5 GB. The database did more instructions (19.35 billion retired micro-ops vs 11.43 billion) and still finished faster: 3.6 seconds became 2.7 on the second run.

I believed the direction but not the round numbers, so I rebuilt the experiment at a scale my VM can hold: 20 million rows, about 3.4 million unique keys, one C program, same two algorithms.

// naive: one open-addressing hash table for all keys
size_t s = hash64(k) & MASK;
while (hk[s] && hk[s] != k) s = (s + 1) & MASK;
// radix: hash, take the top 12 bits, push into 1 of 4096 partitions,
// then aggregate each partition with its own small table
int p = (hash64(keys[i]) >> 52) & 4095;

First, the latency ladder, because it explains everything else. Pointer-chasing a randomly permuted array on this box (AMD EPYC 9D25, L1d 32 KB, L2 1 MB, L3 32 MB, from /sys):

     32 KB :   2.7 ns   (L1)
    256 KB :   7.1 ns
   1024 KB :  17.1 ns   (L2)
   8192 KB :  34.8 ns   (L3)
  32768 KB : 122.4 ns   (L3-sized, but shared/noisy on this VM)
 262144 KB : 222.9 ns   (DRAM)

Two honest caveats before the headline number. This is a cloud VM, not Pivot's bare-metal Genoa box, so my DRAM latency (223 ns) is far worse than their 50–100 ns, and the 32 MB step lands at 122 ns instead of the textbook 10–15 ns — a shared, noisy L3 does not behave like the datasheet. The shape of the cliff is still unmistakable: crossing from cache to DRAM costs roughly 80x the L1 latency here.

Then the GROUP BY itself, 20,000,000 rows, 3,390,516 distinct keys, both algorithms verified to the same count (sum of counts = 20,000,000 exactly):

naive hash : 0.958 s, groups=3390516, sum=20000000
radix 4096 : 0.234 s (aggregate phase only), groups=3390516, sum=20000000
radix end-to-end (count+fill+aggregate): 0.534 s, speedup vs naive: 1.79x

The aggregate phase alone runs 4.10x faster, but that number flatters radix: partitioning is real work, and the end-to-end figure is the one that counts. (An earlier run gave 0.975 s naive / 0.263 s aggregate-only, so treat the second decimal as noise, not signal.) Even with the fill included, radix wins by 1.79x, for exactly Pivot's reason — each partition's hash table is small enough to live in cache, so the random accesses that used to miss to DRAM mostly hit L2/L3 instead.

So the trade is real, and it generalizes beyond databases: when your working set is bigger than cache, you are not buying compute, you are buying memory round-trips. Doing more instructions to make those round-trips shorter is a good deal — 19.35 billion cheap operations beat 11.43 billion operations that each wait 223 ns. The next time a profile shows a hot CPU at 100%, check what fraction of it is actually retiring work before you reach for a faster machine. A faster machine with the same memory wall just stalls faster.

Sources: Pivot, "It's the memory latency, stupid" (Oct 28, 2026) — naive 3.9s/3.6s, 50.1% backend-bound, 16.1% retiring, 76,190,837 DRAM fills; radix 3.3s/2.7s, 23.5%, 32.2%, 25,688,280 fills; full engine 1.848s single-core, 171.8ms on 16 cores. My numbers: this VM, gcc -O2, single thread, code and raw output kept with the run notes.

title: CDC Schema Changes: What Breaks and How to Ship Them
description:
On Friday at 17:40, someone renamed one column in the orders table. The pipeline stayed green all weekend. On Monday, the revenue dashboard showed zero for Saturday and Sunday. Nothing failed, and that was the problem.

This is Part 5 of CDC in Production. In Part 4 the sink learned to survive duplicates, late events and deletes. This time the table itself changes. We'll follow a schema change through the pipeline, look at the registry rules that decide what's allowed, see what Snowflake and the lakehouse can absorb, and finish with a migration pattern that never breaks either side.

Prefer to watch? Here's the 7-minute video version with animated diagrams:

Video link: CDC Schema Changes: What Breaks and How to Ship Them

How a schema change travels

Postgres logical decoding (the feature that turns the write-ahead log into row changes) doesn't carry DDL. So Debezium never sees the ALTER TABLE itself. It notices the new shape on the next row change for that table and refreshes its in-memory schema. That event goes out with the new structure.

If you use Avro, the converter then registers the new structure as a new schema version in Schema Registry, a service that stores every version of each message schema. Versions are grouped under a subject; with the default naming, the value schema for topic shop.public.orders lives under shop.public.orders-value. Before accepting a new version, the registry runs a compatibility check against what's already there.

The converter is configured on the connector (or the Connect worker):

"value.converter": "io.confluent.connect.avro.AvroConverter",
"value.converter.schema.registry.url": "http://schema-registry:8081"

Registry compatibility modes

Compatibility is the rule the registry uses to decide whether a new version may be registered. The default is BACKWARD.

Mode Guarantee Upgrade first
BACKWARD (default) Consumers using the new schema can read data written with the old one Consumers
FORWARD Consumers using the old schema can read data written with the new one Producers
FULL Both directions Either side, independently

By default the check compares only against the latest version. The _TRANSITIVE variants (BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE and so on) compare against every version, which matters if a consumer might replay old data from the start of a topic.

What does that allow in practice, with Avro?

Change BACKWARD FORWARD FULL
Add an optional field (has a default) ✅ ✅ ✅
Remove an optional field ✅ ✅ ✅
Add a required field (no default) ❌ ✅ ❌
Remove a required field ✅ ❌ ❌

All of it comes from one rule in Avro's schema resolution: if the reader's schema has a field with no default, and the data was written without that field, the read fails. With Debezium, a nullable Postgres column becomes an optional field with a null default. A NOT NULL column becomes a required field, unless Debezium can carry the column's default value into the schema (it does this for many defaults; for function defaults, see mistake 4 below).

The rename, two ways

amount_cents became total_cents. To Debezium, that's one field gone and a new one added.

If the column is NOT NULL, the new field is required, with no default. Under BACKWARD, the registry rejects it. The converter throws, and with Kafka Connect's default errors.tolerance=none, the connector task fails. That's loud, and loud is good: someone gets paged on Friday.

In the real incident, the column was nullable. Both fields are optional, so the registry accepts the change and nothing turns red. Snowflake, with schema evolution switched on, adds a TOTAL_CENTS column. The old AMOUNT_CENTS column gets NULL on every new row. Every dashboard still sums AMOUNT_CENTS, so weekend revenue reads zero.

A failed connector is the good outcome. The dangerous schema changes are the ones every system accepts.

What Snowflake absorbs

Schema evolution lets a load add columns to the target table automatically. It needs three things:

ALTER TABLE analytics.orders SET ENABLE_SCHEMA_EVOLUTION = TRUE;

-- The loading role needs EVOLVE SCHEMA (or OWNERSHIP) on the table
GRANT EVOLVE SCHEMA ON TABLE analytics.orders TO ROLE loader;

and a supported loading method: COPY INTO (with MATCH_BY_COLUMN_NAME), Snowpipe, or Snowpipe Streaming. Plain INSERT can't evolve a table.

And it does only two things:

  • it adds new columns, and
  • it drops NOT NULL from columns that are missing in new data.

It never renames and never changes a type.

Type changes through ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN are stricter still:

Change Allowed?
Make a VARCHAR longer ✅
Raise a number's precision ✅
Change a number's scale ❌
Make a VARCHAR shorter ❌
Turn a number into a VARCHAR ❌

So if Postgres moves price from numeric(10,2) to numeric(12,4), Snowflake can't follow in place. The scale changed. You add a new column, backfill it, and switch readers over, which is the pattern at the end of this post.

The lakehouse: more forgiving, not magic

Apache Iceberg tracks every column by a unique field ID, not by its name. Renames and drops are metadata changes, so no data files are rewritten. A new column gets a fresh ID, so it never reads old data by mistake, even if it reuses an old name. Type changes are limited to safe widening: int to long, float to double, or a decimal with more precision and the same scale.

Delta Lake can rename and drop columns only with column mapping enabled:

ALTER TABLE orders SET TBLPROPERTIES (
  'delta.columnMapping.mode' = 'name',
  'delta.minReaderVersion'   = '2',
  'delta.minWriterVersion'   = '5'
);

That's a protocol upgrade you can't undo, and after a rename or drop it can break readers of the table's change data feed.

Here's the catch for both formats: a CDC sink still sees a rename as a dropped field and a new one, because that's what the events say. Unless you rename the table column yourself, you get the same split as in Snowflake.

Expand, then contract

The safe pattern is expand/contract: make the schema bigger first, move everything over, and only then make it smaller. A rename becomes four steps:

-- 1. Expand: add the new column as nullable (or with a constant default)
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN total_cents bigint;

-- 2. Backfill in small batches, and have the application write both columns
UPDATE orders
SET    total_cents = amount_cents
WHERE  total_cents IS NULL
  AND  id BETWEEN 1 AND 50000;

-- 3. Move every reader (views, models, dashboards) to total_cents

-- 4. Contract, weeks later, once nothing reads the old column
ALTER TABLE orders DROP COLUMN amount_cents;

Because amount_cents was nullable, every step only adds or removes an optional field, which the registry accepts in any mode. (Dropping a NOT NULL column removes a required field, which passes BACKWARD but not FORWARD or FULL.) Two practical notes:

  • The backfill is CDC traffic. Every row it updates becomes a change event, which is why it runs in batches.
  • Snowflake won't drop the old column for you. Schema evolution never removes columns. Drop AMOUNT_CENTS in the warehouse yourself once readers have moved.

Two guardrails

Test schemas in CI. Schema Registry has a compatibility endpoint that tells you whether a schema would be accepted, without registering it:

# Wrap the new Avro schema in the request body the registry expects
python3 -c 'import json, sys; print(json.dumps({"schema": open(sys.argv[1]).read()}))' \
  orders-value.avsc > payload.json

curl -X POST \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/vnd.schemaregistry.v1+json' \
  --data @payload.json \
  'http://schema-registry:8081/compatibility/subjects/shop.public.orders-value/versions/latest?verbose=true'
# {"is_compatible":false,"messages":[...]}

Fail the build when is_compatible is false. Remember that a nullable rename passes this check, so it catches only the loud kind of break.

Watch the warehouse. Alert when a new column appears on a captured table, and when a column's null rate jumps:

SELECT DATE_TRUNC('hour', updated_at)              AS hour,
       COUNT(*)                                    AS rows_loaded,
       COUNT_IF(amount_cents IS NULL) / COUNT(*)   AS null_rate
FROM   analytics.orders
WHERE  updated_at >= DATEADD(day, -2, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP())
GROUP  BY 1
HAVING null_rate > 0.2
ORDER  BY 1;

The threshold is yours to pick. Either alert would have caught Friday's rename on Friday night.

Five common mistakes

  1. Renaming a column with a single ALTER. Use expand/contract.
  2. Changing a numeric column's scale in place. Snowflake can't follow.
  3. Setting compatibility to NONE just to get a failed connector running again. You've switched off the only alarm.
  4. Trusting function defaults. Debezium exports a default like CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(6) as a zero value (1970-01-01) in the schema.
  5. Changing a schema during an incremental snapshot. The Postgres connector doesn't support it.

Recap

  • Postgres doesn't send DDL, so the next event carries the new schema.
  • The registry checks compatibility, BACKWARD by default. Optional fields are safe to add or remove; required fields are not.
  • Snowflake adds columns, but never renames or changes types.
  • In the lakehouse, your sink still sees a rename as a drop and an add.
  • So expand, then contract.

This week, find the last schema change on a captured table and check what it did in the warehouse.

The CDC in Production series

  • Part 1: Change Data Capture (CDC) Explained (article · video)
  • Part 2: Debezium Postgres to Kafka: Every Setting Explained (video)
  • Part 3: The Silent CDC Bug: Data Loss With No Errors (video)
  • Previous, Part 4: CDC Deletes, Tombstones and the Idempotent MERGE (video)
  • Part 5: CDC Schema Changes: What Breaks and How to Ship Them (this post · video)
  • Next, Part 6: Running CDC in Production: The WAL Slot Trap (video, out November 2)

If this was useful, the video version has the animated diagrams for every step: watch it on YouTube. Subscribe to Pipeline Whiteboard for more diagram-first data engineering explainers. Next up, in the final part: the WAL slot trap, lag, heartbeats, alerting and runbooks.

title: How Ora benchmarks every major AI agent on Vercel
description:
Ora on Vercel

  • Front end, back end, and agent runtime on one platform

  • Every major agent tested side by side on live sites

  • Hundreds of commits a day from a 16-person engineering team

Ora sends agents onto live websites with instructions to sign up for a product, integrate with it, and pay for it. Agents often fail, and by Ora's estimate, 99% of the web isn't agent-ready. The platform shows customers where and why agents fail, and what to change.

Assaf Elovic, co-founder of Ora, spent years helping agents discover the web. His previous company, Tavily, built a web search engine for AI agents and was acquired by Nebius earlier this year. Search solved half the problem, but an agent that finds a product still has to actually use it. He and co-founder Liad Yosef started Ora to measure how ready the web is for agents, and to fix the parts that aren't.

Today that means spawning agents against live customer sites from journey.ora.ai, where Ora runs a journey and records the cost, latency, and steps an agent needs to finish a task. The platform runs on Vercel, including the agent runtime.

Benchmarking every major agent side by side

Every harness expects its own infrastructure

Agents decompose into two parts: a model, which does the reasoning, and a harness, the software that gives the model its tools and drives it from step to step. Ora's lineup covers the agents customers use most: Claude Code, ChatGPT, Gemini, Hermes, OpenClaw, and eve, Vercel's agent framework. Ora runs each agent on a customer's website and watches how it handles common workflows.

No two harnesses want the same infrastructure. Each expects its own environment and exposes its steps differently, so Ora runs a separate runtime for every harness and traces every step. Ido Finder, who leads engineering at Ora, calls that side-by-side coverage one of the most valuable things ora brings to its customers.

When an agent stalls in a signup flow, the customer sees which step and what it tried. Without the trace, the result is a score with nothing behind it.

One platform under every harness

Ora built this testing system entirely on Vercel. Front end, back end, and the agent runtime share the same deployment path, logs, and authentication. The agent runtime isn't separate infrastructure to operate; it lives where the rest of the product lives.

Ora benchmarked eve, then built on it

Testing eve like any other harness

When Vercel launched eve, Ora gave it no special treatment. eve went through the same benchmark, under the same conditions, as every other harness in the lineup. Ora works with Vercel Engineering as a design partner, and Finder gave the eve team direct access to the platform to dig into the results.

The initial test put eve against Claude Code across hundreds of real journeys on multiple domains. Both harnesses ran the same models, Claude Fable 5 and Haiku 4.5, and every run gave the agent the same job: integrate with a product.

Ora published three numbers from the comparison:

  • 7% fewer steps to reach the goal

  • 2x native success: twice as many tasks finished on the customer's own site instead of falling back to web search

  • 9% more valid endpoints: more of the endpoints the agent found were ones it could actually call

The benchmark fed back into eve, too. One run surfaced a prompt-caching issue, the eve team shipped a fix, and Ora's next round of results measured roughly 15% lower total cost.

The framework behind Ora's own agents

For a company that benchmarks every major harness for a living, this is not a casual choice. After those results, Ora builds on eve.

Because eve follows the Next.js paradigm, there was little to configure, and tools, skills, and connectors take little code. The feature that sealed it was the sandbox override. An agent framework like eve ships with its own sandbox, the isolated environment where the agent executes, runs tools, and touches files. That's a good default for most teams, because you get safe execution for free. But an agent in the framework's own sandbox runs outside the instrumented environment where Ora traces every step. The override lets the team swap that environment in, so eve agents get recorded like every other harness, with nothing new built.

Journey.ora.ai now has eve on both sides, eve is one of the harnesses it tests, and eve is what it runs on.

How 16 engineers ship hundreds of commits a day

The engineering team is 16 people shipping hundreds of commits a day, and day-to-day infrastructure work belongs to their coding agents. A stack that sits in one place lets those agents run it end to end.

Finder puts the time saved at a few hours a week at least. Elovic credits a similar amount to how well coding agents build with Vercel's libraries.

What's next

Ora is adding more products, and the architecture is growing with them. The team is splitting its platform into microservices, all of them on Vercel. New services deploy to the same infrastructure and talk to each other with no extra configuration, and the internal agents built on eve will run as one more service.

By Ora's own measure, 99% of the web still can't handle an agent that shows up to sign up, integrate, and pay.

About Ora: Ora makes the web agent-ready. Companies use ora to benchmark how AI agents discover, navigate, and interact with their websites, and to build the infrastructure agents need to find, use, and transact with them.

Read more

title: Case Converter: Batch-Renaming PascalCase React Components to kebab-case Without Breaking Imports
description:
Last Tuesday we agreed on a file naming rule. Components move to kebab-case, so ChatWidget.tsx becomes chat-widget.tsx, and the old PascalCase files disappear.

The trigger was mundane. Two teammates on macOS kept hitting broken checkouts because DateRange.tsx and daterange.tsx are two files in CI on Linux, but a single file on their laptops. Same repo, two views of it.

Eleven components. Sounds like one slow afternoon.

I spent most of that afternoon on three problems that have nothing to do with converting case: imports pointing at old paths, Git refusing to notice half my renames, and XMLHttpRequestPanel.tsx coming out of my first script as xmlhttprequestpanel.tsx.

Here is what worked, in Python 3.11.1 and Node v22.13.1, plus the shortcut for small batches.

Method 1: a Python 3.11.1 script that keeps Git history

Plain mv loses the fact that a rename happened. git mv keeps it. My script runs git mv per file, then rewrites every import that points at an old name.

import re
import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path

SPLITTER = re.compile(r"(?<=[a-z0-9])(?=[A-Z])|(?<=[A-Z])(?=[A-Z][a-z])")

# Digits next to acronyms: the splitter cannot guess these.
OVERRIDES = {
    "UserAvatar2FA": "user-avatar-2fa",
    "OAuth2Callback": "oauth2-callback",
}

root = Path(sys.argv[1])
plan = {}
for src in sorted(root.glob("*.tsx")):
    target = root / f"{OVERRIDES.get(src.stem) or '-'.join(p.lower() for p in SPLITTER.split(src.stem))}.tsx"
    if target.name != src.name:
        plan[src] = target

for src, dst in plan.items():
    subprocess.run(["git", "mv", str(src), str(dst)], check=True)
    print(f"{src.name:26} -> {dst.name}")

edited = 0
for path in root.glob("*.tsx"):
    text = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    for old, new in ((s.stem, d.stem) for s, d in plan.items()):
        text = re.sub(rf"([./]){old}(?=\")", rf"\g<1>{new}", text)
    if text != path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"):
        path.write_text(text, encoding="utf-8")
        edited += 1

print(f"\nrenamed {len(plan)} files, rewrote imports in {edited} files")

Run it against the component folder, then check that nothing still refers to the old paths.

$ python3 rename_components.py src
ChatWidget.tsx             -> chat-widget.tsx
DateRange.tsx              -> date-range.tsx
Grid2Col.tsx               -> grid2-col.tsx
HTTPClientErrors.tsx       -> http-client-errors.tsx
InvoiceLineItemV2.tsx      -> invoice-line-item-v2.tsx
OAuth2Callback.tsx         -> oauth2-callback.tsx
PDFViewer.tsx              -> pdf-viewer.tsx
SideNavBar.tsx             -> side-nav-bar.tsx
UserAvatar2FA.tsx          -> user-avatar-2fa.tsx
Utils.tsx                  -> utils.tsx
XMLHttpRequestPanel.tsx    -> xml-http-request-panel.tsx

renamed 11 files, rewrote imports in 11 files

$ grep -rn 'from "./[A-Z]' src/*.tsx || echo "(none)"
(none)

Every import got rewritten, so the grep comes back clean, and git mv keeps the batch as 11 renames rather than 11 deletions plus 11 untracked files.

The splitter does the real work. (?<=[a-z0-9])(?=[A-Z]) cuts between a lowercase letter or digit and an uppercase one. (?<=[A-Z])(?=[A-Z][a-z]) cuts before the last capital of an acronym run, which is what turns XMLHttp into XML-Http. Both are zero-width assertions, documented in the Python re reference.

Two names refuse to cooperate. UserAvatar2FA splits into user-avatar2-fa and OAuth2Callback into o-auth2-callback, because the digit rule cannot tell whether a digit attaches forward (2FA) or backward (OAuth2). I gave up on solving that inside the regex and pinned both names in OVERRIDES.

Method 2: the same batch rename in Node v22.13.1

No Python on the machine? The logic ports over directly.

import { execFileSync } from "node:child_process";
import { readdirSync, readFileSync, writeFileSync } from "node:fs";
import path from "node:path";

const root = process.argv[2] ?? "src";
const OVERRIDES = new Map([
  ["UserAvatar2FA", "user-avatar-2fa"],
  ["OAuth2Callback", "oauth2-callback"],
]);
const SPLIT = /(?<=[a-z0-9])(?=[A-Z])|(?<=[A-Z])(?=[A-Z][a-z])/;
const toKebab = (stem) =>
  OVERRIDES.get(stem) ?? stem.split(SPLIT).map((p) => p.toLowerCase()).join("-");

const candidates = readdirSync(root, { encoding: "utf8" })
  .filter((name) => name.endsWith(".tsx"))
  .sort();

const mapping = new Map();
for (const name of candidates) {
  const stem = name.slice(0, -4);
  const target = `${toKebab(stem)}.tsx`;
  if (target === name) continue;
  execFileSync("git", ["mv", path.join(root, name), path.join(root, target)]);
  mapping.set(stem, target.slice(0, -4));
  console.log(`${name.padEnd(26)} -> ${target}`);
}

let edited = 0;
for (const name of readdirSync(root, { encoding: "utf8" })) {
  if (!name.endsWith(".tsx")) continue;
  const file = path.join(root, name);
  const before = readFileSync(file, "utf8");
  let after = before;
  for (const [from, to] of mapping) {
    after = after.replaceAll(new RegExp(`([./])${from}(?=")`, "g"), `$1${to}`);
  }
  if (after !== before) {
    writeFileSync(file, after);
    edited += 1;
  }
}

console.log(`\nrenamed ${mapping.size} files, rewrote imports in ${edited} files`);

String.prototype.split accepts lookbehind in V8, so both assertions work unchanged (MDN covers the lookbehind syntax). The output matched Python line for line: 11 renames, 11 files rewritten, zero leftover imports.

Spot-check the odd names against the Utilvy case converter before trusting either script. If it disagrees with your expectation, the script is usually the wrong one.

Method 3: convert names in a browser tab

Two or three files? Skip the script entirely. Paste the component names into a free case converter, pick kebab-case, copy the result, and pair them up by hand.

It handles whole lists in one paste, so ten names are no slower than one. It runs locally in the tab, which matters on an unreleased branch.

Above a handful of files, go back to a script. The browser gives you the new names, but someone still has to rewrite eleven import blocks, and a web page cannot do that part.

Three things that cost me the afternoon

Straight lowercasing destroys acronym boundaries

My very first line was this:

>>> "XMLHttpRequestPanel".lower()
'xmlhttprequestpanel'

Same for HTTPClientErrors turning into httpclienterrors and PDFViewer into pdfviewer. Every word boundary vanishes, and there is no way back from a flattened string. This browser-based tool keeps those boundaries intact, which makes it a decent oracle when you want to argue with your own regex. Split first, lowercase second.

Renaming the file is only half the job, and the failure is silent

My first rewrite used a guard I thought was clever:

text = re.sub(rf'(?<!/){old}(?=")', new, text)

Every import path in a TypeScript file starts with ./. The guard rejected all of them, and the script printed:

renamed 11 files, rewrote imports in 0 files

Eleven renames, zero rewrites, exit code 0. Nothing broke visibly until the next build. Use a capture group instead of a lookbehind, then grep for from "./[A-Z] before you commit.

Case-insensitive filesystems hide case-only renames

Utils.tsx to utils.tsx changes nothing but case. Fine on Linux, invisible on macOS and Windows, where Git is configured with core.ignorecase. Here is the reproduction on an ext4 disk:

$ git config core.ignorecase true
$ mv Utils.tsx utils.tsx
$ git status --short
 D Utils.tsx

Only a deletion. git ls-files still lists Utils.tsx, while import Utils from "./utils" points at a file Git no longer tracks. Flip the flag and Git sees both halves:

$ git config core.ignorecase false
$ git status --short
 D Utils.tsx
?? utils.tsx

On macOS, step through a temp name: git mv Utils.tsx tmp-utils.tsx && git mv tmp-utils.tsx utils.tsx. Or do the whole batch in CI where the filesystem takes casing seriously.

Pick your approach

Scenario Approach Handled 11 files in
Whole repo to migrate Python 3.11.1 script + git mv one run, imports rewritten
Python unavailable Node v22.13.1 equivalent one run, identical output
Two or three names Browser-based kebab conversion under a minute

Verify in this order: grep for leftover PascalCase imports, then read git status on a case-sensitive filesystem, then commit.

More free browser-based utilities at utilvy.com

title: How to Use a Node.js API for 3 Enabled Feature Flag Checks: Gaming Costs
description:
A feature flag check is useful only when the resulting checkout failure can be assigned to the decision that caused it. Record the evaluated flag state, a stable checkout attempt identifier, the failure class, and the cost bucket in one structured event. Keep high-cardinality payment details out of the event, retain the decision record for the period your reconciliation process requires, and sample only the surrounding diagnostic data.

That is the short answer. The API can return an enabled state with a small JSON response, but the observability boundary should emit an audit-shaped record at the same decision point. A successful response is not proof that the rollout was safe; it is evidence that one request received one evaluation.

Keep the decision record boring.

How can a Node.js API check whether a feature flag is enabled?

In a game checkout, a flag may select a payment flow, a promotion, or a risk rule. The important unit is the checkout attempt, not the HTTP request. Retries, redirects, and client reconnects can produce several requests for one economic action. Use an idempotency key or an equivalent stable attempt ID, then associate every evaluation with that ID.

I would record three states for each decision: the requested flag key, the evaluated boolean, and the evaluation reason. The reason is deliberately constrained: default, targeted, rollout, or error. A missing flag should not silently look like false, because a disabled feature and an evaluation failure have different operational and financial meanings.

The event also needs a cost attribution field. For example, authorization, inventory, fulfillment, or reconciliation can identify the downstream work that failed or must be repeated. This is a business classification, not a price claim. It lets an incident review ask which branch accumulated work without putting card data, player identity, or a raw provider response into the log.

I start with three questions: what did the evaluator decide, what side effect followed, and which cost bucket owns the retry? Those questions keep a feature check attached to an economic action instead of a loose request log.

Implement the decision boundary before the checkout side effect

The flag service interface should return a decision object, while the checkout code owns the audit event. That separation makes a test able to assert both behavior and evidence. Here is a compact Go example of the boundary; the same fields can be serialized by a Node.js API handler when that is the surrounding application runtime.

package checkout

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "io"
)

type FlagDecision struct {
    Key    string
    On     bool
    Reason string
}

type FlagReader interface {
    Evaluate(context.Context, string, string) (FlagDecision, error)
}

type AuditEvent struct {
    AttemptID  string `json:"attempt_id"`
    FlagKey    string `json:"flag_key"`
    Enabled    bool   `json:"enabled"`
    Reason     string `json:"reason"`
    CostBucket string `json:"cost_bucket"`
    Outcome    string `json:"outcome"`
}

func CaptureDecision(ctx context.Context, flags FlagReader, out io.Writer, attemptID string) (bool, error) {
    d, err := flags.Evaluate(ctx, "new_checkout", attemptID)
    if err != nil {
        return false, err
    }
    e := AuditEvent{
        AttemptID: attemptID, FlagKey: d.Key, Enabled: d.On,
        Reason: d.Reason, CostBucket: "authorization", Outcome: "evaluated",
    }
    if err := json.NewEncoder(out).Encode(e); err != nil {
        return false, err
    }
    return d.On, nil
}

The ordering matters. Evaluate and record the decision before creating an authorization or reserving inventory. If the audit write is asynchronous, the event must still carry the same attempt ID and an idempotency key; otherwise a retry can create an apparently new decision. Exactly-once delivery is usually an aspiration at transport level, so make the consumer idempotent and deduplicate on the decision identity.

Which retention choice preserves cost evidence?

The bill is rarely driven by the boolean itself. It is driven by volume, payload size, retention, and the number of derived indexes or exports. In this scenario, the dominant controllable term is often repeated diagnostic payload attached to every checkout retry. A small decision event with bounded fields can stay longer than a verbose request trace, while still supporting reconciliation.

That is a trade-off, not a free optimization. I would retain the decision record and a compact failure classification, then keep full traces for a shorter, explicitly documented window. When a failure is disputed later, the retained event can prove which branch was selected; it cannot reconstruct a discarded request body or a payment processor response. The latter should be recovered from the system of record under its own access controls, not copied into observability storage.

A practical retention review measures three quantities separately: decision events per checkout attempt, bytes per event, and retained days. Do not turn a cost dashboard into a second ledger. Observability can explain why work happened, while the ledger remains authoritative for money and settlement.

The identifier is the anchor.

Record Keep longer Why
Flag decision Yes Proves branch selection and evaluation reason
Failure class Yes Supports cost attribution without raw payloads
Full request trace Usually no Larger, more sensitive, and less durable evidence

How should failure tests distinguish disabled from unknown?

Test the decision contract at the boundary. A disabled flag should skip the new side effect and produce an auditable enabled=false decision. An evaluation error should follow the declared fail-open or fail-closed rule, record reason=error, and produce a different cost attribution path. The choice depends on the operation: showing a cosmetic offer and authorizing a charge do not have the same risk.

Use a deterministic attempt ID in tests and replay the same request twice. The second execution should not create a second authorization, second reservation, or second economic decision. It may create a transport-level retry record, but that record must point to the original decision. This is where an apparently harmless feature-flag example becomes a payment correctness problem.

Keep the rollout review equally concrete. Compare failure counts by flag state and cost bucket, check that the denominator is checkout attempts rather than raw requests, and investigate missing decision events before interpreting a drop as improvement. A missing record is an observability failure, not a zero.

I would stop retaining full checkout payloads in the general-purpose event stream once the decision record, failure class, and authoritative ledger reference are sufficient for the review. The reasoning is specific: a flag event answers which branch was selected, a failure class answers which operational work was affected, and the ledger reference answers what financial state was ultimately recorded. Keeping the payload after those three answers exist adds sensitive material without making the branch decision more trustworthy. That reduces exposure and keeps retention analysis legible, but the cost is slower incident reconstruction when a downstream system omitted its own evidence. The deletion rule therefore needs a tested export or lookup path, an owner for each source of truth, and a review that confirms the lookup still works after the retention window changes. A team that cannot recover the authoritative reference should not delete the diagnostic field merely because the dashboard looks quieter.

The final rule is simple: retain the smallest immutable decision record that can explain branch selection and downstream cost, make retries idempotent, and treat missing telemetry as an explicit failure mode. This serves gaming checkout operations without turning a feature-flag check into a product-specific observability tutorial.

Further reading

  • OpenTelemetry, “Logs signal concepts”: https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/logs/

title: Xbox Wireless Controller Keeps Disconnecting? Test It in 5 Minutes Before You Replace It
description:
Nothing kills a ranked match faster than a controller that drops out mid-fight. Before you spend money on a replacement, run a quick diagnosis — most disconnects come from a short list of fixable causes, and you can narrow it down in about five minutes.

1. Rule out the battery first

Low batteries cause the classic symptom: the pad works fine for a while, then cuts out under vibration or heavy input. Swap in fresh alkalines or a fully charged pack, even if the dashboard still shows a bar or two. If the disconnects stop, you just saved yourself a replacement.

2. Test wired

Plug the controller in over USB and play for a few minutes. If it stays rock solid wired but drops wirelessly, the problem is in the wireless link, not the controller's inputs. If it still drops over USB, suspect the cable, the port, or the controller board itself — try a different cable and a different USB port before concluding anything.

3. Check the wireless environment

Bluetooth and the Xbox wireless adapter both hate interference. Move closer to the console or PC, remove anything between you and the receiver, and unplug nearby USB 3 devices that sit right next to the dongle — they are a known source of 2.4 GHz noise. Other controllers, headsets, and even a microwave in the next room can crowd the band. Retest with fewer wireless devices active.

4. Update firmware and drivers

Outdated controller firmware causes disconnects that look like hardware failure. On Xbox, update through the Accessories app; on PC, update through the Xbox Accessories app from the Microsoft Store and check Windows Update for Bluetooth driver updates. Retest after every update — do not stack three changes at once, or you will never know which one fixed it.

5. Confirm the inputs still work

Once the connection holds, check that every button, trigger, and stick actually registers. A pad that stays connected but misses inputs has a different problem. Open a free online gamepad tester in your browser, press every button, squeeze both triggers through their full travel, and move both sticks in slow circles. Anything that sticks, skips, or fails to reach full range is a hardware fault, not a connection fault.

You can test your Xbox controller online for free — it shows live button, trigger, and stick readings in the browser, no install needed.

When to replace, honestly

Replace the controller if it still disconnects over USB with a known-good cable, after a firmware update, with fresh power. Repair or replace the wireless adapter first if wired play is perfect and only wireless drops. And if the pad disconnects only in one game, check that game's controller settings before blaming hardware — a game-side bug does not need a new controller.

Five minutes of testing beats a blind purchase. Test wired, test wireless, update, then check the inputs — in that order.

title: Death to long-lived static credentials
description:
Fifteen years ago, TLS was something you'd use to protect the most sensitive areas of your app. Then Google, Let's Encrypt, the EFF, and others led the push for HTTPS everywhere, making encryption the default for every request. Without it, anyone between the browser and server can read and tamper with the traffic.

OAuth, OIDC, DBSC, and related standards already provide building blocks for secure authentication, but standards alone do not make secure methods the norm. HTTPS needed tooling that made encryption easy and a sustained push that made it expected. Machine-to-machine authentication still resembles HTTPS in 2010, with some vendors and enterprises leading the way while long-lived static credentials remain the default for many SaaS vendors and infrastructure providers.

At Vercel, we want to make fast and secure the default across the web, including in our own services and the integrations in our Marketplace. We’ve built OIDC UI, a shadcn/ui registry that gives providers trust-policy forms and token verification code. We’re expanding OIDC support across Vercel and setting new authentication requirements for Marketplace providers.

Long-lived static credentials are insecure

Long-lived static credentials are secrets such as API keys and database passwords that applications keep reusing, often with no expiration. As agents take on more useful work, we give them access to our systems, tools, and data through credentials that can grant permissions far beyond the task at hand.

Those credentials can leak into a code repository or chat, be stolen when a service or dependency is compromised, or be exposed when prompt injection leads an agent to reveal them. However it happens, an attacker can use the credential with the permissions it grants until it expires or is revoked. Recent credential-theft and supply-chain incidents across the industry show why encryption at rest isn’t enough when malicious code can read an application’s credentials in production.

Rotating exposed credentials takes time and coordination across the systems that use them, and mistakes can disrupt production. At Vercel, we’ve previously spent thousands of engineering hours on multiple, very painful key rotations out of an abundance of caution, and we never want to have to do this again.

Better solutions already exist

With OIDC, your application can authenticate without storing a long-lived provider key. A trusted issuer provides a signed, short-lived token identifying the application, and the receiving service verifies that token before deciding what access to grant.

A stolen token stops working when it expires, limiting how long that copy can be used even if the leak goes unnoticed. Your application can obtain fresh credentials programmatically, removing the need to distribute and manually rotate a persistent provider key across the systems that use it.

We’ve been prioritizing OIDC across Vercel so applications can access Blob, AI Gateway, and Sandbox without storing long-lived keys for those services. Our OIDC federation has been generally available since 2024, letting applications running on Vercel exchange Vercel-issued identity tokens for temporary AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure credentials under configured project and environment trust policies. But for developers to stop managing long-lived keys, that support has to extend to all the services their applications depend on.

The rest of the web hasn’t followed

We surveyed more than 1,000 SaaS vendors and found that only 8.4% supported secure authentication methods.

But getting vendors to support secure authentication is only part of the problem. Even when a service offers a secure method, developers often choose a static key because it can be simpler to use. We see three main barriers to broader adoption:

  • Tooling and setup that make secure authentication more complicated than using a static key.

  • Added latency from fetching or exchanging tokens on the request path.

  • Weak incentives for vendors to offer and prioritize secure authentication.

Our goal is to make secure authentication the default on Vercel, while also using our Marketplace to help push more vendors to support it.

Our commitment to a more secure web

We have a responsibility to make this change practical across the services we run, the tools developers use, and the integrations we build with partners.

Make secure authentication easier to use

Using a secure token has to be easier than pasting a key, or developers will keep pasting keys. On Vercel, code retrieves an OIDC token with a function call, and a custom audience specifies the service intended to receive it.

With Vercel Connect, applications and agents use their deployment identity to request provider tokens at runtime, without having to store long-lived provider secrets in environment variables. Once the connector is configured and linked to the project and the user’s account is connected, code can request a token for that user with scopes the provider supports.

We’re also extending OIDC support across the Vercel API and CLI to remove the need for long-lived Vercel tokens in deployment workflows.

OIDC UI for API providers

OIDC UI is a shadcn/ui component registry with a trust-policy configurator and a server-side token verifier. It includes provider forms for Vercel, GitHub, GitLab, Google, Bitbucket, AWS, Azure, and custom OIDC issuers. A provider can let customers configure trust for a particular Vercel project’s production environment, then verify incoming tokens against that policy without building the configuration interface and verification code from scratch.

Reduce the performance cost of secure authentication

A static key in an environment variable is already available when a function runs, so reading it requires no network request. Fetching a token or exchanging it for provider credentials can add network latency, so reducing those calls is part of making secure authentication practical.

Vercel Functions receive a platform-issued token in the request header, which the SDK reads without fetching another. The platform reuses unexpired tokens, while Vercel Connect caches provider tokens in process and refreshes them near expiry. Custom-audience and provider exchanges require network calls.

For example, an application can use the Azure SDK to access Cosmos DB with temporary credentials instead of a database key. With Azure configured to trust the Vercel project and its default token audience, the callback supplies a Vercel OIDC token to ClientAssertionCredential, which exchanges it for the Azure access token used by CosmosClient.

Give providers an incentive to support secure authentication

The Vercel Marketplace offers access to third-party databases, content management systems, observability tools, and more. Our goal is for all of these vendors to support short-lived, identity-based authentication, whether they accept OIDC tokens directly or exchange them for temporary credentials. We’re working to make integrations configure that authentication automatically when developers connect a service, so it does not require a separate setup step.

HTTPS everywhere did not win on ergonomics alone. Chrome put a “Not secure” label on plain HTTP, and then it set deadlines. Now we are setting ours. By November 30, 2026, vendors who do not support OIDC auth from Vercel to their services and use long-lived secrets for authentication will have a similar “Not secure” message on their listing. By January 2027, vendors who do not offer secure auth will be delisted. We are holding the Vercel API and our own native integrations to the same bar.

From static to dynamic

Fifteen years ago, encrypting every request felt like overkill. Today, the padlock is so normal that we only notice when it's missing. Secure authentication between services should become just as routine, so developers can connect the systems they need without storing another long-lived secret. Going from static to dynamic has always been the Vercel mission. It started with pages, and now it’s credentials.

Additional resources

  • OIDC federation covers how deployments get short-lived identity tokens, with guides for AWS, GCP, Azure, and your own API.

  • Custom OIDC token audiences scopes each token to the one service meant to receive it.

  • Vercel Connect requests short-lived, scoped provider tokens at runtime, so code and agents never store credentials.

  • Vercel Connect guides walk through building agents this way, from Slack bots to GitHub agents.

Read more

title: Node.js Example OpenAI GPT API Integration for Product Text Summarization
description:
The hard part of using a Node.js example to integrate the OpenAI GPT API for text summarization is not producing one short paragraph. It is keeping the catalog pipeline portable when a provider changes its client library, authentication model, or output behavior. My default is to isolate summarization behind a small adapter, use a chat-completion interface for the first useful result, and keep the input contract provider-neutral.

For a team already standardized on OpenAI, the direct OpenAI API is the shortest path. For a team testing several vendors, Infrai is a reasonable integration layer to try because its public discovery surface exposes schemas and runnable examples before a key is required. That matters when adding a capability should involve inspecting one contract rather than learning another SDK. It is a fit for the adapter boundary, not a reason to pretend every model is interchangeable.

What does portability require in a catalog pipeline?

Start with the data boundary. A catalog record should hand the model a bounded description and a precise instruction: preserve factual attributes, remove sales language, and return a concise summary. The application should own truncation or chunking for long descriptions; letting an SDK silently decide what to drop makes later provider comparisons hard to interpret.

The output should be treated as generated text, not as the source of truth for price, dimensions, or compliance claims. Store the original description beside the summary, record the provider and model selected, and validate the result before publishing it. This is more operational work than calling a model once. It is also what makes a migration measurable.

The useful first test is deliberately small: one record, one bounded prompt, one summary, and a saved request identifier. I initially thought the provider choice would dominate the design. The adapter contract does. If the rest of the catalog service knows a vendor-specific message shape, portability has already been lost.

Keep it boring.

The first failure mode I test is silent truncation: a 12,000-character bound can remove a specification table, while a 45-word output limit can hide a required attribute. I keep those numbers in application configuration, preserve the original description, and compare a direct result with a chunked result before changing providers. That is a concrete boundary, not a benchmark claim.

Which integration path reaches a useful summary fastest?

Option Credentials and setup SDK surface Boundary
OpenAI API One OpenAI API key and the OpenAI client pattern A focused chat-completion call Best when the catalog team already owns this provider and wants the fewest moving parts
Anthropic API A separate provider credential and its messages-oriented client pattern A different request and response contract Good for teams willing to maintain a second adapter and evaluate its output separately
Google Vertex AI Google Cloud project and platform authentication Cloud-platform configuration plus model invocation Useful when identity, governance, and deployment already live in Google Cloud
Infrai One Infrai key for the unified surface A plain REST surface with public discovery and runnable examples Useful when provider portability and capability discovery outweigh direct-vendor simplicity

These are different operational choices, not four interchangeable model names. Direct OpenAI has the cleanest match to the question this article starts from: authenticate with an OpenAI key, instruct a chat model to summarize, and tune temperature and max_tokens. Anthropic and Vertex AI are credible alternatives, but each adds a distinct credential or client contract that the adapter must absorb. Infrai reduces that particular discovery friction across a broad surface: its live discovery reports 295 routes across 20 modules, with schemas and runnable examples exposed per capability.

The trade-off is worth stating plainly. A unified layer adds one more boundary to understand, and a direct provider may be preferable when a team needs provider-specific controls or the specialist's native feature set. Portability is valuable only if the boundary preserves the controls the workload actually needs.

How should a Node.js service integrate OpenAI GPT API text summarization?

The following example keeps the provider-specific work in one function. A Node.js service can use axios or the openai npm package against the same contract; this Python sample keeps the HTTP method, URL, headers, status handling, and retry behavior visible. The model name is a configuration choice; do not treat it as a promise that every model has identical context or output behavior.

import os
import random
import time

import requests


def summarize_description(description: str) -> str:
    api_key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
    bounded_description = description[:12000]
    prompt = (
        "Summarize this product description in 45 words or fewer. "
        "Keep factual product attributes, remove promotional claims, and "
        "do not invent missing information.\n\n"
        f"Product description:\n{bounded_description}"
    )

    for attempt in range(4):
        try:
            response = requests.post(
                "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/chat/completions",
                headers={
                    "Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}",
                    "Content-Type": "application/json",
                },
                json={
                    "model": "deepseek-v4.1-flash",
                    "messages": [
                        {
                            "role": "system",
                            "content": "You produce factual e-commerce catalog summaries.",
                        },
                        {"role": "user", "content": prompt},
                    ],
                    "temperature": 0.2,
                    "max_tokens": 180,
                },
                timeout=60,
            )
            if response.status_code == 429:
                if attempt == 3:
                    response.raise_for_status()
                retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
                delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2**attempt
                time.sleep(delay + random.random())
                continue
            if not response.ok:
                raise RuntimeError(
                    f"Summarization failed with HTTP {response.status_code}: "
                    f"{response.text}"
                )
            content = response.json().get("choices", [{}])[0].get("message", {}).get("content")
            if not content:
                raise RuntimeError("The provider returned no summary text")
            return content.strip()
        except requests.RequestException as error:
            if attempt == 3:
                raise
            time.sleep((2**attempt) + random.random())

    raise RuntimeError("Summarization retry loop ended unexpectedly")

This is intentionally not a bulk-ingestion worker. For long descriptions, split on meaningful boundaries, summarize chunks, then summarize the chunk summaries; otherwise a truncation rule can silently remove the specifications that customers care about. For a large catalog, queue the records, make the consumer idempotent, and retain the original input so a prompt or provider change can be replayed.

Where does the unified layer help, and where does it stop?

The strongest argument for the unified layer here is integration friction. Its API is self-describing, and the discovery result includes request schemas, response schemas, billing metadata, and runnable examples. That lets an engineer inspect a capability before installing a vendor SDK. The supporting benefit is a consistent credential and REST boundary while the catalog service experiments with providers, instead of distributing provider keys and client conventions through every worker.

I would recommend Infrai to a catalog team that expects to test multiple AI providers and wants discovery plus a runnable request to be part of the integration workflow. I would choose direct OpenAI for a single-provider implementation whose main requirement is the OpenAI chat-completion contract, and I would choose a specialist when its native controls or model behavior are a hard requirement.

The capability boundary also matters. Audio transcription is listed but currently unavailable; real-time voice session keys are pending and limited to the western region; there is no dedicated moderation endpoint, so text or image moderation needs a chat model with a JSON schema fallback; and image upscaling is limited to Lanczos. None of those blocks catalog summarization, but they are reasons to keep capability selection explicit instead of assuming the unified surface covers every adjacent workload.

A controlled rollout is the portability test

Begin with a small evaluation set containing short descriptions, long descriptions, missing attributes, and aggressively promotional copy. Compare summaries for factual retention, length, and unacceptable invention. Keep the prompt stable while changing providers; otherwise a provider result and a prompt change become one indistinguishable experiment.

Then ship the adapter behind a feature flag. Record the chosen provider, model, latency, and failure class, but do not publish generated text before validation. A 429 should delay and retry; a malformed or empty response should be visible as a failed record, not converted into a blank catalog field. The operational detail is unglamorous. It is also where portability either survives or disappears.

For one product record, that means retaining the raw description, the normalized prompt version, the provider name, the model name, the response text, and the validation result as separate fields. If the response is too short, contains a missing required attribute, or arrives after a retry, the worker should preserve the response and mark the record for review rather than overwrite the last accepted summary. If a provider is unavailable, the adapter can route the next attempt according to an explicit policy, but the policy must be visible in the record so a later comparison does not confuse provider selection with prompt quality. I would also keep the chunking decision beside the input: a single bounded request and a multi-chunk reduction are different transformations, even when they produce similar prose. That small amount of bookkeeping is the difference between a portable pipeline and a collection of irreproducible calls.

If this boundary matches your system, start with the capability manifest and inspect the available contract before wiring the worker.

References

  • OpenAI Batch API guide
  • OpenAI API documentation
  • Anthropic Messages API
  • Google Vertex AI generative AI documentation

Sources

  • Infrai AI-readable capability manifest
  • OpenAI Batch API guide

title: Designing for Trust: Lessons from Building a Digital Pilgrimage Service
description:
Most product writing about trust is about payments or privacy. When the "product" is a sacred ritual performed on someone's behalf, trust becomes the whole product. At DigitalSnan, a digital pilgrimage service that connects devotees with rituals at Triveni Sangam in Prayagraj, we have had to think hard about how a website, a booking flow and a WhatsApp conversation can respect a centuries-old practice without overselling it.

Here are the design principles we follow. They apply to any service where the customer cannot see the work being done in person.

1. Say exactly what the service is — and what it is not

The first temptation in faith-tech is to borrow the emotional weight of the real thing. We avoid that. A digital snan is not the same as physically bathing in the Sangam, and our copy says so. What we offer is a sankalp (intention) taken in the devotee's name, with rituals performed at the Sangam by local priests, and the experience shared with the family.

Lesson: precise language reduces support tickets and disputes, and earns long-term credibility. Write the honest version of your value proposition first, then make it warm — never the other way round.

2. Proof of service beats promises

Customers booking from Toronto or Melbourne cannot walk to the ghat. So the core artifact is evidence: names spoken during sankalp, photos or video of the ritual, and a clear timeline. We publish samples openly on YouTube and Instagram so people can judge before booking.

Engineering takeaway: treat "proof" as a first-class data object. Each booking should carry a status, timestamps, the media delivered and who performed it. If you can't reconstruct what happened for an order, you have a trust bug.

3. Time zones are a feature, not a footnote

Our audience is split between India and NRI families in the USA, UK, Canada and Australia. Auspicious timings (muhurat) follow the Indian calendar and IST, while families abroad want to watch together on a weekend in their own zone.

  • Always show IST alongside the customer's local time.
  • Store times in UTC; render per viewer.
  • Explain festival dates in plain language — tithi-based dates shift and confuse people searching by Gregorian date.

4. Low-bandwidth, high-clarity communication

Many devotees — often parents and grandparents — are not comfortable with complex web apps. A phone call or WhatsApp message at +91-97943-76889 is frequently the real interface. The website explains and reassures; the human conversation closes the loop.

Lesson: don't force every user into your funnel. Offer an obvious human channel (we also answer at digitalsnanofficial@gmail.com) and make sure what the human says matches the site.

5. Respect the culture in the UI

Small things matter: correct spelling of ritual names, not using sacred imagery as decoration, no countdown-timer pressure around festivals. Dark patterns are bad everywhere; in devotional contexts they are disrespectful.

6. Don't invent social proof

It's tempting for a young startup to pad testimonials or quote big numbers. We don't. Real ritual footage, transparent pricing and fast replies do the work. If you're early, publish your process instead of vanity metrics — process is verifiable.

7. Content as documentation

Much of our "marketing" is really documentation: what happens during a ritual, what the family should prepare, which festivals matter at Prayagraj. Writing explainers forces internal clarity and answers questions customers would otherwise ask one by one.

8. Build for the festival spike

Demand in devotional services is calendar-driven: Kartik Purnima, Makar Sankranti, Mauni Amavasya, Magh Purnima and Mela years bring sharp peaks. Plan capacity (priests, media editing, support replies) ahead of the calendar, cap bookings honestly when full, and never promise delivery windows you cannot meet. A queue with a clear message beats an overpromise.

Closing thoughts

Faith-tech sits at an unusual intersection: ancient practice, global diaspora and ordinary web tooling. The technology is simple — forms, payments, media delivery, messaging. The hard part is the discipline to be honest, precise and humane at every touchpoint.

Curious how a digital pilgrimage service works end to end? Explore digitalsnan.com or watch ritual videos on our YouTube channel.

title: Vercel Sandbox commands now support stdin
description:
Vercel Sandbox now lets you send input to running commands through standard input (stdin). Use it to exchange messages with stdio MCP servers such as agent-browser, or send data to other command-line programs while they run.

In the TypeScript SDK, set stdin: true and detached: true in runCommand(). Use writeStdin() to send input and closeStdin() when you’re done:

You can also set stdin to a Node.js readable stream, such as process.stdin. The SDK forwards the stream’s data and closes the command’s standard input when the stream ends.

In the Python SDK, set stdin=subprocess.PIPE and send input with server.stdin.send(). Call communicate() to close stdin, collect remaining output, and wait for the process to exit:

For commands that receive all their input at once, you can pass input directly to Python’s run_process().

title: I Built PosterPilot: A Cloudinary-Powered Tool to Adapt University Event Posters Without Cropping Important Details
description:
University societies and event organizers regularly create posters for seminars, workshops, competitions, hackathons, and other campus activities.

However, sharing one poster across different platforms can become challenging. Instagram posts, Instagram Stories, and website previews all require different dimensions. Simply resizing an image can crop important information, such as event titles, dates, venue details, or sponsor logos.

To explore how image transformation can solve this problem, I built PosterPilot, a Cloudinary-powered web application that helps users adapt one uploaded event poster into multiple formats.

What is PosterPilot?

PosterPilot is a web-based image adaptation tool designed with university societies and event organizers in mind.

Users upload an event poster once and generate different output formats using Cloudinary image transformations.

The main idea is simple: make poster adaptation easier while giving users control over whether the entire image should remain visible or fill the selected dimensions.

🌐 Live Demo: https://posterpilot.vercel.app
💻 GitHub Repository: https://github.com/alpha5-rdx/posterpilot

The Problem I Wanted to Solve:

Imagine a university society has designed a poster for an upcoming technology event. The society wants to share it in three places:

  • Instagram Square post
  • Instagram Story
  • Website or social media preview

Each platform requires a different image size. Cropping the original poster to fit these dimensions can remove important information.

I wanted to build a simple solution that could generate these formats without requiring users to manually edit the same poster multiple times.

Technology Stack

I used the following technologies:

  1. React: Building the user interface and reusable components.
  2. Vite: Development environment and production build tooling.
  3. JavaScript: Application logic and interactions.
  4. CSS: Responsive styling and layout.
  5. Cloudinary: Image uploading, transformation, delivery, and optimization.
  6. Vercel: Deploying and hosting the application.

The project uses a frontend-only architecture. Cloudinary handles image storage and delivery, so I did not need to build a separate backend for this version.

How Cloudinary Powers PosterPilot?

Cloudinary is the central part of the application.

I integrated Cloudinary's Upload API using an unsigned upload preset. This allows the frontend to upload an image without exposing the Cloudinary API Secret. The application sends the selected image and upload preset to the Cloudinary image upload endpoint: https://api.cloudinary.com/v1_1//image/upload

After a successful upload, Cloudinary returns information such as:

  • Secure image URL
  • Public ID
  • Image dimensions
  • File format
  • File size
  • Asset version

PosterPilot uses the returned image information to generate transformed image URLs.

This approach allows the application to work with one original uploaded image and dynamically generate different versions through Cloudinary transformations.

Five Output Formats

PosterPilot currently supports five predefined formats:

Format: Innsta Square Dimensions: 1080 x 1080
Format: Innsta Story Dimensions: 1080 x 1920
Format: Web/Social Preview Dimensions: 1080 x 1080
Format: LinkedIn Portrait Dimensions: 1080 x 1350
Format: LinkedIn Square Dimensions: 1080 x 1080

Users can preview the generated versions before copying their URLs or downloading the images.

*My Main Feature: No-Crop vs Crop-to-Fill
*
One of the main features I wanted to explore was the difference between preserving the complete image and filling a target canvas.

1. No-Crop Mode

For this mode, I used Cloudinary's c_pad transformation.

Example transformation: c_pad,w_1080,h_1080,b_white/q_auto/f_auto

This transformation fits the original image inside the specified dimensions while preserving the entire image. If the aspect ratios differ, padding is added to complete the canvas.

This is useful when the poster contains important information that should remain visible.

2. Crop-to-Fill Mode

For the alternative mode, I used Cloudinary's c_fill transformation with center gravity.

Example transformation: c_fill,g_center,w_1080,h_1080/q_auto/f_auto

This fills the target dimensions by cropping the image where necessary.

It is useful when users prefer a completely filled canvas and accept that some parts of the original image may be cropped.

Image Optimization and Delivery

I also used two useful Cloudinary transformation parameters:

  • q_auto: Automatically selects an appropriate image quality setting.
  • f_auto: Automatically selects a suitable delivery format based on browser support.

These transformations help optimize image delivery without requiring users to manually create multiple optimized files.

Other Application Features

In addition to image transformations, PosterPilot includes:

  1. Drag-and-drop image upload.
  2. File browsing and image validation.
  3. JPG, PNG, and WebP support.
  4. A 10 MB client-side upload limit.
  5. Upload progress and error handling.
  6. Image replacement and reset functionality.
  7. Copy transformed image URL.
  8. Download transformed images.
  9. Responsive user interface.

Testing and Deployment

After development, I tested the application locally and deployed it using Vercel. I also tested the live application to verify that:

  • Image uploads work with Cloudinary.
  • All three output formats generate correctly.
  • No-Crop and Crop-to-Fill modes update the previews.
  • Generated image URLs can be copied and opened.
  • Transformed images can be downloaded.

The live application is available here: (https://posterpilot.vercel.app)

What I Learned?

Building PosterPilot gave me practical experience with Cloudinary's image upload and transformation capabilities. Some of the important concepts I explored include:

  • Integrating an external image service into a React application.
  • Using unsigned uploads without exposing API secrets.
  • Generating image variations through dynamic transformations.
  • Understanding the difference between padding and cropping.
  • Optimizing images for web delivery.
  • Deploying a frontend application with environment variables.

I also learned that a useful project does not always need a complicated architecture. Sometimes, combining the right service with a focused real-world problem can produce a practical solution.

*What's Next?
*
PosterPilot is an initial version, and there is room for improvement. Some possible future enhancements include:

  • More social media presets.
  • Custom width and height controls.
  • Background color selection for padded images.
  • Batch poster processing.
  • Additional image editing options.

*Final Thoughts
*
PosterPilot started with a simple campus-related problem: adapting event posters into different formats without unnecessarily losing important information.

Through this project, I explored how Cloudinary can make image uploading, transformation, optimization, and delivery easier to integrate into a modern web application.

I'm excited to continue learning, building, and exploring more practical applications of Cloudinary.

I'd appreciate your feedback and suggestions!

title: How long a liquor license takes in Texas, New York City and Los Angeles (data from 1,000+ applications)
description:
Disclosure: I run PourWire, which turns state liquor license and building permit filings into a daily list of restaurants and bars that are about to open. The numbers below come from that pipeline plus the states' own open data. The CSV is public under CC BY 4.0.

The question "how long does a liquor license take" has a different answer in every state, and most answers online are guesses. Here is what the filings say as of October 2026.

The short answer

Where Agency Typical time Measured on
Texas (5 metros) TABC median 24 days from submission to issue (middle half 18 to 34) 144 MB and BG applications filed since June 2026
New York City NY State Liquor Authority applications pending a median of 118 days (middle half 62 to 212); 32% over 6 months 920 restaurant and bar applications pending in the five boroughs
Los Angeles County California ABC median 67 days from application to issue (middle half 54 to 72) 23 issued type 41, 47 and 48 licenses filed since July 2026

How it was measured

Texas. TABC publishes pending applications and issued licenses as two datasets on data.texas.gov. We matched our MB (mixed beverage) and BG (wine and beer) applications in Houston, Dallas-Fort Worth, Austin, San Antonio and Waco-Temple to the original issue date in TABC License Information by owner and permit.

New York City. The SLA queue is the story. data.ny.gov "Current SLA Pending Licenses" lists every application still in review with its received date, so the age of what is waiting today is the honest number. Of the NYC applications we have tracked since June, 25 have been issued so far, a median of 105 days after the SLA received them. That figure is capped by our start date, so the real average is higher.

Los Angeles. California ABC keeps one license number from application to issue, so filing to issue is a direct join. Every new application goes through a 30-day public notice period before ABC investigates, which is why almost nothing issues in under a month (the fastest we saw was 36 days).

Get the data

  • CSV of the wait times with sample sizes and source links: us-liquor-license-applications on GitHub (data/liquor-license-wait-times.csv), plus the last 30 days of new applications across every metro we track, refreshed weekly. Also on Hugging Face.
  • Step by step lookup guides with the license class codes explained:
    • Texas: pending TABC applications, MB, BG and FB
    • New York City: SLA wait times, classes 340, 240 and 370
    • Los Angeles: ABC wait times, types 41, 47 and 48

If you are opening a restaurant, the practical takeaway is to file early in New York, budget about two months in Los Angeles, and expect about a month in Texas. If you sell to new restaurants, the pending lists are a 1 to 4 month head start on who is about to open.

Corrections and better joins are welcome in the GitHub repo issues.
