title: I Built IntentChord to Bring Human Control to AI Coding Agents — Contributors Welcome
description:
AI coding agents can write code, modify files, and report that a task is complete.

But a successful-looking response doesn't necessarily answer some important questions:

  • Was the agent working on the correct source?
  • Was the change within the approved scope?
  • Is the reported result supported by actual evidence?
  • Who decides whether the work is accepted?

These questions led me to build IntentChord.

What is IntentChord?

IntentChord is a local-first, human-governed development workflow that connects an owner's intent to workspace context, confirmed scope, agent-specific execution contracts, evidence-based review, and a final human decision.

Its central principle is simple:

An AI agent's report is not the same as verified execution evidence, and an agent's claim of success is not the owner's approval.

What's in the project?

The repository includes:

  • Task and scope authority management
  • Workspace discovery, indexing, and source-context foundations
  • Governed execution contracts for Codex, Claude Code, and Gemini CLI
  • Execution evidence and report-verification logic
  • Human review and decision workflows
  • A Next.js, React, TypeScript, and PostgreSQL-based application

The project is still evolving and is not presented as a production-certified system.

I'm opening the project to contributors

I've made the source public because I'd like to develop IntentChord with other developers.

I'm particularly interested in contributions involving code quality, testing, developer onboarding, architecture discussions, and improvements to the human-in-the-loop workflow.

There are already beginner-friendly and documentation tasks available in GitHub Issues.

Repository: https://github.com/hesham-m/IntentChord

Contribution opportunities: https://github.com/hesham-m/IntentChord/issues

The project is source-available under PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0, rather than an OSI-approved open-source license. Please review the repository's license and contribution guidelines before contributing.

I'd be interested to hear how other developers handle agent authority, scope changes, and evidence verification in their AI-assisted development workflows.

What would you improve or challenge in this approach?

title: Next.js Prefetching in App Router: How `<Link>` Partial Prefetch Works and Why Your Pages Still Feel Slow
description:
Next.js Prefetching in App Router: How <Link> Partial Prefetch Works and Why Your Pages Still Feel Slow

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

Developers adopt Next.js App Router expecting server components to eliminate client-side waterfalls and prefetching to deliver instant navigation. The reality surprises them: links feel sluggish, dynamic routes block for seconds, and the DevTools network tab shows requests firing only after the user clicks. The prefetch happened, the data arrived, but the navigation still waits.

The confusion stems from three behaviors that collide in production: partial prefetch stops at the first Suspense boundary instead of loading the full page, the router cache expires prefetched data after 30 seconds for dynamic routes, and the client cannot render anything until the server responds with the missing pieces. The result is a server-driven app that feels slower than the client-side SPA it replaced.

Next.js 16.3 introduces partial prefetching as an opt-in feature, giving developers fine-grained control over what loads before navigation. Combined with the new cache components primitive, teams can mark reusable UI as cacheable and let Next.js extract loading shells from any route, not just routes with a loading.tsx file. The client now has enough data to render an instant transition, and the server streams dynamic content as it resolves.

This post explains how App Router prefetching works under the hood, why the default behavior creates slow navigations, and how to adopt the new primitives to make every link click feel instant without breaking dynamic content.

Key Takeaways

  • Next.js App Router partial prefetch (the default) stops at the first Suspense boundary, not the full page, causing slow navigations when routes lack explicit loading shells.
  • The router cache expires prefetched data after 30 seconds for dynamic routes and 5 minutes for static routes, triggering re-fetches on click if the user waits too long.
  • Next.js 16.3's partial prefetching and cache components let developers mark reusable UI as cacheable and control exactly what loads before navigation.
  • Instant Insights in the Next.js DevTools automatically surfaces slow navigations during development, eliminating guesswork about which links need optimization.
  • Full prefetch with prefetch={true} loads the entire destination page ahead of time, but costs bandwidth and can serve stale personalized content if cached data expires.

How Next.js Link Prefetching Actually Works in App Router

The <Link> component in Next.js App Router triggers prefetching when it enters the viewport or when the user hovers over it. The exact behavior depends on the prefetch prop and whether the destination route is static or dynamic.

By default, <Link> uses prefetch="auto", which means Next.js decides what to prefetch based on the route type. For static routes, the full route loads. For dynamic routes, Next.js fetches the route down to the first loading.tsx boundary, a behavior called partial prefetch.

The distinction between static and dynamic routes matters because Next.js treats them differently at build time. A route is static if it contains no dynamic segments (like [id]), no generateStaticParams is missing, and it does not read request-specific data like cookies or headers. Everything else is dynamic.

// app/blog/page.tsx - static route
export default function BlogPage() {
  return <div>Blog posts render at build time</div>;
}

// app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx - dynamic route
export default function PostPage({ params }: { params: { slug: string } }) {
  // Reads dynamic segment, so Next.js treats this as dynamic
  return <div>Post: {params.slug}</div>;
}

When a user hovers over a <Link href="/blog/post-1">, Next.js sends a request to the server. For a static route, the server returns the pre-rendered HTML and RSC payload. For a dynamic route, the server returns only the layout and any shared UI down to the first Suspense boundary, then stops. The page component itself does not load until the user clicks.

The official Next.js documentation (as of version 16.3) describes this behavior in the prefetch prop reference: "For dynamic routes, the partial route down to the nearest segment with a loading.js boundary will be prefetched." If no loading.tsx file exists, the prefetch ends at the layout, and the navigation blocks until the server responds with the page.

The router cache stores prefetched data with a time-to-live (TTL) that depends on the route type. Static routes cache for 5 minutes. Dynamic routes cache for 30 seconds. After the TTL expires, clicking the link triggers a new server request even if the prefetch completed successfully.

This explains why navigations sometimes feel instant and sometimes block. If the user clicks within 30 seconds of hovering, the cached data is fresh and the navigation completes immediately. If the user waits 31 seconds, the cache expires, and the client must wait for the server to re-render the route before the navigation can proceed.

Partial Prefetch vs Full Prefetch: What Gets Loaded When

The prefetch prop on <Link> accepts three values: "auto" (the default), true, and false. Each produces different behavior and costs.

prefetch="auto" defers to Next.js to decide what to load. For static routes, this means the full route. For dynamic routes, this means a partial prefetch that stops at the first loading.tsx boundary. The goal is to balance performance with bandwidth: prefetch enough to make navigation feel instant without loading content the user may never see.

prefetch={true} forces a full prefetch for both static and dynamic routes. The client downloads the entire page, including all data-fetching and rendering, before the user clicks. This guarantees instant navigation but wastes bandwidth if the user never visits the link. It also introduces stale data problems for personalized routes: if the prefetched page contains user-specific content, and the user waits long enough for the cache to expire, clicking the link shows stale content until the server responds with fresh data.

prefetch={false} disables prefetching entirely. The client requests the route only after the user clicks. This saves bandwidth but guarantees a slow navigation because the client must wait for the server to render the page before the transition can complete.

Next.js 16.3 changes the behavior when partial prefetching is enabled via partialPrefetching: true in next.config.ts. With this flag, prefetch="auto" now prefetches the route's app shell (the static and cached content) instead of stopping at the first loading.tsx boundary. The app shell includes layouts, templates, and any components marked with 'use cache', giving the client enough data to render a loading state immediately on click.

Prefetch value Static route behavior Dynamic route behavior Router cache TTL Best for
"auto" (default) Full route Partial (to first loading.tsx) Static: 5min, Dynamic: 30s Most links
true Full route Full route Static: 5min, Dynamic: 30s Critical navigation paths
false No prefetch No prefetch N/A Rarely-visited routes, infinite scroll lists
"auto" (with partialPrefetching: true) App shell + cached content App shell + cached content Configurable per cache tag Next.js 16.3+ apps

The tradeoff between partial and full prefetch becomes clear in a dashboard app. A sidebar contains 20 links to different reports. Full prefetch downloads all 20 pages when the sidebar renders, consuming megabytes of bandwidth and server resources even if the user only views one report. Partial prefetch downloads the shell for each page (layouts, navigation, headers) but waits to load report-specific data until the user clicks. The navigation feels instant because the shell paints immediately, and the data streams in as it resolves.

// app/dashboard/layout.tsx
export default function DashboardLayout({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  return (
    <div className="dashboard">
      <nav>
        {/* Partial prefetch: loads shell, not data */}
        <Link href="/dashboard/sales">Sales Report</Link>
        <Link href="/dashboard/inventory">Inventory</Link>
        <Link href="/dashboard/analytics">Analytics</Link>
      </nav>
      <main>{children}</main>
    </div>
  );
}

The diagram shows why partial prefetch feels faster for the initial shell render but slower for the complete page, while full prefetch either delivers the entire page instantly or serves stale content if the cache expired. Choosing the right strategy depends on whether the route contains dynamic content that changes frequently.

The Router Cache Problem: When Prefetched Data Goes Stale

The router cache in Next.js App Router exists to avoid redundant server requests. When a prefetch completes, Next.js stores the result in memory with a TTL. Subsequent navigations to the same route read from the cache instead of hitting the server, making back-and-forth navigation instantaneous.

The problem surfaces when the TTL expires before the user clicks. For dynamic routes, 30 seconds is short enough that normal user behavior (reading content, scrolling, comparing options) exhausts the cache before the navigation happens. The user clicks, the cache check fails, and the client blocks while waiting for the server to re-render the route.

This behavior surprises developers because the prefetch succeeded. The DevTools network tab shows the request completing with a 200 status. But when the user clicks 35 seconds later, a second identical request fires, and the navigation waits for that response before proceeding. The prefetch wasted bandwidth and delivered no performance benefit.

The stale data problem is worse for personalized routes. Consider a product page that shows the user's cart count in the header. If the page prefetches when the user hovers the link, and the user adds items to the cart before clicking, the prefetched page shows the old cart count until the new server response arrives. The transition looks instant, but the cart count is wrong for 200-300ms, creating a flicker as the correct data streams in.

Next.js addressed this in 16.3 by tying cache invalidation to the 'use cache' directive. When a component or function is marked with 'use cache', Next.js generates a cache key based on the function's arguments and the user's session. If the arguments or session change, the cache key changes, and the cached data is no longer valid. This lets developers opt specific components into granular caching while keeping the rest of the page fresh.

// app/dashboard/sales/page.tsx
import { unstable_cache } from 'next/cache';

async function getSalesData(userId: string) {
  'use cache';
  const response = await fetch(`/api/sales?user=${userId}`);
  return response.json();
}

export default async function SalesPage({ params }: { params: { userId: string } }) {
  const data = await getSalesData(params.userId);

  return (
    <div>
      <h1>Sales Report</h1>
      {/* This data is cached per user and stays fresh across navigations */}
      <pre>{JSON.stringify(data, null, 2)}</pre>
    </div>
  );
}

The official Next.js 16.3 release notes state: "It's more explicit and composable than our previous server-side caching APIs, and now, it also brings client-side caching to Next.js for the first time." The 'use cache' directive integrates with prefetching by letting the router cache store function-level results instead of full routes. When a prefetch happens, Next.js extracts the cached data, bundles it with the shell, and sends it to the client. The user clicks, the shell renders instantly, and only the non-cached dynamic data requires a server round-trip.

The cache key mechanism solves the stale data problem but introduces a new complexity: cache invalidation. If the sales data changes server-side while the client holds a cached copy, the user sees outdated information until the cache expires or the route re-validates. Next.js provides revalidation APIs (revalidatePath, revalidateTag) to expire caches on demand, but developers must call them explicitly when data changes.

Router cache diagram showing TTL expiration and re-fetch behavior

The image illustrates how the router cache expires after the TTL and triggers a new server request, even when the original prefetch completed successfully. The gap between prefetch and click determines whether the navigation feels instant or blocks.

Controlling Prefetch Behavior: Practical Code Examples

Developers control prefetching at three levels: per-link via the prefetch prop, per-route via loading.tsx files, and globally via next.config.ts flags.

The prefetch prop is the most direct control. Setting prefetch={false} disables prefetching for a specific link, useful for links in infinite scroll lists where prefetching would waste bandwidth. Setting prefetch={true} forces a full prefetch, useful for critical navigation paths like the main call-to-action on a landing page.

// app/components/product-list.tsx
'use client';

export default function ProductList({ products }: { products: Product[] }) {
  return (
    <div className="grid">
      {products.map((product) => (
        <Link
          key={product.id}
          href={`/product/${product.id}`}
          // Disable prefetch for long lists to save bandwidth
          prefetch={false}
        >
          {product.name}
        </Link>
      ))}
    </div>
  );
}

The loading.tsx file provides a route-level loading shell that prefetching uses to render an instant transition. When a dynamic route includes a loading.tsx file, partial prefetch stops at that file and sends the loading component to the client. The user clicks, the loading state renders immediately, and the page content streams in as the server resolves data-fetching.

// app/blog/[slug]/loading.tsx
export default function Loading() {
  return (
    <div className="blog-post-skeleton">
      <div className="skeleton-title" />
      <div className="skeleton-author" />
      <div className="skeleton-content" />
    </div>
  );
}

Without loading.tsx, partial prefetch has nothing to send, so the navigation blocks until the full page arrives. The Next.js DevTools Instant Insights panel highlights this as a slow navigation and suggests adding a loading file.

Next.js 16.3 adds two config flags that change prefetching behavior globally. Setting cacheComponents: true enables the new cache components primitive, letting developers mark reusable UI with 'use cache' and have Next.js extract it during prefetch. Setting partialPrefetching: true changes the default prefetch="auto" behavior from "stop at first loading.tsx" to "prefetch app shell plus cached content."

// next.config.ts
import type { NextConfig } from 'next';

const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
  cacheComponents: true,
  partialPrefetching: true,
};

export default nextConfig;

These flags unlock fine-grained control over what loads before navigation. A product page can mark the header, footer, and navigation as cached, while leaving product-specific content (price, availability, reviews) dynamic. The prefetch sends the shell, the user clicks, the shell renders instantly, and the dynamic content streams in.

// app/product/[id]/page.tsx
import { Suspense } from 'react';

async function Header() {
  'use cache';
  return <header>Site Header</header>;
}

async function ProductDetails({ id }: { id: string }) {
  const product = await fetch(`/api/products/${id}`).then(res => res.json());

  return (
    <div>
      <h1>{product.name}</h1>
      <p>{product.price}</p>
    </div>
  );
}

export default function ProductPage({ params }: { params: { id: string } }) {
  return (
    <>
      <Header />
      <Suspense fallback={<div>Loading product...</div>}>
        <ProductDetails id={params.id} />
      </Suspense>
    </>
  );
}

The cache components approach solves the stale data problem by caching at the component level instead of the route level. The header never changes, so it stays cached indefinitely. The product details change frequently, so they skip the cache and fetch fresh data on every navigation. The user sees an instant shell render followed by a smooth stream of dynamic content, no flicker, no stale data.

Next.js 16.3 Instant Navigations and the Future of Prefetching

Next.js 16.3 introduces Instant Navigations, a suite of features designed to make server-rendered apps feel as responsive as client-side SPAs without sacrificing the benefits of server rendering. The headline feature is partial prefetching, which builds on the cache components primitive to extract loading shells from any route, not just routes with a loading.tsx file.

The official Next.js 16.3 announcement states: "Next.js can extract this UI and load it into the client prior to a navigation, making your app feel as snappy as an SPA once users start clicking around it." The key word is "extract." Instead of requiring developers to manually define loading shells in separate files, Next.js analyzes the route's component tree, identifies cached components, and bundles them with the prefetch response. The client receives a ready-to-render shell even if the route has no loading.tsx file.

Partial prefetching also changes how prefetch payloads are structured. In prior versions, a prefetch request returned a monolithic RSC payload containing the entire route. In 16.3, the payload includes three layers: the app shell (layouts, templates, cached components), URL-specific data (dynamic segments, search params), and truly dynamic content (user-specific data, real-time updates). The client renders the app shell immediately, paints URL-specific data as it arrives, and streams dynamic content last.

This staged handoff eliminates the binary choice between instant-but-stale full prefetch and accurate-but-slow partial prefetch. The app shell is always safe to cache because it does not depend on user state or request timing. URL-specific data caches per route, so navigating between products on the same site reuses the shared shell and only fetches product-specific content. Dynamic content bypasses the cache entirely, guaranteeing freshness at the cost of a small delay.

// app/dashboard/[reportId]/page.tsx
import { Suspense } from 'react';

async function DashboardShell() {
  'use cache';
  return (
    <div className="dashboard-layout">
      <nav>Dashboard Navigation</nav>
      <aside>Filters</aside>
    </div>
  );
}

async function ReportData({ reportId }: { reportId: string }) {
  const data = await fetch(`/api/reports/${reportId}`).then(res => res.json());

  return <div>{JSON.stringify(data, null, 2)}</div>;
}

export default function ReportPage({ params }: { params: { reportId: string } }) {
  return (
    <>
      <DashboardShell />
      <Suspense fallback={<div>Loading report...</div>}>
        <ReportData reportId={params.reportId} />
      </Suspense>
    </>
  );
}

The diagram below shows the execution flow when partial prefetching is enabled. The prefetch extracts the app shell, the user clicks, the shell renders instantly, and the report data streams in as the server resolves the fetch.

The Instant Insights panel in the Next.js DevTools automatically detects slow navigations and suggests fixes. If a route lacks a loading shell, the panel shows a warning and generates a prompt that teaches AI agents how to add one. If a route has a loading shell but still feels slow, the panel identifies which components are blocking the critical path and suggests marking them with 'use cache'.

The official documentation (Next.js 16.3 release notes) describes Instant Insights as "a new devtool that automatically surfaces slow navigations." The panel runs in development mode only, monitoring every client-side transition and measuring the time from click to first paint. If the time exceeds a threshold (currently 300ms), the panel flags the navigation as slow and logs the component stack that blocked rendering.

This eliminates the guesswork that plagued prior versions. Developers no longer need to profile every link manually or instrument their code with performance marks. The DevTools highlight the problem, explain the root cause, and provide a concrete fix. All without leaving the browser.

Instant Insights panel in Next.js DevTools showing a slow navigation warning

The image shows the Instant Insights panel flagging a navigation to /dashboard/sales as slow because the route lacks a loading shell. The panel suggests adding a loading.tsx file or marking reusable components with 'use cache' to unlock instant navigation.

Debugging Slow Navigations: Finding the Real Culprit

Slow navigations in Next.js stem from four common causes: missing loading shells, expired router cache, blocking data fetches, and oversized prefetch payloads. Identifying the root cause requires inspecting the network tab, the React DevTools profiler, and the Next.js Instant Insights panel.

The network tab shows when prefetch requests fire and how long they take to complete. A prefetch that completes in 50ms but triggers a second identical request on click indicates a cache expiration problem. The user waited longer than the TTL, so the router cache invalidated the prefetched data and fetched it again.

The React DevTools profiler shows which components are blocking the critical path. If a navigation waits 2 seconds before painting anything, the profiler flame graph reveals which component is running slow. The usual suspects are data-fetching components that call fetch without Suspense boundaries, heavy computations in the render phase, and third-party libraries that block the main thread.

The Instant Insights panel ties these signals together by showing the full navigation trace. The panel logs the click event, the prefetch check, the cache hit or miss, the first paint, and the final layout shift. If the navigation is slow, the panel highlights the step that took the longest and suggests a fix.

The diagram shows the decision tree the router follows during navigation. If the cache is valid, the render happens immediately. If the cache expired, the navigation blocks while waiting for the server response. The gap between cache check and server response is where slowness accumulates.

Fixing slow navigations requires matching the solution to the root cause. If the cache expired, either shorten the time between prefetch and click (by prefetching on hover instead of on viewport entry) or extend the cache TTL by marking components with 'use cache'. If the navigation blocks on data fetches, wrap the slow components in Suspense boundaries and add a loading fallback. If the prefetch payload is too large, reduce it by setting prefetch={false} on low-priority links or splitting the route into smaller chunks.

The useLinkStatus hook (introduced in Next.js 16.2) provides immediate feedback during navigation. When a user clicks a link, the hook returns { pending: true } until the navigation completes, letting developers show a loading indicator without waiting for the server response.

'use client';

import { useLinkStatus } from 'next/link';

export default function NavigationIndicator() {
  const { pending } = useLinkStatus();

  if (!pending) return null;

  return (
    <div className="fixed top-0 left-0 right-0 h-1 bg-blue-500 animate-pulse" />
  );
}

The hook debounces fast navigations by adding a 100ms delay before returning pending: true. This prevents the loading indicator from flashing on screen for navigations that complete in under 100ms, reducing visual noise for instant transitions.

The official Next.js documentation (version 16.3) recommends combining useLinkStatus with CSS transitions to create a smooth loading experience: "You can 'debounce' the hint by adding an initial animation delay (e.g. 100ms) and starting as invisible (e.g. opacity: 0)." This gives the server time to respond before showing any feedback, avoiding flicker on fast networks.

For further reading on Next.js caching and performance, see the related posts Next.js 15 Caching Changes, Next.js App Router Layouts and Templates, and Next.js Caching Mental Model 2026.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why does my Next.js link prefetch but still feel slow when clicked?

The router cache expires prefetched data after 30 seconds for dynamic routes. If the user clicks after the TTL, the client fetches the route again even though the prefetch completed. Use 'use cache' to extend the TTL or reduce the delay between prefetch and click by prefetching on hover.

What is the difference between partial prefetch and full prefetch in App Router?

Partial prefetch loads the route down to the first Suspense boundary, sending the layout and loading shell but skipping page-specific data. Full prefetch loads the entire page including all data. Partial prefetch saves bandwidth but may feel slower if no loading shell exists. Use prefetch={true} to force full prefetch on critical links.

How does Next.js 16.3 partial prefetching change the default behavior?

In Next.js 16.3, enabling partialPrefetching: true makes prefetch="auto" send the app shell plus cached components instead of stopping at loading.tsx. This gives the client enough data to render an instant transition without requiring a separate loading file for every route.

When should I disable prefetching with prefetch={false}?

Disable prefetching for rarely-visited routes, infinite scroll lists, and links that appear in large quantities (like a product catalog with 1000 items). Prefetching wastes bandwidth if the user never clicks the link, and disabling it has no downside if the route is not performance-critical.

How do I debug which component is blocking a slow navigation?

Use the Instant Insights panel in the Next.js DevTools to identify slow navigations, then inspect the React DevTools profiler to see which component is blocking the critical path. The profiler flame graph shows render times per component, revealing bottlenecks like unwrapped data fetches or heavy computations in the render phase.

Making Next.js Navigations Feel Instant Without Breaking Dynamic Content

Next.js prefetching promises instant navigation but delivers slow transitions when the defaults collide with dynamic routes, expired caches, and missing loading shells. The confusion stems from partial prefetch stopping at Suspense boundaries, router cache expiration after 30 seconds, and the client blocking until the server responds with missing data.

Next.js 16.3 fixes this with partial prefetching, cache components, and Instant Insights. Developers mark reusable UI with 'use cache', and Next.js extracts it during prefetch, giving the client enough data to render an instant shell. Dynamic content streams in as the server resolves it, and the DevTools highlight any navigation that takes longer than 300ms, eliminating guesswork about which links need optimization.

Adopting the new primitives requires enabling two flags in next.config.ts and marking cached components with 'use cache'. The payoff is a server-rendered app that feels as responsive as a client-side SPA, with no stale data, no flicker, and no guesswork about when prefetches expire.

title: Building a browser .io strategy game with a Go server
description:
I'm building Warhex.io, a free .io strategy game that runs in the browser. You build a base out of walls, turrets, snipers and barracks, defend key positions and fight players from all over the world in real time. This post is about how the game is put together, in case you are thinking about making a multiplayer browser game of your own.

If you used to play bloble.io or similar base-building .io games, Warhex.io is made for that kind of player. It is an independent project and is not affiliated with bloble.io.

The shape of the stack

  • Server: Go. One authoritative game loop owns the whole match, and clients only send intentions (place a building, move units, buy an upgrade).
  • Transport: WebSockets with a small binary protocol. Every message is one type byte followed by a compact payload, so a camera update or a unit position costs a handful of bytes.
  • Client: plain JavaScript, a canvas renderer and webpack. No game engine. The renderer only draws what the server says exists.
  • Accounts and data: Supabase for login (Discord only) and for things that must survive a restart, like progress and ranking.
  • Community: a Discord bot in Node that syncs the global top 10 to server roles.

Why Go for the game server

A match is a lot of small updates: bullets, units, buildings and health bars changing many times per second. Go gives cheap concurrency (one goroutine per connection, one loop for the world) and predictable memory use, which matters when you want a cheap server to hold many players.

The important rule is that the server decides everything. The client can ask "place a turret here", and the server checks the cost, the position, the limits and who owns the space before it replies. That one rule removes most of the cheating you would otherwise have to chase.

A tiny binary protocol

Text JSON is easy, but at a few hundred updates per second it gets expensive. Our messages look like this:

[ type: 1 byte ][ playerID: 1 byte ][ payload ... ]

On the client a worker decodes each frame by type and hands plain objects to the game. Rarely sent things (a clan list, a chat line) can still use JSON inside the same envelope, so you only pay for binary where it matters.

Boss fights as a game design tool

The most fun feature to build was three world bosses. Each boss is a fortified base made of the same pieces players use, with a shield made of generators. You have to break the shield generators first, then the core. Because bosses reuse the normal building and damage code, there was almost no special-case logic, and balancing them is just changing numbers.

What I would tell my past self

  1. Make the server authoritative from day one.
  2. Keep the protocol small before you need to.
  3. Reuse your own game rules for new content (bosses, events, tutorials).
  4. Put the moderation tools (chat filter, rate limits) in early.
  5. Ship the community (Discord, wiki, guides) alongside the game, not after.

You can play Warhex.io for free at https://warhex.io and join the community at https://discord.gg/CsVHA7R7Vx. There is also a wiki with a full guide at https://warhexio.fandom.com/pt-br/wiki/Warhex.io

Questions about the netcode or the Go server? Ask in the comments and I will answer.

title: Your AI Portal Is Live. Why Do Users Still Get Lost?
description:
A white-label AI portal can be technically online and still feel completely unusable.

That is the awkward gap many teams discover after launch. The domain resolves, the dashboard opens, and the models respond, yet new visitors hesitate. They cannot tell what the product is for, which tool to try, whether the price is predictable, or who will help when something breaks.

The usual reaction is to add more: more navigation items, more models, a louder hero banner, and a longer feature list. That often makes the problem worse. A portal does not earn trust by showing everything it can possibly do. It earns trust by helping a visitor complete one useful task without getting lost.

Treat the homepage like the start of a journey

Before changing colors or uploading a logo, open the site in a private browser window and pretend you know nothing about it.

Within a few seconds, the page should answer three ordinary questions:

  • What can I make here?
  • Where should I begin?
  • What will it cost me?

That does not require a grand slogan. A sentence such as “Create product images and short campaign videos from a prompt” is much more helpful than a vague promise about transforming creativity.

The same principle applies to navigation. A catalog of every available capability may impress the person who configured the site, but it gives a first-time user too many decisions. Put the main workflow first. If the portal is built for marketing teams, image creation, copy generation, and video production probably deserve the most visible positions. Secondary tools can remain available without competing for attention on the opening screen.

A useful test is to ask someone unfamiliar with the project to find the primary feature while sharing their screen. Do not guide them. The pause before their first click is valuable product research.

Branding is mostly consistency

A memorable name and a crisp logo help, but branding falls apart when the details disagree. The browser title uses one name, the login page uses another, and the support documentation points to a third domain. Each mismatch creates a small reason to distrust the site.

Keep the logo simple enough to survive at favicon size. Check it on both light and dark backgrounds, and inspect the mobile header instead of relying on the admin preview. A wide logo with tiny lettering may look fine in the source file and become unreadable once the interface scales it down.

The hero image deserves the same restraint. It should reinforce one job the visitor can perform, not carry the entire business plan. Text baked into an image is especially fragile because responsive layouts may crop it. Important claims and calls to action are safer as real page text.

Login is part of the product, not an admin setting

Authentication is often configured from the administrator's point of view: enable a provider, save the form, and move on. Users experience a longer chain. They click, leave the site for an identity provider, return, and expect to land somewhere sensible.

Test that whole chain while signed out. Try it on a phone. Check what happens after a cancelled login and whether an error offers a practical next step. The best default method is usually the one the target audience already uses, but convenience only matters if the redirect and return path work reliably.

It is also worth checking the first minute after registration. A successful login that drops a new user into an empty, unexplained dashboard is technically correct and emotionally disappointing. A short starter prompt, a sample project, or a direct link to the main tool can make the first session feel intentional.

A custom domain needs an end-to-end check

Adding a domain in an admin panel is only half the work. DNS still has to direct that hostname to the service, and HTTPS has to work once the record propagates.

For an Ace Data Cloud subsite, the documented CNAME target is platform-proxy.acedata.cloud. A typical record for ai.example.com would look like this:

Type:   CNAME
Name:   ai
Target: platform-proxy.acedata.cloud

Before adding it, look for an existing A, AAAA, or CNAME record using the same hostname. Conflicting records can produce confusing results that appear to work for one person and fail for another because of resolver caches.

You can inspect the public result from a terminal:

dig ai.example.com CNAME +short
curl -I https://ai.example.com

Do not stop when dig returns an answer. Open the actual URL, verify that it reaches the correct tenant, and check that the browser reports a valid certificate. Repeat the test away from the network where the site was configured if possible. DNS propagation and local caching have a habit of making the administrator's laptop look healthier than the rest of the internet.

Pricing copy should remove surprises

A pricing table is not clear simply because it contains numbers. Users need to know what the unit represents. A price per generated image, per second of video, per request, and per bundle of credits are not interchangeable.

Work backward from a realistic task. If someone wants a ten-second clip, what is the likely total rather than the smallest unit price? If retries consume credits, say so. If quality or resolution changes the cost, show that relationship close to the selector.

This is also where sustainable operation matters. Pricing below the underlying cost may attract early usage, but it turns every successful customer into a larger problem. Pricing far above it without explaining support, curation, or convenience creates a different trust problem. The interface should make both the unit and the value understandable before the user clicks generate.

Documentation should follow the moment of confusion

Most users do not read a manual from beginning to end. They look for help when something interrupts them. Good documentation mirrors those moments:

  • signing in for the first time
  • choosing the right tool
  • understanding credits and charges
  • improving a weak result
  • reporting a failed task

A short answer with the exact interface label and a current screenshot is often better than a long tour of every feature. Support conversations are an excellent backlog for documentation. When the same question appears twice, turn the answer into a page and link to it from the place where the confusion happens.

Privacy information deserves the same practical treatment. Describe what the site actually collects, which third-party services are involved, how long relevant data is kept, and how a user can ask for help. Copying another company's policy without adapting names, contacts, and data flows is worse than having a shorter policy that reflects reality.

Launch with a small acceptance script

The final review should not happen inside the admin session. Log out and walk through the product as a stranger. Then do it again on a narrow mobile screen.

A lightweight launch script can be written in plain language:

Open the homepage from the public domain.
Understand the main use case without opening a menu.
Create a new account with the default login method.
Find the primary tool and run a small task.
See the price or credit impact before and after the task.
Open help from the point where a beginner would hesitate.
Find a real support contact and the privacy terms.
Repeat the critical path on mobile.

This is not a one-time ceremony. Run the same path after changing authentication, navigation, pricing, or DNS. It catches the kind of breakage that monitoring dashboards often miss because every individual service can be healthy while the user journey is broken.

The strongest portal is rarely the one with the most crowded homepage. It is the one that feels obvious. A visitor arrives, understands the promise, trusts the domain, signs in without friction, predicts the cost, and finishes a useful task. Once that path works, adding more capability becomes an improvement instead of another layer of confusion.

Reference

title: The night shift nobody works: what idle VMs cost, by the hour
description:
A dev VM is used from 8 to 8, five days a week. That is 60 hours. The cloud bills 168. Multiply by every VM in dev and QA and the night shift is the most expensive team you have, and it does nothing.

Control Cloud reads your clouds through the provider API with read-only credentials and puts a number on that, from your own inventory, not from a calculator with guessed inputs.

What a night costs, by the hour

The Overnight bleeding card takes the VMs that are running right now, their hourly rate, and the hours a night you choose. On this demo organization: 16 running VMs, 12 hours a night, $1.51 an hour, $18.16 a night, $127 a week, $6,627 a year. It excludes what bills 24/7 anyway (databases, load balancers, NAT gateways), so the number is what you can actually get back.

Three things that bill for nothing

Under the card, the same page lists the efficiency opportunities it found: unused resources still billing (4 proven orphans: nothing uses them, they are still paid for), disks of stopped VMs (5 disks that keep billing although their VM is off) and off-hours shutdown (the estimated saving of powering dev and QA off at night and on weekends). Each one links to the breakdown in the cost advisor.

Then make it stop

Schedules power resources off and on at set times. Every run lands in the audit log (who, what, when, on which resource), and a run that fails emails the person who created the schedule. A shutdown that fails silently leaves four VMs on all weekend; that one is on the invoice, not in the UI, unless someone tells you.

title: Vercel Agent is now available in Slack code channels
description:
Vercel Agent now works in Slack code channels, a new kind of channel launched today for working with a coding agent. Anyone in the channel can follow the work, give Agent new instructions, and review the code it writes.

Choose Create a code channel from the Slack sidebar, select Vercel as the agent, and describe what you need to get started. You can also ask Agent to create one from an existing channel or thread. It brings that context with it to the new channel.

Use code channels to investigate incidents, write and review code as a team, or manage ongoing work such as dependency upgrades and migrations.

Inside a Vercel Agent code channel:

  • Follow the work: Agent posts relevant deployments, logs, errors, and diffs in the channel as it works.

  • Talk without repeated @Vercel mentions: Agent follows the conversation, recognizes which messages are for it, and continues when the team gives it more work.

  • Review pull requests: Ask Agent for a PR review and it posts its findings in the channel. It can find bugs outside the diff, and explain failing checks and their root causes.

  • Approve every change: Agent is read-only by default and never exceeds the requester's permissions. Before making a change, it drafts a plan and waits for approval. For every action, Vercel records who requested and approved it and what Agent ran.

  • Stop work at any time: The person who created the code channel can cancel an active task.

Vercel Agent in Slack code channels is available in public beta for Pro and Enterprise teams. Add Vercel to Slack, learn about Slack Code, or read the docs.

title: Twilio vs Vonage for SMS Alerts — Property Management Pricing, Features, Node.js
description:
Short answer: For property-management SMS alerts, choose Twilio when global coverage and developer tooling reduce integration work; choose Vonage when high-volume SMS economics matter more; consider a unified REST API when one signup flow must connect SMS, email fallback, and adjacent backend capabilities.

The integration decision is not “which SMS API has the longest feature list?” It is where account creation ends and message delivery begins. Twilio is the stronger default when global coverage, integrations, and developer tooling carry the most weight. Vonage deserves the lead when high-volume SMS economics and the relevant regional carrier relationships matter more. A unified REST surface is useful when the real constraint is wiring both the SMS step and its fallback without multiplying contracts.

What should the signup flow own?

For a tenant signup, the application should create the verification token, store its expiry, and enqueue a notification job. The SMS provider should accept the message and return an identifier. A worker can reconcile delivery state later. That division keeps a carrier response out of the account transaction and gives the product a stable place to decide what “verified” means.

The decision is conditional, but it is not vague. Choose Twilio when its extensive global coverage, integrations, documentation, and SDKs reduce the code your team has to maintain. Choose Vonage when volume SMS and country-specific pricing deserve more weight. Check carrier partnerships for every launch region; a general comparison does not replace that review.

Keep it boring.

For a solo team, I would also evaluate a single REST surface for the boundary between signup, SMS, and an email fallback. Infrai’s public discovery surface is self-describing and exposes request schemas, response schemas, billing details, and runnable examples without requiring a key. The documented capability set also has runnable examples in 10 languages, which turns “how do I wire this?” into a concrete inspection task rather than an SDK-selection exercise.

There is a second, different advantage: one key and one bill cover a broad backend surface. The live discovery set contains 295 routes across 20 modules, including 41 in the communication group. For this workflow, that means the same platform boundary can cover the notification step and adjacent backend work without asking a small team to collect a new credential and reconcile another provider for every capability. It does not make the specialist SMS providers irrelevant.

How should the Node.js boundary look?

Make the provider call an adapter. The signup service should deal in verificationId, providerMessageId, and expiresAt; it should not know whether the transport is Twilio, Vonage, or another REST provider. The adapter should also own status normalization, since a carrier state is evidence about delivery rather than proof that someone opened a link.

Here is the smallest useful shape. It is intentionally transport-neutral, so it can be tested without sending a real message. The production adapter supplies the provider-specific implementation and keeps credentials outside the signup code.

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;

if (!apiKey) {
  throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");
}

const baseUrl = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1";

function delayFor(response: Response, attempt: number): number {
  const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
  return Number.isFinite(retryAfter)
    ? Math.max(1000, retryAfter * 1000)
    : Math.min(8000, 500 * 2 ** attempt);
}

async function discoverSmsBoundary(): Promise<unknown> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/discovery`, {
      method: "GET",
      headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}` },
    });

    if (response.ok) {
      const manifest = (await response.json()) as {
        capabilities: Array<{ method: string; path: string }>;
      };
      return manifest.capabilities.find(
        (capability) =>
          capability.method === "GET" && capability.path === "/v1/sms/status/{id}",
      );
    }

    if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 3) {
      await new Promise((resolve) =>
        setTimeout(resolve, delayFor(response, attempt)),
      );
      continue;
    }

    const detail = await response.text();
    throw new Error(`Discovery failed (${response.status}): ${detail}`);
  }

  throw new Error("Discovery retry budget exhausted");
}

discoverSmsBoundary().then(console.log).catch((error: unknown) => {
  console.error(error);
  process.exitCode = 1;
});

type Verification = {
  verificationId: string;
  providerMessageId: string;
  expiresAt: Date;
};

type DeliveryState = "pending" | "delivered" | "failed" | "unknown";

interface SmsPort {
  sendVerification(input: {
    phoneNumber: string;
    verificationUrl: string;
    idempotencyKey: string;
  }): Promise<{ messageId: string }>;
  readStatus(messageId: string): Promise<DeliveryState>;
}

async function createSignupVerification(
  sms: SmsPort,
  input: { verificationId: string; phoneNumber: string; verificationUrl: string },
): Promise<Verification> {
  const expiresAt = new Date(Date.now() + 15 * 60 * 1000);
  const result = await sms.sendVerification({
    phoneNumber: input.phoneNumber,
    verificationUrl: input.verificationUrl,
    idempotencyKey: `signup-verification:${input.verificationId}`,
  });

  return {
    verificationId: input.verificationId,
    providerMessageId: result.messageId,
    expiresAt,
  };
}

The discovery call is intentionally read-only. It lets the adapter inspect the documented SMS boundary before choosing a provider-specific send implementation, and it honors Retry-After without treating a throttled response as success. The important detail in the send adapter is the idempotency key, not the syntax. A timeout after the provider accepted the message must not create a second link when the worker retries. On the read side, use bounded backoff and surface a non-success response with its body. Do not turn an unknown carrier state into a successful signup.

This also keeps the example honest about the provider boundary. The application owns the 15-minute policy shown here; it is not a claim about a provider’s delivery window. The actual adapter must use the selected provider’s documented request and response shape, and the application must store the returned message ID before it tries to reconcile status.

Is Twilio or Vonage the better SMS transport?

Twilio and Vonage overlap on the features that matter for this flow: delivery receipts and message scheduling are broadly available in both. Twilio has extensive global coverage and strong developer documentation and SDK support. Vonage can offer a cost advantage for volume SMS. Those are useful differences, but they do not answer the regional question. Carrier relationships vary, so test the countries where tenants actually receive messages.

Amazon SNS is a third option when the property platform already has an AWS-shaped operational boundary. It is a reasonable comparison point for teams that want their notification path close to existing AWS controls. It is a worse fit if introducing another cloud-specific integration is the very work the team is trying to avoid. SendGrid is relevant on the other side of the handoff: it can be considered for an email fallback, but it is not an SMS transport for the tenant signup link.

Option Where it fits What to verify before committing
Twilio Global coverage, integrations, and developer-friendly tooling Regional carrier behavior and the ongoing shape of the SDK or HTTP integration
Vonage High-volume SMS where regional pricing is a major input Country-level carrier partnerships and the complete delivery workflow
Amazon SNS A property backend already organized around AWS services Whether the added cloud-specific boundary reduces or increases integration work
SendGrid A separate email fallback owned by an email provider It does not replace the SMS provider for this signup path
Infrai A small team that values public discovery and one backend contract Pull-based status, application-owned anti-abuse policy, and regional SMS readiness

The price comparison should stay in its lane. Pricing changes, and a table of unit prices becomes stale faster than the signup code. For a large alert stream, model the actual destinations and volumes, then compare message creation, delivery-state reads, retries, and fallback work. For a product with many backend capabilities, count the credentials, SDK conventions, and operational handoffs too. Those costs are part of integration effort even when they do not appear on an invoice.

The explicit recommendation is narrow: a property-management team should try Infrai for the signup verification and email-fallback boundary when it wants to discover both capabilities from one public REST surface and keep one credential across the backend. Twilio or Vonage is the better specialist choice when carrier-level regional tooling, mature SMS integrations, or volume economics dominate the decision.

Where does the provider handoff end?

The application should own abuse policy. The available caveats matter here: geographic anti-fraud limits and country-based spend circuit breakers must be built at the business layer. Do not assume the transport provider will enforce the property product’s rules. Store an allowlist or policy decision with the signup attempt, and reject or defer suspicious requests before the send adapter runs.

That policy check is also where the comparison becomes concrete. Suppose a property manager serves several countries and the product team adds a new signup channel late in the release cycle. The transport adapter should receive a request that has already passed the country rule, rate rule, and token-expiry rule; it should not decide any of those things while talking to a carrier. A Twilio or Vonage adapter can then normalize its message identifier into the same internal record, while an email fallback can use a separate adapter with its own code and expiry. A unified REST surface can reduce the number of discovery and credential steps around this handoff, but it cannot choose the allowed geography or make an email OTP hosted for you. Those remain application decisions.

The application should also own the fallback policy. The email side does not provide a hosted OTP interface, so an email verification fallback needs an application-owned code and expiry. There is no SMTP relay, and email scheduling has no cancel route. SMS does have a cancel route, but that difference is a reason to keep cancellation semantics behind the adapter rather than exposing them as a universal notification feature.

Status is pull-based in both namespaces; there are no webhook event pushes. That makes a bounded polling worker part of the design. As of the 2026-10-31 discovery snapshot, the broader platform surface is 295 routes across 20 modules, but that breadth does not change this constraint: the signup UI should not wait on a carrier response. Record the provider message ID, reconcile until the verification expiry, and make unresolved status visible to support without treating it as account failure immediately.

The operational checklist is short enough to enforce in code review. Store the token and expiry internally. Enqueue the send after the signup record is durable. Pass a deterministic idempotency key. Persist the message ID. Reconcile with bounded retries. Keep the token out of logs. Test every destination country and the email fallback separately.

Ship the boundary.

That is the boundary I would use: the property application owns identity and policy, the SMS provider owns transport, and a worker owns reconciliation. If the main friction is discovering and connecting adjacent backend capabilities, start with the public capability reference. If the main friction is carrier behavior in a specific country, stay with the specialist comparison and test that country first.

References

The implementation boundary follows the provider documentation and the communication constraints described above. Regional carrier behavior and current pricing should be checked again before launch.

Sources

  • Twilio SMS documentation: https://www.twilio.com/docs/sms
  • Vonage SMS API documentation: https://developer.vonage.com/en/messaging/sms/overview
  • Amazon SNS SMS documentation: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sns/latest/dg/sms_publish-to-phone.html
  • Google Email sender guidelines: https://support.google.com/a/answer/81126
  • Unified API discovery and capability reference: https://docs.infrai.cc/llms.txt

title: Deleting files safely from a Tauri app: what I learned sending them to the Windows Recycle Bin from Rust
description:
I'm building a disk cleaner for Windows in Rust and Tauri 2. Finding junk isn't the scary part. Deleting it is. If the scanner has a bug, you see a wrong number. If the delete path has a bug, someone loses files.

So the delete path ended up with more code and more tests than anything else in the app. Here's what it does and why. All the snippets are from the real source, trimmed a bit, with the file name on top.

One thing up front: not everything my app removes goes to the Recycle Bin. I'll get to that at the end, because I only fixed how the UI talks about it this week.

1. The webview only gets to delete what a scan returned

In Tauri the UI is a webview calling Rust commands. I treat it like any other client I don't control. If a command takes a list of paths, those paths could be anything.

So the backend remembers what each scan returned, and only those paths can be trashed:

// src-tauri/src/files/guard.rs (simplified)
type Approved = HashMap<ScanKind, HashSet<String>>;
static APPROVED: LazyLock<Mutex<Approved>> = LazyLock::new(Mutex::default);

/// Records the files a scan returned to the UI: only these can be trashed.
/// Protected paths are never recorded.
pub fn approve<'a>(kind: ScanKind, paths: impl IntoIterator<Item = &'a str>) {
    let set = paths
        .into_iter()
        .filter(|path| !is_protected(Path::new(path)))
        .map(str::to_owned)
        .collect();
    approved().insert(kind, set);
}

trash_files checks every path against that set. Anything else is reported as failed and left alone. There's a test for it: a file no scan returned gets reported, and it's still on disk afterwards.

2. "Inside C:\Windows" means folder boundaries

The protected list is what you'd expect. %SystemRoot%, Program Files and ProgramData. $Recycle.Bin and System Volume Information anywhere. pagefile.sys, Recovery, Windows.old and friends at a drive root. Network shares get refused too.

The comparison is where it's easy to slip. A plain starts_with thinks c:\windowsill\notes.txt is inside c:\windows. So paths get normalised first (no \\?\ prefix, lower case, no trailing separator) and then compared on folder boundaries:

// src-tauri/src/files/guard.rs
/// `c:\data` contains `c:\data\x` but not `c:\database`.
pub fn is_within(path: &str, root: &str) -> bool {
    match path.strip_prefix(root) {
        Some("") => true,
        Some(rest) => root.ends_with(SEP) || rest.starts_with(SEP),
        None => false,
    }
}

Yes, there's a test for C:\Windowsill\notes.txt.

3. A path can change between the scan and the delete

By the time someone clicks "Move to Recycle Bin", the scan might be minutes old. In that time a folder on the path could have been swapped for a junction pointing somewhere else. Scans return resolved paths, so right before deleting I resolve the path again and refuse it if it doesn't resolve to itself anymore:

// src-tauri/src/files/guard.rs
/// A regular file (not a link or folder) outside protected locations whose path
/// resolves to itself. A link or junction put in the way since the scan is refused.
fn safe_size(path: &str) -> Option<u64> {
    let meta = Path::new(path).symlink_metadata().ok().filter(std::fs::Metadata::is_file)?;
    let real = normalize(&std::fs::canonicalize(path).ok()?);
    (real == normalize(Path::new(path)) && !is_protected_normalized(&real)).then_some(meta.len())
}

On Windows canonicalize also expands 8.3 short names like PROGRA~1, which is one more way two strings can mean the same folder. The check runs again for every batch, right before Windows sees the paths, since an earlier batch might have sat on a dialog for a while.

4. The trash crate and COM threads

The actual move is done by the trash crate (5.x). On Windows it initialises COM single-threaded. My app already had other commands (the program list, icons) setting COM to multithreaded on the shared command threads. Call trash on one of those and you don't get an error. You get a panic.

The fix is boring. Every Recycle Bin operation gets its own thread:

// src-tauri/src/recycle.rs
/// `trash` initialises COM single-threaded and *panics* when the thread already uses
/// the multithreaded model. A new thread has no COM state, and a panic there only
/// fails this call.
pub fn on_own_thread<T: Send + 'static>(f: impl FnOnce() -> T + Send + 'static) -> Option<T> {
    std::thread::spawn(f).join().ok()
}

If you've got windows-crate COM code and trash in the same Tauri app, it's worth checking which thread each one runs on.

5. Batches, cancels, and "delete permanently?"

One shell operation per file is slow. One giant operation fails as a whole if a single path is bad. I went with batches of 64, and if a batch fails before it even starts, the code falls back to one file at a time so one bad path doesn't hold up the rest.

Windows has opinions too. If a file is too big for the Recycle Bin, Windows asks whether to delete it permanently. If the user says no, I shouldn't ask again for every remaining file:

// src-tauri/src/files/guard.rs (simplified)
const TRASH_BATCH: usize = 64;
const USER_CANCELLED: [i32; 2] = [
    0x8007_04C7_u32 as i32, // HRESULT_FROM_WIN32(ERROR_CANCELLED)
    0x8027_0000_u32 as i32, // COPYENGINE_E_USER_CANCELLED
];

for chunk in paths.chunks(TRASH_BATCH) {
    let chunk: Vec<&String> = chunk.iter().filter(|p| safe_size(p).is_some()).collect();
    match trash::delete_all(&chunk) {
        Ok(()) => {}
        Err(err) if cancelled_by_user(&err) => return, // the user stopped it
        Err(trash::Error::Unknown { .. }) => {}        // ran, but the shell skipped some
        Err(_) => { /* failed before starting: retry one by one */ }
    }
}

6. Let the disk say what moved

The shell's return value doesn't tell you what happened to each file. So after the move, the code just looks. If a path still exists, it's a failure. Only paths that are actually gone count toward "bytes freed":

// src-tauri/src/files/guard.rs
// The file system is the source of truth for what actually moved.
for (path, size) in targets {
    if exists(&path) { report.failed.push(path); }
    else { report.bytes_freed += size; report.deleted.push(path); }
}

That's why the number the app shows can be smaller than what you picked. Files that were in use stay put and show up as failed.

7. Being honest about what doesn't go to the Recycle Bin

This is the part I got wrong.

Large files, duplicates and similar photos go through everything above. Dev build folders (node_modules, target and so on) also go to the Recycle Bin, through a similar check in recycle.rs. Temp files and caches don't. The cleanup rules in junk_rules/mod.rs delete them with std::fs::remove_file, and the confirm text says why: "These are caches and temporary files; apps rebuild them as needed." What they get instead is a couple of different guards. A rule is skipped while its app is running (the comment in the code: "deleting a live cache can corrupt it"), and One-Click Fix and the scheduler only touch files older than 24 hours.

The code was fine with that. My welcome screen wasn't. It told people deleted files go to the Recycle Bin, which just isn't true for caches.

This week (#103) I swapped the native confirm box for an in-app dialog. It lists what's about to go and shows one of two labels: "Can be restored from the Recycle Bin" or "Permanent â€” not moved to the Recycle Bin". Cancel has focus by default. The welcome text now says: "Super Cleaner always asks first. Large files go to the Recycle Bin; caches and temp files are deleted for good."

While I was in there I found 11 of my 26 confirms showing English buttons in the Chinese UI. Turns out that one was on me. My old confirmAction() wrapper defaulted to okLabel = "Continue" and cancelLabel = "Cancel", hardcoded in English, and 11 call sites never passed their own labels. Now okLabel is required and Cancel defaults to the translated string.

If you're writing your own delete path

Don't trust the UI with paths, and only delete what the backend found itself. Normalise before you compare, compare on folder boundaries, and resolve again right before the delete. If anything else in your process touches COM, give trash its own thread. Assume the user, or Windows, will cancel halfway. Count what's actually gone from the disk. And tell people plainly what they can and can't undo, because that's the part I almost shipped wrong.

The code's from Super Cleaner, a Windows cleaner I'm building in Rust + Tauri. It's not public yet. I'll post here when it is.

title: Why Most Directories Fail Developers with 14-Day Queues (And How We Engineered an Instant-Live Launchpad)
description:
If you’ve ever launched a developer tool or side project, you know the dread of the Directory Holding Pattern.

You spend months building your product. You polish the UI, fix the edge cases, write clean docs, and submit your link to five different software launchpads.

Then, you wait.

One directory asks for $49 to "skip the queue." Another takes 17 days to approve your listing. And the third one silently goes live on a random Sunday night while your entire audience is asleep — completely burning your launch momentum.

Makers shouldn't be penalized because an admin queue is backed up.

That’s why I spent the last few months building Astro Discover — an open, hype-free product launchpad with a guaranteed 24-hour spotlight and zero queue delays.

💡 The Core Problem: The Launch Day Limbo

Traditional launchpad moderation models have two major flaws:

  1. The Ghosting Trap: Submissions get buried in queues for weeks. By the time the product is approved, the maker has already moved on to other marketing initiatives.
  2. The Pay-to-Win Fast Track: Platforms create artificial delays just to monetize expedited review tiers.

We wanted to engineer a platform where the maker’s launch day is sacred and protected.

🛠️ The Architectural Solution: 24–48 Hr Turnaround + The "Pending Review" Fail-Safe

Here is the exact mechanism we implemented on Astro Discover:

1. 24–48 Hour Maximum Human Verification

Every submission is screened by a human to prevent malicious phishing, direct executable downloads, and broken links. We keep our queue lean and mean with a 24 to 48-hour SLA.

2. The Auto-Live Fail-Safe (No Lost Launches)

Here’s our biggest innovation: Makers schedule their exact launch day in advance.

If your scheduled launch day arrives and manual review is still in queue over a weekend or holiday, your project still goes live automatically on Today's Launches with a transparent "Pending Review" badge.

  • You never lose your 24-hour spotlight window.
  • The 24-hour spotlight starts cleanly at 12:01 AM IST.
  • Early adopters can still test your project and inspect your tech stack.
  • Once verified, the badge seamlessly flips to approved.

3. Tech Stack Transparency Over Marketing Hype

Developers don't care about corporate buzzwords. Every card on Astro Discover directly exposes:

  • The actual tech stack (React, TypeScript, Go, Python, Rust, etc.)
  • Open-source licensing (MIT, Apache, AGPL)
  • Direct GitHub repository links
  • Verified maker socials

⚡ Zero-Delay Performance & Architecture

We built the frontend on React + Vite + Tailwind CSS with real-time reactive Firestore listeners.

To eliminate "Soft 404" indexing issues and ensure search engine crawlers (Googlebot, Perplexity, ChatGPT) never see an empty screen, we pre-hydrate the baseline tools at zero milliseconds and stream live Firestore upvotes in the background.

🌐 Try Astro Discover

The directory is completely free, open, and requires zero login to browse:

👉 Explore Live Launches: https://astrodiscover.ai.studio

👉 Submit Your Tool & Lock Your Launch Day: https://astrodiscover.ai.studio/submit

What's your worst launchpad experience?

Have you ever lost a launch day or waited weeks for a directory review? How do you usually handle launch timing across timezones? Drop your stories and thoughts below!

title: How to Export Google Ads Transparency Center Data (with Ad Copy) in Python
description:
I wanted something simple: every Google search ad a competitor is running, how long each one has been running, and the actual ad copy — in a spreadsheet.

Google already publishes all of this in the Ads Transparency Center (Google's answer to Meta's Ad Library). It just has no export button and no API. So I scraped it, and ran into something I didn't expect: for most big advertisers, the ad copy isn't there as text at all.

The surprise: most text ads are stored as images

When you open a text ad in the Transparency Center, Google renders it in one of two ways:

  1. A text preview — the headline and description exist as text (in a small JS preview), easy to parse.
  2. A screenshot — a PNG of the ad, nothing else. The words only exist as pixels.

I pulled the first 30 text ads of five large advertisers on Nov 1, 2026 and counted how many had a text version:

Advertiser Text ads checked With a text version
booking.com 30 0
expedia.com 30 0
hubspot.com 30 1
samsung.com 30 7
nike.com 30 21
Total 150 29 (19%)

So if a tool only reads the text preview, the best it can do here is copy for about 1 ad in 5 — and for booking.com and expedia.com, nothing. That's a big hole if "what are my competitors saying?" is the whole point.

Reading the screenshots (the DIY version)

The fix is OCR. Each ad record links to its snapshot image (tpc.googlesyndication.com/archive/simgad/...), and a basic version with Tesseract is a few lines:

import io, requests, pytesseract
from PIL import Image

def read_ad(image_url):
    img = Image.open(io.BytesIO(requests.get(image_url, timeout=20).content)).convert("L")
    img = img.resize((img.width * 2, img.height * 2))          # small text OCRs better when upscaled
    data = pytesseract.image_to_data(img, config="--psm 6", output_type=pytesseract.Output.DICT)
    words = [(w, float(c)) for w, c in zip(data["text"], data["conf"]) if w.strip() and float(c) >= 0]
    text = " ".join(w for w, _ in words)
    confidence = sum(c for _, c in words) / max(len(words), 1)
    return text, confidence

That gets you a blob of text. Turning it into headline / description / display URL reliably took most of the work. The traps I hit:

  1. Not everything in the image is the ad. Many snapshots include a product thumbnail or sitelink buttons on the right. OCR happily reads those and mixes them into the description. Detect and crop them first.
  2. Headline vs. description. Google draws the headline in blue and the description in dark grey, so splitting by color before OCR works far better than guessing from line positions afterwards.
  3. Language. The same advertiser runs ads in dozens of languages. Picking the Tesseract model from the countries the ad ran in (Korean, Japanese, Thai, Arabic, Cyrillic…) fixes most of the garbage.
  4. Trust the confidence score — strictly. My first threshold was 70. At 77, one booking.com description came out as "Book a Hotel near Universal Studios. HEHHE HAHA Quick, Easy Booking." Above 90 the text was mostly clean, apart from cut-off words. Anything lower should be flagged, not trusted.
  5. Some words are simply cut off. The screenshot crops long headlines, so you'll get "Hotels in Downtown Chica…". Nothing to fix there — just know it.
  6. Be gentle with Google. The listing endpoints rate-limit quickly (429s and CAPTCHA pages). Retry a couple of times, then stop — don't hammer.

The no-maintenance version

I packaged all of this as an Apify Actor (Google Ads Transparency & Ad Library Scraper), so I don't have to babysit OCR models or rate limits. Here's how I find a competitor's long-running search ads — the ones they keep paying for:

from apify_client import ApifyClient
import pandas as pd

client = ApifyClient("<YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN>")

run = client.actor("datalume/google-ads-transparency-scraper").call(run_input={
    "domains": ["nike.com"],
    "region": "US",
    "platform": "search",
    "format": "text",
    "minDaysRunning": 30,          # skip short tests
    "sortBy": "longestRunning",
    "maxAdsPerTarget": 50,
})

df = pd.DataFrame(client.dataset(run.default_dataset_id).iterate_items())
good = df[df["copyStatus"] == "ok"]   # high-confidence copy only
good[["daysShown", "firstShown", "headline", "regionCount"]].head(10)

Here's what came back for nike.com (US, search, text ads, run on Nov 1, 2026) — 50 ads, copy for all 50 (38 from the text preview, 12 by OCR, all above 90 confidence). A slice of the longest-running ones:

Days shown First shown Advertiser Headline Countries
1,833 2021-10-25 WPP Media (agency) Zapatillas Air Max 90. Nike MX 8
1,794 2021-10-25 Nike Retail BV Nike - Onlineshop Deutschland 46
1,794 2021-10-25 Nike Retail BV Nike: zapatillas, ropa y más 51
1,793 2021-10-25 Nike Retail BV Nike UK - Online Store 44
1,792 2021-10-25 Nike Retail BV The Official Nike Site - Nike: Shop The Collection (OCR) 39
1,735 2021-10-25 Nike Retail BV NIKE — onlinebutik - Officiella Nike-webbplatsen (OCR) 29
1,384 2022-11-30 Nike, Inc. Training & Gym Equipment. Nike.com (OCR) 1
1,384 2022-11-30 Nike, Inc. (dynamic — Google writes it) 1

A few things jump out in under a minute:

  1. The longest-running ads weren't placed by Nike's own account but by an agency account (WPP Media). A domain search returns every advertiser whose ads point at the domain — useful, but filter by advertiser if you only want the brand itself.
  2. Nike's European "brand" ads have been running since at least October 2021, in roughly 30–50 countries each, with the same handful of lines ("The Official Website. Home Of Everything Nike. Shop The Latest Releases."). That's what a proven, evergreen brand ad looks like.
  3. In the US, 28 of the 31 ads from the Nike, Inc. account have no fixed headline — they're Dynamic Search Ads, where Google writes the headline from the landing page. Nike US leans on DSA and only controls the description. You'd never see that pattern by clicking through ads one at a time.

Also note daysShown is the number of days the ad actually ran, not just last-minus-first: three ads that all "started" on 2021-10-25 show 1,833, 1,794 and 1,688 days.

What else is in each row

  • firstShown, lastShown, daysShown, isActive — how long the ad has been running and whether it's live
  • regions — every country the ad ran in, with the last date shown there
  • headline, description, displayUrl, plus copySource (text or ocr) and copyConfidence
  • transparencyUrl — a link back to the ad on Google's site, so you can check anything by eye

You can also pass advertiser names or IDs instead of domains, filter by country / platform / date, and set onlyNewAds on a daily schedule to get just the new creatives.

Caveats (read these before you trust the numbers)

  • firstShown has a floor. The oldest ads I've seen all show 2021-10-25, which looks like where the Transparency Center's history begins. Read it as "running since at least then", not as the real start date.
  • OCR isn't perfect. Even high-confidence rows can contain a wrong letter ("Al" for "AI") or a cut-off word. Low-confidence rows are kept but marked lowConfidence.
  • Domain searches include other advertisers — agencies, resellers, or anyone whose ads link to that domain or its subdomains (like the WPP Media rows above). Use an advertiser ID if you need exactly one advertiser.

Cost

The Actor charges per ad: $2.00 per 1,000 ads, or $3.50 per 1,000 for text ads where high-confidence copy was extracted (instead of, not on top of, the $2). Countries are included, and rows Google fails to load are free. The 50-ad run above cost $0.18 (50 ads with copy × $0.0035) and took about a minute; with onlyNewAds on a schedule, you only pay for ads you haven't seen before.

Disclosure: I run datalume, the publisher of the Actor used here. Both the Actor and this article were built with AI assistance; every number above comes from real runs on Nov 1, 2026 and was checked against the raw data. Questions welcome in the comments.
