title: Building an Asynchronous WhatsApp Cloud API Webhook Gateway with Sub-50ms Latency
description:
When building production enterprise messaging applications, handling real-time incoming events from the Meta WhatsApp Cloud API requires speed, resilience, and strict cryptographic verification.

Many engineering teams default to legacy Business Solution Providers (BSPs) that introduce intermediate aggregator servers, per-message markups, and artificial queue bottlenecks. At AIsoule, engineered by PrimeSkill Solutions Private Limited (Scheme No. 51, Indore, MP 452006, India), we architected our platform directly on Meta's native Cloud API infrastructure, bypassing all third-party aggregators to achieve 0% markup and sub-50ms event processing latency.

In this deep dive, we'll walk through the implementation of a high-throughput, event-driven WhatsApp Cloud API webhook gateway with HMAC SHA-256 signature verification and real-time audio signaling.

1. The Core Architecture Challenge

Every incoming WhatsApp event—whether it's an inbound customer text, message delivery status (sent, delivered, read), button click, or media upload—is dispatched by Meta's servers as an HTTPS POST request to your configured webhook URL.

┌─────────────────────────┐
│ Meta WhatsApp Cloud API │
└────────────┬────────────┘
             │ HTTPS POST (JSON Payload + X-Hub-Signature-256)
             ▼
┌─────────────────────────┐
│   AIsoule Edge Gateway  │ ──► Verify HMAC Signature (<2ms)
└────────────┬────────────┘
             │ Fast-Ack: HTTP 200 OK (<15ms)
             ▼
┌─────────────────────────┐
│ Async Processing Worker │ ──► CRM Routing & Live WebRTC Signaling
└─────────────────────────┘

If your server takes longer than 3,000 milliseconds to respond with an HTTP 200 OK, Meta considers the request timed out and begins aggressive exponential retry loops. Under heavy broadcast spikes (thousands of replies per minute), synchronous database writes will quickly exhaust your connection pool and cause cascading failures.

2. Step 1: Webhook Challenge Verification (GET Request)

When first registering your webhook in the Meta Developer Portal, Meta sends a GET request with challenge query parameters. Here is the verification logic:

const crypto = require("crypto");
const express = require("express");
const app = express();

const VERIFY_TOKEN = process.env.WHATSAPP_VERIFY_TOKEN || "aisoule_secure_webhook_token_2026";

app.get("/api/whatsapp/webhook", (req, res) => {
  const mode = req.query["hub.mode"];
  const token = req.query["hub.verify_token"];
  const challenge = req.query["hub.challenge"];

  if (mode === "subscribe" && token === VERIFY_TOKEN) {
    console.log("[AIsoule Gateway] Webhook successfully verified by Meta.");
    return res.status(200).send(challenge);
  }

  return res.sendStatus(403);
});

3. Step 2: Cryptographic HMAC SHA-256 Signature Validation

Security is paramount. You must verify that incoming POST payloads originate from Meta and were not spoofed or intercepted. Meta attaches an X-Hub-Signature-256 header formatted as sha256=<hash>.

// Middleware to capture raw buffer for HMAC hashing
app.use(express.json({
  verify: (req, res, buf) => {
    req.rawBody = buf;
  }
}));

const APP_SECRET = process.env.META_APP_SECRET;

function verifyMetaSignature(req, res, next) {
  const signature = req.headers["x-hub-signature-256"];
  if (!signature) {
    return res.status(401).json({ error: "Missing X-Hub-Signature-256 header" });
  }

  const expectedSignature = "sha256=" + crypto
    .createHmac("sha256", APP_SECRET)
    .update(req.rawBody)
    .digest("hex");

  if (!crypto.timingSafeEqual(Buffer.from(signature), Buffer.from(expectedSignature))) {
    console.error("[Security Alert] Invalid webhook HMAC signature!");
    return res.status(403).json({ error: "Invalid signature" });
  }

  next();
}

Using crypto.timingSafeEqual prevents timing attacks that could reveal secret bits.

4. Step 3: Fast-Ack Asynchronous Queue Pattern

To guarantee sub-50ms latency and prevent Meta webhook retries, your gateway should return res.status(200).send("EVENT_RECEIVED") immediately after cryptographic verification, offloading the event payload to a worker queue:

const { Queue } = require("bullmq");
const messageQueue = new Queue("whatsapp-messages", {
  connection: { host: "localhost", port: 6379 }
});

app.post("/api/whatsapp/webhook", verifyMetaSignature, async (req, res) => {
  // FAST-ACK: Return 200 OK immediately
  res.status(200).send("EVENT_RECEIVED");

  const body = req.body;
  if (body.object === "whatsapp_business_account") {
    for (const entry of body.entry || []) {
      for (const change of entry.changes || []) {
        if (change.value && change.value.messages) {
          // Push to asynchronous worker queue
          await messageQueue.add("process-message", {
            businessAccountId: entry.id,
            data: change.value
          }, {
            removeOnComplete: true,
            attempts: 3
          });
        }
      }
    }
  }
});

5. Bridging Chat to Live WebRTC Voice Calling

One of the standout architectural innovations we built into AIsoule is native in-browser WebRTC voice calling.

Traditionally, when a high-intent customer chatting on WhatsApp needs immediate human support, agents must dial an international PSTN number, incurring telecom carrier fees. With our architecture, agents can generate a secure single-use WebRTC voice signaling session link directly inside the WhatsApp chat thread:

  1. Agent generates a session token via our multi-agent conversational CRM.
  2. The customer receives an interactive WhatsApp action button.
  3. Clicking the button opens a secure, browser-native WebRTC audio call connected directly to the agent's live browser desk—delivering HD audio with zero telecom toll charges.

6. Real-World Cost Benchmarks: Zero Markup vs Legacy BSPs

By implementing a direct Meta Cloud API pipeline, organizations eliminate aggregator markups entirely:

Messaging Dimension Legacy Business Solution Providers (BSPs) AIsoule Direct Cloud API Architecture
Reseller Surcharge \$0.005 – \$0.015 per message \$0.00 (Zero Reseller Markup)
Meta Fee Billing Indirect / Bundled with currency margins Direct from Meta with Local GST Invoice
Processing Latency 400ms – 1,200ms (Aggregator hops) <50ms Direct Edge Ingestion
Voice Support External Call Center / PBX Hardware Native In-Browser WebRTC Calling

You can calculate exact conversation fee savings with our Meta Per-Message Pricing Benchmark.

Conclusion & Resources

Building directly on Meta's WhatsApp Cloud API enables engineering teams to create resilient, scalable communications infrastructure without paying unnecessary reseller surcharges.

To explore open developer utilities and embeddable components:

  • Free WhatsApp Link & QR Generator: AIsoule Link Utilities
  • Interactive Floating Chat Widget: AIsoule Widget Generator
  • Official Enterprise Platform: AIsoule Platform

Engineered by PrimeSkill Solutions Private Limited, Scheme No. 51, Indore, MP 452006, India.

Choose between two approval modes:

title: Vercel Sandbox is now globally available

title: AI Gateway now supports asynchronous video generation
description:
Video generation on AI Gateway can now run asynchronously.

By default, generateVideo keeps one HTTP request to AI Gateway open until the result is ready. Because video generation can take seconds or minutes, that request can exceed request timeouts.

With asynchronous generation, your application can receive a webhook, poll for completion, or start a generation and retrieve the result in a later request.

Choose an option based on whether your process can keep running and whether your application can receive webhooks:

Existing generateVideo calls continue to work as before. All four options support text-to-video, image-to-video, reference-to-video, and other video inputs.

Upgrade the SDK

Install the latest versions of the AI SDK and AI Gateway provider:

Use asynchronous video generation

Wait for completion in a Workflow

An easy way to consume the completion webhook is a Workflow SDK. The workflow creates its own webhook URL, passes it to startVideo, and suspends until AI Gateway delivers the completion event. Install the Workflow SDK alongside the AI SDK:

While the video renders, the workflow run is suspended and resumes when AI Gateway delivers the terminal event.

Use a webhook with generateVideo

Pass webhook to generateVideo to wait for a completion event without polling. AI Gateway sends an event when the job completes or fails. The SDK waits for that event, fetches the generated videos, and resolves the original generateVideo call.

The calling process and webhook handler need a shared token and store so the delivery can be matched to the correct generation. generateVideo does not expose the signing secret for this job. See the webhook verification documentation for the complete receiver pattern.

Both the polling and webhook options for generateVideo return result.videos as GeneratedFile objects. The SDK downloads provider-hosted videos, making uint8Array, base64, and mediaType available in either job.

Poll with generateVideo

Add poll to an existing generateVideo call:

AI Gateway starts an asynchronous job, and the SDK sends a short status request at each interval until the job finishes. The calling process must remain running until generateVideo resolves, but no individual request to AI Gateway stays open for the full generation.

Start a job and retrieve it later

startVideo returns an operation as soon as AI Gateway accepts the job, without waiting for rendering to finish. Store that operation and pass it to getVideoStatus later from the same process or another one:

The operation is JSON-serializable, so it can be stored in a database or passed through a queue. Your application controls how long to keep checking the job because it has no built-in timeout.

You can also pass webhookUrl to startVideo to receive a completion event instead of checking the status. The start response includes the signing secret needed to verify the webhook.

Unlike generateVideo, getVideoStatus does not download hosted videos. It returns provider URLs or inline bytes. Hosted URLs can expire, so download any videos you need to keep.

Monitor asynchronous jobs

Every asynchronous generation appears on the AI Gateway Logs page as soon as it starts. Jobs show as Running while generation is in progress and update when they complete or fail.

Under Request Mode, select Async to show only asynchronous jobs. Opening an entry shows the job ID and the request details.

Only asynchronous requests create jobs. A standard generateVideo call appears as a single completed request after the video is ready.

For size limits, idempotency for retried job starts, webhook delivery retries, and other operational details, read the asynchronous video generation documentation or browse all video models.

Read more

title: ACH Return Code R01: Insufficient Funds — Detection and Retry Strategy
description:
ACH Return Code R01: Insufficient Funds — Detection and Retry Strategy

Understanding R01: The Most Common ACH Return

When an ACH debit transaction bounces, the most frequent culprit is NACHA return code R01: Insufficient Funds. This occurs when the receiver's account lacks the balance to cover the transaction at settlement time. For developers building payout systems, handling R01 correctly is critical—it's not a permanent failure, but a timing and liquidity issue.

When R01 Fires

R01 triggers during the ACH settlement window (typically T+1 or T+2), when the Federal Reserve attempts to debit the destination account. The originating bank submits the return file, and your system receives notification via your ACH processor's webhook or API.

Key timing detail: R01 returns arrive 1–2 business days after the original debit attempt. This delay means your reconciliation logic must account for a multi-day window before you know the final state.

Why R01 Matters More Than Other Returns

Unlike R03 (No Account) or R04 (Invalid Account), R01 is reversible and retryable. The account exists, it's valid—the customer simply didn't have enough money at settlement time. This distinction shapes your recovery strategy.

According to Nacha data, R01 represents roughly 35–40% of all ACH returns in consumer and B2B flows. If you're processing high volume, you'll see R01 regularly.

Programmatic Detection and Routing

Here's a minimal example of detecting and categorizing an R01 return in your payout pipeline:

def handle_ach_return(return_code, transaction_id, amount):
    """
    Route ACH returns based on code.
    R01 → retry queue; R03/R04 → manual review; others → dunning.
    """
    if return_code == "R01":
        # Insufficient funds: safe to retry
        schedule_retry(
            transaction_id=transaction_id,
            retry_after_days=3,  # Give customer time to deposit
            max_retries=2
        )
        log_event("R01_INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS", transaction_id, amount)
        return "RETRY_SCHEDULED"

    elif return_code in ["R03", "R04"]:
        # Invalid account: manual intervention required
        escalate_to_support(transaction_id, return_code)
        return "MANUAL_REVIEW"

    else:
        # Other returns: apply dunning logic
        apply_dunning_rule(transaction_id, return_code)
        return "DUNNING_APPLIED"

Building a Retry Strategy for R01

R01 returns demand a thoughtful retry approach:

Attempt Delay Logic
Initial T+1 or T+2 Original ACH debit
Retry 1 T+4 Customer may have deposited; low cost
Retry 2 T+7 Final attempt; consider alternate rail
Fallback T+9+ Switch to Visa Direct or RTP if available

Why this cadence? R01 is often a temporary liquidity event. Waiting 3–4 days gives the customer time to deposit funds, and your retry cost is minimal (ACH retry is ~$0.25 per transaction).

Webhook Integration Pattern

Most ACH processors (Stripe, Dwolla, Treasury Prime) deliver return notifications via webhook. Here's a robust handler:

@app.post("/webhooks/ach-return")
def receive_ach_return(payload):
    """
    Webhook handler for ACH return notifications.
    Payload includes return_code, original_transaction_id, reason_code.
    """
    return_code = payload.get("return_code")
    txn_id = payload.get("transaction_id")
    amount = payload.get("amount")

    # Idempotency: check if we've already processed this return
    if Return.query.filter_by(nacha_id=payload["nacha_id"]).first():
        return {"status": "already_processed"}, 200

    # Log the return
    Return.create(
        transaction_id=txn_id,
        return_code=return_code,
        amount=amount,
        received_at=datetime.utcnow()
    )

    # Route based on code
    action = handle_ach_return(return_code, txn_id, amount)

    return {"status": "processed", "action": action}, 200

Key Takeaways

  • R01 is recoverable. It signals a timing issue, not a closed account or fraud.
  • Retry within 3–7 days. Gives customers time to resolve liquidity and keeps your success rate high.
  • Detect programmatically. Use return_code fields in your webhook payload to auto

Decoding ACH return codes programmatically? The ACH Return Codes API returns the full Nacha R01–R85 set with plain-language descriptions and handling guidance.

title: Fintech Ticket Triage with Node.js RAG: PDF Upload, Semantic Search, and Citations
description:
Short answer: use Node.js for the upload workflow, pgvector for metadata-aware semantic search, and embeddings plus citations as a validated contract; choose a shared OpenAI-compatible runtime only when its breadth is more useful than provider-specific controls.

The practical answer is a small retrieval pipeline: parse the uploaded PDF, split it into overlapping chunks, embed each chunk with its filename, page, and section, retrieve the nearest chunks with pgvector, and pass those chunks and their citation metadata to the answer model. For a fintech support queue, I would make structured output correctness the release gate, not a dashboard score or a fluent demo.

At 3 a.m., the useful page is the one that says a ticket cannot be answered because its evidence is missing or malformed. A page saying “retrieval healthy” is not enough. What page fired, and can the on-call engineer reproduce the answer from the cited source?

What should the page fire on?

Imagine the support worker receives a question about a transfer limit. The user uploaded a policy PDF last week. The worker finds a semantically similar passage, generates an answer, and the UI displays a citation. The failure worth paging on is not that the prose sounds awkward; it is that the returned object has an answer with no source, a source with no page, or a citation whose chunk was not among the retrieved chunks.

Work backwards from that contract. Store each chunk with a stable document identifier, filename, page, section, and chunk position. Keep the exact text used to create the embedding. Then the retrieval result can carry evidence forward instead of asking the answer model to recreate provenance from memory.

The instrumentation change is small: count malformed structured responses, missing citation metadata, and citations that do not resolve to retrieved chunk IDs. Include a request ID and a ticket ID in logs, but never put the uploaded document or payment details into a broad operational log. For a queue handling several document revisions, I would also record the document version beside the chunk ID, because a valid page from yesterday's policy can still be the wrong answer today. The check needs to distinguish a bad model response from a stale retrieval index, then attach the distinction to the page so the responder knows where to start. A threshold that pages on every malformed response will train the team to ignore the page; a threshold that hides all failures makes the citation promise fictional.

The page is binary.

How should a Node.js RAG handle PDF upload and semantic search?

Chunking is a boundary decision, not a magic number. A chunk that is too large brings unrelated policy language into the context; one that is too small can separate a condition from its exception. Overlap helps preserve that relationship, while page and section metadata make the result inspectable. Token counting is useful here because chunk size and top-k context must fit the answer prompt.

One workable record looks like this. It is deliberately boring: the source fields travel with the text instead of being reconstructed after generation.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func postJSON(path string, payload any) ([]byte, error) {
    body, err := json.Marshal(payload)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    base := os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL")
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if base == "" || key == "" {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_BASE_URL and INFRAI_API_KEY are required")
    }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPost, base+path, bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        data, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            wait := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); parseErr == nil {
                wait = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(wait)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("API status %s: %s", resp.Status, data)
        }
        return data, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("rate limit persisted after retries")
}

func main() {
    embedding, err := postJSON("/v1/embeddings", map[string]any{
        "model": os.Getenv("EMBEDDING_MODEL"),
        "input": "What is the daily transfer limit?",
    })
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    chat, err := postJSON("/v1/chat/completions", map[string]any{
        "model": os.Getenv("CHAT_MODEL"),
        "messages": []map[string]string{{
            "role": "user",
            "content": "Answer only from the retrieved chunks and return citation IDs.",
        }},
    })
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Printf("embedding=%d bytes, chat=%d bytes\n", len(embedding), len(chat))
}

The important part is not the Go type. It is the invariant: an answer citation must point to a stored chunk that was actually retrieved. Before calling the chat model, validate that the selected chunks have text, a stable ID, and source metadata. After the call, validate the output schema again. If validation fails, return a review-needed result rather than inventing a citation.

Embeddings solve a different problem. They let semantic retrieval find a passage when the ticket uses different wording from the PDF. They do not prove that the passage is current, applicable to the customer, or sufficient to answer the question. A similarity score is evidence for ranking, not evidence for authorization.

Which implementation should own the retrieval boundary?

There are several reasonable choices, and the operational boundary matters more than the logo.

Option Useful distinction Boundary to test
OpenAI embeddings and chat APIs with Postgres/pgvector Direct model APIs plus a database you control You own chunking, metadata joins, retries, and citation validation
Cohere Embed and Rerank with a vector store Separate retrieval and reranking capabilities Model and reranker behavior must be evaluated against your policy corpus
Vertex AI embeddings and model services A natural fit for teams already operating on Google Cloud IAM, regional availability, and managed-service conventions become part of the incident path
Infrai's OpenAI-compatible surface One consistent contract can put embeddings and chat behind the same integration boundary, while its broader REST surface lets a later capability use another endpoint rather than another client integration Verify readiness, model routing, and response metadata for the capabilities you actually depend on

The first four are not interchangeable and none removes the need for a source contract. pgvector is an extension for Postgres, not a hosted answer engine; it keeps vector similarity close to relational metadata, which is useful when tenant and document permissions must be applied in the same query. A managed vector database can reduce database operations, but it adds a separate consistency and authorization boundary. Anthropic's Claude is another model-provider alternative for answer generation when its model behavior is already approved; it does not remove your need to own PDF parsing, embeddings, vector filtering, or citation checks.

I would choose the OpenAI-compatible path only when the shared contract is worth more than provider-specific controls, and I would choose a direct provider when its retrieval or model behavior is a tested requirement. Infrai is a strong fit for a small ask-your-docs service that expects to add backend capabilities behind one REST shape. It is not a good fit if a team requires a single provider's proprietary retrieval controls, regional guarantees, or an already-certified model path; choose that provider directly then. It is not a reason to skip schema validation, permission filters, or evaluation on real support tickets.

What does a minimal correctness check look like?

The write path creates embeddings for chunks and stores the vector beside the source fields. The read path embeds the ticket, searches pgvector with the tenant and document filters applied, and sends only the selected text plus citation metadata to chat completions. The exact client can vary; the contract should not.

package main

import (
    "errors"
    "fmt"
)

type Retrieved struct {
    ChunkID  string
    Text     string
    Filename string
    Page     int
}

type Answer struct {
    Text       string
    CitationIDs []string
}

func validateAnswer(a Answer, retrieved []Retrieved) error {
    if a.Text == "" || len(a.CitationIDs) == 0 {
        return errors.New("answer must contain text and at least one citation")
    }
    known := make(map[string]bool, len(retrieved))
    for _, r := range retrieved {
        if r.ChunkID == "" || r.Filename == "" || r.Page < 1 || r.Text == "" {
            return errors.New("retrieved evidence has incomplete metadata")
        }
        known[r.ChunkID] = true
    }
    for _, id := range a.CitationIDs {
        if !known[id] {
            return fmt.Errorf("citation %q was not retrieved", id)
        }
    }
    return nil
}

func main() {}

In production, the embedding and chat calls need explicit status handling, authentication from an environment variable, and backoff for rate limits. A write or publish retry also needs an idempotency key. Those are boring details until a queue retries a ticket and creates two audit records. Keep them in the client boundary, where every model provider follows the same rules.

How do you keep false positives from becoming the incident?

The page should represent a user-impacting contract failure, not merely a low similarity score. Start with a small labeled set of tickets: expected answer, acceptable source pages, and cases that must be escalated. Measure citation validity separately from answer quality. A fluent answer with the wrong page is a failure; a refusal with a correct citation may be the desired behavior for an ambiguous policy.

This is where I distrust dashboards. A green retrieval latency chart cannot tell me whether the policy exception disappeared during chunking. A red latency chart may be harmless if the queue is draining and every answer remains grounded. The actionable signal is the trace from ticket to retrieved chunk IDs to validated response.

The false-positive cost is real. If the threshold is too sensitive, humans spend the night reviewing healthy tickets and start suppressing the page. If it is too loose, unsupported financial guidance reaches a customer. Tune the alert around the structured contract and sample the borderline cases; do not let a single aggregate similarity threshold stand in for correctness.

Further reading

  • OpenAI Embeddings guide
  • pgvector: Postgres vector similarity extension
  • Cohere Embed documentation
  • Vertex AI text embeddings documentation
  • Pinecone documentation

title: Always-on tracing for production and preview traffic
description:
With always-on tracing, you can now debug your real user requests without reproducing them.

Always-on tracing continuously collects traces from your production and preview traffic. Unlike session tracing, which only captures requests from your own browser, it samples your live traffic.

You control what's collected with sampling rules. Each rule sets a trace rate for an environment (All, Production, or Preview), optionally scoped to a path prefix like /checkout. Nothing is collected until you add a rule, so you pay only for what you choose to trace.

You can also manage sampling rules from the CLI. vercel traces config set adds a rule, or changes the rate of an existing one when you run it again with the same environment and path prefix:

Infrastructure and outbound fetch spans are captured automatically. To add framework and custom spans, instrument your app with @vercel/otel.

To view a trace, open the Logs or run vercel traces get <request-id>.

Always-on tracing is is now in beta and available to teams on all plans. Tracing is priced at $0.50 per 1M span units. Traces follow your runtime log retention: 1 hour on Hobby, 1 day on Pro and 3 days on Enterprise.

Get started by adding a rule in Settings → Tracing or from the settings icon in Logs. Learn more in the documentation.

title: Stack vs Queue: What Is the Difference? (With Examples)
description:
Originally published on CodingCush.

A stack and a queue are both simple ways of storing items in order, but they differ in one rule: a stack removes the last item you added (LIFO — Last In, First Out), while a queue removes the first item you added (FIFO — First In, First Out). A stack behaves like a pile of plates; a queue behaves like a line of people at a ticket counter.

What Is a Stack?

Imagine the plate pile in a kitchen. You place clean plates on top of each other, and when you need one, you take it from the top. You never pull a plate from the middle unless you enjoy washing the floor as well. That is a stack: new items go on top, and removals also happen at the top. The last plate you placed is the first one you take away — Last In, First Out.

A stack supports two main operations. Push adds an item to the top, and pop removes the item from the top. Most stacks also offer peek (or top), which lets you look at the top item without removing it — the programming equivalent of glancing at the pile before committing.

stack = []

stack.append("page A")   # push
stack.append("page B")   # push
stack.append("page C")   # push

print(stack.pop())       # page C  (last in, first out)
print(stack.pop())       # page B
print(stack)             # ['page A']

This is not a made-up classroom example: your browser's Back button works exactly like this. Every page you visit is pushed onto a history stack, and pressing Back pops the most recent page off. The Undo button in your editor, and the way programmes remember which function called which, use the same idea.

What Is a Queue?

Now picture the queue at a coffee shop. The first person who joined the line is served first, and new arrivals join at the back. Nobody (in a polite country, at least) cuts in at the front. That fairness rule — First In, First Out — is a queue. Adding an item is called enqueue and happens at the back; removing one is called dequeue and happens at the front.

from collections import deque

queue = deque()
queue.append("print job 1")   # enqueue at the back
queue.append("print job 2")
queue.append("print job 3")

print(queue.popleft())        # print job 1  (first in, first out)
print(queue.popleft())        # print job 2
print(queue)                  # deque(['print job 3'])

Queues quietly run much of the software you use daily. Printers work through documents in queue order. Websites place incoming requests in a queue so the server handles them fairly. Downloads, message apps and customer-support tickets all line up in queues. In Python, the official tutorial's Data Structures chapter shows both patterns — lists used as stacks, and queues built for first-in, first-out behaviour — in its Python documentation on data structures.

The official Python Tutorial, Data Structures chapter — its contents list both "Using Lists as Stacks" and "Using Lists as Queues".

Stack vs Queue in One Table

Point Stack Queue
Rule LIFO — Last In, First Out FIFO — First In, First Out
Real-life picture A pile of plates A line at a ticket counter
Insert happens at The top (same end) The back (rear)
Remove happens at The top (same end) The front
Main operations push, pop, peek enqueue, dequeue, front
Everyday examples Browser Back button, Undo, function calls Print jobs, waiting requests, message lines

The single most important row is the first one. If an interviewer asks you nothing else, remember: same-end versus two-ends. A stack works at one end only; a queue works at both ends — in at the back, out at the front.

Why the Removal Cost Differs in Python

Here is a detail that separates a memorised answer from an understood one. In Python, using a list as a stack is fast, because append() and pop() work at the end of the list, where nothing else has to move. A queue built from a plain list is slow, though: removing the first item with pop(0) forces every remaining item to shuffle one place forward. Do that a million times and your programme develops a noticeable limp. That is why the example above uses deque from the collections module, which is built for fast additions and removals at both ends. MDN's reference for JavaScript's Array methods shows the same pattern in another language: push/pop for stack behaviour, and shift for queue behaviour (with the same cost warning in large arrays).

If you enjoyed this comparison, our guide to array vs linked list explains where these structures actually store their items in memory, and it pairs nicely with what you have just read.

A Famous Stack Trick: Checking Balanced Brackets

Here is the example that makes stacks click for most people. Suppose you must check whether the brackets in a line of code are balanced — every opening bracket closed in the right order, as in { [ ( ) ] }. A stack solves it beautifully: walk through the characters, push every opening bracket, and whenever a closing bracket appears, pop the top and check that the pair matches. If the stack is empty at the end, the brackets are balanced.

def is_balanced(text):
    pairs = {")": "(", "]": "[", "}": "{"}
    stack = []
    for ch in text:
        if ch in "([{":
            stack.append(ch)
        elif ch in ")]}":
            if not stack or stack.pop() != pairs[ch]:
                return False
    return len(stack) == 0

print(is_balanced("{ [ ( ) ] }"))   # True
print(is_balanced("{ [ ( ] ) }"))   # False

Notice why a queue would fail here: the closing bracket must match the most recent opener, not the oldest one — and "most recent first" is exactly the stack rule. The mirror-image classic for queues is breadth-first search, where you explore a tree or a map level by level, always visiting the place that has waited longest. Same family of ideas, opposite removal rule.

How Fast Are They? A Quick Big O Note

For interviews, one line about speed is usually enough: push, pop, enqueue and dequeue are all O(1) — constant time — when the structure is built properly, because each operation touches only one end and nothing else has to move. Looking at the top of a stack or the front of a queue is also O(1). Searching for an item inside either one is O(n), because you may have to look at every element — a polite way of saying these two structures are designed for order, not for searching.

Which One Should You Use?

Choose by asking one question: which item should come out next? If the answer is "the most recent one" — undo steps, backtracking through a maze, checking that brackets in code are balanced, reversing a word — you want a stack. If the answer is "the one that has waited longest" — tasks, requests, messages, print jobs, breadth-first search through a tree or a graph — you want a queue. When in doubt, picture the plates and the coffee line; the correct structure usually introduces itself.

Stacks and queues are also the friendly front door to bigger data-structure ideas. Our explainer on what a hash table is covers the other classic beginner structure, the one that trades ordering for lightning-fast lookups by name.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does LIFO and FIFO mean?

LIFO means Last In, First Out: the newest item leaves first, as in a stack. FIFO means First In, First Out: the oldest item leaves first, as in a queue. They are simply the two removal rules written as initials.

Is a stack or a queue used for the browser Back button?

A stack. Each page you visit is pushed on top, and Back pops the latest page off, which is why you retrace your steps in reverse order.

Can one structure act as the other?

Programmers can simulate a queue using two stacks, and vice versa — a favourite interview puzzle — but in everyday code you simply pick the structure whose removal rule matches your problem.

Which is faster, a stack or a queue?

Both are fast when built correctly: their main operations are O(1), constant time. Slowness only appears when you use the wrong tool, like removing from the front of a Python list instead of using a deque.

Conclusion

A stack takes from the top; a queue serves from the front. Plates versus people in a line, LIFO versus FIFO, push/pop versus enqueue/dequeue — once those pictures stick, you will never confuse the two again, in an interview or in real code.

title: Prompt Engineering for Beginners (Part 2): The Anatomy of a Good Prompt
description:
Part 1 of our Prompt Engineering from Scratch series, we explored how AI generates answers, what tokens and context windows are, and why the way we communicate with AI matters.

We learned one important lesson:

Getting better results from AI isn't always about using a more powerful model. Sometimes, it's about giving clearer instructions.

But knowing that we should write better prompts is one thing.

How do we actually write them?

What information should we include? How specific should our instructions be? And how do we know whether our prompt is good enough?

That's exactly what we'll explore in Part 2.

We'll break down six useful components of a well-structured prompt, understand what each one does, and learn how to combine them using simple, real-life examples.

No complicated terminology. No programming knowledge required.

Let's get started.

In Part 2, we'll learn the six useful building blocks of a good prompt, how to combine them, and how to test whether our prompts are working.

And don't worry. You don't need any technical background.

Let's begin with something we all understand.

1. Why Isn't a Simple Prompt Always Enough?

Imagine you're asking a friend to help you write an email.

You say:

Write an email for me.

Your friend would probably have a few questions.

Who is the email for?

What is it about?

Should it sound formal or friendly?

How long should it be?

Without that information, your friend has to guess.

AI faces a similar problem.

A basic prompt

Let's say you type:

Write an email asking for leave.

The AI might produce an email, but it doesn't know important details.

For example:

  • Who are you writing to?
  • Why do you need leave?
  • How many days do you need?
  • What tone should the email use?
  • Should the email be short or detailed?

Now let's make the prompt clearer.

A more detailed prompt 

Write a professional email to my manager
requesting two days of leave.

I need leave on Monday and Tuesday
because of a family commitment.

Keep the email polite and under 120 words.

Include a subject line.

This is much clearer.

You've given the AI the information it needs to create a more suitable response.

Does that guarantee the perfect email?

No.

But it reduces unnecessary guessing.

And that's the foundation of a good prompt.

A good prompt doesn't need complicated words. It needs clear instructions and enough relevant information.

2. The Six Building Blocks of a Good Prompt

When writing a prompt, there are six useful components you can think about.

These components help you explain what you need, how you want the task completed, and what the final answer should look like.

Component What it means Simple example
1. Role Who should the AI act as? Act as a helpful writing assistant.
2. Context What background information does it need? I'm writing to my manager about taking leave.
3. Examples Can you show what a good answer looks like? Here is an example of my writing style.
4. Task What exactly should it do? Write an email requesting two days of leave.
5. Constraints What rules should it follow? Keep it polite and under 120 words.
6. Output Format How should the answer be presented? Include a subject line and email body.

These six components provide a useful framework for writing clear prompts.

But here's something important: you don't need all six components every time.

For a simple question like:

What is the capital of Nepal?

A short prompt is perfectly fine.

For more complicated tasks, such as analyzing a document or writing a detailed report, additional information becomes more valuable.

The goal isn't to make every prompt longer.

The goal is to make every prompt clear enough for its purpose.

Now let's understand each component.

3. Component 1: Role - Who Should the AI Act As?

Imagine you're asking someone for advice.

If you need help preparing for an exam, you might ask a teacher.

If you need help improving your writing, you might ask an editor.

If you need help planning a trip, you might ask a travel guide.

Different roles suggest different ways of approaching a task.

You can use a similar idea when prompting AI.

Without a role 

Help me improve this paragraph.

With a role 

Act as a friendly writing tutor.

Help me improve this paragraph using
simple English.

Explain what you changed and why.

The second prompt gives the AI a clearer direction.

It suggests the type of assistance and explanation you want.

What is a system prompt?

You might hear the technical term system prompt.

In many AI applications, a system message contains higher-level instructions about how the assistant should behave.

For example, an application might instruct its AI assistant to use a particular language or follow certain rules.

However, when you type:

Act as a writing tutor.

into a normal chat, you're generally giving a role instruction as a user, not changing the application's actual system message.

You don't need to access system settings to use role-based prompting.

And a role doesn't give the model magical expertise or guarantee accurate answers.

It simply helps guide how the model approaches and presents the task.

When is this useful?

When you want a particular style of help, such as teaching, editing, planning, or reviewing.

4. Component 2: Context - Give the AI the Background Information

Imagine someone asks you:

What should I do?

You'd probably respond:

About what?

Without knowing the situation, it's difficult to give useful advice.

That's exactly why context matters.

Context is the background information that helps AI understand your situation or task.

Without context 

Write an email requesting leave.

With context 

I'm an employee writing to my manager.

I need two days of leave on Monday
and Tuesday because of a family commitment.

My manager prefers short and
professional emails.

Now the AI knows more about your situation.

It can use that information when preparing the email.

Another example

Imagine you're asking AI to recommend a laptop.

Basic prompt:

Recommend a laptop.

Prompt with context:

I'm a university student.

I mainly use my laptop for online classes,
writing assignments, browsing, and watching videos.

My budget is around $600.

Recommend suitable laptops and explain
why they would fit my needs.

The second prompt gives the model a much clearer picture of what you're looking for.

Can you provide too much context?

No.

More information isn't always better.

Imagine asking someone to help you choose a laptop, then telling them your entire life story.

Most of that information wouldn't help them.

The same applies to AI.

Provide the background details that matter for the task, and avoid including unnecessary personal or sensitive information.

Good context means relevant information, not simply more information.

5. Component 3: Examples - Show the AI What You Want

Sometimes it's easier to show someone what you want than to explain it.

Imagine you're asking a friend to design an invitation card.

Instead of describing every detail, you might show an example and say:

I want something similar to this.

AI can also use examples to understand the pattern, style, or structure you expect.

Without an example 

Rewrite this message professionally.

With an example 

Rewrite my message in a professional
but friendly tone.

Example:

Original:
"Hey, send me the report."

Improved:
"Could you please send me the report
when you have a chance?"

Now rewrite this message:

"I need the meeting details."

The example demonstrates the kind of change you want.

It shows the AI how to make a request sound more polite without changing its meaning.

A little technical detail: Zero-shot and Few-shot prompting

These are two terms you might encounter.

Zero-shot prompting means asking the AI to perform a task without providing examples.

For example:

Rewrite this sentence professionally:

"Send me the file."

Few-shot prompting means providing one or more examples before asking the AI to perform the task.

For example:

Example 1:
"Send me the file."
→ "Could you please send me the file?"

Example 2:
"Call me tomorrow."
→ "Could you please call me tomorrow?"

Now rewrite:
"Give me the document."

The examples help demonstrate the pattern.

However, examples aren't always necessary, and they don't automatically work better than clear instructions.

For simple tasks, a direct instruction may be enough.

We'll explore zero-shot and few-shot prompting in more detail in Part 3.

When should you use examples?

When you want a specific writing style, structure, classification, or repeated pattern.

6. Component 4: Task - Explain Exactly What You Need

This is one of the most important parts of a prompt.

The task tells the AI what it should actually do.

It sounds obvious, but vague tasks can lead to vague answers.

Example 1: Too vague 

Help me with my resume.

What kind of help?

Should the AI check grammar?

Improve the wording?

Shorten it?

Suggest missing sections?

Example 2: Clear task 

Review my resume.

Identify unclear sentences and
suggest improvements.

Keep my existing experience and
achievements accurate.

Do not invent qualifications or
work experience.

Now the AI knows what to focus on.

Another example

Basic:

Summarize this article.

Clearer:

Summarize this article in five bullet points.

Focus on the main findings.

Explain any difficult terms in
simple English.

Notice something?

We haven't used complicated technical language.

We've simply explained the task more clearly.

A useful habit: Before sending a prompt, ask yourself:

If someone who had never met me read this instruction, would they understand what I wanted them to do?

If the answer is no, you may need to make the task clearer.

7. Component 5: Constraints - Set Clear Rules and Limits

Now imagine you're asking someone to write a short speech.

You tell them:

Write a speech about teamwork.

They might write a ten-minute speech.

But you only have two minutes to speak.

The problem isn't necessarily the speech itself.

You forgot to explain the time limit.

That's where constraints come in.

Constraints are the rules or limitations you want the AI to follow.

They help make the output more suitable for your needs.

Example 

Write a short speech about teamwork.

Rules:
- Use simple English.
- Keep it under 200 words.
- Include one everyday example.
- Avoid difficult technical terms.
- End with an encouraging message.

Here, you've made your expectations much clearer.

Common types of constraints

Type Example
Length Keep it under 150 words.
Language Use simple English.
Tone Keep it polite and friendly.
Content Include three practical examples.
Restrictions Don't invent facts or statistics.
Structure Use short paragraphs.

Can constraints be too strict?

Yes.

If you add too many conflicting rules, the AI may struggle to follow them.

For example:

Explain this topic in detail using only ten words.

Those instructions work against each other.

So try to keep constraints realistic and relevant.

Remember: Constraints guide the AI, but they don't guarantee that every rule will always be followed.

That's why checking the final answer is still important.

8. Component 6: Output - Format Decide How the Answer Should Look

Imagine asking someone to organize your monthly expenses.

They could give you a long paragraph describing everything.

Or they could present a simple table.

Which would be easier to understand?

Usually, the table.

That's why output format matters.

Output format tells the AI how you want the final answer to be organized.

Without a format 

Compare online learning and
classroom learning.

The AI might produce several paragraphs.

With a format 

Compare online learning and
classroom learning.

Present the comparison in a table.

Include:
- Cost
- Flexibility
- Interaction
- Advantages
- Disadvantages

Finish with a short summary.

Now the structure is clear.

Common output formats

Format When it's useful
Paragraph Explanations and general writing
Bullet points Short summaries and quick ideas
Numbered steps Instructions and tutorials
Table Comparisons and organized information
Checklist Planning and reviewing tasks
Code Programming-related tasks
JSON When software needs a structured data format

A little technical detail: What is JSON?

JSON is a way to organize information using labels and values.

For example:

{
  "name": "Aarav",
  "age": 22,
  "city": "Kathmandu"
}

You don't need to use JSON in everyday prompting.

It's mainly useful when applications or programs need information in a consistent structure.

For most beginners, requesting a paragraph, table, or list is enough.

The takeaway: Choosing the right output format can make an answer easier to read, check, and use.

9. Putting All Six Components Together

Now let's combine everything we've learned.

We'll use the same email example from the beginning.

Basic prompt 

Write an email asking for leave.

This might work, but it leaves several details unclear.

Structured prompt 

ROLE:
Act as a professional writing assistant.

CONTEXT:
I'm an employee writing to my manager.
I need two days of leave on Monday and
Tuesday because of a family commitment.

EXAMPLE:
Use a polite and professional tone similar to:
"I would like to request your approval
for two days of leave."

TASK:
Write an email requesting the leave.

CONSTRAINTS:
- Keep it under 120 words.
- Use simple and professional language.
- Do not invent additional personal details.

OUTPUT FORMAT:
Include:
1. Subject line
2. Greeting
3. Email body
4. Closing

This prompt gives the AI much clearer instructions.

What changed?

Component What we added
Role Professional writing assistant
Context Leave dates, reason, recipient
Examples Preferred writing tone
Task Write a leave-request email
Constraints Word limit, language, accuracy
Output Format Subject, greeting, body, closing

We haven't used any magic words.

We've simply organized our instructions.

Important: Do we always need six sections?

Absolutely not.

The same request could be written naturally in a few sentences:

Write a polite email to my manager requesting leave on Monday and Tuesday because of a family commitment. Keep it under 120 words, use simple professional English, and include a subject line.

That may be enough.

A well-structured prompt doesn't have to be long or complicated. It just needs to provide the information the task requires.

The six components are a guide, not a rule that every prompt must follow.

10. Basic vs. Structured Prompts: What's the Difference?

Let's compare a few everyday examples.

Situation Basic prompt More structured prompt
Learning Explain photosynthesis. Explain photosynthesis to a 12-year-old using simple English and one everyday example.
Writing Write a birthday message. Write a short, funny birthday message for my best friend. Keep it under 60 words.
Planning Make a study plan. Create a seven-day study plan for someone who can study two hours daily. Present it in a table.
Summarizing Summarize this document. Summarize the document in five bullet points, focusing on the main findings and important numbers.
Comparing Compare these phones. Compare these phones by price, battery, camera, and storage in a table.

Notice that the improved prompts aren't necessarily much longer.

They simply explain what matters.

Does a structured prompt always give a better answer?

Not necessarily.

For straightforward tasks, a simple prompt can work perfectly.

For complicated tasks, clear instructions often help.

And sometimes the model may still make mistakes despite having a well-written prompt.

That's why we need a way to test whether our changes actually improve the result.

11. A Real-World Example: Summarizing a Long Document

This example connects closely with my work testing AI models on real documents.

Imagine you upload a 50-page report and type:

Summarize this report.

The AI might give you a useful general summary.

But suppose you actually need:

  • The report's main purpose
  • Important findings
  • Financial information
  • Major risks
  • Recommendations

Your original prompt didn't mention those expectations.

So you might have to ask several follow-up questions.

Now let's try a more structured approach.

ROLE:
Act as a research assistant.

CONTEXT:
I've uploaded a report that I need
to understand without reading every page.

TASK:
Summarize the report.

Include:
1. The main purpose of the report.
2. Five important findings.
3. Key financial figures, if available.
4. Major risks or limitations.
5. Important recommendations.

CONSTRAINTS:
- Use simple English.
- Keep the summary under 500 words.
- Do not invent missing information.
- Clearly mention if something is not found.

OUTPUT FORMAT:
Use headings and bullet points.

Where possible, include page references
so I can check the original information.

This prompt gives the model a clearer structure.

It also makes the output easier to verify.

For example, if the AI reports a financial figure, you can check the page where that figure appears.

Of course, the model could still overlook information or provide an incorrect page reference.

A structured prompt improves clarity and makes verification easier. It doesn't eliminate the need to check important results.

12. For the Curious: How Developers Use Structured Prompts

If you're not from a technical background, you can skip this section.

Everything we've learned so far is enough to start improving your prompts.

But if you're curious about how developers use these ideas, here's a simple example.

Suppose a developer asks:

Write code to calculate the total price.

The AI doesn't know the programming language, the calculation rules, or how to handle unusual inputs.

A clearer request might look like this:

ROLE:
Act as a Python programming assistant.

CONTEXT:
I'm building a small shopping application.

TASK:
Write a function that calculates the total
price of products in a shopping cart.

CONSTRAINTS:
- Each product has a price and quantity.
- Reject negative prices or quantities.
- Explain the calculation clearly.
- Include two example calculations.

OUTPUT FORMAT:
Return the Python code followed by
a short explanation.

This follows the same six-component idea.

The only difference is the task.

A developer may also provide database information, existing code, error messages, or other technical details.

But the main principle remains the same:

Give the AI enough information to understand the task, and clearly explain how you want the answer.

Generated code still needs to be reviewed and tested before being used in a real application.

13. The Prompt Engineering Workflow

Now that we know how to build a prompt, what should we do if the first answer isn't good enough?

Should we rewrite everything?

Should we keep adding random instructions?

Not necessarily.

A better approach is to improve the prompt step by step.

Here's a simple workflow.

Step 1: Specify Decide What You Want

Before writing a prompt, identify:

  • Your goal
  • The information AI needs
  • The kind of answer you expect
  • Any important rules or limitations

For example:

I want a short explanation of climate change for a young student.

Step 2: Save Keep Your Original Prompt

Don't immediately replace your first prompt.

Keep a copy.

For example:

Version 1:

Explain climate change.

This is your starting point.

You can compare future versions against it.

In technical settings, saving and tracking changes is sometimes called versioning.

But you don't need special software to do this.

A notebook or text document works perfectly.

Step 3: Test Change One Thing at a Time

Let's improve the prompt.

Version 2: Change the audience

Explain climate change to a 12-year-old.

Now compare the answer with Version 1.

Did it become easier to understand?

Next, return to Version 1 and test a different change.

Version 3: Change the length

Explain climate change in 100 words.

Now compare again.

This helps you understand whether specifying the audience or limiting the length made the answer more useful.

If you change five things at once, it becomes harder to identify which change helped.

AI responses can vary even when you use the same prompt, so repeat important tests before drawing strong conclusions.

Step 4: Improve Combine What Works

After comparing the results, you can combine useful instructions.

For example:

Explain climate change to a 12-year-old.

Use simple English.

Keep it under 100 words.

Include one everyday example.

You now have a clearer prompt based on what you've learned.

Step 5: Reuse - Save Your Best Prompts

If a prompt works well for a task you repeat often, save it.

For example:

Explain [TOPIC] to [AUDIENCE].

Use simple language.

Keep the explanation under [WORD LIMIT].

Include [NUMBER] everyday examples.

You can replace the words inside the brackets whenever you need to use the template again.

This is one of the practical benefits of prompt engineering.

Instead of starting from scratch every time, you build a collection of instructions that you can reuse and improve.

A simple workflow to remember

Specify → Save → Test → Improve → Reuse

In professional applications, teams may also track prompt versions, run repeated tests, compare results, and monitor performance after releasing an AI feature.

But for beginners, the same idea starts with something much simpler:

Keep your original prompt, change one thing, and check what happens.

14. Your Prompt Checklist

Before sending an important prompt, ask yourself:

  • [ ] Goal: Have I clearly explained what I want?
  • [ ] Context: Have I provided the necessary background information?
  • [ ] Role: Would specifying a role make the task clearer?
  • [ ] Examples: Would an example help show the result I expect?
  • [ ] Constraints: Have I mentioned important limits or rules?
  • [ ] Output Format: Have I explained how the answer should be presented?
  • [ ] Accuracy: Have I told the AI what to do if information is missing?
  • [ ] Verification: Can I check whether the result is correct?

You don't have to check every box for every question.

Use the ones that matter for your task.

15. Your 5-Minute Exercise: Build Your Own Prompt

Let's practice what we've learned.

Open your preferred AI chatbot.

We'll start with a simple request.

Step 1: Write a basic prompt 

Make a study plan for me.

Read the answer.

Is it suitable for your situation?

Does it know what subject you're studying?

Does it know how much time you have?

Step 2: Add context 

I'm a student preparing for an exam
next week.

I can study for two hours every day.

Make a study plan for me.

Compare the result with your first answer.

Step 3: Add useful constraints 

I'm a student preparing for an exam
next week.

I can study for two hours every day.

Create a seven-day study plan.

Include short breaks.

Keep the activities realistic.

Step 4: Specify the output format 

I'm a student preparing for an exam
next week.

I can study for two hours every day.

Create a seven-day study plan.

Include short breaks.

Present the plan in a table with:
- Day
- Study topic
- Duration
- Activity

Notice how the prompt becomes more specific.

The goal hasn't changed.

You've simply made your expectations clearer.

Step 5: Experiment

Now change only one part of the prompt.

For example:

  • Change the study time from two hours to one hour.
  • Or change the output format from a table to a checklist.
  • Or specify a particular subject.

Compare the results.

Ask yourself:

Which instruction changed the answer, and did that change make it more useful?

That's the habit I want you to develop throughout this series.

16. Quick Recap: The Six Components

Here's everything we've learned in one table.

Component Simple question to ask yourself
Role Who should the AI act as?
Context What does the AI need to know?
Examples Can I show what a good answer looks like?
Task What exactly do I want it to do?
Constraints What rules or limits matter?
Output Format How should the answer look?

And remember:

You don't need all six components for every prompt.

A simple question can have a simple prompt.

A complicated task may need more detail.

The purpose of prompt engineering isn't to make communication complicated.

It's to make it clearer.

What's Coming in Part 3?

In Part 3, we'll explore six useful prompting techniques:

  1. Zero-shot prompting: Asking AI to complete a task without examples.
  2. Few-shot prompting: Showing examples of the kind of answer you want.
  3. Chain-of-thought prompting: Approaches involving intermediate reasoning steps for more complicated tasks.
  4. Role-based prompting: Guiding AI through a particular role.
  5. Constraint-based prompting: Using clear rules and limitations.
  6. Meta-prompting: Using AI to help design or improve prompts.

We'll explain each one using practical examples and discuss when it might be useful.

Final Thoughts

In Part 1, we learned that language models don't automatically know what we expect from them.

Today, we learned how to communicate those expectations more clearly.

And here's the most important lesson:

A good prompt isn't measured by how long or complicated it is. It's measured by how clearly it communicates the task and how useful the result is.

You don't need to use special commands.

You don't need to memorize complicated terms.

And you certainly don't need a programming background.

Start with a simple prompt.

See what works.

Change one thing.

Compare the results.

And keep improving.

That's how you begin developing a prompt-engineering mindset.

One Question Before You Go

What's one task you regularly ask AI to help you with?

Writing emails? Studying? Summarizing documents? Planning your day?

Share your basic prompt in the comments, and let's see how we can improve it using the six components.

This is Part 2 of 6 in my "Prompt Engineering from Scratch" series. I work with and test open-source AI models on real documents, and I'm sharing what I learn along the way.

Follow the series if you'd like to understand AI and learn practical prompting techniques, one step at a time.

Further Reading

  • OpenAI: Prompt Engineering Guide
  • OpenAI: Best Practices for Prompt Engineering
  • Microsoft Learn: Introduction to Prompt Engineering

title: 2026 Node.js Error Tracking Library Integration: Best Practices for Silent Import Failures
description:
2026 Scheduled Import Observability: Proving Results Before Assigning Operational Cost

The constraint changes the design: a scheduled e-commerce import that produces no result may never throw, so a Node.js error-tracking library cannot prove that the job ran. Use the library for exceptions, add an explicit completion record with a stable run identifier, and have a separate heartbeat check detect a missing result before assigning the operational cost to a source or cost center.

Short answer: initialize Sentry, Rollbar, or a similar library before application work, capture uncaught and HTTP errors, and wrap the import boundary for explicit reporting. Then record successful and empty outcomes separately. A missed schedule needs a Healthchecks-style monitor or an equivalent polling check; it is not an error event.

The distinction is easy to miss.

What should the import system prove?

For every scheduled import, I want one answerable question: did the expected result arrive before the business deadline? The completion record should carry job_name, run_id, source, started_at, finished_at, rows, and cost_center. The last field is deliberate. If marketplace, catalog, and inventory feeds share workers, an error count cannot explain whose operational cost is rising.

There are three useful outcomes:

  • failed: the worker reported an exception or an HTTP failure.
  • completed_empty: the run finished, but produced zero rows where zero is suspicious.
  • missing: no completion signal arrived before the deadline.

Only the first outcome is naturally visible to an error-tracking SDK. The other two require an application event and a deadline check. OpenTelemetry describes logs as a signal whose records can carry attributes, which is a useful model for correlating error events, completion events, and deadline checks without pretending they are one signal.

Keep the business cost calculation outside the error tracker. A zero-row result may be a legitimate supplier response, a broken credential, or a scheduler that never fired. The tracker preserves evidence; a small attribution job applies the business rule after the run state is known.

Why does a missing import need another signal?

Absence is not an exception. Consider a nightly catalog import expected by 02:00 UTC. The worker may never start, wait behind a stuck process, or exit before it initializes the library. In all three cases, a design built only around try/catch has no event to send.

The minimum design is a pair of writes: emit an error when a failure is observed, and emit a completion event after the durable result is committed. A scheduler or Healthchecks-style service checks for the latter. Give that check a tolerance window. A deadline that is too strict converts ordinary queue delay into an incident storm, while one that is too generous delays cost attribution.

Use the same run_id in error context, completion log, queue message, and cost ledger. Trace and span fields can help correlate records when available, but this design does not depend on a distributed-trace query or a span tree.

No exception is required.

That is the awkward part. A catalog feed can return a valid response, write zero rows, and leave the error tracker quiet; the system must retain the schedule, source, row count, deadline, and cost center long enough for an attribution job to distinguish a legitimate empty feed from a missed run. I would make that distinction in the workflow, because a library cannot infer whether zero is normal for one supplier on one day. The import worker should also rethrow after reporting an exception. Swallowing it makes the scheduler believe the run succeeded, which corrupts both operational status and cost attribution.

The application contract can stay provider-neutral. This Python example shows the capture boundary for a REST capability; the Node.js worker can implement the same contract through its chosen SDK or HTTP client. The operational limits matter too: use a 10-second request timeout, make four bounded attempts, and treat HTTP 429 as a retryable response rather than a reason to loop forever. Those are explicit client choices, not promises about provider latency.

import os
import time
import uuid

import requests


def capture_error(error_payload):
    api_key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
    base_url = os.environ["INFRAI_BASE_URL"].rstrip("/")
    response_url = f"{base_url}/v1/errors/capture"
    headers = {
        "Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}",
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": str(uuid.uuid4()),
    }

    for attempt in range(4):
        response = requests.post(
            response_url,
            headers=headers,
            json=error_payload,
            timeout=10,
        )
        if response.status_code != 429:
            if not response.ok:
                raise RuntimeError(
                    f"error capture failed: {response.status_code} {response.text}"
                )
            return response.json()

        retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
        delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2**attempt
        time.sleep(delay)

    raise RuntimeError("error capture rate limit did not clear after retries")

The key comes from an environment variable, the method is explicit, a 429 honors Retry-After, and non-success responses remain visible. The idempotency key prevents a retry after a network timeout from recording the same failure twice. Do not send this authorization header to a separate URL returned for another operation.

Which tools fit the evidence?

The comparison should follow the missing proof, not the popularity of a dashboard. Sentry is a natural fit when the main requirement is SDK-based exception capture and context. Rollbar belongs in the same shortlist for application error monitoring. Datadog is a broader observability choice when error records need to sit beside other operational telemetry. None of those labels, by themselves, answers “did this scheduled import produce a result?”

Option Strong fit Boundary for silent imports Cost attribution implication
Sentry Capturing application exceptions with project context A missing completion still needs a positive event and a deadline check Add cost_center and run_id to captured context, then calculate attribution outside the error stream
Rollbar Error monitoring for application failures A worker that never emits an error remains invisible Keep the run ledger separate so a low error count cannot be mistaken for low import cost
Datadog Joining error records with wider observability practice The monitoring design still needs an explicit import-success signal Use a common identifier and meter the workflow independently from incident volume
Healthchecks-style monitoring Detecting a missed scheduled check-in It does not replace stack traces or application context Attribute the missed run to the job and source, then link supporting error records
A plain REST error capability Sending error evidence without installing a provider SDK It is still not a heartbeat or alerting rule engine Preserve the internal event contract and assemble the missing checks separately

That last row is where Infrai can fit. Infrai's one REST API is pure HTTP: no SDK to install, and any language or runtime can send the request. Its API is also self-describing, so the discovery surface can show the request and response contract before a worker is wired to it; that reduces the friction of replacing an SDK-backed capture edge during a provider change. The internal event contract can remain stable while the service behind the capability changes, so swapping the provider does not require changing application code. Infrai also uses one key and one bill across the platform, which reduces credential and invoice sprawl without changing the observability limits. The platform has 295 routes across 20 modules under one key, but that breadth does not turn error capture into a heartbeat monitor or a notification system.

The 2026-10-29 capability snapshot also makes the limitations material. Infrai has no built-in threshold notifications, distributed span-tree query, source-map deobfuscation, session replay, or heartbeat monitoring in the stated capability boundary. Its client-side checking model is polling-based, and the observability facts do not establish a declared filter contract for log search or metric query. Choose Sentry when SDK-centered exception context is the priority, Datadog when a wider observability estate matters more, and a Healthchecks-style tool when missed schedules are the primary failure. Choose the REST capability only when a provider-neutral HTTP contract is more valuable than an integrated debugging suite; it isn't a replacement for one.

How should I integrate the Node.js library?

Install the selected library with npm and initialize it before application work begins. Configure middleware for uncaught exceptions and HTTP errors, then wrap the import worker as well; middleware catches request failures, while a scheduled worker may run outside an HTTP request entirely. Attach user information only where it is appropriate and lawful, and prefer a stable internal identifier over an email address.

The test should be repeatable. Trigger one controlled exception and verify that the report includes the import name and run_id. Run a successful import and verify the completion event. Then suppress the completion event in a test environment and confirm that the heartbeat check marks the run as missing. A green error dashboard with no missing-run test does not establish that the integration works.

The provider-specific SDK is an implementation detail. The durable contract is the useful part: error reports include the run context, successful work emits a completion record, and retries use the same idempotent run identifier. Do not use a trace tree as a substitute for this contract; the available logs may carry trace_id and span_id without providing distributed trace exploration.

A rollout rule that survives provider changes

Start with one import whose business owner can define “late.” Record the expected schedule, allowed delay, source, and cost center before enabling notifications. Compare observed exceptions, completed runs, and expected runs over a fixed test window. The gaps are the product decision.

Keep error capture, completion recording, and missed-run detection as replaceable edges around one internal event contract. This permits a move from Sentry to Rollbar, Datadog, or a plain REST capability without rewriting the import worker's business logic, while keeping the uncomfortable truth visible: an error tracker can explain a failed run, but only a positive completion signal can establish that a run occurred.

Sources

  • OpenTelemetry Logs signal concepts
  • Sentry Node.js documentation
  • Rollbar Node.js documentation
  • Datadog Node.js error tracking
  • Healthchecks.io documentation
