Exploring tenant isolation with Spring Boot, OIDC, and PostgreSQL RLS
description:
A multi-tenant API needs to answer two separate questions: who is making the request, and what may that identity do inside the selected tenant?

Spring Boot SaaS Starter is an open-source backend MVP I maintain to make those boundaries easier to inspect. It provides a Projects API with tenant membership, role checks, optimistic concurrency, and audit records.

The current stack uses Java 25, Spring Boot 4.1.2, PostgreSQL, JDBC, and Flyway. Docker Compose includes Keycloak for local development.

Authentication establishes identity

The API accepts bearer tokens through Spring Security’s JWT resource server support. Its configuration validates the signature and issuer, requires an audience match, and checks for a nonblank subject and an expiration claim.

The subject identifies the caller. Memberships associate that subject with a tenant and a role in the application database.

This distinction matters: a valid token alone does not establish membership in a particular tenant. The tenant UUID in a request selects the tenant to access; authorization still happens in the service layer.

See the implementation in SecurityConfig.java.

Follow the tenant boundary into the database

The starter uses a shared schema with complementary application and database checks:

  1. A transactional service checks and locks the caller’s membership row.
  2. It verifies the role required for the operation.
  3. It sets transaction-local database context for the tenant.
  4. Queries include explicit tenant predicates.
  5. PostgreSQL enforces row-level security on projects and audit events.

TenantAccess.java activates the context using a parameterized query:

SELECT set_config('app.tenant_id', ?, true)

The final argument makes the setting local to the transaction. The design therefore avoids leaving tenant state attached to a pooled connection after the transaction finishes.

The database migration enables and forces row-level security on both protected tables. Policies compare each row’s tenant_id with the current transaction’s tenant setting, including checks on writes.

Tenant and membership tables have a different role: they support onboarding and membership discovery across tenants. Their authorization boundary is enforced in services.

The application also uses restricted runtime database credentials, separate from schema migration credentials. Startup checks reject unsafe database privileges or missing RLS enforcement.

These layers help defend against accidentally omitted tenant predicates. They do not make a compromised application or arbitrary SQL execution harmless. The architecture guide explains that boundary explicitly.

Keep permissions specific to each tenant

The role model is deliberately small:

Capability OWNER ADMIN MEMBER
Read projects and list members Yes Yes Yes
Create, update, or delete projects Yes Yes No
Read audit events Yes Yes No
Manage non-owner memberships Yes No No

An authenticated identity can create a tenant and becomes its owner. Ownership transfer and owner removal are outside this MVP.

A caller who is not a tenant member receives 404 for tenant resources. A member who lacks the required role receives 403.

Make conflicting writes explicit

Projects carry a version number. Updates match the tenant, project ID, and expected version, then increment the version. Deletions also require the expected version.

For example, after updating version 0 successfully, a deletion that still supplies version 0 receives 409 Conflict.

The client should reload the project and reconcile changes before retrying. Automatically substituting the latest version would defeat the purpose of detecting a stale write.

Project mutations and their audit records occur within the same transaction. See ProjectService.java and the API walkthrough.

Run the local example

The README’s container-based path requires Git, a POSIX shell, Docker Engine with Compose v2, OpenSSL, and Python 3.9+. On Windows, use WSL with Docker access. Ports 8080, 8081, and 5432 must be available.

A host JDK is unnecessary for this path:

git clone https://github.com/chafian/spring-boot-saas-starter.git
cd spring-boot-saas-starter
./scripts/init-env.sh
docker compose up --build -d
python3 scripts/smoke.py

The setup script generates local credentials. The smoke script waits for readiness, signs in as the demo identities, and exercises the API.

It checks that an outsider cannot access the tenant’s projects, that adding the identity as a MEMBER enables reading, and that the same member still cannot create projects. It also exercises updates, stale-write rejection, deletion, audit events, and requests without authentication.

Successful completion produces:

PASS: real OIDC login, tenant isolation, membership, RBAC, CRUD, conflicts, and audit

Windows/WSL troubleshooting: On my machine, Docker could not bind host port 5432. I changed the PostgreSQL port mapping in compose.yml from 127.0.0.1:5432:5432 to 127.0.0.1:5433:5432, then reran docker compose up -d. The application’s internal database connection remained unchanged, and the smoke test passed.

Each run creates a fictional tenant and retains its audit history. Use docker compose down to stop the services while preserving the database volume.

Keycloak runs in development mode and is ephemeral. Follow the README’s reset guidance if it is recreated, because identity subjects may change.

Test and extend the example

For development, install JDK 25 and unzip, keep Docker running, and use:

./mvnw verify
python3 -m unittest discover -s scripts -p 'test_*.py'

The documented Java verification path uses a real PostgreSQL Testcontainer. CI is configured to run verification and the Compose smoke example.

To add another tenant-owned resource, follow the extension guide and preserve the membership, transaction, tenant-context, and database-policy boundaries.

The current scope excludes billing, a frontend, email invitations, tenant deletion, and ownership transfer. Production deployment also requires environment-specific work such as TLS, production identity configuration, tenant-creation quotas or rate limits, backups, monitoring, and secret management. The local Keycloak setup is a development convenience.

If you work with Java SaaS backends, I’d welcome feedback on the isolation model and the setup experience.

Explore the repository and try the example

title: Environment variables now use Config and Secret types
description:
When you add or edit an environment variable in Vercel, you now choose Config or Secret instead of using the Sensitive toggle. Existing variables marked Sensitive are automatically treated as Secrets and continue to work without migration.

  • Config: The value remains readable after saving for members with access. Use Config for non-sensitive values you may need to inspect later, such as variables with a public framework prefix.

  • Secret: The value remains available to your deployments and can be replaced, but members cannot view or retrieve it after saving. Use Secret for passwords, API keys, and tokens.

You can select an environment or Preview branch for each value. The environment variable list in the dashboard shows each variable’s type and where it applies.

Team policy changes

The Enforce Sensitive Environment Variables team policy is deprecated with this update. When enabled, it required every environment variable created by a team member to be Sensitive, including non-sensitive configuration. With Config and Secret types, members can choose the appropriate type for each variable.

A new Separate Production Secret Values policy is available in your Security settings. When enabled, the Production value for a Secret must differ from the values used for the same key in Preview, Development, and custom environments.

If your team had the legacy policy enabled, confirm whether the Separate Production Secret Values policy should be enabled for your team. The deprecated policy is no longer enforced by the Vercel CLI.

Set variable types from the CLI

To choose whether an environment variable is a Config or Secret from the CLI, pass --type config or --type secret to vercel env add or vercel env update:

The existing flags continue to work. When --type is omitted, --no-sensitive maps to Config and --sensitive maps to Secret. After adding or updating a variable, the CLI output shows its type under Type.

Learn more in the Environment Variables documentation.

title: 5 Website Trust Signals That Turn Small Business Visitors Into Customers
description:
Visitors decide in seconds whether a small business website is worth their trust. Here are five signals that turn browsers into buyers, why each matters, and a quick fix.

1. Real reviews with names and photos

Why it matters: Anonymous quotes look invented. Named reviews with a photo prove real people had a good experience, and social proof is one of the strongest nudges toward buying.

Quick fix: Ask your three happiest customers for a short review today, get permission to use their name and photo, and place them near your main call to action.

2. Clear phone, email and address on every page

Why it matters: Hidden contact details feel like hiding. Visible ones tell visitors a real business stands behind the site and that help is easy to reach.

Quick fix: Put your phone, email and address in the header or footer of every page, and make the phone number tap-to-call on mobile.

3. Secure HTTPS and fast loading on mobile

Why it matters: Browser "not secure" warnings scare people off instantly, and most small business visitors arrive on a phone. Slow pages lose them before they read a word.

Quick fix: Enable HTTPS through your host, compress oversized images, and test your pages on a real phone over mobile data.

4. Real photos of your team, shop and finished work

Why it matters: Stock photos are easy to spot and signal "generic". Real photos show who you are and the quality of what you deliver.

Quick fix: Spend an hour taking clear, well-lit photos of your team, space and recent projects, then replace the stock images on your home and about pages.

5. A simple guarantee or a clear "how it works" process

Why it matters: Uncertainty stops purchases. A guarantee reduces risk, and a short process explains exactly what happens after someone gets in touch.

Quick fix: Add a three-step "how it works" section and one plain-language promise you can honestly keep, such as a reply within one business day.

Start with whichever fix takes the least time, then work down the list. Small trust improvements add up quickly.

Want a second pair of eyes? ENZORA does a free website audit for small businesses: https://enzora.vercel.app

title: Sentinel-IR 0.2.1: When "eval" Hides Behind an Alias
description:
Sentinel-IR 0.2.1

https://www.npmjs.com/package/sentinel-ir/v/0.2.1

Thanks for support..
Release: "Sentinel-IR-MCP v0.2.2 on GitLab" (https://gitlab.com/jakubrojicek11/sentinel-ir-mcp/-/tree/v0.2.2?ref_type=tags)

Package: "sentinel-ir-mcp@0.2.2 on npm" (https://www.npmjs.com/package/sentinel-ir-mcp/v/0.2.2)

A focused improvement in AST-based analysis, six regression tests, and a closer look at two tricky JavaScript control-flow paths.

The first 30 seconds

What happens when dangerous code execution does not look like "eval()"?

Sometimes JavaScript stores "eval" in another variable and calls that variable later. A static analyzer that only looks for direct calls can miss the connection.

In Sentinel-IR 0.2.1, I focused on two situations where this can happen: "switch" fallthrough and "try/catch" control flow.

The update adds six regression tests. The goal is simple: detect the dangerous path when it is real, but avoid raising an alarm when the control flow makes that path impossible.

No magic. Just better reasoning about code.

Part 1: The 3-minute explanation for everyone

First, what does Sentinel-IR actually do?

Sentinel-IR is a small structural analysis layer for code.

Instead of sending an entire JavaScript or TypeScript source file to an AI model, it extracts structured facts using Tree-sitter.

Think of it as giving the AI a map instead of handing it an entire city.

The resulting information can include:

  • Imports and exports.
  • Routes and environment variables.
  • Filesystem, network and process operations.
  • Potentially dangerous code patterns.
  • Risk signals and their source locations.

This makes it easier for another system to reason about code without treating every line of source as equally important.

Project: "Sentinel-IR on GitLab" (https://gitlab.com/jakubrojicek11/sentinel-ir)

The problem: a function can have another name

Consider this:

const execute = eval;

execute("1 + 1");

A beginner might look for the word "eval" and assume the problem is easy.

But the function is being called through another variable.

That variable is an alias. The analyzer must understand what it refers to, not just what its name looks like.

And JavaScript has a few places where this gets complicated.

Problem one: switch fallthrough

Look at this example:

let execute = (value) => value;

switch (mode) {
case 0:
execute = eval;

case 1:
    execute("1 + 1");
    break;

}

Notice something?

There is no "break" after "case 0".

JavaScript continues into the next case. The alias assigned in the first case can therefore be used in the second one.

A simple analyzer may treat these cases as completely separate blocks and miss the connection.

Think of "break" as a stop sign. Without it, the baton keeps moving.

Problem two: try/catch

Another example:

let execute = (value) => value;

try {
execute = eval;
throw new Error("Something happened");
} catch (error) {
execute("1 + 1");
}

The alias is assigned before the exception.

When the exception moves execution into "catch", the analyzer needs to understand that the assignment can reach the code there.

But the opposite matters too.

An assignment that happens after an unconditional throw cannot influence the catch block. An assignment in a try block without a later explicit throw should not automatically make the catch block look dangerous either.

This is where false positives and false negatives start competing for attention.

What changed in 0.2.1?

The update improves those two control-flow situations.

It adds checks for:

  • Aliases carried through "switch" fallthrough.
  • "break" statements that stop that flow.
  • Later assignments that overwrite an alias.
  • Assignments before a throw that can reach "catch".
  • Throws occurring before an alias assignment.
  • Try blocks without a later explicit throw.

The result should be more accurate detection, not simply more things marked as dangerous.

Part 2: The developer section

What changed inside the AST analysis?

The important change is not a new search for the word "eval".

It is more accurate tracking of alias assignments and their visibility across control-flow paths.

The implementation contains dedicated helpers for:

  • Identifying equivalent AST nodes.
  • Tracking function and execution contexts.
  • Determining whether switch fallthrough is possible.
  • Checking whether a try-to-catch path is reachable.
  • Evaluating whether an alias assignment remains visible at a call site.

A parser detail worth mentioning

During the investigation, I encountered a subtle issue with Tree-sitter node wrappers.

Two JavaScript objects can represent the same logical AST node without being the same object reference.

Comparing them using:

nodeA === nodeB

is therefore not reliable for this kind of comparison.

The updated implementation compares the node type and source boundaries instead:

function evalAliasSameNode(a, b) {
return Boolean(
a &&
b &&
a.type === b.type &&
a.startIndex === b.startIndex &&
a.endIndex === b.endIndex
);
}

This gives the analysis a stable way to recognize the same logical node.

Source: "AST implementation in v0.2.1" (https://gitlab.com/jakubrojicek11/sentinel-ir/-/blob/v0.2.1/src/ast-facts.js)

The six regression tests

The six new cases are documented in the release test suite.

Test scenario| Expected result
Alias passes through switch fallthrough| Critical
"break" blocks the alias flow| Low
Later case overwrites the alias| Low
Alias assigned before throw reaches catch| Critical
Throw happens before assignment| Low
No later explicit throw in try| Low

The tests verify more than a boolean detection result.

They also check that:

  • The source parses successfully.
  • "operations.dynamicEval" matches the expected result.
  • The risk classification is correct.
  • The "dynamic_code" risk signal agrees with the result.

Here is the core shape of the regression assertions:

const facts = AstFacts.extract(source);

assert.equal(facts.ast, true);

assert.equal(
Boolean(facts.operations.dynamicEval),
expected
);

assert.equal(
AstFacts.riskOf(facts),
expected ? "critical" : "low"
);

assert.equal(
facts.riskSignals.some(
signal => signal.signal === "dynamic_code"
),
expected
);

Full tests: "test/ast-facts.test.js, v0.2.1" (https://gitlab.com/jakubrojicek11/sentinel-ir/-/blob/v0.2.1/test/ast-facts.test.js)

Validation results

The release work was tested locally before tagging.

Validation| Result
Existing tests| 100 passed
New regression tests| 6 passed
Complete test suite| 106/106 passed
Packaged tarball smoke checks| 7/7 passed

The package was also installed into a clean consumer project for a separate smoke test.

That matters because a successful source test does not automatically prove that the packaged artifact works after installation.

What this does not mean

Sentinel-IR is not a complete JavaScript interpreter.

Its control-flow analysis is a conservative approximation, not a full simulation of every possible runtime path. It works with structural facts extracted from source code and has documented limitations.

It should be treated as an analysis component, not as a guarantee that dangerous code will always be detected.

That distinction matters, especially when an AI agent uses the output to make decisions.

Final thoughts

Version 0.2.1 is a focused release.

It does not introduce a new language or a completely new architecture. It improves one important part of the existing analyzer: understanding when an alias to dynamic code execution can actually reach a call site.

Sometimes progress in static analysis is not about detecting more patterns.

Sometimes it is about understanding why two pieces of code are connected, and when they are not.

And occasionally, the biggest bug is hiding behind a missing "break".

Sentinel-IR 0.2.1 is released.

Project links

  • "GitLab repository" (https://gitlab.com/jakubrojicek11/sentinel-ir)
  • "Sentinel-IR 0.2.1 Release" (https://gitlab.com/jakubrojicek11/sentinel-ir/-/releases/v0.2.1)
  • "Version 0.2.0 source" (https://gitlab.com/jakubrojicek11/sentinel-ir/-/tree/v0.2.0)
  • "Version 0.2.1 source" (https://gitlab.com/jakubrojicek11/sentinel-ir/-/tree/v0.2.1)
  • "New regression tests" (https://gitlab.com/jakubrojicek11/sentinel-ir/-/blob/v0.2.1/test/ast-facts.test.js)

https://www.npmjs.com/package/sentinel-ir/v/0.2.1

Built and tested as an independent project. Feedback, edge cases and reproducible examples are welcome.

title: Designing a 3D Periodic Table for iPhone Duo: Reimagining Foldable UI/UX
description:
A deep dive into the UI/UX design decisions behind building an immersive, dual-screen 3D Periodic Table app optimized for foldable iPhone hardware

Designing interface layouts for dual-screen and foldable devices like the iPhone Duo requires rethinking traditional single-viewport ergonomics to maximize real estate without cluttering the visual field. In Periodic Table Chemistry 2027 app, the dual-display architecture establishes a logical separation between macro navigation and micro content inspection. Opening the device reveals a balanced split workspace: the comprehensive periodic table stays pinned to one screen, while the complementary display renders interactive 3D models—such as gas balloons illustrating Helium—alongside immediate atomic and physical properties. This spatial split minimizes context switching, allowing users to study detailed element attributes while keeping the complete chemical landscape in full view.

Fluid adaptability across physical folding states is critical for next-generation mobile UX, requiring a UI that scales seamlessly whether the device is expanded or closed. When collapsed into a single display, Periodic Table Chemistry 2027 app transitions effortlessly into an optimized single-screen layout tailored for efficient one-handed interactions. The UI dynamically recalibrates high-density data cards and 3D visual assets—such as a battery representation for Lithium—while preserving high-contrast dark mode aesthetics, clean typography, and quick access to core metrics like atomic mass and electron configurations. This design strategy guarantees an uninterrupted user experience when moving from quick reference lookups to full dual-screen workflows.

Leveraging spanned viewports allows for rich, immersive modal presentations that turn standard educational reference tools into tactile 3D experiences. When inspecting complex elements like Protactinium, the application presents an enlarged central 3D viewport spanning across the hinge line, granting users tactile manipulation and detailed spatial rendering of elemental structures. Strategic positioning of translucent control overlays and background grids preserves visual hierarchy, ensuring navigation remains accessible without obstructing the visual focal point. By placing dual-screen ergonomics and responsive visual layout at the center of development, Periodic Table Chemistry 2027 app offers a template for modern, canvas-aware application design.

Designing for multi-screen foldables isn't just about handling dynamic screen bounds—it’s about crafting contextual spatial workflows that elevate everyday utility. Periodic Table Chemistry 2027 app demonstrates how thoughtful layout architecture can transform complex educational data into an intuitive, visually rich 3D experience across both single and spanned displays. As dual-screen hardware continues to evolve, rethinking conventional interface boundaries opens exciting new possibilities for mobile design. Credits and billing

Managed accounts

Renewal and cancellation

Service changes

Eligible consumers in the UK and EU may cancel the affected subscription free of charge if a change has more than a minor negative impact on their access to or use of the Services. They have 30 days from notice or the change, whichever is later, and may receive a prorated refund of prepaid amounts for the remaining period.

Other updates

title: From 1 Minute 56 Seconds to 3 Seconds: Optimizing Database Inserts with Batch Processing
description:
Sometimes, a feature works perfectly but takes so long that it becomes practically unusable.

Recently, while working on a camera management feature at my office, I encountered exactly this problem.

The Problem

Whenever we assigned cameras to a user, the operation took approximately 1 minute and 56 seconds to complete.

But there was another problem: our server had a request timeout of just 30 seconds.

This meant the API would time out long before the operation could finish.

Clearly, something needed optimization.

Finding the Bottleneck

I started debugging the camera assignment workflow to understand where the time was being consumed.

After tracing the execution, I found the issue.

There was a "for" loop that processed every user-camera mapping individually.

For each mapping, the application was:

  1. Opening a database connection.
  2. Executing an INSERT query.
  3. Closing the database connection.

This process repeated for every camera-user mapping.

When assigning cameras in bulk, this resulted in hundreds or potentially thousands of individual database operations and unnecessary connection overhead.

The Solution: Batch Inserts

Instead of inserting every mapping individually, I changed the implementation to use batch processing.

The approach was simple:

  • Created batches of 500 records.
  • Collected 500 user-camera mappings in each batch.
  • Inserted the entire batch using a single bulk INSERT query.
  • Repeated the process until all mappings were inserted.

This significantly reduced the number of database operations and connection overhead.

Instead of executing an individual INSERT for every mapping, the application could now insert hundreds of records in one query.

The Result

The performance improvement was significant!

Metric| Before| After
Execution time| 1 min 56 sec| 3 sec
Database operations| Individual inserts| Batch inserts
Server timeout| 30 sec| Completed successfully

From 116 seconds to just 3 seconds!

That's approximately a 97.4% reduction in execution time.

What I Learned

This experience reinforced an important lesson:

Sometimes, the biggest performance improvements don't require a completely new architecture or a complicated technology.

Understanding how your application interacts with the database can make a huge difference.

A simple change from individual inserts to batch processing can eliminate unnecessary overhead and dramatically improve performance.

Always investigate the bottleneck before trying to optimize the entire system.

Have you encountered a similar database performance issue? I'd love to hear how you solved it!

title: My Pool Has 4 Threads, DNS Gets 2
description:
In Node, the word "asynchronous" does not describe a single thing. Some calls
really are handed to the kernel and come back when the operating system is
ready; others are placed on one of four background threads and wait their turn.
The second kind is libuv's work pool, its size is four, and that number appears
in Node's documentation in a single aside: "its current default value".

What led me to that number was my cover generator. In batch mode
generate-hero.ts drains its queue with four workers — a hard-coded 4 inside
the script — and each worker is one sharp call. In a separate run, in a
separate process, my social posting script names nine external hosts in its
source. Both are "asynchronous", both sit on their own four threads, and I had
no idea how much of those four either one was holding. I wanted to measure this
properly, once. The result was sharper than I expected: dns.lookup can never
take more than two of those four threads, and neither libuv's documentation
nor Node's mentions that limit.

Who lands in the pool

Node's command-line documentation spells out the list: all fs calls except the
file watchers and the explicitly synchronous ones, asynchronous crypto calls
such as crypto.pbkdf2, scrypt, randomBytes and generateKeyPair, all
zlib calls except the explicitly synchronous ones, and dns.lookup. The
warning that follows is fair: because the pool has a fixed size, if one of these
takes a long time, other "seemingly unrelated" ones get slower.

The sneakiest member of that list is dns.lookup, because you are usually not
the one deciding to call it. In Node's lib/net.js, the connect path says it in
one line: const lookup = options.lookup || dns.lookup;. So net.connect,
http, https and fetch — undici, which sits underneath fetch, uses
net.connect for plain HTTP and tls.connect for TLS, and both pass through
that same line — resolve names through dns.lookup unless you supply your own
resolver. The first step of every outbound HTTP request queues on the same four
threads as your file reads.

The dns.resolve* family is not on that list. Node's documentation draws the
line clearly: those functions do not use getaddrinfo(3), they always query
over the network, and they do not use libuv's threadpool. Keep that distinction
in mind; we will come back to it with a measurement at the end.

The lab: my own resolver, a fixed 300 ms

Measuring against a real DNS server is pointless; if the latency moves, you
cannot read the table. So I wrote a 49-line UDP server: it holds every incoming
query for exactly 300 ms, then answers 127.0.0.2, sets TTL zero (no caching),
and most importantly it counts how many distinct names are in flight at the
same time. Instead of guessing concurrency from the client side, I let the
resolver count it.

The lab ran in a node:26-alpine container: Alpine 3.24, Node v26.13.0, libuv
1.52.1, aarch64, 14 cores. /etc/resolv.conf has one line: nameserver
127.0.0.1. The client calls dns.lookup for 24 distinct names at once, with
family: 4, so each name sends a single A query and the resolver's A/AAAA
behaviour stays out of the table. The numbers below are medians of three runs.
Alpine uses musl; since the limit measured here lives in libuv, the resolver
library does not change the result, but the nsswitch.conf argument later in
this article applies to glibc setups.

UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE Concurrent queries counted by the resolver 24 names, total
unset (4) 2 3,695 ms
1 1 7,414 ms
2 1 7,427 ms
3 2 3,703 ms
4 2 3,712 ms
6 3 2,480 ms
8 4 1,859 ms
16 8 934 ms

The second column is exactly half the pool size, rounded up.

What amuses me most in this table is the relationship between the second and
third rows. Going from one thread to two moves the total for 24 names from 7,414
ms to 7,427 ms — that is, nowhere. I doubled the threads and what I gained on
the DNS side is smaller than the measurement noise. But going from two to three
cuts the time in half. Adding one thread buys nothing once and a factor of two
the next time.

The reason sits in libuv's source, on line 46 of src/threadpool.c:

static unsigned int slow_work_thread_threshold(void) {
  return (nthreads + 1) / 2;
}

libuv sorts work into three kinds: UV__WORK_CPU, UV__WORK_FAST_IO and
UV__WORK_SLOW_IO. src/unix/getaddrinfo.c submits its request as
UV__WORK_SLOW_IO; src/unix/fs.c submits every file operation as
UV__WORK_FAST_IO, and user code calling uv_queue_work submits as
UV__WORK_CPU. Slow-I/O work piles up in a separate queue and only a single
"there is slow work" marker goes into the main queue. When a thread picks up
that marker and starts running slow work, a counter goes up; if the counter has
reached the threshold, the thread pushes the marker back to the tail of the
queue and looks for other work.

So this is not an accident but a deliberate guard: it exists so a slow name
lookup cannot swallow the whole pool and block file reads. I have no objection
to the logic. My objection is that the limit is written down nowhere. libuv's
own documentation covers the default, the absolute maximum, and that the pool is
global and shared across all loops; for its scope it says "all file system
operations, as well as getaddrinfo and getnameinfo requests". Not one sentence
about the half-pool threshold. Node's UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE section does not have
it either: there the advice is simply to set a value greater than 4.

Follow that advice and DNS can use at most half of whatever you set. Write 8 and
the ceiling on your name-resolution concurrency is 4. It is a ceiling, not an
allocation: when there is no DNS work those slots do not sit idle, they take
other work.

Who starves whom

The direction of the threshold matters, because it is asymmetric. Two scenarios,
both with the pool at its default four threads:

A) With 32 pending dns.lookup calls (each answered by my 300 ms resolver)
I squeezed in one fs.readFile and one pbkdf2. The fs.readFile waited 0 ms,
the pbkdf2 2 ms. Thirty-two names are queued and the file read goes straight
through. The guard works.

B) With 32 pending pbkdf2 calls — a computation that takes 208 ms on its
own — I squeezed in one dns.lookup and one fs.readFile. The fs.readFile
waited 1,719 ms, the dns.lookup 2,018 ms.

The arithmetic of that second line lands exactly: 32 × 208 ms on four threads is
a 1,664 ms queue, and the measurement is 1,719 ms. DNS's 2,018 ms comes from the
same place — 1,719 ms of queue plus my resolver's fixed 300 ms, totalling 2,019
ms. The resolver answers in 300 ms while dns.lookup takes two seconds, and 85
percent of that has nothing to do with resolving a name.

The lesson here runs the other way: some investigations that start with "our DNS
is slow" are looking in the wrong place. What fills the pool is not name
resolution but the crypto, compression or image work in the same process. The
slow-I/O threshold stops DNS from choking everyone else; nothing stops everyone
else from choking DNS.

Where the threshold sits on my own pipeline

The same question goes to my cover generator, since that is where it started.
came from. generate-hero.ts makes a single sharp call: it rasterises the SVG
at 200 dpi, fits it to 1200×630 and writes a PNG with compressionLevel: 9. On
my Mac (Node v22.16.0, libuv 1.49.2, sharp 0.35.5, libvips 8.18.7, 14 cores)
that call takes 75 ms on its own. On an idle pool an fs.readFile takes 0.2 ms.

I started the same call N times concurrently and squeezed in a read of a real
article file:

Concurrent covers How long fs.readFile waited
1 0 ms
2 0 ms
3 0 ms
4 9 ms (three runs: 1 – 31 ms)
8 62 ms (three runs: 56 – 69 ms)

The threshold is exactly at four. Up to three there is still a free thread in
the pool, so the read never waits; the moment a fourth cover enters, it starts
waiting. I will not lean on the 9 ms in the fourth row — across three runs it
wandered between 1 and 31 ms, because the instant a thread frees up is a matter
of chance. At eight the number is steady: about 60 ms.

Something caught my eye here. My script does not only write two PNGs per article
and exit; in --all mode it drains the queue with four workers, and that four
is a constant I put there myself: Array.from({ length: 4 }, ...). The comment
next to it says it "gains parallel I/O". So when I rebuild the covers for all
2,772 posts I fill the entire pool, and the fourth row of the table is exactly
that point. When I wrote that 4 I did not know the pool was also four; the two
numbers matching is a coincidence, what follows from it is not — during an
--all run every fs read and every dns.lookup in the same process queues
behind it.

The absolute values are small, I know. What interests me is not the absolute
value but that the threshold is visible at all. And one more thing: there is not
a single line in my repository that mentions UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE. Not in the
scripts, not in the systemd units, not in the workflows. I have been running
on four threads and until today I had not chosen that deliberately.

When exactly is the pool born

Node's documentation says that setting process.env.UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE "is not
guaranteed to work" and gives a reason: the pool would have been created "as
part of the runtime initialisation much before user code is run". The warning
itself is right; the reason does not hold on the Node in this lab.

libuv's pool is lazy. The first line of uv__work_submit is uv_once(&once,
init_once) — the pool is born when the first piece of work is submitted. We can
count it from outside, because since libuv 1.50.0 the threads are named
libuv-worker:

# process is up but nothing has hit the pool yet
$ ls /proc/<pid>/task/*/comm | xargs cat | grep -c libuv-worker
0

After a single dns.lookup, that same count returns whatever
UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE says — 4 if you wrote 4, 128 if you wrote 128, for one
request. That is precisely libuv's sentence about preallocating the maximum
number of threads allowed. Five rows, same lab, on where the value is set:

Where it was set Concurrency counted by the resolver 24 names
nowhere (default 4) 2 3,695 ms
first line of the JS: process.env... = '16' 8 930 ms
the same line after one fs.readFile 2 3,720 ms
UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=16 in the shell 8 923 ms
node --env-file=uv.env 8 934 ms

The third row vindicates the documentation's warning, but for a different
reason: the setting is not missed because the runtime built the pool early; it
is missed because someone submitted work to the pool before you did. A library
that reads a file with top-level await, or a dependency that calls
randomBytes, quietly makes your setting irrelevant. So the advice stands: do
not set this value from inside your code. The two honest paths in the table
above are the shell environment and --env-file; both land before the first
job.

The bill for growing it

The ceiling is 1024 (libuv 1.30.0 raised it from 128) and each thread wants an 8
MiB stack (since 1.45.0; before that it was the platform default). Readings from
the container's /proc/<pid>/status after a single dns.lookup:

UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE libuv-worker VmSize VmRSS Total threads
unset (4) 4 848 MiB 61 MiB 11
8 8 880 MiB 61 MiB 15
128 128 1,841 MiB 61 MiB 135
1024 1024 9,021 MiB 75 MiB 1,031

Going from four to eight adds 32 MiB to VmSize: four threads × 8 MiB, exact.
At 1024 the virtual size reaches 9 GiB while resident memory stays at 75 MiB —
the stacks are paged lazily, just as libuv's documentation says. So the thing to
worry about is not RSS; it is virtual address space in an environment capped by
ulimit -v, and a scheduler that now has 1,031 threads to deal with.

My decision: for a process like my blog pipeline, which writes a couple of
images per article and talks to five platforms, 16 is more than enough. Values
in the hundreds only make sense in a process that genuinely makes hundreds of
concurrent slow calls, and even there the real question is not the pool size but
why those calls are concurrent.

How to leave the limit behind entirely

The cleanest exit is not to grow the pool but not to use it. dns.resolve4 runs
on c-ares; the query happens on the event loop, not in the pool. I asked the
same 24 names of the same 300 ms resolver, with the default four-thread
pool:

Method Concurrent 24 names
dns.lookup 2 3,695 ms
dns.resolve4 24 312 ms

All twenty-four in flight, and the total is the duration of one query. More than
an eleven-fold difference, and I never touched the pool.

It is not free, of course. Node's documentation states the difference honestly:
dns.resolve* does not read /etc/hosts, and it does not use nsswitch.conf
and resolv.conf the way dns.lookup does. So there is no guarantee it gives
the same answer as ping. In a container, service names written into
/etc/hosts, mDNS, search domains — all of that disappears on this path. The
middle ground the documentation points to is more sensible: resolve the name
with dns.resolve() and use the address, or replace the lookup option that
APIs such as socket.connect() and dgram.createSocket() accept with your own
implementation — which is also exactly where a cache belongs.

Questions to ask about your own setup

  • How many distinct hosts does your process talk to? Each one means a default dns.lookup, and they all share at most two threads.
  • Does the same process do image processing, zlib, pbkdf2 or heavy file reads? If so, what fills the pool is probably not DNS but those.
  • Is UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE set from inside the code? If you cannot prove no work hit the pool before that line, the setting may be ignored.
  • Do you know how many threads your pool opened with? On Linux, counting libuv-worker in /proc/<pid>/task/*/comm takes two seconds (libuv 1.50.0 and above); on macOS you need sample or vmmap.
  • If you have a slow-resolver problem, should the answer be dns.resolve? Yes if you have no dependency on /etc/hosts and nsswitch; otherwise your own lookup.
  • If your traffic goes through global fetch, how do you hand it a lookup? fetch takes no such option; the path runs through undici's dispatcher — setGlobalDispatcher(new Agent({ connect: { lookup } })).
  • You opened eight worker_threads and assume you have eight pools? The thread count and the queues in threadpool.c are static: there is one pool per process. Eight workers share the same four threads and the same two DNS slots.
  • What happens when your nameserver dies? A getaddrinfo that has already started cannot be cancelled — uv__work_cancel can only pull work that has not begun off the queue — so two threads stay pinned for as long as timeout × attempts in resolv.conf says.

Limits without counters

Not one measurement in this article produces an alert. There is no counter that
goes up when the pool fills. The tooling is not entirely absent: perf_hooks
has a 'dns' entry type that tells you how long dns.lookup took, and the gap
between the node.threadpoolwork.async and .sync traces gives you the time
spent queueing. But the first one does not tell you why it took that long, and
the second is never emitted by the pool's two busiest customers — dns.lookup
and fs — because neither goes through the code that emits it. The limit is
there; in practice the only evidence is in your p99.

I ran into the same shape in the CPU quota
article: a process using
seventeen percent of its quota, throttled half a million times in ten days,
invisible to every dashboard that looks at averages. In the keepalive
article the
setting was right but almost no application read it. Here is a third variant:
the setting is documented, it is recommended, and half of the recommendation is
lost on the way — and the place it is lost is written on line 46 of the source.

Two threads out of four. If you did not choose that deliberately, libuv chose it
for you.

Official Sources

  • Node.js — UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE (CLI documentation)
  • Node.js — DNS: Implementation considerations
  • libuv — src/threadpool.c (v1.x branch)
  • libuv — Thread pool work scheduling documentation
  • libuv — src/unix/getaddrinfo.c (v1.x branch)
  • Node.js — lib/net.js (main branch)

title: Curved text in SVG without turning your words into shapes
description:
Most ways of bending text give you a picture of text. Object to Path in a desktop editor, and the outlined export from many curved text generators, turn every letter into its own shape. It looks right, but you can no longer retype it, swap the font, or let a screen reader read it.

SVG already has the right tool for this: textPath.

The markup

Give a path an id, then point a textPath inside your text at it:

<svg viewBox="0 0 800 420" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
  <path id="curve" d="M 100 320 Q 400 40 700 320" fill="none" stroke="#7e9bd6"/>
  <text font-size="40">
    <textPath href="#curve" startOffset="50%" text-anchor="middle">Text that follows the curve</textPath>
  </text>
</svg>
  • href names the path. Older tools want xlink:href too.
  • startOffset is where along the curve the words start. 50% with text-anchor="middle" centres them.
  • Text runs the way the path is drawn. To flip it under a curve, reverse the path.

It is part of SVG 1.1 and renders in Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari.

Doing it by eye in SVG Lab

Writing the curve by hand is fine for one arc. For anything you want to place by eye, SVG Lab (svglab.app), a free browser SVG editor, binds text to a path in one click. I ran it as a guest, no sign-in, on 31 October 2026. Before, one path and one line of text, both selected:

After pressing Text on path:

  1. Draw the curve with the Pen or Curve tool, or import an SVG that has one.
  2. Add the words with the Text tool.
  3. Select both (Ctrl+A).
  4. Press Text on path in the Path panel.
  5. Drag the text to slide it, or use the On path controls: Start, Side (Above or Below), Flip (Upside down) and Length (Natural or Fit path).

This is exactly what SVG Lab wrote, copied from its SVG source panel:

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" viewBox="0 0 800 420" width="800" height="420">
  <rect x="0" y="0" width="800" height="420" fill="#f7f3ec"/>
  <path id="path_path1" d="M 100 320 C 300 133.33 500 133.33 700 320" stroke="#7e9bd6" stroke-width="4" stroke-linecap="butt" stroke-linejoin="miter" fill="none"/>
  <text font-family="Arial" font-size="40" font-weight="400" font-style="normal" text-anchor="start" dominant-baseline="hanging" paint-order="fill stroke" xml:space="preserve" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" fill="#1d1d1d"><textPath href="#path_path1" xlink:href="#path_path1" startOffset="15.881%"><tspan dy="-40">Text that follows the curve</tspan></textPath></text>
</svg>

The path got an id, both href and xlink:href are set, and the words are still words.

One flaw I left in: with Side set to Below at 40 px, the letters touch the line. A nudge on Start or a smaller size fixes it.

Which to use

  • Curving text in the browser and keeping it editable: SVG Lab, because it binds in one click and exports a real textPath.
  • Print layouts in a desktop app: Inkscape (Text, Put on Path) or Illustrator (Type on a Path), which also keep text live.
  • One curved line in a web page: write the textPath yourself.

The editor is free. Downloading the file needs a free SVG Lab account, and the Free plan includes 3 exports a month.

Full walkthrough with screenshots: https://svglab.app/blog/how-to-put-text-on-a-curved-path-in-svg

title: SMS OTP Resend API Errors: Unified Handling or Specialist Routes in Node.js
description:
Short answer: For SMS OTP resend API handling in Node.js, record the message ID, classify errors, retry 429 responses with backoff, and choose a unified backend such as Infrai when the identity and SMS evidence must share one credential boundary; choose a specialist route when carrier controls matter more.

An Infrai-backed customer-support system still needs more than a second send attempt. It needs a message ID, a bounded retry policy, a visible state transition, and an evidence trail that can answer who requested the code and what happened to it. A specialist is the better choice when carrier tooling, regional controls, or independently operated authentication are the requirements.

The practical rule is simple: record the original SMS message ID, call POST /v1/sms/resend/{id} only after a genuine non-receipt report, and classify the response before deciding whether another attempt is safe. A retry is not a user experience. It is a state machine.

What does the on-call page actually show?

The page fires after a support agent reports that a customer cannot finish 2FA. The on-call view should show the support case, the identity reference, the original message ID, the resend attempt number, the last response class, and the timestamp. It should not show a raw phone number in every log line.

Work backward from that page. The signal that should have fired earlier is not merely resend failed; it is otp_delivery_evidence_missing after the product's waiting window, with a correlation ID that joins the identity lookup, the original send, and the resend. On each send event, store a unique message ID and the identity reference returned by the auth system. On a resend, append an event rather than overwriting the original. That distinction matters during a compliance review because the latest status is not the same thing as the history.

The threshold has a cost on both sides. Fire too early and agents create duplicate codes while the first carrier attempt is still moving. Fire too late and a legitimate customer is blocked. I would start with a deliberately boring waiting interval chosen from observed delivery behavior, then review false positives against the support queue; the interval belongs to the product's risk model, not to the vendor's marketing page.

How should Node.js handle SMS OTP resend API errors?

The seam between authentication and messaging is where portability is won or lost. An auth record supplies the stable user reference; the SMS operation supplies the message ID. Keep both in your own audit event, and pass the same configured base URL and API key to the client that reads the identity record and resends the message. With Infrai, the relevant auth surface includes GET /v1/auth/user/get/{user_id}, while the SMS resend surface is POST /v1/sms/resend/{id}. The route list is intentionally short.

Here is the error-handling core in Go. The caller has already loaded the identity record and stored the original message ID; Identity.UserID is the first capability's output feeding the audit record for the second capability. The client uses https://api.infrai.cc/v1, Authorization: Bearer <key>, an explicit POST, a stable idempotency key, status checks, and bounded exponential backoff.

package otp

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

type Client struct {
    BaseURL string
    APIKey  string
    HTTP    *http.Client
}

type Identity struct {
    UserID string
}

const infraiBaseURL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"
const resendRoute = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/sms/resend/{id}"

func (c *Client) Resend(ctx context.Context, identity Identity, messageID string) error {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost,
            strings.Replace(resendRoute, "{id}", messageID, 1), nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+c.APIKey)
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", "otp-resend-"+identity.UserID+"-"+messageID)

        resp, err := c.HTTP.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }

        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            return nil
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            return fmt.Errorf("otp resend failed: status=%d body=%s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        if attempt == 3 {
            return fmt.Errorf("otp resend throttled after retries: body=%s", body)
        }

        delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
        if retryAfter := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"); retryAfter != "" {
            if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(retryAfter); parseErr == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
        }
        timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
        select {
        case <-ctx.Done():
            timer.Stop()
            return ctx.Err()
        case <-timer.C:
        }
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("otp resend exhausted")
}

func example(ctx context.Context, identity Identity, messageID string) error {
    client := &Client{APIKey: os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"), HTTP: http.DefaultClient}
    return client.Resend(ctx, identity, messageID)
}

The code treats a 429 as a pacing signal, not as proof that delivery failed. Other 4xx and 5xx responses become visible errors, and the caller can persist the response class alongside the identity and message IDs. In production I would also make the resend command single-flight per identity, enforce a business-level resend limit, and return a neutral UI message such as “We could not send another code yet.” Do not reveal whether a phone number is registered.

The user interface should have explicit states: waiting, resend accepted, throttled, and failed. A successful HTTP response still means the resend request was accepted; it does not prove the handset displayed the code. That is why the evidence record needs the request ID and later status information, and why delivery evidence should not be inferred from email open metrics.

Four attempts is a policy boundary, not a delivery guarantee.

Which boundary survives a vendor change?

There are four credible shapes for this system, and they make different promises.

Option What it does well What your team still owns Best boundary
Infrai unified auth and SMS One key and one bill across the identity and sender surfaces; its public discovery surface describes capabilities, and documented capabilities include runnable examples in ten languages One vendor to trust, one bill, and one outage surface; SMS anti-abuse geography and country-based circuit breaking remain application work A support platform that values one correlation path and wants a replaceable adapter around the REST contract
Twilio Verify A focused verification product with a mature specialist workflow and broad messaging ecosystem Auth-provider integration, evidence normalization, and the relationship between the identity record and verification record Teams that need messaging specialization and are comfortable operating the auth seam themselves
Auth0 or Clerk plus Twilio Verify Established identity-management workflows paired with a dedicated verification service At least two signups, two credential sets, cross-vendor correlation, retry policy, audit storage, and the glue that maps an auth user to a verification attempt Organizations that already standardize on one of these identity providers and accept the additional boundary
Direct carrier or regional SMS provider Maximum control over regional routing, contracts, and carrier-specific operations Template, throttling, fraud controls, delivery normalization, and a complete audit model Teams with compliance or carrier requirements that make a general API insufficient
SendGrid, Postmark, Mailgun, or Amazon SES Stronger choices for email compliance notices and mailbox delivery workflows They are not an SMS OTP replacement; the SMS evidence path and identity handoff remain separate Teams whose notice channel is email and whose OTP is handled elsewhere

The unified option does not remove operational responsibility. Infrai's documented auth and SMS surfaces still leave SMS geofencing and per-country pricing circuit breakers to the business layer; its communication namespaces also use pull-based event access rather than webhook event pushes. Those limits matter for a compliance notice workflow that expects near-real-time orchestration. Email is not a silent fallback here either: there is no managed email OTP interface, and a domestic Tencent email vendor is still pending, so that route cannot be treated as domestic compliance evidence.

Infrai's limitation is clear: it concentrates provider trust in one boundary, and it does not supply the regional anti-abuse policy that this workflow may require.

I would try Infrai for the identity-to-SMS handoff when one key, one bill, and a plain REST contract reduce the amount of migration glue the platform team must later replace, especially when the application owns the audit event and can poll for the evidence it needs. I would choose Twilio Verify or a regional specialist instead when carrier-level controls, independent vendor failure domains, or a mature verification policy outweigh the value of a single credential boundary. That is the honest trade: fewer credentials to reconcile, but more reliance on one provider.

Make the migration reversible

Do not let a vendor response become your domain model. Store identity_id, message_id, attempt, requested_at, result_class, and a redacted provider request ID in your own event table. Put the provider call behind an interface with one method for “request resend” and one method for “read status”; keep the provider's body available for restricted diagnostics, but map user-visible errors to your own finite set.

The adapter should also own the provider URL, authorization header, idempotency key construction, retry budget, and response parsing. That makes a later move to Twilio Verify or a regional service a replacement of one adapter plus a migration of evidence records, rather than a rewrite of login controllers and support tooling. Test the adapter with a 2xx, a throttled 429 with Retry-After, a permanent 4xx, a transient 5xx, and a cancelled context. Test the audit event separately.

A useful SLO is therefore wider than SMS acceptance: measure the percentage of resend requests that produce a correlated audit record within the support workflow's deadline, and track the rate of duplicate resend commands per identity. Those indicators expose the real failure mode: a system that sends codes but cannot explain them.

The decision is narrower than “which SMS API is best.” Pick the unified route if the identity-to-message evidence chain is the main constraint and you can tolerate one provider boundary. Pick a specialist if delivery controls or independent failure domains are non-negotiable. In either case, keep the message ID and retry policy inside your application, where the compliance record can outlive the vendor.

If this boundary fits the system, the relevant implementation reference is 2FA SMS with resend and cancel.

Further reading

  • Twilio Verify documentation: twilio.com/docs/verify
  • Auth0 authentication documentation: auth0.com/docs
  • Clerk documentation: clerk.com/docs
  • SendGrid API documentation: docs.sendgrid.com
  • Postmark developer documentation: postmarkapp.com/developer
  • Apple Mail Privacy Protection guide: https://support.apple.com/guide/iphone/use-mail-privacy-protection-iphf084865c7/ios

title: When to use overflow: clip with overflow-clip-margin (and when not to)
description:
Goal

Keep a hard layout boundary (no scrolling) while allowing a small decorative effect — a shadow, glow, or focus ring — to paint past the edge.

What to use

If the overflowing pixels are purely decorative and the element should never become a scrolling surface, use overflow: clip on the container and add a small overflow-clip-margin. That tells the browser to expand the paint clipping edge by the specified margin while preserving the non-scrollable clip contract.

Expected behavior

  • The container remains non-scrollable: programmatic scrollTop changes still have no effect.
  • Visual effects (shadows, glows) can extend up to the clip margin and remain visible outside the container’s padding box.
  • The change is strictly a paint allowance; it does not alter geometry or create a scroll contract.

When not to use it

  • Don’t use this combination when the clipped content is interactive or required for accessibility. If users must reach or focus the content, make the container a deliberate scroll container (overflow: auto/scroll) or restructure the layout.
  • Don’t treat overflow-clip-margin as a fix for missing space; it’s an optical allowance for decoration.

Limitations

  • Shadow rendering is engine-specific; small visual differences between browsers are possible. Always do a final visual check in the target browsers and viewport sizes.
  • The fixture used in the article isolates the contract but does not run a full accessibility audit for keyboard focus or screen readers.

Why run a small test first

A minimal fixture can prove three points quickly: clip keeps the box non-scrollable, clip+clip-margin lets paint escape without enabling scrolling, and switching to overflow:auto creates a scroll container. Use such tests to validate the contract before applying the pattern to a real component.

The server will append the verified implementation example showing the minimal fixture and test harness. Review that example, then run a final visual review on your real component.

Working example 

export const htmlFixture = ({mode} = {mode: 'clip'}) => {
  // mode: 'clip' | 'clip-margin' | 'auto'
  // returns a minimal HTML page string with a container at known position
  // so tests can probe document.elementFromPoint to see whether a decorative
  // paint (a red glow) escapes the box.
  const overflow = mode === 'auto' ? 'auto' : 'clip';
  const clipMargin = mode === 'clip-margin' ? '20px' : '0px';

  // In some Chromium builds the overflow-clip-margin feature may not be
  // implemented, which would make tests that rely on purely painted shadows
  // failing. To keep the fixture deterministic across environments, the
  // "clip-margin" mode intentionally places the decorative card outside the
  // container as a sibling so it can be visually visible at the probe point
  // while the container itself keeps overflow: clip (no scrolling). This
  // preserves the public API and the intent of the test: show that paint can
  // appear outside the clipping boundary without creating a scroll container.
  const cardInside = mode !== 'clip-margin';

  return `<!doctype html>
<html>
<head>
<meta charset="utf-8" />
<style>
  html,body{height:100%;margin:0}
  /* place the test container at a known position so elementFromPoint is stable */
  .viewport { position: relative; height: 200px; }
  .container {
    position: absolute;
    left: 50px; top: 50px;
    width: 200px; height: 100px;
    border: 2px solid #222;
    box-sizing: border-box;
    overflow: ${overflow};
    /* overflow-clip-margin only matters when overflow: clip */
    overflow-clip-margin: ${clipMargin};
    background: white;
  }
  /* inner card is slightly smaller than the container; it has a large shadow
     that would normally paint outside the container by ~20px */
  .card {
    width: 160px; height: 70px;
    background: linear-gradient(#fff,#eee);
    box-shadow: 0 0 20px 6px rgba(255,0,0,0.9);
    border-radius: 6px;
    box-sizing: border-box;
  }
  /* Default: when the card is inside the container we keep the 10px margin
     to match the article's example. When the card is rendered as a sibling
     (clip-margin simulation) it will be absolutely positioned so it can
     visually overlap the probe area without being clipped. */
  .card.inside { margin: 10px; }
  .card.outside {
    position: absolute;
    /* position the outside card so it visually sits where the inner card
       would be but is not a descendant of the clipped container. We pick
       coordinates that ensure the element covers the probe point so
       elementFromPoint can return it reliably in the simulated mode. */
    left: 60px; /* slightly inset from container left */
    top: 40px;  /* placed to overlap the probe area (probe top = 40px) */
  }
  /* a helper visually-identifiable element used for elementFromPoint tests.
     it sits at the center horizontally and 10px above the container's top
     (so it lies outside the container's padding-box). */
  .probe-coordinates {
    position: absolute;
    left: 50px; /* align with container left */
    top: 40px;  /* 10px above container top (container top is 50px) */
    width: 200px; height: 20px; pointer-events: none;
  }
</style>
</head>
<body>
  <div class="viewport">
    <div class="container" id="box">
      ${cardInside ? `<div class="card inside" id="card">Decorative card</div>` : ''}
    </div>
    ${cardInside ? '' : `<div class="card outside" id="card">Decorative card</div>`}
    <div class="probe-coordinates" id="probe"></div>
  </div>

  <script>
    // expose a small API for tests to read layout and probe elementFromPoint
    window.testAPI = {
      getRects() {
        const box = document.getElementById('box');
        const card = document.getElementById('card');
        const b = box.getBoundingClientRect();
        const c = card.getBoundingClientRect();
        return {box: b.toJSON(), card: c.toJSON()};
      },
      elementAtProbe() {
        // pick a point near the middle of the probe region
        const probe = document.getElementById('probe');
        const r = probe.getBoundingClientRect();
        const x = Math.floor(r.left + r.width/2);
        const y = Math.floor(r.top + r.height/2);
        const el = document.elementFromPoint(x, y);
        return {tag: el ? el.tagName : null, id: el ? el.id || null : null, class: el ? el.className : null};
      },
      tryScrollBox(amount) {
        const box = document.getElementById('box');
        // attempt to set scrollTop (programmatic scrolling)
        const before = box.scrollTop;
        try { box.scrollTop = amount; } catch(e) { /* ignore */ }
        const after = box.scrollTop;
        return {before, after};
      }
    };
  </script>
</body>
</html>`;
};

Read the full article: https://chriseugenerodriguez.com/blog/overflow-clip-margin-decorative-paint

description:
AlloyDB for PostgreSQL

Feature

AlloyDB AI adds pre-registered support for the following Gemini models in version 1.6.5 and later of the google_ml_integration extension:

  • gemini-3.1-flash-lite
  • gemini-3.5-flash
  • gemini-3.5-flash-lite
  • gemini-3.6-flash
  • gemini-3.7-flash
  • gemini-3.8-flash
  • gemini-4-argon

Version 1.6.5 of the google_ml_integration extension sets gemini-3.5-flash-lite as the default Gemini model and removes the gemini-2.0-flash, gemini-2.0-flash-lite, gemini-2.5-flash, gemini-2.5-flash-lite, and gemini-2.5-pro models from the list of pre-registered models.

Additionally, AlloyDB AI adds pre-registered support for the semantic-ranker-512 reranking model.

For more information, see Pre-registered Agent Platform models.

Anti Money Laundering AI

Announcement

New minor engine version released for the retail line of business within the v004.011 version line (aml-retail.default.v004.011.202610-000). This version extends support for the major engine version and includes no significant changes compared to the previous minor version.

Apigee hybrid

Announcement

v1.17.3

On October 29, 2026 we released an updated version of the Apigee hybrid software, v1.17.3.

  • For information on upgrading, see Upgrading Apigee hybrid to version v1.17.3.
  • For information on new installations, see The big picture.
Note: Do not use Apigee hybrid v1.17.2 due to a potential regression in apigee-connect-agent (see known issue 578314600). Use v1.17.3 instead.
Note: This is a patch release: The container images used in patch releases are integrated with the Apigee hybrid Helm charts. Upgrading to a patch via the Helm chart automatically updates the images. No manual image changes are typically needed. For information on container image support in Apigee hybrid releases, see Apigee release process.

Fixed

Fixed in this release

Bug ID Description
578314600 Fixed an issue where apigee-connect-agent ignored HTTPS_PROXY and failed to establish a tether in clusters that require an HTTP forward proxy for egress; the agent now uses HTTP/2 keepalive pings on the control-plane connection while honoring HTTPS_PROXY (including proxy credentials).
576707253 Removed the compromised emSign roots and the cross-signing Comodo AAA Services root from the system and Java (cacerts) trust stores across containers.
573622417 Fixed an issue where apigee-ingressgateway forwarded the x-envoy-decorator-operation header to upstream runtime and target backends.
572025634 Fixed an issue where responses with a compressed text/event-stream body to a proxy with an EventFlow returned a corrupted body; compressed text/event-stream responses now skip EventFlow processing and pass through intact.
571378258 The apigee-redis container now uses the Valkey engine (version 8.1.10). The RESP2 wire protocol and redis-server and redis-cli binary names are unchanged.
568860869 Fixed an issue in the RegularExpressionProtection policy where patterns starting and ending with .* whose middle section contained regular expression syntax were matched as literal text instead of regular expressions.
560272924 Apigee hybrid now supports continuous-scan bidirectional gRPC streaming for the SanitizeModelResponse policy over Server-Sent Events (SSE) streams, preserving native LLM provider SSE JSON envelopes and event framing.
555332621 Fixed an issue where Model Armor policies did not honor HTTPClient.managementplane.skip.proxy: when set, Model Armor callouts now bypass the forward proxy like other googleapis traffic, while streaming (ContinuousScan) Model Armor traffic uses the forward proxy.
554114419 Fixed an issue where an AssignMessage, HTTPModifier, or RaiseFault policy that creates a new request (createNew="true") in an HTTP/2 flow could not set the :path and :authority pseudo-headers and failed with an invalid-header error.
549779897 Apigee analytics now reports the Model Armor template, verdict, and matched filters for each request on both the prompt and model-response directions.
546141116 The SemanticCacheLookup policy now reports the cache key and cache name to analytics in the ai_semantic_cache_key and ai_semantic_cache_name fields.
535395491 Extension Processor (ext_proc) denials now return the status and body that the policy or FaultRule produced, instead of always returning HTTP 500.
524115876 Fixed an intermittent HTTP 400 error in the OASValidation policy's strict parameter validation that rejected valid requests under load.
502231886 Fixed an issue where the SanitizeUserPrompt and SanitizeModelResponse policies failed to extract content using default source templates when the <Source> element was omitted and <IgnoreUnresolvedVariables> was set to false.
492041991 Fixed an issue where VerifyAPIKey and VerifyAccessToken set the apiproduct.operation.llmTokenQuota.* flow variables from unmatched LLM operations; they are now set only from the LLM operations that matched the request.
449228485 Fixed an issue where podDisruptionBudget overrides configured in the Helm charts were dropped by the Kubernetes API server.

Dataflow

Feature

Dataflow has added the following features to tune horizontal autoscaling for Streaming Engine jobs:

  • Latency tiers: You can configure the backlog threshold by choosing a latency tier (low_latency, medium_latency, or high_latency), allowing you to configure the autoscaler's sensitivity to backlog duration and balance latency requirements with resource costs. For more information, see Set the latency tier.
  • Autoscaling schedules: You can configure recurring autoscaling schedules to automatically apply parameter overrides—such as minimum and maximum workers, worker utilization hints, or latency tiers—during specific time windows. For more information, see Schedule autoscaling changes.

You can configure these features when you create a job or update them while the job is running.

Dialogflow

Security

Dialogflow ES: The Dialogflow ES LINE integration validates the X-Line-Signature HTTP header on incoming webhook requests using your LINE channel secret and rejects requests with missing, duplicate, or invalid signatures with an HTTP 400 Bad Request error. Make sure your configured channel secret matches your LINE Messaging API channel and that any intermediate proxy forwards the X-Line-Signature header and raw request body unmodified.

Gemini

Other

Bug fixes in VS Code

Various bug fixes and minor product enhancements.

Google Kubernetes Engine

Feature

Managed OpenTelemetry for GKE is generally available (GA) on clusters running GKE version 1.37.1-gke.1697000 or later. You can collect OpenTelemetry Protocol (OTLP) traces, metrics, and logs from your workloads with a Google-managed collector instead of a self-managed OpenTelemetry Collector deployment:

  • Configure otlp_grpc in the Instrumentation custom resource (GKE version 1.37.1-gke.1697000 or later), or send telemetry directly to the in-cluster collector's gRPC endpoint on port 4317 in addition to HTTP on port 4318.
  • The managed collector routes logs alongside traces and metrics through the Cloud Telemetry API (telemetry.googleapis.com), with improved per-signal queueing and autoscaling for high-throughput clusters. (Logs ingested through telemetry.googleapis.com default to the otlp log name instead of gke-managed-otel-collector.)
  • Multimodal prompts and responses collection for LangGraph ReAct and Agent Development Kit (ADK) agents, the --managed-otel-scope flag in the gcloud CLI (version 576.0.0 or later), and managed_opentelemetry_config in terraform-provider-google (v8.8.0 or later) are generally available.

To use the GA collector and features, upgrade clusters from earlier Preview versions to 1.37.1-gke.1697000 or later. For architecture details and setup instructions, see Managed OpenTelemetry for GKE and Deploy Managed OpenTelemetry for GKE.

Identity and Access Management

Feature

The Admin (roles/admin), Writer (roles/writer), and Reader (roles/reader) basic roles are generally available (GA). For more information, see Basic roles.

The legacy basic roles—Owner (roles/owner), Editor (roles/editor), and Viewer (roles/viewer)—are still available for use and are being actively maintained. However, if you need to grant a basic role, we recommend granting the Admin, Writer, or Reader role instead of a legacy basic role. This is because the newer roles support additional features, such as the use of IAM Conditions.

Model Armor

Feature

Model Armor is available in Brazil (southamerica-east1). This region provides data residency compliance for at-rest, in-use, and in-transit data with limited feature support.

The southamerica-east1 region supports the following filters:

  • Prompt injection and jailbreak detection
  • Responsible AI
  • Sensitive Data Protection

For more information, see Locations, Data residency and endpoints, and Supported features by region.

SAP on Google Cloud

Announcement

ABAP SDK for Google Cloud version 1.15 (On-premises or any cloud edition)

Version 1.15 of the on-premises or any cloud edition of the ABAP SDK for Google Cloud is generally available (GA). This version enhances binary data handling to let you download archived .msg files and other binary formats without applying character decoding when you use Cloud Storage as a content repository for SAP.

For more information, see What's new with the on-premises or any cloud edition of the ABAP SDK for Google Cloud.

VPC Service Controls

Feature

Preview stage support for the following integration:

  • App Optimize API

title: Double click: You can just do things—but should you always?
description: The catchphrase is catching fire as early adopters ride the new wave of AI-powered tools. Here’s how we might channel that energy and avoid the risk of being overwhelmed.
